title: CGGS: Consistency-Augmented Geometric Gaussian Splatting for Ego-centric 3D Scene Generation
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, IEEE Transactions on Image Processing
summary: Challenges remain in ego-centric 3D scene generation due to limited view overlap and the dominant influence of individual perspectives on scene interpretation. These factors hinder the creation of viewpoint-consistent and semantically aligned visual content, as well as the construction of accurate geometric structures. In this paper, we propose CGGS, a text-to-3D framework aiming to enhance 3D-content-awareness and address geometric distortions in ego-centric scene generation. Firstly, the Ego-centric Generator is proposed by fine-tuning a Multi-View Latent Diffusion Model with consistency-augmented loss to generate consistent, high-fidelity 2D content aligned with textual descriptions. Then, Layout Decorator leverages optical flow and point-track correspondence to estimate depth, therefore producing dense point clouds as coarse layouts from the ego-centric 2D priors. Building on this initialization, Geometric Refiner is proposed to enhance 3D Gaussian reconstruction via an entropy-based Mutual Information Depth Loss (MID) combined with a hierarchical optimization scheme for improving visual quality and geometric structure. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that \textcolor{softred}{CGGS} outperforms previous methods in generating coherent and accurate text-driven 3D scenes. Project page: https://cggs-26.github.io/cggs26/.

AI.tldr: CGGS is a text-to-3D framework that enhances ego-centric 3D scene generation by using an Ego-centric Generator with consistency-augmented loss, a Layout Decorator for depth estimation and point cloud construction, and a Geometric Refiner with entropy-based Mutual Information Depth Loss and hierarchical optimization to improve geometric accuracy and visual quality.
AI.motivation: Ego-centric 3D scene generation suffers from limited view overlap and strong individual perspective influence, leading to viewpoint inconsistency, semantic misalignment, and geometric distortions.
AI.method: CGGS consists of three components: (1) Ego-centric Generator fine-tunes a Multi-View Latent Diffusion Model with consistency-augmented loss for consistent 2D generation; (2) Layout Decorator uses optical flow and point-track correspondence for depth estimation and dense point cloud construction; (3) Geometric Refiner applies entropy-based Mutual Information Depth Loss (MID) and hierarchical optimization to improve 3D Gaussian reconstruction.
AI.result: CGGS outperforms previous methods in generating coherent and accurate text-driven 3D scenes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses geometric distortions and enhances 3D-content-awareness in ego-centric scene generation, setting a new state-of-the-art.

title: Lights, Camera, Carbon: Architectural Scaling Laws for Video Generation Energy Consumption
summary: We present a bidirectional framework for estimating the energy consumption of text-to-video (T2V) and text-to-video-audio (T2VA) models from architectural first principles and observable generation parameters such as resolution and duration, requiring no access to weights, model size, or implementation details. Forward, it predicts energy from generation parameters and architectural principles; backward, it recovers architectural scaling behavior from observed inference times, with accuracy serving as a criterion for architectural validity. Building on the established compute-bound nature of video diffusion models, we demonstrate that each model's energy profile obeys theoretically derived scaling laws, decomposing into quadratic and linear terms whose coefficients directly reflect the underlying architectural complexity. Validated across six open-source models spanning 8.3B-27B parameters and three GPU configurations, this decomposition achieves below 3% MAPE across all architectures. This approach offers a standardized, empirically and theoretically grounded framework for sustainability benchmarking across T2V models and architectures.

AI.tldr: A bidirectional framework estimates energy consumption of text-to-video and text-to-video-audio models using only observable generation parameters (resolution, duration) and architectural first principles, achieving <3% MAPE across six models without requiring model weights or implementation details.
AI.motivation: To provide a standardized, accessible framework for sustainability benchmarking of T2V and T2VA models that does not depend on proprietary model details (weights, size, implementation), enabling energy estimation from observable parameters alone.
AI.method: A bidirectional framework: forward prediction estimates energy from generation parameters and architectural principles; backward recovery infers architectural scaling behavior from observed inference times. Builds on compute-bound nature of video diffusion models, decomposing energy into quadratic and linear terms reflecting architectural complexity. Validated on six open-source models (8.3B-27B parameters) across three GPU configurations.
AI.result: Achieves below 3% Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) across all tested architectures and GPU configurations.
AI.conclusion: Offers a standardized, empirically and theoretically grounded framework for sustainability benchmarking across T2V models and architectures, enabling reproducible energy estimation without access to internal model details.

title: High-Performance Real-Time Implicit Strand-Based Hair Rendering via Software Rasterization
summary: In this work we propose an efficient deferred software rasterization pipeline for real-time rendering of strand-based hair using hair meshes. Hair plays a crucial role in creating expressive 3D characters, yet strand-based approaches are often restricted to high-end hardware and typically applied to only a small number of hero characters. Hair meshes have proven to be an efficient representation capable of handling a wide variety of groom styles, but existing mesh shader-based implementations still suffer from significant bottlenecks. In this work, we address these limitations with a software rasterization approach that improves performance and compatibility. Our method enables efficient far-field strand-based hair rendering-even at a single sample per pixel-by combining deferred shading with a strand filtering and reconstruction step, while requiring only minimal hardware support. To further enhance scalability, we introduce a level-of-detail (LOD) scheme that adapts hair representation and shading complexity based on viewing distance and screen-space coverage, reducing computational cost further while preserving visual fidelity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to achieve this combination of efficiency, flexibility, scalability, and broad hardware compatibility.

AI.tldr: Proposes an efficient deferred software rasterization pipeline for real-time strand-based hair rendering using hair meshes, achieving broad hardware compatibility with improved performance and scalability via a LOD scheme.
AI.motivation: Hair meshes suffer from bottlenecks in existing mesh shader-based implementations; strand-based approaches are limited to high-end hardware and few hero characters.
AI.method: Software rasterization pipeline combining deferred shading with strand filtering and reconstruction; uses a LOD scheme that adapts hair representation and shading complexity based on viewing distance and screen-space coverage.
AI.result: Enables efficient far-field strand-based hair rendering even at a single sample per pixel, reducing computational cost while preserving visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: First approach to achieve the combination of efficiency, flexibility, scalability, and broad hardware compatibility for strand-based hair rendering.

title: SleepBand: Single-Source Domain Generalization for Sleep Staging via Physiologically Structured Spectral Modeling
summary: Generalizing sleep staging models to unseen datasets is challenging, and typical domain generalization (DG) methods often rely on multiple source domains or domain labels that are rarely available in practice. We tackle the stricter and more practical setting of single-source domain generalization: training on a single labeled source dataset, without domain labels or access to target data. We present SleepBand, a physiology-guided framework that embeds oscillatory priors via a learnable Morlet filter bank and a structured integration-and-recalibration pipeline. This anchors representations to domain-invariant sleep rhythms (e.g., slow waves, spindles), reducing reliance on dataset-specific artefacts. On five public datasets, SleepBand achieves state-of-the-art SDG performance and remains competitive under leave-one-domain-out (multi-source) DG. Analyses show that the learned filters align with canonical neurophysiology and that robustness stems from focusing on narrowband, physiologically meaningful cues. Our results suggest that principled, physiology-aware inductive biases are a promising path for robust single-domain sleep staging. Code is available at https://github.com/lzcn/sleep-band

AI.tldr: SleepBand is a physiology-guided framework for single-source domain generalization in sleep staging that uses a learnable Morlet filter bank and integration-and-recalibration pipeline to anchor representations to domain-invariant sleep rhythms, achieving state-of-the-art performance on five public datasets without requiring domain labels or target data access.
AI.motivation: Generalizing sleep staging models to unseen datasets is challenging. Typical domain generalization methods rely on multiple source domains or domain labels that are rarely available in practice, motivating the need for a stricter single-source domain generalization (SDG) setting.
AI.method: SleepBand embeds oscillatory priors via a learnable Morlet filter bank and a structured integration-and-recalibration pipeline, anchoring representations to domain-invariant sleep rhythms (e.g., slow waves, spindles) to reduce reliance on dataset-specific artefacts.
AI.result: On five public datasets, SleepBand achieves state-of-the-art SDG performance and remains competitive under leave-one-domain-out (multi-source) DG. Learned filters align with canonical neurophysiology; robustness stems from focusing on narrowband, physiologically meaningful cues.
AI.conclusion: Principled, physiology-aware inductive biases are a promising path for robust single-domain sleep staging.

title: How to Build Digital Humans? From Priors to Photorealistic Avatars
summary: This state-of-the-art report provides an overview of controllable 3D human avatar creation. We describe current 3D avatar systems, which typically consist of three stages: (i) learning priors of human appearance and motion, (ii) creating a personalized avatar, and (iii) animating the avatar. To limit the scope, we focus on the prior learning and avatar creation stages. We define current avatar representations and introduce a taxonomy that categorizes existing work along multiple axes, including body regions and employed priors. We review methods for full-body and head avatars, as well as layered representations that decompose the body into components such as hands, hair, and garments. Finally, we outline common underlying principles, reference key literature for newcomers, and discuss open challenges and future research directions.

AI.tldr: This state-of-the-art report surveys controllable 3D human avatar creation, focusing on prior learning and avatar creation stages. It categorizes methods by body regions (full-body, head, layered components like hands/hair/garments) and priors, outlines underlying principles, and discusses open challenges and future directions.
AI.motivation: To provide a structured overview of controllable 3D human avatar creation, define a taxonomy for categorizing existing work, and serve as a reference for newcomers to understand common principles, key literature, and open challenges in the field.
AI.method: The report defines a taxonomy categorizing avatar representations along multiple axes, including body regions (full-body, head, layered components) and employed priors. It reviews methods across these categories, focusing on prior learning and personalized avatar creation stages, while outlining common underlying principles.
AI.result: A comprehensive taxonomy and survey of controllable 3D avatar creation methods, categorized by body region and priors, with identified key literature and outlined open challenges.
AI.conclusion: The report synthesizes current approaches, identifies gaps and open challenges in controllable 3D avatar creation, and offers future research directions for the field.

title: See the Emotion: A Facial Emoji Proxy Modeling for EEG Emotion Recognition
summary: Despite the high accuracy of EEG-based emotion recognition, existing models remain opaque "black boxes", lacking semantic grounding between abstract neural features and human-interpretable states. In this paper, we reframe EEG explainability as a cross-modal generation task, shifting the paradigm from feature attribution to behavioral visualization. We introduce Facial Emoji Proxy Modeling, a novel framework that translates high-dimensional EEG signals into identity-anonymized facial emojis. Guided by the neuroscientific inspiration of neural-facial association, this approach grounds neural representations in the manifold of observable facial dynamics. Technically, our framework integrates FMENet, a specialized backbone modeling expression-relevant spatial synergies, and the Facial Emoji Learning Branch (FELB), which treats emoji reconstruction as a structured semantic regularizer. Extensive experiments on EAV and MMER benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among EEG-only models. Crucially, it generates semantically faithful facial animations that provide a transparent, privacy-preserving window into the brain's emotional evolution, effectively allowing users to "see the emotion" directly from neural signals. Code is available at https://github.com/xian-sh/SeeEmotion

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Facial Emoji Proxy Modeling, a framework that translates EEG signals into facial emojis to make emotion recognition interpretable. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while providing semantically faithful, privacy-preserving facial animations that allow users to visually perceive emotional states from neural signals.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG-based emotion recognition models are opaque "black boxes" lacking semantic grounding between abstract neural features and human-interpretable emotional states.
AI.method: The framework integrates FMENet (a backbone for modeling expression-relevant spatial synergies) and the Facial Emoji Learning Branch (FELB), which treats emoji reconstruction as a structured semantic regularizer, reframing EEG explainability as a cross-modal generation task.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among EEG-only models on EAV and MMER benchmarks, and generates semantically faithful, privacy-preserving facial animations that reflect the brain's emotional evolution.
AI.conclusion: The approach shifts the paradigm from feature attribution to behavioral visualization, enabling users to "see the emotion" directly from neural signals through interpretable, identity-anonymized facial emoji proxies.

title: SceneFrom3D: Geometry-Conditioned Outdoor 3D Scene Generation via View Scheduling with Object-Level Control
summary: Geometry-conditioned 3D scene generation enables the creation of 3D environments from user-provided geometry, offering direct control over scene structure and object layout. To generate such 3D scenes, current methods commonly adopt a three-stage design that first defines a view schedule, then synthesizes multi-view observations along the scheduled views, and finally reconstructs a 3D representation from the generated images. However, defining the view schedule becomes a major bottleneck for outdoor scenes, where large, unstructured, and unbounded geometry makes it difficult to obtain views that provide sufficient coverage while supporting stable generation. To address this bottleneck, we present SceneFrom3D, a framework that automatically schedules views from outdoor input geometries. SceneFrom3D constructs a directed generation graph whose nodes represent anchor views and whose edges represent interpolation trajectories, defining which views to synthesize, which view pairs to interpolate, and in which order generation should proceed. Beyond automatic view scheduling, SceneFrom3D further improves controllability through object-level conditioning, assigning each object an identity image for appearance guidance and a geometry-adherence parameter for region-wise control over the input geometry. Experiments demonstrate that SceneFrom3D achieves state-of-the-art geometry-conditioned outdoor 3D scene generation, producing high-quality scenes with controllable object appearance and geometry adherence.

AI.tldr: SceneFrom3D is a framework for geometry-conditioned 3D outdoor scene generation that automatically schedules anchor views and interpolation trajectories via a directed generation graph, overcoming the bottleneck of manual view scheduling in large unbounded outdoor environments, and further improves controllability through object-level identity images and geometry-adherence parameters.
AI.motivation: The three-stage pipeline (view schedule → multi-view synthesis → 3D reconstruction) suffers from a major bottleneck in outdoor scenes because large, unstructured, and unbounded geometry makes it difficult to manually define a view schedule that ensures sufficient coverage and stable generation.
AI.method: SceneFrom3D constructs a directed generation graph where nodes are anchor views and edges are interpolation trajectories, automatically determining which views to synthesize, which view pairs to interpolate, and the generation order. It also introduces object-level conditioning via identity images for appearance guidance and geometry-adherence parameters for region-wise control.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on geometry-conditioned outdoor 3D scene generation, producing high-quality scenes with controllable object appearance and geometry adherence.
AI.conclusion: SceneFrom3D effectively addresses the view scheduling bottleneck for outdoor scenes and enhances controllability, achieving superior results in outdoor 3D scene generation.

title: Parallelized Autoregressive Decoding for Omni-Modal Dense Video Captioning
summary: Dense video captioning aims to generate temporally grounded descriptions of video events, benefiting both event-level video understanding and generation. In this domain, autoregressive video large language models have emerged as a prevalent paradigm due to their strong generative and cross-modal modeling capacity. However, generating dense captions under the token-by-token paradigm severely limits inference efficiency and hinders scalability as video length and event density increase. In this work, we propose a parallelized autoregressive framework that not only improves generation efficiency but also enhances temporally grounded captioning performance. Our key insight is to exploit the weak local dependencies across temporally distinct events to restructure the causal dependency graph, thereby enabling lossless parallel generation. Specifically, tokens with weak cross-event dependencies can be decoded in parallel, while tightly coupled tokens within each event retain sequential decoding to preserve local semantic coherence. To realize this insight, we introduce two key components for lossless parallel decoding: (1) a latent global planning mechanism that automatically learns the event-level structure and produces compact tokens encoding global inter-event causality while adaptively aggregating event-level audio-visual semantics, guiding subsequent dependency restructuring and parallel decoding; and (2) an event-factorized parallel decoding mechanism that effectively balances local focus with global inter-event awareness. Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate the clear advantage of our approach in both efficiency and performance in omni-modal event grounding and captioning. Project website: https://github.com/showlab/PadCaptioner.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a parallelized autoregressive framework (PadCaptioner) for dense video captioning that restructures causal dependency graphs to enable lossless parallel decoding of weakly-dependent cross-event tokens, using latent global planning and event-factorized parallel decoding mechanisms to improve both efficiency and performance.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video LLMs generate dense captions token-by-token, which severely limits inference efficiency and hinders scalability as video length and event density increase.
AI.method: (1) A latent global planning mechanism that learns event-level structure and produces compact tokens encoding global inter-event causality while aggregating event-level audio-visual semantics. (2) An event-factorized parallel decoding mechanism that balances local focus with global inter-event awareness, exploiting weak local dependencies across temporally distinct events to restructure the causal dependency graph.
AI.result: Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate clear advantages in both efficiency and performance for omni-modal event grounding and captioning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parallelized autoregressive framework successfully improves generation efficiency and temporally grounded captioning performance by enabling lossless parallel decoding through dependency graph restructuring.

title: Metronome: Bound the Cache, Keep the Beat for Real-Time Interaction Model Serving
summary:
Real-time interaction models -- Moshi, MiniCPM-o, Qwen-Omni -- turn serving into a periodic real-time task: on every frame a session ingests streaming audio and must respond by a recurring wall-clock deadline, while its KV cache grows monotonically and stays pinned for the whole conversation. This regime hides a dangerous failure mode. On a real full-duplex stack, sustained load does not degrade serving gracefully: it falls off a cliff, jumping in one step from milliseconds per frame to a stalled engine when accumulated session state exhausts the KV pool. The collapse is metastable -- identical five-minute runs collapse or survive on run-to-run variance -- and silent: latency and deadline-miss metrics read healthy throughout.
  We show one move restores both stability and observability: bound each session's resident state, and latency starts telling the truth. Metronome's in-engine KV window eliminates the collapse (0/20 vs. 14/20 runs across two batches) and turns per-frame latency into a monotone load signal, on which an online admission controller discovers the schedulable concurrency; without the window, the identical controller over-admits into the wall. A first-order model predicts the collapse time within a few percent on the headline model, and a quality probe validates the bound's design by ablation: the window alone is quality-free in turn-based decoding, and its few pinned attention-sink tokens are what keep free-running generation healthy. Everything is measured end-to-end on real audio, across four interaction models on one GPU.

AI.tldr: Real-time interaction models suffer a metastable collapse under sustained load when session state exhausts the KV cache pool. Metronome introduces an in-engine KV window that bounds session state, eliminating collapse, restoring latency as a truthful load signal, and enabling online admission control.
AI.motivation: Current real-time interaction models (Moshi, MiniCPM-o, Qwen-Omni) operate as periodic real-time tasks where sessions accumulate unbounded KV cache over time. Under sustained load, this causes a sudden, metastable, and silent collapse — latency appears healthy until the engine stalls completely. The motivation is to understand and eliminate this dangerous failure mode.
AI.method: Metronome introduces an in-engine KV window that bounds each session's resident state, preventing unbounded KV cache growth. The method includes: (1) a bounded KV window to eliminate collapse, (2) using per-frame latency as a monotone load signal for online admission control, (3) a first-order model to predict collapse time, and (4) ablation studies to isolate the effect of attention-sink tokens on quality.
AI.result: Metronome's KV window eliminates collapse entirely (0/20 vs. 14/20 runs across two batches). Per-frame latency becomes a monotone load signal, enabling an online admission controller to discover schedulable concurrency — without the window, the same controller over-admits into the wall. The first-order model predicts collapse time within a few percent. The window is quality-free in turn-based decoding, with only attention-sink tokens needed for free-running generation.
AI.conclusion: Bounding session state with an in-engine KV window is a simple, effective fix for the metastable collapse in real-time interaction model serving. It restores both stability and observability, enabling safe admission control without quality degradation.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
summary: Tool-calling benchmarks are increasingly used to rank language-model agents, yet their scores are often treated as ground truth without validating the evaluators themselves. We present a systematic validity and reproducibility audit of four major tool-calling benchmark families: BFCL v4, τ2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, and MCP-Atlas. Across 496 expert-reviewed benchmark tasks, we find 92 evaluator-human disagreements, corresponding to an 18.5% misalignment rate. The failures are not isolated annotation mistakes: deterministic benchmarks exhibit brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths, substring-based communication failures, and reward-basis misalignment, while LLM-judge benchmarks exhibit rubric drift, hallucinated completion, answer-only scoring, and substantial run-to-run variance. In LiveMCPBench, 23 repeated evaluations of the same setup produce scores ranging from 57.9% to 76.8%, a spread of 18.9 percentage points, large enough to change leaderboard conclusions. These results show that current tool-calling scores can reflect evaluator artifacts rather than agent capability. We introduce a unified taxonomy of tool-calling evaluation failures, release trace-level audit artifacts and corrected evaluation components, and argue for decomposed metrics that separately measure tool invocation, task completion, and outcome verification. Our findings suggest that progress in tool-using agents requires benchmarks whose evaluators are themselves reproducible, auditable, and aligned with human judgments of task success. We further introduce Tool-Veritas, a configurable benchmark that combines deterministic state verification with optional qualitative judging, and Harness Lab, an open-source system for benchmark execution, trace inspection, repeated-run comparison, and evaluator debugging.

AI.tldr: Tool-calling benchmarks suffer from 18.5% evaluator-human misalignment. Deterministic benchmarks have brittle state matching and trajectory lock-in; LLM-judge benchmarks show rubric drift and high variance (e.g., 57.9%-76.8% on same setup). The paper introduces a failure taxonomy, corrected artifacts, Tool-Veritas (configurable benchmark), and Harness Lab (debugging system), arguing for decomposed, auditable, and reproducible evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling benchmarks are widely used to rank language-model agents, but their evaluators (both deterministic and LLM-based judges) are rarely validated themselves. This undermines the credibility of leaderboard conclusions and obscures whether scores reflect actual agent capability or evaluator artifacts.
AI.method: Conducted a systematic validity and reproducibility audit across 4 benchmark families (BFCL v4, τ2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, MCP-Atlas) with 496 expert-reviewed tasks. Identified evaluator-human disagreements, categorized failure modes, performed repeated evaluations (23 runs on same setup), and introduced a unified failure taxonomy along with Tool-Veritas (hybrid deterministic+qualitative judging) and Harness Lab (open-source debugging system).
AI.result: Found 92 evaluator-human disagreements (18.5% misalignment). Deterministic benchmarks suffer from brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths, substring failures, and reward-basis misalignment. LLM-judge benchmarks exhibit rubric drift, hallucinated completion, answer-only scoring, and run-to-run variance (18.9 percentage point spread on LiveMCPBench). Released trace-level audit artifacts and corrected evaluation components.
AI.conclusion: Current tool-calling scores can reflect evaluator artifacts rather than genuine agent capability. Progress requires benchmarks with reproducible, auditable evaluators aligned with human judgment. Proposed decomposed metrics (tool invocation, task completion, outcome verification) and released Tool-Veritas and Harness Lab to support this goal.

title: Auditing the Audit: Five Failure Modes in Benchmark-Validity Audits
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the TAIGR Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Governance frameworks ask AI providers and auditors for documented evaluation evidence, and perturbation-based construct-validity audits are a common form of that evidence. We argue the audits are themselves fragile: their conclusions can be silently manufactured by implementation details that readers cannot see in the reported numbers. We name five classes of pipeline failure and demonstrate each in a self-audit over safety benchmarks and open-weight instruction-tuned models. Under a unified six-point due-diligence gate, every cell lands in a non-confirmatory bucket, and no cell reaches confirmatory. The evidence here is a single two-model, five-benchmark case study, and F1--F5 is an illustrative, deliberately non-exhaustive starting taxonomy -- not a comprehensive partition of audit failures. We position the gate as a withholding and disclosure protocol for assurance-grade evidence, supplementary to (not a replacement for) classical construct-validity evidence, and not as a route to benchmark-validity verdicts.

AI.tldr: Perturbation-based construct-validity audits for AI safety are themselves fragile: their conclusions can be silently manufactured by invisible implementation details. The paper identifies five classes of pipeline failures (F1–F5) and demonstrates that under a unified six-point due-diligence gate, all evaluated cells land in non-confirmatory buckets. The gate is proposed as a withholding and disclosure protocol for assurance-grade evidence.
AI.motivation: To expose that perturbation-based construct-validity audits, commonly used as evidence in AI governance frameworks, are fragile and can produce misleading conclusions due to hidden implementation details that readers cannot detect from reported numbers.
AI.method: The authors identify five classes of pipeline failure (F1–F5) and demonstrate each through a self-audit on safety benchmarks and open-weight instruction-tuned models, using a unified six-point due-diligence gate to evaluate confirmatory status.
AI.result: Under the six-point due-diligence gate, every evaluated cell (from a two-model, five-benchmark case study) fell into a non-confirmatory bucket, with no cell reaching confirmatory status.
AI.conclusion: The proposed gate should serve as a withholding and disclosure protocol for assurance-grade evidence, supplementary to classical construct-validity evidence, not as a replacement or a route to benchmark-validity verdicts.

title: Learning 3D Affordances for Blade Insertion in Cluttered Stowing
summary: Many manipulation tasks require reasoning about free-space affordances: discovering volumes where an extended rigid tool can safely navigate, complementary to surface contact affordances for grasping. Robotic stowing is a canonical instance, where a blade must sweep items aside inside cluttered fabric bins to create insertion space. Production stow systems generate millions of such episodes, but standard approaches with unimodal data infer affordances as SE(3) pose distributions, a geometric question asked in the wrong domain. VulcanVoxel keeps inference spatial: a masked autoencoder over 3D occupancy fields reconstructs blade occupancy conditioned on scene geometry, computing feasibility locally at each voxel and recovering multi-modal predictions from unimodal data. Blade affordances are spatial objects, subsets of 3D space defined by geometric feasibility. Pose parameters carry no structure for reasoning whether unobserved placements are feasible, and standard generative objectives including flow matching faithfully learn the unimodal distribution produced by execution policies and cannot recover geometric alternatives. Trained on 10,000 real warehouse stow episodes without human annotation, VulcanVoxel achieves top-5 coverage of 0.89 versus 0.71 for the best pose-based baseline, with a distilled student providing RGB-to-voxel inference in 30 ms. vs. 1.4 s. for voxel-to-voxel. We have released a dataset of real blade insertion cycles with RGB-D observations and pose trajectories at https://www.armbench.com/blade_insertion. html.

AI.tldr: VulcanVoxel uses a masked autoencoder over 3D occupancy fields to predict blade free-space affordances as spatial objects (voxel feasibility) rather than SE(3) pose distributions, achieving superior coverage on real warehouse stow tasks with a fast distilled RGB-to-voxel student model.
AI.motivation: Robotic stowing requires reasoning about free-space affordances for safe tool navigation, but standard pose-based approaches (SE(3) distributions) fail to recover multi-modal geometric alternatives from unimodal execution data, as pose parameters lack structure for reasoning unobserved feasible placements.
AI.method: VulcanVoxel employs a masked autoencoder over 3D occupancy fields that reconstructs blade occupancy conditioned on scene geometry, computing feasibility locally per voxel to recover multi-modal spatial predictions from unimodal data, without human annotation.
AI.result: Trained on 10,000 real warehouse stow episodes, VulcanVoxel achieves top-5 coverage of 0.89 vs. 0.71 for pose-based baselines, with a distilled student achieving RGB-to-voxel inference in 30 ms (vs. 1.4 s for voxel-to-voxel).
AI.conclusion: Blade affordances are better treated as spatial objects (subsets of 3D space) rather than pose distributions; the approach is validated on real-world data and a dataset has been released.

title: iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni Technical Report
summary: General-purpose embodied agents must understand multimodal instructions, anticipate how their environment will evolve, and produce precise control actions over extended horizons. Existing approaches typically specialize in visual-language reasoning, video-based world modeling, or action generation, while cascaded pipelines that first synthesize future observations and then infer actions can introduce interface bottlenecks and compound prediction errors. We present iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni, a unified multimodal foundation model that jointly models vision(videos and images), language, and action within a single Omni framework. Its modality-specific visual-language, video-generation, and action-generation components communicate through shared multimodal self-attention. This design establishes brain-cerebellum collaboration: the vision-language modeland video generation model form a high-level brain for instruction understanding, task planning, progress tracking, and future visual-state prediction, whereas the action generation modelserves as a low-level cerebellum that directly converts planned subgoals and shared multimodal context into executable action chunks. To develop these capabilities, we combine action-annotated and action-free embodied videos from human demonstrations and robot interactions with embodied reasoning, embodied perception, and general-purpose image-text data to construct a comprehensive dataset. We further adopt a four-stage strategy that progressively trains the VLM, VGM, and AGM before jointly fine-tuning the complete model.

AI.tldr: iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni is a unified multimodal foundation model that jointly processes vision, language, and action within a single Omni framework using brain-cerebellum architecture, trained via a four-stage strategy on combined action-annotated and action-free embodied data.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied AI approaches use cascaded pipelines separating visual-language reasoning, world modeling, and action generation, which create interface bottlenecks and compound prediction errors. A unified model is needed to avoid these issues.
AI.method: The model employs a brain-cerebellum design where VLM and video generation model (brain) handle instruction understanding, task planning, and future state prediction, while action generation model (cerebellum) converts subgoals into action chunks. All components communicate via shared multimodal self-attention. Training uses a four-stage progressive strategy on a combined dataset of human demonstrations, robot interactions, embodied reasoning, perception, and general image-text data.
AI.result: The paper presents a unified model that jointly models vision, language, and action within a single framework, but specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The unified Omni framework with brain-cerebellum collaboration and progressive four-stage training can effectively develop embodied agents capable of understanding multimodal instructions, anticipating environment evolution, and producing precise extended-horizon control actions.

title: StructuredEdit: Constraint-Aware Graphic Design Editing via Differentiable Parameter Propagation
comment: 3 page poster short paper.2 Figures, 2 Tables. Planned to submit to SIGGRAPH Asia
summary: Graphic design editing requires precise manipulation of typography, layout, and visual hierarchy under strict design constraints. Following the introduction of large language models, organizations have increasingly promoted vision-language models to enhance productivity. However, current models operate on pixels and achieve only 52% constraint satisfaction on structured design edits, thereby limiting their reliability for professional workflows. We present StructuredEdit, a pipeline that reframes design editing as parameter manipulation rather than pixel generation. Our core technical contribution is Differentiable Parameter Propagation (DPP), a training method that embeds hard design constraints into vision-language model fine-tuning by backpropagating pixel-level constraint violations through a lightweight differentiable rasterizer. A hybrid candidate-and-filter pipeline produces 125k validated edit triplets. The resulting system reaches 89% constraint satisfaction versus 52% for GPT-4V, 0.82 matched-element Intersection over Union, and 76% top-1 font accuracy over the 100 most-frequent design typefaces. In a user study (N=35), editing time drops 33% and correction iterations drop 44% relative to a GPT-4V baseline.

AI.tldr: StructuredEdit reframes design editing as parameter manipulation using Differentiable Parameter Propagation (DPP), achieving 89% constraint satisfaction (vs 52% for GPT-4V), 33% faster editing, and 44% fewer corrections in user studies.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models operate on pixels and achieve only 52% constraint satisfaction on structured design edits, limiting reliability for professional graphic design workflows.
AI.method: StructuredEdit uses a pipeline that reframes design editing as parameter manipulation. The core technical contribution is Differentiable Parameter Propagation (DPP), which embeds hard design constraints into VLM fine-tuning by backpropagating pixel-level constraint violations through a lightweight differentiable rasterizer. A hybrid candidate-and-filter pipeline produces 125k validated edit triplets.
AI.result: 89% constraint satisfaction (vs 52% for GPT-4V), 0.82 matched-element IoU, 76% top-1 font accuracy over the 100 most-frequent typefaces. User study (N=35): 33% reduction in editing time, 44% reduction in correction iterations.
AI.conclusion: StructuredEdit significantly outperforms pixel-based VLM approaches for professional graphic design editing by treating edits as parameter manipulations, enabled by the DPP training method that enforces hard design constraints.

title: Taste-aware music retrieval from audio embeddings
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of MusiCHER-2026, Special Session of IEEE CBMI 2026
summary: Crossmodal correspondences between sound and taste are well established in psychology and neuroscience, but largely absent from content-based multimedia retrieval. We formalise taste-from-audio prediction as a content-based music information retrieval benchmark over a perceptually validated multi-source corpus, comparing ten frozen audio encoders from the four HEAR families under a shared multi-task regression head, with gated late-fusion as a configurable variant. In order to assess the effectiveness of the models, we compute absolute error and rank correlation. The strongest systems predict the five tastes within a macro RMSE of 0.134; on held-out real music their error is less than half a single rater's deviation from the consensus (RMSE 0.13 vs. 0.28), so the model tracks the group consensus more closely than an average human rater, and well below the previous state of the art baseline (0.219). On absolute error the encoders are statistically flat, with a single VGGish matching the best fusion, but gated late-fusion's advantage is confined to rank correlation (macro Pearson r 0.724 vs. 0.666). Operationalised as a content-based retrieval index, the predicted taste space ranks a 309-item pool far more faithfully than a CLAP-text baseline, which sits at chance; ridge probes and an audio-bandstop knockout read the strongest representations against documented sound-taste correspondences.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes taste-from-audio prediction as a music information retrieval benchmark, comparing ten frozen audio encoders from four HEAR families. The best systems predict five tastes with macro RMSE of 0.134, outperforming human raters (0.28) and previous state-of-the-art (0.219). While absolute error is statistically flat across encoders, gated late-fusion improves rank correlation (macro Pearson r 0.724 vs. 0.666). The predicted taste space outperforms a CLAP-text baseline and aligns with documented sound-taste correspondences.
AI.motivation: Crossmodal correspondences between sound and taste are well established in psychology/neuroscience but largely absent from content-based multimedia retrieval, motivating the need to formalize and benchmark taste-from-audio prediction.
AI.method: Ten frozen audio encoders from four HEAR families are compared under a shared multi-task regression head with gated late-fusion as a configurable variant, using a perceptually validated multi-source corpus. Evaluation uses absolute error and rank correlation.
AI.result: Best systems achieve macro RMSE of 0.134, outperforming human raters (RMSE 0.28) and prior SOTA (0.219). VGGish matches best fusion on absolute error; gated late-fusion excels in rank correlation (Pearson r 0.724 vs. 0.666). Predicted taste space outperforms CLAP-text baseline significantly.
AI.conclusion: Taste-from-audio prediction is feasible and can surpass human-level consensus tracking. Gated late-fusion benefits ranking tasks, while individual encoders like VGGish suffice for absolute prediction. The approach operationalizes taste as a content-based retrieval index aligned with known crossmodal correspondences.

title: When Not to Write Memory: Governing False Promotion from Correlated Agent Traces
summary: Long-lived language agents increasingly write reusable memories from their own execution traces. The key safety question is not only what agents should remember, but when they should refuse to write memory at all. Repeated observations across agents are not necessarily independent evidence: the same claim may be copied from a shared source, induced by a shared prompt, stale under a new environment, or valid only in a narrower scope. We study this failure mode as a memory writepath governance problem. We introduce GovMem as a conservative diagnostic reference policy that estimates dependency-aware support, retrieves counterevidence, assigns scope, and outputs one of three decisions: promote, reject, or needs-review. In controlled synthetic stress tests, GovMem reduces false promotion from 0.597 to 0.040 in the default setting while preserving 0.960 recall, at an explicit review burden. In a project-internal 120candidate human-labeled real-trace subset spanning 79 recorded traces and project reports, dependency-aware promotion reduces false promotion from 0.371 for source+scope to 0.032 overall, but held-out false promotion remains 0.111 and the method is highly conservative, with 0.692 review burden and 0.448 direct recall. A final human adjudication of 133 high-impact external codingagent candidates is more severe: none are safe for automatic promotion, and all 11 verification-gate positives are rejected as boilerplate, shared-tool artifacts, file dumps, or non-reusable debugging traces. These results support GovMem primarily as a diagnostic governance design point, not as a generally validated or efficient automatic memory writer: agent memory write paths should be evaluated as risk-controlled evidence-governance systems, while broader external coverage and downstream harm evidence are still needed before stronger claims.

AI.tldr: GovMem is a conservative diagnostic memory governance policy for long-lived language agents that estimates dependency-aware support for memory writes, reducing false promotion rates significantly across synthetic, internal human-labeled, and external coding-agent traces, but remaining too conservative for automatic promotion—supporting its use as a governance design point rather than a deployed writer.
AI.motivation: Long-lived language agents write reusable memories from execution traces, but repeated observations across agents may not be independent evidence—they could be copied from shared sources, induced by shared prompts, stale, or scope-limited. The key safety question is when agents should refuse to write memory, not just what to remember.
AI.method: GovMem implements a dependency-aware diagnostic reference policy that estimates support for candidate memories, retrieves counterevidence, assigns scope, and outputs one of three decisions: promote, reject, or needs-review.
AI.result: In synthetic stress tests: false promotion reduced from 0.597 to 0.040 with 0.960 recall. In 120-candidate human-labeled traces: false promotion from 0.371 to 0.032 overall, but held-out false promotion 0.111, review burden 0.692, recall 0.448. In 133 external coding-agent candidates: none safe for automatic promotion; all 11 verification-gate positives rejected as boilerplate, shared-tool artifacts, file dumps, or non-reusable traces.
AI.conclusion: GovMem is primarily a diagnostic governance design point, not a generally validated or efficient automatic memory writer. Agent memory write paths should be evaluated as risk-controlled evidence-governance systems; broader external coverage and downstream harm evidence are needed before stronger claims.

title: Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models for Electricity Price Forecasting: Contamination Risk, Distributional Shifts, and Covariate Dependence
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have shown strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but their generalization in covariate-driven, non-stationary settings is underexplored. Electricity price forecasting (EPF) presents a challenging testbed due to complex temporal dependencies, distributional shifts, and strong reliance on structural and contextual information. We propose a two-dataset-benchmarking framework for EPF to mitigate contamination risk and enable fair evaluation of TSFMs. We examine key aspects of EPF including point and probabilistic forecasting performance, tail behavior, price spikes, and comparisons against domain-specific methods. We find that TSFMs are highly competitive and often outperform general-purpose baselines. Yet, their performance depends critically on covariate support, and they do not consistently surpass domain-specific methods tailored to EPF. Interestingly, simple ensembles of TSFMs and domain-specific methods appear to have significant potential, suggesting that the two approaches capture complementary predictive information.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates time series foundation models (TSFMs) on electricity price forecasting (EPF), finding they are competitive but rely heavily on covariate support, do not consistently beat domain-specific methods, and that simple ensembles combining both approaches show significant potential.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models have shown strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but their generalization in covariate-driven, non-stationary settings like electricity price forecasting is underexplored.
AI.method: Propose a two-dataset benchmarking framework for EPF to mitigate contamination risk. Evaluate TSFMs on point and probabilistic forecasting, tail behavior, price spikes, and comparisons against domain-specific methods.
AI.result: TSFMs are highly competitive and often outperform general-purpose baselines, but their performance depends critically on covariate support and they do not consistently surpass domain-specific EPF methods. Simple ensembles of TSFMs and domain-specific methods show significant potential.
AI.conclusion: TSFMs and domain-specific methods capture complementary predictive information, and their combination via simple ensembles is a promising direction for EPF.

title: DELTAVID: Enhancing Fine-Grained Spatiotemporal Perception with Cross-Video Differences
summary: Video multimodal large language models have made strong progress on open-ended video understanding, but they still lack precise local spatiotemporal perception. When two videos share almost the same global semantics and differ only in a short time span or a small region, current models often fail to find the change and provide reliable evidence. We propose DELTAVID, a verifiable proxy-task framework that enhances fine-grained spatiotemporal perception with cross-video differences. The key idea is to turn cross-video spot-the-difference into a trainable perception signal, where a model identifies local changes, judges temporal boundaries, and organizes spatial evidence by comparing similar videos. To make this signal scalable to train and reliable to evaluate, we further introduce DELTAVID-10K and DELTAVID-Bench, which convert controllable local differences in real videos into evidence-labeled training and test samples. Experiments show that DELTAVID substantially improves performance on cross-video difference understanding and transfers the learned local evidence ability to general video understanding benchmarks, including MMVU, MLVU, Video-MME, VideoHolmes, VideoMMMU, LVBench, TempCompass, and LongVideoBench. These results show that cross-video differences are not only an effective way to diagnose fine-grained perception failures, but also a scalable proxy supervision that moves Video MLLMs from coarse semantic understanding toward fine-grained spatiotemporal evidence reasoning.

AI.tldr: DELTAVID is a proxy-task framework that enhances fine-grained spatiotemporal perception in Video MLLMs by training them to spot local differences across similar videos, supported by a new dataset (DELTAVID-10K) and benchmark (DELTAVID-Bench). It improves cross-video difference understanding and transfers to multiple general video understanding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current Video MLLMs excel at open-ended video understanding but lack precise local spatiotemporal perception — they fail to detect changes when two videos share nearly identical global semantics but differ in a short time span or small region.
AI.method: DELTAVID introduces a verifiable proxy-task framework that converts cross-video spot-the-difference into a trainable perception signal. The model is trained to identify local changes, judge temporal boundaries, and organize spatial evidence by comparing similar videos. DELTAVID-10K and DELTAVID-Bench provide evidence-labeled training and test samples derived from controllable local differences in real videos.
AI.result: DELTAVID substantially improves performance on cross-video difference understanding, and transfers learned local evidence ability to general video understanding benchmarks including MMVU, MLVU, Video-MME, VideoHolmes, VideoMMMU, LVBench, TempCompass, and LongVideoBench.
AI.conclusion: Cross-video differences serve as both an effective diagnostic tool for fine-grained perception failures and a scalable proxy supervision signal, moving Video MLLMs from coarse semantic understanding toward fine-grained spatiotemporal evidence reasoning.

title: Internal Pluralism and the Limits of Pairwise Comparisons
summary: Local pairwise comparisons are a standard tool for learning how people want decision rules to work, e.g., in participatory design or alignment. However, their use builds in two strong assumptions: that local comparisons are sufficient evidence about how a person wants an automated decision rule to behave, and that people can always answer those comparisons decisively. We investigate how these assumptions may be compromised under internal pluralism: the idea that an individual evaluates decision rules according to multiple authoritative priorities about how the rule should behave. We provide a formal model of such pluralistic preferences over decision rules, which then lets us identify two distinct failures of forced local pairwise comparison data. First, priorities such as proportionality, egalitarianism, and equal treatment are inherently global: what they imply in one case can depend on what happens elsewhere, so local comparisons may fail to capture them. Second, even when priorities are representable locally, tension between strongly-held priorities can generate internal conflict, producing potentially costly behavioral distortions when comparisons are forced. We then use our model to investigate the alternative -- allowing people to report indecision -- and our findings suggest that doing so can considerably reduce the number of queries needed to learn preferences accurately. We conclude by describing how our model points toward preference-learning methods that elicit these priorities directly, yielding more faithful and interpretable accounts of what people value.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges two assumptions of using local pairwise comparisons for learning preferences (e.g., in alignment or participatory design): that local comparisons sufficiently capture how people want decision rules to behave, and that people can answer decisively. Under internal pluralism—where individuals hold multiple authoritative priorities—the authors show local comparisons fail for global priorities (e.g., proportionality, egalitarianism) and forced choices cause costly behavioral distortions. Allowing indecision reduces queries needed, and the model suggests directly eliciting priorities for more faithful preference learning.
AI.motivation: Local pairwise comparisons are widely used to learn how people want automated decision rules to behave (e.g., in participatory design or alignment), but they rely on two strong assumptions: that local comparisons sufficiently capture preferences, and that people can answer decisively. The authors investigate how internal pluralism—where an individual evaluates decision rules according to multiple authoritative priorities—can compromise these assumptions.
AI.method: The authors provide a formal model of pluralistic preferences over decision rules. They use this model to identify two distinct failures of forced local pairwise comparison data: (1) global priorities (e.g., proportionality, egalitarianism, equal treatment) are inherently non-local, so local comparisons fail to capture them; (2) even when priorities are local, tension between strongly-held priorities can create internal conflict and behavioral distortions under forced choices. They also investigate the alternative of allowing people to report indecision.
AI.result: The model shows that forced local pairwise comparisons can fail due to global priorities that depend on context beyond the local pair, and due to internal conflict between multiple priorities causing costly behavioral distortions. Allowing indecision can considerably reduce the number of queries needed to learn preferences accurately.
AI.conclusion: The findings point toward preference-learning methods that directly elicit the underlying priorities rather than relying on local pairwise comparisons, yielding more faithful and interpretable accounts of what people value.

title: Physics-Based Simulation of Contact-Induced Facial Wrinkling
summary: Facial skin dynamics are inherently challenging to simulate due to a combination of geometric, material, and anatomical complexities. Human skin is a nonlinear layered material with spatially heterogeneous attachments to the underlying tissues. During contact events, localized compression and shear induce mechanical instabilities, leading to fine-scale wrinkling patterns governed by a delicate interplay of geometry, boundary conditions, and through-the-thickness stresses. We present a finite element framework to simulate contact-induced wrinkling of facial skin. We model skin as a viscoelastic material with time-dependent relaxation that governs the rate, persistence, and damping of wrinkle formation. We employ high-order prismatic solid-shell elements to resolve through-thickness stresses and high-frequency deformation modes. Central to our approach, we introduce a continuum-based formulation of skin ligaments to model heterogeneous skin attachments and provide anatomically inspired mobility constraints. These skin ligaments control the formation and appearance of facial wrinkles by modulating their amplitude, wavelength, and spatial distribution. We evaluate our method on a set of synthetic examples and compare simulations with real-world footage. These results demonstrate that our skin model produces temporally coherent and visually realistic wrinkle patterns during transient contact.

AI.tldr: A finite element framework that simulates contact-induced facial skin wrinkling using viscoelastic material models, high-order prismatic solid-shell elements, and a continuum-based formulation of skin ligaments to model heterogeneous attachments, producing temporally coherent and visually realistic wrinkle patterns.
AI.motivation: Facial skin dynamics are inherently difficult to simulate due to geometric, material, and anatomical complexities such as nonlinear layered structure, heterogeneous attachments, and mechanical instabilities during contact that produce fine-scale wrinkling patterns.
AI.method: The framework uses: (1) viscoelastic material model with time-dependent relaxation for wrinkle rate/persistence/damping; (2) high-order prismatic solid-shell elements for through-thickness stresses and high-frequency deformations; (3) a continuum-based formulation of skin ligaments modeling heterogeneous attachments and providing anatomically inspired mobility constraints that modulate wrinkle amplitude, wavelength, and spatial distribution.
AI.result: Evaluation on synthetic examples and comparisons with real-world footage demonstrate that the skin model produces temporally coherent and visually realistic wrinkle patterns during transient contact.
AI.conclusion: The proposed finite element framework effectively captures contact-induced facial skin wrinkling by integrating viscoelasticity, high-order elements, and continuum-based ligament constraints, yielding realistic dynamic wrinkle behavior.

title: Towards Standardized Light Field Quality Assessment: Hybrid Subjective Benchmarking and Objective Metric Evaluation
summary: Benchmarking immersive media coding solutions, especially in the standardization context, requires reliable and reproducible subjective quality assessment (QA) procedures, along with objective quality metrics that remain accurate across different distortion types. This paper presents a standardized workflow for light field QA, developed and deployed in the context of JPEG Pleno standardization activities, which integrates benchmark generation, a hybrid subjective evaluation, and objective metric analysis into a common workflow. The benchmark is designed to encompass not only traditional coding-only artifacts but also distortions that arise in processing pipelines in which light field encoding is accompanied with view synthesis and reconstruction techniques. A hybrid subjective method is proposed enabling fine-grained assessment by combining reference-anchored quality rating with targeted pairwise refinement in perceptually ambiguous regions. The reliability of subjective scores is verified using statistical consistency analyses between observers of two cohorts. Finally, a large set of objective metrics is systematically evaluated in terms of global prediction accuracy, local agreement in ambiguous quality regions, and robustness across distortion families. The results show that several metrics achieve strong agreement for coding-only stimuli, but their performance consistently drops when view synthesis distortions are included. The analysis further highlights the importance of view-pooling strategy in the design of future light field quality metrics. The work provides a reproducible and standardization-ready framework for fine-grained light field QA, while identifying key limitations of current objective metrics under emerging coding pipelines. The subjectively annotated dataset is publicly available at https://plenodb.jpeg.org/lfqa/objectivecfp.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a standardized workflow for light field subjective quality assessment and objective metric evaluation, developed within JPEG Pleno standardization. It introduces a hybrid subjective method combining anchored ratings with pairwise refinements, and systematically evaluates objective metrics across coding-only and view synthesis distortions, finding that metric performance degrades with synthesis distortions.
AI.motivation: To establish reliable and reproducible subjective quality assessment procedures and evaluate objective quality metrics for light field coding, particularly in standardization contexts like JPEG Pleno, given that existing metrics fail under emerging processing pipelines involving view synthesis and reconstruction.
AI.method: The workflow integrates benchmark generation, a hybrid subjective evaluation (reference-anchored rating + pairwise refinement in ambiguous regions), and systematic objective metric analysis across coding-only and view-synthesis distortion types. Statistical consistency analyses between two observer cohorts verify subjective reliability. Metrics are evaluated for global accuracy, local agreement, and robustness across distortion families.
AI.result: Several objective metrics achieve strong agreement for coding-only stimuli, but performance drops consistently when view synthesis distortions are included. The view-pooling strategy is identified as critical for future light field quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a reproducible, standardization-ready framework for fine-grained light field QA and identifies key limitations of current objective metrics under emerging coding pipelines. The annotated dataset is publicly available.

title: Adaptive Loss Balancing for Multi-Task Bioacoustic Classification of Bird Species and Call Types
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence (LNAI). Extended version of the ICAART 2026 paper "BirdCallNet: Joint Species and Call-Type Classification."
summary:
Reliable analysis of bird vocalisations in passive acoustic monitoring requires models handling multiple, imbalanced annotation targets. We extend BirdCallNet for joint species and call-type classification on the long-tailed WiWa dataset and investigate how task-loss balancing interacts with pretrained representations and adaptation depth. We evaluate four bird-domain encoders, ConvNeXtBS, EAT, BirdMAE, and ProtoCLR, with separate species and call-type heads under linear probing, attentive probing, and full fine-tuning. A manually tuned fixed objective is compared with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting and Dynamic Weight Averaging across all three adaptation regimes, while GradNorm is evaluated only under full fine-tuning.
  Results indicate that the factorised multi-task formulation yields the most consistent improvements over the combined single-task baseline for call-type recognition, while its effect on species recognition depends on the adaptation regime. Full fine-tuning is not consistently optimal: ConvNeXtBS achieves the highest mean species performance under linear probing, whereas BirdMAE provides the strongest call-type performance under attentive probing. Adaptive weighting benefits species recognition more consistently than call-type recognition. Uncertainty weighting is particularly effective for species recognition under attentive probing, whereas Dynamic Weight Averaging is generally stronger for the same task under full fine-tuning. GradNorm achieves competitive call-type performance for selected backbones but consistently underperforms other weighting strategies for species recognition and incurs higher computational and memory costs. Overall, the preferred loss-balancing strategy depends on the backbone, adaptation regime, and target task, while frozen-backbone adaptation can provide a more favourable performance-efficiency trade-off than end-to-end fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper extends BirdCallNet for joint species and call-type classification on the long-tailed WiWa dataset, investigating how task-loss balancing interacts with pretrained representations and adaptation depth. Results show the factorised multi-task formulation improves call-type recognition, while optimal loss-balancing strategy depends on backbone, adaptation regime, and target task, with frozen-backbone adaptation offering a better performance-efficiency trade-off than full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Reliable analysis of bird vocalisations in passive acoustic monitoring requires models that can handle multiple, imbalanced annotation targets, motivating the need to study multi-task learning strategies for joint species and call-type classification.
AI.method: Extended BirdCallNet for joint species and call-type classification; evaluated four bird-domain encoders (ConvNeXtBS, EAT, BirdMAE, ProtoCLR) with separate heads under linear probing, attentive probing, and full fine-tuning; compared manual fixed objective, homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, Dynamic Weight Averaging, and GradNorm.
AI.result: Factorised multi-task formulation consistently improves call-type recognition over single-task baseline; full fine-tuning not consistently optimal (ConvNeXtBS best under linear probing for species, BirdMAE best under attentive probing for call-type); adaptive weighting benefits species more than call-type recognition; GradNorm achieves competitive call-type performance but underperforms for species recognition with higher costs.
AI.conclusion: Preferred loss-balancing strategy depends on backbone, adaptation regime, and target task; frozen-backbone adaptation can provide a more favourable performance-efficiency trade-off than end-to-end fine-tuning.

title: Better Together, in the Right Order: Classical-then-LLM Optimization for SE
summary:
A growing body of work combines large language models (LLMs) with classical optimizers for software engineering (SE) configuration tasks. Often, the classical optimizer is in charge: it owns the search loop and calls the LLM only to assist in subroutines (e.g. to warm-start the first generation, propose a mutation, or stand in as a surrogate). We report that there is much value in the reverse approach: seeding an LLM with the results from a cheap classical learner.
  We call this method SNAP2. Applied to over 100 SE tasks, it is the single best of all methods studied, reaching the top tier on 85% of tasks, ahead of the same LLM run alone (75%) and ahead of every method in which the classical optimizer retains control. It is also less expensive: relative to the LLM-alone method, it uses roughly 30% fewer tokens and runs 1.4x faster, since the classical setup performs the inexpensive work, and the LLM is invoked only to finish.
  We conclude that it is unwise to study classical learners or LLMs in isolation: there is much value in combining the two, and in the order that combination is applied.

AI.tldr: SNAP2 combines cheap classical learners with LLMs by first running the classical optimizer and then seeding the LLM with its results, outperforming LLM-alone and classical-optimizer-driven methods on 85% of 100+ SE tasks while using 30% fewer tokens and running 1.4x faster.
AI.motivation: Prior work combines LLMs with classical optimizers but keeps the classical optimizer in control of the search loop, only using the LLM for subroutines. The authors hypothesize that reversing this order—seeding an LLM with cheap classical learner results—yields better performance and efficiency.
AI.method: SNAP2 first runs a cheap classical learner (e.g., simple heuristic or search) on software engineering configuration tasks, then uses the results to seed/fine-tune an LLM prompt, letting the LLM finish the optimization. Evaluated on over 100 SE configuration tasks against baselines including LLM-alone and classical-optimizer-controlled methods.
AI.result: SNAP2 reaches the top tier on 85% of tasks (vs. 75% for LLM-alone), outperforms all methods where the classical optimizer retains control, uses ~30% fewer tokens, and runs 1.4x faster than LLM-alone.
AI.conclusion: Studying classical learners or LLMs in isolation is unwise; combining them in the right order (cheap learner first, then LLM) provides substantial benefits in both performance and cost.

title: QuantFlow: A Federated Mamba-Based Post-Transformer Foundation Model for Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time-series forecasting supports decisions in finance, en-ergy, transportation, public health, and industrial monitoring. Recent foundation models improve transfer across forecast-ing tasks, but many depend on centralized data and Trans-former attention, which restricts their use for long, high-di-mensional, and privacy-sensitive signals. This paper presents QuantFlow, a probabilistic forecasting framework that com-bines inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders, quantile regression, and federated learning. Each variable is embedded over the complete ob-servation window, processed in forward and reverse direc-tions, and projected to five conditional quantiles. TSMixup expands temporal diversity through Dirichlet-weighted inter-polation while preserving sequence structure. Experiments cover cryptocurrency, traffic, electricity, Electricity Trans-former Temperature, influenza, and weather data. QuantFlow obtains mean squared errors of 0.2834 on ETTm1 and 0.2218 on Weather, and a 20-client non-IID deployment retains use-ful accuracy after three communication rounds without cen-tralizing raw records. The results indicate that selective state-space modelling is a promising basis for scalable, uncer-tainty-aware, and privacy-conscious time-series prediction, while also revealing limitations on irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon generalization.

AI.tldr: QuantFlow combines inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders, quantile regression, and federated learning for probabilistic time-series forecasting, achieving competitive MSE (0.2834 on ETTm1, 0.2218 on Weather) and retaining accuracy in 20-client non-IID federated settings after 3 rounds without centralizing raw data.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation models for time-series forecasting rely on centralized data and Transformer attention, limiting their use for long, high-dimensional, and privacy-sensitive signals.
AI.method: QuantFlow uses inverted sequence embedding (embedding each variable over the full observation window), bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders (forward and reverse processing), quantile regression (projecting to five conditional quantiles), TSMixup (Dirichlet-weighted interpolation for temporal diversity), and federated learning for privacy preservation.
AI.result: Mean squared errors of 0.2834 on ETTm1 and 0.2218 on Weather; 20-client non-IID federated deployment retains useful accuracy after three communication rounds; limitations observed on irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon generalization.
AI.conclusion: Selective state-space modeling (Mamba) is a promising basis for scalable, uncertainty-aware, and privacy-conscious time-series prediction, though challenges remain for irregular signals and long-horizon tasks.

title: Interpretable machine learning predicts Parkinson's disease severity using motion-corrected QSM MRI and multiband multiecho fMRI features
comment: 16 pages from main manuscript and 17 pages from supplementary information
summary:
Introduction: Objective neuroimaging biomarkers may improve Parkinson's disease motor assessment by capturing brain variation not directly observable from clinical examination. We used interpretable machine learning to predict current motor severity, measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III, from QSM and multiband multi-echo resting-state fMRI-derived ReHo features.
  Methods: Regional QSM and ReHo features were extracted from 28 participants, including 24 individuals with Parkinson's disease and 4 controls. Thirteen feature-set experiments evaluated imaging-only, clinical-only, imaging-plus-clinical, full, reduced, and multimodal inputs. Support vector regression, Elastic Net, Random Forest, and XGBoost models were trained using nested cross-validation. Performance was assessed using pooled held-out R^2, RMSE, MAE, Pearson correlation, permutation testing, and the proportion of participants predicted within +/-5 MDS-UPDRS Part III points.
  Results: Imaging-only models carried meaningful predictive signal, whereas the clinical-only model performed weakly. Full fMRI, full QSM, and clinical variables provided the strongest global fit, explaining 45.4% of variance in motor severity. Selected QSM plus clinical variables produced the most clinically close predictions, with 75.0% of participants predicted within +/-5 points and the lowest MAE among top-performing models. SHAP highlighted cerebellar, thalamic, striatal, insular, and motor cortical features.
  Conclusion: QSM and multiband multi-echo fMRI-derived ReHo capture distinct, interpretable dimensions of Parkinson's disease motor severity. These findings show that structural and functional imaging contribute differently depending on the clinical prediction goal.

AI.tldr: QSM and multiband multi-echo fMRI-derived ReHo features, combined with machine learning, predict Parkinson's disease motor severity (MDS-UPDRS Part III), with imaging-only models carrying meaningful signal and combined QSM+clinical features achieving the most clinically accurate predictions (75% within ±5 points).
AI.motivation: Objective neuroimaging biomarkers may improve Parkinson's disease motor assessment by capturing brain variation not directly observable from clinical examination.
AI.method: 28 participants (24 PD, 4 controls); regional QSM and ReHo features extracted; 13 feature-set experiments (imaging-only, clinical-only, imaging+clinical, full, reduced, multimodal); SVR, Elastic Net, Random Forest, XGBoost with nested cross-validation; evaluated by R², RMSE, MAE, Pearson r, permutation testing, ±5-point accuracy; SHAP for interpretability.
AI.result: Imaging-only models carried meaningful signal; clinical-only model performed weakly. Full fMRI, full QSM, and clinical variables explained 45.4% of variance. Selected QSM+clinical variables achieved 75% within ±5 points and lowest MAE. SHAP highlighted cerebellar, thalamic, striatal, insular, and motor cortical regions.
AI.conclusion: QSM and multiband multi-echo fMRI-derived ReHo capture distinct, interpretable dimensions of PD motor severity; structural and functional imaging contribute differently depending on the clinical prediction goal.

title: ASK in the Dark: Uncertainty-Gated LLM Assistance under Partial Observability
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI Joint Workshop on Planning for Complex Real-World Applications and Bridging the Gap Between AI Planning and (Reinforcement) Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning agents operating under partial observability must act on incomplete information, making them natural candidates for guidance from small language models (SLMs) that carry broad reasoning priors. Yet integrating SLM guidance into this setting has proven difficult: across all test environments, vanilla uncertainty-gated approaches achieve an overwrite rate at or near zero, meaning the SLM almost never contributes an independent action. We trace this failure to the bare egocentric prompt, which provides insufficient context for genuine reasoning, and identify it as a context problem rather than a capacity problem. We propose ASK+, which supplies the SLM with trajectory-aware context (a partially revealed map, visited positions, and action history) and structured chain-of-thought reasoning, converting it from a passive redundancy check into a more informative consultant that occasionally corrects the policy. We further establish that the predictive entropy signal used for selective querying measures action uncertainty rather than state uncertainty and remains informative in POMDPs, making uncertainty-gated assistance viable beyond fully observable settings. The stateful prompt drives substantial gains: on DoorKey, where vanilla ASK matches PPO (both 89%), ASK+ reaches 93% success; on FourRooms, success climbs from 53% to 70%; on HigherLower, accuracy reaches 73.7%, matching the SLM-only upper bound. Across all environments, Qwen3.5-2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-4B, confirming that prompt design and selective gating dominate the impact of model scale, enabling guidance without large models.

AI.tldr: ASK+ enhances partial-observability RL by providing SLMs with trajectory-aware context (map, positions, action history) and structured CoT reasoning, enabling effective uncertainty-gated guidance that outperforms vanilla methods and matches larger models through superior prompt design.
AI.motivation: Standard SLM-guided RL under partial observability fails because bare egocentric prompts lack sufficient context for genuine reasoning—this is a context problem, not a capacity problem. The authors aim to make uncertainty-gated SLM assistance viable in POMDPs.
AI.method: ASK+ provides SLMs with trajectory-aware context (partially revealed map, visited positions, action history) and structured chain-of-thought reasoning.
