It uses predictive entropy for selective querying, which measures action uncertainty rather than state uncertainty and remains informative in POMDPs.
AI.result: DoorKey: 93% (vs vanilla ASK/PPO 89%); FourRooms: 70% (vs 53%); HigherLower: 73.7% (SLM-only upper bound). Qwen3.5-2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-4B, showing prompt design dominates model scale.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design and selective gating dominate the impact of model scale, enabling effective SLM guidance without large models. The stateful prompt converts the SLM from a passive check into an informative consultant.

title: Glare Mitigation using a Differentiable Unified Glare Rating
comment: 15 pages, 16 figures. Published in Proceedings of the Eurographics Symposium on Rendering (EGSR) 2026, Symposium Track. This is the authors' version; the definitive version is available at the Eurographics Digital Library
summary: Recent research in differentiable light transport extends the utility of computer graphics algorithms beyond traditional image generation, offering powerful tools for physical inverse design. In architectural and automotive applications, visual discomfort from glare is a critical design rating, traditionally quantified by the discrete CIE Unified Glare Rating (UGR). The standard UGR formulation relies on strict binary thresholds, making it fundamentally incompatible with smooth gradient-based inverse rendering. In this paper, we introduce a continuous, fully differentiable proxy for UGR. To resolve the severe optimisation instabilities caused by Monte Carlo variance at low sample densities, we introduce a differentiable optical scattering pass that simulates the Point Spread Function (PSF) of the human eye to heal fractured evaluation masks. We replace the discrete UGR step function with a tunable sigmoid boundary, enabling gradients to flow smoothly from the psychophysical measure back to the physical scene parameters. We deploy this differentiable framework to systematically reduce glare across three radiometric domains: surface-side microgeometry roughening, boundary-side index of refraction (IOR) optimisation, and source-side emitter gobo masking. By transforming a passive perceptual evaluation into an active loss landscape, our framework provides a robust, physics-based pipeline for optimizing visual comfort in complex global illumination environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces a continuous, differentiable proxy for CIE Unified Glare Rating (UGR) to enable gradient-based inverse rendering for glare reduction, using a differentiable optical scattering pass (PSF simulation) and tunable sigmoid boundary to replace discrete UGR thresholds, deployed across microgeometry, IOR, and gobo masking domains.
AI.motivation: The standard UGR formulation relies on strict binary thresholds, making it fundamentally incompatible with smooth gradient-based inverse rendering, thus preventing optimization of visual comfort (glare) in physically-based differentiable rendering.
AI.method: (1) A differentiable optical scattering pass simulating the human eye's PSF to heal fractured evaluation masks caused by Monte Carlo variance; (2) Replacing discrete UGR step function with a tunable sigmoid boundary for smooth gradients; (3) Deploying the framework across three domains: microgeometry roughening, IOR optimization, and emitter gobo masking.
AI.result: Enables systematic glare reduction across three radiometric domains (surface-side, boundary-side, source-side) by transforming passive perceptual UGR evaluation into an active differentiable loss landscape.
AI.conclusion: Provides a robust, physics-based pipeline for optimizing visual comfort in complex global illumination environments using differentiable light transport.

title: ResearchStudio-Reel: Automate the Last Mile of Research from Paper to Poster, Video, and Blog
summary: Research dissemination, turning a paper into a poster, a talk video, and a blog post, is still a manual last mile. Prior automation treats each artifact in isolation that each re-extract the paper from scratch, usually ship one-way renders the author cannot reopen in PowerPoint or Word, and gates quality on soft VLM-preference scores that plateau while load-bearing sections still read as empty. We argue this last mile is best built as a composition of skills: thin agent-readable contracts that share one upstream extractor and wrap deterministic primitives in a measured-fill loop whose exits are hard pass/fail render gates. We instantiate this as ResearchStudio-Reel, five Claude Code and Codex skills organized into one shared extractor (Paper2Assets), three editable generators (Paper2Poster, Paper2Video, Paper2Blog), and one interactive convergence layer (Paper2Reel). Paper2Assets extracts each paper once into a shared bundle that can be reused by every downstream skill; The three generators produce a print-ready poster, a synchronized talk video, and a bilingual blog that stay factually consistent and round-trip through PowerPoint or Word; Paper2Reel then binds all three into a self-contained HTML viewer whose section-level clicks jump the video, slides, captions, and blog to matching content. On the Paper2Poster benchmark, our posters lead every aesthetic and information sub-criterion against both prior automated systems and single-shot frontier LLMs, surpassing the authors' own on aesthetics under two held-out VLM judges and winning overall on 84% to 93% of papers; capability audits further show that, by uniquely pairing narration-aligned on-slide highlights with a bilingual blog gated by layout-aware DOCX repair, ResearchStudio-Reel is the only pipeline to ship all three editable artifacts. Project is available at https://aka.ms/ResearchStudio

AI.tldr: ResearchStudio-Reel automates research dissemination by using a shared extractor and three editable generators (poster, video, blog) with hard render gates, achieving superior quality and round-trip editability in PowerPoint/Word.
AI.motivation: Research dissemination (paper→poster, talk video, blog post) remains a manual "last mile." Prior approaches treat each artifact in isolation, re-extract from scratch, produce one-way renders that can't be edited, and rely on soft VLM-preference scores that plateau while key sections remain empty.
AI.method: A composition of skills: thin agent-readable contracts sharing one upstream extractor (Paper2Assets) with deterministic primitives in a measured-fill loop, gated by hard pass/fail render checks. Five Claude Code/Codex skills: Paper2Assets, Paper2Poster, Paper2Video, Paper2Blog, and Paper2Reel (an interactive HTML viewer).
AI.result: On Paper2Poster benchmark, posters lead all aesthetic and information sub-criteria vs. prior automated systems and frontier LLMs, surpassing authors' own posters on aesthetics. Wins 84-93% of papers overall. Only pipeline to ship all three editable artifacts with narration-aligned highlights and layout-aware DOCX repair.
AI.conclusion: The composition-of-skills paradigm with hard render gates and round-trip editability outperforms isolated automation approaches, making the dissemination "last mile" fully automatable while maintaining quality and editability.

title: DETECT-3B-Omni is Agnostic of Content and Demographics
summary: A trustworthy and GDPR-compliant deepfake audio detector must base its decisions on acoustic artifacts, not on what is being said or who is speaking. We present a large-scale study of semantic independence for Resemble AI's detector, DETECT-3B-Omni. Using 10,240 audio samples from diverse US English speakers across 30 states, generated through 8 different AI voice-cloning systems, we test whether detection accuracy depends on spoken content (benign versus malicious), speaker gender, speaker age, or speaker region. Using equivalence testing, our results show that the accuracy difference between any two of these groups is at most 2 percentage points, at 99% confidence. The detector therefore identifies AI-generated audio with equivalent accuracy regardless of what the audio says or who the speaker is.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates through a large-scale study (10,240 samples) that Resemble AI's DETECT-3B-Omni deepfake audio detector achieves semantic independence, with accuracy differences between demographic and content groups bounded by at most 2 percentage points at 99% confidence, confirming GDPR-compliant operation based on acoustic artifacts rather than speech content or speaker identity.
AI.motivation: To verify that deepfake audio detectors are GDPR-compliant and trustworthy by ensuring decisions are based solely on acoustic artifacts rather than biased by spoken content (benign vs. malicious), speaker gender, speaker age, or speaker region.
AI.method: Large-scale study using 10,240 audio samples from diverse US English speakers across 30 states, generated via 8 different AI voice-cloning systems. Semantic independence tested across spoken content type, speaker gender, age, and region using equivalence testing.
AI.result: Accuracy difference between any two demographic or content groups is at most 2 percentage points at 99% confidence, demonstrating equivalent detection accuracy regardless of what the audio says or who the speaker is.
AI.conclusion: Resemble AI's DETECT-3B-Omni detector achieves semantic independence, identifying AI-generated audio with equivalent accuracy irrespective of spoken content or speaker characteristics, thus meeting GDPR compliance and trustworthiness requirements.

title: The Moving Target: A Longitudinal Audit of Trustworthiness Drift Across Twelve Checkpoints of Open-Source Chat LLMs
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures; accepted as a poster at the ICML 2026 TAIGA Workshop
summary: Model cards quote trust-benchmark scores without recording when they were measured, and the same number is routinely carried across successive checkpoints of one release line as if the model behind it had not shifted. We test whether it has shifted by auditing four open-source release lines, Yi, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemma, at three successive generations each, on a fixed basket of trust benchmarks under multiple prompt templates. Mean absolute adjacent-generation drift lands well above an independence-based no-drift reference null, and the gap persists when we drop a benchmark, drop a release line, or switch to strict scoring. We therefore conclude that a trust score attached to a release line should not be carried forward to the next checkpoint without remeasurement; it should instead be reported as a checkpoint-bound, dated artefact, which we package as a longitudinal model card. Closed APIs, larger models, canonical benchmark protocols, and fixed month-cadence rules lie outside the audited scope and require their own evaluation.

AI.tldr: Trust scores from model cards are not updated across successive model checkpoints, even though the models shift. An audit of four open-source release lines over three generations each shows significant drift in trust benchmarks, indicating that trust scores should be checkpoint-bound and dated rather than carried forward.
AI.motivation: Model cards quote trust-benchmark scores without recording when they were measured, and the same score is routinely carried across successive checkpoints of a release line without remeasurement, even though the underlying model may have shifted.
AI.method: Audited four open-source release lines (Yi, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma) at three successive generations each, on a fixed basket of trust benchmarks under multiple prompt templates. Measured mean absolute adjacent-generation drift and compared against a no-drift reference null. Conducted robustness checks by dropping benchmarks, dropping a release line, and switching to strict scoring.
AI.result: Mean absolute adjacent-generation drift is significantly above the no-drift reference null, and the gap persists across all robustness checks (dropping a benchmark, dropping a release line, switching to strict scoring).
AI.conclusion: A trust score attached to a release line should not be carried forward to the next checkpoint without remeasurement; it should be reported as a checkpoint-bound, dated artefact (longitudinal model card). Closed APIs, larger models, canonical benchmark protocols, and fixed month-cadence rules require their own evaluation as they lie outside the audited scope.

title: GRAFT: Grafted Reference Audio for Fine-grained Pronunciation in Zero-shot Text-to-Speech
summary: We present GRAFT, a per-word pronunciation conditioning mechanism for text-to-speech neural codec language modeling. Existing systems reach high intelligibility and naturalness but inherit the ambiguity of text and mispronounce rare proper nouns, loanwords and technical terms. Even phoneme-conditioned models offer no direct acoustic handle for per-word pronunciation. GRAFT controls the pronunciation of a chosen word from a short spoken sample of it, encoded with the model's own speech tokenizer and bound to the word's position in the prompt. Voice conversion during training-data construction disentangles the hint speaker from the target speaker, so the hint may come from any voice while the output stays in the target voice. In a blind English listening study, human raters rank GRAFT first by a clear margin, judging its rendering of the difficult word closest to a reference recording of that word. On a five-language objective benchmark, GRAFT reduces target-word phoneme error rate by 22-39% over the identical text-only backbone and outperforms competitive open-source zero-shot systems, both phoneme- and text-conditioned, on target-word pronunciation, while preserving speaker similarity and naturalness.

AI.tldr: GRAFT is a per-word pronunciation conditioning mechanism for text-to-speech neural codec language modeling that improves pronunciation of rare words by using a short spoken sample of the target word, disentangled from the target speaker via voice conversion, achieving significant improvements in phoneme error rate and human preference.
AI.motivation: Existing TTS systems mispronounce rare proper nouns, loanwords, and technical terms because text-to-speech models inherit the ambiguity of text, and even phoneme-conditioned models lack direct acoustic control over per-word pronunciation.
AI.method: GRAFT controls pronunciation of a chosen word by encoding a short spoken sample of it using the model's own speech tokenizer, binding it to the word's position in the prompt. Voice conversion during training-data construction disentangles the hint speaker from the target speaker, allowing the hint to come from any voice while preserving the target voice in the output.
AI.result: In a blind English listening study, human raters ranked GRAFT first by a clear margin. On a five-language objective benchmark, GRAFT reduced target-word phoneme error rate by 22-39% over the identical text-only backbone and outperformed competitive open-source zero-shot systems on target-word pronunciation while preserving speaker similarity and naturalness.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT effectively addresses the pronunciation problem for rare and ambiguous words in TTS by leveraging spoken hints with speaker disentanglement, achieving superior pronunciation accuracy without sacrificing voice quality or naturalness.

title: Reliability-Aware Monocular Depth Supervision for Sparse-View Neural Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. All authors contributed equally
summary: Sparse-view neural reconstruction is challenging in outdoor driving scenes, where cameras usually move along a narrow forward-facing trajectory and provide limited multi-view overlap. Although monocular depth estimators can provide dense geometric priors, their predictions are noisy, and not uniformly reliable across image regions. In this work, we study monocular depth supervision for sparse-view neural reconstruction. We use Depth Anything V2 as a dense monocular depth prior, align its predictions to metric depth using scale-shift fitting, and apply depth supervision selectively through photometric masks generated from an RGB-only baseline model. We evaluate this strategy on two representative scene representations: Mip-NeRF-360 and Splatfacto. On KITTISeq02 under an every2 sparse-view setting, masked monocular depth supervision gives only marginal rendering gains for Mip-NeRF-360 and does not improve metric geometry. In contrast, Splatfacto benefits more clearly, improving PSNR from 14.903 to 15.932 and reducing RMSE from 0.542 to 0.100. Additional KITTISeq05 experiments and matched-ratio mask ablations further show that the gains for Splatfacto come from selecting reliable low-error regions rather than simply reducing the number of depth-supervised pixels. Additional experiments on the Bicycle scene show that depth supervision can improve geometry while hurting RGB rendering quality when multi-view coverage is already strong. Overall, our results suggest that monocular depth priors are useful for under-constrained sparse-view reconstruction, but should be applied selectively and with moderate weighting.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates selective monocular depth supervision (using Depth Anything V2) for sparse-view neural reconstruction in outdoor driving scenes, finding that while it improves Splatfacto (PSNR +1.029, RMSE -0.442), it yields marginal gains for Mip-NeRF-360 and can hurt RGB quality when multi-view coverage is already strong.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view neural reconstruction in outdoor driving scenes is challenging due to narrow forward-facing camera trajectories with limited multi-view overlap; while monocular depth estimators can provide dense priors, their predictions are noisy and unreliable across regions, motivating the need for selective depth supervision strategies.
AI.method: Use Depth Anything V2 as dense monocular depth prior with metric alignment via scale-shift fitting; apply depth supervision selectively via photometric masks derived from an RGB-only baseline model; evaluate on Mip-NeRF-360 and Splatfacto under KITTI Seq02/Seq05 and Bicycle scene settings.
AI.result: Masked monocular depth supervision gives marginal rendering gains for Mip-NeRF-360 and no metric geometry improvement; Splatfacto benefits more clearly (PSNR: 14.903→15.932, RMSE: 0.542→0.100); gains stem from selecting reliable low-error regions, not merely reducing supervised pixels; in well-covered scenes (Bicycle), depth supervision improves geometry but degrades RGB quality.
AI.conclusion: Monocular depth priors are useful for under-constrained sparse-view reconstruction but must be applied selectively and with moderate weighting to avoid harming RGB quality when multi-view coverage is sufficient.

title: Automated Data Readiness for Scientific AI
summary: Leadership computing facilities steward large-scale scientific datasets that routinely require substantial transformation before serving as AI training data. However, no existing framework fully unifies automated transformation, readiness assessment, provenance tracking, and agent-native deployment. We present REDI, an open-source framework that addresses this gap through a unified five-stage pipeline (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, and output) with per-stage instrumentation for reproducibility and deployment as an agent-callable skill; companion tool SetGo automates FAIR compliance and catalog publication. Evaluated across climate, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion, REDI transforms all datasets from raw to AI-ready, with outputs validated against domain-expert references, and preliminary results show near-ideal parallel scaling to 100 nodes on Frontier for the climate case. Provenance-instrumented profiling reveals file I/O as the dominant pipeline cost, with format selection a first-order optimization lever. These results establish REDI as a cross-domain platform providing automated data readiness for scientific AI, transforming data preparation bottlenecks into reproducible, reusable community assets.

AI.tldr: REDI is an open-source framework that unifies automated transformation, readiness assessment, provenance tracking, and agent-native deployment for scientific datasets across climate, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion, with companion tool SetGo for FAIR compliance. It uses a five-stage pipeline (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, output) and demonstrates near-ideal parallel scaling to 100 nodes on Frontier, with file I/O identified as the dominant cost.
AI.motivation: Leadership computing facilities steward large-scale scientific datasets that routinely require substantial transformation before serving as AI training data, but no existing framework fully unifies automated transformation, readiness assessment, provenance tracking, and agent-native deployment.
AI.method: REDI implements a unified five-stage pipeline (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, output) with per-stage instrumentation for reproducibility and deployment as an agent-callable skill; companion tool SetGo automates FAIR compliance and catalog publication.
AI.result: Evaluated across climate, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion, REDI transforms all datasets from raw to AI-ready with outputs validated against domain-expert references; near-ideal parallel scaling to 100 nodes on Frontier for the climate case; proven-instrumented profiling reveals file I/O as dominant cost and format selection as first-order optimization lever.
AI.conclusion: REDI establishes a cross-domain platform providing automated data readiness for scientific AI, transforming data preparation bottlenecks into reproducible, reusable community assets.

title: Trajectory Variance: AnUnsupervised Measure of Developmental Vocal Plasticity in Birdsong
summary: How much does a vocalization change over the course of development? We propose trajectory variance, a per-vocalization plasticity score that answers this question without type labels. A displacement model learns to predict age-conditioned shifts in autoencoder latent space; the variance of its predictions across target ages quantifies how much each vocalization would change if produced at different developmental stages. Evaluated on three zebra finches (183K-274K vocalizations, 40-101 days post-hatch), trajectory variance separates learned song syllables from innate calls (Cohen's d = 0.29-0.57, AUC = 0.58-0.67, after controlling for duration), while no nonparametric baseline achieves consistent separation. Trajectory variance also correlates with spectral flatness across all three birds (r = -0.48 to -0.75): more plastic vocalizations tend to have more tonal, structured spectra.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes trajectory variance, a per-vocalization plasticity score that measures how much a vocalization would change across development without requiring type labels. It uses a displacement model to predict age-conditioned shifts in autoencoder latent space. Tested on three zebra finches with 183K-274K vocalizations, it separates learned song syllables from innate calls and correlates with spectral flatness, indicating more plastic vocalizations have more tonal structures.
AI.motivation: To quantify vocalization plasticity over development without relying on type labels, enabling automated measurement of how individual vocalizations change across developmental stages.
AI.method: A displacement model learns to predict age-conditioned shifts in autoencoder latent space; trajectory variance is computed as the variance of these predictions across target ages, yielding a per-vocalization plasticity score.
AI.result: Trajectory variance separates learned song syllables from innate calls (Cohen's d = 0.29-0.57, AUC = 0.58-0.67 after controlling for duration) and correlates with spectral flatness (r = -0.48 to -0.75) across three zebra finches.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory variance is an effective unsupervised metric for quantifying vocalization plasticity, outperforming nonparametric baselines, and reveals that more plastic vocalizations tend to be more tonal and structured.

title: OmniPresent: Generating Coherent Presentation Suites from Scientific Papers
summary: Transforming static research papers into dynamic media such as posters, slides, and videos is essential for effective dissemination but remains a labor-intensive challenge. Existing automated approaches often treat these formats in isolation and consequently fail to maintain semantic consistency across the entire presentation suite. We address this fragmentation by formalizing the task of unified presentation suite generation and proposing $\textbf{OmniPresent}$ to orchestrate the creation of coherent deliverables. Our framework adopts a renderable HTML representation to enable centralized content planning and a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop that actively resolves conflicts across modalities. We further facilitate scalable research in this domain by releasing $\textbf{OmniPreBench}$, a comprehensive dataset comprising over one thousand papers with paired artifacts, and establishing a rigorous VLM-based evaluation protocol. Empirical results confirm that our method generates high-quality and faithful presentation suites that significantly surpass strong baselines in both accuracy and visual appeal.

AI.tldr: OmniPresent is a framework that transforms research papers into coherent multi-format presentation suites (posters, slides, videos) using HTML-based centralized planning and a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop, supported by the OmniPreBench dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing automated approaches treat different presentation formats (posters, slides, videos) in isolation, failing to maintain semantic consistency across the entire presentation suite, while manual creation remains labor-intensive.
AI.method: Formalizes unified presentation suite generation; uses a renderable HTML representation for centralized content planning; employs a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop to resolve cross-modal conflicts; releases OmniPreBench dataset with 1000+ papers and paired artifacts; establishes a VLM-based evaluation protocol.
AI.result: The method generates high-quality, faithful presentation suites that significantly surpass strong baselines in both accuracy and visual appeal.
AI.conclusion: OmniPresent effectively addresses fragmentation in presentation suite generation by ensuring semantic consistency across modalities, and the dataset and evaluation protocol facilitate scalable research in this domain.

title: Federated Learning for Object Detection: Enabling Collaborative Drone Learning Without Centralizing Data
summary:
Object detection is a fundamental capability for AI-driven perception in safety-critical drone and edge-vision systems, including disaster response, operational security environments, infrastructure monitoring and defense applications. Robust model performance in such environments depends on large, continuously updated datasets. However, training high-performing detectors typically requires centralizing aerial imagery, which raises privacy, regulatory, storage, and bandwidth challenges. This is especially problematic in distributed drone deployments, where visual data is generated onboard and is often impractical or undesirable to transfer to a centralized infrastructure.
  In this work, we apply Federated Learning (FL) for object detection, enabling drones to improve a shared model while keeping image data local and private. We implement a federated object detection pipeline using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset, and compare it with Single-drone and Centralized baselines using mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.50 and 0.50-0.95. In our experiments, the proposed FL approach remains close to Centralized training while dramatically improving over Single-drone training, with the best lightweight model (YOLO26 nano), suitable for deployment even on very limited edge infrastructure, achieving relative gains of 52.89% and 67.80% in mAP@0.50 and mAP@0.50:0.95, respectively. These results show that FL enables scalable, high-performing, and privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets without data centralization.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Federated Learning (FL) for object detection in distributed drone systems, enabling privacy-preserving model improvement without centralizing aerial imagery. Using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset, the FL approach achieves performance close to Centralized training while significantly outperforming Single-drone training—the YOLO26 nano model shows 52.89% and 67.80% relative gains in mAP@0.50 and mAP@0.50:0.95, respectively.
AI.motivation: Training high-performing object detectors for safety-critical drone applications requires large, continuously updated datasets, but centralizing aerial imagery raises privacy, regulatory, storage, and bandwidth challenges. This is especially problematic in distributed drone deployments where onboard data is impractical or undesirable to transfer to centralized infrastructure.
AI.method: The authors apply Federated Learning (FL) for object detection using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset. They compare FL with Single-drone and Centralized baselines using mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.50 and 0.50:0.95, employing the YOLO26 nano lightweight model suitable for edge infrastructure.
AI.result: The proposed FL approach remains close to Centralized training while dramatically improving over Single-drone training. The YOLO26 nano model achieves relative gains of 52.89% in mAP@0.50 and 67.80% in mAP@0.50:0.95 compared to Single-drone training.
AI.conclusion: FL enables scalable, high-performing, and privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets without requiring data centralization, making it suitable for safety-critical edge-vision applications.

title: Do Diabetic Foot Ulcer Segmentation Models Generalize? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark of CNN and Transformer Architectures
summary: Deep learning models for diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) segmentation routinely report high accuracy, but they are almost always trained and tested on the same dataset, leaving their behaviour on data from a different clinical source largely unmeasured. We benchmark three representative segmentation architectures -- U-Net and DeepLabV3+ (convolutional) and SegFormer-B2 (Transformer) -- under an identical, leakage-screened protocol: training on the combined FUSeg/AZH wound data and evaluating, without fine-tuning, on two independent external datasets (DFUC2022 and Medetec). All models achieve strong in-domain performance (Dice 0.80--0.83) but degrade substantially across datasets. The degradation is, however, architecture-dependent: SegFormer-B2 generalizes best on both external sets (DFUC2022 Dice 0.557, Medetec Dice 0.786), outperforming both convolutional models, while the more complex DeepLabV3+ generalizes worse than the simpler U-Net. Per-image failure analysis on 2,160 images across both external test sets confirms that SegFormer-B2 produces the fewest catastrophic failures on DFUC2022 (31.1%), compared with U-Net (38.5%) and DeepLabV3+ (43.0%). The consistent ranking across two independent external sources, confirmed by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p < 0.001 on both datasets), indicates that architecture family, not model complexity, drives cross-hospital generalization.

AI.tldr: Deep learning models for diabetic foot ulcer segmentation show high in-domain performance (Dice 0.80-0.83) but degrade substantially on external datasets. SegFormer-B2 (Transformer) generalizes best across datasets (DFUC2022 Dice 0.557, Medetec Dice 0.786), outperforming convolutional models, with architecture family (not complexity) being the key driver of cross-hospital generalization.
AI.motivation: Current DFU segmentation models are typically trained and tested on the same dataset, leaving their cross-dataset generalization behavior largely unmeasured.
AI.method: Benchmarked U-Net, DeepLabV3+ (convolutional), and SegFormer-B2 (Transformer) under an identical, leakage-screened protocol: trained on combined FUSeg/AZH data, evaluated without fine-tuning on two external datasets (DFUC2022 and Medetec). Used per-image failure analysis on 2,160 images and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
AI.result: All models achieve in-domain Dice 0.80-0.83 but degrade on external data. SegFormer-B2 generalizes best (DFUC2022 Dice 0.557, Medetec Dice 0.786). DeepLabV3+ generalizes worse than simpler U-Net. SegFormer-B2 has fewest catastrophic failures (31.1% vs 38.5% for U-Net, 43.0% for DeepLabV3+). Rankings are consistent across both datasets (p < 0.001).
AI.conclusion: Architecture family, not model complexity, drives cross-hospital generalization for DFU segmentation. Transformer-based models (SegFormer-B2) generalize better than convolutional architectures across clinical sources.

title: SwarmResearch: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Open-Ended Discovery
summary: Long-running coding agents such as autoresearch can persistently discover optimizations for open-ended problems. However, they tend to converge onto a single high-level approach, then proceed with low-level edits while missing other superior approaches to the problem. We hypothesize two harness-level design choices contribute to this behavior: accumulating context in a single long-running agent and only exposing a single program state to edit. We introduce SwarmResearch, an orchestrator-subagent harness in which a Shepherd Agent uses global context to steer a population of Search Agents, each operating with local context in their respective git branch. On open-ended optimization tasks, SwarmResearch discovers better or comparable solutions to state-of-the-art LLM-guided evolution and multi-agent techniques on 13/15 tasks, driven by higher-level exploration. Compared with fixed scaling of serial and parallel agents, SwarmResearch's orchestrator-guided scaling discovers better-performing solutions by adapting parallelism at different search depths.

AI.tldr: SwarmResearch introduces an orchestrator-subagent harness (Shepherd Agent + Search Agents in git branches) that outperforms existing LLM-guided optimization methods on 13/15 tasks by enabling higher-level exploration and adaptive parallelism, overcoming the convergence issue of long-running coding agents.
AI.motivation: Long-running coding agents (e.g., autoresearch) tend to converge onto a single high-level approach and then only make low-level edits, missing superior alternative solutions. This is hypothesized to stem from accumulating context in a single long-running agent and exposing only one program state to edit.
AI.method: SwarmResearch employs a two-level architecture: a Shepherd Agent with global context that steers a population of Search Agents, each operating with local context in their respective git branch, enabling parallel exploration of diverse approaches.
AI.result: SwarmResearch discovers better or comparable solutions than state-of-the-art LLM-guided evolution and multi-agent techniques on 13/15 open-ended optimization tasks. Its orchestrator-guided scaling outperforms fixed scaling of serial/parallel agents by adapting parallelism at different search depths.
AI.conclusion: The orchestrator-subagent design with global steering and local parallel exploration effectively addresses the convergence problem in long-running coding agents, achieving superior performance through higher-level exploration and adaptive parallelism.

title: Provable Pruning for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting via Coresets
comment: 39 pages, 15 figures, including supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/waseem-m/3dgs_provable_coresets
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis, but practical scenes often contain millions of Gaussians, making compression essential for deployment on limited hardware. Existing reduction methods are effective but mostly heuristic: they provide no multiplicative approximation guarantee for the rendered objective, and thus rely heavily on costly post-pruning finetuning to recover quality. We ask a basic question: can a 3DGS scene be provably replaced by a much smaller weighted subset (coreset) while preserving the objective of interest? We first show that, in the unrestricted setting, no non-trivial multiplicative 3DGS coreset exists. We then show that multiplicative guarantees are not impossible, but resolution-dependent. For a prescribed rendering resolution, such as representative views or grids of views/rays, we provide the first weighted coreset construction theorem for 3DGS. The construction samples Gaussians by sensitivity: provable importance scores measuring each Gaussian's role in the full-scene objective. Finally, under explicit validity and log-transmittance stability assumptions, we turn this objective guarantee into a rendering guarantee. Empirically, our method is strongest where deployment needs it most: aggressive compression with no or minimal recovery compute. In prune-only and very short finetuning regimes, it achieves state-of-the-art performance, showing that principled importance estimation can be both theoretically meaningful and practically useful. Open-source code is available at https://github.com/waseem-m/3dgs_provable_coresets.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first provable coreset construction for 3D Gaussian Splatting, showing that multiplicative approximation guarantees are resolution-dependent, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in aggressive compression regimes with minimal finetuning.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS compression methods are heuristic with no multiplicative approximation guarantees for the rendered objective, and rely heavily on costly post-pruning finetuning to recover quality. The authors ask whether a 3DGS scene can be provably replaced by a much smaller weighted subset (coreset) while preserving the objective.
AI.method: The authors first prove no non-trivial multiplicative 3DGS coreset exists in the unrestricted setting, then show resolution-dependent multiplicative guarantees are possible. They construct a weighted coreset by sampling Gaussians according to sensitivity scores—provable importance measures. Under log-transmittance stability and validity assumptions, they convert the objective guarantee into a rendering guarantee.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance in prune-only and very short finetuning regimes, demonstrating that principled importance estimation is both theoretically grounded and practically effective for aggressive compression with minimal recovery compute.
AI.conclusion: Theoretically principled importance-based coreset construction for 3DGS is feasible under resolution-dependent conditions, and offers practical advantages where deployment constraints require aggressive compression with little to no finetuning.

title: EEG-Based Imagined Speech Decoding Using a Hybrid CNN-SNN Architecture
summary: Imagined speech decoding using EEG signals has emerged as a promising frontier in brain-computer interface (BCI) research, particularly to restore communication for individuals with severe speech impairments. However, decoding imagined speech remains a complex task due to the non-stationary, low-amplitude, and highly variable nature of EEG signals. Existing methods often rely on classical machine learning or deep learning models that fail to exploit spike-based temporal dynamics or event-driven firing mechanisms of biological neurons, which are naturally modeled by spiking neural networks (SNNs). In this study, we propose a hybrid decoding pipeline that extracts temporal representations using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) followed by biologically inspired temporal classification via SNNs. To our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate SNNs into EEG-based imagined speech decoding. Experimental results show that the proposed CNN-SNN architecture achieves an accuracy of 80.13% on the 2020 BCI Competition III benchmark, surpassing existing methods reported in the literature (up to 70.19%) under comparable evaluation settings. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of spike-based temporal decoding for imagined speech, highlighting the promise of biologically grounded pipelines for next generation neuromorphic BCI applications.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN-SNN architecture is proposed for EEG-based imagined speech decoding, achieving 80.13% accuracy on the BCI Competition III benchmark, significantly outperforming existing methods (up to 70.19%). This is the first study integrating spiking neural networks for this task, demonstrating the potential of biologically inspired spike-based temporal decoding for neuromorphic BCI applications.
AI.motivation: Imagined speech decoding from EEG signals is crucial for restoring communication in individuals with severe speech impairments, but existing methods fail to exploit the spike-based temporal dynamics and event-driven firing mechanisms naturally modeled by spiking neural networks (SNNs).
AI.method: A hybrid CNN-SNN pipeline: CNNs extract temporal representations from EEG signals, followed by biologically inspired temporal classification via SNNs for spike-based temporal decoding.
AI.result: The CNN-SNN architecture achieves 80.13% accuracy on the 2020 BCI Competition III benchmark, surpassing existing methods (up to 70.19%) under comparable evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Spike-based temporal decoding via the hybrid CNN-SNN approach effectively improves imagined speech decoding performance, highlighting the promise of biologically grounded pipelines for next-generation neuromorphic BCI applications.

title: Attributing Structured-Output Gains in Function Calling: Interface Alignment versus Procedural Transfer
summary: Structured-output benchmarks reward both task decisions and interface compliance, so prompt-induced function-calling gains require attribution before they can be interpreted as transferable skill. We introduce a four-layer gain-attribution protocol for prompt-prepended skill injection, combining canonicalized rescoring, format-only controls, repaired/balanced induction, and portability checks. Applied to the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) and scoped with API-Bank, MATH-500, and MultiHop-RAG, the protocol shows that several apparent gains are better attributed to interface alignment than to procedural transfer: format-only prompts match or exceed full skills in key BFCL cells, repaired/balanced induction removes the largest sub-frontier gains, and API-Bank target-native gains are matched within 0.5 percentage points (pp) by length-matched generic procedural prompts. These findings treat format compliance as a useful engineering capability while clarifying what a structured-output score certifies. We release BFCL-CANONICAL and recommend canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines for function-calling skill-gain attribution. Code and data are available at https://github.com/couragec/skill-injection-attribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a four-layer attribution protocol to distinguish genuine skill transfer from format compliance gains in structured-output benchmarks, showing that many apparent function-calling improvements on BFCL and API-Bank are actually due to interface alignment rather than procedural skill transfer.
AI.motivation: Structured-output benchmarks conflate task decision quality with interface compliance, making it unclear whether prompt-induced gains reflect transferable skill or mere format alignment. The authors aim to disentangle these factors to clarify what structured-output scores actually certify.
AI.method: A four-layer gain-attribution protocol: (1) canonicalized rescoring, (2) format-only controls (prompts with structure but no skill content), (3) repaired/balanced induction, and (4) portability checks across benchmarks (BFCL, API-Bank, MATH-500, MultiHop-RAG).
AI.result: Format-only prompts match or exceed full skills in key BFCL cells; repaired/balanced induction removes the largest sub-frontier gains; API-Bank target-native gains are matched within 0.5 pp by length-matched generic procedural prompts.
AI.conclusion: Format compliance is a useful engineering capability but should not be conflated with transferable procedural skill. The authors recommend canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines for proper function-calling skill-gain attribution.

title: Post-Generation Curation of Synthetic Images via Homogeneous-Heterogeneous Splitting
summary: Recent generative models can produce high-quality synthetic images, offering scalable training training data for data-hungry models. Existing approaches to exploiting this potential typically involve 1) training or fine-tuning generators, or 2) using lightweight post-hoc adaptation like prompt engineering or inference-time guidance, making them generator-specific and expertise-intensive. We study a complementary question: given a fixed pool of generated images, can downstream utility be improved purely by selecting an informative subset? The answer is yes. We show that effective selection must counter a structural bias of modern generators: they tend to over-produce canonical modes of each class while underrepresenting intra-class variation. Building on this insight, we split each real class into a canonical Homogeneous (HO) subset and a non-redundant Heterogeneous (HE) subset, then score synthetic images by a fidelity-diversity criterion that rewards semantic alignment while penalizing canonical redundancy. The method is generator-agnostic and requires no retraining. Across multiple benchmarks, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines and matches the real-data performance with up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. The same criterion remains effective when applied on top of stronger task-tuned generators, with gains on both classification and segmentation tasks. Post-generation selection is therefore not a substitute for better generators, but a complementary mechanism for improving the utility of synthetic data.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that selecting an informative subset from a fixed pool of generated images, using a fidelity-diversity criterion that reduces canonical redundancy, can significantly improve downstream task performance without modifying the generator.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for leveraging synthetic images require training/fine-tuning generators or expertise-intensive post-hoc adaptation. The authors ask whether downstream utility can be improved purely by selecting an informative subset from a fixed pool of generated images, without generator modification.
AI.method: The method splits each real class into canonical Homogeneous (HO) and non-redundant Heterogeneous (HE) subsets, then scores synthetic images using a fidelity-diversity criterion that rewards semantic alignment while penalizing canonical redundancy. It is generator-agnostic and requires no retraining.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines and matches real-data performance with up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. Gains are shown on both classification and segmentation tasks, even when applied on top of stronger task-tuned generators.
AI.conclusion: Post-generation selection is not a substitute for better generators but a complementary mechanism for improving synthetic data utility by addressing the structural bias of generators toward over-producing canonical modes.

title: How many labels do you need? A decision framework for cross-habitat marine species recognition
comment: 29 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Includes supplementary appendix
summary:
Automated image recognition is increasingly used to scale ecological monitoring beyond manual annotation, yet ecologists lack evidence-based guidance on how much labelling effort reliable deployment at new sites requires. We present a decision framework quantifying the trade-off between labelling effort and recognition accuracy when transferring vision systems across marine habitats. The benchmark spans five datasets, three oceans, and three taxonomic groups (fish, corals, invertebrates), from tropical reefs in the Great Barrier Reef and French Polynesia to a temperate Danish fjord. We evaluated four recognition models (DINOv2, CLIP, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B4) under four adaptation strategies (linear probing, LoRA, Visual Prompt Tuning, full fine-tuning) across three protocols: within-habitat transfer across 20 reef sites (240 runs), cross-dataset geographic transfer along a difficulty gradient (40 runs), and few-shot adaptation curves with 0-100 labelled samples per class (648 runs). Frozen self-supervised foundation features (DINOv2 + linear classifier, 1,538 trainable parameters) generalised to unseen reef sites at least as well as fully fine-tuned convolutional baselines four orders of magnitude larger; they learned species-diagnostic, habitat-invariant representations, whereas baselines encoded habitat-specific shortcuts that fail at new sites. As few as 10-20 labelled images per species sufficed to deploy reliable recognition at a new site, cutting annotation effort by roughly an order of magnitude.
  Solution. Programmes expanding to new sites can deploy reliable recognition by pairing a frozen, open foundation model (DINOv2) with a simple linear classifier and annotating only 10-20 images per species - roughly 1-4 hours per site. The framework lets programmes budget labelling effort against expected accuracy across sites, ecosystems, and platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks vision models and adaptation strategies for transferring ecological image recognition across marine habitats, finding that frozen DINOv2 features with a linear classifier generalize well across sites and require only 10-20 labelled images per species for reliable deployment at new sites.
AI.motivation: Ecologists lack evidence-based guidance on how much labelling effort is needed to reliably deploy image recognition systems at new sites, creating a trade-off between annotation cost and recognition accuracy that needs quantification.
AI.method: The study spans five datasets across three oceans and three taxonomic groups (fish, corals, invertebrates), evaluating four recognition models (DINOv2, CLIP, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B4) under four adaptation strategies (linear probing, LoRA, Visual Prompt Tuning, full fine-tuning) across three transfer protocols: within-habitat transfer (20 reef sites, 240 runs), cross-dataset geographic transfer (40 runs), and few-shot adaptation curves (0-100 labelled samples per class, 648 runs).
AI.result: Frozen DINOv2 + linear classifier (1,538 parameters) matched fully fine-tuned convolutional baselines four orders of magnitude larger; it learned species-diagnostic, habitat-invariant representations while baselines encoded habitat-specific shortcuts. Only 10-20 labelled images per species sufficed for reliable recognition at new sites, reducing annotation effort by ~10x.
AI.conclusion: Programmes expanding to new sites can deploy reliable recognition by pairing frozen DINOv2 with a linear classifier and annotating only 10-20 images per species (~1-4 hours per site), enabling principled budgeting of labelling effort against expected accuracy.

title: Object-Centric Environment Modeling for Agentic Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve through accumulated experience, but free-form textual memories become difficult to maintain, validate, and reuse as interactions grow. Recent symbolic approaches learn executable skills or programmatic world models, yet often store local procedures or assume simplified dynamics. We propose Object-Centric Environment Modeling (OCM), which organizes experience into an executable object-centric environment model. OCM maintains two connected code bases: object knowledge, which defines environment entities and mechanisms as Python classes, and procedure knowledge, which records reusable interaction patterns that must import and use the object model. OCM works in an online setting: after each episode, OCM reflects on the trajectory, updates both knowledge bases, and verifies that all procedures execute against the updated object model. During future interaction, the agent uses progressive knowledge disclosure to inspect compact code signatures first and read source code only when needed. Experiments show that OCM achieves the best average rank across benchmarks and reduces invalid actions, demonstrating that agents can benefit from building object-centric environment models.

AI.tldr: OCM organizes LLM agent experience into an executable object-centric environment model with two connected code bases (object knowledge and procedure knowledge), achieving better performance and fewer invalid actions through online learning and code-based memory.
AI.motivation: Free-form textual memories for LLM agents are difficult to maintain, validate, and reuse as interactions grow; existing symbolic approaches store local procedures or assume simplified dynamics.
AI.method: OCM maintains object knowledge (Python classes for environment entities/mechanisms) and procedure knowledge (reusable interaction patterns). After each episode, it reflects on trajectories, updates both knowledge bases, and verifies procedure executability. During interaction, progressive knowledge disclosure inspects code signatures first, reading source code only when needed.
AI.result: OCM achieves the best average rank across benchmarks and reduces invalid actions.
AI.conclusion: Agents can benefit from building object-centric environment models for more structured, verifiable, and reusable memory.

title: Track the Noise, Move the World:3D-Grounded Motion-Consistent Noise for Controllable Video Generation
summary: Modern image-and-text-to-video diffusion models can synthesize highly realistic videos by iteratively denoising an initial Gaussian noise tensor conditioned on reference image and text inputs. However, existing approaches still lack precise and unified controllability over both object motion and camera motion within a single generation process. We present UniCaMo, a unified framework that enables simultaneous control of object trajectories and camera viewpoints by directly constructing the input noise of the diffusion model. Specifically, UniCaMo builds a shared 3D-grounded motion-consistent noise space across latent video frames. Sparse 3D point tracks are used to warp the Gaussian noise of the reference frame along desired object trajectories, while a virtual spherical noise representation provides globally consistent noise values for newly revealed scene regions under camera motion. By combining local track-guided noise warping with global sphere-based noise sampling, UniCaMo maintains geometric and temporal consistency under both object movement and viewpoint changes. Because UniCaMo modifies only the input noise, it requires no auxiliary adapters, control branches, or architectural changes to the underlying video diffusion model. With lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on large pretrained video diffusion models, including Wan 2.1 (14B), UniCaMo achieves state-of-the-art results in both video quality and motion controllability on standard controllable video generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: UniCaMo enables simultaneous control of object trajectories and camera viewpoints in video diffusion models by constructing a 3D-grounded motion-consistent noise space, using local track-guided noise warping and global sphere-based noise sampling, requiring no architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Existing image-and-text-to-video diffusion models lack precise and unified controllability over both object motion and camera motion within a single generation process.
AI.method: UniCaMo constructs a shared 3D-grounded motion-consistent noise space across latent video frames. It uses sparse 3D point tracks to warp Gaussian noise of the reference frame along desired object trajectories, and a virtual spherical noise representation for globally consistent noise values under camera motion. Only input noise is modified; no auxiliary adapters or architectural changes are needed, with lightweight LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results in both video quality and motion controllability on standard controllable video generation benchmarks, demonstrated on large pretrained models including Wan 2.1 (14B).
AI.conclusion: UniCaMo achieves unified simultaneous control of object and camera motion by manipulating only the input noise space, offering a simple yet effective approach without architectural modifications.

title: TokAN: Accent Normalization Using Self-Supervised Speech Tokens
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing (TASLP)
summary: Accent normalization (AN) seeks to convert non-native (L2) accented speech into standard (L1) speech while preserving speaker identity. The current techniques either require naturally recorded parallel L1-L2 speech for training, or suffer from quality degradation when supervised by synthesized targets. In this paper, we present TokAN, a token-based accent normalization framework that operates on self-supervised discrete speech tokens extracted from a L1-L2 jointly trained vector-quantization (VQ) tokenizer, without the need of synthetic supervisory speech. An autoregressive encoder-decoder model performs token-to-token conversion, translating L2-accented token sequences into the tokens of standard voice. We also introduce reinforcement learning (RL) post-training based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using word error rate and accent classifier confidence as complementary rewards. A non-autoregressive flow-matching synthesizer recovers the Mel-spectrogram from the converted tokens, conditioned on the source speaker embedding. We also develop a flow-matching duration predictor that supports total-duration-aware synthesis, making TokAN applicable to duration-critical tasks such as voice dubbing and live casting. Experiments on seven English accents demonstrate that TokAN reduced the word error rate from 12.40% to 9.89% after supervised fine-tuning, and further to 9.23% after RL post-training, consistently outperforming frame-to-frame, direct flow-matching, and prompt-based token-conversion baselines in terms of accent reduction and intelligibility.

AI.tldr: TokAN is a token-based accent normalization framework that converts non-native (L2) accented speech into standard (L1) speech using self-supervised discrete speech tokens, an autoregressive encoder-decoder for token-to-token conversion, RL post-training with GRPO, and a flow-matching synthesizer with duration control, achieving superior accent reduction and intelligibility across seven English accents.
AI.motivation: Existing accent normalization techniques either require naturally recorded parallel L1-L2 speech pairs for training, which are scarce and expensive, or suffer from quality degradation when relying on synthesized supervisory targets.
AI.method: 1) Uses a VQ tokenizer jointly trained on L1 and L2 speech to extract self-supervised discrete tokens. 2) An autoregressive encoder-decoder model performs token-to-token conversion from L2 to L1 tokens. 3) RL post-training via GRPO with word error rate and accent classifier confidence as rewards. 4) A non-autoregressive flow-matching synthesizer recovers Mel-spectrograms conditioned on source speaker embedding. 5) A flow-matching duration predictor enables total-duration-aware synthesis for duration-critical tasks.
AI.result: On seven English accents, TokAN reduced WER from 12.40% to 9.89% after supervised fine-tuning, and further to 9.23% after RL post-training, consistently outperforming frame-to-frame, direct flow-matching, and prompt-based token-conversion baselines.
AI.conclusion: TokAN provides an effective token-based framework for accent normalization without requiring natural parallel speech, and the RL post-training further improves performance, making it suitable for duration-critical applications like voice dubbing and live casting.

title: AgentLTL: A Trace-Verification Framework for Measuring, Enforcing, and Training Procedural Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents are usually evaluated by final-answer correctness or LLM judges. Neither captures how an answer was produced. In safety-critical settings, the procedure itself is part of correctness. In this paper, we introduce AgentLTL, a language derived from First-Order Linear Temporal Logic (FO-LTL) that expresses procedural rules over agent traces. It yields a deterministic, judge-free compliance score. In this framework, a single specification drives two usages. The first is harnessing: the constraints score completed traces, or gate tool calls by checking each prefix online, before execution. The second is finetuning: the score serves as a dense reward. On a benchmark spanning ordering, branching, iteration, and grounding, block-and-warn harnessing improves compliance on five of seven models. Finetuning with the same reward yields +38 and +17.5 percentage point gains in accuracy and compliance on held-out patterns, including unseen tool-name aliases. These findings are consistent with the model acquiring procedural structure rather than memorizing surface tool names and procedures.

AI.tldr: AgentLTL uses First-Order Linear Temporal Logic to define procedural rules over agent traces, yielding deterministic compliance scores for both harnessing (online gating) and finetuning (dense reward), improving compliance and accuracy across multiple models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluation methods (final-answer correctness, LLM judges) fail to capture procedural correctness of how answers are produced, which is crucial in safety-critical settings.
AI.method: AgentLTL is a language derived from FO-LTL that expresses procedural rules over agent traces. A single specification drives two usages: (1) harnessing—scoring completed traces or gating tool calls online before execution, and (2) finetuning—using the score as a dense reward signal.
AI.result: Block-and-warn harnessing improves compliance on 5/7 models. Finetuning yields +38 pp accuracy and +17.5 pp compliance gains on held-out patterns, including unseen tool-name aliases.
AI.conclusion: The model acquires procedural structure rather than memorizing surface tool names and procedures, demonstrating generalizable procedural learning.

title: A Granularity-Aware EEG Feature Framework for Psychopathology Dimension Prediction
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a noninvasive approach for examining neurophysiological correlates of dimensional psychopathology, yet systematic evidence across EEG paradigms and feature granularities remains limited. Here, we develop a granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline that organizes multi-scale descriptors into global, regional, and channel levels. Using the Healthy Brain Network (HBN) cohort, we evaluate the prediction of four psychopathology dimensions: p-factor, internalizing, externalizing, and attention problems, across four EEG paradigms. Given the heterogeneity of pediatric psychopathology and the moderate reliability of questionnaire-derived scores, this setting represents a challenging feasibility test rather than a clinical screening scenario. Tree-based models and granularity-balanced feature selection showed promising improvements over conventional approaches in selected conditions, although effect sizes remained modest. Visualization of selected markers revealed dimension-specific spatial and spectral patterns that were broadly aligned with existing neurophysiological knowledge. An exploratory cross-dataset sanity check on the independent PEARL cohort suggested that the proposed selection principle remains technically feasible under protocol shifts, without claiming cross-dataset generalizability. Overall, multi-scale EEG features contain weak but detectable signals related to dimensional psychopathology, and granularity-aware selection may serve as a useful feature-reduction strategy for future EEG-based phenotyping studies.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline (global, regional, channel levels) to predict dimensional psychopathology (p-factor, internalizing, externalizing, attention problems) across four EEG paradigms using the HBN cohort. Tree-based models with granularity-balanced feature selection show modest improvements; cross-dataset sanity check on PEARL cohort confirms technical feasibility. Multi-scale EEG features contain weak but detectable signals for dimensional psychopathology.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate whether multi-scale EEG features across different paradigms and granularities can capture neurophysiological correlates of dimensional psychopathology, addressing the gap in evidence across EEG paradigms and feature granularities.
AI.method: Granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline organizing multi-scale descriptors into global, regional, and channel levels; tree-based models with granularity-balanced feature selection; evaluated on HBN cohort (four psychopathology dimensions, four EEG paradigms) with an exploratory cross-dataset sanity check on PEARL cohort.
AI.result: Granularity-balanced feature selection showed promising but modest improvements over conventional approaches. Dimension-specific spatial and spectral patterns aligned with existing neurophysiological knowledge. Cross-dataset sanity check suggested technical feasibility under protocol shifts, but effect sizes remained modest throughout.
AI.conclusion: Multi-scale EEG features contain weak but detectable signals for dimensional psychopathology; granularity-aware selection serves as a useful feature-reduction strategy for EEG-based phenotyping, though the setting is better framed as a feasibility test than a clinical screening tool.

title: Inpainting U-Net for seamless pedestrian-level wind prediction across urban morphologies
summary: Pedestrian-level wind prediction is essential for urban design and wind-comfort assessment, but high-fidelity simulations such as LES remain computationally expensive for rapid evaluation. This study develops a two-stage U-Net framework for efficient prediction of time-averaged pedestrian-level wind speed over realistic urban morphologies. The model is trained and evaluated using the UrbanTALES dataset, which contains realistic city configurations under different approaching wind directions. In the first stage, a baseline U-Net model (M1) predicts wind fields patch-by-patch from normalised building height and fetch information. This formulation allows application to urban domains of arbitrary size, but independent patch inference can introduce discontinuities at patch boundaries. To address this, a second U-Net model (M2) is introduced as an inpainting-based refinement model. M2 uses a larger contextual window containing the initial M1 prediction and local morphology to reduce discontinuities using neighbouring flow information. During full-field inference, M2 is applied iteratively using a Gauss-Seidel scheme until convergence. Results show that M1 captures the main spatial distribution of pedestrian-level wind speed and performs well in low- and moderate-velocity regions, although high-velocity peaks are less accurate. M2 substantially reduces patch-boundary artefacts and improves spatial coherence. Across unseen urban cases, the framework reproduces mean velocity and spatial variability reasonably well, while maximum velocities remain underestimated. Overall, the proposed framework provides an efficient and flexible surrogate model for high-resolution pedestrian-level wind prediction across realistic urban morphologies.

AI.tldr: A two-stage U-Net framework (M1 + M2 with Gauss-Seidel inpainting) predicts pedestrian-level wind speeds over realistic urban morphologies using the UrbanTALES dataset, achieving efficient, spatially coherent predictions with reduced patch-boundary artefacts.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity simulations like LES are computationally expensive for rapid pedestrian-level wind prediction in urban design and wind-comfort assessment.
AI.method: Two-stage U-Net framework: Stage 1 (M1) predicts wind fields patch-by-patch from building height and fetch data; Stage 2 (M2) performs inpainting-based refinement with a larger contextual window, applied iteratively via a Gauss-Seidel scheme to reduce patch-boundary discontinuities.
AI.result: M1 captures main spatial distribution well in low/moderate-velocity regions but is less accurate for high-velocity peaks. M2 substantially reduces patch-boundary artefacts and improves spatial coherence. The framework reproduces mean velocity and spatial variability reasonably for unseen urban cases, though maximum velocities remain underestimated.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an efficient and flexible surrogate model for high-resolution pedestrian-level wind prediction across realistic urban morphologies.

title: MedCalc-Pro: Solving Complex Medical Calculations with LLM Agents
summary: Current benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in medical calculation are largely based on simplified settings, where each patient case corresponds to a single calculator and the required tool is explicitly specified in the query. However, real clinical scenarios often require multiple calculators for joint evaluation, nested-scale calculation, and fuzzy queries that do not directly specify the target calculator. To this end, we propose a new medical calculation benchmark, MedCalc-Pro, which covers three progressively challenging task settings: single-calculator, multi-calculator, and nested-calculator calculation settings. MedCalc-Pro contains 2,268 real-world clinical cases, covering 77 medical calculators across 14 clinical departments. Meanwhile, to address the limited performance of existing frameworks and methods in complex clinical scenarios, we further propose a more generalizable agent framework that supports multi-tool selection and nested-tool calling, while suppressing parameter error propagation through structured validation and evidence review. We conduct systematic comparisons across open-source, closed-source, and medical-specialized LLMs, and the results show that our framework achieves the best performance across all three task settings. This work provides a new benchmark and method for evaluating and applying LLMs in challenging medical calculation scenarios.

AI.tldr: MedCalc-Pro is a new medical calculation benchmark with 2,268 clinical cases across 77 calculators and 14 departments, covering single, multi, and nested-calculator settings. The authors also propose a generalizable agent framework supporting multi-tool selection and nested-tool calling with structured validation, achieving state-of-the-art performance across all task settings.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs on medical calculations in simplified settings (single calculator, explicit query), which fails to reflect real clinical complexity requiring multiple calculators, nested-scale calculations, and fuzzy queries.
AI.method: Proposed MedCalc-Pro benchmark with three task settings (single-calculator, multi-calculator, nested-calculator) containing 2,268 real clinical cases across 77 calculators and 14 departments. Also proposed a generalizable agent framework with multi-tool selection, nested-tool calling, structured validation, and evidence review to suppress parameter error propagation.
AI.result: The proposed agent framework achieved best performance across all three task settings (single, multi, nested) when compared systematically against open-source, closed-source, and medical-specialized LLMs.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a more realistic benchmark (MedCalc-Pro) for evaluating LLMs in complex medical calculation scenarios and demonstrates an effective agent framework that generalizes well across challenging settings.

title: Fast 3D Foundation Model Initialized Gaussian Splatting
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at ICECET 2026
summary: This paper introduces a fast method for high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction without traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM). The proposed approach leverages 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) for camera pose and point-cloud initialization, then jointly optimizes both camera poses and Gaussian primitives using a depth-guided loss function. This enables fast convergence even from rough initialization with as few as 50-60 input views. To further improve reconstruction quality in sparse-view scenarios, an MLP-based pose refinement module is introduced alongside depth-guided supervision from the foundation model. Extensive experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and RobustNeRF demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive reconstruction quality (23.61 dB PSNR, 0.19 LPIPS) while reducing training time to approximately three minutes per scene. The proposed method produces ready-to-use 3DGS models at a fraction of the time required by existing pipelines, making it suitable for near real-time applications in robotics, VR, and autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: A fast 3DGS reconstruction method that bypasses SfM by using 3D Foundation Models for initialization and joint optimization of poses and Gaussians with depth-guided loss, achieving high-quality results (~23.61 dB PSNR) in ~3 minutes per scene.
AI.motivation: Traditional 3DGS pipelines rely on time-consuming SfM (e.g., COLMAP) for initialization, which is a bottleneck for near real-time applications. This work aims to eliminate SfM while maintaining reconstruction quality and accelerating training.
AI.method: (1) Uses 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) for camera pose and point-cloud initialization; (2) Jointly optimizes camera poses and Gaussian primitives with a depth-guided loss function; (3) Introduces an MLP-based pose refinement module for sparse-view scenarios; (4) Leverages depth-guided supervision from the foundation model.
AI.result: Achieves 23.61 dB PSNR and 0.19 LPIPS on benchmark datasets (Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, RobustNeRF), with training time reduced to ~3 minutes per scene using as few as 50-60 input views.
AI.conclusion: The method produces ready-to-use 3DGS models at a fraction of the time of existing pipelines, demonstrating suitability for near real-time applications in robotics, VR, and autonomous navigation.

title: Information-Geometric Superposed Vowel Evaluation: Part 1. Moraic Syllabary (Japanese)
summary: This paper explains the principles and provides examples of a new method for distinguishing between FAKE human speech synthesized by generative AI and natural speech. Since synthetic speech is generated based on information from a limited set of training spectra, the variety of vowels - which are key to identifying individuals - is limited. In contrast, natural speech exhibits a more diverse distribution of vowel spectra due to the flexibility of the human articulatory organ. In this paper, using Japanese - a Syllabary limited to five vowel phonemes, each of which corresponds one-to-one with a specific sound - as an example, we outline a method for distinguishing between synthetic and natural speech reading the same text by analyzing the spectral distributions. If we normalize the spectra of speech sounds and regard them as probability density functions for the frequency bands received by the hair cells of the human cochlea, and evaluate the distance between spectra using the Wasserstein metric, the Wasserstein distances between the vowels of synthetic speech are short. By preserving this distance and performing a topological mapping using persistent homology, the spectral probability density functions of synthetic and natural speech can be decomposed into clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a method to distinguish AI-generated synthetic speech from natural human speech by analyzing vowel spectral distributions using Wasserstein distance and persistent homology, demonstrating with Japanese speech samples.
AI.motivation: With the rise of generative AI capable of synthesizing highly realistic human speech, there is a growing need for reliable methods to detect fake or synthetic speech. The paper aims to address this problem by leveraging the inherent limitations in vowel diversity found in synthetic speech compared to natural speech.
AI.method: The method involves normalizing speech spectra as probability density functions (representing frequency bands received by cochlear hair cells), computing Wasserstein distances between vowel spectra, and applying persistent homology for topological clustering to separate synthetic and natural speech clusters.
AI.result: The Wasserstein distances between vowels in synthetic speech are shorter than those in natural speech, and persistent homology-based topological mapping successfully decomposes spectral probability density functions into distinct clusters corresponding to synthetic versus natural speech.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Wasserstein distance and persistent homology-based approach can effectively distinguish between synthetic and natural speech by capturing differences in vowel spectral diversity, demonstrated using Japanese as a test case.

title: A Survey of LLM-Driven Penetration Testing: Taxonomy, Co-Evolution, and Open Challenges
summary: Agents4Pentest, an emerging class of LLM-based autonomous penetration testing systems, has become a rapidly growing area in security research. Despite this growth, the field still lacks a unified taxonomy, a systematic understanding of how agent architectures and evaluation benchmarks have co-evolved, and a clear characterization of remaining capability and reliability gaps. This survey addresses these gaps through a systematic analysis of 81 papers between 2023 and 2026. We organize the literature into six categories: evaluation benchmarks, general-purpose systems, domain-specific frameworks, CTF-based systems, defense-oriented research, and surveys. We further trace a four-phase architectural evolution from text-only reasoning agents to agents trained with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), showing that each transition is driven by a distinct capability bottleneck. Our analysis yields several key findings. First, RLVR marks a shift in capability acquisition from imitation of expert demonstrations to reward-driven self-improvement, enabling agents to discover previously undocumented attack strategies. Second, CTF platforms have evolved from evaluation testbeds into dual-purpose infrastructure for both agent evaluation and RL training. Third, domain-specific frameworks improve efficiency through recurring specialization mechanisms, but their gains remain largely confined to narrow task classes and are difficult to compare across domains because existing evaluations rely on different benchmarks. Fourth, the field is expanding beyond offensive automation toward adversarial defense and security compliance. Across these categories, we identify three structurally linked open challenges: evaluation reliability, limited performance on multi-stage attack scenarios, and scarcity of high-quality training data.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically analyzes 81 papers (2023-2026) on LLM-based autonomous penetration testing, organizing them into six categories and tracing a four-phase architectural evolution toward RLVR.
