AI.motivation: Standard conformal prediction for vision tasks uses flat coordinate charts (e.g., yaw-pitch, Euler angles) to define residuals/scores, but many outputs naturally lie on curved manifolds (sphere, SO(3)). The authors hypothesize that this mismatch introduces systematic geometric distortion near singularities, silently breaking coverage guarantees.
AI.method: The authors analyze conformal scoring on curved output spaces theoretically and empirically. They compute slice-conditional coverage on four datasets (ETH-XGaze, Gaze360, BIWI, AFLW2000-3D) near singularities (pitch >70° for gaze, pitch >60° for head pose near gimbal lock). They prove scalar thresholding cannot fix the distortion because it rescales set size but not axis ratios, and propose using coordinate-free geodesic scoring instead.
AI.result: Slice-conditional coverage at 90% nominal drops by 30-50 percentage points in singular regions: to 38.9% (ETH-XGaze), 42.0% (Gaze360) for gaze pitch >70°; to 57.5% (BIWI), 55.2% (AFLW2000-3D) for head pose pitch >60° near gimbal lock, while marginal coverage stays near 90%. Riemannian volume density strongly correlates with coverage collapse. Geodesic scoring eliminates the distortion with no retraining and negligible cost.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction on curved spaces requires geometrically aware scoring to maintain coverage guarantees uniformly. Coordinate-free geodesic scoring is a simple, effective fix.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Seeking Diagnostic Reasoning with Large Language Models
summary: Recent reasoning-centric Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant strides, yet they predominantly operate on a passive-inference pattern that assumes complete information. In contrast, real-world clinical intelligence is inherently an iterative investigative process requiring strategic evidence acquisition. To bridge this gap, we formalize medical diagnosis as an Iterative Evidence-Seeking Task. We leverage Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to elicit intrinsic reasoning within a closed-loop environment, guided by a novel suite of rewards that enforce diagnostic precision and examination consistency. To facilitate this, we introduce the Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based Examination Simulator (RAGES), a high-fidelity clinical oracle that provides realistic, knowledge-grounded follow-up evidence. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate that our framework enables LLMs to transition from passive responders to autonomous assistants. Notably, our model demonstrates comparable performance to larger and reasoning-enhanced baselines, while RAGES proves superior to vanilla LLMs in generating biologically plausible clinical feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework that transforms LLMs from passive responders into autonomous clinical assistants by formalizing medical diagnosis as iterative evidence-seeking, using Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based Examination Simulator (RAGES) for realistic evidence acquisition.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning-centric LLMs operate on a passive-inference pattern assuming complete information, whereas real-world clinical diagnosis requires iterative, strategic evidence acquisition. The paper aims to bridge this gap by formalizing medical diagnosis as an iterative evidence-seeking task.
AI.method: The authors formalize medical diagnosis as an Iterative Evidence-Seeking Task, leverage Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to elicit intrinsic reasoning in a closed-loop environment, introduce a suite of rewards enforcing diagnostic precision and examination consistency, and develop RAGES (Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based Examination Simulator) as a high-fidelity clinical oracle for realistic follow-up evidence.
AI.result: The framework enables LLMs to transition from passive responders to autonomous assistants, achieving comparable performance to larger and reasoning-enhanced baselines. RAGES demonstrates superiority over vanilla LLMs in generating biologically plausible clinical feedback.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully bridges the gap between passive LLM inference and active clinical reasoning, enabling autonomous diagnostic capabilities through iterative evidence-seeking with reinforcement learning and realistic simulation.

title: CARD: Cross-component Audio Representation Distillation for Encoder-Free Audio Captioning
summary: Modern automated audio captioning systems pair a frozen audio encoder with a large language model (LLM) via a trainable projector, incurring the encoder's inference cost and bottlenecking the model through its fixed acoustic features. We present CARD, an encoder-free audio captioning model that removes the encoder at inference: a 13.2M projector feeds a frozen LLM with merged LoRA adapters, while the teacher used to train it is discarded. CARD distills a pretrained audio teacher (CLAP-HTSAT) into the model, but rather than injecting it into the LLM alone, it routes the teacher's representations across components: perceptual stages to the projector and semantic stages to the LLM. This placement improves CIDEr-D by +12.18 over an LLM-only distilled model on AudioCaps and by +5.21 on Clotho, reaching 55.4 against a 66.4 encoder-kept upper bound with no encoder at inference, showing that where a teacher's knowledge is placed matters as much as its presence.

AI.tldr: CARD is an encoder-free audio captioning model that distills knowledge from a pretrained audio teacher into a frozen LLM via a lightweight projector, routing different teacher representations (perceptual → projector, semantic → LLM) to improve performance, achieving strong results without the inference cost of a separate audio encoder.
AI.motivation: Existing automated audio captioning systems rely on a frozen audio encoder paired with an LLM via a trainable projector, which incurs the encoder's inference cost and limits the model through fixed acoustic features. The goal is to remove the encoder at inference time while maintaining high captioning quality.
AI.method: CARD removes the audio encoder at inference by using a 13.2M parameter projector to feed a frozen LLM with merged LoRA adapters. It distills knowledge from a pretrained CLAP-HTSAT teacher, but instead of injecting teacher features only into the LLM, it routes perceptual-stage representations to the projector and semantic-stage representations to the LLM.
AI.result: CARD achieves CIDEr-D improvements of +12.18 over an LLM-only distilled model on AudioCaps and +5.21 on Clotho, reaching 55.4 against a 66.4 encoder-kept upper bound with no encoder at inference.
AI.conclusion: Where a teacher's knowledge is placed within the model architecture matters as much as its presence; routing different representational stages to different components (projector vs. LLM) significantly improves performance in encoder-free audio captioning.

title: A large-scale dataset of Android applications and their SDK dependencies
summary: Mobile applications (apps) increasingly rely on third-party Software Development Kits (SDKs) to provide services such as advertising, analytics, authentication, crash reporting, and location services. These components form an important, but often hidden, layer of the mobile ecosystem. Here, we present a large-scale dataset linking Android apps to the third-party SDKs they integrate. The dataset was constructed by combining app package files (APKs) and metadata from AndroZoo with SDK detection rules provided by Exodus Privacy. We implemented a reproducible, static-analysis pipeline that downloads APKs, inspects their compiled code, and detects SDKs through code-level signature matching: the released dataset contains 334,719 unique app-version observations (associated with 99,722 Android apps) and 246 third-party SDKs - including app-level metadata such as categories, comments, file size, download counts, ratings and SDK-level metadata such as categories, code roots, code versions, names. The dataset supports the construction of a large-scale app-SDK dependency network and its projection onto both layers; in addition, SDKs are mapped to their corresponding operating companies, enabling provider-level analysis of technological concentration and upstream control in the mobile ecosystem. To support reproducible research, the pipeline and dataset are publicly released on GitHub and Zenodo; more broadly, the project provides a reusable research infrastructure for studying third-party technological dependencies, data-collection capabilities, and privacy infrastructures across Android apps.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale dataset linking 99,722 Android apps to 246 third-party SDKs, constructed using static analysis of APKs from AndroZoo and SDK detection rules from Exodus Privacy. The dataset includes app and SDK metadata, supports dependency network analysis, and enables provider-level study of technological concentration in the mobile ecosystem. The reproducible pipeline and dataset are publicly released.
AI.motivation: Third-party SDKs form a critical but often hidden layer in the mobile ecosystem, yet large-scale, reproducible datasets linking apps to their integrated SDKs have been lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap to enable systematic study of technological dependencies, data collection practices, and privacy implications.
AI.method: The authors combined APK files and metadata from AndroZoo with SDK detection rules from Exodus Privacy, implemented a reproducible static-analysis pipeline that downloads APKs, inspects compiled code, and detects SDKs via code-level signature matching.
AI.result: The released dataset contains 334,719 unique app-version observations (99,722 Android apps) and 246 third-party SDKs, along with app-level metadata (categories, comments, file size, download counts, ratings) and SDK-level metadata (categories, code roots, code versions, names). SDKs are mapped to their operating companies.
AI.conclusion: The dataset supports construction of large-scale app-SDK dependency networks and provider-level analysis of technological concentration. The project provides a reusable research infrastructure for studying third-party dependencies, data-collection capabilities, and privacy infrastructures across Android apps.

title: Training Hybrid Block Diffusion Language Models with Partial Bidirectionality
summary: High-throughput long-context generation is one of the central challenges for large language models. Generation is typically memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound: each decoding step must stream the accumulated key/value (KV) cache from memory, so bandwidth demand grows with context length while only one token is emitted. Two parallel approaches have therefore emerged: reducing memory access with efficient attention variants and linear-time mixers such as Mamba, or increasing parallel computation by generating blocks of tokens at once. However, technical challenges arise when combining these two ideas. Earlier hybrid diffusion models such as DiffuMamba use bidirectional Mamba mixing, including a reverse-direction scan relative to causal generation. This reverse scan needs to scan the entire sequence, so its states are not prefix-only and cannot be precisely reused as a cache even when diffusion is performed block by block. We propose a BDLM Mamba--attention hybrid that addresses this challenge by restricting the reverse Mamba scan to the active denoising block, which enables exact caching across blocks. In an 87M-parameter DCLM sweep, BDLM Mamba-H achieves the best C4-en validation perplexity compared to BDLM attention and full-sequence baselines. At 350M parameters, it remains competitive with BDLM attention. For long-context inference, BDLM Mamba-H reaches 19.7x the throughput of full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens and 3.7x the throughput of BDLM attention at 262K, showing that Mamba hybrids are a potential long-context diffusion architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BDLM Mamba-H, a hybrid Mamba-attention diffusion model that restricts reverse Mamba scans to the active denoising block, enabling exact KV cache reuse. This achieves 19.7x throughput over full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens and 3.7x over BDLM attention at 262K tokens, while maintaining competitive perplexity.
AI.motivation: High-throughput long-context generation is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound due to KV cache streaming costs. Two parallel solutions (efficient attention/linear mixers and block-wise generation) face technical challenges when combined, particularly the reverse-direction scan in hybrid diffusion models like DiffuMamba cannot be precisely cached, limiting throughput.
AI.method: BDLM Mamba-H restricts the reverse Mamba scan to only the active denoising block (instead of the full sequence), enabling exact cache reuse across denoising blocks. This is a hybrid architecture combining Mamba and attention, designed for block-wise diffusion-based long-context generation.
AI.result: At 87M parameters, BDLM Mamba-H achieves best C4-en validation perplexity among baselines. At 350M, competitive with BDLM attention. For long-context inference: 19.7x throughput vs full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens; 3.7x throughput vs BDLM attention at 262K tokens.
AI.conclusion: Mamba hybrids are a potential long-context diffusion architecture, offering significant throughput gains while maintaining competitive quality.

title: MAGE: View-guided Point Cloud Completion with Efficient Modality Alignment and Adaptive Geometry Enhancement
summary: View-based point cloud completion aims to recover a complete 3D shape from a partial point cloud, guided by a single-view image. However, existing approaches often suffer from limited performance due to weak modality alignment and limited self-geometry enhancement. To overcome these challenges, we propose a unified geometry-aware framework that integrates efficient modality alignment and adaptive geometry enhancement, mainly to address cross-modal geometric inconsistency of view-guided point cloud completion. Specifically, we propose a geometry-aware modality alignment by integrating a shared self-attention Transformer and cross-modality reconstruction supervision, which aims to bring features of the image and point cloud close to each other in a shared latent space describing the 3D object. To enhance the perception of global shape and local geometric details, we propose an adaptive geometry-aware self-attention module, which simultaneously considers local geometry-aware attention computation and the spatially-variant feature fusion. In addition, we apply a geometry-perceptive anchor refinement module to reorganize the anchor points (representing a local region of the shape) under appropriate supervision, further boosting the completion performance of our method. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance over existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/weizequan/MAGE.

AI.tldr: Proposes MAGE, a unified geometry-aware framework for view-based point cloud completion that integrates modality alignment, adaptive geometry enhancement, and anchor refinement, achieving superior performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing view-based point cloud completion methods suffer from weak cross-modal alignment (image vs. point cloud) and limited self-geometry enhancement, leading to geometric inconsistencies and suboptimal completion quality.
AI.method: (1) Geometry-aware modality alignment via shared self-attention Transformer and cross-modality reconstruction supervision to align image and point cloud features in a shared latent space. (2) Adaptive geometry-aware self-attention module with local geometry-aware attention and spatially-variant feature fusion for global shape and local detail perception. (3) Geometry-perceptive anchor refinement module to reorganize anchor points under appropriate supervision.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate superior performance over existing approaches. Code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified geometry-aware framework effectively addresses cross-modal geometric inconsistency in view-guided point cloud completion through better modality alignment and adaptive geometry enhancement, outperforming existing methods.

title: Beyond Forecasting: The Belief-to-Trade Layer in Prediction-Market Agents
summary: Forecasting future events has attracted growing attention as a testbed for general-purpose AI. A natural way to ground this evaluation is let the models trade in the prediction markets. Trading, however, requires more than forecasting. Moreover, recent benchmarks report a substantial gap between calibrated probability scores and the trading results. We propose Raven-Agent, to the best of our knowledge, the first autonomous trading agent for prediction markets. On a controlled replay over an archived decision set, our architecture achieves the only positive return and the only positive risk-adjusted return among all tested policies. We have released our code in https://github.com/Alchemist-X/predict-raven .

AI.tldr: Raven-Agent is the first autonomous trading agent for prediction markets, achieving the only positive returns (both raw and risk-adjusted) among all tested policies in controlled replay experiments.
AI.motivation: Forecasting future events is a testbed for general-purpose AI, and prediction markets offer a natural evaluation environment. However, trading requires more than just forecasting, and existing benchmarks show a gap between calibrated probability scores and actual trading results, motivating the need for a dedicated autonomous trading agent.
AI.method: The authors propose Raven-Agent, an autonomous trading agent for prediction markets. They evaluate it via controlled replay over an archived decision set, comparing it against multiple baseline policies.
AI.result: Raven-Agent achieves the only positive return and the only positive risk-adjusted return among all tested policies on the controlled replay benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Raven-Agent demonstrates that autonomous trading in prediction markets is feasible and outperforms existing policies, highlighting the importance of designing agents specifically for trading rather than relying solely on forecasting capabilities.

title: SynSFX: Multi-Model Sound Effects Synthesis Dataset for Deepfake Detection and Evaluation
summary: While audio deepfake detection has advanced significantly, representative detectors show limited generalization to synthetic sound effects. Existing environmental audio datasets such as EnvSDD provide important initial resources, but remain limited in scale and generation provenance for studying isolated sound-effect deepfakes. To support this direction, we present SynSFX, a large-scale corpus of 43374 clips (26452 synthetic, 16922 real) spanning 7 popular text-to-audio models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SynSFX, a large-scale dataset of 43,374 audio clips (26,452 synthetic, 16,922 real) from 7 text-to-audio models, aimed at addressing the limited generalization of audio deepfake detectors to synthetic sound effects.
AI.motivation: Existing audio deepfake detectors show limited generalization to synthetic sound effects, and current environmental audio datasets like EnvSDD are insufficient in scale and generation provenance for studying isolated sound-effect deepfakes.
AI.method: The authors construct SynSFX, a large-scale corpus comprising 43,374 clips (26,452 synthetic and 16,922 real) sourced from 7 popular text-to-audio models.
AI.result: SynSFX provides a significantly larger and more diverse dataset for sound-effect deepfake research, spanning multiple generation sources.
AI.conclusion: SynSFX addresses the gap in scalable, provenance-diverse resources for studying and improving deepfake detection on synthetic sound effects.

title: Can Coding Agents Implement Missed Compiler Optimizations? Evaluating LLM Agents on LLVM Peephole Optimizations
summary:
Coding agents built on large language models are now capable of patching sizable real-world codebases, yet whether they can develop compiler optimizations remains an open question. To study this question, we introduce PeepholeBench, an evaluation framework whose tasks are constructed from real-world missed peephole optimizations reported against LLVM's InstCombine pass. Since missed peephole optimizations are typically fixed with small, localized patches, they offer a well-scoped but demanding testbed for coding agents: a correct fix demands rigorous reasoning about program semantics along with familiarity with optimizer-specific conventions. PeepholeBench derives its tasks from 21 resolved LLVM issues and 19 merged pull requests (PRs), supplies agents with only the issue context that existed before each fix, and assesses the resulting patches for both correctness and profitability.
  With PeepholeBench, we benchmark state-of-the-art coding agents on fixing missed peephole optimizations in LLVM's InstCombine pass, measuring their patches against the corresponding human-written fixes. We observe a tension between correctness and profitability, and no agent matches human developers on both dimensions at once. The dominant failure modes are overly narrow transformations and misuse of LLVM-specific mechanisms, errors that existing test suites rarely expose. Together, these results establish PeepholeBench as a realistic and challenging benchmark for coding agents, and suggest future directions for building agents that can more dependably assist compiler optimization development.

AI.tldr: PeepholeBench evaluates coding agents' ability to fix missed peephole optimizations in LLVM's InstCombine pass, showing no agent matches human performance on both correctness and profitability, with failures from overly narrow transformations and misuse of LLVM-specific mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLM-based coding agents can develop compiler optimizations, particularly fixing missed peephole optimizations in real-world codebases like LLVM.
AI.method: Constructed PeepholeBench from 21 resolved LLVM issues and 19 merged PRs, providing agents with pre-fix issue context and evaluating patches for correctness and profitability against human-written fixes.
AI.result: No agent matches human developers on both correctness and profitability simultaneously; dominant failures are overly narrow transformations and misuse of LLVM-specific mechanisms not caught by existing test suites.
AI.conclusion: PeepholeBench is a realistic, challenging benchmark for coding agents in compiler optimization, highlighting a correctness-profitability tradeoff and pointing to directions for more dependable agent-based compiler development.

title: Less Tokens, Better Forecasts: Sparse Residual Routing for Efficient Weather Prediction
summary: Existing ViT-based weather forecasting models apply uniform computation across all spatial tokens, even though nearby atmospheric grid points often contain similar values and large regions evolve smoothly over time. This makes much of the intermediate per-token computation redundant. Standard token-efficiency methods, such as pruning or merging, reduce cost by removing or fusing tokens. However, weather forecasting is a spatiotemporal dense prediction problem in which a history of atmospheric states must be mapped to future values on the original latitude-longitude grid. Thus, every grid cell must retain a physically meaningful representation, especially under autoregressive rollout. We introduce Sparse-Reslim, a parameter-free plug-in routing module that makes sparse token processing compatible with this fixed-grid requirement. Sparse-Reslim routes only 25% of spatial tokens through the expensive middle transformer blocks and treats those blocks as residual updates: it computes the change produced for the routed tokens and scatters only this delta back to the full sequence. Unselected tokens keep their pre-routing representations exactly, so no grid cell is dropped or replaced by a mask token, and no fusion layer or additional parameters are introduced. Across ERA5 resolutions up to the operational 0.25\textdegree{} standard and two model families, a deterministic Transformer and a diffusion model, Sparse-Reslim improves forecast accuracy on every evaluated variable while substantially reducing cost: training is about 2.5x faster in the main settings and reaches 3.18x speedup at 0.25\textdegree{}, with over 2.2x lower peak memory. A controlled decomposition shows that the accuracy gain comes primarily from sparse routing itself, while random token selection provides an additional regularization benefit without selector overhead.

AI.tldr: Sparse-Reslim is a parameter-free routing module that processes only 25% of spatial tokens through expensive transformer blocks in weather forecasting models, treating them as residual updates. It improves forecast accuracy while achieving ~2.5x training speedup (up to 3.18x at 0.25° resolution) and >2.2x lower peak memory across deterministic and diffusion model families on ERA5 data.
AI.motivation: Existing ViT-based weather forecasting models apply uniform computation across all spatial tokens, but nearby atmospheric grid points contain similar values and evolve smoothly, making intermediate per-token computation redundant. Standard token-efficiency methods (pruning/merging) are incompatible with spatiotemporal dense prediction where every grid cell must retain a physically meaningful representation on the original grid.
AI.method: Sparse-Resmit is a parameter-free plug-in routing module that routes only 25% of spatial tokens through expensive middle transformer blocks. It treats these blocks as residual updates: computes the change for routed tokens and scatters only this delta back to the full sequence. Unselected tokens keep their pre-routing representations exactly, ensuring no grid cell is dropped or replaced.
AI.result: Improves forecast accuracy on every evaluated variable on ERA5 data (up to 0.25° resolution). Training is ~2.5x faster in main settings, reaches 3.18x speedup at 0.25°, with over 2.2x lower peak memory. Works across deterministic Transformer and diffusion model families. Accuracy gain comes primarily from sparse routing itself; random token selection provides additional regularization benefit.
AI.conclusion: Sparse token processing via residual updates is compatible with fixed-grid dense prediction requirements in weather forecasting, achieving both higher accuracy and significantly reduced computational cost without adding parameters or requiring token fusion layers.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Last-Layer Adaptation of RETFound for Referable Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Under Dataset Shift
comment: 12 pages, 8 tables, 6 figures. Code available at https://github.com/kmardhani/uncertainty-aware-retfound
summary: This paper presents a safety-centered empirical evaluation of uncertainty-aware last-layer adaptation for referable diabetic retinopathy screening using RETFound, a self-supervised vision-transformer retinal foundation model used here as a frozen feature encoder, and the public APTOS 2019 and DDR diabetic retinopathy fundus image datasets. We compare a cached-feature softmax head, post-hoc temperature scaling, variational Bayesian last-layer heads, a diagonal Laplace last-layer approximation, and an SNGP-style cached-feature head. On APTOS, uncertainty-aware operating points improved sensitivity and selective-referral behavior. The strongest APTOS selective-referral result deferred approximately 20 percent of cases and reduced accepted-case false negatives to zero while preserving high accepted-case specificity. However, threshold tuning also reduced false negatives at high false-positive cost, so false-negative reduction alone was not unique to Bayesian modeling. On DDR, native Bayesian heads qualitatively reproduced the APTOS direction but with weaker tradeoffs, while the APTOS-trained SNGP checkpoint transferred poorly and failed to provide useful external selective-referral behavior. These results highlight the value of safety-centered evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy: uncertainty-aware last-layer heads can improve internal safety-oriented operating points, but trustworthy retinal screening claims require explicit safety-coverage evaluation and second-dataset validation under shift.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates uncertainty-aware last-layer adaptation methods for diabetic retinopathy screening using RETFound, finding that these methods can improve safety-oriented operating points on APTOS (deferring ~20% of cases to reduce false negatives to zero) but show weaker results on DDR and poor transferability, emphasizing the need for safety-coverage evaluation and second-dataset validation.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether uncertainty-aware last-layer adaptation methods improve safety outcomes (sensitivity, selective-referral behavior) in diabetic retinopathy screening beyond aggregate accuracy metrics, and to assess their reliability under distribution shift.
AI.method: Compared six approaches: cached-feature softmax head, post-hoc temperature scaling, variational Bayesian last-layer heads, diagonal Laplace last-layer approximation, and SNGP-style cached-feature head, using RETFound as a frozen feature encoder on APTOS 2019 and DDR datasets.
AI.result: On APTOS, uncertainty-aware methods deferred ~20% of cases and reduced accepted-case false negatives to zero with high specificity. However, threshold tuning alone also reduced false negatives at high false-positive cost. On DDR, Bayesian heads showed weaker tradeoffs; SNGP transferred poorly.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware last-layer heads can improve internal safety-oriented operating points, but trustworthy screening claims require explicit safety-coverage evaluation and second-dataset validation under shift.

title: Human-Centric Reflective Architecture for Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making
summary: The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) across diverse areas of human activity-ranging from everyday tasks to safety-critical applications-aims to enhance decision-making effectiveness with minimal human feedback. Concurrently, it seeks to align decisions with human expectations, preferences, and needs while mitigating risks associated with AI non-determinism. However, humans frequently over- or under-rely on AI recommendations, and current AI systems remain poorly calibrated to human expectations. To address these challenges, we introduce a human-AI collaborative decision-making framework designed to augment human capabilities and align AI agents with human preferences and expectations. Specifically, this paper (a) formulates the collaborative decision-making task as a stochastic game between an AI agent and a human player, and (b) proposes the Human-Centric Reflective Architecture (HCRA), which integrates human-calibrated models with reinforcement learning agents that leverage linguistic feedback in an iterative, reflective process. Evaluation results demonstrate that HCRA enhances decision-making effectiveness and delivers high-quality recommendations.

AI.tldr: HCRA is a human-AI collaborative decision-making framework that formulates collaboration as a stochastic game between an AI agent and a human player. It integrates human-calibrated models with reinforcement learning agents using linguistic feedback in an iterative reflective process to reduce over-/under-reliance and improve alignment between AI recommendations and human expectations.
AI.motivation: Humans frequently over- or under-rely on AI recommendations, and current AI systems are poorly calibrated to human expectations, creating risks in both everyday and safety-critical applications.
AI.method: The paper (a) formulates collaborative decision-making as a stochastic game between an AI agent and a human player, and (b) proposes HCRA, which integrates human-calibrated models with reinforcement learning agents that leverage linguistic feedback in an iterative, reflective process.
AI.result: HCRA enhances decision-making effectiveness and delivers high-quality recommendations.
AI.conclusion: HCRA addresses misalignment and calibration issues in human-AI collaboration by combining game-theoretic formulation with reflective reinforcement learning from linguistic feedback, improving decision quality and alignment with human expectations.

title: Adaptive Diversity-Uncertainty Active Learning with Redundancy Control for Bioacoustic Event Classification
comment: BioDCASE 2026 Challenge, Task 4: Active Learning for Bioacoustics, 1st Place (1/14)
summary: Active learning is a promising framework for reducing annotation costs in large-scale bioacoustic monitoring, where expert labeling is expensive and data distributions are highly heterogeneous across environments. However, existing sample selection strategies often rely on static criteria that do not adapt to the evolving reliability of model predictions during training. This limitation can lead to suboptimal exploration-exploitation trade-offs and redundant sample selection. We propose an active learning strategy for multilabel bioacoustic event classification that jointly models predictive uncertainty, embedding-space diversity, and intra-batch redundancy. The method introduces an adaptive weighting scheme that progressively shifts from diversity-driven exploration in high-uncertainty regimes toward uncertainty-driven exploitation as the model becomes more confident, reflecting the increasing reliability of the classifier. To further improve annotation efficiency, a greedy Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) procedure is used to enforce diversity among selected samples within each acquisition batch. We evaluate the proposed approach within the BioDCASE 2026 Task 4 active learning framework on terrestrial (BirdSet) and marine (ATBFL) benchmarks using pretrained audio embeddings and a fixed annotation budget. Experimental results show consistent improvements in learning efficiency and competitive in terms of macro mean Average Precision (mAP) and Area Under the Learning Curve (AULC) across heterogeneous acoustic domains. The gains are particularly pronounced on structured terrestrial soundscapes, while performance remains competitive under noisier marine conditions. These findings demonstrate that adaptive acquisition strategies combining uncertainty estimation, embedding-space diversity, and redundancy-aware batch construction provide an effective and robust solution for [...].

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an active learning strategy for multilabel bioacoustic classification that adaptively balances diversity-driven exploration and uncertainty-driven exploitation using an adaptive weighting scheme and Maximum Marginal Relevance for batch selection, showing consistent improvements on BirdSet and ATBFL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing active learning strategies for bioacoustic monitoring rely on static selection criteria that do not adapt to the evolving reliability of model predictions, leading to suboptimal exploration-exploitation trade-offs and redundant sample selection.
AI.method: The method jointly models predictive uncertainty, embedding-space diversity, and intra-batch redundancy. It uses an adaptive weighting scheme that shifts from diversity-driven exploration in high-uncertainty regimes to uncertainty-driven exploitation as model confidence grows, plus a greedy Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) procedure to enforce diversity within each acquisition batch.
AI.result: Evaluated on BioDCASE 2026 Task 4 framework using BirdSet (terrestrial) and ATBFL (marine) benchmarks, the method shows consistent improvements in learning efficiency, competitive mAP and AULC, with pronounced gains on structured terrestrial soundscapes and competitive performance under noisier marine conditions.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive acquisition strategies combining uncertainty estimation, embedding-space diversity, and redundancy-aware batch construction provide an effective and robust solution for reducing annotation costs in heterogeneous bioacoustic monitoring.

title: LLMoxie: Exploring Agentic AI for Scientific Software Development
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to ACM SIGKDD 2026 Workshop: Agentic AI for Scientific and Societal Advances (SciSoc Agents and LLMs). Describes an agentic AI platform for scientific software engineering with governed multi-cloud inference, structured multiagent workflows, and domain-aware coding support (cs.SE, cs.MA, cs.AI)
summary: In this paper, we describe LLMoxie, an institutional AI platform whose three-tiered architecture supports multi-cloud and on-premise inference, a LiteLLM/MLflow control plane for authentication, budgeting, PII masking, and observability, and an application augmentation layer for AI coding agents. Layered on top, an open-source RSE-Plugins ecosystem encodes accumulated RSE knowledge as a Plugin-Agent-Skill hierarchy spanning scientific Python practice, domain-specific knowledge, a six-phase research-and-implement workflow, and project lifecycle management. Scientific software is judged less by raw code quality than by whether it can be cited, audited, reproduced, and extended. Off-the-shelf AI coding agents, optimized against commercial software benchmarks, are poorly calibrated for this setting: they ignore the conventions of the scientific Python libraries they invoke, mishandle sensitive or embargoed data, and leave decision trails that are difficult to reconstruct after the fact. We report on twenty months of practice at a university-based research software engineering (RSE) center, where RSEs embedded across astronomy, earth and climate science, agriculture, and health projects worked to close this gap. We characterize the recurring infrastructure, governance, and process challenges of adopting Agentic AI inside a multi-domain RSE center, describe the platform and plugin design, and distill operational lessons from real scientific software deployments. Together, the platform and plugins shift AI coding agents from generic code generators into domain-aware collaborators that respect community norms and produce auditable provenance of technical reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMoxie is an institutional AI platform with a three-tiered architecture (multi-cloud/on-premise inference, LiteLLM/MLflow control plane, application augmentation layer) combined with an open-source RSE-Plugins ecosystem (Plugin-Agent-Skill hierarchy) that adapts AI coding agents for scientific software development. After 20 months of practice across multiple scientific domains, the system shifts agents from generic code generators to domain-aware collaborators that respect community norms and produce auditable provenance.
AI.motivation: Off-the-shelf AI coding agents are optimized for commercial software benchmarks and poorly calibrated for scientific software, which requires citability, auditability, reproducibility, and extensibility. They ignore scientific Python conventions, mishandle sensitive/embargoed data, and leave difficult-to-reconstruct decision trails.
AI.method: A three-tiered platform architecture (multi-cloud/on-prem inference → LiteLLM/MLflow control plane for auth, budgeting, PII masking, observability → application augmentation layer for AI coding agents) plus an open-source RSE-Plugins ecosystem encoding accumulated RSE knowledge as a Plugin-Agent-Skill hierarchy spanning scientific Python practice, domain-specific knowledge, six-phase research-and-implement workflow, and project lifecycle management.
AI.result: Twenty months of practice at a university-based RSE center across astronomy, earth and climate science, agriculture, and health projects. Characterized recurring infrastructure, governance, and process challenges of adopting Agentic AI in multi-domain RSE centers.
AI.conclusion: The platform and plugins shift AI coding agents into domain-aware collaborators that respect community norms and produce auditable provenance of technical reasoning in scientific software settings.

title: On the Design Space of Discrete Diffusion Online Adaptation for Molecular Optimization
comment: Submitted to The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
summary: Molecular optimization often starts from a pretrained generative model that captures a broad prior over valid molecular structures. At test time, however, the goal is not to sample from this prior, but to use a limited oracle budget to shift generation toward task-specific high-reward molecules. We study this adaptation problem for discrete diffusion models. Each online round couples several choices. The loop must decide which candidates to evaluate, how rewards become model updates, which feedback to reuse, and how far to move beyond the pretrained prior. These choices have mostly been studied in isolation, leaving open whether they complement one another, become redundant, or interfere inside a full online adaptation loop. We conduct controlled studies across six small-molecule binding-affinity tasks and three protein-fitness tasks. We find that acquisition, reward shaping, and model debiasing provide complementary routes to higher reward, especially for small molecules. Replay further stabilizes learning, while validity penalties keep small-molecule exploration on the valid molecular manifold. Together, these findings point to a practical recipe for feedback-efficient molecular optimization: online fine-tuning with acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, and validity control. This recipe outperforms offline fine-tuning and inference-time search baselines under matched oracle-call budgets and GPU-hour accounting. The gains are largest when high-reward candidates require larger shifts from the pretrained prior.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to adapt pretrained discrete diffusion models for molecular optimization under limited oracle budgets, systematically comparing different design choices (acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, validity control) and finding they complement each other, leading to a practical recipe that outperforms offline fine-tuning and inference-time search baselines.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization typically starts from a pretrained generative model, but the test-time goal is to shift generation toward task-specific high-reward molecules under a limited oracle budget. The key choices (which candidates to evaluate, how rewards become model updates, what feedback to reuse, how far to move beyond the prior) have mostly been studied in isolation, leaving open whether they complement, become redundant, or interfere inside a full online adaptation loop.
AI.method: Controlled studies across six small-molecule binding-affinity tasks and three protein-fitness tasks, comparing acquisition, reward shaping, model debiasing, replay, and validity penalties within an online fine-tuning framework for discrete diffusion models.
AI.result: Acquisition, reward shaping, and model debiasing provide complementary routes to higher reward, especially for small molecules. Replay stabilizes learning, while validity penalties keep small-molecule exploration on the valid manifold. The combined recipe outperforms offline fine-tuning and inference-time search baselines under matched oracle-call budgets and GPU-hour accounting, with largest gains when high-reward candidates require larger shifts from the pretrained prior.
AI.conclusion: The findings point to a practical recipe for feedback-efficient molecular optimization: online fine-tuning with acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, and validity control.

title: Dual-Adaptive SAM3: Hierarchical Routing over Low-Rank Expert Layers for Parameter-Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
summary: The Segment Anything Model with Concepts (SAM3) heralds a new paradigm for open-vocabulary segmentation through natural language interaction, offering significant potential for medical image analysis. However, effectively adapting such a powerful vision-language model to the diverse and nuanced domain of medical imaging remains a key challenge. Naive fine-tuning is parameter-inefficient, while standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) methods introduce prohibitive computational overhead, limiting their clinical applicability. To address this, we propose Dual-Adaptive SAM3 (DA-SAM3), a novel framework that achieves both high segmentation accuracy and extreme parameter efficiency via a dual-adaptive specialization mechanism. Our first adaptation is task-aware: a Dynamic Expert Router (DER) that sparsely activates the most relevant experts by jointly reasoning about the visual input and the textual concept prompt, mimicking a clinical consultation process. Our second adaptation is parameter-aware: a Decomposed Parameterized Experts (DPE) design that represents each expert as a shared frozen base (inherited from the pretrained SAM3) and a lightweight trainable low-rank delta, reducing MoE parameter overhead by over 80\%. Extensive experiments on multiple public medical segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that Dual-Adaptive SAM3 not only matches or exceeds the accuracy of fully fine-tuned SAM3 and standard MoE baselines, but also achieves a notable 5\% gain over current state-of-the-art methods, with interpretable results validating its effectiveness. The code is available at: https://github.com/Reconsider80/DA-SAM3.

AI.tldr: DA-SAM3 introduces a dual-adaptive specialization mechanism (task-aware Dynamic Expert Router + parameter-aware Decomposed Parameterized Experts) to efficiently adapt the SAM3 vision-language model for medical image segmentation, achieving high accuracy with over 80% reduction in MoE parameters and 5% improvement over SOTA.
AI.motivation: Adapting SAM3 (open-vocabulary segmentation model) to medical imaging is challenging due to domain diversity. Naive fine-tuning is parameter-inefficient, and standard MoE methods introduce prohibitive computational overhead, limiting clinical applicability.
AI.method: Proposes DA-SAM3 with two adaptations: (1) Task-aware Dynamic Expert Router (DER) sparsely activates relevant experts by jointly reasoning about visual input and textual concept prompts; (2) Parameter-aware Decomposed Parameterized Experts (DPE) represents each expert as a shared frozen base (from pretrained SAM3) plus a lightweight trainable low-rank delta, reducing MoE parameters by over 80%.
AI.result: Matches or exceeds accuracy of fully fine-tuned SAM3 and standard MoE baselines; achieves 5% gain over current state-of-the-art methods on multiple public medical segmentation benchmarks; provides interpretable results.
AI.conclusion: DA-SAM3 effectively adapts SAM3 to medical imaging with high accuracy and extreme parameter efficiency, validating dual-adaptive specialization as a viable approach for clinical deployment.

title: Silicon Sampling via Cross-Survey Transfer
summary: Silicon sampling-using large language models (LLMs) to simulate human survey respondents-has emerged as a promising approach for augmenting traditional survey research. However, most evaluations rely on distributional comparisons rather than individual-level prediction, which risks conflating pattern matching with coherent respondent-level prediction. We propose cross-survey transfer, a more rigorous evaluation framework in which an LLM is given a respondent's answers to one set of questions and must predict their answers to entirely different questions from the same survey. Using data from the Taiwan Election and Democratization Study (TEDS) 2024, three open-weight LLMs (27B-120B parameters), and supervised machine learning baselines, we find that: (1) zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy on genuinely unseen items, closing to within 6 percentage points (pp) of a supervised random forest trained on same-population data; (2) a stable construct predictability hierarchy emerges, from 67% for partisan attitudes to 23% for sovereignty; and (3) variance collapse and safety alignment effects-two commonly cited LLM limitations-turn out to be more nuanced than previously reported, with variance collapse affecting supervised models as well and alignment effects varying dramatically across model families. These findings clarify both the promise and boundaries of silicon sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cross-survey transfer as a rigorous evaluation framework for silicon sampling (using LLMs as simulated survey respondents). Testing on TEDS 2024 data with three open-weight LLMs, they find zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy on unseen items (within 6pp of a supervised random forest), identify a predictability hierarchy across constructs (67% for partisan attitudes to 23% for sovereignty), and reveal that variance collapse and safety alignment effects are more nuanced than commonly reported.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs as survey respondents rely on distributional comparisons rather than individual-level prediction, which may conflate pattern matching with coherent respondent-level prediction. A more rigorous evaluation framework is needed.
AI.method: Proposes cross-survey transfer evaluation: given a respondent's answers to one set of questions, predict their answers to entirely different questions from the same survey. Uses TEDS 2024 data, three open-weight LLMs (27B-120B parameters), and supervised ML baselines (random forest).
AI.result: (1) Zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy on unseen items, within 6pp of a supervised random forest; (2) construct predictability ranges from 67% (partisan attitudes) to 23% (sovereignty); (3) variance collapse and safety alignment effects are more nuanced than previously reported, with variance collapse also affecting supervised models and alignment effects varying across model families.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify both the promise and boundaries of silicon sampling, showing it works reasonably well for some constructs but poorly for others, and that common criticisms need re-examination.

title: Towards Robust Uncertainty-Aware Speaker Modeling
summary: Speaker embeddings aggregate frame-level acoustic features into compact representations for speaker recognition. Recent uncertainty-aware speaker modeling approaches further characterize the reliability of speaker embeddings by estimating their associated uncertainty. However, existing methods often suffer from inaccurate uncertainty estimation and uncertainty miscalibration under domain shifts. To address these challenges, we propose a robust uncertainty modeling framework from both estimation and adaptation perspectives. Specifically, we introduce an Inter- and Intra-Speaker-Aware Uncertainty Softmax that incorporates both inter-speaker separability and intra-speaker variability into uncertainty learning, enabling uncertainty estimates to better capture the reliability of speaker embeddings. Furthermore, we propose an Uncertainty-Calibrated Domain Adaptation (UCDA) framework to mitigate uncertainty miscalibration caused by domain mismatch. Extensive experiments on both in-domain and cross-domain benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves uncertainty reliability and speaker recognition robustness.

AI.tldr: Proposes a robust uncertainty modeling framework for speaker embeddings that improves uncertainty estimation via Inter- and Intra-Speaker-Aware Uncertainty Softmax and mitigates miscalibration under domain shifts via Uncertainty-Calibrated Domain Adaptation, achieving more reliable uncertainty and robust speaker recognition.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty-aware speaker modeling approaches suffer from inaccurate uncertainty estimation and uncertainty miscalibration under domain shifts, limiting their reliability in real-world speaker recognition.
AI.method: (1) Inter- and Intra-Speaker-Aware Uncertainty Softmax that incorporates both inter-speaker separability and intra-speaker variability into uncertainty learning. (2) Uncertainty-Calibrated Domain Adaptation (UCDA) framework to mitigate uncertainty miscalibration caused by domain mismatch.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in uncertainty reliability and speaker recognition robustness on both in-domain and cross-domain benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses uncertainty estimation and calibration challenges in speaker embeddings, leading to more robust speaker recognition under domain shifts.

title: SMOCS: A Streaming Framework for Simplified Deployment, Monitoring, and Optimization of ML Systems in Production
summary: Machine learning has demonstrated significant potential for real-time monitoring, optimization, and control of scientific facilities. However, deploying and maintaining ML models in operational environments remains a substantial engineering challenge. Each facility presents unique data protocols, non-standard formats, and infrastructure constraints, forcing teams to rebuild integration pipelines for every new application. We present SMOCS (Streaming Monitoring Optimization and Control System), a Kafka-based containerized framework that addresses this challenge through three contributions: 1) a layered abstraction over Apache Kafka that separates infrastructure from application logic, 2) a three-thread agent architecture that temporally decouples data ingestion, model training, and real-time inference enabling continuous online learning from live data streams, and 3) a configuration-driven deployment model that enables domain experts to operate ML pipelines without software engineering expertise. SMOCS is facility platform-agnostic, fault-isolated by design, and horizontally scalable through Docker containerization. The framework is publicly available as open-source software on the Jefferson Lab Github.

AI.tldr: SMOCS is a Kafka-based containerized framework that separates infrastructure from application logic, decouples data ingestion/training/inference via a three-thread agent architecture, and enables configuration-driven ML pipeline deployment for scientific facilities without requiring software engineering expertise.
AI.motivation: Deploying and maintaining ML models in operational scientific facilities is a substantial engineering challenge due to unique data protocols, non-standard formats, and infrastructure constraints, forcing teams to rebuild integration pipelines for every new application.
AI.method: 1) A layered abstraction over Apache Kafka separating infrastructure from application logic; 2) A three-thread agent architecture temporally decoupling data ingestion, model training, and real-time inference for continuous online learning; 3) A configuration-driven deployment model enabling domain experts to operate ML pipelines without software engineering expertise.
AI.result: SMOCS is facility platform-agnostic, fault-isolated by design, and horizontally scalable through Docker containerization. It is publicly available as open-source software on the Jefferson Lab Github.
AI.conclusion: SMOCS addresses the engineering challenge of ML deployment in scientific facilities by providing a reusable, scalable, and accessible framework that eliminates the need for rebuilding integration pipelines for each new application.

title: Labeled-Data-Free Meta-Learning: Efficient Task Generation Using Pre-trained Models and Unlabeled Data
summary: Meta-learning without labeled data is crucial for real-world applications, where obtaining labeled datasets can be expensive or restricted due to privacy concerns. Data-Free Meta-Learning (DFML) addresses this challenge by leveraging pre-trained models without access to training data. However, existing DFML methods rely on model inversion to generate training data, a process that is generally difficult and computationally expensive due to the need to generate high-dimensional data matching the original distribution. To address this limitation, we propose a novel meta-learning setting that avoids model inversion by jointly leveraging pre-trained models and unlabeled data. Our method generates meta-training tasks by assigning soft labels from pre-trained models to unlabeled data. Since the quality of these tasks can vary, we introduce a task-weighting mechanism based on task confidence and class distribution balance to ensure effective meta-learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach substantially reduces computational cost and improves generalization, achieving up to 104-fold speedup and 8.4 percent to 36.4 percent improvements in few-shot classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art DFML methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new Data-Free Meta-Learning (DFML) setting that avoids computationally expensive model inversion by using pre-trained models to assign soft labels to unlabeled data, combined with a task-weighting mechanism based on task confidence and class distribution balance, achieving up to 104-fold speedup and 8.4%-36.4% accuracy improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing DFML methods rely on model inversion to generate training data, which is difficult and computationally expensive due to the need to generate high-dimensional data matching the original distribution. The goal is to avoid this limitation while still performing meta-learning without labeled data.
AI.method: The method generates meta-training tasks by assigning soft labels from pre-trained models to unlabeled data, and introduces a task-weighting mechanism based on task confidence and class distribution balance to handle varying task quality.
AI.result: Substantial reduction in computational cost (up to 104-fold speedup) and 8.4% to 36.4% improvements in few-shot classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art DFML methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses the limitations of existing DFML methods by avoiding model inversion, reducing computational overhead, and improving generalization performance.

title: Additive Causal Construction for Transferable and Reconfigurable Cross-System Learning in Multi-Source Image Fusion
summary: In multi-source image fusion scenarios, heterogeneous inputs are typically driven by distinct generative mechanisms and can be viewed as a composition of multiple causal systems. However, cross-system discrepancy (CSD) and cross-system entanglement (CSE) commonly arise during the fusion process, often leading to significant performance degradation under out-of-distribution (OOD) predictions. To address the CSD and CSE issues, we propose the additive causal construction (ACC) framework, which characterizes information fusion at two levels: firstly, it establishes causal "anchors" shared among multiple systems through intervention consistency to enable causal graph transferability (CGT); and secondly, it formalizes the fusion process as causal construction and models the reliability of constructed paths through uncertainty quantification to ensure causal graph reconfigurability (CGR). Building upon this, we revisit the traditional causal representation learning (CRL) with ACC and propose ACC-CRL as a learnable instantiation of the framework. The method explores joint causal content representations across systems via content-mechanism decoupling, and performs response alignment under shared anchors to mitigate CSD. Furthermore, it incorporates structural uncertainty to adaptively regulate the fusion process, thereby suppressing unstable CSE. We conduct systematic experiments on synthetic data (ColorMNIST) and real-world multi-center medical imaging tasks (microvascular invasion (MVI) prediction). The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves OOD generalization while maintaining in-distribution (ID) performance, validating the effectiveness and robustness of the ACC-CRL strategy based on mechanism alignment and uncertainty modeling in open environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Additive Causal Construction (ACC) framework and its learnable instantiation ACC-CRL to address cross-system discrepancy (CSD) and cross-system entanglement (CSE) in multi-source image fusion, improving out-of-distribution generalization via causal anchors, mechanism decoupling, and uncertainty-guided fusion regulation.
AI.motivation: Multi-source image fusion suffers from cross-system discrepancy (CSD) and cross-system entanglement (CSE), which cause severe performance degradation under out-of-distribution (OOD) predictions due to heterogeneous generative mechanisms across systems.
AI.method: The ACC framework operates at two levels: (1) establishing causal "anchors" via intervention consistency for causal graph transferability (CGT), and (2) formalizing fusion as causal construction with uncertainty quantification for causal graph reconfigurability (CGR). The ACC-CRL instantiation performs content-mechanism decoupling, response alignment under shared anchors to mitigate CSD, and structural uncertainty-based adaptive regulation to suppress CSE.
AI.result: Experiments on ColorMNIST (synthetic) and real-world multi-center microvascular invasion (MVI) prediction show significant OOD generalization improvement while maintaining in-distribution performance, validating robustness of the ACC-CRL strategy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism alignment and uncertainty modeling approach effectively addresses CSD and CSE in open environments, offering a principled causal framework for multi-source image fusion.

title: APeB: Benchmarking Personalization Ability of Large Language Model Agents
summary: LLM-powered agents struggle with personalization when users issue raw, underspecified queries. In this setting, agents must infer latent intent, extract preferences from noisy interaction histories, and select among competing alternatives. Existing benchmarks rarely test this capability, as they often rely on user-refined queries or simplified histories. We introduce personalized product search (PPS), a testbed for agentic personalization under raw queries and diverse histories. We construct Agent Personalized Benchmark (APeB) from action logs, pairing underspecified intents with rich histories and user-viewed candidate items. Evaluating state-of-the-art LLMs with multi-step agent workflows, we find that models handle explicit queries well but struggle with early-stage queries requiring intent and preference discovery. Rubric analysis attributes this gap mainly to ineffective history use. A simple history-aware query-refinement pipeline, VQRA, yields consistent gains, highlighting the need for dedicated history-utilization modules in personalized agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PPS/APeB benchmark for testing LLM agents on personalized product search with raw queries, finds models struggle with intent discovery especially due to poor history utilization, and proposes VQRA for improvement.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents fail to personalize under raw, underspecified user queries because they must infer latent intent and extract preferences from noisy histories; existing benchmarks avoid this challenge by using refined queries or simplified histories.
AI.method: Constructs APeB benchmark from action logs with underspecified intents, rich histories, and candidate items; evaluates state-of-the-art LLMs using multi-step agent workflows; proposes VQRA, a history-aware query-refinement pipeline.
AI.result: Models perform well on explicit queries but poorly on early-stage queries requiring intent/preference discovery; rubric analysis shows the main failure is ineffective history use; VQRA yields consistent performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Dedicated history-utilization modules are critical for improving personalization in LLM-powered agents, as demonstrated by VQRA's success.

title: Listen, Think, Transcribe: Continuous Latent Test-Time Scaling for ASR
summary: End-to-end ASR models transcribe in a single pass, leaving no room for the decoder to revisit hard inputs. We propose LatentASR, a parameter-efficient method that adds continuous latent test-time scaling to a frozen ASR backbone. Two small trainable modules drive it: a Latent Adapter that iteratively refines a few latent prefix positions through bounded, stabilized updates, and a Value Head that predicts whether extra computation will help and halts the loop early. The Qwen3-ASR-0.6B backbone stays fully frozen, and we train only ~4M extra parameters. We activate this loop with a deliberately small, diverse 500-utterance training set. Under this minimal-data regime, standard adaptation methods all regress: full fine-tuning, LoRA, and prompt tuning each increase WER. LatentASR is the only tested method that reduces WER on both clean benchmarks (FLEURS -2.54% and VoxPopuli -0.47% relative). The reductions are concentrated on intrinsically hard inputs. On accented and code-switched speech (ASCEND), LatentASR achieves a 16.0% relative CER reduction. Across 30 FLEURS languages (23,049 utterances), the multilingual WER decreases uniformly across resource tiers, confirming that the adapter generalizes without overfitting. Dynamic halting preserves most of the clean-set reduction at a fraction of the compute, skipping roughly half of all utterances at the entry gate. Our results show that a small, carefully chosen activation set can switch on test-time scaling inside a frozen ASR model without corrupting the model itself, converting fixed per-utterance compute into input-dependent compute where it is most needed.

AI.tldr: LatentASR adds continuous latent test-time scaling to a frozen ASR backbone using only ~4M trainable parameters and a small 500-utterance set, reducing WER on clean benchmarks (FLEURS -2.54%, VoxPopuli -0.47%), achieving 16.0% CER reduction on accented/code-switched speech, and generalizing across 30 FLEURS languages without overfitting.
AI.motivation: End-to-end ASR models transcribe in a single pass, leaving no room for the decoder to revisit hard inputs; the authors aim to add test-time scaling to a frozen ASR model without corrupting it.
AI.method: Two small trainable modules are added to a frozen Qwen3-ASR-0.6B backbone: a Latent Adapter that iteratively refines latent prefix positions through bounded stabilized updates, and a Value Head that predicts whether extra computation will help and halts the loop early. Only ~4M parameters are trained on a small, diverse 500-utterance set.
AI.result: LatentASR reduces WER on FLEURS (-2.54% relative) and VoxPopuli (-0.47% relative), achieves 16.0% relative CER reduction on ASCEND (accented/code-switched speech), and shows uniform WER reduction across all resource tiers in 30 FLEURS languages (23,049 utterances). Dynamic halting skips roughly half of all utterances at the entry gate.
AI.conclusion: A small, carefully chosen activation set can switch on test-time scaling inside a frozen ASR model without corrupting the model itself, converting fixed per-utterance compute into input-dependent compute where it is most needed.

title: Benefits of Applying Software Design Patterns to Backend Rust Applications
summary: Software design patterns' effects on code quality have mostly been studied in the context of object-oriented languages. In the programming language Rust, which comes with novel language concepts, compile-time safety guarantees and a distinct type system, there has been little research on design patterns. This work investigates how patterns affect software quality and compile-time enforcement of invariants through a case study on three representative components of production backend applications. An evaluation framework based on criteria derived from the SQuaRE quality model, incorporating benchmarking, static code analysis and expert interviews, is developed to assess the refactored code. The patterns typestate and newtype are applied to address existing code smells in the selected use cases. While the typestate pattern improves faultlessness and testability significantly, it comes at the cost of more structural code that can degrade readability. Code with extensive branching logic and a high number of invariants is likely to benefit most from the pattern. The newtype pattern combined with the "Parse, don't validate" principle offers high returns in software quality at a low cost and prevents invalid states during runtime. Overall, this work provides an initial empirical assessment of design patterns in Rust and establishes a foundation for further studies involving additional use cases and patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically assesses how design patterns (typestate and newtype) affect software quality and compile-time invariant enforcement in Rust, using a case study on three production backend components evaluated via SQuaRE-based criteria, benchmarking, static analysis, and expert interviews.
AI.motivation: Software design patterns' effects on code quality have been well-studied in object-oriented languages, but little research exists on patterns in Rust, which features novel language concepts, compile-time safety guarantees, and a distinct type system.
AI.method: A case study on three representative production backend components; an evaluation framework based on SQuaRE quality model criteria with benchmarking, static code analysis, and expert interviews; application of typestate and newtype patterns to address code smells.
AI.result: The typestate pattern significantly improves faultlessness and testability but increases structural code that may reduce readability. The newtype pattern combined with "Parse, don't validate" offers high quality gains at low cost and prevents invalid runtime states.
AI.conclusion: This work provides an initial empirical assessment of design patterns in Rust and establishes a foundation for further studies involving additional use cases and patterns.

title: Trading Confidence: Comprehensive Uncertainty Estimation in Algorithmic Trading
comment: Accepted at the Pacific Asia Conference on Information Systems (PACIS 2025). 17 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach in financial trading, enabling agents to learn optimal strategies through direct market interaction. However, financial markets are highly uncertain, with price fluctuations driven by stochastic volatility, model limitations, and regime shifts. Traditional RL models struggle in dynamic environments, often failing to adapt to sudden market disruptions, leading to suboptimal trading decisions. To address this challenge, we propose an uncertainty-aware RL framework that integrates distributional, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty estimations. Our approach enhances uncertainty estimation using SHAP-weighted reconstruction uncertainty, MC Dropout, and an LSTM-based technical indicator consensus mechanism. Experimental results on five major U.S. stock indices demonstrate that RL agents equipped with uncertainty estimation significantly outperform traditional models in return and risk management. This study advances uncertainty estimation in RL-based financial trading, with future research extending its application to other asset classes and alternative RL architectures for greater adaptability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an uncertainty-aware Reinforcement Learning framework that integrates distributional, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty estimations using SHAP-weighted reconstruction uncertainty, MC Dropout, and LSTM-based technical indicator consensus, demonstrating superior performance on five U.S. stock indices.
AI.motivation: Financial markets suffer from stochastic volatility, model limitations, and regime shifts, making traditional RL models fail to adapt to sudden market disruptions and produce suboptimal trading decisions.
AI.method: The framework integrates three uncertainty types: distributional, epistemic, and aleatoric. It uses SHAP-weighted reconstruction uncertainty, MC Dropout, and an LSTM-based technical indicator consensus mechanism to enhance uncertainty estimation in RL trading agents.
AI.result: RL agents equipped with uncertainty estimation significantly outperform traditional models in both return and risk management across five major U.S. stock indices.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware RL improves financial trading performance; future work will extend to other asset classes and alternative RL architectures.

title: Symmetry-Structured Neural Completion of Islamic Geometric Patterns from Sparse Control Geometry
summary: Islamic geometric patterns are governed by exact rotational symmetry and strict construction rules. This paper treats these rules as formal geometric knowledge and embeds them in a neural completion framework, rather than leaving them to be learned statistically from data. Given sparse control geometry and a target symmetry order, the system completes the pattern as a vector graph by predicting edges and refinements of bounded curves over a candidate lattice whose edges are organised into rotational orbits under the cyclic group. Symmetry is enforced either by constraining predictions within these orbits or by projecting them onto them during inference. The orbit-tied variant provides a constructive guarantee: for any input and any orbit-level selection rule, it produces exact N-fold symmetry, preserves anchor points, and keeps all refinements within prescribed bounds. These properties are verified numerically. The study focuses on rotational symmetry, and all quantitative results are obtained from procedurally generated graphs inspired by Islamic geometric design rather than from a historical corpus. On clean inputs, enforcing exact validity produces no measurable loss in fidelity. When control geometry is missing, an unstructured decoder loses fidelity and breaks symmetry; retraining on corrupted inputs recovers much of the fidelity but not exact validity. Symmetry-structured inference, by contrast, keeps violations at zero throughout. The results show that augmentation and symmetry structure address distinct failure modes: augmentation improves fidelity under corruption, while symmetry structure guarantees validity. The framework therefore provides a knowledge-constrained, guarantee-backed approach to neural completion for scalable vector ornaments whose validity depends on exact geometric structure.

AI.tldr: The paper embeds formal geometric rules of Islamic patterns (rotational symmetry, construction constraints) into a neural completion framework, enforcing exact N-fold symmetry via orbit-tied predictions rather than learning it from data. This guarantees validity (zero symmetry violations) without sacrificing fidelity, unlike unstructured decoders that break symmetry under corruption even with augmentation.
AI.motivation: Islamic geometric patterns require exact rotational symmetry and strict construction rules, but purely data-driven neural methods cannot guarantee these formal constraints. The authors aim to embed explicit geometric knowledge into a completion framework to ensure validity by construction rather than relying on statistical learning.
AI.method: The system takes sparse control geometry and a target symmetry order, then completes a vector graph over a candidate lattice whose edges are organized into rotational orbits under the cyclic group. Predictions are either constrained within these orbits (orbit-tied) or projected onto them during inference. Symmetry is enforced explicitly rather than learned.
AI.result: On clean inputs, exact symmetry enforcement incurs no measurable fidelity loss. Under missing control geometry, unstructured decoders lose fidelity and break symmetry; retraining on corrupted data recovers fidelity but not exact validity. The symmetry-structured approach keeps symmetry violations at zero throughout. Augmentation and symmetry structure address distinct failure modes.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a knowledge-constrained, guarantee-backed approach to neural completion for scalable vector ornaments where exact geometric structure is essential. Augmentation and symmetry structure are complementary: augmentation handles fidelity under corruption, while symmetry structure guarantees validity.

title: Organizational Memory for Agentic Business Process Execution
summary: LLM-based agents offer new opportunities for automating business process execution beyond the limits of rule-based systems. However, general-purpose LLMs lack the organization-specific knowledge required for reliable execution, which is typically fragmented across human-oriented artifacts such as policies, process models, and standard operating procedures. While such knowledge can technically be encoded in individual prompts or agent-specific retrieval setups, this approach does not scale in enterprises, as it gives rise to knowledge silos and rule duplicates, and makes consistent updates and learning across agents difficult. We argue that this calls for an organizational memory for agentic business process execution: a shared, governed, and agent-consumable reference layer of evolving organization-specific procedural knowledge about how work should be executed. We derive requirements for such a memory, propose an architecture for its curation and consumption, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a proof-of-concept based on a procurement scenario.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an organizational memory architecture for LLM-based agents to share, govern, and consume organization-specific procedural knowledge, addressing scalability issues of siloed agent-specific knowledge setups in enterprise business process execution.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs lack organization-specific knowledge needed for reliable business process execution. Current approaches (individual prompts or agent-specific retrieval) create knowledge silos, rule duplicates, and hinder consistent updates, making them unscalable in enterprises.
AI.method: The authors derive requirements for an organizational memory, propose an architecture for its curation and consumption, and demonstrate it via a proof-of-concept procurement scenario.
AI.result: A proof-of-concept demonstration in a procurement scenario showing the effectiveness of the proposed organizational memory architecture for agentic business process execution.
AI.conclusion: An organizational memory—a shared, governed, and agent-consumable reference layer of evolving procedural knowledge—is needed to enable scalable and consistent agentic business process execution across enterprises.

title: Context-Aware ASR for Mandarin Technical Lectures
summary: Technical lectures mix Mandarin speech with English technical terms. These terms carry the core meaning of the lecture, yet they occupy few characters. Character error rate (CER) therefore hides their recognition failures. We study whether lecture context helps recognize these terms. We build a term-rich Mandarin AI/ML lecture benchmark, and we define term-centric metrics that measure technical-term recognition directly. We then propose a two-pass, reference-free decoding method. The first pass runs segment-only ASR. We extract the most frequent technical terms from the first-pass hypotheses, and we prompt the recognizer with this self-built glossary in the second pass. Across five ASR backbones, the first-pass glossary raises term recall for every model and holds or lowers CER on all five. On Breeze-ASR-25 it lifts term recall from 52.50% to 60.13% while lowering CER, and a hybrid that adds a small external term list reaches 62.05% recall and 82.73% term precision.
