Lecture context, recovered from the model's own output, is a practical signal for technical-term recognition. Term-centric evaluation exposes errors that CER misses.

AI.tldr: A two-pass, reference-free decoding method uses self-extracted technical terms from first-pass ASR hypotheses to prompt the recognizer, improving term recall by up to ~10% on a Mandarin AI/ML lecture benchmark while maintaining or reducing CER.
AI.motivation: CER hides recognition failures of rare but semantically critical English technical terms in Mandarin lectures; term-centric metrics are needed to expose these errors.
AI.method: Proposes a two-pass decoding: (1) segment-only ASR extracts frequent technical terms from hypotheses; (2) self-built glossary prompts the recognizer in the second pass. A hybrid variant adds a small external term list.
AI.result: Across five ASR backbones, first-pass glossary improves term recall for all models while holding or lowering CER. On Breeze-ASR-25: term recall 52.50%→60.13% with lower CER; hybrid reaches 62.05% recall and 82.73% term precision.
AI.conclusion: Lecture context recovered from the model's own output is a practical signal for technical-term recognition; term-centric evaluation reveals errors that CER misses.

title: From Codebases to LLMs: Non-Inclusive Naming in Linux Foundation Repositories
summary: Since 2020, the Linux Foundation and the multi-organization Inclusive Naming Initiative (INI) have encouraged open-source projects to replace non-inclusive terms such as master/slave and whitelist/blacklist. Although these recommendations have been widely adopted, there is limited empirical evidence on their long-term adoption across Linux Foundation (LF) projects or their implications for AI-assisted software development. In this paper, we present NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework that detects non-inclusive terminology across source code and related software artifacts using the INI vocabulary. Using NISCAN, we conduct the first ecosystem-scale study of inclusive naming across 461 Linux Foundation repositories. Our analysis shows that non-inclusive terminology has declined by approximately 47% since 2020, yet adoption remains incomplete: 62.7% of repositories still contain at least one Tier-1 non-inclusive identifier, while most remaining terminology resides outside source code in documentation, comments, configuration files, and other software artifacts. We further show that repository size, programming language, project functionality, and ecosystem are stronger predictors of term inclusiveness in LF repositories rather than foundation governance. To examine the implications for AI-assisted software development, we conduct a case study evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from surrounding program context. The results show that historical naming decisions remain embedded in model predictions even after identifiers have been renamed. Overall, our study findings provide the first ecosystem-scale assessment of inclusive naming adoption within the Linux Foundation and highlight the importance of addressing terminology residue to support responsible naming and ethically sourced code generation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework for detecting non-inclusive terminology, and conducts the first ecosystem-scale study across 461 Linux Foundation repositories. It finds a 47% decline in non-inclusive terms since 2020, but 62.7% of repos still contain Tier-1 terms, mostly outside source code. A case study with LLMs reveals that historical non-inclusive identifiers can be reconstructed from context even after renaming.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread recommendations (since 2020) from Linux Foundation and Inclusive Naming Initiative to replace non-inclusive terms like master/slave and whitelist/blacklist, there is limited empirical evidence on long-term adoption across LF projects and the implications for AI-assisted software development.
AI.method: The authors built NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework using the INI vocabulary, and analyzed 461 LF repositories. They also conducted a case study on LLMs (likely code models) to test whether they reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from surrounding context after renaming.
AI.result: Non-inclusive terminology declined ~47% since 2020; 62.7% of repositories still contain at least one Tier-1 non-inclusive term; most remaining terminology is in documentation, comments, config files, not source code. Repository size, language, project functionality, and ecosystem are stronger predictors of inclusiveness than foundation governance. LLMs can reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from context even after renaming.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first ecosystem-scale assessment of inclusive naming adoption within the Linux Foundation, highlighting that addressing terminology residue (especially outside source code) is critical, and that LLMs may perpetuate historical bias even after identifiers are renamed, underscoring the need for responsible naming and ethically sourced code generation.

title: Reward Granularity in RLVR: Comparing Process and Outcome Reward Structures for Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving mathematical reasoning in language models. Yet most RLVR work rewards only the final answer (outcome-based rewards), leaving the impact of step-level process supervision (process rewards) underexplored especially for small models that lack the capacity to self-correct under sparse feedback. We systematically compare five reward conditions applied to Qwen2.5-0.5B fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on GSM8K: a no-RL baseline, process-only, outcome-only, and three hybrid weightings ($λ\in \{0.9, 0.5, 0.1\}$ process weight). Process-only supervision achieves 63.73% test accuracy versus 53.75% for outcome-only, a nearly 10-percentage point gap while yielding reasoning traces with higher step validity and lower deviation from ground-truth chain length. Hybrid rewards generally correlate positively with process weight, with one notable anomaly: the low-process / high-outcome configuration ($λ=0.1$) underperforms pure outcome supervision, suggesting conflicting optimization signals. Error analysis using GPT-4o as a judge reveals distinct failure mode distributions: process models generate structurally inconsistent but arithmetically grounded traces, while outcome models produce concise but derivation-error-prone chains. Our results demonstrate that reward granularity is a first-order design decision for RLVR, with process-level supervision substantially improving both accuracy and trace fidelity in small language models.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how different reward granularities (process vs. outcome supervision) affect RLVR training of small language models (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on GSM8K. Process-only rewards achieve 63.73% accuracy vs. 53.75% for outcome-only, with better step validity and trace fidelity. Hybrid reward weighting correlates positively with process weight, but low-process/high-outcome hybrid underperforms pure outcome supervision, indicating conflicting signals.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate the underexplored impact of process-level (step-wise) rewards versus outcome-level (final answer) rewards in RLVR for small language models, which lack the capacity to self-correct under sparse feedback.
AI.method: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B using GRPO on GSM8K under five reward conditions: no-RL baseline, process-only, outcome-only, and three hybrid weightings (λ=0.9, 0.5, 0.1 process weight). Error analysis via GPT-4o as judge to categorize failure modes.
AI.result: Process-only achieves 63.73% vs 53.75% for outcome-only (~10pp gap). Hybrid rewards correlate positively with process weight; λ=0.1 underperforms pure outcome supervision. Process models produce structurally inconsistent but arithmetically grounded traces; outcome models produce concise but derivation-error-prone chains.
AI.conclusion: Reward granularity is a first-order design decision for RLVR; process-level supervision substantially improves both accuracy and trace fidelity in small language models.

title: Criterion-Conditional In-Context Learning: Evaluating Criterion-Shift Adaptation in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models can perform new tasks without parameter updates through in-context learning (ICL), whose core mechanism is utilizing the support set for task induction. In the standard ICL setting, once the task is induced, its decision criterion remains fixed. However, in real-world applications, many tasks exhibit a stable high-level intent, while their decision criteria shift according to specific requirements. Thus, we introduce a new setting, denoted as Criterion-Conditional In-Context Learning (CC-ICL), where models must infer the latent criterion from context and adjust predictions accordingly under fixed task semantics. To evaluate this capability, we propose two complementary metrics, Criterion Invariance and Criterion Sensitivity, capturing the model's robustness and adaptability under criterion shifts. We further construct CC-Bench, a multi-domain benchmark that supports evaluation under the CC-ICL setting. By employing a dual-level data hierarchy, CC-Bench enables legitimate ground-truth variation conditioned on the active criterion even when the task remains fixed. Experiments on CC-Bench reveal that most models exhibit a rigid boundary bias, struggling to align their decisions with the latent criterion. We also find that even a simple multi-criterion training strategy can significantly reduce this bias, improving Criterion Sensitivity and enabling 7B-scale models to surpass proprietary models without degrading general multimodal performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Criterion-Conditional In-Context Learning (CC-ICL), a new setting where vision-language models must infer shifting decision criteria from context while maintaining fixed task semantics. The authors propose CC-Bench, a multi-domain benchmark with dual-level data hierarchy, and two metrics (Criterion Invariance and Criterion Sensitivity). Experiments show most models have rigid boundary bias, but a simple multi-criterion training strategy significantly improves performance, enabling 7B-scale models to surpass proprietary models.
AI.motivation: Real-world tasks often have stable high-level intents but shifting decision criteria. Standard ICL assumes fixed decision criteria once a task is induced, which fails to capture this realistic scenario. The authors aim to address this gap by formalizing CC-ICL and providing evaluation tools.
AI.method: (1) Formalizing the CC-ICL setting. (2) Proposing two metrics: Criterion Invariance (robustness to irrelevant criteria shifts) and Criterion Sensitivity (ability to adapt predictions to latent criteria). (3) Constructing CC-Bench, a multi-domain benchmark with a dual-level data hierarchy (task-level + criterion-level) enabling legitimate ground-truth variation under fixed tasks. (4) Proposing a multi-criterion training strategy to reduce rigid boundary bias.
AI.result: Most models exhibit rigid boundary bias, struggling to align decisions with latent criteria. The proposed multi-criterion training strategy significantly reduces this bias, improving Criterion Sensitivity and enabling 7B-scale models to outperform proprietary models without degrading general multimodal performance.
AI.conclusion: CC-ICL is a valuable new setting for real-world vision-language tasks. Current models struggle with criterion shifts, but a simple training strategy can substantially close this gap, demonstrating that scale alone is insufficient and targeted training is needed for criterion-conditional reasoning.

title: Embodied Operators and Benchmarking: Toward Reusable and Deployable Embodied Intelligence Systems
summary: Embodied intelligence systems require not only end-to-end policy models, but also reusable functional modules that transform multimodal observations, robot states, human demonstrations, and task contexts into structured representations, decisions, trajectories, control references, and system services. This work defines these modules as embodied operators and studies them as independent yet composable units in embodied intelligence pipelines. We clarify their definition boundary, emphasizing task semantics, standardized input-output contracts, deployability, reusability, and multi-layer optimizability. We further construct a taxonomy covering five categories: detection and segmentation, spatial localization and 3D understanding, hand motion recovery, embodied foundation models and task-decision operators, and planning, control, and system support operators. For each category, we summarize representative functions, technical paradigms, application roles, and practical limitations. Beyond taxonomy, we propose a multi-dimensional benchmark framework that evaluates embodied operators in terms of correctness, end-to-end efficiency, resource usage, temporal stability, portability, interface compatibility, deployment reliability, and downstream task utility. We also discuss workflow-level operator acceleration and open challenges in operator composition, data standardization, world models, VLA safety, edge deployment, and real-world application value. Overall, this work argues that embodied operators should be optimized and evaluated as holistic deployable components, providing a foundation for reusable, scalable, and verifiable embodied intelligence systems.

AI.tldr: This paper defines "embodied operators" as independent, reusable, and composable modules in embodied intelligence pipelines, covering five categories (detection/segmentation, spatial/3D understanding, hand motion recovery, embodied foundation models, planning/control/support). It proposes a multi-dimensional benchmark for evaluating operators on correctness, efficiency, resource usage, stability, portability, interface compatibility, reliability, and downstream utility, and discusses optimization challenges and future directions.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligence systems need not only end-to-end policy models but also reusable functional modules. The paper aims to formally define these modules as "embodied operators" and provide a systematic taxonomy, benchmark framework, and discussion of optimization challenges to enable reusable, scalable, and verifiable embodied intelligence.
AI.method: The authors define embodied operators with clear criteria (task semantics, standardized I/O contracts, deployability, reusability, multi-layer optimizability). They construct a five-category taxonomy covering detection/segmentation, spatial/3D understanding, hand motion recovery, embodied foundation models/task-decision operators, and planning/control/system support operators. They propose a multi-dimensional benchmark evaluating correctness, end-to-end efficiency, resource usage, temporal stability, portability, interface compatibility, deployment reliability, and downstream task utility.
AI.result: A taxonomy of five embodied operator categories with representative functions, paradigms, applications, and limitations. A multi-dimensional benchmark framework for holistic operator evaluation. Identification of open challenges: operator composition, data standardization, world models, VLA safety, edge deployment, and real-world application value.
AI.conclusion: Embodied operators should be optimized and evaluated as holistic deployable components, forming a foundation for reusable, scalable, and verifiable embodied intelligence systems.

title: $C^3$ASD: Multi-Level Consistency-Driven Representation Learning
summary: Active Speaker Detection determines whether a visible person in a video is speaking at each moment. While recent audio-visual fusion methods perform well on clean data, they degrade under real-world corruptions such as background noise, occlusion, or simultaneous modality degradation. We attribute this limitation to the absence of explicit consistency constraints that promote robust, semantically aligned representations across modalities. Without such guidance, models tend to learn fragile modality-specific shortcuts that fail under corrupted conditions. We propose $C^3$ASD, a multi-level consistency-driven framework with three complementary constraints: embedding-level inter-modality consistency aligns audio-visual representations during speech; sequence-level intra-modality consistency separates speaking and non-speaking clusters via track-aware contrastive learning; and prediction-level consistency stabilizes fusion through knowledge distillation. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements under diverse audio, visual and joint corruptions, while maintaining competitive performance on clean data.

AI.tldr: C³ASD is a consistency-driven framework for Active Speaker Detection that uses three levels of constraints (embedding, sequence, prediction) to improve robustness against real-world corruptions like noise and occlusion, while maintaining clean data performance.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-visual fusion methods for Active Speaker Detection perform well on clean data but degrade under real-world corruptions (noise, occlusion, simultaneous modality degradation) because they lack explicit consistency constraints, leading models to learn fragile modality-specific shortcuts.
AI.method: C³ASD introduces a multi-level consistency framework with three constraints: (1) embedding-level inter-modality consistency aligning audio-visual representations during speech; (2) sequence-level intra-modality consistency separating speaking/non-speaking clusters via track-aware contrastive learning; (3) prediction-level consistency stabilizing fusion through knowledge distillation.
AI.result: Significant improvements under diverse audio, visual, and joint corruptions, while maintaining competitive performance on clean data.
AI.conclusion: Explicit multi-level consistency constraints effectively improve ASD robustness against real-world corruptions without sacrificing clean-data performance.

title: Was It Never Collected, or Rewritten Away? A Commit-Provenance Dataset Separating Ingestion Gaps from Upstream History Edits across the World of Code
summary: Any global mirror of open-source version control is incomplete, but the reasons a commit is missing are not interchangeable: a project may have force-pushed it away (so it no longer exists upstream), or the mirror may never have ingested it (a true collection gap). We release a commit-provenance dataset that separates these cases at scale by comparing two views of the same commit graph: the GHArchive event stream, a historical witness of what GitHub advertised at push time, and the World of Code (WoC) V2604 object database, an accumulated union of periodic fetches that never deletes a collected commit. Walking each reference's PushEvent chain reconstructs force-pushes structurally (a before that is not the prior head breaks the fast-forward chain; no recorded flag exists across eras), and joining every advertised commit against WoC membership yields a three-way label. Over 1,118,116,350 advertised commits, 53.35% are present in WoC, 6.47% are rewritten (orphaned by a later force-push, an upstream edit and a correct absence), and 40.18% are never-ingested (the candidate collection gap). About one missing-commit case in fifteen is a rewrite the project erased, not a mirror gap. We release the force-push witness (166,710,831 events over 19,926,250 repositories) and a per-project rollup (78,125,788 repositories; force-pushing observed in 25.47%, a rewritten commit in 12.85%). We treat the 40% never-ingested share as an upper bound on the collection gap and state five reasons it overcounts. The dataset makes mirror-completeness reporting honest, flags rewritten commits as duplicate patch sources for contribution counting, and corrects a 10.82% corpus-wide undercount that history editing imposes on commit-based productivity, with a released per-project correction factor. All artifacts ship as a self-contained, independently hosted replication package keyed to WoC V2604.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a commit-provenance dataset that distinguishes between two types of missing commits in open-source version control mirrors: force-pushed (rewritten) commits vs. never-ingested (collection gaps). By cross-referencing GHArchive event streams with WoC object databases across 1.1B+ advertised commits, the authors find 53.35% present, 6.47% rewritten, and 40.18% never-ingested. They release force-push witness data and per-project correction factors for commit-based productivity metrics.
AI.motivation: Global mirrors of open-source version control are inherently incomplete, but missing commits arise from two distinct causes: force-pushes (upstream edits) and collection gaps (mirror never ingested them). Existing systems conflate these cases, making mirror-completeness reporting inaccurate and biasing downstream analyses like contribution counting and productivity metrics.
AI.method: The authors compare two views of the same commit graph: GHArchive event stream (historical witness of what GitHub advertised at push time) and WoC V2604 object database (accumulated union of periodic fetches). They reconstruct force-pushes structurally by walking each reference's PushEvent chain, detecting broken fast-forward chains. Every advertised commit is joined against WoC membership to produce a three-way label: present, rewritten (force-pushed), or never-ingested.
AI.result: Over 1,118,116,350 advertised commits: 53.35% present in WoC, 6.47% rewritten (force-pushed), 40.18% never-ingested. The force-push witness contains 166,710,831 events over 19,926,250 repositories. Of 78,125,788 repositories analyzed, 25.47% showed force-pushing, 12.85% had a rewritten commit. A 10.82% corpus-wide undercount in commit-based productivity is attributed to history editing.
AI.conclusion: The dataset enables honest mirror-completeness reporting, differentiates rewritten commits from collection gaps, and corrects commit-based productivity undercounts. The 40% never-ingested share is treated as an upper bound on the collection gap with five stated reasons for overcounting. All artifacts are released as a self-contained replication package keyed to WoC V2604.

title: Poisson-Gamma Modeling of Inter-Relational Dependencies in Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). 20 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables
summary: Dynamic knowledge graphs are ubiquitous in today's AI applications, as we represent molecular structures, social relationships, and language information using these graph models. As knowledge graphs evolve over time and are often noisy and incomplete, modeling their temporal and relational dependencies becomes crucial for downstream tasks. To address these challenges, this paper proposes PGRE (Poisson-Gamma Relational Evolution), a probabilistic model for modeling inter-relational dependencies in dynamic knowledge graphs. PGRE represents multi-relational temporal links via a Poisson-Bernoulli formulation. It introduces Gamma-distributed latent variables to capture entity-factor associations and cross-relation dependencies mediated by shared latent communities. A Gamma Markov process further models the temporal evolution of these latent variables, enabling principled characterization of relational dynamics. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that PGRE achieves competitive performance in link prediction, particularly in sparse settings, while revealing meaningful relational evolution patterns in dynamic knowledge graphs.

AI.tldr: PGRE (Poisson-Gamma Relational Evolution) is a probabilistic model for dynamic knowledge graphs that uses Poisson-Bernoulli formulation and Gamma-distributed latent variables with a Gamma Markov process to capture inter-relational dependencies and temporal evolution, achieving competitive link prediction especially in sparse settings.
AI.motivation: Dynamic knowledge graphs are noisy, incomplete, and evolve over time. Modeling both temporal and relational dependencies is crucial for downstream applications, yet existing methods struggle with sparse settings and capturing cross-relation dependencies.
AI.method: PGRE uses a Poisson-Bernoulli formulation for multi-relational temporal links, introduces Gamma-distributed latent variables to capture entity-factor associations and cross-relation dependencies via shared latent communities, and employs a Gamma Markov process to model temporal evolution of latent variables.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance in link prediction, particularly in sparse settings, and reveals meaningful relational evolution patterns in dynamic knowledge graphs.
AI.conclusion: PGRE is an effective probabilistic model for dynamic knowledge graphs that captures temporal and relational dynamics, with particular strength in sparse data scenarios.

title: Classroom Behavior Monitoring with YOLO An Empirical Study in Higher Education Settings
summary: Classroom behavior monitoring plays a vital role in evaluating student engagement and improving teaching effectiveness. Traditional observation methods remain subjective and lack scalability. This study introduces a real-world dataset of classroom videos collected at the Banking Academy of Vietnam (BAV-Classroom dataset), annotated with nine distinctive behavioral categories. State-of-the-art Computer Vision models were evaluated and compared, with YOLOv11 achieving the best performance. Experimental results indicate that students' concentration often decreases notably during the final part of lectures, highlighting challenges in sustaining engagement. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying computer vision for automated classroom monitoring, providing valuable insights for academic quality management.

AI.tldr: This study introduces the BAV-Classroom dataset for automated classroom behavior monitoring, evaluates state-of-the-art computer vision models (with YOLOv11 achieving best performance), finds that student concentration decreases during the final part of lectures, and demonstrates the feasibility of automated monitoring for academic quality management.
AI.motivation: Traditional classroom behavior observation methods are subjective and lack scalability, motivating the need for an automated, objective approach to monitor student engagement and improve teaching effectiveness.
AI.method: The authors collected a real-world classroom video dataset (BAV-Classroom) at the Banking Academy of Vietnam, annotated with nine behavioral categories. They evaluated and compared several state-of-the-art Computer Vision models, with YOLOv11 achieving the best performance.
AI.result: YOLOv11 outperformed other state-of-the-art models on the BAV-Classroom dataset. Experimental results revealed that students' concentration notably decreases during the final part of lectures, indicating challenges in sustaining engagement.
AI.conclusion: Automated computer vision-based classroom monitoring is feasible and can provide valuable insights for academic quality management, particularly in identifying engagement patterns such as declining attention toward lecture end.

title: Reflective Dialogue or Prompt Refinement? Effects of Tutor Scaffolding on Students' Independent LLM Use for Programming
comment: Best paper award, Published in AIED 2026: The 27th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide personalized support in learning, several studies have raised concerns regarding their use in education. Importantly, learning depends on how students engage with LLMs. This study examined how two types of LLM-based tutors shape students' prompting practices, learning, and subsequent LLM-use: a Socratic-Guidance (SG) tutor, which structures interaction through dialogic questioning, and a Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor that guides the formulation of effective prompts. We conducted a two-phase study in a graduate-level mobile robotics course: 66 students used either the SG or PR tutor during a 6-week intervention, followed by 52 students using an unconstrained LLM during a 3-week course project. Results show that while the SG- and PR tutors led to similar task performance and prompting patterns during guided use, they differ in learning outcomes and later LLM-use. SG-students, relative to PR-student, achieved higher learning gains in later sessions, and were more likely to adopt understanding-driven prompting strategies, which are predictive of higher understanding, when using an unconstrained LLM. Although learners perceived the SG tutor as less efficient, the findings suggest that Socratic guidance supports the development of students' capacity to learn with LLMs over time, highlighting its importance for LLM tutor design.

AI.tldr: This study compares two LLM-based tutors—Socratic-Guidance (SG) and Prompt-Refinement (PR)—in a graduate robotics course, finding that while both yield similar task performance during guided use, SG tutors produce higher learning gains and foster understanding-driven prompting strategies when students later use an unconstrained LLM, despite being perceived as less efficient.
AI.motivation: Several studies have raised concerns about LLM use in education, and learning outcomes depend critically on how students engage with LLMs. This work investigates whether different LLM tutor designs can shape students' prompting practices and learning trajectories.
AI.method: Two-phase study in a graduate-level mobile robotics course: Phase 1 (6-week intervention) had 66 students using either a Socratic-Guidance (SG) tutor (dialogic questioning) or a Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor (guiding effective prompt formulation). Phase 2 (3-week course project) had 52 students using an unconstrained LLM to assess transfer effects.
AI.result: SG and PR tutors led to similar task performance and prompting patterns during guided use, but SG students achieved higher learning gains in later sessions and were more likely to adopt understanding-driven prompting strategies when using an unconstrained LLM. Understanding-driven prompting was predictive of higher understanding. Learners perceived the SG tutor as less efficient.
AI.conclusion: Socratic guidance supports the development of students' capacity to learn with LLMs over time, highlighting its importance for LLM tutor design despite lower perceived efficiency.

title: OmniFocus: Query-Guided Modality-Balanced Token Compression for Omni-Modal Large Language Models
summary: Omni modal large language models (OmniLLMs) have attracted wide attention for their ability to jointly process audio and video, but they generate large token sequences under audio-visual inputs, leading to substantial inference cost. Existing audio-visual token compression methods often rely on unimodal guidance, overlooking the temporal locality of query-relevant evidence in audio-visual inputs and implicitly assuming that the two modalities share a temporally aligned information density distribution. We propose \textbf{OmniFocus}, a training-free query-guided token compression method for OmniLLMs that performs independent importance estimation for video and audio, enabling a modality-symmetric compression design that preserves modality-specific salient evidence while maintaining audio-visual alignment, thereby mitigating the modality bias issue that can arise from unimodal-guided compression. Experiments on the Qwen2.5-Omni model family across four audio-visual benchmarks show that OmniFocus maintains strong compressed performance at low token retention ratios and outperforms existing baselines on several major benchmark scores at 25\% token retention. On DailyOmni with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B at 25\% token retention, OmniFocus maintains 59.40 accuracy while delivering up to 1.38$\times$ prefill speedup relative to the full-token baseline, highlighting a favorable practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: OmniFocus is a training-free, query-guided token compression method for OmniLLMs that independently estimates importance for video and audio, enabling modality-symmetric compression to preserve salient evidence while maintaining cross-modal alignment. It achieves strong results at low token retention ratios (e.g., 25%) on Qwen2.5-Omni models across four benchmarks, delivering up to 1.38× prefill speedup with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-visual token compression methods rely on unimodal guidance, overlooking temporal locality of query-relevant evidence and assuming temporally aligned information density across modalities, which leads to modality bias and suboptimal compression.
AI.method: OmniFocus performs query-guided, independent importance estimation for video and audio modalities, followed by a modality-symmetric compression design that preserves modality-specific salient evidence while maintaining audio-visual alignment, all without requiring additional training.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B at 25% token retention on DailyOmni, OmniFocus achieves 59.40 accuracy with 1.38× prefill speedup. It outperforms existing baselines on multiple benchmarks at low token retention ratios.
AI.conclusion: OmniFocus offers a favorable practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off for OmniLLM inference, mitigating modality bias and maintaining strong performance under aggressive token compression.

title: A Preliminary Study on Explaining Risk of Code Changes using LLM-Based Prediction Models
summary: Predictions by machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) models are often received skeptically unless they are paired with intelligible explanations. In the context of just-in-time defect prediction, highlighting small portions of a software change (diff) -- beyond rule-based lints -- where risk may be concentrated has not yet been extensively investigated. In this work, we leverage attention weights from an LLM-based Diff Risk Score (DRS) model to highlight parts of a diff that the model focuses on when predicting risk. We aggregate token-level attention into interpretable code units (lines, hunks, and files), and present the top-K units to developers as a lightweight form of guidance during code review. We evaluate our approach using expert-labeled changes that have caused real outages. Results show that the highlighted snippets cover expert-labeled outage-causing change lines 53.85% of the time when highlighting the top-2 hunks, while requiring developers to review 26.28% of the changed lines on average. Because attention is produced during standard model inference, the approach is scalable for large development workflows and can be surfaced in the code review UI with low additional latency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using attention weights from an LLM-based Diff Risk Score (DRS) model to highlight risky code regions in software diffs for just-in-time defect prediction, showing that top-2 hunks cover 53.85% of actual outage-causing lines while requiring review of only 26.28% of changed lines.
AI.motivation: ML/AI predictions are often met with skepticism without intelligible explanations, and highlighting risk-concentrated portions of software diffs beyond rule-based lints has not been extensively investigated in just-in-time defect prediction.
AI.method: Uses attention weights from an LLM-based Diff Risk Score (DRS) model to identify which parts of a diff the model focuses on, then aggregates token-level attention into interpretable code units (lines, hunks, files) and presents the top-K units as guidance during code review.
AI.result: Highlighted snippets cover expert-labeled outage-causing change lines 53.85% of the time when highlighting the top-2 hunks, requiring developers to review only 26.28% of changed lines on average.
AI.conclusion: The attention-based highlighting approach is scalable for large development workflows, introduces low additional latency, and can be surfaced in code review UIs as a lightweight guidance mechanism.

title: Dynamic Regret for Non-Stationary Linear Bandits via Misspecification Reductions
summary: Many online decision-making problems involve both round-specific feasible actions and drifting reward models: eligible ad impressions, feasible prices, and available treatments can change over time, while user preferences, demand curves, and patient responses may evolve. Motivated by these applications, we study non-stationary linear bandits with round-specific feasible decision sets. Existing methods that obtain the optimal \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) dependence, where \(P_T\) is the path length of the reward-parameter sequence, impose an orthogonal-structure assumption on round-specific decision sets, which can be restrictive in contextual applications. We address this gap through a unified misspecification-reduction viewpoint: after partitioning the horizon into blocks, we relate each block's dynamic regret to regret against a fixed-parameter linear bandit benchmark, with the within-block parameter drift entering as bounded misspecification. Restarting algorithms with misspecification-dependent regret guarantees then yields the optimal \(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3}\) dynamic-regret dependence for both linear bandits with general compact decision sets and \(K\)-armed contextual linear bandits.

AI.tldr: The paper studies non-stationary linear bandits with round-specific feasible decision sets, achieving optimal \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) dynamic regret without assuming orthogonal decision-set structure, by using a misspecification-reduction framework with restarting algorithms.
AI.motivation: Existing methods achieving optimal dynamic regret for non-stationary linear bandits require an orthogonal-structure assumption on round-specific decision sets, which is restrictive in many contextual applications like ad impressions, pricing, and treatment assignment. The authors aim to remove this assumption while retaining optimal regret guarantees.
AI.method: The paper employs a unified misspecification-reduction viewpoint: partition the horizon into blocks, relate each block's dynamic regret to regret against a fixed-parameter linear bandit benchmark (treating within-block parameter drift as bounded misspecification), and then restart algorithms that have misspecification-dependent regret guarantees.
AI.result: Achieves the optimal \(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3}\) dynamic-regret dependence for both linear bandits with general compact decision sets and \(K\)-armed contextual linear bandits, without requiring orthogonal-structure assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The misspecification-reduction framework effectively removes the restrictive orthogonal-structure assumption, enabling optimal dynamic regret for non-stationary linear bandits in broader real-world settings.

title: Evaluating Intellectual Property Guardrails of Generative Image Models: A Technical Report
summary: Generative image models are capable of producing images that bear a strong resemblance to, or replicate, recognizable intellectual property (IP). In this technical report, we present a benchmark and automated evaluation pipeline to test for evidence of IP guardrails in generative image models along with the propensity for these models to generate images with recognizable IP. The IP categories we tested include fictional characters, celebrity likeness, and commercial logos and do not encompass the full range of IP which may be implicated by image generation models. We evaluated fourteen widely used text-to-image models, including three self-hosted open weights models and eleven private models. While all of the private models were observed to refuse generations at some level due to IP guardrails, the frequency of generation refusals varied substantially among models. The refusal rates also varied considerably across the different IP categories tested. Commercial logos were refused least frequently and were successfully generated at the highest rate, on average. Though the rate varies, all models tested readily generated images containing recognizable IP as of March 2026.

AI.tldr: This report presents a benchmark for testing IP guardrails in text-to-image generative models, evaluating 14 models (3 open-weight, 11 private) across fictional characters, celebrity likenesses, and commercial logos. Results show all private models have IP guardrails but refuse at varying rates; commercial logos are refused least and generated most. As of March 2026, all models still readily generate recognizable IP.
AI.motivation: Generative image models can produce images that replicate or strongly resemble recognizable intellectual property (IP), raising legal and ethical concerns. The authors aim to systematically benchmark and evaluate the effectiveness of IP guardrails across different models and IP categories.
AI.method: The authors constructed a benchmark and automated evaluation pipeline to test IP guardrails in text-to-image models. They evaluated 14 models (3 self-hosted open-weight, 11 private) across three IP categories: fictional characters, celebrity likenesses, and commercial logos.
AI.result: All private models exhibited some level of generation refusal due to IP guardrails, but refusal rates varied substantially across models and IP categories. Commercial logos had the lowest refusal rate and highest successful generation rate. As of March 2026, all tested models still readily generated images containing recognizable IP.
AI.conclusion: IP guardrails in generative image models are inconsistent and insufficient; commercial logos are particularly vulnerable. Despite guardrails, all models as of March 2026 can generate recognizable IP, indicating a need for stronger and more uniform protections.

title: When Aggregate Alignment Misleads: Auditing Policy Repair Without Per-State Expert Actions
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly used to edit, refine, and repair decision policies, but evaluating these edits is difficult when per-state expert action labels are unavailable. We study this problem in a hotel-pricing simulator where an agentic policy editor receives only region-level diagnostic feedback: summaries of how its price distribution differs from a benchmark policy across time, inventory, and market regions. The editor cannot observe benchmark actions, benchmark source code, reward numbers, or held-out outcomes, and may only propose constrained edits to a target-action table. On 5,000 held-out episodes, a multi-restart LLM editor reaches RevPAR 108.47 (95% CI 107.61 - 109.34), close to the benchmark policy's 108.75 (107.81 - 109.68), with paired gap (LLM minus benchmark) -0.276 and 95% CI [-0.692, 0.146]. A cheap diagnostic projection already recovers much of the revenue (107.90), so the LLM editor's distinctive gain is not raw revenue lift alone: it also reduces episode composition distance from 1.153 to 0.609. This is the strongest non-benchmark repair result. This profile is not explained by restart search alone: non-semantic proposers with up to 2,500 evaluations fall 8.77 - 14.57 RevPAR points short. Nor is it explained by plausible prompt format: a shuffled-diagnostic control breaks region-error correspondence and falls to RevPAR 94.30. The match is genuine but partial. A tree editor achieves stronger pooled alignment, 0.214 versus 0.266, and stronger reference-state D1, 0.328 versus 1.197, yet revenue falls to 98.91. These results show that agentic policy repair should be evaluated by whether diagnostic feedback becomes reliable closed-loop outcome, not by a single behavioral distance.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based agentic policy editor, using only region-level diagnostic feedback (not per-state labels or benchmarks), nearly matches a benchmark policy's revenue (RevPAR 108.47 vs 108.75) and significantly reduces episode composition distance, outperforming non-semantic proposers and shuffled-diagnostic controls, though a tree editor achieves better alignment at the cost of lower revenue, suggesting evaluation should focus on closed-loop diagnostic reliability rather than single behavioral metrics.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether agentic AI systems can effectively edit and repair decision policies when only coarse, region-level diagnostic feedback is available, without access to per-state expert labels, benchmark actions, source code, or reward numbers.
AI.method: A multi-restart LLM editor operates in a hotel-pricing simulator, receiving only region-level diagnostic summaries about price distribution differences from a benchmark. It proposes constrained edits to a target-action table, evaluated on 5,000 held-out episodes. Comparisons include a cheap diagnostic projection baseline, non-semantic proposers (up to 2,500 evaluations), a shuffled-diagnostic control, and a tree editor.
AI.result: LLM editor achieves RevPAR 108.47 (CI: 107.61-109.34), near benchmark's 108.75; paired gap -0.276 (CI: -0.692, 0.146). Episode composition distance reduces from 1.153 to 0.609. Non-semantic proposers fall 8.77-14.57 RevPAR short; shuffled-diagnostic control drops to 94.30. Tree editor has better alignment (0.214 vs 0.266) and D1 (0.328 vs 1.197) but revenue only 98.91.
AI.conclusion: Agentic policy repair should be evaluated by whether diagnostic feedback becomes a reliable closed-loop outcome signal, not by a single behavioral distance metric.

title: UniSkip-Mamba: A Frequency-Aware State Space Model for Audio-Visual Temporal Forgery Localization
summary: With the proliferation of AI-generated content, sophisticated multimedia manipulation has raised critical concerns about malicious applications such as opinion manipulation and evidence fabrication, making Audio-Visual Temporal Forgery Localization (AV-TFL) an urgent research frontier. Existing TFL methods have progressed along two main paradigms: Transformer-based temporal modeling and channel-wise multimodal fusion. While these approaches capture temporal dependencies and cross-modal correlations, they process all frequency components indiscriminately, leading to overfitting on high-frequency noise and limited robustness under real-world data degradation. Through systematic frequency domain analysis, we find that forgery-discriminative patterns concentrate in the low/mid-frequency range (normalized frequency 0-0.15), while high-frequency components primarily introduce noise, removing them even improves detection performance by +1.4%. Based on this phenomenon, we propose UniSkip-Mamba, a frequency-aware State Space Model framework that incorporates Unified Multimodal Sequence Fusion to preserve cross-modal phase relationships, and Skip-Scanning Mamba Blocks that implement frequency-aware regularization through a novel Group-Scan-Merge mechanism, naturally biasing learning toward discriminative low/mid-frequency patterns (0-0.15) while maintaining representational completeness. We achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance: 63.4% AP@0.95 on LAV-DF (+9.8% improvement) and 63.58% mAP on AV-Deepfake1M (+14.32% improvement), with 6x faster inference. Our frequency-domain analysis provides theoretical justification from a signal processing perspective for why skip-scanning inherently improves both accuracy and robustness.

AI.tldr: UniSkip-Mamba is a frequency-aware State Space Model for Audio-Visual Temporal Forgery Localization that exploits the finding that forgery-discriminative patterns reside in low/mid-frequency (0-0.15 normalized), achieving SOTA performance (63.4% AP@0.95 on LAV-DF, +9.8%) with 6x faster inference via Unified Multimodal Sequence Fusion and Skip-Scanning Mamba Blocks.
AI.motivation: AI-generated multimedia manipulation (opinion manipulation, evidence fabrication) makes Audio-Visual Temporal Forgery Localization urgently needed, yet existing Transformer-based and multimodal fusion methods process all frequency components indiscriminately, causing overfitting to high-frequency noise and limited robustness under real-world data degradation.
AI.method: (1) Frequency-domain analysis revealing forgery-discriminative patterns in low/mid-frequency range (0-0.15 normalized), with high-frequency removal improving detection by +1.4%. (2) UniSkip-Mamba framework with Unified Multimodal Sequence Fusion to preserve cross-modal phase relationships, and Skip-Scanning Mamba Blocks implementing frequency-aware regularization via a Group-Scan-Merge mechanism that biases learning toward discriminative low/mid-frequency patterns while maintaining representational completeness.
AI.result: 63.4% AP@0.95 on LAV-DF (+9.8% improvement), 63.58% mAP on AV-Deepfake1M (+14.32% improvement), 6x faster inference.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain analysis provides theoretical justification from a signal processing perspective for why skip-scanning inherently improves both accuracy and robustness, establishing frequency-aware modeling as a promising direction for AV-TFL.

title: A Systematic Methodology for Evaluating Failure Independence in LLM-Generated Code
summary: N-Version Programming (NVP) improves software reliability by executing multiple independent implementations and combining outputs, but its adoption is limited by high cost and the assumption of failure independence, which empirical studies have challenged. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) reduce the cost of generating multiple implementations, shifting focus to whether their failures are independent. We propose the first systematic methodology to assess failure independence in LLM-generated code and apply it to 224 problems across twelve models, five languages, and three prompting strategies. We analyze both structural and behavioral diversity (i.e., whether implementations fail on the same test cases), complemented by N-version reliability analysis under majority voting and manual inspection of the generated code. Structural diversity analysis shows that implementations from the same model are highly similar, while different models produce more distinct solutions. The same trend appears in behavioral diversity, with implementations from different models showing higher diversity yet still failing on the same tests far more often than expected under independence. N-version reliability analysis reinforces this: three- and five-version ensembles realize only 0.43 and 0.44 of the reliability gain achievable under independence, dropping below 0.3 when ensembles are built from the same model. Manual fault analysis shows that even different failure patterns often share root causes. Overall, these results suggest LLM-generated solutions do not satisfy NVP's failure independence assumption, though heterogeneous models help partially. They also validate our methodology as a tool for systematically evaluating failure independence as models evolve.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated code fails to satisfy N-version Programming's failure independence assumption; implementations from different models show higher diversity but still fail on the same tests far more often than expected, achieving only 0.43–0.44 of the theoretical reliability gain under independence.
AI.motivation: N-version Programming (NVP) improves reliability via multiple independent implementations, but adoption is limited by high cost and questionable failure independence assumptions. LLMs reduce generation cost, but it is unclear whether LLM-generated code exhibits independent failures.
AI.method: Proposed the first systematic methodology to assess failure independence in LLM-generated code, analyzing structural diversity (code similarity) and behavioral diversity (test failure overlap) across 12 models, 5 languages, 3 prompting strategies, and 224 problems, complemented by N-version reliability analysis and manual fault inspection.
AI.result: Same-model implementations are structurally highly similar; different models produce more distinct solutions. Behavioral diversity is higher across models, yet failure overlaps exceed independence expectations. Three- and five-version ensembles achieve only 0.43 and 0.44 of the reliability gain possible under independence, dropping below 0.3 for same-model ensembles. Different failure patterns often share root causes.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated solutions do not satisfy NVP's failure independence assumption, though heterogeneous models offer partial improvement. The proposed methodology provides a systematic framework for evaluating failure independence as models evolve.

title: Variable Bit-width Quantization: Learning Per-Group Precision for "Bigger-but-Smaller" Language Models
summary: Low-bit quantization shrinks language models but treats precision as a single global hyper-parameter: every weight uses the same bit-width. We introduce Variable Bit-width Quantization (VBQ), a training-time method in which each contiguous group of 64 weights learns its own resolution from {1,2,4,8} bits via a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, trained jointly by an alternating optimization that gives the precision logits a clean, task-aligned signal. VBQ discovers a consistent, strongly heterogeneous allocation within individual projection types, not merely across layers, impossible to express with per-layer methods: 69% of groups collapse to 1 bit, the LM head averages 1.09 bits, while the first MLP block keeps ~2.5 bits. This pattern is stable enough to freeze into a fixed recipe and reuse without further search. The recipe yields a "bigger-but-smaller" regime: a 131M model at 1.82 mean bits reaches perplexity 4.2 on TinyStories, beating a 55M FP16 model (PPL 4.4) at 3.8x less storage, and lets a 1.46B model on FineWeb-Edu match a 593M FP16 control at ~3.7x less storage with 2.5x more parameters. As quality-per-byte, VBQ is 3.9-8.4x more efficient than FP16. The recipe maps directly to packed low-bit storage, so it also accelerates inference: with custom fused dequantize-and-multiply kernels, memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decode is faster at equal output, and the speedup grows with scale (parity at 131M, 1.9x at 1.0B, 4.7x at 9B on Apple silicon). A distributional analysis (KL divergence and argmax-flip rate) reveals a striking mechanism: deeper layers progressively self-heal the quantization error injected by early layers. The win is a from-scratch, train-time phenomenon; scaling the search economically beyond 1.5B parameters remains open. VBQ reframes precision as a learnable, non-uniform resource and shows that spending a fixed bit budget unevenly beats spending it uniformly.

AI.tldr: VBQ introduces variable bit-width quantization where each contiguous group of 64 weights learns its own precision (1,2,4,8 bits) via Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, achieving 3.9-8.4x better quality-per-byte than FP16. A 131M model at 1.82 mean bits beats a 55M FP16 model, and the method shows that deeper layers self-heal quantization errors, with consistent allocation patterns that can be frozen into reusable recipes.
AI.motivation: Standard low-bit quantization treats precision as a single global hyper-parameter where every weight uses the same bit-width, failing to leverage the fact that different weights can tolerate different levels of quantization. The goal is to reframe precision as a learnable, non-uniform resource to achieve better efficiency.
AI.method: VBQ uses a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation over {1,2,4,8} bits for each contiguous group of 64 weights, trained via alternating optimization to provide task-aligned signals to precision logits. The learned allocation patterns are frozen into fixed recipes for reuse without further search, and custom fused dequantize-and-multiply kernels accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound inference.
AI.result: 69% of groups collapse to 1 bit; LM head averages 1.09 bits; first MLP block keeps ~2.5 bits. A 131M model at 1.82 mean bits achieves PPL 4.2 on TinyStories, beating a 55M FP16 model (PPL 4.4) at 3.8x less storage. A 1.46B model matches a 593M FP16 control at ~3.7x less storage. VBQ is 3.9-8.4x more efficient than FP16 in quality-per-byte. Inference speedup reaches 1.9x at 1.0B and 4.7x at 9B on Apple silicon.
AI.conclusion: VBQ reframes precision as a learnable, non-uniform resource; spending a fixed bit budget unevenly beats spending it uniformly. Deeper layers progressively self-heal quantization errors from earlier layers. The win is a from-scratch, train-time phenomenon, though scaling the search beyond 1.5B parameters remains an open challenge.

title: RotateAttention: RoPE-Aware Rotation and Range Rectification for INT4 Quantized Attention in Video Generation
summary: In \textbf{DiT-based video generation models equipped with 3D Rotary Position Embeddings (3D RoPE)}, the attention mechanism remains a primary computational bottleneck due to its quadratic complexity with respect to sequence length. While quantized \textbf{FlashAttention} offers a promising path toward hardware acceleration, existing low-bit quantization methods overlook two critical challenges in this setting: \textbf{1)} applying online rotation matrices -- a widely used technique for mitigating outliers in Queries ($Q$) and Keys ($K$) -- is difficult to reconcile with \textbf{RoPE}; and \textbf{2)} the non-negative attention matrix $P = \exp(QK - \max(QK))$ makes symmetric quantization waste half of the 4-bit dynamic range. In this work, we observe that the outlier distributions of $Q$ and $K$ are strongly affected by the dimensional partitioning of \textbf{3D RoPE}. Based on this finding, we propose \textbf{RotateAttention}, an efficient \textbf{mixed-precision INT4 FlashAttention} framework tailored for \textbf{DiT-based video generation models with 3D RoPE}, using selective \textbf{FP16 fallback} for accuracy-sensitive attention blocks and denoising steps. RotateAttention introduces two core techniques: \textbf{1) RoPE-aware Rotation}, which employs either mergeable rotation matrices that can be fused into RoPE or negligible-overhead matrices to mitigate RoPE-induced outliers in $Q$ and $K$; and \textbf{2) Range-optimized $P$ Quantization}, which uses fixed scales and zero-points to fully exploit the \textbf{INT4 numerical range} with minimal computational overhead. Experiments show that \textbf{RotateAttention} preserves video generation quality nearly identical to full-precision baselines while achieving up to 1.68$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 2.2$\times$ kernel-level acceleration.

AI.tldr: RotateAttention is a mixed-precision INT4 FlashAttention framework for DiT-based video generation with 3D RoPE, achieving up to 1.68× end-to-end speedup by addressing RoPE-induced outliers and optimizing asymmetric quantization of non-negative attention matrices.
AI.motivation: Existing low-bit quantization for FlashAttention in DiT-based video generation with 3D RoPE faces two challenges: (1) online rotation matrices for outlier mitigation conflict with RoPE; (2) symmetric quantization wastes half the INT4 range on non-negative attention matrices P = exp(QK - max(QK)).
AI.method: Two core techniques: (1) RoPE-aware Rotation — uses mergeable rotation matrices fused into RoPE or negligible-overhead matrices to mitigate RoPE-induced Q/K outliers; (2) Range-optimized P Quantization — applies fixed scales and zero-points to fully exploit INT4 range. Selective FP16 fallback is used for accuracy-sensitive attention blocks and denoising steps.
AI.result: Preserves video generation quality nearly identical to full-precision baselines, with up to 1.68× end-to-end speedup and 2.2× kernel-level acceleration.
AI.conclusion: RotateAttention effectively enables efficient 4-bit quantized FlashAttention for 3D RoPE-based video diffusion models by addressing both RoPE-outlier interactions and asymmetric quantization waste.

title: From Mobile Data to Business Insights: An End-to-End Analytics Framework for Large-Scale Urban Mobility Analysis and Decision Support
summary: Real time location data derived from mobile applications is a powerful tool for addressing various urban challenges, including tourism planning, parking management, bus route optimization, and resource allocation. Besides, it offers invaluable insights for shaping strategic decisions in commercial domains such as location based services, market share analysis, and behavioral profiling. In this expansive study, we aim to address all of the aforementioned challenges by investigating the behaviors and patterns of smartphone users within urban environments, particularly in the domains of tourism, transportation, and retail. Our approach encompasses the development of a sophisticated data platform from inception to implementation, which includes the formulation of use cases, architectural design, and implementation of modules. We employ state of the art techniques and technologies, including data anonymization, ETL pipelines, and utilizing Google BigQuery and Vertex AI for data processing and machine learning model development. A modular architecture based on reusable analytical building blocks was developed to generate data products that support multiple stakeholder driven use cases. Additionally, we apply interactive data visualization techniques via Power BI to facilitate the effective interpretation of analytical findings by stakeholders. The developed models address a wide range of mobility analytics tasks, including mobility profiling, frequent trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin destination pattern analysis. The results demonstrate the framework's ability to capture user mobility dynamics at fine spatial and temporal resolutions, providing actionable insights for urban planning and strategic business decision making.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive data platform built on mobile location data to analyze urban mobility patterns across tourism, transportation, and retail domains. It integrates Google BigQuery, Vertex AI, and Power BI with a modular architecture to support tasks like mobility profiling, trajectory mining, anomaly detection, and origin-destination analysis, yielding actionable insights for urban planning and business strategy.
AI.motivation: Real-time location data from mobile apps can address urban challenges (tourism, parking, transit optimization) and support commercial decisions (location-based services, market analysis), but a comprehensive platform integrating these capabilities is lacking.
AI.method: The authors developed a data platform from conception to implementation, including use case formulation, modular architecture design with reusable analytical building blocks, ETL pipelines, data anonymization, Google BigQuery and Vertex AI for processing and ML, and Power BI for interactive visualization.
AI.result: The models successfully perform mobility profiling, frequent trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin-destination pattern analysis, capturing user mobility dynamics at fine spatiotemporal resolutions.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides actionable insights for urban planning and strategic business decision-making, demonstrating its effectiveness in analyzing smartphone user behaviors across tourism, transportation, and retail domains.

title: Quantum-Inspired Harmonic Decision Models: A Computational Framework for Music Generation
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures. Preprint. Code and evaluation data available at GitHub
summary:
This paper introduces a quantum-inspired computational framework for harmonic decision-making in music. The proposed approach formulates harmonization as an optimization problem within a structured combinatorial space, where multiple candidate chord sequences are evaluated under interacting musical constraints. The model combines an interference-based harmonization stage with a classical optimization procedure grounded in tonal harmony. The quantum-inspired component enables the parallel consideration of multiple harmonic alternatives, while the classical stage refines the resulting sequences to ensure structural coherence and stylistic plausibility.
  The framework is evaluated on selected musical examples, including Autumn Leaves and It's a Long Way to Tipperary. Quantitative analysis shows that the optimization stage significantly reduces chord density, increases harmonic stability, and improves functional organization. At the same time, expert evaluation highlights the importance of stylistic context, demonstrating that increased harmonic complexity is not always perceived as more natural. The results suggest that harmonic generation can be interpreted as a structured decision-making process in a constrained search space. The proposed approach provides a computational model that integrates domain-specific knowledge with an interference-based search mechanism.
  Although preliminary, this work indicates that quantum-inspired methods may offer a useful framework for modeling complex decision processes in creative domains such as music. The proposed framework contributes to ongoing research on quantum-inspired models of cognition and decision-making in complex biological and creative systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum-inspired computational framework for music harmonization that combines an interference-based search mechanism with classical optimization, evaluated on jazz standards. The hybrid approach reduces chord density, increases harmonic stability, and improves functional organization, though expert evaluation reveals that complexity does not always align with perceived naturalness.
AI.motivation: To develop a computational model for harmonic decision-making in music that integrates domain-specific musical knowledge with quantum-inspired search mechanisms, treating harmonization as a structured optimization problem in a constrained combinatorial space.
AI.method: A two-stage hybrid framework: (1) a quantum-inspired interference-based stage that enables parallel evaluation of multiple harmonic alternatives, followed by (2) a classical optimization stage grounded in tonal harmony theory that refines chord sequences for structural coherence and stylistic plausibility.
AI.result: Quantitative results show significant reduction in chord density, increased harmonic stability, and improved functional organization. Expert evaluation indicates that increased harmonic complexity is not always perceived as more natural, highlighting the importance of stylistic context.
AI.conclusion: Harmonic generation can be interpreted as a structured decision-making process in a constrained search space. Quantum-inspired methods offer a useful framework for modeling complex decision processes in creative domains like music, contributing to research on quantum-inspired models of cognition and decision-making.

title: EvoOtter: Evolutionary Reproduction Test Generator
summary: Before fixing an issue, it is useful to first reproduce it by generating a bug reproduction test (BRT). However, generating a BRT is itself a challenging task, because issue descriptions tend to be informal, making it difficult to determine whether a candidate BRT indeed fails for the reason in the issue. Prior work has attempted to tackle this problem via inference scaling, using large language models to generate many BRTs and patches, then using execution feedback to select and improve them. Unfortunately, this is expensive and the feedback is unreliable. This paper explores evolutionary programming for BRT generation to sharpen the feedback, while enhancing evolutionary programming to keep costs in check. Our new approach, EvoOtter, controls test execution costs via successive halving. Furthermore, it controls LLM costs via batched crossover for an entire generation in a single LLM call, as well as via rule-based code mutations, with a new fitness score tailored for BRTs. As a result, EvoOtter generates state-of-the-art quality BRTs at the fraction of the cost of prior inference-scaling approaches to this problem. More broadly, this paper points at how to efficiently and effectively combine evolutionary programming with large language models for software engineering.

AI.tldr: EvoOtter combines evolutionary programming with LLMs to efficiently generate bug reproduction tests at state-of-the-art quality and lower cost than prior inference-scaling methods.
AI.motivation: Generating bug reproduction tests (BRTs) is challenging because issue descriptions are informal, making it hard to verify if a candidate BRT fails for the correct reason. Prior inference-scaling approaches using LLMs are expensive and rely on unreliable execution feedback.
AI.method: EvoOtter uses successive halving to control test execution costs, batched crossover for an entire generation in a single LLM call to control LLM costs, rule-based code mutations, and a novel fitness score tailored for BRTs.
AI.result: EvoOtter generates state-of-the-art quality BRTs at a fraction of the cost of prior inference-scaling approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates how to efficiently and effectively combine evolutionary programming with LLMs for software engineering tasks like BRT generation.

title: Bootstrap Flow-Map Tree Sampling Enables Online Feedback Driven Search
summary: In many scientific and engineering domains, maximizing discovery within a limited sampling budget demands strategic, observation-guided exploration. While generative models have enabled training-free reward alignment, current methods typically excel in local searches within narrow regions of the underlying distribution. These approaches struggle when preferences are unknown a priori and only revealed through sequential feedback-a scenario demanding broad exploration to uncover high-utility regions. To address this, we introduce Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree (a.k.a BFMT), a novel computationally efficient sampling framework designed for history-aware global search and alignment under sampling budget constraints. BFMT enables full tree-path construction from any tree depth using a single function evaluation, drastically reducing computational overhead while providing critical foresight for sequential sampling. By enabling dynamic transition time steps scheduling, BFMT efficiently allocates its sampling budget, smoothly transitioning from broad global exploration to fine-grained local refinement of high-utility modes discovered through exploration. Extensive experiments and ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks demonstrate that BFMT substantially outperforms baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: BFMT is a computationally efficient sampling framework that enables history-aware global exploration and alignment under budget constraints by constructing full tree-paths from any depth with a single function evaluation and dynamic scheduling of transition time steps.
AI.motivation: Existing generative model alignment methods excel in local searches within narrow distribution regions but struggle when preferences are unknown a priori and only revealed through sequential feedback, requiring broad exploration to uncover high-utility regions under limited sampling budgets.
AI.method: BFMT (Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree) constructs full tree-paths from any tree depth using a single function evaluation, reducing computational overhead, and employs dynamic transition time steps scheduling to smoothly transition from global exploration to local refinement of high-utility modes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks show BFMT substantially outperforms baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: BFMT provides an effective solution for budget-constrained global search and alignment where preferences are unknown and sequentially revealed, bridging the gap between broad exploration and fine-grained local refinement.

title: Reliability-Aware CT-MRI Registration: A Quality Engineering Framework with Stability Analysis and Risk Classification
summary: Multimodal CT-MRI registration is central to image-guided radiotherapy, surgical navigation, and diagnostic workflows, but most pipelines report only aggregate quality metrics without per-case reliability signals. We propose a reliability-aware framework that converts registration quality into Green/Yellow/Red risk categories using data-learned thresholds. CT images were registered to T1-weighted MRI using rigid and affine transformations on 90 paired slices from 18 patients across brain, abdominal, and neck anatomies. Reliability was assessed using Delta NMI, Delta SSIM, Dice overlap, registration stability, and inverse consistency error, combined into a single score R. Thresholds learned from training patients were applied unchanged to held-out test patients. Affine registration outperformed rigid registration on NMI and SSIM, yielding 44% Green classifications versus 33% for rigid. Reliability-filtered registrations improved the average alignment profile compared with unfiltered methods. Per-anatomy analysis showed substantial variation, with stronger reliability for abdominal registrations than brain registrations. Weight sensitivity analysis identified Dice overlap as the dominant reliability component. The proposed framework provides an interpretable quality-control layer for multimodal registration, while risk thresholds reflect statistical rather than clinical validation.

AI.tldr: A reliability-aware framework is proposed to classify multimodal CT-MRI registration quality into Green/Yellow/Red risk categories using data-learned thresholds combining Delta NMI, Delta SSIM, Dice overlap, stability, and inverse consistency into a single score R, tested on 90 paired slices from 18 patients across brain, abdominal, and neck anatomies.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal CT-MRI registration pipelines report only aggregate quality metrics without providing per-case reliability signals, limiting their clinical trustworthiness.
AI.method: CT images were registered to T1-weighted MRI using rigid and affine transformations on 90 paired slices from 18 patients across brain, abdominal, and neck anatomies. Reliability combined Delta NMI, Delta SSIM, Dice overlap, registration stability, and inverse consistency error into a single score R with data-learned thresholds for Green/Yellow/Red classification.
AI.result: Affine registration achieved 44% Green classifications vs. 33% for rigid; reliability-filtered registrations improved average alignment; abdominal registrations showed stronger reliability than brain; Dice overlap was the dominant reliability component.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an interpretable quality-control layer for multimodal registration, with the caveat that risk thresholds reflect statistical rather than clinical validation.

title: Efficient bias mitigation in T2I diffusion models using Concept Graphs
summary: Text-to-Image diffusion models often propagate harmful bias inherited from the training data. Existing bias mitigation techniques typically intervene only at the text encoder or provide inference-time guidance, often leading to generations that collapse into semantically incoherent outputs. To address these limitations, we introduce CO-ALIGN (Concept Ontology Alignment), a novel bias mitigation approach based on concept-graph alignment that operates on the model's internal concept ontology. By aligning concepts within the text encoder and denoiser, CO-ALIGN achieves substantial bias reduction while preserving generative integrity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of concept-graph alignment across three paradigms: text-encoders, denoisers and joint text-denoiser ontology alignment. CO-ALIGN outperforms the state of the art, improving fairness by $30\%$, $ΔFID=11.4$ in image quality, $2.8\%$ in image fidelity, all while reducing semantically incoherent outputs by $88\%$. Beyond bias mitigation, we show that CO-ALIGN benefits other downstream tasks as well. In particular, our experiments demonstrate that better-aligned internal ontologies enhance concept unlearning robustness across multiple unlearning techniques.

AI.tldr: CO-ALIGN introduces concept-graph alignment across text encoder and denoiser to mitigate bias in text-to-image diffusion models, achieving superior fairness (+30%), image quality (ΔFID=11.4), fidelity (+2.8%), and reducing incoherent outputs by 88%, while also improving concept unlearning robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing bias mitigation techniques either intervene only at the text encoder or provide inference-time guidance, often resulting in semantically incoherent outputs. The paper aims to overcome these limitations by aligning concepts within the model's internal concept ontology.
AI.method: CO-ALIGN (Concept Ontology Alignment) performs concept-graph alignment on the model's internal concept ontology, operating across three paradigms: text-encoder alignment, denoiser alignment, and joint text-denoiser ontology alignment.
AI.result: Outperforms state of the art with 30% fairness improvement, ΔFID=11.4 in image quality, 2.8% improvement in image fidelity, and 88% reduction in semantically incoherent outputs. Also enhances concept unlearning robustness across multiple techniques.
AI.conclusion: Concept-graph alignment is an effective bias mitigation strategy that preserves generative integrity and benefits downstream tasks like concept unlearning, demonstrating the value of aligning internal ontologies in diffusion models.

title: Determinants and Limits of LLM Security-Tool Orchestration: A Study with HexStrike-AI
summary: Large language model agents driving security tool suites over the Model Context Protocol are increasingly common. Yet the factors that bound their capability remain poorly characterized: how much depends on the model versus the client that drives it, whether constraining the agent to the orchestrator's own tools helps, and where capability is limited by reasoning rather than by missing tools. Using HexStrikeAI, an open-source orchestrator that exposes 150+ tools, as a testbed, we follow a methodology that evaluates the system, diagnoses its failures, and applies targeted improvements. We run 86 picoCTF challenges across seven categories and three difficulty tiers, under three tool-access regimes and three model/client configurations (774 trials). We then apply corrections to existing tools, agent-behavior changes, and eleven new capability tools, and re-run the previously-unsuccessful trials. The diagnosis isolates the driving client as a first-order factor for a fixed model (a 2.1 * gap between two DeepSeek clients) and a monotonic difficulty gradient, with the largest gains in the mid tier. The overall solve rate rises from 55.4% to 72.0%, and every configuration improves significantly (paired McNemar p < 0.001, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals). The residual failures are reasoning- or environment-bound rather than missing-tool. A 60-run stability sub-study finds single-run verdicts reproducible (17/20 unanimous). We discuss what the results imply for how such orchestrators should be evaluated, and we are explicit about the limits: the study uses a single benchmark, the fixes were tuned on the same challenges they were evaluated on, and the client effect is demonstrated for one model only, so its generality to other models remains a hypothesis.
