AI.tldr: Using HexStrikeAI (150+ tools) across 86 picoCTF challenges (774 trials), the paper finds that the orchestrator client drives 2.1× performance gap between two DeepSeek clients, and targeted fixes raise solve rates from 55.4% to 72.0%, with residual failures due to reasoning/environment limits rather than missing tools.
AI.motivation: Despite increasing use of LLM agents driving security tools via MCP, the factors bounding their capability (model vs. client, effect of tool constraints, reasoning vs. missing-tool failures) remain poorly characterized.
AI.method: 86 picoCTF challenges across 7 categories and 3 difficulty tiers, 3 tool-access regimes × 3 model/client configurations (774 trials). Diagnosis, correction of existing tools, agent-behavior changes, and 11 new capability tools; re-run on previously-unsuccessful trials. Stability sub-study with 60 runs.
AI.result: Driving client is a first-order factor (2.1× gap between DeepSeek clients); monotonic difficulty gradient with largest gains in mid tier. Solve rate improves from 55.4% to 72.0% (p < 0.001). Residual failures are reasoning- or environment-bound, not missing-tool. 17/20 unanimous verdicts in stability study.
AI.conclusion: Orchestrator evaluation must account for client effects; client effect demonstrated for only one model, generality remains a hypothesis; fixes tuned on the same benchmark; single-benchmark limitation.

title: CoFEND: A Cross-Modal Fusion End-to-End Network for Cold-Start Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction
summary: Cold-start drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction for new drugs is critical for minimizing unexpected adverse drug reactions. The key challenge is to capture similarity between new and known drugs. However, such similarity is closely associated with complex relationships and mechanisms among drugs, enzymes, transporters, molecular structures, and other biomedical entities. Existing methods have three limitations in capturing such similarity: (1) only partial relationships and mechanisms are considered, which overlooks cross-modal information and yields incomplete or biased similarity modeling; (2) similarity computation between new and known drugs is conducted separately across modalities and performed offline for cold-start DDI prediction, leading to misalignment between similarity computation and DDI prediction; and (3) existing interpretability analyses are typically single-modality and focus primarily on key determinants of the perpetrator drug, while the underlying causes of susceptibility for the victim drug are seldom investigated. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel Cross-Modal-Fused End-to-End Learning Network (CMF-ELN) with three components. First, diverse multimodal information is leveraged to construct four types of drug-centered knowledge graphs, enabling comprehensive similarity modeling under reconstruction-based supervision. Second, a four-channel graph autoencoder is designed to fuse cross-modal similarity within an end-to-end learning framework. Finally, a two-stage interpretability scheme is devised to precisely localize key factors for both perpetrator and victim drugs. Extensive experiments on two real datasets demonstrate that CMF-ELN achieves significantly higher prediction accuracy and more comprehensive interpretability of mechanisms than its peers.

AI.tldr: CMF-ELN is a cross-modal, end-to-end network for cold-start DDI prediction that fuses four types of drug-centered knowledge graphs via a four-channel graph autoencoder and provides two-stage interpretability for both perpetrator and victim drugs, outperforming existing methods on real datasets.
AI.motivation: Cold-start DDI prediction for new drugs is critical for preventing adverse drug reactions, but existing methods capture drug similarity incompletely due to ignoring cross-modal information, misaligning similarity computation with prediction, and lacking victim-drug interpretability.
AI.method: (1) Constructs four types of drug-centered knowledge graphs from multimodal data for comprehensive similarity modeling; (2) Designs a four-channel graph autoencoder for cross-modal similarity fusion in an end-to-end learning framework; (3) Devises a two-stage interpretability scheme to localize key factors for both perpetrator and victim drugs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two real datasets show CMF-ELN achieves significantly higher prediction accuracy and more comprehensive mechanism interpretability than its peers.
AI.conclusion: CMF-ELN effectively addresses cross-modal fusion, end-to-end alignment, and dual-side interpretability limitations in cold-start DDI prediction, outperforming existing methods on both accuracy and interpretability.

title: Homer: Understanding Long-form Videos with Hierarchical Memory and Agentic Reasoning
summary: Multimodal large language models excel on short clips but struggle on hour-long videos in an online setting, where frames are processed incrementally under limited memory. Existing online methods either retain compact visual representations that lack semantic structure, or build higher-level memory stores organized around temporal proximity rather than explicit causal links, leaving multi-hop narrative reasoning to be reconstructed by the LLM at every query. We bridge this gap with \textsc{Homer}, a Hierarchical Online Memory Exploration and Reasoning framework. \textsc{Homer}'s memory mirrors the multi-scale structure of long videos, ranging from raw perception, to recurring entities, to events connected by explicit temporal and causal relations. Its agentic reasoner then explores this memory the way humans do, locating the relevant scene, looking up details, and composing the answer through multi-round memory retrieval, with a harness that verifies and corrects each step. \textsc{Homer} outperforms the previous best agent method by $+5.5$, $+10.8$, and $+4.4$ points on M3-Bench-robot, M3-Bench-web, and Video-MME-Long, and consistently lifts three various LLM backbones, indicating a model-agnostic structural capability for grounded retrieval over long videos.

AI.tldr: HOMER is a hierarchical online memory framework for hour-long video understanding that organizes memories from raw perception to events with temporal/causal links, and uses an agentic reasoner with multi-round retrieval to achieve state-of-the-art results on long-video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing online video methods struggle with long videos because they either keep compact visual representations lacking semantic structure, or build memory stores organized by temporal proximity rather than explicit causal links, forcing the LLM to reconstruct multi-hop narrative reasoning at every query.
AI.method: HOMER constructs a hierarchical memory mirroring the multi-scale structure of long videos (raw perception → recurring entities → events with temporal/causal relations), and uses an agentic reasoner that explores memory through human-like multi-round retrieval (locating scene → looking up details → composing answer), with a harness that verifies and corrects each step.
AI.result: Outperforms previous best agent method by +5.5, +10.8, and +4.4 points on M3-Bench-robot, M3-Bench-web, and Video-MME-Long respectively, and consistently improves performance across three different LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: HOMER demonstrates a model-agnostic structural capability for grounded retrieval over long videos, showing that hierarchical memory organization with explicit causal relations and agentic multi-step retrieval is effective for hour-long video understanding.

title: Personalized Causal Recourse: A Human-In-The-Loop Approach
comment: Accepted at the 4th World Conference on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI 2026)
summary: Algorithmic recourse addresses the challenge of providing tailored recommendations to users affected by unfavorable machine learning decisions, in potentially high-stakes scenarios. Traditional approaches to recourse often rely on the closest counterfactual explanations or assume a priori knowledge of a user's causal structure, resulting in interventions that overlook individual contexts and specific feature interactions. To overcome these limitations, we study a human-in-the-loop framework that iteratively approximates the user's structural causal model through interactive queries via Bayesian inference before producing recourse recommendations. This framework exploits humans' feedback to improve the identification of causal effects, allowing personalized recourse that is plausible, cost-effective, and aligned with the actual causal dependencies of each user. As a proof of concept, we evaluate this framework through simulated human responses. Our simulations across linear and non-linear causal models show promising results, though challenges remain in capturing complex, non-linear structures, emphasizing the importance of accurate approximations and robust noise distribution modeling.

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop framework that uses Bayesian inference to iteratively approximate users' structural causal models via interactive queries, enabling personalized algorithmic recourse that is plausible, cost-effective, and aligned with individual causal dependencies.
AI.motivation: Traditional recourse methods rely on closest counterfactuals or assume a priori knowledge of causal structures, overlooking individual contexts and specific feature interactions. This work aims to overcome these limitations by incorporating human feedback to personalize recourse recommendations.
AI.method: A human-in-the-loop framework that iteratively approximates the user's structural causal model through interactive queries, using Bayesian inference to improve identification of causal effects before generating recourse recommendations.
AI.result: Simulations across linear and non-linear causal models show promising results; challenges remain in capturing complex non-linear structures, highlighting the need for accurate approximations and robust noise distribution modeling.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables personalized, plausible, and cost-effective recourse aligned with individual causal dependencies, though further work is needed for non-linear models and robust noise modeling.

title: Diagnosis-Driven Automatic Repair for Agentic Workflow via Symbolic Inference
summary: Platform-orchestrated agentic workflows have become a popular paradigm for developing LLM-based applications. However, their reliability remains a major challenge due to the uncertainty of LLM outputs, complex inter-node dependencies, and heterogeneous tool interactions. Existing agentic workflow optimization and agent enhancement methods primarily rely on trajectory-level feedback. Without explicitly identifying the underlying failure root causes, their resulting repair plans are often insufficiently targeted. We propose FlowFixer, a diagnosis-driven automated repair framework for agentic workflows. FlowFixer first transforms workflow executions into unified symbolic traces and performs symbolic inference to derive executable behavioral specifications that capture node correctness, temporal dependencies, and causal relationships. Based on specification verification, it conducts failure attribution and root cause analysis, and then generates targeted repair patches. To reduce verification costs, FlowFixer further employs a multi-dimensional pre-execution assessment to filter infeasible repairs before dynamic verification. We evaluate FlowFixer on workflow failures collected from three popular development platforms: Dify, Coze and n8n. Results show that FlowFixer achieves a repair success rate of 71.3%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by 11.9% to 27.6%. It also improves failure attribution accuracy by 4.8% to 33.1% and root cause analysis accuracy by 15.3% to 38.8%. This work offers a new perspective on reliable diagnosis and repair of agentic workflows through symbolic modeling and inference.

AI.tldr: FlowFixer is a diagnosis-driven automated repair framework for agentic workflows that uses symbolic tracing and inference to identify failure root causes and generate targeted repair patches, achieving 71.3% repair success rate on Dify, Coze, and n8n platforms, outperforming baselines by 11.9%–27.6%.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic workflow optimization and agent enhancement methods rely on trajectory-level feedback without explicitly identifying underlying failure root causes, resulting in insufficiently targeted repair plans.
AI.method: FlowFixer transforms workflow executions into unified symbolic traces, performs symbolic inference to derive executable behavioral specifications (capturing node correctness, temporal dependencies, and causal relationships), conducts failure attribution and root cause analysis via specification verification, generates targeted repair patches, and employs multi-dimensional pre-execution assessment to filter infeasible repairs before dynamic verification.
AI.result: FlowFixer achieves 71.3% repair success rate on Dify, Coze, and n8n platforms, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by 11.9% to 27.6%, improving failure attribution accuracy by 4.8% to 33.1% and root cause analysis accuracy by 15.3% to 38.8%.
AI.conclusion: This work offers a new perspective on reliable diagnosis and repair of agentic workflows through symbolic modeling and inference.

title: In-span learning: adapting reduced-order models using their own predictions
summary: Reduced-order models compress high-dimensional dynamics into low-dimensional representations that can be evaluated rapidly, but they lose accuracy when online dynamics drift beyond the training data. Adaptive methods address this by updating the subspace online with external, out-of-span information, such as full-order corrections or sensor snapshots. We discovered that a complementary and previously unexploited in-span adaptation channel exists within the current reduced subspace. By streaming the model's own predictions through an incremental singular-value decomposition with forgetting, we obtain a trajectory-informed spectral preconditioner, in which the subspace is unchanged but the basis is reweighted and realigned toward the modes visited by the dynamics. This enables the model to absorb future out-of-span corrections more effectively. We expose aspects of this mechanism on a three-dimensional spiral and confirm it on viscous Burgers and Fisher-KPP dynamics. We also discuss how in-span learning can be viewed as a dynamical-systems analogue of in-context learning. More broadly, in-span learning suggests a new principle for computational science, revealing that model-generated trajectories contain more usable information than previously recognized.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces in-span learning, a novel adaptive method for reduced-order models that reweights and realigns the existing subspace basis using the model's own predictions via incremental SVD with forgetting, improving future out-of-span correction absorption without requiring external data.
AI.motivation: Reduced-order models compress high-dimensional dynamics but lose accuracy when online dynamics drift beyond training data. Existing adaptive methods use external (out-of-span) information like full-order corrections or sensor snapshots, but no prior work exploited the information within the current reduced subspace itself.
AI.method: The method streams the model's own predictions through an incremental singular-value decomposition (SVD) with forgetting, producing a trajectory-informed spectral preconditioner. The subspace remains unchanged, but the basis is reweighted and realigned toward modes visited by the dynamics.
AI.result: The mechanism is exposed on a 3D spiral and confirmed on viscous Burgers and Fisher-KPP dynamics. In-span learning improves the model's ability to absorb future out-of-span corrections.
AI.conclusion: In-span learning reveals that model-generated trajectories contain more usable information than previously recognized, suggesting a new principle for computational science. It is also positioned as a dynamical-systems analogue of in-context learning.

title: CPR: Chained Perceptual Refinement for Coarse-to-Fine Medical Image Classification
summary: High resolution medical images contain fine grained, spatially sparse cues that are critical for diagnosis, yet preserving full resolution incurs substantial computational and memory costs. Most deep models process images uniformly, leading to redundant computation or loss of diagnostic detail under downsampling. We propose Chained Perceptual Refinement, CPR, a coarse to fine framework that formulates medical image analysis as a sequential global to local decision process. Starting from a low resolution global view, CPR dynamically predicts the location and spatial extent of refinement regions, extracts high resolution evidence from the original image, and incrementally integrates it with global context. By keeping the backbone input size fixed while contracting the perceptual field, CPR preserves diagnostic fidelity with constant peak GPU memory. Extensive experiments on five medical imaging datasets and multiple backbone architectures demonstrate that CPR consistently outperforms both fixed resolution and multi scale state of the art baselines, achieving improvements of up to 2.27 percentage points over the second best method. It also achieves up to a 19.6 fold reduction in GFLOPs at matched accuracy, establishing a superior accuracy and efficiency trade off for high resolution medical image analysis. The code is available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: CPR is a coarse-to-fine framework for medical image analysis that dynamically predicts refinement regions, extracts high-resolution evidence, and integrates it with global context, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: High-resolution medical images contain fine-grained, spatially sparse diagnostic cues, but processing them at full resolution incurs high computational and memory costs, while downsampling risks losing diagnostic detail.
AI.method: CPR formulates analysis as a sequential global-to-local decision process: starting from a low-resolution global view, it dynamically predicts the location and spatial extent of refinement regions, extracts high-resolution evidence from the original image, and incrementally integrates it with global context while keeping backbone input size fixed.
AI.result: Outperforms fixed-resolution and multi-scale baselines on five medical imaging datasets, with up to 2.27 percentage points improvement over the second best method and up to 19.6x GFLOPs reduction at matched accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CPR establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image analysis, preserving diagnostic fidelity with constant peak GPU memory.

title: Demonstrating Generalization Failures via Mixtures of Conditional Policies
summary: Post-training of frontier language models is conducted on curated task suites, and inevitably leaves a distribution shift between training and deployment environments. This exposes developers to generalization failures, which are relatively poorly understood. To better understand such generalization failures, we believe the community should construct clean demonstrations under simplified conditions. To facilitate this, we propose a simple and flexible way to construct language models which fail to generalize in controllable ways when subsequently trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on a given distribution of training tasks. Our construction uses Supervised Fine-Tuning on a dataset of a mixture of transcripts corresponding to a collection of 'conditional policies', which can each independently be assigned certain behaviors on each different task distribution, to obtain a model that is then well approximated as a 'mixture of conditional policies.' We observe that RL training then selects for policies that obtain the highest reward on the training distribution. This can produce striking behaviors: in a controlled setting with two distributions containing identical questions prepended with two different 'trigger strings', RL training on either distribution actively degrades performance on the other to zero, even though the underlying task is identical. We also use our construction to illustrate two novel ways in which generalization may fail in future language models, corresponding to distribution shifts of task coverage and temporal context respectively. While our construction is deliberately simple and may not closely resemble 'natural' generalization failures, the resulting 'model organisms' are of interest for alignment stress-testing and generalization science, and can be used as existence proofs that training success and generalization can come apart in structured ways.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to construct language models that exhibit controllable generalization failures under RL post-training, using a mixture of conditional policies from SFT. It demonstrates that RL training can actively degrade performance on out-of-distribution tasks, revealing structured ways training success and generalization can diverge.
AI.motivation: Frontier language models undergo post-training on curated task suites, causing distribution shifts between training and deployment environments that lead to poorly understood generalization failures. The authors aim to create simplified, controllable demonstrations of such failures for better study.
AI.method: The authors construct models via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a mixture of transcripts from various 'conditional policies,' each assigned different behaviors per task distribution. The resulting model approximates a 'mixture of conditional policies.' RL training is then applied on a specific task distribution, selecting policies that maximize reward.
AI.result: RL training on one distribution actively degrades performance on another to zero, even when underlying tasks are identical but prepended with different 'trigger strings.' The construction also illustrates two novel generalization failure modes: distribution shifts of task coverage and temporal context.
AI.conclusion: The resulting 'model organisms' serve as existence proofs that training success and generalization can systematically come apart, useful for alignment stress-testing and generalization science—even though the construction is simplified and may not mirror natural failures exactly.

title: CoACT: Action-Preserving Observation Compression for Coding Agents
summary: LLM-based coding agents solve software-engineering tasks through iterative interactions with development environments, where returned observations accumulate in the context and become a major source of inference cost. Observation compression reduces this cost by shortening observations before they are appended to the context. However, existing methods still exhibit an unsatisfactory efficiency-effectiveness trade-off, as they do not explicitly model how compression affects the agent's subsequent behavior. This paper proposes CoACT, an action-preserving observation compression method for coding agents. CoACT is built on next-action preservation (NAP), which requires a compressed observation to induce the same next action as the raw observation. By checking the agent's immediate next action, NAP provides a practical signal for whether a compression preserves the information needed for continued task solving. During training, a teacher model first generates multiple compressed candidates of each observation. CoACT then uses an action-preservation reward based on NAP to filter out candidates that would change the agent's next action, and uses a length-reduction reward to choose compact candidates as supervision for a lightweight compressor. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified with three agentic models show that CoACT reduces average total token consumption by 33.0% while maintaining task-solving effectiveness close to the uncompressed agent.

AI.tldr: CoACT proposes an action-preserving observation compression method for LLM-based coding agents that reduces token consumption by 33% while maintaining task-solving effectiveness by explicitly ensuring compressed observations preserve the agent's next action.
AI.motivation: Existing observation compression methods for coding agents exhibit an unsatisfactory efficiency-effectiveness trade-off because they do not explicitly model how compression affects the agent's subsequent behavior.
AI.method: CoACT introduces next-action preservation (NAP), which requires compressed observations to induce the same next action as raw observations. A teacher model generates compressed candidates, then an action-preservation reward (based on NAP) filters out candidates that alter the agent's next action, while a length-reduction reward selects compact candidates to supervise a lightweight compressor.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified across three agentic models, CoACT reduces average total token consumption by 33.0% while maintaining task-solving effectiveness close to that of the uncompressed agent.
AI.conclusion: Action-preserving compression via NAP provides a practical signal for maintaining task-solving performance while significantly reducing inference costs, addressing the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off in LLM-based coding agents.

title: Missingness as Signal: Channel-Independent Spectrogram Learning for Clinical Time Series Prediction
summary: Clinical time series prediction in intensive care units remains challenging due to heterogeneous physiological variables and informative missingness. The presence or absence of a measurement can reflect clinical decisions and patient severity, and thus missingness can serve as a predictive signal rather than a simple data artifact. This work presents CISM, a Channel-Independent Spectrogram framework with a Missingness stream for clinical multivariate time series prediction. CISM converts each clinical variable into a variable-wise time-frequency spectrogram, preserves variable identity through variable-aligned encoding, and aligns an explicit missingness stream with the spectrogram representation. Experiments on an in-hospital mortality task derived from MIMIC-IV show that CISM achieves the highest mean AUROC (0.7225), AUPRC (0.3308), and F1 (0.3808) among the compared time series, missingness-aware, vision, and time-frequency baselines. Ablation studies further show that observation patterns provide a meaningful informative signal. Pixel-level mask injection improves performance over plain spectrogram inputs and recovers much of this predictive value. The aligned missingness stream contributes a further, complementary gain in both AUROC and AUPRC. These results highlight the importance of modeling observation patterns as structured signals in clinical time series prediction.

AI.tldr: CISM is a Channel-Independent Spectrogram framework with a Missingness stream for clinical time series prediction that converts variables into spectrograms, preserves variable identity, and aligns missingness patterns as predictive signals, achieving state-of-the-art results on MIMIC-IV mortality prediction.
AI.motivation: Clinical time series prediction in ICUs is challenging due to heterogeneous physiological variables and informative missingness, where the presence/absence of measurements reflects clinical decisions and patient severity, making missingness a predictive signal rather than noise.
AI.method: CISM converts each clinical variable into a variable-wise time-frequency spectrogram, applies variable-aligned encoding to preserve variable identity, and aligns an explicit missingness stream with the spectrogram representation for multivariate time series prediction.
AI.result: On MIMIC-IV in-hospital mortality task, CISM achieves the highest mean AUROC (0.7225), AUPRC (0.3308), and F1 (0.3808) among time series, missingness-aware, vision, and time-frequency baselines.
AI.conclusion: Observation patterns provide meaningful predictive signals; pixel-level mask injection improves performance over plain spectrograms; the aligned missingness stream offers complementary gains, highlighting the importance of modeling observation patterns as structured signals in clinical time series prediction.

title: H-OPD: Confidence Aware Heterogeneous Multi-Teacher Multimodal On-policy Distillation
comment: Technical report(work-in-progress). Code will be available at \url{https://github.com/buptyqx/H-OPD}
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently emerged as an effective post-training paradigm by providing supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, existing OPD methods for multimodal reasoning usually rely on a static teacher routing, assigning each sample to a single teacher based on modality or task type. This ignores that visual grounding and abstract reasoning may dominate different decoding steps, making a single teacher insufficient for the full trajectory. To this end, H-OPD is proposed as a confidence-aware heterogeneous multi-teacher OPD framework for multimodal reasoning. By verifying the complementarity of heterogeneous teachers in the same reasoning process, H-OPD replaces task or sample level teacher routing with token-level teacher arbitration along the shared student trajectory. H-OPD employs vision-to-language description transfer to enable text-only teachers to access key visual semantics, and uses a confidence-aware arbitration mechanism to dynamically combine vision-language teacher and text-only teachers at each token. Extensive evaluations over 11 widely-used reasoning benchmarks showcase the superior performance of our method.

AI.tldr: H-OPD is a confidence-aware heterogeneous multi-teacher on-policy distillation framework that performs token-level teacher arbitration (instead of static sample-level routing) to dynamically combine vision-language and text-only teachers for improved multimodal reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing OPD methods for multimodal reasoning use static teacher routing (assigning each sample to a single teacher based on modality/task type), which ignores that visual grounding and abstract reasoning may dominate different decoding steps. This makes a single teacher insufficient for the full trajectory.
AI.method: H-OPD replaces task/sample-level teacher routing with token-level teacher arbitration along the shared student trajectory, uses vision-to-language description transfer to enable text-only teachers to access visual semantics, and employs a confidence-aware arbitration mechanism to dynamically combine vision-language and text-only teachers at each token.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations over 11 widely-used reasoning benchmarks show superior performance of H-OPD compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Token-level dynamic teacher arbitration across heterogeneous teachers outperforms static sample-level routing, confirming the complementarity of different teachers within the same reasoning process for multimodal tasks.

title: MentalThink: Shaping Thoughts in Mental SVG World
summary: We introduce MentalThink, a visual-symbolic reasoning paradigm that equips Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with an executable mechanism for "mental" visualization. The core of MentalThink is a think-with-SVG pipeline, where the model learns to generate, render, and interpret scalable vector graphics (SVG) code as an intermediate visual representation for multi-turn reasoning. By creating structured vector sketches, the model can externalize spatial hypotheses, inspect them through deterministic rendering, and reason within a constrained geometric space, effectively mimicking the human process of mental imagery. We instantiate this paradigm through a two-stage training framework, combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for SVG syntactic alignment with multi-turn Reinforcement Learning (RL) to encourage iterative inspection, revision, and refinement of intermediate visual hypotheses. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MentalThink achieves superior performance on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks (e.g., 55.1% on VSIBench, 76.0% on MindCube), showing that executable vector graphics provide a verifiable visual workspace for dynamic perspective taking, visual reflection, and compositional scene construction.

AI.tldr: MentalThink introduces a visual-symbolic reasoning paradigm where Multimodal LLMs generate, render, and interpret SVG code as intermediate visual representations for multi-turn spatial reasoning, achieving strong results on spatial benchmarks via a two-stage SFT + RL training framework.
AI.motivation: Existing Multimodal LLMs struggle with spatial understanding and multi-step visual reasoning because they lack an explicit mechanism for "mental visualization" — the ability to dynamically construct, inspect, and revise internal visual representations akin to human mental imagery.
AI.method: A think-with-SVG pipeline where the model generates SVG code, renders it deterministically, and interprets the rendered output for multi-turn reasoning; trained via a two-stage framework: SFT for SVG syntax acquisition followed by multi-turn RL for iterative inspection and refinement of visual hypotheses.
AI.result: 55.1% on VSIBench, 76.0% on MindCube, outperforming prior methods on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Executable vector graphics (SVG) serve as a verifiable visual workspace that enables MLLMs to perform dynamic perspective taking, visual reflection, and compositional scene construction, effectively mimicking human mental imagery processes.

title: BeSpec: Behavior-Level Specification Alignment for Code Generation
summary:
LLMs have made substantial progress on automated code generation from natural-language descriptions of desired behavior (intent). Most existing methods improve generated programs through execution-guided code refinement: they generate a candidate solution, execute it, and patch the implementation using feedback, while leaving the underlying specification unchanged. This workflow implicitly assumes that the LLM's understanding of the intent is already correct and complete. In practice, however, intents are often ambiguous or underspecified. As a result, even a capable model may produce a correct implementation of the wrong intent, making specification mismatch a central bottleneck.
  This paper presents BeSpec, a behavioral model-based approach to specification alignment. BeSpec treats the task description as partial evidence about the intended behavior of the correct program. It first builds an explicit behavioral model, which are checkable properties that valid outputs must satisfy. BeSpec then generates candidate programs, executes them on probe inputs, and compares their observed behavior with the predicted behaviors. When observed behavior does not match the predicted behaviors, BeSpec either refines the specification or rejects the candidate program.
  We evaluate BeSpec with three LLMs on four benchmarks: CodeContests, xCodeEval, APPS, and the contamination-free LiveCodeBench. Against nine baselines, BeSpec achieves the highest Pass@1 and average pass rate across all settings, improving average Pass@1 over the strongest baseline by 8.1%--25.3% relative across the three LLMs. A failure analysis shows that after alignment, most remaining errors stem from algorithmic difficulty rather than misunderstood specifications, while ablation studies confirm that each major component of BeSpec contributes positively.

AI.tldr: BeSpec improves LLM code generation by building explicit behavioral models from task descriptions, then iteratively comparing program behavior against predicted behaviors to align specifications and reject mismatched programs. It achieves 8.1-25.3% relative improvement in Pass@1 over baselines across three LLMs and four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing execution-guided code refinement assumes the LLM correctly understands the intent, but specifications are often ambiguous or underspecified, leading to "correct implementation of the wrong intent." Specification mismatch is a central bottleneck.
AI.method: BeSpec treats the task description as partial evidence, builds an explicit behavioral model (checkable properties valid outputs must satisfy), generates candidate programs, executes them on probe inputs, and compares observed vs. predicted behaviors. When mismatched, it either refines the specification or rejects the candidate.
AI.result: Evaluated with three LLMs on CodeContests, xCodeEval, APPS, and LiveCodeBench. BeSpec achieves highest Pass@1 and average pass rate against nine baselines, improving average Pass@1 by 8.1%-25.3% relative across LLMs.
AI.conclusion: After alignment, remaining errors are mostly due to algorithmic difficulty rather than misunderstood specifications. Ablation studies confirm all major components contribute positively.

title: A Precedent-Guided Co-Scientist for Side-Effect-Aware Drug Redesign
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on AI for Science
summary: We propose PRECEDE, a precedent-guided co-scientist for side-effect-aware drug redesign that revises a parent compound to mitigate a specified side effect while preserving therapeutic function. Rather than isolated molecular generation, PRECEDE frames redesign as evidence-grounded reasoning over drug--side-effect associations, biomedical knowledge graphs, and precedents of safety-driven optimization, coordinated by an LLM orchestrator with explicit policies and human-review checkpoints. We position PRECEDE as a human-supervised AI-for-science workflow in which hypotheses remain auditable, falsifiable, and bounded by prior pharmacology.

AI.tldr: PRECEDE is a precedent-guided, LLM-orchestrated AI co-scientist for side-effect-aware drug redesign that revises parent compounds to mitigate specified side effects while preserving therapeutic function, using evidence-grounded reasoning over drug-side-effect associations, knowledge graphs, and safety precedents within a human-supervised, auditable workflow.
AI.motivation: To enable side-effect-aware drug redesign by grounding molecular generation in evidence-based reasoning over biomedical knowledge and prior safety precedents, rather than isolated molecular generation.
AI.method: PRECEDE employs an LLM orchestrator with explicit policies and human-review checkpoints to coordinate reasoning over drug-side-effect associations, biomedical knowledge graphs, and precedents of safety-driven optimization.
AI.result: A human-supervised AI-for-science workflow that produces auditable, falsifiable hypotheses bounded by prior pharmacology for revising parent compounds to mitigate side effects.
AI.conclusion: PRECEDE positions itself as a precedent-guided co-scientist that treats drug redesign as evidence-grounded reasoning under human oversight, ensuring hypotheses remain auditable and grounded in established pharmacological knowledge.

title: Token-level Response-visual Attention Guidance for Multimodal LLMs Knowledge Distillation
summary: While knowledge distillation (KD) is widely adopted for training lightweight models by leveraging supervision from larger teacher models, relying solely on output token distributions has proven insufficient for compressing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Since output tokens are a byproduct of the model attending to visual inputs, prior works have explored explicitly distilling attention to provide a direct supervisory signal. While promising, the precise utility of which attention signals to distill remains under-explored. In this work, we challenge the conventional reliance on prompt-to-vision attention by revealing that downstream performance correlates strongly with response-to-vision attention similarity to the teacher, but negligibly with that of prompt-conditioned attention. Furthermore, we observe that attention distributions exhibit significant variance across individual tokens, indicating that a uniform distillation objective is suboptimal. To this end, we introduce Token-level Response-visual Attention Guidance (TRAG), a distillation objective that 1) shifts the focus to response-to-vision signals and 2) employs token-specific objectives by adaptively weighting the Kullback-Leibler divergence based on attention entropy, effectively guiding the student to mirror the teacher's precise visual focus. Extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that TRAG significantly outperforms prior distillation baselines.

AI.tldr: TRAG is a knowledge distillation method for MLLMs that shifts focus from prompt-to-vision attention to response-to-vision attention and uses token-specific, entropy-weighted KL divergence objectives, significantly outperforming prior distillation baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge distillation methods for MLLMs rely on output token distributions or prompt-to-vision attention signals, but the utility of different attention signals is under-explored. The authors aim to identify which attention signals correlate with downstream performance and design a better distillation objective.
AI.method: The authors propose TRAG (Token-level Response-visual Attention Guidance), which: 1) shifts distillation focus from prompt-to-vision to response-to-vision attention signals, and 2) employs token-specific objectives by adaptively weighting KL divergence based on attention entropy to handle variance across individual tokens.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that TRAG significantly outperforms prior distillation baselines on multiple benchmarks. The key empirical finding is that downstream performance correlates strongly with response-to-vision attention similarity to the teacher, but negligibly with prompt-conditioned attention similarity.
AI.conclusion: Response-to-vision attention is more critical than prompt-to-vision attention for effective KD in MLLMs, and token-level adaptive weighting based on attention entropy yields substantial improvements over uniform distillation objectives.

title: Applying Answer Set Programming with Fuzzy Membership Functions: a Case Study
comment: A shorter version of this paper has been accepted at the 24th International Workshop on Nonmonotonic Reasoning (July 17-19, 2026, Lisbon, Portugal)
summary: Human reasoning often operates through qualitative concepts expressed by linguistic labels such as high, low, expensive, or cheap, whose interpretation depends on context and is usually vague, despite being rooted in numerical data. This paper explores a novel fuzzy-logic-based qualitative extension of Answer Set Programming (ASP) to bridge numerical information and qualitative reasoning. The underlying language, formally introduced in a separate work, provides a principled framework that avoids rigid thresholds and supports robust reasoning under vagueness. Focusing on a representative use case, we illustrate how the framework integrates numerically grounded inputs (such as outputs of machine learning models) with symbolic reasoning over qualitative labels. Key features, including learning-based membership functions and semantically enriched predicates, enable the combination of expert knowledge, contextual factors, and subjective interpretations within a unified declarative setting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fuzzy-logic-based qualitative extension of Answer Set Programming (ASP) that bridges numerical data and qualitative reasoning using linguistic labels, avoiding rigid thresholds and supporting reasoning under vagueness through learning-based membership functions and semantically enriched predicates.
AI.motivation: Human reasoning relies on qualitative concepts (e.g., high, cheap) that are context-dependent and vague, yet they stem from numerical data. Existing ASP frameworks lack support for handling such vague, numerically-grounded qualitative information, motivating the need for a principled integration.
AI.method: The proposed framework extends ASP with fuzzy logic to handle qualitative labels. It uses learning-based membership functions and semantically enriched predicates to integrate numerically grounded inputs (e.g., ML model outputs) with symbolic reasoning, combining expert knowledge, context, and subjective interpretations in a declarative setting.
AI.result: Through a representative use case, the framework demonstrates effective integration of numerical inputs with qualitative symbolic reasoning, avoiding rigid thresholds and maintaining robustness under vagueness.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy-logic-based qualitative ASP extension provides a principled approach to bridge numerical information and qualitative reasoning, enabling flexible, context-aware decision-making without hard thresholds.

title: CAFÉ, an automated feedback tool to approach Formal Methods
summary: We present CAFÉ, a learning platform designed to introduce computer science students to Formal Methods (FM). CAFÉ aims to scaffold students' structural thinking (in contrast with operational thinking) by promoting the practice of Graphical Loop Invariant Based Programming (GLIBP). In the GLIBP approach, students solve loop-based problems by first constructing a Graphical Loop Invariant (GLI) before deriving the corresponding code. The GLI is an informal diagrammatic representation of the loop invariant. It illustrates the variables involved in the loop, their properties, and the relationships between them. To enable automated feedback, students complete a blank GLI, a box-based version of the GLI. Beyond evaluating the code students submit, CAFÉ provides personalized feedback on students' GLI and its alignment with the code. In this demo, we walk through CAFE from both a student's and a teacher's perspective. We show how the tool supports GLI design and provides feedback. We then present how a teacher can encode programming challenges together with a corresponding blank GLI.

AI.tldr: CAFÉ is a learning platform that teaches Formal Methods to computer science students through Graphical Loop Invariant Based Programming (GLIBP), where students create visual loop invariants before writing code, with automated feedback on both diagrams and code.
AI.motivation: To scaffold students' structural thinking (as opposed to operational thinking) when learning Formal Methods, addressing the challenge of teaching loop invariant concepts in programming education.
AI.method: Students solve loop-based problems by first constructing a Graphical Loop Invariant (GLI) — an informal diagrammatic representation of the loop invariant showing variables, properties, and relationships — before deriving code. Students complete a blank box-based GLI, and CAFÉ provides automated feedback on the GLI and its alignment with submitted code. The demo covers both student and teacher perspectives, including how teachers encode programming challenges with corresponding blank GLIs.
AI.result: A demonstration of the CAFÉ platform from both student and teacher perspectives, showing support for GLI design, automated feedback provision, and teacher configuration of programming challenges with blank GLIs.
AI.conclusion: CAFÉ offers a novel approach to teaching Formal Methods by emphasizing structural thinking through graphical loop invariant construction, with automated personalized feedback bridging diagrammatic reasoning and code implementation.

title: Individual Parameters in Weight-Sparse Transformers Appear Interpretable
summary: A central goal of mechanistic interpretability is to understand how neural networks work and what each individual component does. Dominant circuit-finding approaches focus on a specific behavior and reverse-engineer the role of components on the associated sub-distribution. However, past work has shown that components can have different functions that are active on different subsets of the input distribution. In this work we ask whether a single weight can be understood globally across the full training distribution by characterizing when it matters (the inputs on which ablating it changes the model's predictions). We introduce an automated LLM pipeline that writes a short, human-readable description of when a weight matters and verifies it on held-out text, crediting a weight only if its description generalizes. Across two sparse and two dense transformers, the fraction of weights that are interpretable (in this sense) is higher in sparse transformers than in dense ones, a gap that widens once unreliable descriptions are discarded. Our results show that a meaningful fraction of a sparse transformer model's weights can be interpreted: 12 to 31% of weights have a single short description that identifies what the weight is used for.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether individual weights in neural networks can be globally interpreted across the full training distribution, rather than just in specific behavioral contexts. The authors develop an automated LLM pipeline that generates and verifies human-readable descriptions of when a weight matters, finding that 12-31% of weights in sparse transformers have a single interpretable description, with sparse transformers outperforming dense ones.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability approaches focus on specific behaviors and reverse-engineer components on associated sub-distributions, but components can have different functions on different input subsets. The authors aim to understand whether a single weight can be understood globally across the full training distribution by characterizing when it matters (inputs where ablating it changes model predictions).
AI.method: The authors introduce an automated LLM pipeline that writes short, human-readable descriptions of when a weight matters and verifies them on held-out text. A weight is credited only if its description generalizes to unseen data. The method is applied across two sparse and two dense transformers to compare interpretability rates.
AI.result: The fraction of interpretable weights (those with a single short description that identifies what the weight is used for) is higher in sparse transformers than in dense ones, and this gap widens once unreliable descriptions are discarded. In sparse transformers, 12-31% of weights meet this interpretability criterion.
AI.conclusion: A meaningful fraction of a sparse transformer model's weights can be globally interpreted, demonstrating that individual weights can have consistent, describable functions across the full training distribution, particularly in sparse architectures.

title: An automated method of identifying incorrectly labelled images based on the sequences of loss functions of deep learning networks
comment: Presented at the 6th EAI International Conference on IoT as a Service (IoTaaS 2020). Published by Springer in LNICST, vol 346, 2021
summary: Deep learning is widely applied in medical image analysis, but up to 10% of manually labelled images may be incorrect, degrading model performance. This paper proposes an automated method to identify incorrectly labelled medical images by analyzing sequences of loss functions from deep learning classification networks over multiple training epochs. Identified images can be reviewed and relabelled by experts, improving dataset quality and model performance. Two experiments validate the method on a fundus image dataset for referable diabetic retinopathy screening. In the first, 6% (648) of 10,788 gold-standard labels were intentionally flipped. The method identified 75.31% (488) of the flipped samples, with only 4.85% (492) false positives among correctly labelled samples. In the second, reviewing and correcting the 980 identified samples (9.1% of the dataset) and retraining the model improved best accuracy on an independent test set from 95.93% (with 6% label noise) to 96.50% (with 1.5% noise), approaching the ideal 96.57% (with 0% noise). The results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in improving model performance through automated label quality control.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated method to identify incorrectly labelled medical images by analyzing loss function sequences from deep learning networks over multiple training epochs. Experiments on a diabetic retinopathy dataset show it can detect 75% of intentionally flipped labels with low false positive rate, and correcting identified samples improved accuracy from 95.93% (6% noise) to 96.50% (1.5% noise), approaching the ideal 96.57% (0% noise).
AI.motivation: Up to 10% of manually labelled medical images may be incorrect, degrading deep learning model performance. There is a need for automated methods to identify and correct erroneous labels to improve dataset quality.
AI.method: The method analyzes sequences of loss functions from deep learning classification networks over multiple training epochs to identify incorrectly labelled images. Identified images are then reviewed and relabelled by experts.
AI.result: In Experiment 1: 75.31% (488/648) of flipped labels were identified with only 4.85% (492) false positives. In Experiment 2: correcting 980 identified samples (9.1% of dataset) improved test accuracy from 95.93% (6% noise) to 96.50% (1.5% noise), approaching the ideal 96.57% (0% noise).
AI.conclusion: The method effectively improves model performance through automated label quality control, demonstrating its potential for practical medical image analysis applications.

title: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs
summary:
As AI models continue to develop powerful capabilities, it becomes critical that we are able to verify that their output is aligned with our intentions. A recent line of work focuses on verification via debate, a model of interactive proofs where two competing powerful provers, or AI models, debate each other to convince a weak verifier, or a human, of the correctness of their claim. However, debate assumes that the two AI models possess equal abilities and that one of them is truthful, which may not be realistic.
  In this work, we show \emph{how to avoid debate}: we initiate the study of \emph{single-prover} interactive proofs for AI safety. Prior results in single-prover interactive proofs do not immediately carry over to the AI safety setting: for example, they do not work when the computation has access to an oracle, such as to human judgment or an external database such as the web. We present doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations (also known as relativizing proofs), in the settings where (1) the computation is robust, in the sense that the output does not change if at most a small fraction of the answers to oracle queries are incorrect, or (2) the oracle is a low-degree polynomial. These results suggest that interactive verification is possible even without debate, under structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces single-prover interactive proofs for AI safety as an alternative to debate-based verification, showing they work for oracle-aided computations under robustness or low-degree polynomial conditions.
AI.motivation: Debate-based verification assumes two equally capable AI models with one being truthful, which is unrealistic. The authors aim to eliminate debate by developing single-prover interactive proofs suitable for AI safety settings where oracle access (e.g., human judgment, external databases) is involved.
AI.method: The authors propose doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations under two conditions: (1) the computation is robust (output stable under small fractions of incorrect oracle answers), or (2) the oracle is a low-degree polynomial.
AI.result: Single-prover interactive proofs can work for AI safety without debate when oracle access is structured (low-degree polynomial) or noise-tolerant (robust computation).
AI.conclusion: Interactive verification for AI safety is possible without debate under structured or noise-tolerant oracle access conditions.

title: Detection of LLM-assisted Code Plagiarism Using k-gram Software Birthmarks
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, submitted to the 8th World Symposium on Software Engineering (WSSE 2026)
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have significantly lowered the technical barrier to software plagiarism. By transforming existing source code while preserving its functionality, modern LLMs can generate semantically identical program that may evade traditional plagiarism detection techniques.
  Among such attacks, code paraphrasing modifies the syntax and structure of a program while preserving its behavior. This paper investigates whether software birthmarks can detect such LLM-assisted plagiarism. As a starting point, we employ k-gram software birthmarks based on unique k-grams of Java opcodes, with k ranging from 1 to 6.
  We employ three contemporary LLMs: ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Claude-Haiku-4.5. The dataset consists of individually compilable source files extracted from actively maintained BSD-2-Clause licensed Java projects. We further compare five similarity measures for birthmark matching: cosine similarity, Dice index, Jaccard coefficient, Simpson index, and edit-distance-based similarity.
  The results demonstrate that k-gram software birthmarks remain effective for detecting LLM-assisted plagiarism. Among the evaluated models, ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini generated the most difficult-to-detect clones. Furthermore, the findings confirm the higher performance of coding-oriented models for plagiarism task.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether k-gram software birthmarks (based on Java opcode k-grams, k=1-6) can detect LLM-assisted code plagiarism. Testing three LLMs (ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude-Haiku-4.5) on BSD-2-Clause Java projects with five similarity measures, results show birthmarks remain effective; ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini produced the hardest-to-detect clones, and coding-oriented models performed better at plagiarism.
AI.motivation: LLMs have lowered the barrier to software plagiarism by enabling code paraphrasing that preserves functionality while evading traditional detection. The paper investigates whether software birthmarks can still detect such LLM-assisted plagiarism.
AI.method: Used k-gram software birthmarks (unique k-grams of Java opcodes, k=1-6) with five similarity measures (cosine, Dice, Jaccard, Simpson, edit-distance). Tested on compilable source files from BSD-2-Clause Java projects using three LLMs: ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Claude-Haiku-4.5.
AI.result: K-gram software birthmarks remain effective for detecting LLM-assisted plagiarism. ChatGPT-5.1-Codex-Mini generated the most difficult-to-detect clones. Coding-oriented models showed higher performance for plagiarism tasks.
AI.conclusion: Software birthmarks based on k-grams of Java opcodes are a viable defense against LLM-assisted code plagiarism, though detection difficulty varies across models.

title: Rank-Order N-of-M Codes for Sparse Distributed Memory: Disentangling Representation and Learning Effects in Noise Robustness Against Contemporary Neuromorphic Architectures
comment: 14 pages, 8 tables, 2 figures. Revisits rank-order sparse distributed memory for continual learning and memory-augmented AI. Includes comparisons with CALM and SpikingMamba, statistical evaluation, and real embedding experiments
summary: Large language models remain limited as continual learning systems, motivating renewed interest in Sparse Distributed Memory (SDM) as an explicit online episodic memory. CALM (Nechesov and Ruponen, 2025) identifies its threshold-binary encoder as an open design question. This paper evaluates rank-order N-of-M encoding (Furber et al., 2007) as an alternative. We make three contributions. First, a faithful reimplementation validates the published architecture by confirming exact equivalence between WheelSDM and RankOrderSDM (cosine similarity 1.0000 across 10 seeds) and reproducing the documented divergence of RDLIF neurons under interference. Second, multi-seed capacity experiments show RankOrderSDM outperforming StandardSDM by 13.4 percentage points at saturation in the scaled configuration and by 0.8 percentage points at the published architecture scale. Third, BER robustness experiments disentangle representation and learning effects, showing that the large robustness gain arises primarily from the interaction of rank-order encoding with MAX-Hebbian learning, while the encoder alone provides only a small advantage under matched learning conditions. Experiments on GloVe-100 embeddings confirm this small but consistent encoding benefit on real structured data, whereas sentence embeddings exhibit a ceiling effect at low memory load. A secondary analysis shows that idealized rank-order encoding requires half the component-level encoding energy of SpikingMamba's SI-LIF neurons at four-bit precision, although decoder costs dominate overall system energy. These results identify which components of the original rank-order SDM architecture provide measurable benefits for contemporary memory-augmented AI systems, offering practical guidance for architectures such as CALM.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates rank-order N-of-M encoding as an alternative to threshold-binary encoding in Sparse Distributed Memory (SDM) architectures. The authors validate a reimplementation of WheelSDM/RankOrderSDM, show capacity improvements of up to 13.4 percentage points over StandardSDM, and decompose robustness gains to show the interaction of rank-order encoding with MAX-Hebbian learning is primarily responsible. Energy analysis reveals rank-order encoding requires half the component-level energy of SI-LIF neurons at 4-bit precision.
AI.motivation: Large language models remain limited as continual learning systems, motivating renewed interest in Sparse Distributed Memory (SDM) as an explicit online episodic memory. The CALM architecture identified the threshold-binary encoder as an open design question, which this paper addresses by evaluating rank-order N-of-M encoding.
AI.method: The paper makes three contributions: 1) Faithful reimplementation validating exact equivalence between WheelSDM and RankOrderSDM (cosine similarity 1.0000 across 10 seeds) and reproducing RDLIF neuron divergence under interference; 2) Multi-seed capacity experiments comparing RankOrderSDM to StandardSDM; 3) BER robustness experiments disentangling representation and learning effects, plus energy analysis comparing rank-order encoding to SI-LIF neurons.
AI.result: RankOrderSDM outperforms StandardSDM by 13.4 percentage points at saturation (scaled) and 0.8 percentage points (published scale). Robustness gains primarily arise from rank-order encoding interacting with MAX-Hebbian learning, not encoder alone. GloVe-100 experiments show small encoding benefit; sentence embeddings show ceiling effect. Rank-order encoding requires half the component-level energy of SI-LIF neurons at 4-bit.
AI.conclusion: The results identify which components of rank-order SDM architecture provide measurable benefits for contemporary memory-augmented AI systems, offering practical guidance for architectures such as CALM.

title: CIPHER: Causal Intervention Pathways for Healthcare Equity and Robustness
summary: Deep learning models for medical diagnosis frequently exhibit substantial performance disparities across sensitive subgroups (e.g., race, sex), even when average accuracy is high. While generative data augmentation offers a route to mitigate this, existing strategies are suboptimal; they typically address only one or two dependency channels between sensitive attributes and image features. We formalize the medical image formation process via a structural causal model, revealing that sensitive attributes actually influence image content through four distinct pathways-a structural complexity neglected by prior works. Based on this insight, we introduce CIPHER (Causal Intervention Pathways for Healthcare Equity and Robustness), a framework designed to systematically intervene on all four causal paths. To achieve this, CIPHER utilizes a diffusion backbone equipped with classifier-free guidance and null-text inversion. This technical design enables the faithful reconstruction of patient-specific anatomy while allowing for the precise, editable synthesis of counterfactuals required to break sensitive dependency chains. We tested CIPHER using chest X-ray and dermoscopy benchmarks across both standard and shifted data distributions. By employing a multi-pathway intervention strategy, our model reduced worst-group disparities by an average of 35.8% compared to disease-conditioned synthesis baselines, while also improving total diagnostic accuracy

AI.tldr: CIPHER is a causal framework using diffusion models with classifier-free guidance and null-text inversion to intervene on four causal pathways linking sensitive attributes to medical image features, reducing worst-group disparities by 35.8% and improving overall diagnostic accuracy.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for medical diagnosis exhibit substantial performance disparities across sensitive subgroups (e.g., race, sex) even when average accuracy is high, and existing generative data augmentation strategies are suboptimal because they address only one or two dependency channels between sensitive attributes and image features.
AI.method: The authors formalize the medical image formation process via a structural causal model, revealing four distinct causal pathways from sensitive attributes to image content. Based on this, they propose CIPHER, which uses a diffusion backbone with classifier-free guidance and null-text inversion to systematically intervene on all four causal paths, enabling faithful reconstruction of patient-specific anatomy and precise editable synthesis of counterfactuals to break sensitive dependency chains.
AI.result: On chest X-ray and dermoscopy benchmarks across both standard and shifted data distributions, CIPHER reduced worst-group disparities by an average of 35.8% compared to disease-conditioned synthesis baselines, while also improving total diagnostic accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Multi-pathway causal intervention is more effective than existing single/dual-path approaches for reducing subgroup disparities in medical imaging, and CIPHER's diffusion-based design successfully achieves this, improving both fairness and overall accuracy.

title: The Role of Rigor in Artificial Intelligence
comment: To appear in D. Rickles and T. Thebault (eds.) Philosophy of Rigor (Routledge, 2026)
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved extraordinary capabilities despite lacking many of the conceptual and scientific foundations associated with mature disciplines. Unlike traditional sciences, where reliable technology typically emerges from theoretical understanding, modern AI has progressed largely through performance-driven iteration and "alchemical" experimentation. This tension motivates a systematic analysis of AI through the lens of rigor. We introduce a three-part framework consisting of conceptual rigor (clarifying foundational concepts), epistemic rigor (establishing scientific understanding), and operational rigor (ensuring reliable performance and deployment). Using this framework, we analyze competing conceptions of intelligence and understanding, the strengths and limitations of the empirical approach to deep learning, the power and pitfalls of benchmarks, and the obstacles to theory development posed by modern AI systems. We argue that the distinctive trajectory of AI arises from how forms of rigor interact across paradigms, resulting in the primacy of operational rigor in modern deep learning. This perspective helps explain both AI's rapid advances and its persistent uncertainties, while clarifying the challenges involved in transforming AI into a mature science and reliable technology.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes AI's unusual development path—achieving remarkable capabilities without mature scientific foundations—and introduces a three-part framework (conceptual, epistemic, operational rigor) to explain why operational rigor dominates modern deep learning, accounting for both its rapid advances and persistent uncertainties.
AI.motivation: AI has achieved extraordinary capabilities while lacking the conceptual and scientific foundations typical of mature disciplines, unlike traditional sciences where reliable technology emerges from theoretical understanding. This tension motivates a systematic analysis of AI through the lens of rigor.
AI.method: The paper introduces a three-part framework: (1) conceptual rigor (clarifying foundational concepts), (2) epistemic rigor (establishing scientific understanding), and (3) operational rigor (ensuring reliable performance and deployment). It applies this framework to analyze competing conceptions of intelligence, the empirical approach to deep learning, benchmarks, and obstacles to theory development.
AI.result: The distinctive trajectory of AI arises from how forms of rigor interact across paradigms, resulting in the primacy of operational rigor in modern deep learning. This explains both AI's rapid advances and its persistent uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The framework clarifies the challenges involved in transforming AI into a mature science and reliable technology, highlighting that AI's unusual development path is a consequence of its unique rigor dynamics.

title: Compression, structure, and executor capability: a controlled real-cost decomposition of language-model agent skill optimisation
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Data and reproduction script: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21148499
summary: Agent skills, reusable instruction artefacts supplied to a tool-using language model, are increasingly optimised by shortening, structural rewriting, stronger-model compilation, and scoped loading, on the assumption that a smaller or better-organised skill lowers cost while preserving success. That assumption is rarely tested with quality and real monetary cost measured on the same runs and the contributing factors separated. This study reports a controlled decomposition over ten skill-delivery conditions, 40 software-engineering tasks, and three repetitions per cell (1,200 rollouts), separating no-skill execution, raw skills, deterministic shortening, linear and structured rendering from a shared semantic ledger, scoped loading, and the compiler and executor model tiers. Quality is the verifier pass rate at task level; cost is solve-stage token cost at standard provider prices, with a token-volume-normalised view for robustness and compilation cost amortised separately. The task is the unit of inference, intervals are task-clustered, and the contrast family is multiplicity-controlled. Deterministic shortening is close to the raw baseline but does not establish non-inferiority within the preset margin. Structured rendering and scoped loading lower pass rate on the compact executor without lowering cost, and structured rendering is indistinguishable from linear text at matched content. The only contrast surviving correction is executor capability, which raises pass rate by 27 percentage points at roughly five times the real cost, with compiler tier showing no robust effect. Under real prices no optimised representation reaches a practical break-even. The evidence indicates that executor capability is the dominant lever and that no representation strategy improves over the raw skill on either executor tier.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of 1,200 rollouts across 10 skill-delivery conditions shows that executor capability (27% pass rate improvement at 5× cost) is the dominant lever, while deterministic shortening, structured rendering, and scoped loading fail to improve quality or reduce cost compared to raw skills.
AI.motivation: The assumption that optimizing agent skills through shortening, rewriting, and structured loading lowers cost while preserving success is rarely tested with quality and real monetary cost measured jointly on the same runs.
AI.method: Controlled decomposition over 10 skill-delivery conditions, 40 software-engineering tasks, 3 repetitions per cell (1,200 rollouts), separating no-skill, raw skills, deterministic shortening, linear/structured rendering, scoped loading, and compiler/executor model tiers. Quality measured by verifier pass rate; cost by token cost at standard provider prices with token-volume-normalized view.
AI.result: Deterministic shortening didn't establish non-inferiority. Structured rendering and scoped loading lowered pass rate on compact executor without lowering cost. Structured rendering indistinguishable from linear text. Only executor capability survived correction: +27pp pass rate at ~5× cost. No representation strategy improved over raw skill on either executor tier.
AI.conclusion: Executor capability is the dominant lever for quality; no representation strategy (shortening, structuring, scoping) beats the raw skill baseline. Under real prices, no optimized representation reaches practical break-even.

title: MABLE: Masked Autoencoding with Bi-Lipschitz Decoding for Embeddings and Graph Metric Learning
summary: We propose MABLE (Masked Autoencoding with Bi-Lipschitz Decoding for Embeddings and Graph Metric Learning), a self-supervised framework for learning node and graph embeddings from large, heterogeneous graphs, demonstrated here on geospatial mineral-exploration data. MABLE combines masked reconstruction with fixed cosine-similarity losses that align matched augmented views while keeping unpaired embeddings well spread. A bi-Lipschitz feature decoder ties a low-dimensional reconstruction component of each node embedding to feature similarity, while matched-node consistency shapes the remaining context used by graph pooling. Lipschitz-controlled pooling helps stabilize graph-level representations under perturbations of retained node embeddings, while augmentation alignment trains robustness to masking, node dropping, and sampling variation. Across local copper and regional Arabian Shield studies, MABLE embeddings provide complementary downstream signal and produce coherent embedding-derived layers for hypothesis generation without learned discriminators or hard-negative selection.

AI.tldr: MABLE is a self-supervised framework for learning node and graph embeddings from large, heterogeneous graphs, demonstrated on geospatial mineral-exploration data, combining masked reconstruction with bi-Lipschitz decoding and augmentation alignment to produce robust embeddings without labeled data or hard-negative mining.
AI.motivation: To learn robust node and graph embeddings from large, heterogeneous graphs in a self-supervised manner, specifically for geospatial mineral-exploration data where labeled data is scarce and hard-negative selection is challenging.
AI.method: MABLE combines masked autoencoding with bi-Lipschitz feature decoding, fixed cosine-similarity losses for augmentation alignment, and Lipschitz-controlled graph pooling to stabilize representations under perturbations.
AI.result: Across local copper and regional Arabian Shield studies, MABLE embeddings provide complementary downstream signal and produce coherent embedding-derived layers for hypothesis generation without learned discriminators or hard-negative selection.
AI.conclusion: MABLE enables effective self-supervised graph representation learning on heterogeneous geospatial data, generating useful embeddings for mineral-exploration hypothesis generation without requiring supervised discriminators or explicit negative sampling.

title: Evaluating Agentic Harness Systems for Autonomous Computational Pathology
summary: Autonomous computational pathology (ACP) converts high-level pathology analysis goals into executable, traceable and clinically bounded workflows. Realizing this capability requires adapting general agentic harness systems to pathology-specific tasks, tools, evidence standards and clinical claim boundaries. We contribute ACP-Bench, a framework that adapts existing harness systems from computational pathology support toward ACP workflow capability. ACP-Bench evaluates 41 pathology workflow tasks, including 24 biomarker, 7 morphology and 10 prognosis tasks spanning 6 body-system groups and 9 endpoint families. The benchmark evaluates 9 models and 3 harness groups (Claude Code, Codex and Open Code), yielding 369 complete trajectories. ACP-Bench evaluates each trajectory across workflow execution, diagnostic performance and clinical-boundary alignment, combining expert-adjudicated process audits, diagnostic assessment and pathologist-validated safety review. Across evaluated systems, workflow initiation, task interpretation and diagnostic reporting were more mature than tool-bound execution, result binding and reflective workflow revision, and formal end-to-end completion remained rare. ACP-Bench provides a reusable standard for auditing whether agentic systems can operationalize pathology workflows before claims of reliable clinical autonomy.

AI.tldr: ACP-Bench is a framework for evaluating autonomous computational pathology systems across 41 workflow tasks, finding that while workflow initiation and diagnostic reporting are relatively mature, end-to-end autonomous execution and tool-bound tasks remain challenging.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between general agentic AI systems and the specific requirements of computational pathology, including pathology-specific tools, evidence standards, and clinical claim boundaries.
AI.method: ACP-Bench evaluates 41 pathology workflow tasks (24 biomarker, 7 morphology, 10 prognosis) across 6 body-system groups and 9 endpoint families, testing 9 models with 3 harness groups (Claude Code, Codex, Open Code), yielding 369 trajectories. Evaluation combines expert-adjudicated process audits, diagnostic assessment, and pathologist-validated safety review across workflow execution, diagnostic performance, and clinical-boundary alignment.
AI.result: Workflow initiation, task interpretation, and diagnostic reporting showed relative maturity, while tool-bound execution, result binding, and reflective workflow revision were less developed. Formal end-to-end completion remained rare across all evaluated systems.
AI.conclusion: ACP-Bench provides a reusable standard for auditing agentic systems' operationalization of pathology workflows before claims of reliable clinical autonomy can be made.

title: Robust Feasible Route Construction through Collaborative Partition Optimization
summary: Large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems (CVRPs) are commonly solved by partitioning customers into smaller routing problems that can be optimized independently. While this substantially reduces computational complexity, independently constructed routing solutions may leave some customer demand unserved even when sufficient resources exist elsewhere in the fleet. We present Collaborative Routing Constructors (CoRC), a routing framework that enables independently solved subproblems to exchange customers and vehicles during optimization rather than relying solely on a fixed partition or a subsequent global re-optimization stage. Computational experiments on AGS benchmark instances and synthetic instances containing up to 200,000 customers compare CoRC against independent routing, post-routing global re-optimization, and state-of-the-art, end-to-end routing frameworks. Across all evaluated partitioning strategies, CoRC consistently constructs feasible routing solutions where competing partition-based methods do not.
