Furthermore, it remains effective on problem instances for which the evaluated end-to-end routing frameworks did not produce solutions under the same computational budget. These results demonstrate that collaboration between routing subproblems provides a robust and scalable approach for feasible large-scale route construction.

AI.tldr: CoRC is a routing framework that enables independently solved subproblems to exchange customers and vehicles during optimization, achieving feasible solutions for large-scale CVRPs (up to 200K customers) where partition-based and end-to-end methods fail.
AI.motivation: Partition-based CVRP solvers often leave customer demand unserved even when sufficient fleet resources exist elsewhere, because subproblems are solved independently without cross-partition coordination.
AI.method: CoRC allows subproblems to exchange customers and vehicles during optimization rather than relying on fixed partitions or post-hoc global re-optimization.
AI.result: CoRC consistently constructs feasible solutions on AGS and synthetic instances (up to 200K customers) where competing partition-based and end-to-end methods cannot, and remains effective when end-to-end frameworks fail under the same computational budget.
AI.conclusion: Collaboration between routing subproblems is a robust and scalable approach for feasible large-scale route construction.

title: A Measurement Study on the Adoption of Pledges and Unveils in the OpenBSD Operating System
comment: Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution and Reengineering (SANER 2026), Limassol, IEEE, pp. 1-6
summary: The paper presents a longitudinal measurement study on the adoption of the pledge and unveil system calls in OpenBSD. These system calls are used to sandbox programs and libraries. Given a dataset covering 19 releases, many programs and libraries were modified to use the system calls already before their introductions in official releases. The adoption rates have also steadily grown; a linear trend provides a coarse but sensible heuristic. Although particularly programs residing in /usr/bin and /usr/sbin have been modified to use the system calls, the sizes of programs and libraries do not correlate well with the amounts of pledge and unveil system calls invoked. Regarding the pledges made, standard input and output operations have frequently been requested, although the full fine-grained arsenal offered by pledge has generally been utilized in OpenBSD. The same observation is seen in that particularly read operations to given paths have frequently been unveiled. All in all, the measurement results indicate that the adoption of system call minimization and sandboxing techniques is not necessarily as troublesome as has often been discussed in the literature.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a longitudinal measurement study on the adoption of pledge and unveil system calls in OpenBSD across 19 releases, finding steady adoption growth, frequent use of standard I/O operations, and that adoption is less troublesome than previously discussed.
AI.motivation: To empirically assess the adoption of system call minimization and sandboxing techniques (pledge and unveil) in OpenBSD, challenging the prevailing notion that such approaches are prohibitively difficult.
AI.method: Longitudinal measurement study analyzing 19 OpenBSD releases, examining adoption rates of pledge and unveil system calls across programs and libraries, correlating with program/library sizes and types.
AI.result: Adoption rates grew steadily following a linear trend; programs in /usr/bin and /usr/sbin were most modified; program/library size does not correlate well with pledge/unveil usage; standard I/O operations were most commonly pledged; read operations were most commonly unveiled.
AI.conclusion: The adoption of system call minimization and sandboxing techniques is not as troublesome as often discussed in the literature.

title: Transfer Learning in High-dimensional Ising Models
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICML 2026
summary: In high-dimensional Ising model estimation, target sample sizes are often limited, and effectively using auxiliary binary datasets of unknown relevance remains challenging. To address this, we propose Trans-Ising, a transfer learning method that combines a loss-based source screening rule with a two-stage estimation procedure. The method first identifies informative auxiliary sources using held-out target pseudolikelihood to prevent negative transfer. It then computes an initial estimator via pooled nodewise $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression, followed by a target-only correction step using a folded-concave penalty. Theoretically, we establish fixed-node $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ error bounds, exact graph selection consistency, and the conditional consistency of the screening rule. Through extensive simulations and real-data analyses, we demonstrate that Trans-Ising achieves lower estimation errors than both target-only estimation and naive data pooling.

AI.tldr: Trans-Ising is a transfer learning method for high-dimensional Ising model estimation that uses a loss-based source screening rule and two-stage estimation to effectively leverage auxiliary binary datasets, with theoretical guarantees and empirical superiority over target-only and naive pooling approaches.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional Ising model estimation often faces limited target sample sizes, and existing methods struggle to effectively utilize auxiliary binary datasets whose relevance to the target task is unknown.
AI.method: The method combines a loss-based source screening rule (using held-out target pseudolikelihood to identify informative auxiliary sources and prevent negative transfer) with a two-stage estimation procedure: first, pooled nodewise ℓ1-regularized logistic regression computes an initial estimator; second, a target-only correction step using a folded-concave penalty refines the estimate.
AI.result: Theoretically, fixed-node ℓ2 and ℓ1 error bounds, exact graph selection consistency, and conditional consistency of the screening rule are established. Empirically, Trans-Ising achieves lower estimation errors than both target-only estimation and naive data pooling in simulations and real-data analyses.
AI.conclusion: Trans-Ising effectively addresses negative transfer in Ising model estimation with limited target samples by screening relevant auxiliary sources and applying a principled two-stage transfer learning procedure.

title: CV-DCLR: Causal-Visual Dynamic Label Refinement for Robust Zero-Shot Learning
summary: Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) facilitates knowledge transfer via shared semantic spaces. However, a critical bottleneck in this paradigm is Semantic Entanglement, where visual representations are inevitably conflated with visually similar semantic concepts, such as distinguishing the intrinsic traits of a Wolf from the shared features of a Husky. Existing global alignment methods often indiscriminately maximize correlations between visual and semantic modalities, leading models to overfit spurious similarities rather than capturing distinctive class identities. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose the Causal-Visual Dynamic Label Refinement (CV-DCLR) framework. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on superficial visual statistics, CV-DCLR recalibrates visual-semantic associations via a Dual-Stream Mutual Correction Mechanism. This includes a Visual Likelihood Stream to model observational patterns and a Causal Importance Stream that verifies the structural necessity of candidate prototypes through Counterfactual Intervention. Acting as a logical filter, our adaptive gating mechanism dynamically modulates feature responses to amplify genuine causal traits while suppressing visually plausible but structurally irrelevant distractors. Extensive experiments on the CUB, SUN, and AWA2 benchmarks under a rigorous Semantic Entanglement Injection protocol demonstrate that CV-DCLR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in high-ambiguity scenarios. Specifically, while existing models suffer catastrophic degradation under entanglement, our framework maintains robust performance, effectively disentangling true class identities from semantic confounders.

AI.tldr: CV-DCLR is a ZSL framework that uses a Dual-Stream Mutual Correction Mechanism with counterfactual intervention and adaptive gating to disentangle visually similar but semantically distinct concepts, outperforming SOTA on CUB, SUN, and AWA2 under semantic entanglement.
AI.motivation: Existing ZSL methods suffer from Semantic Entanglement, where visual representations conflate semantically similar classes (e.g., Wolf vs. Husky), and global alignment methods overfit spurious correlations rather than capturing true class identities.
AI.method: CV-DCLR employs a Dual-Stream Mutual Correction Mechanism with a Visual Likelihood Stream (observational patterns) and a Causal Importance Stream (counterfactual intervention to verify structural necessity), plus an adaptive gating mechanism that dynamically amplifies causal traits while suppressing irrelevant distractors.
AI.result: CV-DCLR significantly outperforms SOTA methods on CUB, SUN, and AWA2 under a Semantic Entanglement Injection protocol, maintaining robust performance where existing models suffer catastrophic degradation.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual causal reasoning combined with dynamic label refinement effectively disentangles true class identities from semantic confounders in high-ambiguity ZSL scenarios.

title: Agent Reinforcement Learning via Pivotal-Aware Self-Feedback Retry
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong decision-making capabilities in long-horizon interactive tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage failed trajectories: full retries incur high interaction costs, while experience retrieval tends to dilute critical experience signals. To address this, we propose PivoARL, a self-feedback retry framework for experience exploitation in LLM agents. PivoARL identifies the pivotal erroneous turn through structured reflection and performs local retry only from the corresponding pivotal state, thereby reusing the correct prefix and reducing redundant interactions. From an information-gain perspective, we further show that pivotal retry concentrates useful experience signals near the error boundary, mitigating the signal dilution caused by state-agnostic experience utilization. Based on this insight, we design a pivotal-aware credit assignment mechanism that rewards correct prefixes while isolating erroneous suffixes, and optimize reflection quality through implicit reflection returns. We conduct a systematic evaluation on 4 agent tasks and 7 search-based QA benchmarks. Results show that PivoARL achieves significant improvements on Pass@2/3 across all tasks, with an average gain of about 11.5\% over MetaRL. Moreover, benefiting from contrastive preference signals induced by pivotal turns, PivoARL also consistently improves Pass@1 on over 80\% of the tasks. On Minesweeper environment, PivoARL improves over GiGPO by more than 45\% and reduces interaction turns by about 42\% on average compared with full-retry methods. Code is available at https://github.com/yuki-younai/PivoARL.

AI.tldr: PivoARL is a self-feedback retry framework that improves LLM agents' ability to learn from failed trajectories by identifying pivotal erroneous turns, performing local retries from those points, and using a pivotal-aware credit assignment mechanism to concentrate useful experience signals near error boundaries, achieving ~11.5% average improvement over MetaRL on agent tasks and up to 45% improvement on Minesweeper while reducing interaction turns by ~42%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to effectively leverage failed trajectories: full retries are costly and experience retrieval dilutes critical error signals.
AI.method: PivoARL identifies the pivotal erroneous turn via structured reflection, performs local retry from that state only (reusing correct prefix), and uses pivotal-aware credit assignment that rewards correct prefixes while isolating erroneous suffixes, with implicit reflection returns to optimize reflection quality.
AI.result: Achieves ~11.5% average improvement over MetaRL on Pass@2/3 across 4 agent tasks and 7 QA benchmarks; improves Pass@1 on >80% tasks; improves over GiGPO by >45% on Minesweeper; reduces interaction turns by ~42% vs full-retry methods.
AI.conclusion: Pivotal turn-based local retry with contrastive preference signals effectively concentrates experience near error boundaries, enabling more efficient and effective learning from failures in LLM agents.

title: A Model-Based Framework for Developing DTs in Industry 4.0
summary: With the rise of Industry 4.0 driven by the integration of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and the Internet of Things (IoT), the use of Digital Twins (DTs) has significantly increased over the past decade, as they provide detailed insights and support well-informed decision-making. However, the lack of standardized methodologies, in addition to the time and resources involved for building them remains an important challenge.  Building on the idea that engineering models of the physical twin (PT) are often available, we propose a tool-supported framework that automates the derivation of DTs by leveraging existing structural and behavioral models of the PT and extending them with additional models to build a comprehensive DT. To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, we applied it to four different use cases, in which we automatically derived DT instances from (1) models of their PT, (2) configuration of our generic framework and (3) minimal ad hoc additional development for connecting the DT to the PT. These experiments illustrate the applicability of our framework for building DTs in contexts that satisfy our assumptions and requirements. By simply configuring the framework, we are able to derive a DT aligned with its operational purpose.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a tool-supported framework that automates the derivation of Digital Twins from existing engineering models of the physical twin, reducing time and resources needed for DT development. Feasibility is demonstrated across four use cases.
AI.motivation: Despite the increased use of Digital Twins in Industry 4.0, the lack of standardized methodologies and the significant time/resources required to build them remain major challenges.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that leverages existing structural and behavioral models of the physical twin, extends them with additional models, and automates DT derivation using configuration and minimal ad hoc development for DT-PT connection.
AI.result: Applied to four different use cases, the framework successfully derived DT instances automatically from PT models, framework configuration, and minimal additional development, demonstrating applicability in contexts meeting the stated assumptions.
AI.conclusion: By simply configuring the framework, a DT aligned with its operational purpose can be derived, reducing manual effort and addressing the standardization gap in DT development.

title: Back to Basics: Improving Molecular Understanding in LLMs via SMILES-Graph Translation
summary: Recent advances in molecular large language models have led to strong performance on molecular understanding and generation tasks, yet these gains often come without reliable structural grounding. In particular, existing approaches conflict with the chemistry principle that structure determines function: despite their downstream success, current molecular LLMs perform poorly on basic structure recognition, suggesting that they fail to capture molecular graphs from canonical SMILES. To remedy this, we propose MolBasic, a structure-first framework that strengthens structural comprehension via SMILES-Graph translation. MolBasic is built around a multi-level structure perception benchmark, where bidirectional SMILES-Graph conversion serves as the core task to align sequential and topological representations. On top of this foundation, we employ a progressive learning scheme with a standardized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to steer models from structure acquisition toward higher-level molecular reasoning. Experiments show that MolBasic substantially improves structural understanding and yields robust gains on downstream tasks, including property prediction and objective optimization, supporting our structure-first paradigm.

AI.tldr: MolBasic is a structure-first framework for molecular LLMs that improves structural grounding by using SMILES-Graph translation as a core task, combined with a multi-level benchmark and progressive Chain-of-Thought learning, leading to better performance on structure recognition and downstream molecular tasks.
AI.motivation: Current molecular LLMs achieve strong performance on generation and understanding tasks but lack reliable structural grounding — they fail to capture molecular graphs from canonical SMILES, contradicting the chemistry principle that structure determines function.
AI.method: MolBasic is built on (1) a multi-level structure perception benchmark with bidirectional SMILES-Graph conversion as the core task to align sequential (SMILES) and topological (graph) representations, and (2) a progressive learning scheme using a standardized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to transition models from structure acquisition to higher-level molecular reasoning.
AI.result: MolBasic substantially improves structural understanding and yields robust gains on downstream tasks, including property prediction and objective optimization, supporting the structure-first paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The structure-first paradigm (prioritizing structural comprehension via SMILES-Graph alignment before tackling higher-level tasks) is effective for molecular LLMs, bridging the gap between representation learning and principled chemistry.

title: DynaWM: A Base-VLA-Guided World Foundation Model for Moving-Object Manipulation
summary: Although vision-language-action (VLA) models have received widespread attention, many challenges remain in manipulating dynamic moving objects. In most existing approaches, end-to-end forward or inverse dynamics models, i.e., world models, are incorporated into high-performance base VLA architectures, which may degrade the performance of well-pretrained base VLA models due to inappropriate fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose DynaWM, a base-VLA-guided world foundation model that adapts to a wide variety of fine-tuned and coarse-tuned base-VLA checkpoints for moving-object manipulation. DynaWM uses a Mamba-3-based action encoder to encode the base action chunk produced by the base VLA into an action-conditioning representation, a V-JEPA 2.1 vision encoder to extract features from multi-view observation history, and a proprioceptive state encoder to encode robotic-arm proprioceptive states. These feature representations jointly condition a flow-matching DiT to regenerate motion-aware action trajectories for moving-object manipulation. For systematic evaluation, we construct the DynaGrasp-32 benchmark, covering six categories of moving-object manipulation tasks, including velocity variation, trajectory variation, and multi-object manipulation, as well as the DynaGrasp-1600 dataset, which consists of 32 scenarios, 1,600 demonstration trajectories, and approximately 1.53M images. For fine-tuned base-VLA checkpoints, DynaWM achieves percentage improvements of 7.19, 45.31, 1.88, and 10.94 over SmolVLA, X-VLA, π0, and π0.5, respectively. For coarse-tuned base-VLA checkpoints, performance increases by 35.13, 44.06, 35.69, and 26.13 percentage, respectively. Ablation experiments show that visual encoding enhances success by 27.50%, while reducing success by 45.44% if action conditioning is removed.

AI.tldr: DynaWM is a base-VLA-guided world foundation model using Mamba-3, V-JEPA 2.1, and flow-matching DiT to manipulate dynamic moving objects, outperforming baselines on the DynaGrasp-32 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models incorporate world models via fine-tuning, which degrades well-pretrained base VLA performance for dynamic moving-object manipulation. DynaWM aims to adapt various base-VLA checkpoints without performance degradation.
AI.method: DynaWM uses (1) Mamba-3-based action encoder for base action chunk encoding, (2) V-JEPA 2.1 vision encoder for multi-view observation features, (3) proprioceptive state encoder, all jointly conditioning a flow-matching DiT to regenerate motion-aware action trajectories.
AI.result: For fine-tuned base-VLAs: +7.19% (SmolVLA), +45.31% (X-VLA), +1.88% (π0), +10.94% (π0.5). For coarse-tuned: +35.13%, +44.06%, +35.69%, +26.13%. Ablation: visual encoding +27.50%, removing action conditioning -45.44%.
AI.conclusion: DynaWM effectively guides various base-VLA checkpoints for dynamic object manipulation while avoiding degradation from direct fine-tuning, validated on the DynaGrasp-32 benchmark and DynaGrasp-1600 dataset.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Traffic Signal Control
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for adaptive traffic signal control. However, in safety-critical infrastructure like traffic control, the opaque, black-box nature of deep RL models poses challenges for transportation agency acceptance, regulatory compliance, operational trust, troubleshooting, and fine-tuning. To bridge this gap between high-performance optimization and human-comprehensible interpretability, this effort introduces a novel, explainable entity centric RL framework for safe and transparent traffic signal control. Rather than processing traffic states through monolithic, flat vectors, the proposed architecture disaggregates real-time intersection observations into distinct, high-dimensional lane entities and phase temporal configurations to inherently preserve the structural topology and geometric configurations of the intersection. Relational dependencies and inter-lane conflicts are dynamically extracted via a dual-stage attention network featuring sequential multi-head cross-attention and self-attention blocks. This design yields a real time affinity matrix that quantifies the direct influence of signal phases on specific approach volumes and queues, providing full visual and analytical interpretability. To ensure strict operational reliability, a deterministic action-masking interface is integrated directly into the Proximal Policy Optimization pipeline, explicitly blocking invalid phase transitions to guarantee absolute compliance with established signal timing and safety constraints. Evaluated in a microscopic simulation environment, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in delay minimization. More importantly, the emergent attention weights align precisely with established traffic engineering principles, offering an auditable, trust-enabling, and deployable architecture for next-generation adaptive traffic control systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an explainable entity-centric reinforcement learning framework for traffic signal control that uses dual-stage attention networks to process lane entities and phase configurations, integrates deterministic action masking for safety compliance, and achieves superior delay minimization with fully interpretable attention weights aligned with traffic engineering principles.
AI.motivation: Deep RL models for traffic signal control are opaque black-box systems, hindering adoption in safety-critical infrastructure due to lack of interpretability, regulatory compliance challenges, and difficulties in troubleshooting and fine-tuning.
AI.method: A framework that (1) disaggregates traffic states into high-dimensional lane entities and phase temporal configurations preserving intersection topology, (2) uses dual-stage attention (multi-head cross-attention + self-attention) to extract relational dependencies and inter-lane conflicts, producing a real-time affinity matrix for full interpretability, and (3) integrates a deterministic action-masking interface into the PPO pipeline to block invalid phase transitions and enforce safety constraints.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in delay minimization in microscopic simulation; attention weights align precisely with established traffic engineering principles.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an auditable, trust-enabling, and deployable architecture for next-generation adaptive traffic control systems, bridging high-performance optimization with human-comprehensible interpretability.

title: Flow-A11y: Flow-Aware Accessibility Testing
summary: Modern web applications increasingly expose accessibility barriers through interaction flows rather than static page snapshots. Keyboard traps, focus loss, modal leakage, delayed status updates, dynamic controls, and changing page regions often become observable only after users perform concrete actions. These behaviors are directly related to dynamic WCAG criteria, yet they remain difficult to automate because their assessment depends on runtime interaction evidence and is still commonly performed through manual inspection. We present Flow-A11y, a flow-aware accessibility testing system for interaction-dependent WCAG criteria. Given a target page and a natural-language scenario, Flow-A11y executes the flow in a real browser, records an ordered runtime trace, constructs criterion-specific evidence packets, gates unsupported judgments, and emits auditable findings grounded in resolvable runtime evidence. Evaluated on 19 real public-web scenarios covering 45 dynamic WCAG criteria, Flow-A11y achieves over ten times higher oracle agreement than a generic browser-agent audit, while its evidence-calibration layer improves fail precision from 23.5% to 41.4% and eliminates invalid evidence references. These results show that runtime traces provide actionable evidence for assessing interaction-dependent accessibility behavior. They demonstrate a practical path toward automating dynamic WCAG criteria that page-level scanners cannot assess and that have traditionally required manual evaluation.

AI.tldr: Flow-A11y is a flow-aware accessibility testing system that executes user interaction flows in real browsers, captures ordered runtime traces, and constructs evidence packets to assess dynamic WCAG criteria that page-level scanners cannot handle, achieving over 10× higher oracle agreement than generic browser-agent audits and improving fail precision from 23.5% to 41.4%.
AI.motivation: Dynamic WCAG criteria (e.g., keyboard traps, focus loss, modal leakage) are inherently interaction-dependent and cannot be detected via static page snapshots. These are currently assessed through manual inspection because automation lacks runtime interaction evidence.
AI.method: Flow-A11y takes a target page and a natural-language scenario, executes the flow in a real browser, records an ordered runtime trace, constructs criterion-specific evidence packets, gates unsupported judgments, and emits auditable findings grounded in resolvable runtime evidence.
AI.result: On 19 real public-web scenarios covering 45 dynamic WCAG criteria, Flow-A11y achieves over 10× higher oracle agreement than a generic browser-agent audit. Its evidence-calibration layer improves fail precision from 23.5% to 41.4% and eliminates invalid evidence references.
AI.conclusion: Runtime traces provide actionable evidence for assessing interaction-dependent accessibility behavior, demonstrating a practical path toward automating dynamic WCAG criteria that traditionally required manual evaluation.

title: Do ECG Foundation Models Transfer to Rare Cardiac Diseases? Evidence from Brugada Syndrome Detection
summary: Background: Foundation models (FMs) trained on large-scale unlabeled physiological data have emerged as a promising paradigm for medical artificial intelligence. Their ability to capture clinically meaningful, transferable representations for rare diseases remains largely unproven. This study investigates whether FM pre-training provides genuine clinical generalization benefits beyond improved optimization for rare electrocardiographic (ECG) phenotypes. Methods: We systematically evaluated nine publicly available ECG FMs for Brugada syndrome detection on the BrSwiss cohort (294 patients, 87 cases) and the independent external HUCA cohort (363 patients, 76 cases), under three strategies (from-scratch training, linear probing, full fine-tuning) across several configurations, including a 3% data ablation and zero-shot cross-site transfers. Results: Pre-training was necessary for high-capacity architectures unable to converge from scratch (AUC gain up to 0.411, p < 0.05), but gave no significant gain for compact architectures already converged on labeled data alone. On full BrSwiss, the best fine-tuned FM (ECG-CPC, AUC = 0.962) only marginally exceeded the strongest supervised baseline (ECG-CPC from scratch, AUC = 0.932; p = 0.091). At matched training-set size, the data-efficiency advantage on BrSwiss-3% (AUC gain = 0.055, p < 0.01) did not replicate on HUCA. Under zero-shot cross-site transfer, FM-based pipelines did not generalize better than supervised baselines, all approaching chance-level performance. Conclusion: For Brugada syndrome detection, FM pre-training is mechanical rather than semantic, providing optimization stability rather than transferable clinical knowledge. These findings challenge the assumption that large-scale pre-training inherently encodes clinically meaningful representations, highlighting the central role of model architecture and data-domain alignment.

AI.tldr: Foundation model pre-training for Brugada syndrome ECG detection provides optimization stability (helping high-capacity models converge) but fails to deliver semantically transferable clinical knowledge, as evidenced by marginal or non-significant improvements over supervised baselines and chance-level zero-shot cross-site generalization.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether foundation model pre-training on large-scale unlabeled physiological data provides genuine clinical generalization benefits beyond improved optimization, specifically for rare electrocardiographic phenotypes like Brugada syndrome.
AI.method: Systematically evaluated nine public ECG foundation models on two cohorts (BrSwiss, HUCA) under three strategies (from-scratch, linear probing, full fine-tuning), including 3% data ablation and zero-shot cross-site transfer.
AI.result: Pre-training gave significant AUC gains (up to 0.411) only for architectures that failed to converge from scratch; best FM (ECG-CPC, AUC=0.962) marginally exceeded supervised baseline (AUC=0.932, p=0.091); data-efficiency gain on BrSwiss-3% (AUC+0.055, p<0.01) did not replicate on HUCA; zero-shot cross-site transfer was at chance level for all pipelines.
AI.conclusion: FM pre-training for Brugada syndrome detection is mechanical (optimization stability) rather than semantic (transferable clinical knowledge), challenging the assumption that large-scale pre-training inherently encodes clinically meaningful representations and highlighting the importance of model architecture and data-domain alignment.

title: Latent Visual Cache for Video Reasoning
summary: Video reasoning requires Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to remain grounded in dense evidence, yet existing systems largely adopt "read-once, generate-many" paradigm, in which visual grounding weakens during generation. This phenomenon has been widely observed and is known as Visual Anchoring Decay. To fill this gap, we introduce Latent Video Cache (Latent-VC), a recurrent latent visual cache inserted into the decoder to preserve compact visual memories throughout reasoning. The cache is trained with supervised contrastive cache alignment and vision-grounded GRPO with a latent grounding reward, while maintaining strict train-inference alignment through native decoder hidden states. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, Latent-VC consistently outperforms strong CoT and SFT+GRPO baselines across six video benchmarks, with especially clear gains on grounding-intensive and long-video tasks. In addition, it also achieves higher accuracy with substantially shorter responses, suggesting that latent visual caching improves video reasoning by preserving visual evidence rather than relying on longer textual chains.

AI.tldr: Latent Video Cache (Latent-VC) is a recurrent latent visual cache inserted into the decoder to preserve compact visual memories throughout reasoning, addressing Visual Anchoring Decay in video LMMs. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, it outperforms strong baselines across six video benchmarks with shorter responses, achieving higher accuracy by preserving visual evidence rather than relying on longer textual chains.
AI.motivation: Existing LMMs adopt a "read-once, generate-many" paradigm where visual grounding weakens during generation (Visual Anchoring Decay), leading to degraded video reasoning performance, especially on grounding-intensive and long-video tasks.
AI.method: Introduces Latent-VC, a recurrent latent visual cache inserted into the decoder to preserve compact visual memories. Trained with supervised contrastive cache alignment and vision-grounded GRPO with a latent grounding reward, maintaining strict train-inference alignment through native decoder hidden states.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms strong CoT and SFT+GRPO baselines across six video benchmarks, with clear gains on grounding-intensive and long-video tasks. Achieves higher accuracy with substantially shorter responses.
AI.conclusion: Latent visual caching improves video reasoning by preserving visual evidence rather than relying on longer textual chains, effectively mitigating Visual Anchoring Decay.

title: Can Conversational Temporal Dynamics Improve Depression Detection in Dyads? A Preliminary Investigation in Multi-Modality Perspectives
summary: Automatic depression detection from clinical interviews typically models the semantic content and acoustic characteristics of participant speech. However, the interactional timing between the clinician and participant remains comparatively under-modeled. We investigate conversational temporal dynamics, specifically dyadic turn-pair timing, as a primary modality fused with self-supervised encoders. Evaluated on the DAIC-WOZ dataset, we compare a compact 24-dimensional timing module against frozen WavLM-large and RoBERTa-large baseline detectors. This temporal module achieves the highest single-modality performance on the development set. Furthermore, a convex-weighted late fusion strategy improves overall performance to 0.804 and 0.669 macro-F1 on the development and test sets, respectively. The learned fusion effectively assigns zero weight to acoustics, demonstrating that conversational timing serves as a lightweight, interpretable complement for dyadic depression screening.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using conversational turn-pair timing between clinician and participant as a lightweight, interpretable modality for automatic depression detection. A compact 24-dimensional timing module outperforms frozen WavLM-large and RoBERTa-large baselines in single-modality evaluation, and convex-weighted late fusion achieves 0.804/0.669 macro-F1 on dev/test sets, with acoustics receiving zero fusion weight.
AI.motivation: Acoustic and semantic features are commonly used for automatic depression detection from clinical interviews, but the interactional timing between clinician and participant—a key aspect of conversational dynamics—remains underexplored. The paper aims to investigate whether dyadic turn-pair timing can serve as a primary modality for depression screening.
AI.method: Proposes a compact 24-dimensional temporal module capturing dyadic turn-pair timing features from clinical interviews. This module is evaluated alone and fused via convex-weighted late fusion with frozen WavLM-large (acoustic) and RoBERTa-large (semantic) self-supervised encoders on the DAIC-WOZ dataset.
AI.result: The timing module achieves the highest single-modality performance on the development set. Convex-weighted fusion yields 0.804 macro-F1 on dev and 0.669 on test. The learned fusion assigns zero weight to the acoustic modality, indicating timing alone complements semantics effectively.
AI.conclusion: Conversational timing is a lightweight, interpretable, and effective complement to existing modalities for dyadic depression screening, potentially replacing heavier acoustic features in certain settings.

title: Towards Automatically Inferring Constraints to Identify Implicit Assumptions in Data Analysis
summary: High-level languages such as R or Python are used frequently to analyze and visualize data in the form of scripts or notebooks. However, these artifacts suffer from reproducibility issues due to what we frame as implicit assumptions made by the authors. Such assumptions range from package versions and shapes of involved data tables, to manual and often undocumented setup steps. Within this work, we provide a unified, example-driven perspective on implicit assumptions in data analysis backed by an explorative proof-of-concept implementation. With this perspective, we propose the use of static analysis techniques to identify such assumptions and to make them explicit in the form of code constraints, focusing on the inclusion of data-analysis-specific issues. Such constraints can then be used to automatically transform these scripts into executable and reproducible artifacts, to check these assumptions at runtime, and to serve as documentation to support code reuse and comprehension.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses reproducibility issues in high-level data analysis scripts (R, Python) caused by implicit assumptions (package versions, data shapes, manual setup steps), proposing static analysis to identify and make these assumptions explicit as code constraints for automated reproducibility, runtime checking, and documentation.
AI.motivation: Data analysis scripts and notebooks written in high-level languages like R or Python suffer from reproducibility issues due to implicit assumptions made by authors, such as package versions, data table shapes, and undocumented manual setup steps.
AI.method: The authors propose using static analysis techniques to identify implicit assumptions in data analysis code and make them explicit as code constraints, focusing on data-analysis-specific issues.
AI.result: An explorative proof-of-concept implementation demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed approach for detecting and explicating implicit assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Making implicit assumptions explicit as constraints enables automatic transformation of scripts into reproducible artifacts, runtime assumption checking, and improved documentation for code reuse and comprehension.

title: Can Model Merging Improve Aggregation in DiLoCo?
summary: Model merging techniques, which aggregate independently finetuned models into one to combine their capabilities, have become a topic of significant interest in recent years, with a broad array of methods having been proposed to tackle this problem. Simultaneously, an emerging trend in distributed learning has been the use of methods such as local SGD and DiLoCo, which greatly reduce communication costs by periodically aggregating the independently trained local models. However, these communication-efficient methods have been shown to degrade in performance relative to the FLOP-matched data-parallel gold standard as the number of independent local models grows and as the number of local training steps before global communication is increased. In this work, we draw an explicit analogy between the pseudo-gradient aggregation step in local SGD/DiLoCo and task arithmetic-based model merging, establishing a straightforward way to utilize merging methods in the context of distributed optimization. We then evaluate multiple state-of-the-art model merging methods in this setting and identify one method in particular, Iso-C, as a promising approach for improving DiLoCo. We find that DiLoCo SGD with Iso-C aggregation outperforms not only simple pseudo-gradient averaging but even the momentum-based DiLoCo, despite lacking a momentum mechanism itself. Building on this finding, we propose IsoLoCo, which adapts Iso-C for distributed training by equipping it with Nesterov momentum. Our empirical evaluations on language model pre-training across varying numbers of local workers show that IsoLoCo significantly outperforms DiLoCo, with the gap between them widening as the number of workers increases. This advantage remains present across model sizes and inner step counts, confirming that merging-inspired aggregation is an effective strategy for low-communication distributed training.

AI.tldr: This paper draws an analogy between model merging techniques and the pseudo-gradient aggregation step in communication-efficient distributed training (local SGD/DiLoCo). It applies model merging methods, particularly Iso-C, to improve DiLoCo, and proposes IsoLoCo (Iso-C with Nesterov momentum). Empirical results on language model pre-training show IsoLoCo significantly outperforms DiLoCo, with the gap widening as the number of workers increases.
AI.motivation: Communication-efficient distributed training methods like local SGD and DiLoCo suffer performance degradation as the number of local models or local steps increases. The paper aims to bridge model merging and distributed optimization to improve aggregation quality and mitigate this degradation.
AI.method: The authors establish an explicit analogy between pseudo-gradient aggregation in local SGD/DiLoCo and task arithmetic-based model merging. They evaluate state-of-the-art merging methods, identify Iso-C as promising, and propose IsoLoCo which adapts Iso-C with Nesterov momentum for distributed training.
AI.result: DiLoCo SGD with Iso-C aggregation outperforms simple pseudo-gradient averaging and momentum-based DiLoCo. IsoLoCo significantly outperforms DiLoCo across varying numbers of workers, model sizes, and inner step counts, with the gap widening as workers increase.
AI.conclusion: Merging-inspired aggregation is an effective strategy for low-communication distributed training, and IsoLoCo offers a practical improvement over existing DiLoCo methods.

title: Privacy-Preserving Industrial Ergonomics: mmWave-Based Automated REBA Scoring and Pose Estimation
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Automation and Computing (ICAC 2026)
summary: Work-related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WMSDs) require continuous ergonomic assessments. While Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) is a gold-standard observation tool, manual monitoring is labor-intensive, and vision-based automation leads to privacy concerns. This paper proposes a novel end-to-end multi-task learning framework for privacy-preserving ergonomic assessment using millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar. A spatio-temporal backbone reconstructs 3D human skeletons, which serves as the biomechanical foundation for a subsequent regression head to generate REBA risk scores. To overcome the sparsity of radar point clouds, we utilise a multi-objective loss function incorporating biomechanical limits and temporal smoothness constraints. Furthermore, we implement an oversampling strategy to address the imbalance of high-risk postures in existing datasets. Experimental results on MMFi dataset demonstrate that our framework achieves a Categorical Accuracy of 77.78% and real-time performance with an inference latency of 5.70 ms. Our method reaches a High-risk REBA MAE of 0.93, which significantly outperforms both direct regression and two-stage pipelines in high-risk scenarios, providing a robust solution for non-invasive industrial ergonomic assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-task learning framework using mmWave radar to perform privacy-preserving ergonomic assessment by reconstructing 3D skeletons and regressing REBA risk scores, achieving 77.78% accuracy and 5.70 ms inference latency.
AI.motivation: Manual ergonomic monitoring is labor-intensive and vision-based automation raises privacy concerns, motivating the need for a non-invasive, privacy-preserving automated assessment method.
AI.method: An end-to-end multi-task learning framework with a spatio-temporal backbone reconstructing 3D human skeletons from mmWave radar point clouds, followed by a regression head for REBA scores. Uses a multi-objective loss with biomechanical and temporal constraints, plus oversampling to address high-risk posture imbalance.
AI.result: 77.78% Categorical Accuracy, 5.70 ms inference latency, High-risk REBA MAE of 0.93 on the MMFi dataset, outperforming direct regression and two-stage pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust, non-invasive, privacy-preserving solution for real-time industrial ergonomic assessment, particularly effective for high-risk scenarios.

title: Bridging Interleaved Multi-Modal Reasoning as a Unified Decision Process
summary: Unified multi-modal models (UMMs) have shown promising interleaved text-image reasoning capabilities, yet effectively optimizing such multi-turn generation via reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Existing approaches apply RL exclusively to text steps, relegating image generation to supervised surrogates, preventing policy gradients from propagating through the full interleaved trajectory across heterogeneous modalities. This leaves the potential of RL for UMMs largely untapped. In the paper, we introduce \textbf{BRAID} (\textbf{B}ridging inte\textbf{R}le\textbf{A}ved mult\textbf{I}-modal reasoning as a unified \textbf{D}ecision process), a simple framework that casts multi-turn text-image-text reasoning as a unified Markov decision process (MDP), enabling joint optimization of textual and visual generation via a single, principled RL objective. BRAID computes a shared trajectory-level advantage and propagates it coherently into both text tokens and image denoising paths, each optimized through its modality-native policy gradient mechanism. To further address long-horizon credit assignment, BRAID employs a vision-language model (VLM) judge that scores each intermediate image on its reasoning utility, supplying dense turn-level feedback to sharpen learning at critical visual branches. Experiments on spatial reasoning and visual perception benchmarks show that BRAID consistently outperforms various baselines, confirming that a unified MDP formulation with vision-thinking guidance is essential for effective multi-modal reasoning.

AI.tldr: BRAID is a framework that casts multi-turn text-image-text reasoning as a unified Markov decision process, enabling joint RL optimization of both textual and visual generation through a shared trajectory-level advantage and dense turn-level feedback from a VLM judge, outperforming baselines on spatial reasoning and visual perception tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing RL approaches for unified multi-modal models apply RL exclusively to text steps and use supervised surrogates for image generation, preventing policy gradients from propagating through full interleaved text-image trajectories and leaving the potential of RL for UMMs untapped.
AI.method: BRAID formulates multi-turn text-image-text reasoning as a unified MDP with (1) a shared trajectory-level advantage propagated coherently into both text tokens and image denoising paths, each optimized via modality-native policy gradient mechanisms, and (2) a VLM judge that scores intermediate images on reasoning utility to supply dense turn-level feedback for long-horizon credit assignment.
AI.result: BRAID consistently outperforms various baselines on spatial reasoning and visual perception benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A unified MDP formulation with vision-thinking guidance is essential for effective multi-modal reasoning via RL.

title: Copper: Unifying Correctness and Performance Specification in Code Generation
summary: Generative AI has made remarkable progress in producing functionally correct code, yet ensuring both correctness and performance remains an open challenge. We present Copper, a framework that combines formal verification with performance-aware specification to generate code that is provably correct and efficiently executable. Our approach integrates AI-driven code synthesis with formal verification tools, and automated performance profiling loops. Evaluated on a diverse set of algorithmic and real-world programming tasks, Copper produces solutions that satisfy strict correctness guarantees while delivering significant improvements in runtime and memory efficiency compared to baseline AI-generated code. This work demonstrates that it is feasible to bridge the gap between trustworthiness and performance in AI-assisted programming, offering a practical pathway toward reliable, high-performance code generation.

AI.tldr: Copper is a framework that combines formal verification, performance-aware specifications, and AI-driven code synthesis to generate code that is both provably correct and efficiently executable, outperforming baseline AI-generated code in runtime and memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: Generative AI produces functionally correct code but ensuring both correctness and performance remains an open challenge. The work aims to bridge the gap between trustworthiness and performance in AI-assisted programming.
AI.method: Copper integrates AI-driven code synthesis with formal verification tools and automated performance profiling loops, guided by performance-aware specifications.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse algorithmic and real-world tasks, Copper produces solutions with strict correctness guarantees and significant improvements in runtime and memory efficiency over baseline AI-generated code.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to bridge the gap between trustworthiness and performance in AI-assisted programming, offering a practical pathway toward reliable, high-performance code generation.

title: Out-of-distribution Neural Inference in Dynamical Ising Models
summary: Neural networks are increasingly used to infer hidden physical structure from dynamical observations, yet it remains unclear whether their out-of-distribution performance reflects transferable physical rule learning. We address this question in a controlled inverse problem: reconstructing interaction graphs of a kinetic Ising model from Glauber magnetization trajectories. Across convolutional, graph, Transformer, and hybrid architectures, we find that data-driven training produces distinct and reproducible statistical strategies under topology and temperature shifts. Edge-population diagnostics reveal that Transformer-based models tend to preserve the link density of the training ensemble, whereas convolutional models can collapse toward sparse- or no-link predictions that appear out-of-distribution stable by exploiting the majority no-link class. Thus, high in-distribution accuracy and apparent out-of-distribution robustness do not necessarily imply a learned dynamics-to-structure rule. Instead, neural reconstruction can be governed by architecture-dependent statistical priors. Our results identify a concrete failure mode of standard data-driven learning in physical inverse problems and motivate rule-guided principles for machine-learning-assisted scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Neural network reconstruction of Ising model interaction graphs from dynamical data is governed by architecture-dependent statistical priors rather than learned physical rules, causing out-of-distribution performance to reflect dataset statistics (e.g., link density) rather than transferable dynamics-to-structure mappings.
AI.motivation: To determine whether neural networks' out-of-distribution performance in inferring hidden physical structure reflects genuine transferable learning of physical rules or is instead driven by architecture-dependent statistical biases.
AI.method: Controlled inverse problem of reconstructing interaction graphs of a kinetic Ising model from Glauber magnetization trajectories, comparing convolutional, graph, Transformer, and hybrid architectures under topology and temperature distribution shifts using edge-population diagnostics.
AI.result: Transformer models preserve training ensemble link density; convolutional models collapse toward sparse/no-link predictions exploiting the majority no-link class. High in-distribution accuracy and apparent out-of-distribution robustness do not imply learned physical rules.
AI.conclusion: Standard data-driven learning in physical inverse problems has a concrete failure mode where architecture-dependent statistical priors dominate; motivates rule-guided principles for machine-learning-assisted scientific discovery.

title: Fusion: A Framework for Unified Sequential Token AdaptatIon in VisiOn TraNsformers
summary: Vision Transformers achieve strong image classification accuracy but process all image regions with nearly the same computation, even when many regions are redundant or uninformative. Recent adaptive inference methods reduce this cost by selectively compressing tokens or terminating inference early, but combining these mechanisms often causes unstable intermediate representations and accuracy degradation. We introduce Fusion, a unified adaptive inference framework that coordinates token merging, early exiting, and token pruning through a simple staged design: tokens are merged first, confidence is evaluated next, and pruning is applied only to samples that continue inference. This ordering allows the three mechanisms to operate cooperatively rather than competitively. Fusion further includes lightweight routing modules that adapt compression strength to each input and support inference-time adjustment of the accuracy--latency trade-off without retraining. On ImageNet-1k with DeiT-S, Fusion matches or surpasses state-of-the-art adaptive ViT methods at comparable compute budgets while reducing calibration error by up to $4\times$ and inference energy by $48\%$. Experiments across ImageNet-100, CIFAR-100, and ImageNette with multiple ViT backbones demonstrate consistent transferability without dataset-specific tuning.

AI.tldr: Fusion is a unified adaptive inference framework for Vision Transformers that coordinates token merging, early exiting, and token pruning in a staged design (merge → evaluate → prune), achieving strong accuracy with reduced computation, lower calibration error (up to 4×), and 48% inference energy savings on ImageNet-1k with DeiT-S.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers process all image regions with similar computation despite many being redundant/uninformative; existing adaptive methods (token compression, early exiting, pruning) are typically used separately or compete with each other, causing unstable representations and accuracy drop.
AI.method: A three-stage ordered pipeline: (1) token merging to reduce redundancy, (2) confidence evaluation for early exit decisions, (3) token pruning applied only to samples continuing inference. Lightweight routing modules adapt compression strength per input and allow accuracy-latency trade-off adjustment at inference without retraining.
AI.result: On ImageNet-1k with DeiT-S, Fusion matches/surpasses SOTA adaptive ViT methods at comparable compute, reduces calibration error by up to 4×, and inference energy by 48%. Consistent transferability across ImageNet-100, CIFAR-100, ImageNette with multiple ViT backbones without dataset-specific tuning.
AI.conclusion: The staged design (merge → evaluate → prune) enables cooperative operation of three adaptive mechanisms, yielding efficient, accurate, and well-calibrated inference that generalizes across datasets and backbones.

title: Folding, Reasoning, and Scaling with Open-source Drug Discovery Engine
summary: Accurately modeling biomolecular interactions is a central bottleneck in biology and therapeutic discovery. Here, we introduce Open Drug Discovery Engine (OpenDDE), an open-source, all-atom biomolecular foundation model that uses co-folding as the entry point to a scalable AI-driven drug discovery engine. Rather than treating structure prediction as an isolated endpoint, OpenDDE is designed as a shared structural reasoning layer for modeling sequence-structure-function relationships across biomolecular complexes, enabling complex structure prediction today while providing a foundation for de novo design, affinity estimation, structure-conditioned optimization, and more. OpenDDE integrates advances in all-atom architecture, atomic latent reasoning, inference optimization, and large-scale data processing to achieve IsoDDE-level co-folding accuracy within a reproducible and openly accessible framework. We also identify two scaling-law directions for co-folding models, revealing practical routes for continued improvement through data, model, inference, and training scaling. By releasing training code, inference pipelines, checkpoints, and benchmarks, OpenDDE aims to democratize access to frontier biomolecular intelligence, accelerate global collaboration, and lay an open foundation for next-generation drug discovery systems that can move from predicting molecular structures toward designing, scoring, and optimizing therapeutic candidates for human health.

AI.tldr: OpenDDE is an open-source, all-atom biomolecular foundation model using co-folding as a shared structural reasoning layer for modeling biomolecular interactions, achieving IsoDDE-level accuracy while providing infrastructure for drug discovery tasks like structure prediction, de novo design, and affinity estimation.
AI.motivation: Accurately modeling biomolecular interactions is a central bottleneck in biology and therapeutic discovery, and existing approaches treat structure prediction as an isolated endpoint rather than a reusable reasoning layer.
AI.method: OpenDDE integrates all-atom architecture, atomic latent reasoning, inference optimization, and large-scale data processing; identifies two scaling-law directions for co-folding models (data/model/inference/training scaling).
AI.result: Achieves IsoDDE-level co-folding accuracy within a reproducible and openly accessible framework.
AI.conclusion: OpenDDE democratizes access to frontier biomolecular intelligence and lays an open foundation for next-generation drug discovery systems that move from structure prediction toward designing, scoring, and optimizing therapeutic candidates.

title: Detecting Architectural Drift in Safety-Critical Firmware through Runtime Trace Analysis
comment: accepted at 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026)
summary: Maintaining consistency between architectural design and runtime-observed behavior is challenging in long-lived safety-critical firmware. This paper presents a runtime-informed methodology for detecting architectural drift in ISO 26262-compliant firmware. The approach collects hardware-assisted execution traces, abstracts them into message exchanges among firmware components, and compares the resulting runtime behavior with design-time sequence diagrams through a deterministic differencing step. The computed delta identifies discrepancies as confirmed, missing, additional, or inverted, while a constrained LLM-based step generates a human-readable report only to support expert review. We evaluate the methodology in an industrial firmware context through agreement-based validation and a practitioner survey. Results over 26 test cases show strong agreement between the generated deltas and expert-curated references, while practitioners perceive the reports as useful for interpreting drift, reducing manual analysis effort, and supporting safety-oriented documentation activities. The findings suggest that combining runtime trace analysis, deterministic architectural differencing, and constrained LLM-based reporting can practically support architectural drift detection in evolving safety-critical firmware.

AI.tldr: A runtime-informed methodology detects architectural drift in safety-critical firmware by comparing hardware execution traces against design-time sequence diagrams, using deterministic differencing and constrained LLM-based reporting, validated through industrial case studies.
AI.motivation: Maintaining consistency between architectural design and runtime behavior is challenging in long-lived safety-critical firmware (e.g., ISO 26262), where undetected architectural drift can compromise safety compliance.
AI.method: Collects hardware-assisted execution traces → abstracts them into message exchanges among firmware components → compares runtime behavior with design-time sequence diagrams via deterministic differencing → classifies discrepancies (confirmed, missing, additional, inverted) → uses a constrained LLM to generate a human-readable report for expert review.
AI.result: Evaluated on 26 test cases in an industrial firmware context; strong agreement between generated deltas and expert-curated references; practitioners found the reports useful for interpreting drift, reducing manual analysis effort, and supporting safety-oriented documentation.
AI.conclusion: Combining runtime trace analysis, deterministic architectural differencing, and constrained LLM-based reporting practically supports architectural drift detection in evolving safety-critical firmware.

title: SE-UNet: Singular Equivariant Imaging for Real-World Constrained Generation
summary: While diffusion models have revolutionized image synthesis, their application to real-world inverse problems is often hampered by the need for massive datasets and the difficulty of imposing strict physical constraints. In this work, we introduce \textbf{SE-UNet} (Singular Equivariant UNet), a framework designed to solve ill-posed imaging tasks without extensive pre-training. By treating generation as an optimization problem constrained by geometric equivariance ($D_4$ group) and singular value gating, SE-UNet effectively standardizes the solution space. We demonstrate that these strong inductive biases allow for state-of-the-art zero-shot inpainting results (80\% missing pixels) on CIFAR-10. Our method surpasses Deep Image Prior (DIP) baselines by over 4 dB in PSNR and exhibits a characteristic "singular snap" convergence -- rapidly locking into the signal manifold. SE-UNet thus offers a data-efficient pathway for constrained generation, aligning with the ReALM-GEN goal of bridging theoretical priors with practical deployment.

AI.tldr: SE-UNet is a zero-shot image generation framework that solves ill-posed inverse problems by combining geometric equivariance (D4 group) and singular value gating as strong inductive biases, achieving state-of-the-art inpainting results (80% missing pixels) on CIFAR-10 without pre-training, surpassing DIP by over 4 dB PSNR.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models require massive datasets and struggle to impose strict physical constraints when applied to real-world inverse problems; the goal is to develop a data-efficient solution that does not rely on extensive pre-training.
AI.method: SE-UNet treats image generation as an optimization problem constrained by D4 group geometric equivariance and singular value gating, which collectively standardize the solution space and provide strong inductive biases for zero-shot learning.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot inpainting with 80% missing pixels on CIFAR-10, surpassing Deep Image Prior baselines by over 4 dB in PSNR, and exhibits rapid "singular snap" convergence behavior.
AI.conclusion: SE-UNet provides a data-efficient pathway for constrained generation, bridging theoretical priors with practical deployment in ill-posed imaging tasks.

title: Evaluating LLM Uncertainty in Long-Form Generation Using Deterministic Ground Truth
comment: Accepted to the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). Code available at https://github.com/IdoAmit198/SALT
summary: As LLMs generate increasingly long outputs, effective uncertainty estimation must identify errors at fine-grained levels rather than discard entire responses. While such methods exist, evaluating uncertainty at any resolution (token to an entire generation) is challenging and highly sensitive to label imperfections, making zero-noise benchmarks essential; yet, long-form generation benchmarks tend to rely on fallible labels rather than deterministic ground truth. We introduce Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target (SALT), a benchmark of six procedurally generated tasks with single deterministic long textual ground truths, enabling unit-level evaluation of correctness, calibration, and ranking without external judges. Equipped with SALT, our analysis of 50+ LLMs reveals key insights: We identify which confidence functions dominate each uncertainty aspect and show that confidence ranking largely breaks at atomic resolution, even when clearer separability emerges at coarser line-level units. SALT further enables controlled atom-level interventions throughout generation, revealing two separable drivers of future errors: propagation from corrupted prefixes, dominated by global context correctness, and bounded degradation from increasing answer-context length. Finally, we demonstrate that reasoning, via Chain-of-Thought prompting or internalized through training, introduces a trade-off, improving accuracy while degrading confidence ranking. These findings directly impact risk-critical applications requiring reliable error identification and mitigation.

AI.tldr: SALT is a benchmark with deterministic ground-truth long-form text for evaluating uncertainty estimation in LLMs at fine-grained (atomic) resolution, revealing that confidence ranking breaks at atomic level, that errors arise from two separable drivers (propagation and length degradation), and that reasoning (CoT) trades improved accuracy for worse calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimation methods for long-form LLM generation lack fine-grained evaluation benchmarks with deterministic ground truth, relying instead on fallible labels; this makes it impossible to assess uncertainty at atomic resolution without label noise, motivating a zero-noise benchmark.
AI.method: The authors introduce SALT (Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target), a benchmark of six procedurally generated tasks with single deterministic long textual ground truths. They analyze 50+ LLMs to evaluate confidence functions at unit-level (atomic to entire generation) for correctness, calibration, and ranking, and perform controlled atom-level intervention experiments.
AI.result: Confidence ranking largely breaks at atomic resolution (while clearer separability emerges at coarser line-level units). Two separable drivers of future errors are identified: (1) error propagation from corrupted prefixes (dominated by global context correctness), and (2) bounded degradation from increasing answer-context length. Reasoning (CoT or internalized) improves accuracy but degrades confidence ranking.
AI.conclusion: The findings directly impact risk-critical applications requiring reliable error identification and mitigation, highlighting a trade-off between accuracy and calibration when reasoning is employed.

title: Which Algorithm Specification Formats Help Language Models Implement Machine Learning Algorithms?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to implement algorithms from research manuscripts, but papers often leave implementation choices implicit. This study examines how the written format of an algorithm specification affects first-pass LLM implementation accuracy. We compare ordinary prose, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode, PDF-like extracted pseudocode, Markdown fields, YAML-like specifications, JSON-like specifications, and Python code stubs across five machine learning tasks, three models, and four experimental settings, yielding 4,020 generated implementations. Hidden tests evaluate details that often determine correctness, including tie-breaking, array shapes, numerical rules, return structures, and invalid-input behavior. Under the core-information setting, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode has the largest average format effect, with YAML-like specifications and ordinary prose close behind. Under complete information, GPT-5.4 mini shows no format differences in the matched comparisons, whereas Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2 3B still do. Code stubs do not consistently improve correctness despite specifying the function signature. The results support a writing recommendation: authors should state the interface, computation steps, numerical rules, and boundary-case behavior explicitly, instead of relying on a particular surface format to carry those details.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates how different algorithm specification formats (prose, LaTeX pseudocode, PDF pseudocode, Markdown, YAML, JSON, Python stubs) affect LLM implementation accuracy across 5 ML tasks, 3 models, and 4 settings (4,020 implementations), finding LaTeX pseudocode has the largest positive effect under core-information settings, while code stubs do not consistently improve correctness.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to implement algorithms from research manuscripts, but papers often leave implementation choices implicit. The authors aim to determine how the written format of algorithm specifications affects first-pass LLM implementation accuracy to guide better writing practices.
AI.method: Compared seven specification formats (ordinary prose, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode, PDF-like extracted pseudocode, Markdown fields, YAML-like, JSON-like, Python code stubs) across five ML tasks, three models (GPT-5.4 mini, Gemma 3 4B, Llama 3.2 3B), and four experimental settings, generating 4,020 implementations. Hidden tests evaluated correctness on tie-breaking, array shapes, numerical rules, return structures, and invalid-input behavior.
AI.result: Under the core-information setting, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode showed the largest average format effect, with YAML-like specifications and ordinary prose close behind. Under complete information, GPT-5.4 mini showed no format differences, while smaller models still did. Code stubs did not consistently improve correctness despite specifying the function signature.
AI.conclusion: Authors should explicitly state the interface, computation steps, numerical rules, and boundary-case behavior rather than relying on a particular surface format to carry those details.

title: SHiPPO: Recurrent Memory with Transported Polynomial Projections
summary: HiPPO gives recurrent states memory semantics as coefficients of online polynomial projections, but in fixed channel coordinates. Modern selective SSMs, by contrast, rely on token-dependent control and channel interaction. We introduce SHiPPO (Sylvester HiPPO), a transported projection-memory prior that lifts HiPPO coefficient memories into a moving channel frame. For any fixed or realized right-transport path, SHiPPO transports the approximation family and channel metric together; conditional on that path, the state is ordinary HiPPO in a tied moving frame and follows Sylvester coefficient dynamics, preserving the left online-memory operator while adding right-action transport. For selective-SSM execution, we derive a restricted group-local realization with controller-compatible right actions, exponential-adjusted updates, exact block-affine scan, and recurrent decoding. We also give a simultaneous-reducibility criterion identifying when right transports collapse to static mixing plus independent scalar or blockwise banks. Controlled diagnostics show that larger current-token write rank improves ordinary prediction error but cannot recover order-sensitive changes to already-written memory; transported-memory variants recover this signal, which disappears when the transport pathway is removed. A finite-field associative-recall diagnostic with interleaved bindings, operations, and queries provides complementary autoregressive evidence while leaving the preferred right-action realization open. Taken together, these results support SHiPPO as a mechanistically grounded transported-memory prior, with evidence focused on memory mechanisms rather than broad sequence-modeling dominance.

AI.tldr: SHiPPO extends HiPPO's memory states by transporting polynomial projection coefficients along a moving channel frame, enabling selective SSMs to recover order-sensitive memory changes that fixed-coordinate HiPPO cannot capture.
AI.motivation: HiPPO provides recurrent state memory through online polynomial projections but operates in fixed channel coordinates, limiting its ability to capture token-dependent interactions and order-sensitive changes in already-written memory. Modern selective state space models require such flexibility.
AI.method: SHiPPO introduces a transported projection-memory prior that lifts HiPPO coefficient memories into a moving channel frame via a right-transport path. It uses Sylvester coefficient dynamics preserving the left online-memory operator while adding right-action transport. A restricted group-local realization is derived for selective-SSM execution with exponential-adjusted updates and exact block-affine scan.
AI.result: Larger current-token write rank improves ordinary prediction error but cannot recover order-sensitive changes to already-written memory; transported-memory variants successfully recover this signal. A simultaneous-reducibility criterion identifies when right transports collapse to static mixing plus independent banks.
AI.conclusion: SHiPPO is a mechanistically grounded transported-memory prior that provides evidence for memory mechanisms rather than broad sequence-modeling dominance, with an open question for the preferred right-action realization.

title: CLABTOOLKIT: An Open-Source Toolkit for Routine Processing, Manipulation, and Visualization of Neuroimaging Data
comment: Presented at OHBM 2026 in Bordeaux, France. Submitted to Aperture Neuro
summary: Neuroimaging research requires manipulating heterogeneous data structures, including raw MRI volumes, volumetric parcellations, cortical surface meshes, tractograms, and connectivity matrices, across tools with incompatible interfaces and file formats, forcing researchers to repeatedly re-implement routine but technically demanding operations. We present CLABTOOLKIT, an open-source Python package that consolidates these operations into a single, coherent framework by representing volumetric, surface, and streamline data as interoperable Python objects. Five core data structures (Parcellation, Surface, AnnotParcellation, Tractogram, and Connectome) encapsulate common neuroanatomical entities and provide consistent methods for loading, processing, and exporting data across standard neuroimaging formats (e.g., NIfTI, GIFTI, FreeSurfer annotations, TCK/TRK), including connectome generation from a parcellation and scalar-map projection onto tractogram streamlines. Complementary modules support BIDS dataset management, FreeSurfer integration, diffusion MRI processing, morphometric analysis, graph-theoretical network analysis, and GPU-accelerated multi-panel visualization via PyVista. The toolkit comprises 19 modules organised into six layers, exposing 13 object-oriented classes with 234 methods and 207 standalone functions, and a JSON-based configuration system enables workflow customization without code changes. Unlike existing neuroimaging libraries, which typically address these tasks separately, CLABTOOLKIT combines color and lookup-table management, parcellation manipulation, multi-surface visualization, and tractography utilities within a single framework. CLABTOOLKIT is compatible with Python 3.9-3.12 and released under the Apache 2.0 license. Source code, documentation, and example workflows are available at https://github.com/connectomicslab/clabtoolkit.

AI.tldr: CLABTOOLKIT is an open-source Python package that unifies volumetric, surface, and streamline neuroimaging data into five core interoperable data structures, providing consistent I/O, processing, visualization, and analysis across diverse formats and tools, along with BIDS management, FreeSurfer integration, diffusion MRI, morphometry, graph analysis, and GPU-accelerated visualization.
AI.motivation: Neuroimaging research requires manipulating heterogeneous data structures across tools with incompatible interfaces and file formats, forcing researchers to repeatedly re-implement routine but technically demanding operations.
AI.method: CLABTOOLKIT represents volumetric, surface, and streamline data as interoperable Python objects via five core data structures (Parcellation, Surface, AnnotParcellation, Tractogram, Connectome), with consistent I/O across NIfTI, GIFTI, FreeSurfer annotations, TCK/TRK formats. It comprises 19 modules in six layers, 13 classes with 234 methods and 207 functions, plus a JSON-based configuration system.
AI.result: The toolkit consolidates operations including connectome generation from parcellation, scalar-map projection onto tractogram streamlines, BIDS management, FreeSurfer integration, diffusion MRI processing, morphometric analysis, graph-theoretical network analysis, and GPU-accelerated multi-panel visualization via PyVista. It combines color/LUT management, parcellation manipulation, multi-surface visualization, and tractography utilities in one framework.
AI.conclusion: CLABTOOLKIT addresses fragmentation in neuroimaging software by providing a single, coherent framework that reduces the need for researchers to re-implement common operations, and is released as open-source under Apache 2.0 license for Python 3.9-3.12.

title: Harness-Aware Self-Evolving: Co-Evolving Model Weights, Harness, and Task Solutions
summary: Self-evolving frameworks usually optimize task solutions while treating the surrounding harness as fixed. We introduce Harness-Aware Self-Evolving (HASE), an agentic reinforcement-learning framework in which a single model can generate task solutions or edit selected harness components in a multi-turn action space. HASE enables a single Qwen3-8B model to match the text-classification performance of a GPT-OSS-120B model that uses Claude Code as the harness proposer. In alpha factor mining, HASE outperforms the reported GPT-OSS-120B baseline. HASE also repairs imperfect evaluation components and converges to state-of-the-art performance in circle-packing algorithm discovery. These results show that HASE improves the harness and the solution through one unified agentic process.

AI.tldr: HASE is a reinforcement-learning framework where a single model can both generate task solutions and edit its surrounding harness, achieving GPT-OSS-120B-level text classification, outperforming it in alpha factor mining, and reaching SOTA in circle-packing algorithm discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving frameworks optimize task solutions while treating the surrounding harness (evaluation pipelines, reward functions, etc.) as fixed, limiting adaptability and performance.
AI.method: Harness-Aware Self-Evolving (HASE) — an agentic reinforcement-learning framework with a multi-turn action space where one model can generate task solutions or edit selected harness components.
AI.result: HASE enables a single Qwen3-8B model to match GPT-OSS-120B (with Claude Code as proposer) on text classification, outperforms it on alpha factor mining, repairs imperfect evaluation components, and converges to SOTA in circle-packing algorithm discovery.
