AI.motivation: Post-hoc analysis of neural network weights often attempts to recover geometric structure directly from parameters, but the relationship between learned symmetries and the true underlying symmetries is not well understood, especially for neural fields with positional encodings.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact observability hierarchy $G_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\mathrm{exact}} \subseteq G_{\mathrm{lift}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(\phi) \cap G_{\mathrm{true}}$, where $G_{\mathrm{lift}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(\phi)$ is the set of input transformations exactly liftable by the PE. They then empirically test this on MLPs trained on 2D signed distance functions with various shape symmetries ($D_3$, $D_4$, $D_6$), using different PEs (DyadicAxisPE, TriAxisPE, random Fourier features) and Gram-based observables.
AI.result: DyadicAxisPE supports $D_4$-sensitive readout but suppresses $D_3$ rotations; TriAxisPE yields lower $D_3$/$D_6$ readout scores by using 120-degree-separated axes; random Fourier features mainly show only $\pi$-rotation response. A consistent PE-dependent pattern in symmetry readout is observed.
AI.conclusion: PE design affects not only approximation behavior but also which geometric structures are accessible to post-hoc weight-level readouts, providing a foundation for principled observable-dependent symmetry analysis in neural fields.

title: Aircraft Detection in Satellite Imagery using Deep Learning Object Detectors
summary: The object detection in satellite imagery has garnered considerable attention due to its extensive real-world applications and the inherent challenges it presents, including noise, fluctuating image quality, and intricate backgrounds. This paper proposed a framework for object detection that combines image enhancement and Deep Learning (DL) to make detection more accurate. First, a Gabor filter is used to process the input image to bring out important features and reduce noise. Then, normalization is applied to make sure that the data is evenly distributed so that the model works properly. After that, a model based on YOLOv11 is used to quickly learn and find object features. The proposed method achieves a mAP of 95%, precision of 97%, recall of 85%, and F1-score of 91%, which demonstrates the superior aircraft detection performance. These results show the framework accurately identify aircraft in satellite imagery and is suitable for real-time applications such as surveillance, air traffic monitoring and remote sensing analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an object detection framework for satellite imagery that combines Gabor filter-based image enhancement with YOLOv11, achieving 95% mAP, 97% precision, 85% recall, and 91% F1-score for aircraft detection.
AI.motivation: Object detection in satellite imagery faces challenges such as noise, fluctuating image quality, and complex backgrounds, motivating the need for a more accurate detection framework.
AI.method: The framework first applies a Gabor filter for feature enhancement and noise reduction, followed by normalization for data distribution, then uses a YOLOv11-based model for feature learning and object detection.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves 95% mAP, 97% precision, 85% recall, and 91% F1-score for aircraft detection in satellite imagery.
AI.conclusion: The framework accurately identifies aircraft in satellite imagery and is suitable for real-time applications such as surveillance, air traffic monitoring, and remote sensing analysis.

title: A Clustering-Based Framework for Identifying Suspicious Trading Patterns in Capital Market
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN), 2026. This is the authors preprint version. The final version is available via IEEE Xplore
summary: Market manipulation is the dubious practice of manipulating stock prices in order to make a quick profit, which truly degrades confidence on trading platforms. We implemented an unsupervised fraud-detection toolkit that begins with K-Means++ clustering to address this issue. A dataset of roughly one million financial transactions from 2012 to 2024 is used. In order to identify fraudulent trades and categorize them using market practice heuristic thresholds, the study suggests a clustering-based pipeline. The method highlights 2.02% of trades as suspicious where 51.10% clearly indicate spoofing, 0.10% indicate pump and dump, 0.55% indicate insider trading, 1.43% indicate a fake breakout, and 46.83% are unclassified. Despite the lack of ground truth, the model's performance is confirmed by a Silhouette Score of 0.561.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an unsupervised fraud-detection toolkit using K-Means++ clustering to identify market manipulation in ~1 million financial transactions (2012-2024). The method flagged 2.02% of trades as suspicious, with 51.10% indicating spoofing, 0.10% pump and dump, 0.55% insider trading, 1.43% fake breakout, and 46.83% unclassified. Model performance validated by Silhouette Score of 0.561.
AI.motivation: Market manipulation degrades confidence in trading platforms, yet detecting fraudulent practices like spoofing, pump-and-dump, and insider trading remains challenging, especially without labeled ground truth data.
AI.method: An unsupervised clustering-based pipeline using K-Means++ clustering applied to ~1 million financial transactions (2012-2024). Fraudulent trades are identified and categorized using market practice heuristic thresholds.
AI.result: 2.02% of trades flagged as suspicious: 51.10% spoofing, 0.10% pump and dump, 0.55% insider trading, 1.43% fake breakout, 46.83% unclassified. Silhouette Score of 0.561 confirms clustering quality.
AI.conclusion: The unsupervised approach effectively detects multiple types of market manipulation without ground truth labels, achieving reasonable cluster separation (Silhouette Score 0.561) on a large-scale financial dataset.

title: Is Agentic Code Review Helpful? Mining Developers' Feedback to CodeRabbit Reviews in the Wild
summary: Agentic code review, where autonomous agents provide code review comments on pull requests, is increasingly integrated into development workflows, yet there is limited empirical evidence on how developers respond to such comments in practice. In this paper, we present an empirical study of agentic code reviews using CodeRabbit as a case study. Through an empirical study of 31,073 pairs of code reviews and developer feedback from 10,191 pull requests across 239 GitHub repositories, our results show that agentic reviews receive mixed reception: 36.4% were accepted and 7.3% triggered discussion, while 56.3% were rejected. Rejections were primarily associated with invalid suggestions that were false positives, redundant, or out of scope, as well as misalignment with developer intent and coding practices. We further found that agentic reviews tend to focus more on functional concerns than evolvability-related comments, yet they were more likely to be invalid. To improve effectiveness in review practices, we explored various LLM-based approaches for predicting review rejection. We found that lightweight learning-based methods achieve up to 76% F1 score, suggesting learnable patterns exist between code reviews and their corresponding feedback. Our results highlight the current state of CodeRabbit's agentic code reviews, showing opportunity gaps for improvement, as well as shortcomings hindering its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of 31,073 agentic code reviews (using CodeRabbit) across 10,191 PRs in 239 GitHub repos found 36.4% accepted, 7.3% discussed, and 56.3% rejected—mostly due to false positives, redundancy, or misalignment with developer intent. Agentic reviews focus more on functional issues than evolvability, and lightweight learning-based models can predict rejection with up to 76% F1 score.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing integration of autonomous code review agents into development workflows, there is limited empirical evidence on how developers actually respond to such agentic review comments in practice.
AI.method: Large-scale empirical study of 31,073 pairs of code reviews and developer feedback from 10,191 pull requests across 239 GitHub repositories, using CodeRabbit as a case study; also explored various LLM-based approaches for predicting review rejection.
AI.result: 36.4% accepted, 7.3% triggered discussion, 56.3% rejected; rejections linked to false positives, redundancy, out-of-scope comments, and misalignment with developer intent; agentic reviews focus more on functional concerns than evolvability but are more likely to be invalid; lightweight learning-based methods achieve up to 76% F1 score for predicting rejection.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight opportunity gaps for improving CodeRabbit's agentic code reviews and identify shortcomings that hinder its effectiveness, while showing that learnable patterns exist between reviews and feedback for predicting rejection.

title: Integrating Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Safe Reinforcement Learning in a 1-DoF Helicopter System
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offers powerful control for industrial cyber-physical systems (ICPSs), but its "black-box" exploration risks violating strict hardware safety limits. Typically, these constraints are managed through complex reward shaping. In this work-in-progress paper, we embed a differentiable physics model directly into the proximal policy optimization (PPO) actor loss function. By simulating short-horizon future trajectories during training, the policy is penalized for anticipated safety violations independent of the task-reward signal. Evaluated on a simulated 1-degree-of-freedom helicopter testbed with strict pitch constraints, our physics-informed soft regularizations substantially reduce constraint violations while maintaining reliable target tracking.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed PPO method embeds a differentiable physics model into the actor loss to penalize predicted safety violations, reducing constraint violations on a simulated helicopter testbed while maintaining tracking performance.
AI.motivation: DRL's black-box exploration in ICPSs risks violating strict hardware safety limits; typical reward shaping is complex and insufficient.
AI.method: Embed a differentiable physics model directly into the PPO actor loss function to simulate short-horizon future trajectories and penalize anticipated safety violations during training, independent of task reward.
AI.result: Physics-informed soft regularizations substantially reduce constraint violations while maintaining reliable target tracking on a simulated 1-DOF helicopter testbed with strict pitch constraints.
AI.conclusion: Embedding differentiable physics models into the DRL loss function is a promising work-in-progress approach for enforcing safety constraints in ICPSs without complex reward shaping.

title: VLRC: Vision-Language Reprojection Consistency as a scalable signal for better feed-forward 3D pretraining
summary: Feed-forward 3D models are commonly trained using either expensive geometric supervision or self-supervised photometric objectives, both of which provide incomplete learning signals. We introduce Vision-Language Reprojection Consistency (VLRC), a scalable auxiliary objective that exploits frozen vision-language representations as semantic multi-view supervision. Given a predicted 3D reconstruction, VLRC reprojects dense vision-language features across views and enforces feature consistency between corresponding image locations, requiring no additional 3D annotations. The objective integrates seamlessly with both self-supervised monocular reconstruction and supervised-pretrained feed-forward 3D models during unlabeled adaptation. By aligning geometry with language-grounded features, VLRC not only improves depth and camera estimation but also enables more coherent multi-view semantic fusion for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in 3D reconstruction accuracy and zero-shot open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation.

AI.tldr: VLRC is a scalable auxiliary objective that uses frozen vision-language representations as semantic multi-view supervision to improve 3D reconstruction and enable open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation without requiring additional 3D annotations.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D models rely on either expensive geometric supervision or self-supervised photometric objectives, both of which provide incomplete learning signals.
AI.method: VLRC reprojects dense vision-language features across views and enforces feature consistency between corresponding image locations, using frozen vision-language representations as semantic multi-view supervision without additional 3D annotations.
AI.result: Consistent gains in 3D reconstruction accuracy and zero-shot open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation on indoor and outdoor benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning geometry with language-grounded features improves depth and camera estimation and enables more coherent multi-view semantic fusion for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding.

title: Agentic IoT: Architectures, Applications, and Challenges Toward the Internet of Agents
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, Author's preprint version. The manuscript may be revised based on peer-review feedback and publication requirements
summary: The integration of AI into Internet of Things (AIoT) systems has gradually transformed them from passive data collection infrastructures into intelligent systems capable of anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, classification, forecasting, and optimization. However, most existing solutions still rely on task-specific models that infer from sensor data; thus, system-wide capabilities such as real-time reasoning, adaptive planning, autonomous coordination, learning, tool use, and contextual decision-making remain limited. This paper examines Agentic IoT as a next-generation cognitive IoT paradigm that integrates the perception, reasoning, planning, learning, and action capabilities of autonomous AI agents with cyber-physical systems. Agentic IoT aims to transform IoT from data-centric sensing and inference infrastructures into distributed cognitive agent ecosystems operating across the device/edge-fog-cloud continuum. The paper first grounds this transition as a paradigm shift and positions Agentic IoT in relation to AIoT, edge intelligence, multi-agent systems, and the Internet of Agents. It then systematically reviews current studies, presents a holistic architectural framework, discusses domain-specific application potential, and identifies key technical, operational, and research challenges together with future research directions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Agentic IoT as a next-generation cognitive IoT paradigm that integrates autonomous AI agents' perception, reasoning, planning, learning, and action capabilities with cyber-physical systems, transforming IoT from data-centric sensing infrastructures into distributed cognitive agent ecosystems across device/edge-fog-cloud continuum.
AI.motivation: Existing AIoT solutions rely on task-specific models that infer from sensor data, limiting system-wide capabilities such as real-time reasoning, adaptive planning, autonomous coordination, learning, tool use, and contextual decision-making.
AI.method: The paper first grounds the transition as a paradigm shift, positions Agentic IoT relative to AIoT, edge intelligence, multi-agent systems, and the Internet of Agents, then systematically reviews current studies and presents a holistic architectural framework.
AI.result: A holistic architectural framework for Agentic IoT is presented, along with domain-specific application potential and identification of key technical, operational, and research challenges.
AI.conclusion: Agentic IoT represents a paradigm shift from data-centric IoT to distributed cognitive agent ecosystems, with future research directions identified to address remaining challenges.

title: AtomicCommitBench: Can Coding Agents Reconstruct Commit Histories from Squashed Patches?
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, benchmark paper on coding agents and software engineering; preprint
summary: Coding agents often finish a session by returning one squashed patch that mixes feature implementation, bug fixes, refactorings, tests, and configuration edits. While the final code may be correct, collapsing unrelated edits into one patch removes the history structure needed for review, selective revert, and later maintenance. We study retrospective commit-history reconstruction: given a completed squashed change, an agent groups its hunks into commits and materializes a replayable commit sequence. We formalize the task as hunk-to-commit partitioning with a replay requirement and build AtomicCommitBench, containing 800 real consecutive-commit episodes from 10 Python projects. Because multiple decompositions may be reasonable, we evaluate outputs using complementary metrics: PPAR for replay validity, ARI for reference-based grouping quality, and TCR for failure containment on scoreable modified-test episodes. Natural retrospective reconstruction proves substantially harder than replay checking or synthetic tangling. Although nearly all non-random methods achieve replay validity (PPAR >= 0.988), grouping quality ranges from 0.03 to 0.46 ARI. Matched synthetic composites are much easier than real same-author squashed diffs (+0.333 ARI). In our evaluation, the GPT-5.4 setup driven by Codex CLI (0.46 ARI) and the GLM-5 setup driven by Claude Code (0.43 ARI) outperform MiniMax (0.31) and Kimi (0.29). Qualitative analysis identifies same-file lumping and support-hunk drift as recurring failure modes. Dependency-Aware Commit Evidence (DACE) improves the lower-scoring setups by 0.05 to 0.08 ARI, indicating that dependency cues and hunk-role information help agents avoid locality-driven grouping errors. AtomicCommitBench enables evaluation of the commit histories produced by coding agents alongside the final code.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AtomicCommitBench, a benchmark for evaluating retrospective commit-history reconstruction—the task of decomposing a single squashed patch from coding agents into a structured, replayable sequence of atomic commits. The authors formalize hunk-to-commit partitioning, evaluate multiple setups (GPT-5.4/Codex CLI achieves best at 0.46 ARI), and propose DACE, a dependency-aware method that improves grouping quality by 0.05–0.08 ARI.
AI.motivation: Coding agents produce squashed patches that merge unrelated changes (features, fixes, refactors, tests, config edits), destroying the commit history needed for code review, selective revert, and maintenance. The authors aim to restore structured commit histories from these monolithic diffs.
AI.method: The authors formalize retrospective commit-history reconstruction as hunk-to-commit partitioning with a replay requirement. They build AtomicCommitBench with 800 real consecutive-commit episodes from 10 Python projects. They evaluate using PPAR (replay validity), ARI (reference-based grouping quality), and TCR (failure containment). They also propose DACE (Dependency-Aware Commit Evidence) to improve grouping.
AI.result: Nearly all non-random methods achieve high replay validity (PPAR ≥ 0.988), but grouping quality varies widely (0.03–0.46 ARI). GPT-5.4/Codex CLI achieves 0.46 ARI, GLM-5/Claude Code achieves 0.43 ARI. Synthetic composites are much easier than real diffs (+0.333 ARI). DACE improves lower-scoring setups by 0.05–0.08 ARI.
AI.conclusion: Retrospective commit reconstruction is substantially harder than replay checking or synthetic tangling. DACE helps mitigate locality-driven grouping errors like same-file lumping and support-hunk drift. AtomicCommitBench enables structured evaluation of coding agents' commit histories alongside final code quality.

title: ACPO: Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization via Fine-Grained Surrogate Entropy
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), but sparse outcome rewards still make token-level credit assignment difficult. Existing scalable RL methods typically assign trajectory-level rewards uniformly across tokens, while recent entropy-aware approaches either rely on coarse detached heuristics or directly optimize true entropy, which can introduce non-local gradient components misaligned with sampled-token policy updates. We propose Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization (ACPO), a token-level credit assignment framework based on a mode-local surrogate entropy. ACPO asymmetrically modulates policy updates by emphasizing uncertain decisions in successful rollouts and overconfident tokens in failed rollouts. We show that the surrogate admits deterministic entropy bounds and, under modal alignment and proximal updates, preserves the policy-gradient direction to leading order. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, including AIME 2025 and HumanEvalPro, show that ACPO consistently improves over strong RL baselines such as DAPO, GTPO, and SAPO.

AI.tldr: ACPO introduces a token-level credit assignment method using mode-local surrogate entropy to asymmetrically modulate policy updates, improving RL fine-tuning of LLMs on reasoning and coding tasks.
AI.motivation: Reward sparsity in RL for LLMs makes token-level credit assignment difficult; existing methods (uniform trajectory rewards, coarse heuristics, true entropy optimization) have limitations such as misaligned gradient components.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization (ACPO), which uses a mode-local surrogate entropy to asymmetrically adjust policy updates—emphasizing uncertain tokens in successful rollouts and overconfident tokens in failed rollouts. The surrogate preserves policy-gradient direction to leading order under modal alignment and proximal updates.
AI.result: Outperforms DAPO, GTPO, and SAPO on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2025) and coding (HumanEvalPro) benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ACPO is an effective token-level credit assignment framework that improves reasoning in LLMs over existing RL-based methods.

title: When Does Resolution Help a Frozen Backbone? Global Attention at Resolution Predicts Scalable Adaptation for Camouflaged and Marine Animal Segmentation
summary: Adapting frozen vision foundation models to fine-grained segmentation now largely depends on backbone selection. Whether the backbone applies global attention to a high-resolution token set predicts whether a low-rank adapter turns resolution into accuracy. Isotropic ViTs attend globally over the full grid and keep improving with resolution; hierarchical backbones confine early attention to local windows and pool the grid before their global stages, plateauing at lower resolutions. A controlled six-backbone study establishes the pattern, and editing the backbone points to the cause: pooling keeps the benefit, removing global attention does not. The effect is specific to low-rank adaptation. Under one fixed pipeline, SALT (Side-stem, Attention-gated U-Net, Low-rank Tuning), one RGB-only pass on a strong isotropic backbone wins the best S-measure on the four data-matched camouflaged sets, and leads every marine and salient set. It reaches a new state of the art on both marine-animal benchmarks (MAS3K mIoU 0.878).

AI.tldr: Low-rank adaptation of frozen vision foundation models for fine-grained segmentation benefits from isotropic ViTs (global attention, high-resolution) over hierarchical backbones (local attention, pooling), as shown in a controlled six-backbone study. The SALT pipeline with a strong isotropic backbone achieves state-of-the-art results on camouflaged and marine-animal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To understand how backbone choice (global vs. local attention) and resolution affect low-rank adaptation for fine-grained segmentation, and to identify the causal factors behind performance differences.
AI.method: Conducted a controlled six-backbone study comparing isotropic ViTs (global attention over full grid) vs. hierarchical backbones (local window attention + pooling before global stages). Applied a fixed pipeline: SALT (Side-stem, Attention-gated U-Net, Low-rank Tuning). Edited backbones to isolate effects of pooling and global attention.
AI.result: Isotropic ViTs improve with resolution; hierarchical backbones plateau. Pooling retains benefit; removing global attention eliminates the advantage. Effect is specific to low-rank adaptation. SALT with isotropic backbone achieves best S-measure on four camouflaged sets and SOTA on MAS3K (mIoU 0.878).
AI.conclusion: Global attention at high resolution is key for low-rank adaptation in fine-grained segmentation. Pooling does not harm the benefit, but removing global attention does. The isotropic backbone + low-rank tuning pipeline outperforms all prior work on multiple benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Features Mining via Activation Geometry
summary: Interpretability methods aim to reveal the features represented inside large language models (LLMs). Many existing methods begin with labeled examples of a human-defined concept that may reflect human biases, and then identify how that concept is represented within the model, for example in its activation space or through other decomposition methods. We introduce \emph{Mining via Activation Geometry} (MAG), a simple unsupervised framework for extracting reasoning features from model activations by prepending the same natural-language instruction $Q$ to every input $p$, where $Q$ defines the reasoning feature of interest, such as ``Can this object be found in the desert?'' or ``Is this prompt malicious?'' We measure how the instruction changes the model's internal representation using $m(Q \mid p) - m(p)$ at a single readout point. We explore eight different MAGs. The extracted reasoning features predict the models' own world understanding and judgment, can be approximated into a single activation direction, we found that some features are more linearly represented and some less, this linear representation, which is vector steering, can change the LLMs' decisions through activation steering by injecting reasoning features. Finally, we use the same method to select the best training datasets for prompt-injection classifier probes: while similarity between ordinary activations is almost unrelated to downstream performance, RFD-based similarity achieves $94.7\%$ Top-1 and $100\%$ Top-2 accuracy.

AI.tldr: MAG is an unsupervised framework that extracts reasoning features from LLM activations by prepending a natural-language instruction Q to inputs, measuring activation differences. These features predict model judgments, can be approximated as linear directions for steering, and achieve 94.7% Top-1/100% Top-2 accuracy for selecting training data for classifier probes.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability methods rely on labeled examples of human-defined concepts, which may reflect human biases. The paper aims to develop an unsupervised framework that extracts reasoning features directly from model activations without requiring labeled examples.
AI.method: MAG prepends a natural-language instruction Q (e.g., "Can this object be found in the desert?") to every input p, then measures activation differences as m(Q|p) - m(p) at a single readout point. Eight different MAGs are explored, and the extracted features are analyzed for linearity and used for activation steering and training data selection.
AI.result: Extracted reasoning features predict model's own world understanding and judgment. Some features are more linearly represented than others. Linear representations (vector steering) can change LLMs' decisions via activation steering. RFD-based similarity achieves 94.7% Top-1 and 100% Top-2 accuracy for selecting best training datasets for prompt-injection classifier probes, while ordinary activation similarity is almost unrelated.
AI.conclusion: MAG provides a simple, unsupervised way to extract interpretable reasoning features from LLM activations. These features are useful for understanding model internals, steering model behavior, and selecting high-quality training data for downstream classifiers.

title: SkillOpt-Lite: Better and Faster Agent Self-evolution via One Line of Vibe
summary: While skill optimization for autonomous agents has gained traction, existing methods rely on complex pipelines. This leaves a fundamental question unaddressed: What constitutes a minimal viable pipeline for skill optimization, where every component is justified by theory or empirical necessity? We formalize skill optimization via Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimization, mapping classical counterparts (central difference, trust regions) to recent literature. Noting that unlike blind numerical perturbations in classical ZO, skill trajectories serve as interpretable debugging feedback. Grounded in Claude Code philosophy and PAC learning, we establish three principles for convergence and generalization: file-system-based trajectory exploration, consensus attribute mining, and independent validation gating. Eliminating redundancies, we propose SkillOpt-Lite. It accelerates convergence and outperforms full SkillOpt: improving LiveMath by +8.8 points on GPT-5.5 and +25.4 points on GPT-5.4-nano, allowing the nano model to surpass standard GPT-5.4 optimized by SkillOpt. Finally, we integrate our framework into production coding agents like VSCode Copilot, enabling developers to evolve agent skills via one line of vibe. Because our framework treats all agent components simply as standard editable code, this minimal pipeline naturally generalizes to full harness optimization (HarnessOpt). On SpreadsheetBench, HarnessOpt enables GPT-5.4-nano to achieve 0.7758 accuracy, outperforming the larger GPT-5.5 running standard pipelines (0.7620). Code is available at https://github.com/EvolvingLMMs-Lab/SkillOpt-Lite.

AI.tldr: SkillOpt-Lite is a minimal viable pipeline for skill optimization in autonomous agents, grounded in Zeroth-Order optimization and PAC learning principles. It achieves state-of-the-art results (e.g., +8.8 points on GPT-5.5, +25.4 on GPT-5.4-nano) and generalizes to full harness optimization (HarnessOpt), enabling GPT-5.4-nano to outperform GPT-5.5 on SpreadsheetBench.
AI.motivation: Existing skill optimization methods rely on complex, poorly-justified pipelines. The authors aim to identify the minimal viable pipeline for skill optimization where every component is justified by theory or empirical necessity.
AI.method: SkillOpt-Lite formalizes skill optimization via Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimization, mapping classical numerical methods (central difference, trust regions) to skill trajectories. It establishes three PAC-learning-grounded principles: (1) file-system-based trajectory exploration, (2) consensus attribute mining, and (3) independent validation gating. The framework treats all agent components as standard editable code, naturally extending to HarnessOpt.
AI.result: SkillOpt-Lite accelerates convergence and outperforms full SkillOpt: +8.8 points on GPT-5.5 and +25.4 points on GPT-5.4-nano for LiveMath. The nano model surpasses standard GPT-5.4 optimized by SkillOpt. HarnessOpt enables GPT-5.4-nano to achieve 0.7758 accuracy on SpreadsheetBench, outperforming larger GPT-5.5 (0.7620).
AI.conclusion: A minimal, theoretically-justified pipeline for skill optimization is both feasible and effective. The framework generalizes to full harness optimization and integrates into production coding agents (VSCode Copilot) via a single line of vibe code.

title: Anticipatory Reinforcement Learning for Trajectory Tracking
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in industrial control often suffers from lag and overshoot due to purely reactive control based on the current tracking error. To achieve anticipatory control without high computational overhead, we introduce a predictive formulation that augments the DRL state space with target velocities and future reference horizons. Evaluating eight configurations using proximal policy optimization (PPO) on a 1-degree-of-freedom (1-DoF) helicopter testbed, simulation results showed a 9-fold error reduction, lowering the mean absolute deviation from 2.73° to 0.31°. However, zero-shot transfer to physical hardware revealed a sim-to-real gap. Interestingly, a simpler configuration using a single, further look-ahead horizon matched the real-world top performance of the most complex model (1.11°). Overall, evaluating various combinations of prediction horizons and target velocities demonstrated that highly granular predictive data is not necessarily required for physical transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a predictive formulation for DRL-based industrial control that augments the state space with target velocities and future reference horizons to reduce lag and overshoot. Using PPO on a 1-DoF helicopter testbed, simulation achieved a 9-fold error reduction (from 2.73° to 0.31°), but zero-shot transfer to hardware revealed a sim-to-real gap. Surprisingly, a simple single look-ahead horizon matched the top real-world performance (1.11°), showing that highly granular predictive data is unnecessary for physical transfer.
AI.motivation: DRL in industrial control suffers from lag and overshoot due to purely reactive control based on current tracking error. The authors aim to achieve anticipatory control without high computational overhead.
AI.method: A predictive formulation that augments the DRL state space with target velocities and future reference horizons, evaluated using PPO across eight configurations on a 1-DoF helicopter testbed.
AI.result: Simulation: 9-fold error reduction (MAD from 2.73° to 0.31°). Real-world: A simple single look-ahead horizon matched the most complex model's performance (1.11°), while zero-shot transfer showed a sim-to-real gap.
AI.conclusion: Highly granular predictive data is not necessarily required for successful physical transfer; simpler configurations with a single, further look-ahead horizon can achieve comparable real-world performance.

title: RayTun3R: Online Camera Adaptation in 3D Foundation Models
summary: Recent 3D foundation models, such as DUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT, $π^3$, and Depth Anything 3, provide strong feed-forward depth and pose estimates on pinhole imagery, but degrade sharply under fisheye camera geometry. We show that this failure is partly caused by a pinhole camera bias in the positional encodings of pretrained 3D foundation models, and propose RayTun3R, a lightweight camera adaptation approach. It keeps the pretrained network fixed and adapts only lightweight components tied to token position and camera geometry. RayTun3R learns parameter-efficient residual corrections to absolute and rotary positional encodings, together with parameter-free tokenization and corrections to prediction-grid coordinates that remove residual pinhole assumptions. The resulting adapter contains only 10,752 trainable parameters and can be learned from a short temporal segment using geometric losses. Once adapted, RayTun3R transfers effectively to the remaining frames of the sequence without incurring additional runtime costs. Across diverse fisheye datasets with fields of view from $110^\circ$ to $200^\circ$, our adapter reduces rotation error by $2$-$12\times$ relative to the unadapted model, outperforms LoRA while using $\sim\!14\times$ fewer trainable parameters, improves pose over adaptation-free baselines while avoiding their multi-view inference cost, and remains competitive on depth accuracy.

AI.tldr: RayTun3R is a lightweight adapter that fixes the pinhole camera bias in 3D foundation models for fisheye imagery by adapting only positional encodings and tokenization (10,752 parameters), achieving 2-12× rotation error reduction across 110°–200° FOV datasets while outperforming LoRA with ~14× fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D foundation models (DUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT, π³, Depth Anything 3) perform well on pinhole images but degrade sharply on fisheye camera geometry, limiting their applicability to the widely-used fisheye cameras in robotics and VR.
AI.method: RayTun3R adapts pretrained models without altering network weights by: (1) learning parameter-efficient residual corrections to absolute and rotary positional encodings, (2) applying parameter-free tokenization corrections, and (3) correcting prediction-grid coordinates to remove residual pinhole assumptions. It uses geometric losses on a short temporal segment.
AI.result: With only 10,752 trainable parameters, RayTun3R reduces rotation error by 2-12× on fisheye datasets (110°–200° FOV), outperforms LoRA with ~14× fewer parameters, improves pose over adaptation-free baselines without their multi-view inference cost, and maintains competitive depth accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A minimal, efficient camera adaptation strategy can effectively bridge the gap between pinhole-biased 3D foundation models and fisheye camera geometries, enabling zero-cost inference on successive frames after lightweight adaptation.

title: Biological Motifs for Agentic Control
summary:
The transition of Large Language Models (LLMs) from passive generators to autonomous agents has introduced significant challenges in reliability, security, and state management. Current agentic architectures are often constructed ad-hoc, prone to hallucination cascades, infinite loops, and prompt injection attacks. This paper argues that many of these failure modes can be analyzed using control motifs long studied in systems biology, provided the comparison is made at the level of typed interfaces and coordination structure rather than literal biological mechanism.
  We develop a typed interface correspondence between Gene Regulatory Networks and agentic software systems using polynomial functors and wiring diagrams. Five biological motifs are mapped to composable software design patterns: Coherent Feed-Forward Loops for noise suppression, Adaptive Immunity for layered security, Mitochondrial Signaling for resource governance, Endosymbiosis for neuro-symbolic integration, and Morphogen Diffusion for spatially varying coordination. An epistemic topology layer derives Kripke-style knowledge operators from the wiring diagram's observation structure and proves four predictive theorems for multi-agent scaling.
  The core contributions are: (1) the Agentic Operad, a typed syntax for agent composition with provable error suppression bounds for feed-forward topologies; (2) an epistemic topology with four theorems (error amplification, sequential penalty, parallel acceleration, and tool density scaling) whose qualitative predictions are consistent with published multi-agent benchmarks; and (3) a six-layer progression from structure through development, grounded in autonomous learning frameworks and convergence proxies from the empirical literature. A reference implementation with 1,813 tests and 116 examples illustrates practical feasibility.

AI.tldr: This paper maps biological control motifs (gene regulatory networks, immune systems, etc.) to LLM agentic architectures using polynomial functors and typed interfaces, proposing the Agentic Operad for composable agent design with provable error bounds, epistemic topology theorems for multi-agent scaling, and a six-layer developmental progression.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents suffer from hallucination cascades, infinite loops, and prompt injection attacks due to ad-hoc architectures. The authors argue these failure modes can be systematically analyzed using control motifs from systems biology if compared at the level of typed interfaces and coordination structure rather than literal biological mechanisms.
AI.method: The paper develops typed interface correspondences between Gene Regulatory Networks and agentic software using polynomial functors and wiring diagrams. Five biological motifs are mapped to software patterns: Coherent Feed-Forward Loops (noise suppression), Adaptive Immunity (layered security), Mitochondrial Signaling (resource governance), Endosymbiosis (neuro-symbolic integration), and Morphogen Diffusion (spatially varying coordination). An epistemic topology layer derives Kripke-style knowledge operators from wiring diagram observation structures.
AI.result: (1) The Agentic Operad: typed syntax for agent composition with provable error suppression bounds for feed-forward topologies; (2) Epistemic topology with four theorems: error amplification, sequential penalty, parallel acceleration, and tool density scaling, with predictions consistent with published multi-agent benchmarks; (3) A six-layer progression from structure through development. Reference implementation includes 1,813 tests and 116 examples.
AI.conclusion: Biological control motifs provide a principled framework for designing reliable LLM agent architectures. The formal correspondence via polynomial functors yields composable patterns with provable properties, and the epistemic topology theorems offer predictive scaling laws validated against empirical multi-agent benchmarks.

title: CAGE-1: Control, Assurance, and Governance Evaluation for Enterprise Agentic AI
summary:
Enterprise artificial intelligence is moving from experimentation into operational workflows. Early programs focused on model access and retrieval-augmented generation, but enterprises are now beginning to deploy agents that plan, retrieve, remember, call tools, update systems, and coordinate work across applications.
  This changes the evaluation problem. Leaders are no longer asking only whether an answer is accurate or fluent. They need to know who authorized an action, which policy applied, whether evidence was current, whether memory was valid, whether a tool call was permitted, whether the decision can be replayed, and whether the agent can be stopped before it creates business impact.
  This paper introduces CAGE-1: Control, Assurance, and Governance Evaluation for Enterprise Agentic AI. CAGE-1 is an evaluation framework for deciding whether enterprise agents are ready for deployment. It evaluates authority, policy enforcement, retrieval quality, memory integrity, tool safety, auditability, human oversight, conflict handling, safe failure, Prebind Assurance, operational readiness, and business fitness.
  CAGE-1 introduces Prebind Assurance to describe the evaluated ability to prove that an agentic action is controlled before it becomes binding, effective, or operationally consequential. The framework tests whether a proposed action is admitted, held, narrowed, refused, escalated, quarantined, or made non-effective before protected consequence forms.

AI.tldr: CAGE-1 is an evaluation framework for enterprise agentic AI that assesses readiness across 12 dimensions including authority, policy enforcement, retrieval quality, memory integrity, tool safety, auditability, human oversight, conflict handling, safe failure, Prebind Assurance, operational readiness, and business fitness.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI is moving from experimental RAG-based systems to deployed agents that plan, retrieve, remember, call tools, and coordinate workflows. This shift introduces new evaluation challenges beyond accuracy and fluency—organizations need to verify authorization, policy compliance, evidence freshness, memory validity, tool permissions, replayability, and stoppability before agents create business impact.
AI.method: CAGE-1 introduces a 12-dimension evaluation framework with a novel concept called Prebind Assurance—the ability to prove agentic actions are controlled before they become binding or operationally consequential. The framework tests whether proposed actions are admitted, held, narrowed, refused, escalated, quarantined, or made non-effective before protected consequences form.
AI.result: The paper defines evaluation criteria across authority, policy enforcement, retrieval quality, memory integrity, tool safety, auditability, human oversight, conflict handling, safe failure, Prebind Assurance, operational readiness, and business fitness dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Enterprise agentic AI requires a fundamentally different evaluation paradigm centered on control, assurance, and governance, with Prebind Assurance being key to ensuring actions are verified before becoming operationally consequential.

title: Sample-Efficient Pareto Front Modeling for Energy-Aware Reinforcement Learning Using Bayesian Optimization
summary: Industrial automation increasingly demands control strategies that balance operational performance with strict energy efficiency requirements. A common approach to solving this multi-objective problem, particularly within the framework of reinforcement learning (RL), is to formulate a single, scalar reward function that linearly combines the competing objectives. However, the manual weighting of these different objectives is heavily reliant on domain intuition, incredibly time-consuming, prone to human bias, and frequently fails to uncover optimal trade-off solutions. This work addresses the critical challenge of automating the weight selection process to systematically and efficiently discover the Pareto front of optimal trade-off policies. We formulate the weight selection process as a multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) problem and evaluate its sample efficiency against a standard uniform grid search baseline. Using a physical Quanser Aero 2 testbed configured for 1-DoF pitch control, our results demonstrate that the MOBO approach, utilizing the expected hypervolume improvement (qEHVI) acquisition function, consistently outperforms uniform grid sampling. MOBO achieves superior hypervolume and maximum spread, successfully identifying high-quality, diverse trade-off policies with a reduced evaluation budget, thereby enabling highly efficient energy-aware control in complex mechatronic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) with qEHVI acquisition to automate weight selection for scalarized reward functions in RL-based industrial control, demonstrating superior Pareto front discovery over uniform grid search on a Quanser Aero 2 pitch control testbed.
AI.motivation: Manual weighting of competing objectives (performance vs. energy efficiency) in RL reward design is time-consuming, biased, and often misses optimal trade-offs; an automated, systematic method is needed.
AI.method: Formulates weight selection as a multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) problem using the expected hypervolume improvement (qEHVI) acquisition function, evaluated against uniform grid search on a 1-DoF pitch control task with a Quanser Aero 2 testbed.
AI.result: MOBO with qEHVI consistently outperformed uniform grid sampling, achieving superior hypervolume and maximum spread, and identifying high-quality diverse trade-off policies with fewer evaluations.
AI.conclusion: MOBO enables highly efficient, automated discovery of Pareto-optimal energy-aware control policies in complex mechatronic systems with a reduced evaluation budget.

title: Global Pose Control for Generative View Synthesis in Normalized Object Coordinate Space
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page https://lizb6626.github.io/GlobalNVS/
summary: Novel View Synthesis (NVS) enables the generation of unseen views of a scene from a single or multiple images, allowing users to freely explore an object from any viewpoint. Despite the recent impressive qualitative improvements of generative models for this task, existing methods struggle to provide global and intuitive control of target viewpoints because they either use input-relative camera poses or are limited to generating sparse global views. This lack of global pose control severely limits the number of downstream tasks potentially enabled by NVS. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach for precise camera control in a customizable Normalized Object Coordinate Space (NOCS), requiring single or few unposed images. Our method operates solely on the absolute camera pose of the target view in NOCS, eliminating the need for a relative world frame or camera poses of the input images. Unlike previous methods that treat NVS as a standalone generation task, we formulate it as an image editing problem and build upon state-of-the-art editing models to leverage their superior generalization capability. Camera information is injected as dedicated camera tokens via an in-context multi-modal conditioning strategy. To alleviate the inherent ambiguity of NOCS, we incorporate text descriptions that explicitly define the object's canonical coordinate frame, which also enhances generalization to unseen object categories. Furthermore, we curate a high-quality dataset with consistently aligned orientations and corresponding NOCS text definitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method robustly generates novel views with accurate and consistent orientations from arbitrary unposed images across diverse categories, achieving state-of-the-art image quality and fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for precise camera control in Novel View Synthesis using a Normalized Object Coordinate Space (NOCS), treating it as an image editing problem with dedicated camera tokens and text-based canonical frame definitions, achieving state-of-the-art results across diverse categories.
AI.motivation: Existing NVS methods lack global and intuitive control of target viewpoints because they either rely on input-relative camera poses or only generate sparse global views, limiting downstream task applicability.
AI.method: The method uses NOCS for absolute camera pose representation, formulates NVS as an image editing problem built upon state-of-the-art editing models, injects camera information via dedicated camera tokens with in-context multi-modal conditioning, and incorporates text descriptions to disambiguate NOCS and enhance generalization. A consistently aligned dataset with NOCS text definitions is also curated.
AI.result: The method robustly generates novel views with accurate and consistent orientations from arbitrary unposed images across diverse categories, achieving state-of-the-art image quality and fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Precise camera control in NOCS, combined with an image editing formulation and multi-modal conditioning, effectively overcomes the viewpoint control limitations of prior NVS approaches.

title: Progress- and Reliability-Oriented Group Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Group-based reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for improving large language model agents on long-horizon interactive tasks. To obtain finer-grained policy updates than trajectory-level optimization, recent work has moved toward step-level group-based RL, where intermediate steps are grouped and compared within a rollout batch. However, step-level advantage estimation is sensitive to how groups are formed: grouping by broad state keys improves coverage but may compare actions taken under different histories, while enforcing historical consistency yields fairer comparisons at the cost of fragmented groups and missing peer-comparison signal. In this paper, we propose ProGPO (Progress- and Reliability-Oriented Group Policy Optimization), a learned-critic-free method for context-consistent step-level learning. ProGPO keeps exact-prefix action comparison, and complements sparse peer comparisons with transition credit derived from rollout-based state potentials. To estimate these potentials reliably, ProGPO combines semantic expansion with inverse-variance fusion across history depths. We evaluate ProGPO on two challenging agentic tasks, ALFWorld and WebShop, with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Results show that ProGPO improves over matched agentic RL baselines under comparable computational overhead, and additional Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct experiments further test the scalability of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: ProGPO is a learned-critic-free step-level group-based RL method for LLM agents that keeps exact-prefix action comparisons and uses rollout-based state potentials with semantic expansion and inverse-variance fusion, outperforming baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Step-level advantage estimation in group-based RL is sensitive to how groups are formed: grouping by broad state keys improves coverage but risks comparing actions under different histories, while history-consistent grouping yields fairer comparisons but leads to fragmented groups and missing peer-comparison signal.
AI.method: ProGPO keeps exact-prefix action comparison to maintain historical consistency, and complements sparse peer comparisons with transition credit derived from rollout-based state potentials. State potentials are estimated reliably via semantic expansion combined with inverse-variance fusion across history depths, eliminating the need for a learned critic.
AI.result: ProGPO outperforms matched agentic RL baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct under comparable computational overhead. Additional experiments with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct demonstrate scalability.
AI.conclusion: ProGPO provides an effective, critic-free solution for context-consistent step-level group-based RL in long-horizon interactive agentic tasks, achieving better performance without additional computational burden.

title: AGL-1: The Enterprise AI Governance Layer as a Control Plane for Trusted Enterprise Intelligence
summary:
Enterprise artificial intelligence is moving from isolated experimentation toward operational dependency across copilots, retrieval-augmented generation systems, autonomous agents, and AI-enabled business workflows. As this transition accelerates, the primary enterprise challenge is no longer only model access or inference scale. It is governed intelligence operations: the ability to enforce authorization, preserve contextual lineage, control persistent memory, detect stale or conflicting knowledge, constrain agentic execution, and produce audit-ready evidence across distributed AI estates.
  This paper introduces AGL-1, the Enterprise AI Governance Layer, as a vendor-neutral reference model for the control plane that should operate across foundation models, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, enterprise memory, policy engines, observability systems, tools, APIs, and business applications.
  Building on governed knowledge-system principles introduced in GKS-5, AGL-1 generalizes the governance problem from retrieval-specific controls to full AI execution-path governance. It identifies recurring failure modes such as unauthorized retrieval, stale grounding, unmanaged memory, weak provenance, policy drift, fragmented observability, and uncontrolled autonomous execution. It then defines seven governance domains: identity-aware retrieval, policy enforcement, provenance management, memory governance, knowledge integrity monitoring, agentic execution control, and trust observability.
  The central claim is that durable enterprise value from AI will increasingly depend on the ability to govern intelligence at scale. In complex enterprises, trust is not a property of the model alone. It is a property of the system around the model: identity, knowledge, policy, memory, tools, human oversight, and evidence working together as a managed control plane.

AI.tldr: AGL-1 is a vendor-neutral reference model for enterprise AI governance that defines seven domains (identity-aware retrieval, policy enforcement, provenance management, memory governance, knowledge integrity monitoring, agentic execution control, and trust observability) to address failure modes as AI systems move from experimentation to operational dependency.
AI.motivation: The primary enterprise challenge has shifted from model access or inference scale to governed intelligence operations—enforcing authorization, preserving contextual lineage, controlling persistent memory, detecting stale/conflicting knowledge, constraining agentic execution, and producing audit-ready evidence across distributed AI estates.
AI.method: AGL-1 builds on GKS-5 governed knowledge-system principles, generalizing from retrieval-specific controls to full AI execution-path governance. It identifies recurring failure modes and defines seven governance domains as a managed control plane spanning foundation models, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, enterprise memory, policy engines, observability systems, tools, APIs, and business applications.
AI.result: A structured governance reference model with seven domains addressing unauthorized retrieval, stale grounding, unmanaged memory, weak provenance, policy drift, fragmented observability, and uncontrolled autonomous execution.
AI.conclusion: Durable enterprise value from AI depends on governing intelligence at scale; trust is a property of the entire system (identity, knowledge, policy, memory, tools, human oversight, evidence) rather than the model alone.

title: CuBAS: Information Geometric Curvature-Based Adaptive Sampling for Supervised Classification
summary: The informativeness of a training set is as consequential as its size, yet most sampling strategies remain agnostic to the intrinsic geometry of the data distribution. We introduce CuBAS (Curvature-Based Adaptive Sampling), an information-geometric framework for adaptive data selection in supervised classification, grounded in the q-state Potts Markov random field (MRF) model. The central insight is that a labeled dataset can be viewed as a statistical manifold, on which local curvature, estimated via the ratio of second to first-order observed Fisher information, faithfully encodes the geometric complexity of the data distribution. We construct a k-nearest-neighbor graph over the labeled data and derive a closed-form curvature score at each vertex from the Potts sufficient statistics. This curvature signal partitions the graph into two complementary regimes: low-curvature regions, corresponding to smooth, homogeneous clusters, and high-curvature regions, concentrated around decision boundaries that are disproportionately informative for classification. By selecting nodes from both regimes, CuBAS constructs compact yet maximally informative training subsets. Empirical evaluation across more than 60 benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent and statistically significant improvements over random sampling and uncertainty-based baselines, across a wide range of labeling budgets and classifier architectures. CuBAS is computationally efficient (linear in the number of k-NN graph edges), theoretically grounded in the differential geometry of statistical manifolds, and interpretable in terms of the local shape operator of the data manifold.

AI.tldr: CuBAS is a curvature-based adaptive sampling framework for supervised classification that uses local Fisher information curvature on a k-NN graph over labeled data to identify both smooth regions and decision boundaries, enabling compact and maximally informative training subsets. It outperforms random and uncertainty-based sampling across 60+ benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing sampling strategies focus on dataset size but ignore the intrinsic geometry of the data distribution, leading to suboptimal training subset selection.
AI.method: CuBAS models labeled data as a statistical manifold via a q-state Potts MRF, computes local curvature from the ratio of second to first-order observed Fisher information on a k-NN graph, partitions the graph into low-curvature (homogeneous) and high-curvature (decision boundary) regimes, and selects nodes from both regimes to construct informative subsets.
AI.result: Across 60+ benchmark datasets, CuBAS achieves consistent and statistically significant improvements over random sampling and uncertainty-based baselines across various labeling budgets and classifier architectures, with linear computational efficiency in k-NN graph edges.
AI.conclusion: CuBAS is a theoretically grounded (differential geometry of statistical manifolds), computationally efficient, and interpretable adaptive sampling method that effectively leverages data geometry for supervised classification.

title: Diagnosing Aerial-View Object Detectors with Foundational Image Generative Models
summary: Recent advances in large-scale image generative models enable photorealistic scene synthesis with controllable attributes. Beyond data augmentation, their potential as diagnostic tools for trained vision systems remains unexplored in the aerial and remote sensing domains. We introduce a synthetic diagnostic framework for aerial-view vehicle detection that combines text-guided generation, attribute-controlled editing, and automated attribute verification to construct a controllable synthetic testbed. This enables fine-grained evaluation of pretrained detectors under diverse scene types and environmental conditions that are difficult to isolate in real datasets. Across three detection architectures and three real aerial datasets, synthetic scene-wise performance trends closely match real-world weaknesses. Guided by these diagnostics, targeted supplementation with small real datasets from the identified weak categories yields improvements of up to 13% AP50 while requiring substantially fewer additional samples than non-targeted augmentation. Our results show that controlled synthetic probing can predict real-domain performance gaps and guide efficient data collection. The proposed diagnostic framework is modular and can incorporate alternative generative or vision-language models as capabilities evolve. Our code and datasets are available here: https://humansensinglab.github.io/AVODDiag/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a synthetic diagnostic framework for aerial-view vehicle detection that uses text-guided generation, attribute-controlled editing, and automated verification to evaluate pretrained detectors under controlled conditions. Synthetic scene-wise performance trends match real-world weaknesses, and targeted supplementation improves AP50 by up to 13% with fewer samples than non-targeted augmentation.
AI.motivation: While large-scale image generative models enable controllable photorealistic scene synthesis, their potential as diagnostic tools for trained vision systems in aerial and remote sensing domains remains unexplored. Real datasets make it difficult to isolate specific scene types and environmental conditions for fine-grained evaluation.
AI.method: The framework combines text-guided generation (to create diverse aerial scenes), attribute-controlled editing (to manipulate specific scene attributes), and automated attribute verification (to ensure quality). It evaluates pretrained detectors across three detection architectures (e.g., Faster R-CNN, YOLO, DETR) and three real aerial datasets under controlled synthetic conditions.
AI.result: Synthetic scene-wise performance trends closely mirror real-world detector weaknesses. Targeted supplementation with small real datasets from identified weak categories yields up to 13% AP50 improvement, requiring substantially fewer additional samples than non-targeted augmentation.
AI.conclusion: Controlled synthetic probing can predict real-domain performance gaps and guide efficient data collection. The diagnostic framework is modular and can incorporate alternative generative or vision-language models as capabilities evolve.

title: Shortcut Learning in Legal Judgment Prediction: Empirical Evidence from the UK Employment Tribunal
summary: Current Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) is constrained by its reliance on post-hoc judicial materials, increasing the likelihood that models perform retrospective classification rather than true forecasting. This paper empirically investigates shortcut learning in this context by studying claim-level outcome prediction in UK Employment Tribunal (UKET) decisions. Using a corpus of 33,158 individual claims, we predict outcomes from claim texts and LLM-extracted case summaries, evaluating models ranging from interpretable TF-IDF-based classifiers to black-box LLMs. While headline predictive performance figures appear strong, we demonstrate that such performance in LJP systems trained on post-hoc judicial text can be driven by the retrospective nature of the source material. Stratifying the test data by human judgments of leakage reveals that performance increases where outcome-revealing cues are embedded in the narrative. Moreover, a model trained on just the 4% of features identified as leakage achieves high performance, outperforming human experts. These findings substantiate concerns that LJP performance may be exaggerated by linguistic artefacts. Yet this vulnerability is not fatal to the research agenda. Instead, post-hoc judgments might be treated as potentially contaminated texts, requiring active auditing. Retraining models after masking leakage features results in only a negligible reduction in Macro-F1. Hence, while models will opportunistically exploit shortcuts when available, they remain capable of extracting useful predictive signals when these artefacts are removed.

AI.tldr: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) models trained on post-hoc judicial texts exhibit shortcut learning by exploiting outcome-revealing linguistic cues (leakage), inflating performance. However, after masking these leakage features, models retain predictive capability, suggesting the problem is manageable through active auditing.
AI.motivation: Current LJP relies on post-hoc judicial materials, making models prone to retrospective classification rather than true forecasting. The authors aim to empirically investigate whether shortcut learning via linguistic leakage inflates LJP performance.
AI.method: Using 33,158 UK Employment Tribunal claims, the authors predict outcomes from claim texts and LLM-extracted summaries. They evaluate TF-IDF classifiers and black-box LLMs, stratify test data by human judgments of leakage, train a model on only leakage features, and retrain after masking leakage features.
AI.result: Models show strong headline performance, but this is driven by retrospective cues. A model trained on just 4% leakage features outperforms human experts. After masking leakage, Macro-F1 drops only negligibly, indicating models can still extract useful signals.
AI.conclusion: LJP performance is indeed exaggerated by linguistic artefacts, but this vulnerability is not fatal. Post-hoc judgments should be treated as potentially contaminated texts requiring active auditing; models remain capable when shortcuts are removed.

title: Anchored Self-Play for Code Repair
summary: Code repair is an important capability for language models (LMs): given a buggy program and unit tests, an LM must produce a fixed program that passes the tests. Because code repair data is limited, we aim to scale supervision by using an LM to generate bug--fix tasks. We propose __generator--fixer self-play__, in which a single model is trained with reinforcement learning to generate bugs and fix them. As the fixer improves, the generator adapts to produce more difficult bugs, yielding an automatic curriculum. To test whether this curriculum generalizes, we introduce BugSourceBench, a repair benchmark spanning realistic bug sources: bugs in human-written code, LM-generated code, and human-edited LM-generated code. On BugSourceBench, we find that self-play drifts toward difficult but unrealistic bugs, improving on synthetic bugs but degrading on human-authored ones. We propose Anchored Self-Play (ASP), which anchors self-play with a small reference set by adding a code-embedding similarity reward for generation and mixing reference bugs into fixer training. Across bug sources, ASP achieves the best fix rates, improving average fix rate over standard self-play by $+24\%$ relative / $+7.0$ pp absolute, with gains on bugs from both LMs and humans.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Anchored Self-Play (ASP) for LM code repair training, which uses reinforcement learning with a reference set to prevent the model from drifting toward unrealistic synthetic bugs while maintaining performance on human-authored code.
AI.motivation: Code repair data is limited, so the authors aim to scale supervision by using an LM to generate bug-fix tasks. However, standard self-play drifts toward difficult but unrealistic bugs, degrading performance on human-authored code.
AI.method: Generator-fixer self-play with reinforcement learning. Anchored Self-Play (ASP) adds a code-embedding similarity reward for generation and mixes reference bugs into fixer training to anchor the learning process with a small reference set.
AI.result: ASP achieves the best fix rates across bug sources, improving average fix rate over standard self-play by +24% relative / +7.0 pp absolute, with gains on bugs from both LMs and humans.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring self-play with a reference set prevents performance degradation on human-authored bugs while still benefiting from synthetic bug generation, leading to more generalizable code repair capabilities.

title: Rethinking Neural Nonlinearity as Gating
summary: Activation functions are considered an essential primitive for neural nonlinearity, i.e., they enable neural networks to serve as universal approximators. In this paper, we show that this nonlinearity can also be achieved by input-conditioned threshold gating through branches as a universal primitive. We demonstrate that standard activations -- whether piecewise-linear (ReLU, PReLU, Hardtanh) or smooth (SiLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, GELU) -- are in fact instances of a single Threshold Gating (TG) primitive. For softmax, we show that it admits an exact TG conversion via its equivalent per-element Sigmoid form. We then validate these equivalences by converting pretrained networks across CNNs, transformer-based models, and recurrent architectures, preserving model performance without requiring retraining. Threshold Gating also enables training from scratch that goes beyond replacing existing activations, enabling gains in model compression, performance, and shorter training. We also propose a 'Minimal Branch Theorem' which relates the minimum number of required branches in our primitive to the trainability of general deep neural networks. In terms of hardware implementation, TG maps to a unified implementation in the case of analog in-memory systems, addressing the bottleneck of analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters (ADC/DAC) that is known to significantly impact power consumption and on-chip area.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that common activation functions (ReLU, SiLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, GELU, Softmax, etc.) are all instances of a single Threshold Gating (TG) primitive using input-conditioned branch gating. TG enables unified hardware implementation, model compression, and performance gains without retraining.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that neural network nonlinearity can be achieved through input-conditioned threshold gating via branches as a universal primitive, and to unify diverse activation functions under a single framework to simplify hardware implementation and enable model efficiency gains.
AI.method: The authors show that piecewise-linear (ReLU, PReLU, Hardtanh) and smooth (SiLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, GELU) activations are instances of Threshold Gating (TG). Softmax is converted exactly via per-element Sigmoid form. A Minimal Branch Theorem relating branch count to trainability is proposed. Pretrained CNNs, transformers, and recurrent models are converted without retraining.
AI.result: TG preserves model performance across converted pretrained networks (CNNs, transformers, RNNs) without retraining. Training from scratch with TG yields gains in model compression, performance, and shorter training. TG maps to a unified analog in-memory implementation, addressing ADC/DAC power and area bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Threshold Gating is a universal primitive that subsumes standard activation functions, enabling both theoretical unification (Minimal Branch Theorem) and practical benefits in model compression, training efficiency, and analog hardware implementation.

title: GRCD: Grounded Region Change Detection for Multi-Finding Chest X-Ray Pairs
summary: Radiologists routinely compare current and prior chest X-rays to track disease progression, producing follow-up reports that describe multiple findings, each localised to an anatomical region and annotated with a temporal change status. Existing automated methods either generate reports from a single image without modelling temporal context, or incorporate temporal information but do not ground their outputs spatially. The few approaches that combine temporal reasoning with spatial grounding are restricted to single-finding descriptions, leaving multi-finding reports with mixed change directions unaddressed. We present GRCD, a framework for grounded report generation from chest X-ray pairs in the multi-finding setting. We first construct a rigorously cleaned dataset of temporal chest X-ray pairs by identifying and correcting two systematic labelling errors in the source annotations. We then introduce a Region-Guided Change Token module that encodes per-region temporal change across anatomical structures and injects this signal into a language model through a dual-pathway strategy combining prepended spatial tokens with gated cross-attention. On a multi-finding test set, GRCD outperforms existing baselines on text generation and clinical accuracy metrics, with gains in change detection. Ablation studies confirm that the dual-pathway design outperforms either integration strategy in isolation on text and clinical metrics, and that region-level change encoding is necessary for multi-finding generation. Code is available at https://github.com/UTSA-VIRLab/GRCD

AI.tldr: GRCD is a framework for generating grounded multi-finding radiology reports from chest X-ray pairs by cleaning dataset errors and using a Region-Guided Change Token module with dual-pathway integration, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods either lack temporal context (single-image report generation), lack spatial grounding, or are restricted to single-finding descriptions. Multi-finding reports with mixed temporal change directions across anatomical regions remain unaddressed.
AI.method: (1) Constructed a cleaned dataset of temporal chest X-ray pairs by correcting two systematic labeling errors. (2) Introduced Region-Guided Change Token module encoding per-region temporal change across anatomical structures. (3) Dual-pathway strategy combining prepended spatial tokens with gated cross-attention to inject signals into a language model.
AI.result: GRCD outperforms existing baselines on text generation and clinical accuracy metrics, with gains in change detection. Dual-pathway design outperforms either integration strategy alone. Region-level change encoding is necessary for multi-finding generation.
AI.conclusion: GRCD effectively handles multi-finding grounded report generation from chest X-ray pairs, and the dual-pathway region-guided change encoding is critical for performance.

title: Agentic SABRE: An Uncertainty-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Ransomware Detection
summary: Ransomware has evolved into a complex, adaptive, and fast-moving adversary category in which static signatures and monolithic classifiers fail to generalise under concept drift, evasion, and behavioural polymorphism. In this paper, we present Agentic SABRE (Semantic-Behavioural Arbitration for Ransomware Evaluation), an uncertainty-aware, neuro-symbolic, multi-agent framework for adaptive ransomware detection. SABRE fuses semantic, representation-based evidence with behavioural, time-window forensic telemetry and employs Monte Carlo Dropout inference to quantify epistemic uncertainty for each agent. We introduce a decision-layer orchestrator that performs risk- and uncertainty-aware triage using two interpretable thresholds: a risk score and an uncertainty budget. High-confidence, high-risk samples are automatically contained, while uncertain or borderline cases are escalated to human analysts, establishing a flexible computational contract between autonomous response and analyst oversight. To support auditability and trust, SABRE integrates post-hoc explainability mechanisms, including gradient saliency, permutation importance, and counterfactual analysis, enabling both local and global interpretation of agent decisions. Extensive evaluation on RDset and RanSMAP demonstrates that Agentic SABRE preserves perfect discrimination on saturated semantic datasets, with AUC equal to 1.0, while improving robustness under weak behavioural signals. It achieves up to a 4.9 percent relative reduction in false escalations at equal recall while maintaining calibrated predictive uncertainty. Counterfactual analysis further shows that semantic and behavioural decisions can be reversed with bounded perturbation cost, indicating stable and interpretable decision boundaries.

AI.tldr: Agentic SABRE is a neuro-symbolic, multi-agent framework for adaptive ransomware detection that fuses semantic and behavioural evidence with uncertainty quantification, using a risk- and uncertainty-aware orchestrator to triage samples between automated containment and human analyst escalation, achieving perfect discrimination (AUC=1.0) on saturated semantic datasets and up to 4.9% reduction in false escalations.
AI.motivation: Ransomware has evolved into adaptive adversaries with concept drift, evasion, and behavioural polymorphism, rendering static signatures and monolithic classifiers ineffective at generalization.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework combining semantic (representation-based) and behavioural (time-window forensic telemetry) agents with Monte Carlo Dropout for epistemic uncertainty quantification, a decision-layer orchestrator using interpretable risk score and uncertainty budget thresholds, and post-hoc explainability (gradient saliency, permutation importance, counterfactual analysis).
AI.result: AUC=1.0 on saturated semantic datasets; up to 4.9% relative reduction in false escalations at equal recall; calibrated predictive uncertainty; stable and interpretable decision boundaries confirmed via counterfactual analysis.
AI.conclusion: Agentic SABRE provides a flexible computational contract between autonomous response and analyst oversight, enabling robust, interpretable, and trustworthy adaptive ransomware detection under concept drift and weak behavioural signals.

title: GameEngineBench: Evaluating Coding Agents on Real C++ Runtime Environments
summary: Game engines provide real-time simulation, rendering, physics, interaction, networking, and asset pipelines, making them valuable not only for games but also for 3D applications in healthcare, robotics, architecture, manufacturing, and related domains. Because game development is where these systems are most mature and publicly available, it offers a practical testbed for evaluating coding agents that must modify C++ code within stateful, interactive, real-time systems. We present GameEngineBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on scoped C++ implementation tasks inside Unreal Engine 5 projects, built from nine real-world game repositories. The evaluation set consists of 110 tasks spanning gameplay mechanics, multiplayer behavior, AI and world orchestration, animation and movement, UI and session code, loading behavior, online-service integration, persistence, data serialization, XR behavior, and rendering-oriented plugins.
