These tasks require models to make native C++ changes that compile and satisfy behavioral tests within executable Unreal Engine projects. Across twelve evaluated configurations, the strongest model reaches 55.5\% pass@1, while 31 tasks remain unsolved by every configuration. Our results demonstrate that frontier coding agents continue to struggle with deeply integrated C++ development for real-time interactive software, highlighting game-engine benchmarks as a valuable complement to existing software engineering evaluations.

AI.tldr: GameEngineBench is a benchmark with 110 C++ tasks across 9 Unreal Engine 5 game repositories for evaluating coding agents. The best model achieves 55.5% pass@1, with 31 tasks unsolved by any configuration, showing frontier coding agents struggle with real-time interactive C++ development.
AI.motivation: Game engines are broadly used beyond gaming (healthcare, robotics, architecture), and game development provides a mature, publicly available testbed for evaluating coding agents on C++ code within stateful, interactive, real-time systems—a domain underrepresented in existing software engineering benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors built GameEngineBench from nine real-world Unreal Engine 5 game repositories, creating 110 tasks spanning 11 categories (gameplay, multiplayer, AI, animation, UI, loading, online services, persistence, serialization, XR, rendering). Tasks require native C++ changes that compile and pass behavioral tests in executable UE5 projects. Twelve model configurations were evaluated using pass@1 metric.
AI.result: The strongest model achieves 55.5% pass@1; 31 tasks remain unsolved by all 12 evaluated configurations.
AI.conclusion: Frontier coding agents still struggle with deeply integrated C++ development for real-time interactive software, and game-engine benchmarks serve as a valuable complement to existing software engineering evaluations.

title: Decentralised Federated Learning over Temporal Networks: The Role of Heterogeneities
summary: Decentralised federated learning, based on peer-to-peer communication, is increasingly proposed for on-device training of machine learning models, promising a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient training process with no risk of single-point failure. However, the role of structural and temporal inhomogeneities in such fully decentralised settings remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate their effects when model parameters are locally averaged during aggregation. We show that the decentralised federated learning process is governed, both in the early phase and the late, stationary limit, by the same dynamics as a lazy random-walk diffusion process on temporal networks. Based on this mapping, we demonstrate that the typical experimental scenario used in decentralised federated learning leads to unrealistically rapid convergence because of ignoring the temporal and structural inhomogeneities inherent in the communication network. We analyse real-world temporal networks and find that inhomogeneities most often dramatically slow down diffusion, hence the convergence process.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that decentralized federated learning's convergence dynamics mirror lazy random-walk diffusion on temporal networks, and that real-world structural/temporal inhomogeneities dramatically slow convergence, making typical experimental setups unrealistically optimistic.
AI.motivation: To understand how structural and temporal inhomogeneities in peer-to-peer communication networks affect the convergence of decentralized federated learning, as prior work largely overlooked these real-world network properties.
AI.method: The authors map decentralized federated learning (with local averaging of model parameters) to a lazy random-walk diffusion process on temporal networks, analyzing both early-phase and stationary-limit dynamics. They validate this mapping by comparing typical experimental scenarios against real-world temporal network data.
AI.result: Typical experimental setups in decentralized federated learning ignore temporal and structural inhomogeneities, leading to unrealistically rapid convergence. Real-world temporal networks exhibit inhomogeneities that most often dramatically slow down diffusion and thus the convergence process.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized federated learning convergence is governed by the same dynamics as lazy random-walk diffusion on temporal networks; real-world communication inhomogeneities must be accounted for to avoid overestimating convergence speed.

title: HAS-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Human-Agent Systems under Configurable Human Participation
summary: Large language models increasingly operate in settings where humans are active collaborators rather than passive task providers. We introduce HAS-Framework, a graph-based framework that represents humans and LLM-powered agents as first-class participants with explicit roles, permissions, communication paths, and action authority. Building on this framework, HAS-Bench evaluates Human-Agent Systems under configurable human participation across agency levels, interaction channels, and persona policies. The benchmark measures both task outcomes and process-level collaboration behavior, including clarification quality, feedback utilization, control calibration, safety, initiative, and interaction cost. Experiments across six domains show that human participation can substantially improve task completion and failure recovery, but the gains depend on when, how, and by whom human input is exercised.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HAS-Framework, a graph-based framework for modeling human-LLM agent collaboration, and HAS-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates such systems across varying human participation levels, interaction channels, and persona policies, measuring both task outcomes and process-level behaviors like clarification, feedback, safety, and cost. Experiments across six domains show human participation improves task completion and recovery, but effectiveness depends on timing, manner, and source of human input.
AI.motivation: Large language models increasingly operate in settings where humans are active collaborators rather than passive task providers, yet existing frameworks lack explicit modeling of human roles, permissions, communication paths, and action authority in Human-Agent Systems.
AI.method: The authors propose HAS-Framework, a graph-based representation that treats humans and LLM-powered agents as first-class participants with explicit roles, permissions, communication paths, and action authority. Building on it, HAS-Bench evaluates systems under configurable human participation across agency levels, interaction channels, and persona policies, measuring both task outcomes and process-level collaboration behavior.
AI.result: Experiments across six domains show that human participation can substantially improve task completion and failure recovery, but the gains depend on when, how, and by whom human input is exercised.
AI.conclusion: Human participation improves LLM-agent task performance and failure recovery, but the effectiveness is contingent on the timing, manner, and source of human intervention, highlighting the need for careful design of human-agent collaboration dynamics.

title: LogSemFuse: Semantic Evidence Fusion for Explainable Log Anomaly Detection
summary: Log anomaly detection is critical for reliability monitoring and failure diagnosis in modern software systems. Existing model-based detectors provide useful anomaly signals, but they can still miss anomalous sessions and typically expose only scores or labels rather than the operational semantics behind a decision. This lack of semantic evidence limits their ability to explain why a session is anomalous, even when the final anomaly label is correct. The gap matters in practice because operators need to distinguish urgent failures from benign deviations and trace suspicious sessions back to concrete operational behavior. LLMs can recover richer log semantics, but using them as standalone detectors or repeatedly generating free-form explanations can be costly and difficult to reuse. We present LogSemFuse, an evidence-guided plug-in framework that enhances existing backbone detectors without replacing their original pipelines. LogSemFuse combines backbone predictions with reusable semantic evidence from local event patterns, LLM-based semantic reasoning, and cluster-derived executable rules to produce both anomaly decisions and evidence-based explanations. The resulting output reports the final label together with the semantic evidence that supports it, such as fired local patterns, triggered rules, and LLM rationale. We evaluate LogSemFuse on HDFS, BGL, and Liberty using DeepLog, LogAnomaly, LogBERT, and NeuralLog as backbones. LogSemFuse improves every non-perfect baseline, preserves the already perfect case, recovers 98.8% of backbone false negatives, and produces explanations preferred over direct LLM explanations in a human study. These gains require only modest and stable inference-time overhead, showing that semantic augmentation can improve detection effectiveness and interpretability without imposing large runtime costs.

AI.tldr: LogSemFuse is a plug-in framework that enhances existing log anomaly detectors by combining their predictions with reusable semantic evidence from local patterns, LLM reasoning, and cluster-derived rules, improving detection effectiveness and providing explainable outputs with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing model-based log anomaly detectors often miss anomalous sessions and provide only scores/labels without operational semantics, making it hard for operators to distinguish urgent failures from benign deviations or trace suspicious behaviors.
AI.method: LogSemFuse is an evidence-guided plug-in framework that augments backbone detectors by fusing their predictions with semantic evidence from three sources: local event patterns, LLM-based semantic reasoning, and cluster-derived executable rules. It produces both anomaly decisions and evidence-based explanations.
AI.result: LogSemFuse improves every non-perfect baseline, preserves already perfect cases, recovers 98.8% of backbone false negatives, and produces explanations preferred over direct LLM explanations in a human study, with modest and stable inference-time overhead.
AI.conclusion: Semantic augmentation via LogSemFuse can improve detection effectiveness and interpretability without imposing large runtime costs, offering a practical enhancement for existing log anomaly detectors.

title: Understanding electricity consumption behaviour through Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Understanding how households consume electricity in response to socioeconomic and climatic drivers is important for decision-makers designing energy policies in a changing climate and under geopolitical tensions. Consumers respond differently to thermal stress depending on income, consumption habits and the surrounding built environment, a nonlinear behaviour that most approaches oversimplify. In this study, households are treated as agents interacting with complex environments, and Inverse Reinforcement Learning is used to represent their consumption behaviour as model implied reward functions. Specifically, we observe how these reward functions change when households undergo socioeconomic and climatic shocks. The framework is tested on different clusters of electricity consumption profiles in Italy. Clusters' reward functions are retrieved and used to understand how cooling behaviour changes from summer 2021 to summer 2022 and 2023, before, during and after the energy crisis and a heatwave. We find that these shocks reshaped cooling behaviour heterogeneously across consumer groups, in directions conditioned by their prior habits and built environment. Across the 2021 to 2023 summers, we identify a spectrum of responses: transient adjustments that receded as the shocks eased, durable shifts persisting into 2023, and consumers exhibiting negligible change. At the intradaily scale, groups comparable in socioeconomic and environmental context but differing in their daily timing of consumption responded distinctly, identifying time of use as a separate dimension of behavioural heterogeneity. Energy policies and demand-response schemes should therefore account not only for who consumers are and where they live, but for when they consume and whether their response to a shock persists.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Inverse Reinforcement Learning to model household electricity consumption behaviors as reward functions, testing how socioeconomic and climatic shocks (energy crisis and heatwave) reshaped cooling behavior across different consumer clusters in Italy from 2021-2023, revealing heterogeneous, persistent, and time-of-use-dependent responses.
AI.motivation: Understanding how households consume electricity in response to socioeconomic and climatic drivers is important for decision-makers designing energy policies in a changing climate and under geopolitical tensions. Most approaches oversimplify the nonlinear behavior of consumers responding to thermal stress.
AI.method: Households are modeled as agents interacting with complex environments; Inverse Reinforcement Learning is used to represent consumption behavior as model-implied reward functions. The framework observes how reward functions change under socioeconomic and climatic shocks, tested on different clusters of electricity consumption profiles in Italy.
AI.result: Shocks reshaped cooling behavior heterogeneously across consumer groups, conditioned by prior habits and built environment. A spectrum of responses was identified: transient adjustments, durable shifts persisting into 2023, and negligible change. Groups comparable in socioeconomic/environmental context but differing in daily consumption timing responded distinctly.
AI.conclusion: Energy policies and demand-response schemes should account not only for who consumers are and where they live, but for when they consume and whether their response to a shock persists.

title: Signal from Space: Detecting Schools and Towers to Bridge the Digital Divide
summary: Reliable internet access is essential for modern education, yet millions of school-aged children especially in developing regions remain offline due to unconnected schools. The Giga Initiative aims to connect every school to the internet, but doing so at scale requires efficient methods to map schools and assess surrounding connectivity infrastructure without relying on sparse or noisy third-party datasets. In this work, we propose a scalable, vision-only framework that uses high-resolution satellite imagery and transfer learning to address both tasks simultaneously. By adapting pre-trained object detection models to new geographical regions with minimal labeled data, we detect schools and cell towers directly from space. We then analyze the spatial relationship between detected schools and nearby towers as a proxy for connectivity availability. This purely imagery-driven pipeline enables large-scale infrastructure mapping, reduces dependency on auxiliary data, and supports data-driven prioritization of connectivity investments in underserved areas. Our approach is demonstrated on real satellite imagery from Lesotho, showing strong performance across this region.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a scalable vision-only framework using satellite imagery and transfer learning to simultaneously detect schools and cell towers, analyze their spatial proximity as a connectivity proxy, and support internet connectivity mapping for the Giga Initiative, demonstrated effectively in Lesotho.
AI.motivation: Reliable internet access is essential for modern education, yet millions of school-aged children, especially in developing regions, remain offline due to unconnected schools. Scaling up school connectivity requires efficient mapping of schools and surrounding connectivity infrastructure without relying on sparse or noisy third-party datasets.
AI.method: A scalable, vision-only framework using high-resolution satellite imagery and transfer learning. Pre-trained object detection models are adapted to new regions with minimal labeled data to detect both schools and cell towers. Spatial relationships between detected schools and towers are then analyzed as a proxy for connectivity availability.
AI.result: The approach demonstrated strong performance on real satellite imagery from Lesotho, showing the feasibility of purely imagery-driven large-scale infrastructure mapping without dependency on auxiliary data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables large-scale infrastructure mapping, reduces dependency on auxiliary datasets, and supports data-driven prioritization of connectivity investments in underserved areas.

title: Do GUI Agents Believe Their Eyes? Diagnosing State-Belief Reliance on Pixels versus Structure
summary: Multimodal GUI agents read an interface through two redundant channels: the rendered pixels of a screenshot and a serialized structure such as a DOM or accessibility tree. Before acting, an agent forms a belief about the current interface state, but existing benchmarks score task success, element grounding, or attack resistance and do not ask whether that belief is drawn from the pixels. We formalize visual state reliance, the attribution of a state belief to pixels, structure, or priors, and measure it with paired single-channel interventions over 310 real web, mobile, and desktop probes. Every probe is scored by deterministic forced choice, with no model-generated item and no model judge. Our central metric is the Perception-Fusion Gap, the fraction of probes a model perceives correctly yet resolves toward structure under conflict. Across five models from three vendors, textual state beliefs defer to structure while image-only accuracy stays near ceiling, and Perception-Fusion Gap is positive for every model; non-text identity, by contrast, stays largely pixel-bound. The substitution is specific to the serialized-text and indexed-action channel, and coordinate-action agents are largely immune. For textual conflicts, a white-box ablation traces the effect to a single copied structural value, and in two live environments the conflict drives wrong actions and real task failure. Visual state reliance therefore gives a measurable diagnostic of whether agent state beliefs are visually grounded, and the errors it exposes propagate to actions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Perception-Fusion Gap metric to measure whether multimodal GUI agents visually ground their state beliefs or rely on structural text representations. Testing five models on 310 probes, the authors find that textual state beliefs consistently defer to structure over pixels, leading to action errors and task failures.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for multimodal GUI agents evaluate task success, grounding, or attack resistance, but fail to assess whether an agent's beliefs about interface state are actually drawn from visual (pixel) information versus alternative channels like DOM or accessibility trees.
AI.method: Formalizes visual state reliance through paired single-channel interventions across 310 real web, mobile, and desktop probes. Uses deterministic forced-choice scoring (no model-generated items or judges). Introduces the Perception-Fusion Gap (PFG) metric—the fraction of probes a model perceives correctly yet resolves toward structure under conflict. Includes white-box ablation and live environment validation.
AI.result: Across five models from three vendors: (1) textual state beliefs defer to structure while image-only accuracy remains near ceiling; (2) PFG is positive for all models; (3) non-text identity remains mostly pixel-bound; (4) substitution is specific to serialized-text and indexed-action channels (coordinate-action agents are largely immune); (5) a single copied structural value drives the effect; (6) conflict drives wrong actions and real task failures in live environments.
AI.conclusion: Visual state reliance is a measurable diagnostic of whether agent state beliefs are visually grounded. The errors exposed by PFG propagate to actions, meaning agents are not truly "seeing" interfaces but rather reading structural text, which has practical consequences for reliability.

title: AutoCedar: An Agentic Framework for Verifier-Guided Access Control Policy Synthesis
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly used to turn natural-language requirements into code. In access control, that shortcut is dangerous: a generated policy can compile and read correctly while granting access that no one approved. The difficulty is not only writing policy code. It is fixing what the requirements mean before code is written, and then checking that the final policy actually satisfies that intent. We present AutoCedar, a verifier-guided system that first turns natural-language access-control requirements into a reviewed, checkable target, and then synthesizes Cedar policies against that target. AutoCedar decomposes schema and policy authoring into small intent atoms: reviewable claims about vocabulary and behavior. Once those atoms pass mechanical validation and human intent review, the model proposes a candidate policy, the verifier checks it against the approved target, and each failure is turned into a repair signal that tells the model whether to broaden, narrow, or restructure the policy without changing the target. Because the model's work is split into small problems, each grounded in reviewed intent and backed by verifier feedback, end-to-end policy authoring becomes tractable. AutoCedar converges on all 221 tasks of CedarBench, our benchmark of authorization tasks paired with executable semantic boundaries. Across three requirements-corpus case studies covering healthcare, education, and conference management, AutoCedar converts noisy prose and extracted access-control fragments into reviewed schemas, formal checks, and a globally verified Cedar policy store for each scenario.

AI.tldr: AutoCedar is a verifier-guided system that decomposes natural-language access-control requirements into reviewable intent atoms, synthesizes Cedar policies against formally verified targets, and uses repair signals from verification failures to iteratively fix policies. It achieves convergence on all 221 CedarBench tasks and is validated across three real-world case studies.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated access-control policies are dangerous because they can compile and read correctly while granting unintended access. The core difficulty is not just writing policy code but fixing requirements ambiguity before coding and verifying that the final policy matches intended behavior.
AI.method: AutoCedar decomposes schema and policy authoring into small, reviewable "intent atoms" (claims about vocabulary and behavior). It uses a verifier to check candidate policies against an approved target, and each verification failure generates a repair signal (broaden, narrow, or restructure). The model iteratively refines policies without changing the target.
AI.result: Converges on all 221 tasks in CedarBench. Validated across three case studies (healthcare, education, conference management), converting noisy prose into reviewed schemas, formal checks, and globally verified Cedar policies.
AI.conclusion: By splitting policy generation into small, verifier-grounded problems with reviewed intent, end-to-end policy authoring becomes tractable and safe for access control.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Evaluating Scenario Compatibility in Generative Population Synthesis
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
summary: Scenario-based transportation analysis specifies future assumptions through aggregate population targets, whereas generative population synthesis models produce detailed individual-level realizations. When scenario targets are imposed on generative models, current practice relies on deterministic marginal calibration, implicitly assuming that the targets are compatible with the model's learned structural support. However, whether scenario-level constraints lie within the generative support--and how strongly they distort structural uncertainty--remains largely unexamined. We propose an ensemble-based Bayesian updating framework to quantify scenario compatibility in conditional population synthesis. A population-aware conditional variational autoencoder is developed to learn a distribution over plausible population structures while preserving aggregate fidelity. An ensemble of realizations sampled from the learned prior provides an empirical approximation of structural uncertainty. Scenario targets are treated as probabilistic evidence over aggregate statistics, and posterior weights are obtained through Bayesian updating across the ensemble. Scenario compatibility is quantified using effective sample size (ESS), which measures posterior concentration and the compression of structural uncertainty induced by conditioning. Experiments demonstrate that scenario impact depends not only on target magnitude but also on alignment with the learned joint structure, and reveal structural failure modes when targets fall outside prior ensemble support. The proposed framework provides a probabilistic diagnostic model for evaluating scenario feasibility and structural consistency before downstream projection and transportation planning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ensemble-based Bayesian updating framework with a population-aware conditional variational autoencoder to quantify whether scenario-level aggregate targets are compatible with the learned structural support of generative population synthesis models, using effective sample size (ESS) as a diagnostic metric.
AI.motivation: Current practice imposes scenario targets on generative models via deterministic marginal calibration, implicitly assuming compatibility with the model's learned structural support, yet it remains unexamined whether scenario constraints lie within that support or how strongly they distort structural uncertainty.
AI.method: A population-aware conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) learns a distribution over plausible population structures while preserving aggregate fidelity. An ensemble of realizations from the learned prior approximates structural uncertainty. Scenario targets are treated as probabilistic evidence, and posterior weights are computed via Bayesian updating. Scenario compatibility is quantified using effective sample size (ESS), measuring posterior concentration and compression of structural uncertainty.
AI.result: Experiments show that scenario impact depends on alignment with the learned joint structure, not just target magnitude, and reveal structural failure modes when targets lie outside prior ensemble support.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a probabilistic diagnostic model for evaluating scenario feasibility and structural consistency before downstream projection and transportation planning.

title: Biomechanics-aware Multi-view Markerless Motion Capture of Dexterous Hand Movements
summary: Markerless motion capture (MMC) techniques have been widely beneficial in biomechanical analysis of human movement; however, application to complex motions of the hand lags other musculoskeletal systems. The primary goal of this study was to evaluate the performance of a biomechanical reconstruction method that implements a gradient-based optimization approach with a biomechanical model in the loop for tracking dexterous, unconstrained hand movements using MMC. Using a custom, 8-camera setup, we acquired 121 video recordings from 6 participants performing 11 different tasks that spanned 6 hand postures, 5 object manipulation tasks, and involved motion of the proximal upper limb joints. Performance of the proposed MMC pipeline was directly compared to a more commonly adopted two-stage reconstruction method that first triangulates 2D keypoints from computer vision pose estimation algorithms to 3D and then enforces biomechanical constraints by solving a constrained inverse kinematics problem. Relative performance was assessed qualitatively by visual inspection and quantitatively using a computer vision metric. Our method generated solutions for all 121 video recordings; the two-stage method did not converge for 15% of the recordings. Across the remaining videos, our method produced more biomechanically plausible hand kinematics than the two-stage method and was more robust to occlusion effects during tasks that involved objects. The relative robustness of the end-to-end method suggests that it is more effective in utilizing the available 2D digital keypoint information. Automatic and biomechanically meaningful tracking of hand kinematics during dexterous movements has the potential to support clinical evaluation, rehabilitation monitoring, and studies of human motor control.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a gradient-based biomechanical reconstruction method for markerless motion capture of dexterous hand movements, showing it outperforms a two-stage method in convergence, biomechanical plausibility, and robustness to occlusion across 121 recordings of 11 hand tasks.
AI.motivation: Markerless motion capture (MMC) has been beneficial for biomechanical analysis but lags in application to complex hand motions. The study aims to evaluate a biomechanical reconstruction method using gradient-based optimization with a biomechanical model in the loop for tracking dexterous, unconstrained hand movements.
AI.method: Using an 8-camera setup, 121 video recordings from 6 participants performing 11 tasks (6 hand postures, 5 object manipulations, proximal upper limb motions) were acquired. The proposed MMC pipeline (end-to-end gradient-based optimization with biomechanical model in the loop) was compared to a two-stage method (triangulation of 2D keypoints to 3D + constrained inverse kinematics). Performance assessed qualitatively via visual inspection and quantitatively via a computer vision metric.
AI.result: The proposed method converged for all 121 recordings, while the two-stage method failed for 15%. Across successful recordings, the proposed method produced more biomechanically plausible hand kinematics and was more robust to occlusion during object manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end gradient-based method is more effective at utilizing 2D keypoint information, offering automatic and biomechanically meaningful hand tracking that could support clinical evaluation, rehabilitation monitoring, and studies of human motor control.

title: Server-side Anti-cheat in FPS games for Aimbot detection using Deep learning and Machine learning
summary: Modern video games are becoming more complex day by day. Most of these modern games are multiplayer first-person shooter (FPS) games. The rising popularity of FPS games emphasizes the need to combat cheating for fair and enjoyable gaming. As the number of players using cheating techniques like aimbots, wallhacks, and speed hacks is also increasing, we need a way to detect players who are using cheating tools to gain an unfair advantage over regular players. In this system, we focus exclusively on detecting aimbot cheats. Players who use aimbot cheats generally do not prioritize other aspects of the game. To distinguish between regular and cheating players, we identify specific features encompassing time-series data such as aim velocity, number of shots, distance to target, and more, along with behavioral data such as utility usage, player movement, and other gameplay patterns. Utilizing these features, we construct a server-side aimbot detection classifier named 'YAACS'. YAACS comprises a parser, a deep learning model, and intermediary connection utilities designed for integration with the game server. The proposed system achieves a classification accuracy of 88.6% with a false positive rate of 0.97% using a Stacked LSTM with Dense layers trained on sequences of 128 ticks (Tick Delta Negative=56, Tick Delta Positive=24), outperforming the Decision Tree baseline which achieves a higher accuracy of 96.2% but at a false positive rate of 2.68%, 2.76x worse than the best LSTM configuration. These results demonstrate that incorporating temporal context through sequence modelling is critical for minimising false accusations in FPS cheat detection.

AI.tldr: YAACS is a server-side aimbot detection system for FPS games that uses a Stacked LSTM with Dense layers trained on time-series and behavioral features (aim velocity, shots, distance, utility usage, movement) over 128-tick sequences, achieving 88.6% accuracy with a 0.97% false positive rate — 2.76x lower than the 96.2% accurate Decision Tree baseline (2.68% FPR) — demonstrating that temporal context via sequence modeling is crucial for minimizing false accusations.
AI.motivation: The rising popularity of multiplayer FPS games has led to increased cheating via aimbots, wallhacks, and speed hacks, undermining fair gameplay. Existing detection methods are insufficient, and there is a need for a server-side system that can accurately detect aimbot users while minimizing false accusations (false positives).
AI.method: The system extracts time-series features (aim velocity, shots, distance to target) and behavioral features (utility usage, player movement, gameplay patterns) from gameplay data. A Stacked LSTM with Dense layers (sequence length 128 ticks) is trained as a binary classifier. The system includes a parser, deep learning model, and intermediary utilities for server integration.
AI.result: YAACS achieves 88.6% classification accuracy with a 0.97% false positive rate using Stacked LSTM. A Decision Tree baseline achieves higher accuracy (96.2%) but with 2.68% FPR — 2.76x worse than the LSTM. Tick Delta Negative=56, Tick Delta Positive=24 for the 128-tick sequences.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating temporal context through sequence modeling (LSTM) is critical for minimizing false accusations in FPS cheat detection. The trade-off between accuracy and false positive rate favors the LSTM approach, as low false accusations are more important for fair gameplay than marginally higher accuracy.

title: Don't Blame the Large Language Model: How Scaffolding Evolution Shapes Coding Agent Quality
summary: Coding agents, autonomous systems that use large language models (LLMs) to resolve software engineering tasks, rely on agentic scaffolding: a middleware layer in between a developer and a large language model that orchestrates system prompts, tool execution, context management, and iterative reasoning loops. While these scaffoldings evolve at extreme velocities, no study has examined how this evolution affects agent quality (i.e., effectiveness and efficiency) over time. Practitioners regularly report quality regressions after scaffolding updates, yet consistently attribute them to the underlying model rather than the scaffolding itself. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting the first controlled longitudinal study that isolates the scaffolding's contribution. Unlike prior work that fixes the scaffolding and varies the model, we fix the model and vary only the scaffolding, evaluating 35 sequential releases to measure their impact on agent effectiveness and efficiency. We first empirically study the development and release evolution of five major open-source scaffoldings (i.e., Codex, Qwen Code, Gemini, OpenCode, and OpenHands), revealing extreme release velocities exceeding two releases per day and thousands of issues within months. We then perform a controlled deep dive into 35 sequential releases of the Qwen Code CLI, evaluating each against 50 stratified SWE-bench Verified tasks while holding the underlying LLM constant. We trace the resulting quality fluctuations to specific development patterns and architectural components, and illustrate our findings with concrete qualitative evidence linking individual pull requests to measured quality shifts.

AI.tldr: This first controlled longitudinal study isolates scaffolding's contribution to coding agent quality by fixing the LLM and varying only the scaffolding across 35 sequential releases, revealing extreme release velocities (>2 releases/day), quality fluctuations traceable to specific architectural changes, and a common misattribution of scaffolding-induced regressions to the underlying model.
AI.motivation: No prior study has examined how the rapid evolution of agentic scaffolding (middleware orchestrating LLMs) affects agent effectiveness and efficiency over time, and practitioners commonly misattribute scaffolding-induced quality regressions to the underlying model rather than the scaffolding itself.
AI.method: (1) Empirical study of development/release evolution of five open-source scaffoldings (Codex, Qwen Code, Gemini, OpenCode, OpenHands); (2) Controlled deep dive into 35 sequential releases of Qwen Code CLI evaluated on 50 stratified SWE-bench Verified tasks with the LLM held constant; (3) Tracing quality fluctuations to specific development patterns, architectural components, and individual pull requests.
AI.result: Extreme release velocities exceeding two releases per day and thousands of issues within months were observed. Quality fluctuations were traced to specific development patterns and architectural components, with concrete qualitative evidence linking individual pull requests to measured quality shifts.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding evolution significantly impacts agent quality independently of the underlying LLM, and regressions previously attributed to models may actually stem from scaffolding changes, highlighting the need for controlled scaffolding evaluation in coding agent development.

title: Reduced-Order Models: The Mother of World Models
summary: World models -- compressed latent representations of an environment that support action-conditioned prediction and planning -- are typically presented as a product of modern self-supervised learning. This paper argues that the functional anatomy of a world model was independently developed, deployed, and formally analyzed decades earlier in the model-order-reduction (MOR) and control literature, under different names and for a different purpose: the real-time operation of physical systems. We trace the anatomy across three communities. Low-dimensional models of turbulence built on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) supplied latent dynamics learned from data of a chaotic environment; eigenface methods in early computer vision supplied the encoder-decoder half, including a primitive runtime validity check; and measurement-based POD frameworks for facility thermal control assembled the complete loop -- POD coefficients as latent state, parametric dependence on actuator setpoints as action conditioning, modal reconstruction as decoding, and, critically, a priori analytical error bounds as a verification layer that certified when the model's predictions could be trusted in closed loop. We then examine what each tradition possesses that the other lacks: MOR contributes verification, physical grounding, and extreme data efficiency; learned world models contribute nonlinear representation, transferability, and horizon. We argue that the outstanding obstacle to deploying world models in systems that cannot fail -- power, thermal, process control -- is not predictive fidelity but verifiability, and we outline a research agenda for physics-grounded, verifiable world models that unifies the two lineages.

AI.tldr: This paper traces the origins of world models (compressed latent representations for action-conditioned prediction/planning) to decades-earlier work in model-order-reduction and control literature, showing that the complete architecture was developed across three communities (turbulence modeling, eigenface methods, thermal control). It argues the key obstacle for deploying world models in safety-critical systems is verifiability, not predictive fidelity, and proposes a research agenda unifying MOR (verification, physical grounding, data efficiency) with learned world models (nonlinear representation, transferability, horizon).
AI.motivation: To correct the historical narrative that world models originated from modern self-supervised learning, and to identify verifiability as the critical missing component preventing deployment of world models in safety-critical systems.
AI.method: Historical tracing of the functional anatomy of world models across three communities: (1) POD-based low-dimensional turbulence models (latent dynamics), (2) eigenface methods in computer vision (encoder-decoder with runtime validity checks), (3) measurement-based POD for thermal control (complete closed-loop system with analytical error bounds). Comparative analysis between MOR and learned world models.
AI.result: Identified that MOR contributes verification, physical grounding, and extreme data efficiency, while learned world models contribute nonlinear representation, transferability, and horizon. The key finding is that verifiability—not predictive fidelity—is the outstanding obstacle for deploying world models in safety-critical domains like power, thermal, and process control.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a research agenda for physics-grounded, verifiable world models that unify the MOR and learned world model lineages, emphasizing the need for verification layers that certify when model predictions can be trusted in closed-loop operation.

title: Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B: Compressing Hybrid MoE LLMs
summary: We present Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B, a compressed variant of Nemotron-3-Super optimized for interactive deployment. We designed the model to maximize server throughput under high user throughput constraints. In interactive serving workloads on a single 8xB200 node, Puzzle-75B-A9B achieves approximately 2x higher server throughput than Nemotron-3-Super at matched user throughput constraints. In ultra-long-context deployment on a single H100 GPU, the compressed model increases 1M-token concurrency from 1 request to 8 requests. Puzzle-75B-A9B is constructed using a multi-stage pipeline that combines the Iterative Puzzle compression framework with knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, quantization, and a Multi-Token Prediction head. The compression process jointly optimizes heterogeneous MoE pruning, active parameter budget, and Mamba pruning to improve inference efficiency while preserving model quality. We evaluate Puzzle-75B-A9B on a broad suite of reasoning, coding, multilingual, long-context, and agentic benchmarks. Despite substantial compression, the model retains strong downstream accuracy relative to the parent model across a wide range of tasks. These results demonstrate that large hybrid MoE models can be substantially optimized for deployment efficiency while maintaining strong downstream capability.

AI.tldr: Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B is a compressed variant of Nemotron-3-Super achieving ~2x server throughput on 8xB200 nodes and 8x concurrency improvement for 1M-token contexts on a single H100, using a multi-stage compression pipeline combining iterative puzzle compression, knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, quantization, and Multi-Token Prediction head with heterogeneous MoE pruning, active parameter budget optimization, and Mamba pruning.
AI.motivation: To optimize large hybrid MoE models for interactive deployment under high user throughput constraints, maximizing server throughput while preserving model quality.
AI.method: Multi-stage pipeline combining Iterative Puzzle compression framework with knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, quantization, and Multi-Token Prediction head; jointly optimizes heterogeneous MoE pruning, active parameter budget, and Mamba pruning.
AI.result: ~2x higher server throughput than Nemotron-3-Super on single 8xB200 node under matched user throughput; increased 1M-token concurrency from 1 to 8 requests on single H100 GPU; retains strong downstream accuracy across reasoning, coding, multilingual, long-context, and agentic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Large hybrid MoE models can be substantially optimized for deployment efficiency while maintaining strong downstream capability.

title: Fault Detection and Explainable Classification in Automotive HIL Validation via Denoising Autoencoders and In-Context Large Language Models
summary: Validating automotive software systems produces large multivariate test recordings that are still examined through effort-intensive manual review and rule-based evaluation, which detects faults beyond predefined rules poorly. Machine and deep learning have advanced fault diagnosis, yet most supervised models require large labelled datasets, generalise poorly to unseen conditions, and offer little insight into their decisions. We propose a generalisable and explainable two-phase framework for fault detection and classification during real-time validation. A denoising autoencoder trained only on healthy signals first flags abnormal behaviour through reconstruction-error analysis, removing the need for fault labels. Each abnormal window is then encoded as compact textual statistical evidence relative to a time-aligned healthy reference and classified by a frozen large language model under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, returning the predicted class, ranked alternatives, a confidence value, the fault location, and a short evidence-based explanation. Eight open-source models are evaluated across two powertrains and three driving regimes. The detector attains average F1-scores of 0.97 across powertrains and 0.98 across regimes, with average mean error below 0.03. Zero-shot prompting proves insufficient (best 0.519 F1-score), whereas few-shot prompting reaches perfect discrimination under stable regimes, showing that prompting strategy, rather than parameter count, governs classification quality: a nine-billion-parameter model surpasses every zero-shot medium and large model. Mistral Small 24B is adopted as the main pipeline model for its balance of accuracy, class-balanced reliability, calibration, and inference cost, giving engineers interpretable diagnostic reports and more efficient validation.

AI.tldr: A two-phase framework using a denoising autoencoder for anomaly detection and a frozen large language model (few-shot prompted) for explainable fault classification in automotive software validation, achieving high F1-scores (0.97–0.98) without requiring labelled fault data.
AI.motivation: Manual review and rule-based evaluation of multivariate test recordings detect faults beyond predefined rules poorly; supervised ML/DL models require large labelled datasets, generalise poorly, and lack interpretability.
AI.method: Two-phase framework: (1) A denoising autoencoder trained solely on healthy signals detects anomalies via reconstruction-error analysis. (2) Abnormal windows are encoded as compact textual statistical evidence relative to a healthy reference and classified by a frozen LLM under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, returning class, ranked alternatives, confidence, fault location, and explanation.
AI.result: Detector achieves average F1-scores of 0.97 (powertrains) and 0.98 (driving regimes). Zero-shot insufficient (best 0.519 F1), few-shot reaches perfect discrimination under stable regimes. Prompting strategy governs quality more than parameter count. Mistral Small 24B selected as main model for balance of accuracy, calibration, and inference cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables generalisable, explainable fault diagnosis without labelled fault data, with few-shot prompting being key; Mistral Small 24B provides practical deployment balance.

title: OpFlow: Learning Opportunity-Conditioned Choice Potentials for Robust OD Flow Prediction
summary: Origin-destination (OD) flow prediction is central to urban analytics, yet deep models trained on raw counts remain vulnerable to distribution shift. The core problem is that raw count supervision cannot distinguish transferable choice mechanisms from environment-specific shortcuts. Raw OD count mixes two objects: how much demand an origin produces and how that demand is allocated across destinations. We argue that the transferable object is the exposure-to-choice law that maps spatial conditions to relative destination preferences. We propose OpFlow, a mechanism-constrained framework that learns row-centered choice potentials and reconstructs flows by combining the induced allocation with a separately calibrated origin scale. Under distribution shift, spatial exposures and the induced allocations are allowed to vary; what transfers is the conditional map from exposure states to relative choice potentials. Theoretically, we characterize the identifiable row-centered potential and show that classical spatial interaction laws are restricted log-potential cases. Controlled synthetic shifts and a real-world experiment show OpFlow improves robustness under environment shifts.

AI.tldr: OpFlow is a mechanism-constrained framework that separates origin demand scale from destination choice potentials, enabling transferable OD flow prediction under distribution shift by learning exposure-to-choice laws rather than raw count patterns.
AI.motivation: Deep models trained on raw OD counts are vulnerable to distribution shift because raw count supervision conflates origin demand volume with destination choice mechanisms, making it impossible to distinguish transferable choice processes from environment-specific shortcuts.
AI.method: OpFlow learns row-centered choice potentials (exposure-to-choice mapping) and reconstructs flows by combining induced allocation with a separately calibrated origin scale. Under distribution shift, spatial exposures and allocations vary while the conditional map from exposure states to relative choice potentials transfers.
AI.result: Theoretically shows identifiable row-centered potential and classical spatial interaction laws as restricted log-potential cases. Empirically demonstrates improved robustness under controlled synthetic shifts and real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing OD flow into origin scale and choice-based allocation, where only the choice mechanism transfers, yields more robust predictions under environmental distribution shifts than raw count-based models.

title: Conversational Human Audio-visual Talking Dialogue Generation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026 as a main paper
summary: Large-scale dyadic interactive audio-visual dialogue (DIAD) datasets provide fundamental data resources for developing humanoid interactive virtual agents and digital humans. However, collecting such data is time-consuming, expensive, and ethically sensitive. To address this, we propose CHAT, a new dyadic interactive audio-visual dialogue generation (DIADG) framework that generates diverse, paired, and mutually responsive speech-face dialogue clips from a single textual prompt. CHAT unifies large language models and talking face models with interactive audio and facial behaviour refinement modules, enabling the generation of aligned dyadic dialogue clips with diverse contents and facial identities. Experiments show that CHAT outperforms existing related methods designed for similar tasks under both objective and subjective evaluations. Moreover, our synthesised CHAT-AVD-50k dataset serves as effective pre-training data for downstream interactive head generation, consistently improving PerFRDiff and ReactDiff on REACT 2024. CHAT offers a scalable alternative to the costly and ethically sensitive collection of real dyadic interaction data.

AI.tldr: CHAT is a framework that generates paired, responsive speech-face dialogue clips from text prompts, unifying LLMs and talking face models with refinement modules. It outperforms existing methods and its synthetic dataset CHAT-AVD-50k improves downstream interactive head generation models.
AI.motivation: Collecting large-scale dyadic interactive audio-visual dialogue (DIAD) datasets is time-consuming, expensive, and ethically sensitive, yet such data is essential for developing humanoid interactive virtual agents and digital humans.
AI.method: CHAT unifies large language models and talking face models with interactive audio and facial behaviour refinement modules to generate diverse, aligned dyadic dialogue clips with varied contents and facial identities from a single text prompt.
AI.result: CHAT outperforms existing related methods under both objective and subjective evaluations. The synthetic CHAT-AVD-50k dataset effectively serves as pre-training data, consistently improving PerFRDiff and ReactDiff on REACT 2024.
AI.conclusion: CHAT offers a scalable alternative to the costly and ethically sensitive collection of real dyadic interaction data for developing interactive virtual agents and digital humans.

title: Decentralized Aggregation of LLM Predictions via Wagering Mechanisms
summary: It is increasingly common to aggregate predictions from multiple LLMs, each with domain expertise or access to private tools and data, to improve collective prediction performance. In decentralized settings, aggregation weights need to be determined without access to models' private information and should remain robust to strategic reporting. We propose a family of advantage-aligned wagering mechanisms for LLM aggregation (WALLA), in which each model reports a prediction and a learned wager, and predictions are aggregated using wagers as weights. WALLA introduces a leave-one-out baseline into the net payout function, yielding three desirable properties: (1) dominant-strategy incentive compatibility of prediction under arbitrary belief structure, (2) advantage--wager alignment, where the optimal wager is proportional to the model's expected score advantage, and (3) prediction-agnostic wager optimization, enabling decentralized learning of wager policies without requiring optimal predictions. We further instantiate two mechanism variants that trade off normality and no-arbitrage while maintaining a bounded worst-case deficit for the mechanism. Experiments on question-answering and forecasting benchmarks across heterogeneous models and private-information settings show that WALLA matches centralized aggregation methods in predictive performance, while simultaneously achieving decentralized learning, advantage-aligned aggregation weights, uncertainty awareness, and incentive-compatible prediction.

AI.tldr: WALLA introduces wagering mechanisms for decentralized LLM aggregation that are incentive-compatible, advantage-aligned, and enable decentralized learning of wager policies, matching centralized performance on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To enable decentralized aggregation of LLM predictions where models have domain expertise, private tools/data, and may behave strategically, without requiring access to private information.
AI.method: Proposes advantage-aligned wagering mechanisms (WALLA) where each model reports both a prediction and a learned wager; aggregation weights are the wagers. A leave-one-out baseline in the payout function ensures dominant-strategy incentive compatibility, advantage-wager alignment (optimal wager proportional to expected score advantage), and prediction-agnostic wager optimization. Two variants trade off normality and no-arbitrage with bounded worst-case deficit.
AI.result: On QA and forecasting benchmarks with heterogeneous models and private information, WALLA matches centralized aggregation methods in predictive performance while achieving decentralized learning, advantage-aligned weights, uncertainty awareness, and incentive-compatible prediction.
AI.conclusion: WALLA effectively addresses the challenge of decentralized, incentive-compatible LLM aggregation with theoretical guarantees and empirical performance comparable to centralized approaches.

title: Graph-Aware Fuzzing for Graph Database Management Systems
summary: Graph Database Management Systems (GDBMSs) are essential infrastructure for managing interconnected data. Existing GDBMS testing methods primarily rely on differential and metamorphic testing. The result consistency oracles of these methods constrain inputs to queries that are comparable across engines or transformations, leaving single engine runtime failures, such as crashes and memory errors, insufficiently explored. Developing dedicated fuzzers for GDBMSs faces two key challenges: (1) generating valid and structurally diverse queries under complex graph constraints, and (2) guiding exploration to capture topology dependent execution behavior. To address these challenges, we propose GRAF, a black box fuzzing framework for GDBMS query engines. First, GRAF introduces graph context aware query generation based on cascading dependency resolution. It instantiates parameterized Cypher skeletons generated by a Large Language Model (LLM) by jointly resolving labels, relationship types, properties, values, and variable scopes against the active graph state. This process produces structurally diverse queries while eliminating syntactic and semantic violations. Second, GRAF applies five graph specific mutation operators guided by execution state feedback, including execution time, result size, and system status. This feedback steers exploration away from unproductive queries and expensive traversals, while prioritizing local mutations around abnormal executions. We evaluated GRAF against three existing approaches on six widely used GDBMSs. GRAF consistently improves line coverage by 31.6% to 41.1% over the strongest baseline on each target. In 12 hour fuzzing, it triggered 25 unique bugs, compared to six from all baselines combined. Overall, GRAF discovered 34 previously unknown bugs, with 32 confirmed by developers and 23 assigned CVEs.

AI.tldr: GRAF is a black-box fuzzing framework for Graph Database Management Systems that uses LLM-generated query skeletons with graph-context-aware instantiation and graph-specific mutation operators guided by execution feedback, achieving 31.6-41.1% better line coverage than baselines and discovering 34 previously unknown bugs (32 confirmed, 23 CVEs).
AI.motivation: Existing GDBMS testing methods rely on differential/metamorphic testing with result consistency oracles, which constrain inputs to comparable queries across engines/transformations. This leaves single-engine runtime failures (crashes, memory errors) underexplored. Developing dedicated fuzzers faces challenges of generating valid, structurally diverse queries under complex graph constraints and guiding exploration to capture topology-dependent execution behavior.
AI.method: GRAF is a black-box fuzzing framework with two key components: (1) Graph context-aware query generation using cascading dependency resolution, which instantiates LLM-generated parameterized Cypher skeletons by jointly resolving labels, relationship types, properties, values, and variable scopes against the active graph state; (2) Five graph-specific mutation operators guided by execution state feedback (execution time, result size, system status) to steer exploration away from unproductive/traversal-heavy queries and prioritize mutations around abnormal executions.
AI.result: Evaluated against three existing approaches on six GDBMSs. GRAF improved line coverage by 31.6%-41.1% over the strongest baseline per target. In 12-hour fuzzing, triggered 25 unique bugs (vs. 6 from all baselines combined). Overall discovered 34 previously unknown bugs, 32 confirmed by developers, 23 assigned CVEs.
AI.conclusion: GRAF effectively addresses the limitations of existing GDBMS testing by combining LLM-driven query generation with graph-aware mutation and feedback-guided exploration, significantly outperforming prior approaches in coverage and bug discovery.

title: Transition Information Density: Morphological Trajectories, Synesthetic Perception, and Structured Interpolation in Neural Training (or: The Synesthetic AI)
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Empirical results from structured interpolation training across four representational mediums. Pipeline scripts, experimental data, and the Synesthesia Grid algorithm available upon reasonable request
summary: Standard machine learning training presents data as discrete endpoint pairs, omitting the structure of the space between them. This paper introduces Transition Information Density (TID) -- the information content recoverable from structured intermediate states between categorically distinct training endpoints -- and Positional Identity, the defined location of an intermediate state on the A-to-B continuum. Both constructs are grounded in three empirical contexts: grapheme-color synesthesia, the Synesthesia Grid (a boundary-contour morphing algorithm instantiating TID in visual morphological space), and a four-condition training experiment across four representational mediums. Probes trained on structured interpolation at defined Positional Identities (C3) exhibit substantially lower intrinsic dimensionality than volume-matched controls (C2) in Phonetic/Linguistic (C3: 3.33 vs. C2: 10.81) and Semantic Description (C3: 4.59 vs. C2: 8.67) mediums. Visual and cross-modal mediums do not show this effect, establishing a modality boundary condition. A fixed-N=50 comparison confirms that Positional Identity structure, not sample count, drives the effect. Resolution N scales monotonically with representational richness. Pooled TwoNN analysis reveals globally collapsed representations in visual space (0.075) and globally consistent representations in phonetic space (0.977). The paper contributes a formal definition of TID and Positional Identity, a nine-metric shape characterization framework, and a four-condition experimental design isolating trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity as distinct factors.

AI.tldr: Introduces Transition Information Density (TID) and Positional Identity as constructs for leveraging structured intermediate states between training endpoints, showing in experiments that structured interpolation (C3) reduces intrinsic dimensionality in phonetic/linguistic and semantic domains compared to volume-matched controls (C2), with modality-specific boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: Standard ML training treats data as discrete endpoint pairs, ignoring the structure of the space between them. The paper aims to formalize and experimentally validate the value of structured intermediate states for representation learning.
AI.method: Defines TID (information recoverable from intermediate states) and Positional Identity (location on the A-to-B continuum). Conducts a four-condition training experiment across four representational mediums (Phonetic/Linguistic, Semantic Description, Visual, Cross-modal), comparing probes trained on structured interpolation (C3) against volume-matched controls (C2) using intrinsic dimensionality analysis, fixed-N=50 comparisons, resolution scaling, and pooled TwoNN analysis.
AI.result: C3 probes show substantially lower intrinsic dimensionality than C2 in Phonetic/Linguistic (3.33 vs. 10.81) and Semantic Description (4.59 vs. 8.67). Visual and cross-modal mediums show no such effect. Fixed-N comparison confirms Positional Identity structure drives the effect. Resolution N scales monotonically with representational richness. Pooled TwoNN shows globally collapsed visual representations (0.075) vs. globally consistent phonetic representations (0.977).
AI.conclusion: Formally defines TID and Positional Identity, contributes a nine-metric shape characterization framework, and a four-condition experimental design that isolates trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity as distinct factors. Establishes modality-specific boundary conditions for the utility of structured interpolation.

title: Prior Bias in Vision Language Models on UML Diagram Interpretation
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to software engineering artifacts, especially UML class diagrams whose meaning depends on visual notation. Yet, it is unclear whether VLMs actually read such diagrams or instead answer from pretrained priors about how classes typically relate. We introduce a controlled UML benchmark in which each prior-conforming diagram is paired with its prior-conflicting counterpart that (1) preserves the same class names and layout while (2) reverses only the relation arrow. We evaluate eight open-source VLMs from two model families, InternVL3.5 and Qwen3, alongside two closed-source frontier models GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 Mini. Across the eight open-source models, reversing the arrow reduces relation-direction accuracy by 33.48% on average, while GPT-5.4 Mini retains a 10% gap. In the harder three-class condition, accuracy drops sharply by 45.28% for open-source models, and even 18.62% for the GPT-5.4 family on average. Scaling provides only limited improvements and is family-dependent. Our benchmark presents a diagnostic prior-driven failure in diagram-grounded software understanding. Our artifact is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UMLKnowledgeConflict-8461.

AI.tldr: VLMs heavily rely on pretrained priors rather than actual visual understanding when reading UML class diagrams; reversing arrow direction causes a 33.48% average accuracy drop in open-source models, with limited improvement from scaling.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether VLMs truly understand UML class diagrams visually or instead exploit pretrained priors about typical class relationships, as prior work has not systematically disentangled visual grounding from prior-driven guessing in software engineering artifacts.
AI.method: A controlled UML benchmark where each prior-conforming diagram is paired with a prior-conflicting counterpart preserving class names and layout but reversing only the relation arrow. Evaluated on 8 open-source VLMs (InternVL3.5, Qwen3) and 2 closed-source models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini).
AI.result: Arrow reversal reduces relation-direction accuracy by 33.48% on average for open-source models; GPT-5.4 Mini retains a 10% gap. In three-class conditions, open-source models drop 45.28%, GPT-5.4 family drops 18.62%. Scaling yields limited, family-dependent improvements.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs exhibit prior-driven failure in diagram-grounded software understanding, with visual grounding being substantially weaker than reliance on statistical regularities from pretraining data.

title: MechMath Agent Team: LLM Driven Agents for Mathematical Research
summary: AI reasoning has become a central focus in contemporary artificial intelligence, largely driven by the success of large language models. However, mathematical research, which is characterized by non-linear derivation paths, rigorous logical requirements, and protracted exploration cycles, poses severe challenges for existing reasoning systems. To overcome these limitations, we present the MechMath Agent Team (MMAT), which is a large language model driven agent designed to serve as a co-pilot throughout the full cycle of mathematical research. We design a tripartite Harness Architecture that decouples system responsibilities into Control, Execution, and Augmentation planes, thereby reconciling rigorous logical control with the agility demanded by open-ended research. Building upon this framework, we instantiate three specialized agents: a Knowledge Base Manager, a Natural Language Prover, and a Formal Language Prover, all operating in a closed loop to produce formally certified mathematical proofs. We evaluate MMAT on open problems in Number Theory, Algebraic Complexity Theory, Differential Algebra, Operator Algebra, and Inequalities. Across a two-month deployment, 11 problems have been solved, demonstrating its capacity to act as a co-pilot throughout the entire research cycle. The contributions are threefold: a general decoupled Harness Architecture for multi-agent mathematical reasoning, its concrete instantiation in the MMAT system, and empirical validation on a diverse suite of open problems.

AI.tldr: MMAT is an LLM-driven multi-agent system with a decoupled Harness Architecture (Control, Execution, Augmentation) that solves open mathematical research problems, demonstrated by solving 11 problems across Number Theory, Algebraic Complexity Theory, Differential Algebra, Operator Algebra, and Inequalities over two months.
AI.motivation: Mathematical research poses severe challenges for existing AI reasoning systems due to non-linear derivation paths, rigorous logical requirements, and protracted exploration cycles, which current LLM-based systems cannot adequately handle.
AI.method: A tripartite Harness Architecture decoupling system responsibilities into Control, Execution, and Augmentation planes, with three specialized agents (Knowledge Base Manager, Natural Language Prover, Formal Language Prover) operating in a closed loop to produce formally certified proofs.
AI.result: Across a two-month deployment on open problems in Number Theory, Algebraic Complexity Theory, Differential Algebra, Operator Algebra, and Inequalities, 11 problems were solved, demonstrating capability as a co-pilot throughout the full research cycle.
AI.conclusion: The contributions are a general decoupled Harness Architecture for multi-agent mathematical reasoning, its concrete instantiation in MMAT, and empirical validation on diverse open problems.

title: EvoEye: Self-Evolving Runtime Monitoring for Autonomous Driving Systems
summary: Runtime monitoring is essential for detecting impending hazards in autonomous driving systems (ADSs). However, existing ADS runtime monitors have fixed detection capabilities: rule-based monitors cover only manually specified hazards, while learning-based monitors depend heavily on their initial training data and may retain substantial prediction errors. We therefore propose EvoEye, which identifies the current monitor's errors, generates informative executions accordingly, and updates the monitor through self-evolution. To enable effective self-evolution, EvoEye combines a capable runtime monitor with targeted scenario acquisition. FusionMonitor learns cross-module temporal interactions for collision prediction, while BlindSpotEvolver converts current prediction errors into search guidance and uses density-aware mutation to acquire informative executions for subsequent monitor updates. We evaluate EvoEye on Baidu Apollo with CARLA in representative highway and urban scenarios. FusionMonitor improves frame-level Recall by up to 37.8 percentage points at a false positive rate of 0.05, with 2.49 ms latency and 2.8-4.2 seconds of median warning time. Under the same budget, BlindSpotEvolver outperforms uniform and violation-oriented sampling by up to 13.2 F1 points on previously missed unsafe contexts.

AI.tldr: EvoEye is a self-evolving runtime monitoring system for autonomous driving that identifies monitor errors, generates informative executions to improve detection, and combines a cross-module temporal fusion monitor (FusionMonitor) with a blind-spot-driven scenario acquisition method (BlindSpotEvolver) to achieve significant recall and F1 improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing ADS runtime monitors have fixed detection capabilities—rule-based monitors cover only manually specified hazards, and learning-based monitors depend on initial training data and retain substantial prediction errors—necessitating a self-evolving approach.
AI.method: EvoEye combines FusionMonitor (a runtime monitor learning cross-module temporal interactions for collision prediction) with BlindSpotEvolver (which converts current prediction errors into search guidance and uses density-aware mutation to acquire informative executions for monitor updates).
AI.result: On Baidu Apollo with CARLA, FusionMonitor improves frame-level Recall by up to 37.8 pp at 0.05 FPR with 2.49 ms latency and 2.8-4.2 s median warning time; BlindSpotEvolver outperforms uniform and violation-oriented sampling by up to 13.2 F1 points under the same budget.
AI.conclusion: EvoEye demonstrates that self-evolution through targeted error-driven scenario acquisition and monitor updates effectively overcomes fixed detection limitations in ADS runtime monitoring.

title: Joint distribution of upstream runoff governs downstream river-discharge prediction uncertainty in distributed ML models
summary: Uncertainty quantification of hydrological predictions is necessary to inform operational decisions. Recent generative machine-learning methods have advanced probabilistic streamflow prediction, but have remained confined to lumped models that predict a basin outlet directly. At the same time, deterministic LSTM runoff models are increasingly applied at grid or catchment scale and routed through river networks to produce spatially continuous, physically consistent discharge fields. This technical note argues that moving probabilistic prediction from lumped to distributed models introduces a specific new requirement: the joint distribution of upstream runoff generation must be sampled jointly. In lumped inference, the model predicts the outlet distribution directly and can modulate spread from basin attributes. In distributed inference, downstream discharge is obtained by routing many upstream runoff predictions, so independent local sampling averages uncertainty away. Using Japan as a case study, we train two probabilistic basin-scale runoff LSTMs and route their runoff through a Hayami routing scheme. Randomly matching upstream ensemble members produces severely under-dispersed downstream ensembles, whereas a simple quantile matching strategy restores much of the spread of the direct basin-scale reference. The shift from lumped to distributed probabilistic hydrology therefore requires explicit attention to the spatial joint structure of runoff uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that moving probabilistic streamflow prediction from lumped to distributed models requires sampling the joint distribution of upstream runoff jointly, as independent local sampling averages uncertainty away; a quantile matching strategy restores spread in downstream ensembles.
AI.motivation: Operational decisions require uncertainty quantification of hydrological predictions, but existing generative ML methods for probabilistic prediction are limited to lumped models. There is a need to extend probabilistic prediction to distributed models that produce spatially continuous discharge fields.
AI.method: Two probabilistic basin-scale runoff LSTMs are trained for Japan, their runoff routed through a Hayami routing scheme. Randomly matching upstream ensemble members is compared to a quantile matching strategy for constructing downstream ensembles.
AI.result: Randomly matching upstream ensemble members produces severely under-dispersed downstream ensembles, while quantile matching restores much of the spread observed in the direct basin-scale reference.
AI.conclusion: Transitioning from lumped to distributed probabilistic hydrology requires explicit attention to the spatial joint structure of runoff uncertainty; independent local sampling is insufficient for maintaining ensemble spread.

title: Cancelable Biometric Template Protection Based on Multi-Instance Fusion: A Contralateral Iris Approach
summary: Biometric templates are vulnerable to theft if stored without protection. Unlike passwords, a compromised iris cannot be reissued. Although existing cancelable biometric schemes address this problem, most still require an external key or token, introducing an additional attack surface. This paper proposes a cancelable contralateral iris template protection scheme that eliminates the need for a separate token or stored secret, satisfying the three requirements of ISO/IEC 24745: irreversibility, unlinkability, and confidentiality. The method fuses three enrollment samples per eye using Majority Vote Fusion to produce a stable template, and applies a salt-based bit permutation derived from the subject's enrollment ID. Combining the left- and right-permuted templates via a bitwise XOR produces a single Protected Fused Template. Since left and right iris patterns are statistically independent, fusing contralateral irises improves the accuracy of the system. An attacker must possess both iris codes and both salts to recover any useful information, yielding a larger effective key space than single-iris schemes. Experiments on three datasets, CASIA-IrisV4-Interval, CASIA-IrisV2 (two devices), and CASIA-Iris-Thousand, yield EERs of $0.36$\%, $4.88$\%, $10.80$\%, and $3.35$\%, respectively; the highest value reflects the more challenging cross-device scenario. These results demonstrate that our contralateral approach outperforms unprotected baselines while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art cancelable methods. %In addition, an ablation study confirms the benefit on both recognition performance and security. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first scheme to combine tokenless multi-instance fusion and contralateral binding under ISO/IEC 24745.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cancelable iris template protection scheme that fuses left and right iris patterns using a salt derived from the subject's enrollment ID, eliminating the need for an external token while satisfying ISO/IEC 24745 requirements for irreversibility, unlinkability, and confidentiality.
AI.motivation: Biometric templates are vulnerable to theft; compromised irises cannot be reissued. Existing cancelable schemes require external keys/tokens, introducing additional attack surfaces. A tokenless solution is needed.
AI.method: Fuses three enrollment samples per eye via Majority Vote Fusion; applies salt-based bit permutation using the enrollment ID; combines left and right permuted templates via bitwise XOR to produce a Protected Fused Template.
AI.result: EERs of 0.36% (CASIA-IrisV4-Interval), 4.88% and 10.80% (CASIA-IrisV2 two devices), and 3.35% (CASIA-Iris-Thousand); outperforms unprotected baselines; competitive with state-of-the-art cancelable methods.
AI.conclusion: First scheme to combine tokenless multi-instance fusion and contralateral binding under ISO/IEC 24745; demonstrates improved accuracy and security through contralateral iris fusion.

title: LLM-as-a-Tutor: Policy-Aware Prompt Adaptation for Non-Verifiable RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for non-verifiable instruction following increasingly relies on LLM judges with prompt-specific rubrics as reward signals. While recent methods adapt these rubrics to the evolving policy during training, the training prompts themselves remain static, drawn from fixed corpora. This static approach often results in a critical misalignment between prompt difficulty and policy capability, leaving the judge unable to recover a discriminative reward signal when prompts fail to elicit quality variance among rollouts. To address this misalignment, we introduce LLM-as-a-Tutor, a framework that extends the LLM's role from judge to tutor: a single model serves as an examiner that pairwise-compares policy rollouts to detect non-challenging prompts, and as a generator that appends atomic constraints to them. This append-only design monotonically raises difficulty in step with the policy's capability, producing a self-calibrating training signal without external difficulty schedules.
