On three complex instruction-following benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms both policy-unaware baselines and prior policy-adaptive methods that adapt rubrics or rewrite prompts, suggesting prompt adaptation as a missing axis of policy-awareness in non-verifiable RL.

AI.tldr: LLM-as-a-Tutor extends the LLM judge role to a tutor that detects non-challenging prompts and generates atomic constraints, monotonically increasing task difficulty in sync with policy capability, outperforming prior methods on complex instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Static training prompts in RL for non-verifiable instruction following cause misalignment between prompt difficulty and policy capability, preventing the judge from recovering a discriminative reward signal when prompts fail to elicit quality variance among rollouts.
AI.method: A single LLM serves as both an examiner (pairwise-comparing policy rollouts to detect non-challenging prompts) and a generator (appending atomic constraints to those prompts), using an append-only design that monotonically raises difficulty in step with policy capability.
AI.result: Outperforms both policy-unaware baselines and prior policy-adaptive methods (that adapt rubrics or rewrite prompts) on three complex instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Prompt adaptation is a missing axis of policy-awareness in non-verifiable RL, and self-calibrating training signals can be produced without external difficulty schedules.

title: Semantic-aware and Self-improving Program Reduction via Agentic Large Language Models
summary:
Reducing bug-triggering programs to their minimal essential form is a fundamental task in debugging language processors such as compilers and interpreters. Existing reduction techniques are limited by their reliance on predefined, syntax-driven transformations that lack semantic understanding of the target program, and by their inability to learn from past reduction experiences.
  We present a new approach that recasts program reduction as an autonomous reasoning task powered by agentic Large Language Models (LLMs). Instead of applying fixed transformation rules, our method enables an LLM to analyze program semantics, formulate reduction hypotheses, and iteratively refine its approach based on execution outcomes. Successful reduction experiences are further distilled into reusable strategies, allowing the system to continuously improve over time.
  We realize this approach in PROJ, a framework built around two collaborative components: a reducer agent that performs semantic-aware, case-specific program reduction, and a reflector agent that extracts and accumulates transferable reduction knowledge. Extensive experiments on 90 benchmarks spanning three programming languages show that PROJ consistently produces smaller reduced programs than all existing state-of-the-art reducers while maintaining high efficiency.

AI.tldr: PROJ uses LLM agents for semantic-aware program reduction, outperforming existing syntax-driven reducers by producing smaller programs and learning from past experiences.
AI.motivation: Existing reduction techniques rely on predefined, syntax-driven transformations lacking semantic understanding, and cannot learn from past reduction experiences.
AI.method: A framework with two collaborative LLM agents: a reducer agent for semantic-aware, case-specific reduction, and a reflector agent that extracts and accumulates transferable reduction knowledge from successful experiences.
AI.result: On 90 benchmarks across three programming languages, PROJ consistently produces smaller reduced programs than all existing state-of-the-art reducers while maintaining high efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Recasting program reduction as an autonomous reasoning task with LLMs yields better results than fixed transformation rules, with the ability to continuously improve through distilled reusable strategies.

title: PhenoNEST: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Ontology-Aware Multimodal Plant Phenotyping and Trait Discovery
summary: High-throughput plant phenotyping generates valuable data that often remains trapped in unstructured text and isolated RGB images. To bridge this semantic gap, we propose a framework for constructing a multimodal granular Knowledge Graph (KG) to monitor genotype-phenotype interactions across time and experiments. In this work, we focus on wheat Triticum aestivum as a representative target crop to validate our methodology across complex canopy environments. Our pipeline first distills noisy field notes to extract entities and relations, dynamically constructing the KG by converting unique instances into hierarchical class entities via RDF-typing. These graph nodes are then aligned with standardized ontologies (PO, RO, WTO) using PlantDeBERTa. To visually ground the constructed graph, a Vision-Language Model paired with a wheat-segmentation ViT generates attention-based softmaps, linking specific KG entities directly to image pixels. We introduce a central observation node Plant_Obs_Id to connect these multimodal subgraphs temporally. Evaluated on 500 curated WisWheat samples using Pointing Game accuracy, Visual Word Sense Disambiguation (VWSD), and rank-based metrics, our neuro-symbolic approach successfully maps complex field observations to a structured graph. This enables automated field note auditing, temporal stress monitoring, and precise spatial trait localization for wheat breeders.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework for constructing a multimodal granular Knowledge Graph from high-throughput wheat phenotyping data, integrating unstructured field notes and RGB images via RDF-typing, ontology alignment (PO, RO, WTO) with PlantDeBERTa, and vision-language grounding with attention-based softmaps, validated on 500 WisWheat samples for automated field note auditing, temporal stress monitoring, and spatial trait localization.
AI.motivation: High-throughput plant phenotyping data (field notes and RGB images) remains unstructured and isolated, creating a semantic gap that prevents effective monitoring of genotype-phenotype interactions across time and experiments.
AI.method: 1) Distills noisy field notes to extract entities/relations; 2) Dynamically constructs KG by converting instances to hierarchical class entities via RDF-typing; 3) Aligns graph nodes with standardized ontologies (PO, RO, WTO) using PlantDeBERTa; 4) Grounds graph visually via a Vision-Language Model + wheat-segmentation ViT generating attention-based softmaps; 5) Introduces Plant_Obs_Id as central observation node to connect multimodal subgraphs temporally.
AI.result: Evaluated on 500 curated WisWheat samples using Pointing Game accuracy, Visual Word Sense Disambiguation (VWSD), and rank-based metrics, achieving successful mapping of complex field observations to a structured graph.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic framework enables automated field note auditing, temporal stress monitoring, and precise spatial trait localization for wheat breeders.

title: E-TraMamba: A New Paradigm for Efficient Long-Term 3D Feature Tracking with Event Cameras
summary: Event-based 3D tracking enables low-latency and high-speed perception, while existing CNN- and Transformer-based trackers struggle to capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies in sparse, noisy event streams, especially under real-time and efficiency constraints. To address these challenges, we present E-TraMamba, the first Mamba-based framework for 3D feature tracking on event data. This new framework adopts a linear state-space model for efficient long-range modeling and integrates a lightweight affine-transform predictor to maintain stable tracking under motion blur and occlusion. We also design an effective scheme to fuse multi-scale cues -- local spatiotemporal patches, correlation maps, and positional embeddings -- into a unified representation that enables stable and smooth 3D tracking. We construct a large-scale synthetic dataset, named EvD-PointOdyssey, which is generated with monocular rendering and provides synchronized event streams, depth maps, and accurate 3D trajectories for training and evaluating event-based 3D tracking models. Extensive experiments on event-based benchmarks demonstrate that E-TraMamba achieves state-of-the-art performance, delivering over $2\times$ longer feature lifetimes under strict accuracy thresholds (e.g., 0.1 m), with higher tracked-feature ratios and lower RMSE than all baselines. These results make E-TraMamba a strong candidate for low-latency visual odometry, real-time SLAM, and interactive robotics.

AI.tldr: E-TraMamba is the first Mamba-based framework for event-based 3D feature tracking, using a linear state-space model for efficient long-range modeling and a lightweight affine-transform predictor. It fuses multi-scale cues and achieves SOTA performance with over 2× longer feature lifetimes under strict accuracy thresholds.
AI.motivation: Existing CNN- and Transformer-based trackers struggle to capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies in sparse, noisy event streams under real-time and efficiency constraints.
AI.method: E-TraMamba adopts a linear state-space model (Mamba) for efficient long-range modeling, integrates a lightweight affine-transform predictor for stable tracking under motion blur/occlusion, and fuses multi-scale cues (local spatiotemporal patches, correlation maps, positional embeddings). Also introduces the EvD-PointOdyssey synthetic dataset with synchronized event streams, depth maps, and 3D trajectories.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance: over 2× longer feature lifetimes under strict accuracy thresholds (0.1 m), higher tracked-feature ratios, and lower RMSE than all baselines on event-based benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: E-TraMamba is a strong candidate for low-latency visual odometry, real-time SLAM, and interactive robotics.

title: Agent Step Value: State-Transition Measurement with State-Grounded LLM Evaluators
summary: Most agent evaluations collapse a multi-step trace into a final answer, a success flag, or a trajectory-level score. These aggregates obscure the diagnostic question developers need most: which action changed the state in a useful direction? We introduce Agent Step Value (ASV), a state-transition measurement framework that scores each observed action by the change it induces in a state-grounded evaluator's distribution over fixed candidate outcomes. ASV renders redacted before/after state projections, uses a stateless LLM evaluator to assign candidate log scores, and reports both gold-free belief diagnostics and offline oracle validation metrics. A label-free rationale pass separates evaluator deliberation from one-token option scoring, preserving candidate likelihoods while exposing leakage and floor-score events. On 100 reviewed open-QA evidence-seeking tasks with live PubMed retrieval, a partially live DeepSeek actor, and DeepSeek log-probability scoring, ASV evaluates 1,100 steps and 2,200 states. Under the fixed-layout rationale-conditioned protocol, mean gold-margin gain is -2.335 (trajectory-bootstrap 95\% CI [-3.395, -1.272]), entropy movement is 0.000, and mean Bayesian surprise is 2.693. ASV therefore localizes constructive and destructive belief pivots that final-answer scores and entropy-only step metrics miss. We release the standalone ASV Eval toolkit.

AI.tldr: Agent Step Value (ASV) is a framework that scores each action in a multi-step agent trace by measuring the change it induces in a state-grounded evaluator's belief distribution over outcomes, outperforming aggregate final-answer or trajectory-level scores by localizing constructive and destructive belief pivots across 1,100 steps on PubMed retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing agent evaluations collapse multi-step traces into final answers, success flags, or trajectory-level scores, obscuring the diagnostic information of which individual actions changed the state in a useful direction.
AI.method: ASV scores each observed action by the change it induces in a state-grounded evaluator's distribution over fixed candidate outcomes, using redacted before/after state projections, a stateless LLM evaluator for candidate log scores, and a label-free rationale pass that separates deliberation from one-token scoring while preserving likelihoods and exposing leakage/floor-score events.
AI.result: On 100 open-QA evidence-seeking tasks with PubMed retrieval and DeepSeek actor/scoring, ASV evaluated 1,100 steps and 2,200 states, yielding mean gold-margin gain of -2.335 (95% CI [-3.395, -1.272]), entropy movement of 0.000, and mean Bayesian surprise of 2.693 under the fixed-layout rationale-conditioned protocol.
AI.conclusion: ASV localizes constructive and destructive belief pivots that final-answer scores and entropy-only step metrics miss, providing more granular diagnostic information for agent development.

title: SkillFab: An Agent-Native Skill Production Platform
summary:
SkillFab is an agent-native platform for turning missing capabilities into reviewed, reusable Agent Skills. At runtime, agents first search for reusable skills; when no adequate skill exists, the unmet capability becomes a demand-first issue before any repository or implementation branch needs to exist. Development then proceeds through a SkillFab-managed repository, Git-ingested commit evidence, maintainer review, and registry publication. The same lifecycle is exposed through web, REST, and MCP surfaces, so humans, scripts, and external agents operate on shared state rather than separate task logs. The current system uses scoped Git push URLs, native range commit ingestion, workflow-state reads, and workflow-event histories to make long-running agent work reviewable and recoverable. We document the platform model, architecture, implemented capabilities, and three case studies: an end-to-end OS-detect skill run, a Docker research package that converts operational practice into reusable skill knowledge, and an external optimization case showing how improved skill artifacts can enter SkillFab as reviewable, versioned submissions.
  Deployment: https://skillfab.ai.

AI.tldr: SkillFab is an agent-native platform that enables agents to identify missing capabilities, create, review, and publish reusable Agent Skills through a structured lifecycle with Git-based commit tracking and multiple interface surfaces (web, REST, MCP).
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between agents encountering missing capabilities and the creation of reviewed, reusable skills, enabling demand-first development before any repository exists.
AI.method: The platform uses a lifecycle where agents search for reusable skills; unmet capabilities become demand-first issues; development proceeds through SkillFab-managed repository, Git-ingested commit evidence, maintainer review, and registry publication. Exposed via web, REST, and MCP interfaces with scoped Git push URLs, native range commit ingestion, workflow-state reads, and workflow-event histories.
AI.result: Implemented an end-to-end OS-detect skill run, a Docker research package converting operational practice into reusable skill knowledge, and an external optimization case for reviewable, versioned submissions.
AI.conclusion: SkillFab demonstrates a viable agent-native lifecycle for skill creation, review, and reuse, enabling long-running agent work to be reviewable and recoverable.

title: Unbiased Alignment for Large Language Models with Noisy Preferences
summary: The alignment of large language models with human preferences is commonly achieved through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or Direct Preference Optimization. However, these methods are vulnerable to the significant noise prevalent in real-world preference datasets. To address this critical issue, we present a theoretical framework for unbiased alignment, introducing the Unbiased Reward Model (URM) loss and the Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization (UDPO) loss. By mathematically correcting the distortion induced by preference noise, our novel objectives enable unbiased model training directly from noisy datasets, without requiring clean ground-truth supervision. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses demonstrating that our methods are noise-tolerant, parameter downward compatible, and classification-calibrated. Comprehensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/cswjl/unbiased-alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces theoretical frameworks (URM and UDPO losses) that enable unbiased alignment of LLMs with human preferences directly from noisy preference datasets, without requiring clean ground-truth supervision, by mathematically correcting preference noise.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment methods (RLHF, DPO) are vulnerable to significant noise prevalent in real-world preference datasets, which degrades model performance. The paper aims to address this critical robustness issue.
AI.method: The authors propose the Unbiased Reward Model (URM) loss and Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization (UDPO) loss, which mathematically correct the distortion induced by preference noise, enabling unbiased training directly from noisy datasets without clean supervision.
AI.result: The proposed methods outperform state-of-the-art baselines across diverse datasets, with rigorous theoretical guarantees of noise-tolerance, parameter downward compatibility, and classification calibration.
AI.conclusion: The URM and UDPO losses provide a theoretically grounded, noise-tolerant approach to unbiased alignment, eliminating the need for clean ground-truth data while achieving superior empirical performance.

title: SPLIT: Training-Free AI-Generated and Partially Edited Video Detection via Spatial Patch-Level Incoherence and Temporal Roughness
summary: Deploying AI-generated video detectors in real-world services demands an ultra-low false positive rate (FPR) on real videos to avoid falsely rejecting authentic content, a regime where standard metrics such as AUROC fail to reflect actual operating behavior. We introduce Spatial Patch-Level Incoherence and Temporal Roughness (SPLIT), a training-free detector that operates on patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder to detect both fully generated and partially edited videos. SPLIT computes two complementary signals: Two-step Temporal Roughness (TTR), capturing non-smooth patch trajectories via one-step and two-step feature variation contrast, and Local Spatial Motion Incoherence (LSMI), measuring spatially inconsistent temporal changes through gradients of a feature-space motion field. The two are fused multiplicatively with gamma correction to sharpen real-fake separation at strict thresholds. We further propose a service-aligned evaluation protocol based on Fake Recall at fixed FPR with real-only threshold calibration and cross-real threshold transfer. Across three benchmarks (FakeParts, GenVideo, and ViF-Bench), SPLIT achieves the highest Fake Recall at FPR = $0.1\%$, substantially outperforming supervised and training-free baselines while remaining robust to post-processing with negligible overhead. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mldljyh/SPLIT .

AI.tldr: SPLIT is a training-free AI-generated video detector that uses Spatial Patch-Level Incoherence and Temporal Roughness signals to detect both fully generated and partially edited videos, achieving state-of-the-art performance at ultra-low false positive rates with a service-aligned evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Real-world deployment of AI-generated video detectors demands ultra-low false positive rates on real videos to avoid falsely rejecting authentic content, but standard metrics like AUROC fail to capture operating behavior in this regime. Existing methods also struggle with both fully generated and partially edited videos.
AI.method: SPLIT operates on patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder with two complementary signals: Two-step Temporal Roughness (TTR) measuring non-smooth patch trajectories via one-step and two-step feature variation contrast, and Local Spatial Motion Incoherence (LSMI) measuring spatially inconsistent temporal changes through gradients of a feature-space motion field. These are fused multiplicatively with gamma correction. A service-aligned evaluation protocol based on Fake Recall at fixed FPR with real-only threshold calibration and cross-real threshold transfer is also proposed.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks (FakeParts, GenVideo, ViF-Bench), SPLIT achieves the highest Fake Recall at FPR=0.1%, substantially outperforming supervised and training-free baselines while remaining robust to post-processing with negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: SPLIT provides an effective, training-free solution for AI-generated video detection optimized for real-world deployment constraints, with publicly available code.

title: ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suite from ML Conference Outcomes
summary: Large language models have made research ideation increasingly accessible, yet effective idea development requires more than generating candidate directions. Researchers must ground a problem in current literature, identify meaningful bottlenecks, differentiate from existing solutions, and evaluate risks before committing to implementation. We present ResearchStudio-Idea as a reusable skill suite for this first mile of research ideation. The suite includes Paper-Search, a standalone multi-source literature search skill; Scoop-Check, a standalone prior-art collision checker for novelty claims; and IdeaSpark, the end-to-end skill that composes evidence grounding, pattern-guided generation, collision retrieval, audit, and idea-card rendering into one workflow. IdeaSpark is constructed from a corpus of 1,947 machine learning conference papers collected from ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS between 2021 and 2025, including Oral papers, a separately tracked high-citation subset, and rejected submissions. Analysis of these outcomes reveals 31 recurring ideation sub-patterns, consolidated into 15 reusable ideation patterns. Each pattern is operationalized as a structured card containing research contexts, bottleneck types, differentiation strategies, supporting precedents, and common failure modes. Given a research problem and an evidence bundle, IdeaSpark evaluates evidence readiness, reconstructs the surrounding research context, identifies unresolved bottlenecks, selects relevant patterns, instantiates one candidate direction, retrieves potentially conflicting prior work, and performs outcome-informed auditing. This workflow transforms reusable ideation patterns into traceable research proposals. Blind automated-judge evaluations show that IdeaSpark consistently produces stronger research proposals than no-skill and generic-skill baselines while maintaining competitive novelty.

AI.tldr: ResearchStudio-Idea is a reusable skill suite for the first mile of research ideation, comprising Paper-Search (multi-source literature search), Scoop-Check (prior-art collision checker), and IdeaSpark (end-to-end ideation workflow). Built from 1,947 ML conference papers (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS 2021-2025), it identifies 31 ideation sub-patterns consolidated into 15 reusable patterns, each operationalized as structured cards. Blind automated-judge evaluations show IdeaSpark produces stronger research proposals than baselines while maintaining competitive novelty.
AI.motivation: Research ideation requires more than generating candidate directions; researchers must ground problems in literature, identify bottlenecks, differentiate from solutions, and evaluate risks before implementation. The paper aims to develop a reusable skill suite to support this process.
AI.method: Constructed a corpus of 1,947 ML conference papers (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS 2021-2025) including Oral papers, high-citation subsets, and rejected submissions. Analyzed outcomes to identify 31 recurring ideation sub-patterns consolidated into 15 reusable patterns. Each pattern is operationalized as a structured card with research contexts, bottleneck types, differentiation strategies, supporting precedents, and failure modes. IdeaSpark workflow: evaluates evidence readiness, reconstructs research context, identifies bottlenecks, selects patterns, instantiates candidate directions, retrieves conflicting prior work, and performs outcome-informed auditing.
AI.result: Blind automated-judge evaluations show IdeaSpark consistently produces stronger research proposals than no-skill and generic-skill baselines while maintaining competitive novelty.
AI.conclusion: The workflow transforms reusable ideation patterns into traceable research proposals, demonstrating that structured pattern-guided ideation outperforms unguided or generic approaches in research proposal quality.

title: LogNLQ: Natural-Language Log Querying with Parser-Induced and Semantically Grounded Schemas
summary: Logs are essential for system monitoring and failure diagnoses in modern software systems, yet querying them through natural language remains an open challenge. Existing approaches either treat logs as plain text, generate queries for schema-light backends, or assume predefined relational schemas, but none addresses a fundamental obstacle: raw logs carry no executable schema over which structured queries can be defined and run. To address these limitations, we present LogNLQ, a framework that formulates natural-language log querying as executable SQL generation over parser-induced and semantically grounded schemas. LogNLQ parses raw logs into template-partitioned relational tables, then applies dual-granularity semantic grounding to annotate both templates and parameter columns with interpretable names and descriptions. At query time, relevant schema candidates are retrieved via semantic search, and a large language model (LLM) generates executable SQL constrained to the retrieved context. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce LogNLQ-Bench, an execution-verified benchmark of 8,895 queries over four real-world log datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that LogNLQ consistently outperforms all representative baselines by wide margins, with especially pronounced gains on analytically complex scenario queries.

AI.tldr: LogNLQ is a framework that converts natural language log queries into executable SQL by parsing raw logs into relational tables with semantically grounded schemas, using LLMs for SQL generation constrained by retrieved schema candidates. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LogNLQ-Bench, a new benchmark of 8,895 execution-verified queries.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches fail to support natural language querying on raw logs because logs lack executable schemas needed for structured query definition and execution.
AI.method: LogNLQ (1) parses raw logs into template-partitioned relational tables, (2) applies dual-granularity semantic grounding to annotate templates and parameter columns, (3) retrieves relevant schema candidates via semantic search at query time, and (4) uses an LLM to generate executable SQL constrained to the retrieved context.
AI.result: LogNLQ consistently and significantly outperforms all representative baselines, with especially strong gains on analytically complex scenario queries, validated on LogNLQ-Bench (8,895 execution-verified queries across four real-world datasets).
AI.conclusion: LogNLQ effectively bridges the gap between raw logs and structured querying via parser-induced schemas and semantic grounding, enabling accurate NL-to-SQL for log analysis.

title: From Global to Local: Efficient Regional Weather Downscaling with Global Weather Foundation Model
summary: Accurate regional weather prediction requires resolving fine-scale structure while remaining consistent with global dynamics. Traditional limited area models rely on computationally expensive simulations, while many learning-based approaches frame the problem as super-resolution, overlooking statistical and physical mismatches across scales. We propose a foundation-model-driven downscaling framework that learns regional refinements of global forecasts by augmenting a pretrained weather model backbone with lightweight, multi-scale prediction heads operating directly in its latent space. Despite being trained on substantially coarser inputs, the pretrained backbone supports regional adaptation at resolutions corresponding to a two-order-of-magnitude increase in grid-cell resolution, without the need for retraining. The proposed approach uses regional numerical simulations as training targets and is evaluated not only against gridded datasets but also against ground-based weather station observations, enabling analysis of systematic biases between global reanalysis, regional simulations, and in-situ weather station observations. Our experiments show improved accuracy in comparison to NWP on most of the metrics at the fraction of computational cost. Moreover, we observe that building on a latent space of globally pre-trained weather foundation model offers better downscaling capabilities than the standard image-based super-resolution approaches.

AI.tldr: A foundation-model-driven downscaling framework augments a pretrained weather model with lightweight multi-scale prediction heads to produce regional refinements from coarse global forecasts, achieving two-order-of-magnitude resolution increases without retraining, and outperforming NWP at a fraction of computational cost.
AI.motivation: Accurate regional weather prediction requires resolving fine-scale structure while maintaining consistency with global dynamics; traditional limited area models are computationally expensive, and learning-based super-resolution approaches overlook statistical and physical mismatches across scales.
AI.method: The framework augments a pretrained global weather foundation model backbone with lightweight, multi-scale prediction heads operating in its latent space, learning regional refinements from coarse global inputs. It uses regional numerical simulations as training targets and leverages the pretrained backbone to support up to two-order-of-magnitude resolution increases without retraining.
AI.result: Improved accuracy over NWP on most metrics at a fraction of computational cost; the latent-space approach of a globally pretrained foundation model outperforms standard image-based super-resolution methods.
AI.conclusion: Building on the latent space of globally pretrained weather foundation models offers superior downscaling capabilities compared to standard super-resolution, enabling efficient and accurate regional weather prediction.

title: ProLaViT: Learning Progressive Latent Visual Thoughts in Structured Latent Space
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress but still struggle with complex visual reasoning tasks requiring multi-step perception and logical deduction. While explicit visual generation incurs prohibitive computational costs, existing latent approaches often rely on external experts or lack rigorous cognitive logic. In this paper, we introduce ProLaViT (Progressive Latent Visual Thought), a framework empowering MLLMs to perform structured visual derivation in the continuous latent space. Unlike works dependent on heterogeneous external models, ProLaViT leverages an endogenous self-distillation mechanism, utilizing the model's own visual encoder to supervise latent thoughts. To facilitate this, we construct a scalable programmatic synthesis pipeline enabling the model to internalize algorithmic precision without inference time tools. We design two reasoning paradigms: (1) Coarse-to-Fine Causal Chain for spatial tasks, guiding attention from global context to local targets. (2) Dialectical Reasoning Chain for logical tasks, incorporating counter-factual thinking for verification. Furthermore, we propose a Distance-Weighted Diversity Loss to impose topology-aware constraints, preventing feature degeneration by enforcing semantic distinctiveness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProLaViT outperforms baselines on vision-centric benchmarks, achieving superior accuracy and interpretability with high efficiency.

AI.tldr: ProLaViT introduces a framework for multimodal LLMs to perform structured visual reasoning in latent space via self-distillation and programmatic synthesis, using two reasoning paradigms (coarse-to-fine and dialectical chains) and a diversity loss, achieving superior accuracy and interpretability.
AI.motivation: MLLMs struggle with complex visual reasoning requiring multi-step perception and logical deduction; explicit visual generation is computationally prohibitive, while existing latent approaches rely on external experts or lack rigorous cognitive logic.
AI.method: ProLaViT employs endogenous self-distillation using the model's own visual encoder to supervise latent thoughts, a scalable programmatic synthesis pipeline, two reasoning paradigms (Coarse-to-Fine Causal Chain for spatial tasks and Dialectical Reasoning Chain for logical tasks with counter-factual verification), and a Distance-Weighted Diversity Loss for topology-aware constraints.
AI.result: ProLaViT outperforms baselines on vision-centric benchmarks with superior accuracy, interpretability, and high efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Progressive latent visual thought is an effective and efficient approach for structured visual reasoning in MLLMs without relying on external models or explicit generation.

title: Why Pure Reasoning is Not Enough: Nature as the Source of Mathematical Innovation
summary:
We advance the hypothesis that human mathematical reasoning, constrained by both the undecidability and the computational intractability of even modest logical fragments, relies fundamentally on pattern matching from domains external to pure deduction. The most prolific reservoir of such patterns is the natural world, whose physical laws and biological systems have undergone billions of years of ``pre-computation'' and already exhibit surprisingly innovative solutions. To ground this claim, we trace the history of the Fourier transform and relevant mathematics, from the vibrating string controversy to the hear equation and subsequent formalisms prevalent in mathematics. At each critical juncture, a physics problem forced the acceptance or creation of a mathematical tool that pure formal reasoning failed to anticipate or, worse, human reasoning had resisted.
  We further survey the landscape of logical complexity, from NP-hard propositional satisfiability to the non-elementary decision-procedures for monadic second-order theories, to demonstrate that even when a logic is decidable, the resources required for worst-case deduction are astronomically prohibitive. We argue that these barriers make physics-inspired pattern matching not just a historical accident but a cognitive necessity. Finally, we draw the consequence for artificial intelligence: if pure reasoning is constitutively insufficient, then any system aiming at human-level mathematical creativity must embed a vast store of cross-domain patterns rather than rely on deduction alone. This furnishes a principled justification for the enormous scale of contemporary large language models.

AI.tldr: Human mathematical reasoning relies on physics-inspired pattern matching rather than pure deduction, due to fundamental logical complexity barriers (undecidability, intractability). This justifies the massive scale of LLMs as they embed cross-domain patterns.
AI.motivation: To argue that pure deductive reasoning is constitutively insufficient for mathematical creativity due to logical complexity barriers (undecidability, NP-hardness, non-elementary complexity), and that physics-inspired pattern matching from the natural world is a cognitive necessity.
AI.method: Historical analysis of the Fourier transform's development (vibrating string problem → heat equation → formalisms) to show physics forced mathematical innovations that pure reasoning resisted. Survey of logical complexity landscape (SAT, monadic second-order theories).
AI.result: At each critical juncture in the history of Fourier analysis, physical problems compelled mathematical breakthroughs that formal reasoning could not anticipate or actively resisted. Logical complexity barriers make worst-case deduction astronomically prohibitive even for decidable logics.
AI.conclusion: Pure reasoning is constitutively insufficient; human-level mathematical creativity requires vast cross-domain pattern stores. This provides a principled justification for the enormous scale of large language models.

title: Inferring the Shape of Data Frames in R Programs using Abstract Interpretation
summary:
Data frames are a fundamental data structure in many data analysis tasks and are widely used in programming languages like R. Due to their omnipresence in data analysis, there are many functions that operate on their shape and content, for example, to clean and transform study data. However, languages like R do not offer static guarantees on data frames making it difficult to reason about their shape at a specific point in the program.
  In this paper, we present a novel static analysis to infer the shape of data frames in R programs using abstract interpretation by tracking the ensured and potential column names, as well as the potential number of columns and rows. For this, we use a reduced product domain and define abstract semantics for the most commonly used data frame operations, such as mutating, filtering, and subsetting. We evaluate the correctness and accuracy of our analysis on a selection of 78 executable real-world R scripts achieving empirical evidence for soundness by never under-approximating the data frame shape. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability of our analysis to infer the shape of data frames on a large dataset of 33,314 real-world R scripts by inferring concrete shape constraints for 42.1 % and exact shapes for 0.9 % of the data frame operations, improving to 58.7 % and 4.2 % if all datasets read in these scripts are available to our analysis. Using the inferred data frame shapes, we identified 40 real-world R scripts containing potential invalid data frame accesses. This shows the potential of our analysis to significantly support researchers in using data frames in data analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel static analysis using abstract interpretation to infer data frame shapes (column names, column/row counts) in R programs, achieving soundness on 78 real-world scripts and identifying 40 scripts with potential invalid data frame accesses.
AI.motivation: R lacks static guarantees on data frames, making it difficult to reason about their shape at specific program points, which hinders safe data manipulation and analysis.
AI.method: The authors developed a static analysis based on abstract interpretation using a reduced product domain that tracks ensured and potential column names along with the possible number of columns and rows. They defined abstract semantics for common data frame operations (mutating, filtering, subsetting) and evaluated it on real-world R scripts.
AI.result: On 78 executable scripts, the analysis achieved soundness with no under-approximation. On 33,314 scripts, it inferred concrete shape constraints for 42.1% and exact shapes for 0.9% of data frame operations (improving to 58.7% and 4.2% when datasets were available). It identified 40 scripts with potential invalid data frame accesses.
AI.conclusion: The static analysis effectively infers data frame shapes in R programs, providing sound guarantees and demonstrating potential to support researchers by catching invalid data frame accesses in real-world code.

title: A harmonised dataset for Earth system foundation models
summary: Foundation models for Earth systems have so far been trained primarily on physical climate and weather data, with limited representation of the human systems that both drive and respond to environmental change. The lack of a unified global training resource that combines climate, land, ocean, cryosphere, infrastructure, hazards, and socioeconomic data on a common grid hinders progress toward truly multimodal Earth system foundation models. We present WorldTensor, a harmonised global dataset that aligns hundreds of environmental and socioeconomic variables to a standardised 0.25$^\circ$ spatial grid and annual temporal framework. WorldTensor integrates reanalysis products, remote sensing, emissions inventories, land use reconstructions, hydrological observations, infrastructure and hazard datasets, and socioeconomic indicators within a single representation designed for machine learning workflows. To build the dataset, we regridded inputs across heterogeneous native resolutions and projections, rasterised point and vector datasets into spatially meaningful gridded fields, and reconciled temporal coverages ranging from daily observations to sparse multiyear socioeconomic snapshots. All outputs are distributed as NetCDF files with standardised coordinates, variable metadata, and a common CF metadata convention. WorldTensor provides a reproducible resource for training and evaluating foundation models that learn coupled dynamics across environmental and human systems at planetary scale.

AI.tldr: WorldTensor is a harmonised global dataset that aligns hundreds of environmental and socioeconomic variables onto a standardised 0.25° grid for training multimodal Earth system foundation models, integrating climate, land, ocean, cryosphere, infrastructure, hazards, and socioeconomic data.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation models for Earth systems focus primarily on physical climate and weather data, lacking representation of human systems that drive and respond to environmental change. There is no unified global training resource combining climate, land, ocean, cryosphere, infrastructure, hazards, and socioeconomic data on a common grid.
AI.method: WorldTensor aligns hundreds of variables to a standardised 0.25° spatial grid and annual temporal framework by regridding heterogeneous native resolutions and projections, rasterising point and vector datasets into gridded fields, and reconciling temporal coverages from daily observations to sparse multiyear socioeconomic snapshots. Outputs are distributed as NetCDF files with standardised coordinates, variable metadata, and CF metadata convention.
AI.result: A harmonised global dataset integrating reanalysis products, remote sensing, emissions inventories, land use reconstructions, hydrological observations, infrastructure and hazard datasets, and socioeconomic indicators in a single ML-ready representation.
AI.conclusion: WorldTensor provides a reproducible resource for training and evaluating foundation models that learn coupled dynamics across environmental and human systems at planetary scale.

title: Holo-Captioning: Toward the Text Equivalent of 3D Scenes
summary: This work introduces holo-captioning, a novel task that strives to seek the text equivalent of 3D scenes. As the initial step, we formulate holo-captioning as generating a structured textual description that comprehensively depicts all entities within a 3D scene -- including their semantic tags, spatial locations, attributes, and inter-entity relations. To tackle this challenging task, we first develop an effective captioning engine to produce detailed descriptions of individual entity instances and instance pairs, and contribute a large-scale benchmark comprising over 15K scenes for training and evaluation. Building upon this foundation, we propose HoloScribe, a novel model that features an instance-aware decoupled pipeline for generating structured holo-captions, and further incorporates anchor-aware instance linking to identify relational instance pairs. Additionally, we propose a comprehensive evaluation metric named HoloScore, and provide a human-curated test set to ensure reliable model assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that HoloScribe significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 3D dense captioners and 3D LLM generalists, underscoring the effectiveness of our approach. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/holocap/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces holo-captioning, a task of generating structured textual descriptions of 3D scenes covering entity semantics, locations, attributes, and relations. The authors build a benchmark of 15K+ scenes, propose HoloScribe with an instance-aware decoupled pipeline and anchor-aware instance linking, and introduce HoloScore evaluation metric. HoloScribe outperforms existing 3D dense captioners and 3D LLMs.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between 3D scene understanding and natural language by defining a new task (holo-captioning) that produces comprehensive, structured text descriptions of 3D scenes, going beyond existing 3D dense captioning which lacks structured entity-level detail.
AI.method: (1) A captioning engine for detailed descriptions of individual entity instances and instance pairs; (2) HoloScribe model with an instance-aware decoupled pipeline for generating structured holo-captions and anchor-aware instance linking for identifying relational instance pairs; (3) A large-scale benchmark (>15K scenes); (4) HoloScore evaluation metric with a human-curated test set.
AI.result: HoloScribe significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 3D dense captioners and 3D LLM generalists on the proposed benchmark and evaluation metric.
AI.conclusion: The proposed holo-captioning task and HoloScribe model establish a new paradigm for 3D scene-to-text generation, with the benchmark, metric, and model collectively advancing structured 3D scene understanding.

title: Compressing the Validation Bottleneck: An Agentic Self-Driving Lab for Scientific Discovery
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop ; AI Scientist Competition
summary: Agentic AI-for-Science can automate ideation, planning, and analysis, but final validation still depends on real experiments. A self-driving lab (SDL) can execute those experiments, yet the loop still has bottlenecks: the agent may spend too many rounds on low-value experiments, or each round may require a high-cost experiment. We target these two physical bottlenecks with one agent. First, a prior-aware agentic DOE loop uses domain knowledge and past results to propose feasible and informative next experiments, reducing trials-to-target. Second, a cost-aware surrogate agent predicts high-cost, high-resolution measurements from low-cost, low-resolution measurements. It chooses between a high- and a low-cost measurement based on the predicted uncertainty. We examine these directions in the biology and materials domains, respectively. Together, under a single agent, these components aim to accelerate the SDL loop by reducing both the number of loops and the cost per experiment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a dual-component agentic framework for self-driving labs (SDL) that reduces both the number of experimental trials (via prior-aware DOE) and the cost per experiment (via cost-aware surrogate modeling), accelerating the overall AI-for-Science loop.
AI.motivation: Current AI-for-Science loops using self-driving labs suffer from two physical bottlenecks: agents waste rounds on low-value experiments (too many iterations) and each round may involve expensive high-resolution measurements (high cost per iteration).
AI.method: Two components under a single agent: (1) a prior-aware agentic design-of-experiments (DOE) loop that leverages domain knowledge and past results to propose feasible and informative experiments, reducing trials-to-target; (2) a cost-aware surrogate agent that predicts high-cost, high-resolution measurements from low-cost, low-resolution inputs, and dynamically selects between measurement types based on uncertainty.
AI.result: Reduces both the number of experimental loops (via informed DOE) and the per-experiment cost (via selective surrogate prediction), with validation in biology (DOE direction) and materials (cost-aware surrogate direction).
AI.conclusion: Integrating prior-aware experimental design and cost-aware surrogate modeling under a single agent can significantly accelerate the SDL loop by tackling its two primary physical bottlenecks simultaneously.

title: Balancing Microservices and Monolithic Architectures
comment: Published in Feedforward, IEEE Computer Society Santa Clara Valley Chapter, Volume 5, Issue 3, July 2026, pp. 28-33. Case Study. 6 pages, 1 table
summary: Enterprise software teams face a fundamental architectural choice: build a single unified application or decompose functionality into independently deployable services. This article examines monolithic and microservices architectures, analyzing their technical benefits, tradeoffs, and practical implications for scalability, reliability, deployment, and organizational complexity. It discusses how teams can evaluate these architectural approaches based on system size, business requirements, operational maturity, and long-term maintainability.

AI.tldr: This article compares monolithic vs. microservices architectures for enterprise software teams, analyzing tradeoffs in scalability, reliability, deployment, and organizational complexity, and provides guidance on choosing based on system size, business needs, operational maturity, and maintainability.
AI.motivation: Enterprise software teams need guidance on the fundamental architectural choice between building a single unified application (monolithic) or decomposing into independently deployable services (microservices), given the significant implications for system qualities and team productivity.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of monolithic and microservices architectures across key dimensions: scalability, reliability, deployment complexity, and organizational impact, with consideration of contextual factors like system size, business requirements, and operational maturity.
AI.result: The article identifies that neither architecture is universally superior; the optimal choice depends on contextual factors including system scale, business needs, team operational maturity, and long-term maintainability goals.
AI.conclusion: Teams should evaluate architectural decisions based on their specific context rather than following trends, balancing the tradeoffs between monolithic simplicity and microservices flexibility against their organizational capabilities and requirements.

title: Statistically Meaningful Geometry (SMG) Beyond the Euclidean Paradigm, with Application to Generative AI
summary: Conventional uniform convergence bounds and empirical risk minimization break down in massive over-parameterized models, such as large language transformers and biological sequence networks. With near-infinite unconstrained internal degrees of freedom, their optimization landscapes develop flat vertical gauge valleys, rendering classical generalization metrics vacuous and inducing severe pathologies, specifically generative hallucination and catastrophic forgetting. We introduce the Statistically Meaningful Geometry (SMG) framework, an information-geometric paradigm lifting deterministic parametric models into infinite-dimensional non-parametric Orlicz statistical manifolds. Modeling the total state space as a differential fiber bundle ($\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{B}, π, \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{H}, ω$), we establish a Two-Fold Inference Paradigm. We formalize an Ehresmann connection 1-form $ω$ as a dynamic geometric filter that strips away vertical gauge noise (Structural Internal Directions, or SID) and isolates learning trajectories along the strictly non-degenerate horizontal distribution (Statistical Variational Directions, or SVD$χ$). We prove that under connection-filtered pre-training, out-of-distribution predictive variance is strictly upper-bounded by the finite diameter of the identifiable quotient base manifold $\mathcal{B}$, establishing a hard geometric containment of generative hallucinations. By projecting downstream updates onto the orthogonal complement of the historical horizontal carriage, we formalize the SMG Sequential Adaptation Flow, proving the total non-asymptotic elimination of catastrophic forgetting. SMG replaces empirical fine-tuning heuristics with coordinate-free topological constraints, bridging advanced differential geometry with structural reliability in AI.

AI.tldr: SMG framework uses information geometry and differential fiber bundles to resolve generalization failures in over-parameterized models by filtering vertical gauge noise (hallucinations) and enforcing orthogonal projection (no forgetting).
AI.motivation: Classical uniform convergence and ERM break down in massively over-parameterized models (LLMs, biological sequence networks) due to flat vertical gauge valleys that render generalization metrics vacuous and cause hallucination and catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: Lifts parametric models into infinite-dimensional Orlicz statistical manifolds; models state space as a differential fiber bundle with Ehresmann connection 1-form ω that filters vertical gauge noise (SID) from horizontal learning directions (SVDχ); uses SMG Sequential Adaptation Flow via orthogonal projection of downstream updates.
AI.result: Out-of-distribution predictive variance strictly bounded by finite diameter of identifiable quotient base manifold (hard geometric containment of hallucinations); total non-asymptotic elimination of catastrophic forgetting via orthogonal complement projection.
AI.conclusion: SMG replaces empirical fine-tuning heuristics with coordinate-free topological constraints, bridging differential geometry with structural reliability in AI.

title: Learning Taxonomic Trees with Hierarchical Representation Regularization for Large Multimodal Models
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICML 2026
summary: Taxonomies provide key information about the semantic relationships between concepts and the inherent organization of vision and language. Despite their impressive capabilities, large multimodal models (LMMs) often lack taxonomic knowledge, leading to low hierarchical visual recognition (HVR) consistency. These models typically only rely on language modeling objectives during fine-tuning and lack explicit taxonomy-aware regularization. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Representation Regularization ($HiR^2$), a simple plug-and-play regularizer that improves hierarchical consistency in LMMs. Specifically, we introduce a semantic-aware visual tree construction framework that extracts coarse-to-fine visual features from intermediate LLM layers guided by textual cues. The regularizer combines two complementary objectives: a taxonomic entailment loss that enforces hierarchy via hyperbolic entailment cones in the Lorentz model, and a discriminative dispersive loss that promotes angular separation of semantically similar embeddings on the unit sphere without disturbing the radial hierarchical structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $HiR^2$ effectively captures taxonomic structures across diverse LMMs and fine-tuning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ICST-MIPL/HiR2_ICML2026.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HiR^2, a plug-and-play regularizer that improves hierarchical visual recognition consistency in large multimodal models by introducing taxonomic entailment and discriminative dispersive losses without sacrificing language modeling performance.
AI.motivation: Large multimodal models (LMMs) lack taxonomic knowledge and hierarchical visual recognition consistency because they rely solely on language modeling objectives during fine-tuning without explicit taxonomy-aware regularization.
AI.method: HiR^2 introduces (1) a semantic-aware visual tree construction framework that extracts coarse-to-fine visual features from intermediate LLM layers guided by text, (2) a taxonomic entailment loss using hyperbolic entailment cones in the Lorentz model, and (3) a discriminative dispersive loss that promotes angular separation on the unit sphere while preserving radial hierarchy.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show HiR^2 effectively captures taxonomic structures across diverse LMMs and fine-tuning methods.
AI.conclusion: HiR^2 is a simple, plug-and-play regularizer that improves hierarchical consistency in LMMs without disturbing their original capabilities.

title: VLA Grounder: Language-Conditioning Space Optimization for Black-Box VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are commonly treated as end-to-end action policies conditioned on natural-language task descriptions. In practice, however, their behavior often depends sharply on how the instruction is phrased, suggesting that language is not merely a task label but an optimizable conditioning input. We study whether frozen VLA policies can be improved by optimizing language space rather than updating action weights. Our method introduces a language-conditioning space policy that translates a human instruction into a short VLA-grounded command using object appearance, spatial relations, and target-grounding cues. The language-conditioning space policy is initialized with a failure-derived command-space prior and optimized with reinforcement learning from sparse task-completion rewards, while the downstream VLA remains fully frozen. This yields language-conditioning space optimization: RL discovers which VLA-grounded commands best elicit successful behavior from the frozen action policy. Experiments on RL4VLA and VL-Think show that language-conditioning space optimization improves success on instruction-sensitive, symbolic, and multi-object manipulation tasks, demonstrating that language can serve as an optimizable variable for a robot foundation models. Website: https://tttonyalpha.github.io/vla_grounder

AI.tldr: This paper proposes optimizing the language-conditioning space of frozen VLA models using reinforcement learning to generate better VLA-grounded commands, improving task success without updating action weights.
AI.motivation: VLA models are sensitive to instruction phrasing; language is not merely a task label but an optimizable conditioning input. The authors aim to improve frozen VLA policies by optimizing language space rather than updating action weights.
AI.method: A language-conditioning space policy translates human instructions into VLA-grounded commands using object appearance, spatial relations, and target-grounding cues. It is initialized with a failure-derived prior and optimized via RL from sparse task-completion rewards while the downstream VLA remains frozen.
AI.result: Experiments on RL4VLA and VL-Think show improved success on instruction-sensitive, symbolic, and multi-object manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Language can serve as an optimizable variable for robot foundation models, enabling better performance from frozen VLA policies without modifying action weights.

title: Why3-py: A Tool for Formal Verification of Hypothesis Testing and Meta-Analysis in Python
summary: The reproducibility crisis in scientific research has received widespread recognition, thereby increasing the importance of meta-analyses that integrate statistical analyses from multiple studies. However, statistical methods often have ambiguous and implicit underlying assumptions, which can lead to their erroneous applications and interpretations. To address this issue, we propose a formal verification framework for statistical programs written in Python. Specifically, we present Why3-py, a Python front-end for the Why3 verification platform that transforms Python programs into verification-oriented WhyML representations suitable for formal verification, addressing the challenges arising from Python's dynamic typing and runtime polymorphism. Furthermore, we extend the StatWhy tool to support the verification of meta-analysis methods. These tools enable users to identify overlooked assumptions and misuse of analyses, and to verify the correctness of Python programs for hypothesis testing and for meta-analyses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Why3-py, a Python front-end for the Why3 verification platform, and extends StatWhy to support formal verification of statistical programs, particularly meta-analysis methods, to address reproducibility issues caused by ambiguous statistical assumptions.
AI.motivation: The reproducibility crisis in scientific research increases the importance of meta-analyses, but statistical methods often have ambiguous implicit assumptions leading to erroneous applications. The authors aim to address this by enabling formal verification of statistical Python programs.
AI.method: The authors develop Why3-py, a Python front-end for the Why3 verification platform that transforms Python programs into verification-oriented WhyML representations, handling challenges from Python's dynamic typing and runtime polymorphism. They also extend the StatWhy tool to support verification of meta-analysis methods.
AI.result: The tools enable users to identify overlooked assumptions and misuse of analyses, and to verify the correctness of Python programs for hypothesis testing and meta-analyses.
AI.conclusion: Formal verification of statistical programs can help mitigate the reproducibility crisis by ensuring correct application of statistical methods and proper handling of underlying assumptions.

title: FedAvg for HAR: Exploring the Tradeoff Between Personalized and Generalization Accuracy
summary: The federated learning (FL) paradigm fosters distributed pervasive computing combined with artificial intelligence techniques, allowing for optimized data usage and improved mitigation of privacy concerns. Indeed, model training occurs on the client's local devices, and model parameters are subsequently shared with a centralized server. However, there is a need to find a tradeoff between models' personalization and generalization capabilities. In this paper, we design and implement several testing scenarios devoted to evaluating and comparing the centralized, local, and federated paradigm performances. We also design and implement a scenario that emulates a change in clients' data. We then present experimental results of the FedAvg algorithm applied to the Human Activity Recognition (HAR) domain to understand the trade-off between personalized and generalized accuracy. Results show that, although FedAvg confirms a higher degree of personalization capabilities while keeping a high degree of generalization with respect to the traditional centralized learning, this result is not so obvious under stressful conditions, such as when varying class distribution over clients.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the trade-off between personalization and generalization in federated learning (FL) for Human Activity Recognition (HAR). Using the FedAvg algorithm, the authors design and evaluate centralized, local, and federated paradigms, including a scenario simulating client data distribution shifts. Results show FedAvg achieves better personalization than centralized learning while maintaining high generalization, but this advantage diminishes under stressful conditions like non-IID class distribution across clients.
AI.motivation: The need to find a balance between model personalization (tailoring to individual clients) and generalization (performing well across clients) in federated learning, especially for pervasive computing and privacy-sensitive applications like HAR.
AI.method: Design and implementation of multiple testing scenarios comparing centralized, local, and federated learning paradigms. A data shift scenario emulating changes in clients' data is included. The FedAvg algorithm is applied to the HAR domain for experimental evaluation.
AI.result: FedAvg demonstrates higher personalization capabilities while maintaining strong generalization compared to centralized learning. However, under stressful conditions (e.g., varying class distribution across clients), this advantage becomes less clear.
AI.conclusion: Federated learning (FedAvg) offers a beneficial trade-off between personalization and generalization for HAR, but its robustness degrades under non-IID data distributions, highlighting the need for further improvements in handling heterogeneous client data.

title: Measuring Harness-Induced Belief Divergence in Multi-Step LLM Agents
summary: Software-agent benchmarks usually report whether an agent solves a task, but the agent reaches that outcome through a harness that controls what it sees, which actions it can take, which failures are repaired, which states are verified, and which evidence is logged. We show that this harness can change the agent's multi-step beliefs even when the task, environment, and base LLM are fixed. We introduce a belief-rollout diagnostic that elicits structured K-step trajectories over progress, risk, recoverability, constraints, failure mode, uncertainty, future success, repair cost, and next action under alternative harnesses. We define a cross-harness belief divergence and decompose it into an arrival term for immediate interface shifts and a growth term for horizon-dependent belief changes. On controlled coding tasks and public-benchmark stress tests, blocked actions, compressed repairs, selective verification, and cost-aware evidence pruning often preserve terminal success while changing the beliefs that drive later decisions. We further introduce BIWM, a no-training protocol that canonicalizes observations, logs censored branches, expands repair traces, records verification masks, executes risky branches in shadow, and aligns belief trajectories across harness views. The results suggest that harness design is an experimental variable in agent evaluation, not an implementation detail. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hik289/Harness-induce-bias.git.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the harness (interface controlling agent perception, actions, repairs, verification, and logging) changes an agent's multi-step beliefs even when task, environment, and base LLM are fixed. It introduces belief-rollout diagnostics, cross-harness belief divergence, and BIWM protocol to demonstrate that harness design is an experimental variable in agent evaluation, not an implementation detail.
AI.motivation: Software-agent benchmarks typically report whether a task is solved but overlook how the harness—controlling observation, actions, repairs, verification, and logging—shapes agent behavior and beliefs. The authors aim to demonstrate that harness design significantly impacts agent evaluation and should be treated as an experimental variable.
AI.method: The paper introduces a belief-rollout diagnostic that elicits structured K-step trajectories over aspects like progress, risk, recoverability, etc. It defines cross-harness belief divergence decomposed into an arrival term (immediate interface shifts) and a growth term (horizon-dependent belief changes). The BIWM protocol canonicalizes observations, logs censored branches, expands repair traces, records verification masks, executes risky branches in shadow, and aligns belief trajectories across harness views.
AI.result: On controlled coding tasks and public-benchmark stress tests, blocked actions, compressed repairs, selective verification, and cost-aware evidence pruning often preserve terminal success while changing the beliefs that drive later decisions.
AI.conclusion: Harness design is an experimental variable in agent evaluation, not an implementation detail.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Ask a large language model (LLM) whether a pointer dereference is safe, and it can often produce a plausible justification for ``yes''. The difficulty is that a fluent justification is not a proof. This gap is precisely where automated vulnerability detection lives: deciding, for a given operation in source code, whether a memory safety defect such as a null dereference, use-after-free, or double free can actually occur. We trace the unreliability of LLM-based vulnerability detection to a mechanism, the premature discharge of safety obligations, and argue that the remedy is not better prompting but a separation of roles: the component that interprets the code must not also be the one that decides a safety obligation is met.
  In this paper, we present LeanGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework that assigns each act to the side equipped for it. On the neural side, an LLM serves strictly as a semantic filter over candidate facts extracted from the abstract syntax tree (AST): it prunes spurious facts and keeps the real ones, but never discharges an obligation or decides the verdict on its own. On the symbolic side, the surviving facts are compiled into a verification model in Lean 4 (a formal proof assistant whose kernel accepts a conclusion only when it is formally proved), where every dangerous operation must be matched by a guard that provably covers it in scope; absent such a guard, the obligation stays open rather than being argued away. Because a function rarely arrives with full context, this symbolic model is necessarily partial: an unproved obligation is not yet a defect. An evidence-aware adjudicator therefore weighs the symbolic and neural verdicts by the quality of each. We instantiate the framework on five CWE classes to ask how far this division of labor can be pushed.

AI.tldr: LeanGuard is a neuro-symbolic framework for memory safety detection that separates the LLM's role to a semantic filter over AST-extracted facts, while using Lean 4 for formal verification of safety obligations, with an evidence-aware adjudicator combining both verdicts.
AI.motivation: LLM-based vulnerability detection is unreliable because LLMs prematurely discharge safety obligations with fluent but unproven justifications. The key insight is that the component interpreting code should not also decide whether safety obligations are met.
AI.method: LeanGuard separates neural and symbolic roles: (1) LLM acts strictly as a semantic filter pruning spurious facts from AST, never deciding verdicts; (2) surviving facts are compiled into a Lean 4 verification model where dangerous operations must be matched by provable guards; (3) an evidence-aware adjudicator weighs both symbolic (unproved obligations ≠ defects) and neural verdicts by quality.
AI.result: The framework is instantiated on five CWE classes to evaluate how far this division of labor can be pushed in memory safety detection (null dereference, use-after-free, double free).
AI.conclusion: The remedy for unreliable LLM-based vulnerability detection is not better prompting but a separation of roles: neural components filter, symbolic components verify, and an adjudicator reconciles partial evidence.

title: CSympNet-ID: conformal-symplectic map learning for linearly damped Hamiltonian systems
summary: Learning dissipative dynamics from discrete observations is essential for reliable long-horizon prediction and physically meaningful parameter identification. For linearly damped Hamiltonian systems, the exact flow is generally not symplectic but conformally symplectic, contracting the canonical symplectic form by a scalar factor that reflects the net dissipation. We propose Conformal Symplectic Networks with damping identification (CSympNet-ID), a discrete-time map-learning framework that learns the one-step flow map directly from snapshot pairs while enforcing exact discrete conformal symplecticity by construction, without penalty terms or projection. The architecture composes an exact symplectic neural core with explicit diagonal scaling layers whose factors are parameterized exponentially by a scalar damping-rate parameter, thereby guaranteeing positivity and interpretability of the learned dissipation factor. We establish a scaling-conjugacy factorization for conformal symplectic maps and derive a pointwise-in-step density result for CSympNet-ID. We evaluate an irregular-step damped oscillator, a damped spring-mass chain, a damped nonlinear cubic oscillator, and additional high-dimensional extensions. CSympNet-ID gives the most favorable overall results among the compared models in the reported experiments, particularly in data-scarce regimes, target contraction-law recovery, and high-dimensional tests where unstructured baselines degrade rapidly.

AI.tldr: CSympNet-ID is a framework that learns discrete-time damped Hamiltonian dynamics by enforcing exact conformal symplecticity and identifying the damping rate, outperforming baselines in data-scarce, contraction-recovery, and high-dimensional settings.
AI.motivation: Learning dissipative dynamics from discrete observations is essential for reliable long-horizon prediction and physically meaningful parameter identification, yet existing methods often fail to preserve the conformal symplectic structure of linearly damped Hamiltonian systems.
AI.method: The architecture composes an exact symplectic neural core with explicit diagonal scaling layers parameterized exponentially by a scalar damping-rate parameter, guaranteeing positivity and interpretability. It also establishes a scaling-conjugacy factorization and derives a pointwise-in-step density result.
AI.result: CSympNet-ID achieves the most favorable overall results among compared models, particularly in data-scarce regimes, target contraction-law recovery, and high-dimensional tests where unstructured baselines degrade rapidly.
AI.conclusion: Exact discrete conformal symplecticity can be enforced by construction without penalty terms or projection, enabling reliable long-horizon prediction and physically interpretable damping identification in dissipative Hamiltonian systems.

title: R3D: Quantitative 3D Spatial Reasoning for Egocentric Wearables
summary: Quantitative 3D spatial reasoning from egocentric RGB-D video is a critical capability for next-generation wearable assistants. Yet existing benchmarks do not reflect the challenges of handling (1) natural egocentric video, (2) posed RGB-D video inputs, and (3) challenging quantitative 3D spatial reasoning Q&A. To fill this gap, we introduce R3D-Bench (Reasoning in 3D), a benchmark of 3,033 quantitative spatial reasoning questions across 15 types -- spanning multiple-choice, distance-based, and volumetric reasoning questions -- built on top of 57 egocentric video sequences from Aria Digital Twin. To set a strong baseline on this dataset, we introduce R3D, a model-agnostic spatial tool-calling framework. In contrast to existing approaches that directly embed 3D information into the model's input representation, R3D constructs a 3D scene from video using segmentation and depth-lifted object representations. It provides this information to an LLM through eight composable spatial tools. On R3D-Bench, R3D with Qwen3-VL 235B achieves 73.5% mean relative accuracy, substantially outperforming the best depth-enabled baseline (CuTR+Tools, 61.9%) and the best RGB-only baseline (Gemini 3 Flash, 46.5%).

AI.tldr: R3D-Bench is a new benchmark of 3,033 quantitative 3D spatial reasoning questions from egocentric RGB-D video (Aria Digital Twin), and R3D is a spatial tool-calling framework that constructs 3D scenes via segmentation and depth-lifted objects, enabling an LLM to answer via eight composable tools. R3D with Qwen3-VL 235B achieves 73.5% accuracy, outperforming depth-enabled (61.9%) and RGB-only baselines (46.5%).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fail to capture the challenges of quantitative 3D spatial reasoning from natural egocentric RGB-D video, such as handling egocentric viewpoints, posed video inputs, and complex spatial Q&A. The paper aims to fill this gap by creating a benchmark and a strong baseline method.
AI.method: R3D is a model-agnostic spatial tool-calling framework that constructs a 3D scene from video using segmentation and depth-lifted object representations, then provides this information to an LLM via eight composable spatial tools for answering quantitative 3D reasoning questions.
AI.result: On R3D-Bench, R3D with Qwen3-VL 235B achieves 73.5% mean relative accuracy, significantly outperforming the best depth-enabled baseline (CuTR+Tools, 61.9%) and the best RGB-only baseline (Gemini 3 Flash, 46.5%).
AI.conclusion: The R3D framework provides a strong baseline for quantitative 3D spatial reasoning from egocentric RGB-D video, demonstrating that constructing explicit 3D scene representations and using composable spatial tools substantially improves performance over existing approaches.

title: Heaviside Continuity of Rolling Coefficients for Eliminating Epistemic Entropy in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent outputs that can be wrong. Unlike humans, who often exhibit cues when providing false information, LLMs produce errors that are difficult to detect because autoregressive decoding provides no mechanism for verifying intermediate reasoning before state progression. We introduce Heaviside Continuity of Rolling Coefficients (HCRC), a verification-first execution framework that reformulates inference as predicate-gated state transitions governed by a Heaviside Gate. HCRC combines model confidence with independent verification signals from a parallel worker architecture, allowing execution to advance only when predefined correctness predicates are satisfied. This prevents invalid intermediate states from propagating, reducing epistemic entropy without modifying the underlying model. We evaluate HCRC on software-engineering and reasoning tasks across thirteen proposers from four providers. On capable proposers, the gate reduces the false-completion rate (FCR) from 4--7% to 0% while remaining latency-competitive and, in some settings, faster than the unwrapped model. On weaker proposers, it converts false completions into honest halts instead of corrupting downstream state. Beyond benchmarking, HCRC has operated for months as the production control plane of an agentic coding environment, authorizing file mutations, verification-driven progress reporting, and memory compaction. These results establish HCRC as a general framework for verification-driven LLM execution, showing that reliable reasoning can be achieved through principled execution control rather than model scale alone.

AI.tldr: HCRC is a verification-first execution framework that uses a Heaviside Gate to condition LLM state transitions on predicate satisfaction, reducing false completions to 0% on capable models and converting errors to honest halts on weaker ones, validated across software-engineering and reasoning tasks and deployed in production.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate fluent but potentially incorrect outputs with no verification mechanism during autoregressive decoding, unlike humans who exhibit cues when providing false information.
AI.method: HCRC reformulates inference as predicate-gated state transitions using a Heaviside Gate, combining model confidence with independent verification signals from a parallel worker architecture to allow execution only when predefined correctness predicates are satisfied.
AI.result: On capable proposers, false-completion rate reduced from 4-7% to 0% with competitive latency; on weaker proposers, false completions converted to honest halts. Framework deployed for months as production control plane in an agentic coding environment.
AI.conclusion: Reliable reasoning can be achieved through principled execution control (verification-driven execution) rather than model scale alone, establishing HCRC as a general framework for verification-driven LLM execution.

title: Refused in Chat, Written in Code: Workflow-Level Jailbreak Construction in IDE Coding Agents
