Experimental results demonstrate a 91.8% task completion rate with a median per-request latency of 2.2 seconds, 96.0% safety compliance on the dedicated safety-critical evaluation subset, and an average operational cost of $0.0324 per appointment, yielding a significant cost reduction compared to manual human scheduling. These findings show that carefully scoped and rigorously safeguarded LLM-based agents can reliably automate complex healthcare operational workflows while maintaining safety guarantees and achieving substantial cost efficiency. The source code and system implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/Hadi-Hsn/CareConnect.

AI.tldr: CareConnect is a safety-first conversational agent that uses LLM function calling, RAG, and deterministic safety guardrails to automate healthcare appointment scheduling. It achieves 91.8% task completion, 96.0% safety compliance, $0.0324 cost per appointment, and 2.2s median latency on a 680-scenario benchmark.
AI.motivation: Healthcare appointment scheduling suffers from manual coordination, legacy system fragmentation, and high administrative overhead, limiting provider availability and patient access to care.
AI.method: CareConnect combines LLM function calling, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and layered deterministic safety guardrails, orchestrating eight domain-specific tools for appointment management and facility information retrieval, with emergency detection and medical intent refusal mechanisms.
AI.result: 91.8% task completion, 96.0% safety compliance on safety-critical subset, 2.2s median latency, $0.0324 average cost per appointment — significant cost reduction vs. manual human scheduling.
AI.conclusion: Carefully scoped and rigorously safeguarded LLM-based agents can reliably automate complex healthcare operational workflows while maintaining safety guarantees and achieving substantial cost efficiency.

title: Correct but Slow: An Empirical Study of the GPU Kernel Evaluation Gap in Modern Domain-Specific Languages
summary:
Modern GPU domain-specific languages (DSLs), such as Triton and TileLang, are increasingly used to implement specialized deep-learning kernels and as target languages for automated kernel-generation systems. Existing DSL-kernel evaluations establish correctness through reference-based numerical validation -- necessary, but silent on replacement quality: a functionally valid kernel may still fall far below the throughput of the optimized library operator it is intended to replace.
  We study this correctness-performance gap using 22 Triton and TileLang kernels from five operator categories on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 GPUs, asking whether correctness-based evaluation identifies kernels unsuitable as library replacements, why such failures occur, and how they can be detected without exhaustive benchmark coverage. The study yields three results. \emph{First}, correctness-based evaluation can admit severe slowdowns: an idiomatic TileLang LayerNorm kernel passes KernelBench's correctness check while running more than 300$\times$ slower than the PyTorch baseline. \emph{Second}, the causes differ by kernel family. TileLang normalization and reduction slowdowns are mainly repairable authoring defects, such as sequential reductions and unnecessary dtype conversions, whereas convolution and large general matrix multiplication (GEMM) retain residual gaps after optimization due to code-generation and autotuning-coverage limits; vendor-library algorithm selection contributes only marginally. \emph{Third}, two lightweight checks -- library-relative efficiency and roofline utilization -- are complementary screening criteria: together they flag every functionally valid but inefficient kernel in our suite and separate repairable authoring defects from structural residuals.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the gap between correctness and performance in GPU DSL kernels (Triton, TileLang), finding that functionally valid kernels can be 300×+ slower than library baselines, and proposes two lightweight screening checks (library-relative efficiency and roofline utilization) to detect such inefficiencies without exhaustive benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Existing DSL-kernel evaluations rely on reference-based numerical validation to establish correctness, but this approach is silent on replacement quality—a functionally valid kernel may still underperform the optimized library operator it is meant to replace, creating a correctness-performance gap that current evaluation practices overlook.
AI.method: The study analyzes 22 Triton and TileLang kernels across five operator categories on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 GPUs, investigating whether correctness-based evaluation identifies unsuitable library replacements, why performance failures occur, and how to detect them without exhaustive benchmark coverage.
AI.result: (1) Correctness-based evaluation can admit severe slowdowns (e.g., a TileLang LayerNorm kernel passes correctness checks but runs 300× slower than PyTorch). (2) Causes differ: TileLang normalization/reduction slowdowns are repairable authoring defects (sequential reductions, unnecessary dtype conversions), while convolution/GEMM have residual gaps from code-generation and autotuning-coverage limits. (3) Two lightweight checks—library-relative efficiency and roofline utilization—together flag every functionally valid but inefficient kernel and separate repairable defects from structural residuals.
AI.conclusion: Correctness-based evaluation alone is insufficient for assessing kernel replacement quality. Library-relative efficiency and roofline utilization are complementary, lightweight screening criteria that can detect performance-deficient kernels and distinguish authoring defects from fundamental code-generation limitations.

title: Differentiate the Evaluator, Not the Program: An Efficient Runtime Representation for Neuro-Symbolic Learning
summary:
AI systems increasingly propose executable scientific models whose value depends on both their symbolic structure and their fitted continuous parameters. This makes parameter calibration the bottleneck of program-and-parameter co-search: an outer loop can generate thousands of candidate programs, but each needs an inner gradient-based optimization before it can be assessed. Staging each candidate into its own differentiable graph makes individual models fast but sacrifices the program-as-data property that keeps search fluid; interpreter-based approaches preserve programs as runtime data but pay interpreter overhead that dominates the numerical work.
  We present the Native Differentiable Virtual Machine (NDVM), a runtime representation that differentiates executable programs without compiling each candidate into a separate graph. NDVM separates symbolic structure from differentiable numeric state: tags, symbols, environments, and control remain native runtime data, while numeric payloads live in dense batched buffers with exact reverse-mode gradients recorded along the realized execution trace, so one evaluator walk is amortized across large populations of parameter vectors. A locked cost model of a real differentiable self-hosted Scheme interpreter motivates the design. We realize NDVM as a native runtime with forward and gradient equivalence to the reference backend, about 60x per-lane batch amortization, near-linear multicore scaling, and two independent front ends. In fixed-budget co-search over LLM-proposed programs, NDVM reaches high-quality solutions about 24x sooner in wall-clock time, suggesting runtime differentiation as a practical systems foundation for scientific discovery workflows.

AI.tldr: NDVM is a runtime representation that differentiates executable programs without compiling each candidate into a separate graph, achieving ~60x per-lane batch amortization and ~24x faster wall-clock time in program-and-parameter co-search for scientific discovery.
AI.motivation: Parameter calibration is the bottleneck in program-and-parameter co-search because each candidate program requires inner gradient-based optimization. Existing approaches either sacrifice the program-as-data property (differentiable graphs) or pay interpreter overhead that dominates numerical work.
AI.method: NDVM separates symbolic structure (tags, symbols, environments, control) as native runtime data from differentiable numeric state in dense batched buffers with exact reverse-mode gradients recorded along the realized execution trace, amortizing one evaluator walk across large populations of parameter vectors.
AI.result: ~60x per-lane batch amortization, near-linear multicore scaling, two independent front ends, and gradient equivalence to the reference backend. In fixed-budget co-search, NDVM reaches high-quality solutions ~24x sooner in wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: Runtime differentiation is a practical systems foundation for scientific discovery workflows, significantly accelerating the bottleneck of parameter calibration in program-and-parameter co-search.

title: VISTA: Auditing Semantic Divergence in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models can exhibit visual concept-conditioned divergence: given images containing demographic features, corporate logos, or ideological symbols, some models produce unusually uniform responses that differ from what peer models say about the same input. These behaviors evade text-only audits because visual concepts cannot be isolated or substituted the way text tokens can. We present VISTA (Visual Inconsistency Screening Through Analysis), a black-box cross-model audit that couples semantic entropy with distribution-based divergence to flag model-specific anomalies. In a controlled study, we implant concept-conditioned stances in three VLMs via fine-tuning on small biased datasets and confirm that VISTA detects them. Auditing six VLMs across 19 topics, VISTA surfaces 142 high-suspicion cases (1.2%) and identifies selective refusal as a previously unreported divergence pattern, where models refuse demographic queries at rates varying from 0 to 65% across groups.

AI.tldr: VISTA is a black-box cross-model audit that detects visual concept-conditioned divergence in vision-language models by coupling semantic entropy with distribution-based analysis, successfully identifying implanted biases and discovering selective refusal patterns.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can exhibit visual concept-conditioned divergence (e.g., biased responses to demographic features, logos, or symbols) that evades text-only audits because visual concepts cannot be isolated or substituted like text tokens.
AI.method: VISTA (Visual Inconsistency Screening Through Analysis) is a black-box cross-model audit that combines semantic entropy with distribution-based divergence to flag model-specific anomalies without requiring access to model internals.
AI.result: In controlled studies, VISTA detected implanted concept-conditioned stances in three VLMs fine-tuned on biased datasets. Auditing six VLMs across 19 topics revealed 142 high-suspicion cases (1.2%) and identified selective refusal as a previously unreported divergence pattern.
AI.conclusion: VISTA effectively detects visual concept-conditioned biases in VLMs that text-only audits miss, revealing selective refusal as a new form of bias where models refuse demographic queries at rates varying from 0 to 65% across groups.

title: Diffusion-Guided Uncertainty-Aware Delayed Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning in real world environments often suffers from severe performance degradation due to delayed feedback. Existing approaches typically mitigate performance degradation caused by observation delays by constructing augmented states or predicting the true states. However, these methods often overlook the inherent discrepancy between delayed state and true states induced by stochastic MDP. We theoretically prove the existence of such a discrepancy and show that it leads to the degradation of the optimal policy. To address this challenge, we propose Diffusion Guided Uncertainty Aware Delayed Policy Optimization (DUPO). Our method explicitly models the relationship between delayed state message and the current state using a diffusion model, and leverages the resulting discrepancy estimates to weight delayed policies. Extensive experiments on continuous robotic control tasks with multiple stochastic delays demonstrate that DUPO consistently outperforms existing methods and remains effective even under long and random delay scenarios.

AI.tldr: DUPO uses diffusion models to explicitly model state discrepancies caused by delayed feedback in reinforcement learning, achieving superior performance on continuous robotic control tasks with stochastic delays.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning suffers from performance degradation due to delayed feedback in real-world environments. Existing methods that construct augmented states or predict true states overlook the inherent discrepancy between delayed and true states induced by stochastic MDP, which theoretically degrades optimal policy.
AI.method: DUPO (Diffusion Guided Uncertainty Aware Delayed Policy Optimization) explicitly models the relationship between delayed state messages and current states using a diffusion model, then leverages the resulting discrepancy estimates to weight delayed policies.
AI.result: DUPO consistently outperforms existing methods on continuous robotic control tasks with multiple stochastic delays, remaining effective even under long and random delay scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the discrepancy between delayed and true states via diffusion models is an effective approach for addressing delayed feedback in RL, particularly under challenging stochastic delay conditions.

title: Obey, Diverge, Collapse: Blind Obedience to Incorrect Instructions Drives Code LLMs to Irrecoverable Code Semantic Collapse
summary: Code language models are now trusted collaborators in production workflows for debugging, refactoring, and iterative repair, and every benchmark that evaluates them assumes the instructions they act on are correct. We study what happens when that assumption breaks. We evaluate code language models across four experiments designed to assess whether models resist or obey incorrect instructions in single-pass and iterative repair settings, using the RunBugRun dataset of algorithmic Python problems with deterministic test cases. Our findings reveal a striking behavioral pattern: models correctly identify an incorrect instruction as wrong, then follow it anyway. This compliance unknowingly introduces errors beyond the original bug, and the corrupted code state cannot be recovered through subsequent self-guided iterative repair, which fails to converge across passes. We term this Blind Obedience, characterize the Ghost (Unknown) Errors it introduces, quantify the proportion of cases where semantic corruption proves irrecoverable, and show that extended reasoning cannot reverse it. These findings surface behavioral properties invisible to pass-rate evaluation, with direct consequences for code language models deployed in production settings.

AI.tldr: Code language models exhibit "Blind Obedience": they correctly identify incorrect instructions as wrong but follow them anyway, introducing irrecoverable errors that self-guided repair cannot fix.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume instructions given to code language models are always correct. This paper investigates what happens when that assumption fails—a realistic scenario in production debugging and refactoring workflows.
AI.method: Four experiments evaluating code language models in single-pass and iterative repair settings using the RunBugRun dataset (algorithmic Python problems with deterministic test cases), comparing model behavior on correct vs. incorrect instructions.
AI.result: Models can detect incorrect instructions but comply with them anyway, introducing additional errors beyond the original bug ("Ghost Errors"). Self-guided iterative repair fails to recover from this corrupted state and does not converge across passes. Extended reasoning does not reverse the phenomenon.
AI.conclusion: Blind Obedience introduces semantic corruption that is often irrecoverable, revealing behavioral properties invisible to pass-rate evaluation with direct implications for production deployment of code language models.

title: When Geometry Aligns: Dihedral Hidden-State Transformations in UNet, ViT, and DiT Architectures
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs), 2026
summary: Diffusion architectures now encompass convolutional UNets as well as transformer-based designs such as Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), inspired by Vision Transformers (ViTs), yet the effects of structured geometric perturbations within these architectures remain poorly understood. We study this question through a unified framework that applies reflection-based elements of the dihedral group to intermediate hidden states as controlled internal interventions, contrasting geometrically consistent and inconsistent variants. Using activation-level diagnostics, including Self-Consistency Shift (SCS), Activation Mass Scatter (AMS), and Drift, we analyze feature stability and geometric drift. We find that consistent transformations improve stability, while inconsistent ones induce predictable, architecture-specific failures. In the main Stable Diffusion 2.1 U-Net study, we evaluate seven intervention modes over three seeds and complement the internal diagnostics with image-level FID, KID, CLIP score, and LPIPS diversity. Taken together with supporting ViT and controlled DiT analyses, these results establish geometric consistency as a key principle for stable hidden-state interventions in spatially structured vision and diffusion models.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how structured geometric perturbations affect diffusion architectures (UNets, DiTs, ViTs) using a unified framework of dihedral group reflection-based interventions. Using activation-level diagnostics (SCS, AMS, Drift) and image-level metrics (FID, KID, CLIP, LPIPS), it finds that geometrically consistent transformations improve feature stability while inconsistent ones cause predictable, architecture-specific failures, establishing geometric consistency as a key principle for stable hidden-state interventions.
AI.motivation: The effects of structured geometric perturbations within diffusion architectures (convolutional UNets, transformer-based DiTs/ViTs) remain poorly understood, motivating a systematic study of geometric consistency in hidden-state interventions.
AI.method: A unified framework applies reflection-based elements of the dihedral group to intermediate hidden states as controlled internal interventions. Activation-level diagnostics (Self-Consistency Shift, Activation Mass Scatter, Drift) and image-level metrics (FID, KID, CLIP score, LPIPS diversity) are used across UNet (Stable Diffusion 2.1), ViT, and DiT architectures.
AI.result: Consistent geometric transformations improve feature stability, while inconsistent ones induce predictable, architecture-specific failures. In Stable Diffusion 2.1 U-Net, seven intervention modes were evaluated over three seeds.
AI.conclusion: Geometric consistency is established as a key principle for stable hidden-state interventions in spatially structured vision and diffusion models.

title: CONFLUX: A Latent Diusion Model for 3D Chest-CT Synthesis with RL Post-Training
summary: Controllable generative models of 3D medical images can synthesize volumes with specified clinical attributes, but this demands samples that are simultaneously high-fidelity, natively 3D, and faithful to the requested conditioning. We present CONFLUX, a latent diffusion model for chest computed tomography (CT): a 3D variational autoencoder compresses each volume, and a rectified-flow transformer generates in the latent space. Generation is conditioned on structured radiological metadata (18 abnormality findings, sex, age, and reconstruction kernel) through adaptive layer normalization. The model leads strong volumetric baselines on tri-planar Frechet distance (FID 32.3 vs. 74.6 for MAISI) while exposing direct control over clinical attributes. To strengthen that control we add an online reinforcement-learning post-training stage (group-relative policy optimization) that rewards how reliably a classifier recovers the requested findings from each generated volume. Judged by a separate, independent classifier, post-training removes 47% of the shortfall relative to real-scan reliability. We release the model and a ~200k synthetic chest-CT dataset with conditioning metadata spanning a wide variety of clinical findings.

AI.tldr: CONFLUX is a latent diffusion model for 3D chest CT synthesis conditioned on clinical metadata, using a 3D VAE + rectified-flow transformer with RL-based post-training (GRPO) to improve attribute fidelity, achieving 32.3 FID and reducing conditioning shortfall by 47%.
AI.motivation: Existing controllable generative models for 3D medical images struggle to simultaneously achieve high fidelity, native 3D generation, and faithful adherence to specified clinical attributes (e.g., radiological findings).
AI.method: A latent diffusion model combining a 3D variational autoencoder (VAE) for compression with a rectified-flow transformer in latent space, conditioned on structured radiological metadata via adaptive layer normalization. An online RL post-training stage (group-relative policy optimization, GRPO) rewards classifier-based recovery of requested clinical findings.
AI.result: CONFLUX achieves FID 32.3 vs. 74.6 for MAISI on tri-planar Frechet distance. Post-training with GRPO removes 47% of the shortfall relative to real-scan reliability, as judged by an independent classifier.
AI.conclusion: CONFLUX demonstrates that latent diffusion with rectified flow and RL-based post-training can produce high-fidelity, controllable 3D medical image synthesis that faithfully respects clinical conditioning, with the model and a ~200k synthetic dataset released publicly.

title: ASSEMCAD: Production-Ready CAD Assembly Generation from Natural Language
summary: Recent advances in large language models and programmatic CAD have significantly improved Text-to-CAD generation for individual parts. However, production-ready mechanical assembly generation remains largely unsolved. Unlike single-part modeling, assemblies require coordinated reasoning over multiple components, functional interfaces, assembly relations, engineering principles, and physical consistency. Consequently, directly generating executable CAD code is insufficient for constructing mechanically valid and reusable assemblies. We present AssemCAD, an axiom-grounded framework for production-ready CAD assembly generation from natural language. Instead of representing an assembly as monolithic CAD code, AssemCAD first constructs an axiomatic Assembly Specification consisting of typed parts, geometry-backed ports, executable mates, and engineering axioms. Each assembly relation is explicitly grounded in one or more engineering principles, making the resulting specification interpretable, reusable, and verifiable. To realize this specification, AssemCAD introduces a port- and mate-based CAD assembly library that executes symbolic assembly relations through deterministic mate transformations and validates declared interfaces using concrete B-Rep geometric evidence. Built on this representation and library, AssemCAD further supports on-demand synthesis of reusable parametric component factories for both standard and open-world geometries. Experiments on AssemBench show that AssemCAD substantially improves assembly preservation and physical validity over code-centric CAD generation baselines, while generalizing across different foundation-model backbones. By combining axiom-grounded assembly reasoning with deterministic geometric execution, AssemCAD extends Text-to-CAD from isolated part generation toward production-ready mechanical assembly design.

AI.tldr: AssemCAD is an axiom-grounded framework that generates production-ready mechanical assemblies from natural language, using typed parts, geometry-backed ports, executable mates, and engineering axioms to ensure physical validity and reusability, outperforming code-centric CAD generation baselines on AssemBench.
AI.motivation: Production-ready mechanical assembly generation from text remains unsolved because it requires coordinated reasoning over multiple components, functional interfaces, assembly relations, engineering principles, and physical consistency, which direct CAD code generation cannot adequately handle.
AI.method: AssemCAD first constructs an axiomatic Assembly Specification with typed parts, geometry-backed ports, executable mates, and engineering axioms. It then uses a port- and mate-based CAD assembly library to execute symbolic assembly relations via deterministic mate transformations and validates interfaces using B-Rep geometric evidence. It also supports on-demand synthesis of reusable parametric component factories.
AI.result: Experiments on AssemBench show that AssemCAD substantially improves assembly preservation and physical validity over code-centric CAD generation baselines, and generalizes across different foundation-model backbones.
AI.conclusion: By combining axiom-grounded assembly reasoning with deterministic geometric execution, AssemCAD extends Text-to-CAD from isolated part generation toward production-ready mechanical assembly design.

title: LLM-Driven CI-CD Workflow Intelligence for Cyber Systems Engineering
summary: CI/CD workflows have become executable operational policy: they decide what gets built, tested, released, and deployed, and they mediate how maintainers interact with delivery infrastructure. That makes them an important measurement point for cyber-systems engineering. Recent large language model (LLM) work shows that workflow stages can be recognized directly from configuration files, but stage labels alone do not tell us whether a workflow is brittle, unusual for its ecosystem, or worth revising first. We present an LLM-based CI/CD analysis pipeline that combines repository enrichment, anti-pattern detection, stage mining, and recommendation generation over a large GitHub corpus. Starting from 59,550 repositories with at least 1,000 stars, we identify 34,225 projects with CI/CD and collect 127,559 configuration files. Across 75,201 analyzed workflows, the anti-pattern detector reports 434,769 findings, dominated by reliability and maintainability issues. Across 59,906 configurations, stage usage differs significantly by language ($χ^2 = 4168.88$, $p < 0.001$, Cramer's $V = 0.063$), and domain analysis shows distinct operational profiles, including higher release and cache usage in mobile projects. For repository-level recommendation generation, few-shot prompting performs best overall, averaging 8.25 recommendations per repository with 96.1% YAML-valid snippets. Taken together, the results argue for CI/CD observability that combines diagnosis, context, and human review rather than treating workflow mining as a stage-classification problem alone.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-based CI/CD analysis pipeline that analyzes 75,201 workflows from 34,225 GitHub repositories, detecting 434,769 anti-patterns (dominated by reliability/maintainability issues), finding significant language-specific stage usage differences, and generating 8.25 recommendations per repo with 96.1% YAML-valid snippets, arguing for CI/CD observability that combines diagnosis, context, and human review.
AI.motivation: CI/CD workflows serve as executable operational policy governing build, test, release, and deployment processes, making them critical measurement points for cyber-systems engineering. Existing LLM work can recognize workflow stages from config files, but stage labels alone fail to indicate whether a workflow is brittle, unusual, or worth revising.
AI.method: An LLM-based CI/CD analysis pipeline combining repository enrichment, anti-pattern detection, stage mining, and recommendation generation over a large GitHub corpus of 59,550 repositories (≥1,000 stars), yielding 34,225 projects with CI/CD and 127,559 configuration files.
AI.result: Across 75,201 workflows: 434,769 anti-pattern findings (dominated by reliability/maintainability issues); significant language-specific stage usage differences (χ²=4168.88, p<0.001, Cramer's V=0.063); distinct operational profiles in mobile projects (higher release and cache usage); few-shot prompting achieved 8.25 recommendations/repo with 96.1% YAML-valid snippets.
AI.conclusion: The results argue for CI/CD observability that combines diagnosis, context, and human review rather than treating workflow mining as a stage-classification problem alone.

title: Modular Foundation Models for Time-Series Perception in Digital Twins
summary: Engineering Digital Twins and Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) systems rely on robust perception modules to extract actionable information from heterogeneous and non-stationary time-series data. However, most existing approaches remain task-specific, data-hungry, and difficult to integrate into scalable monitoring and decision-making pipelines. Moreover, purely data-driven models often lack robustness and transferability across varying operating conditions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a modular foundation model for time-series perception based on a collection of pretrained representation encoders. The framework leverages self-supervised learning on heterogeneous datasets to learn transferable and task-agnostic representations, which can be reused across multiple PHM tasks. A gating mechanism is introduced to dynamically select relevant encoders for a given target dataset, enabling conditional computation and adaptive model composition. The selected representations are projected into a shared latent space and aggregated using a Transformer-based self-attention module that explicitly models cross-encoder interactions. The resulting architecture supports multiple downstream tasks, including imputation, long-term forecasting, and few-shot learning, through lightweight task-specific heads, while keeping pretrained encoders frozen during adaptation. Extensive ablation studies demonstrate the complementary roles of self-supervised pretraining, encoder selection, representation alignment, and adaptive aggregation. Experimental results on the ETT benchmark show competitive performance across tasks, while a real-world industrial case study on virtual sensing for hydro-generator rotor temperature highlights the practical relevance of the approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a modular foundation model for time-series perception that uses pretrained representation encoders with self-supervised learning, a gating mechanism for dynamic encoder selection, and Transformer-based self-attention aggregation to handle multiple PHM tasks (imputation, forecasting, few-shot learning) with competitive performance on ETT benchmarks and a real-world hydro-generator virtual sensing case study.
AI.motivation: Existing PHM and digital twin perception modules are task-specific, data-hungry, and difficult to scale; purely data-driven models lack robustness and transferability across varying operating conditions.
AI.method: A modular foundation model with: (1) a collection of pretrained representation encoders via self-supervised learning on heterogeneous datasets; (2) a gating mechanism for dynamic encoder selection and conditional computation; (3) projection to a shared latent space; (4) Transformer-based self-attention for cross-encoder interaction modeling; (5) lightweight task-specific heads for downstream tasks while keeping encoders frozen.
AI.result: Competitive performance across imputation, long-term forecasting, and few-shot learning on ETT benchmark; successful real-world application to hydro-generator rotor temperature virtual sensing; ablation studies confirm the importance of self-supervised pretraining, encoder selection, representation alignment, and adaptive aggregation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modular foundation model achieves transferable, task-agnostic time-series perception that can be efficiently adapted to multiple PHM tasks, demonstrating both benchmark competitiveness and practical industrial relevance.

title: REAL-OW: Rehearsal-free Open World Object Detection with Low-Rank Adaptation and Dual-Stage Objectness Modeling
summary: Open-World Object Detection (OWOD) requires detectors to identify previously unseen objects as unknown and incrementally incorporate them into the set of known categories, while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Existing frameworks rely heavily on exemplar replay to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but in some real applications, storing raw data conflicts with data access restrictions and leads to data exposure risks, while incurring significant memory overhead. In this paper, we propose REAL-OW, a novel rehearsal-free framework that decouples incremental knowledge through a collaborative adapter architecture based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Specifically, we deploy General Adapters (GAs) in the backbone to enable the significance-aware refinement of cross-task universal representations, while Specific Adapters (SAs) in the decoder provide orthogonal storage for task-specific expertise. To resolve representation drift in objectness modeling under rehearsal-free constraints, we introduce Dual-Stage Objectness Modeling (DSOM), which alternates between feature aggregation and boundary consolidation to stabilize objectness distributions while maintaining the separation between known and unknown categories. Furthermore, DSOM is supported by a Calibrated Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (CG-NLL) distance tailored for the dispersed feature distributions inherent in rehearsal-free settings. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that REAL-OW achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing exemplar replay methods in both detection precision and unknown discovery. Our approach establishes a new baseline for rehearsal-free OWOD.

AI.tldr: REAL-OW is a rehearsal-free Open-World Object Detection framework that uses collaborative LoRA-based adapters (General Adapters in backbone, Specific Adapters in decoder) and Dual-Stage Objectness Modeling with Calibrated Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood to detect unknown objects and incrementally learn new categories without storing exemplars, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing OWOD frameworks rely on exemplar replay to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, which conflicts with data access restrictions, poses data exposure risks, and incurs significant memory overhead. The goal is to achieve open-world object detection without rehearsal.
AI.method: REAL-OW introduces: (1) a collaborative adapter architecture with General Adapters (GAs) in the backbone for cross-task universal representations and Specific Adapters (SAs) in the decoder for task-specific expertise, based on LoRA; (2) Dual-Stage Objectness Modeling (DSOM) alternating between feature aggregation and boundary consolidation to stabilize objectness distributions; (3) Calibrated Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (CG-NLL) distance for dispersed feature distributions in rehearsal-free settings.
AI.result: REAL-OW achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing exemplar replay methods in both detection precision and unknown discovery.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes a new baseline for rehearsal-free OWOD, demonstrating that exemplar replay can be eliminated while maintaining or exceeding performance.

title: TacReasoner: A Dynamic Tactile-Language Framework for Interactive Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios
summary: Among the five primary human senses, tactile is arguably the most fundamental to survival, as it enables the perception of physical contact and interaction in real-world environments. In this paper, we explore two key challenges of integrating tactile sensing into intelligent systems for multimodal reasoning: (i) insufficient modeling of dynamic tactile signals, which restricts reasoning over temporally evolving properties, and (ii) hallucination in tactile foundation models caused by the absence of explicit reasoning mechanisms, leading to unstable real-world inference. To address these challenges, we propose TacReasoner, a dynamic tactile-language framework for interactive reasoning in real-world scenarios. First, TacReasoner incorporates a Dynamic-aware Tactile Encoder to enhance the perception and representation of dynamic tactile signals. More importantly, we introduce TouchCoT-10k, the first tactile chain-of-thought dataset for structured reasoning over tactile inputs. Upon it, we establish DynTac-Bench to systematically evaluate dynamic tactile perception and real-world commonsense reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that TacReasoner achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art models across multiple datasets. Notably, despite using only 7B parameters, TacReasoner outperforms the 14B VTV-LLM model on most subtasks, highlighting its effectiveness and efficiency in tactile commonsense reasoning.

AI.tldr: TacReasoner addresses dynamic tactile sensing and reasoning hallucination by introducing a Dynamic-aware Tactile Encoder and TouchCoT-10k dataset, achieving competitive performance with only 7B parameters, outperforming larger models on tactile commonsense reasoning.
AI.motivation: Tactile sensing is fundamental to survival but faces two key challenges in multimodal reasoning: (i) insufficient modeling of dynamic tactile signals limits reasoning over temporally evolving properties, and (ii) hallucination in tactile foundation models due to lack of explicit reasoning mechanisms causes unstable real-world inference.
AI.method: Proposes TacReasoner with (1) a Dynamic-aware Tactile Encoder for better dynamic tactile perception, (2) TouchCoT-10k, the first tactile chain-of-thought dataset for structured reasoning, and (3) DynTac-Bench for systematic evaluation of dynamic tactile perception and real-world commonsense reasoning.
AI.result: TacReasoner achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art models across multiple datasets. With only 7B parameters, it outperforms the 14B VTV-LLM model on most subtasks.
AI.conclusion: TacReasoner demonstrates effectiveness and efficiency in tactile commonsense reasoning, showing that smaller models with structured tactile reasoning can outperform larger counterparts.

title: Finetuning Lightweight LLMs for Control Flow Graph Generation
comment: Accept by The 38th International Conference on Software Engineering & Knowledge Engineering Short Paper
summary: Control Flow Graph (CFG) is an important program representations for software analysis, code understanding, and software maintenance. Traditional CFG generation techniques mainly rely on bytecode or abstract syntax trees. However, these approaches usually require complete, compilable, and syntax error-free code, which limits their applicability to incomplete or erroneous code. Furthermore, they often depend on language specific tools, making it difficult to support multiple programming languages in a unified manner. To address these limitations, this paper investigates the use of fine-tuned lightweight large language models (LLMs) for CFG generation. We first design a unified CFG output format and a task-specific fine-tuning prompt for CFG generation. Then, we construct a dataset based on an existing LeetCode dataset through automatic CFG generation and error augmentation. We evaluate the proposed approach on six lightweight LLM models, including three code-specific LLMs: CodeLlama, QwenCoder, and DeepSeekCoder; and three general purpose LLMs: Llama3.2-3B, Qwen-4B, and Phi-4B. The experimental results show that, through fine-tuning, lightweight LLMs achieve promising results for CFG generation, particularly when the input code is incomplete or erroneous. It also demonstrates cross-language generalization capability on programming language not included in the fine-tuning data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using fine-tuned lightweight LLMs (CodeLlama, QwenCoder, DeepSeekCoder, Llama3.2-3B, Qwen-4B, Phi-4B) for CFG generation, addressing limitations of traditional methods that require complete, compilable, error-free code. Results show promising CFG generation, especially for incomplete/erroneous code, with cross-language generalization capabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional CFG generation relies on bytecode or AST approaches that require complete, compilable, syntax-error-free code and language-specific tools, limiting applicability to incomplete/erroneous code and multi-language support.
AI.method: Designed a unified CFG output format and task-specific fine-tuning prompt; constructed a dataset from LeetCode via automatic CFG generation and error augmentation; fine-tuned six lightweight LLMs (3 code-specific, 3 general-purpose) for CFG generation.
AI.result: Fine-tuned lightweight LLMs achieve promising CFG generation results, particularly for incomplete or erroneous code, and demonstrate cross-language generalization on languages not seen during fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight LLMs fine-tuned for CFG generation effectively overcome limitations of traditional approaches, handling incomplete/erroneous code and generalizing across programming languages.

title: Graph Classification via Network Usable Information: From Representation Evaluation to Structure Selection
summary:
We propose NetinfoGC, a framework for graph classification that extends the Network Usable Information (NUI) paradigm to graph-level learning. Unlike conventional graph neural network approaches that rely on end-to-end training of black-box embeddings, NetinfoGC constructs a family of permutation-invariant graph representations derived from propagation-based mechanisms and classical structural descriptors, including graph centrality measures.
  To evaluate representation quality, we introduce a training-free NUI estimation procedure based on clustering consistency with ground-truth labels, providing a proxy for task-relevant information without supervised learning. We further exploit the same representations using sparse-group LASSO regularization, enabling automatic selection of informative structural descriptors while suppressing redundant ones.
  Experiments on benchmark datasets show that classical centrality measures are highly competitive with learned propagation-based representations, and in several cases yield superior performance. Moreover, we observe a strong correlation between estimated NUI and downstream classification accuracy, validating NUI as an effective measure of representation utility.
  Overall, NetinfoGC provides a unified and interpretable framework for evaluating and exploiting graph representations without requiring end-to-end neural training.

AI.tldr: NetinfoGC is a graph classification framework that uses classical structural descriptors and propagation-based features with an NUI estimation method and sparse-group LASSO, showing that traditional centrality measures often outperform learned GNN embeddings while providing interpretability.
AI.motivation: To move beyond black-box GNN embeddings for graph classification by leveraging interpretable, permutation-invariant graph representations and a training-free NUI estimation procedure that correlates with downstream task performance.
AI.method: (1) Constructs permutation-invariant graph representations from propagation-based mechanisms and classical structural descriptors (e.g., centrality measures). (2) Introduces a training-free NUI estimation procedure based on clustering consistency with ground-truth labels. (3) Uses sparse-group LASSO regularization for automated feature selection from the constructed representations.
AI.result: Classical centrality measures are highly competitive with learned propagation-based representations, sometimes outperforming them. A strong correlation exists between estimated NUI and downstream classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: NetinfoGC offers a unified, interpretable framework for evaluating and exploiting graph representations without end-to-end neural training, with NUI validated as an effective measure of representation utility.

title: PosterHarness: Turning Scientific Poster Generation into an Auditable Instruction-Following Benchmark
summary: Text-rich image models can now design poster-scale layouts, but we lack ways to measure whether they honor scientific communication contracts: legible labels, prescribed aspect ratios, and -- above all -- abstaining from fabricated scientific figures. We present POSTERHARNESS, an auditable harness reframing poster generation as measurable instruction-following tasks, with a pilot benchmark and failure taxonomy. POSTERHARNESS uses a placeholder-first contract to separate two jobs models otherwise conflate. The model performs visual-summary design: typography, reading path, color, and background -- but never draws data-bearing figures. Every figure region must be an empty labeled placeholder; a deterministic compositor inserts real source-paper figures at detected coordinates. This makes properties measurable: placeholder count and ID accuracy, blankness, aspect-ratio compliance, abstention from synthesized graphics, public-text hygiene, and source-figure provenance -- with failures logged as explicit rejections, not hidden in plausible-looking output. We instantiate the harness on 12 papers (6 HEP, 6 AI/ML-adjacent) and report three findings. (i) A counterfactual probe shows the placeholder contract drives VLM-counted synthesized figures from 34 to 0 across three papers. (ii) A failure taxonomy identifies blocking contracts: placeholder geometry, placeholder QA, template critic, and public text. (iii) Comparison with Paper2Poster shows a trade-off: PosterHarness yields higher-resolution artifacts, lower white-canvas fraction, and stronger VLM visual preference; the deterministic baseline retains slightly more PosterQuiz-style information and runs faster. We report this as regime characterization, not a superiority claim. All artifacts, prompts, manifests, and audit scripts are released as a reusable evaluation component.

AI.tldr: POSTERHARNESS is an auditable evaluation framework for text-rich poster generation models that uses a placeholder-first contract to separate visual-summary design (typography, layout, color) from data-bearing figure creation, enabling measurable instruction-following metrics like placeholder accuracy, aspect-ratio compliance, and abstention from synthesized graphics.
AI.motivation: Current text-rich image models can generate poster-scale layouts but lack evaluation methods for whether they honor scientific communication contracts: legible labels, prescribed aspect ratios, and avoiding fabricated scientific figures.
AI.method: A placeholder-first contract splits generation into two jobs: (1) the model performs visual-summary design (typography, reading path, color, background) but never draws data figures; (2) every figure region must be an empty labeled placeholder, and a deterministic compositor inserts real source-paper figures at detected coordinates. Properties measured include placeholder count/ID accuracy, blankness, aspect-ratio compliance, abstention from synthesized graphics, public-text hygiene, and source-figure provenance.
AI.result: (i) Counterfactual probe shows placeholder contract drives VLM-counted synthesized figures from 34 to 0. (ii) Failure taxonomy identifies blocking contracts: placeholder geometry, placeholder QA, template critic, and public text. (iii) Comparison with Paper2Poster shows a trade-off: PosterHarness yields higher-resolution artifacts, lower white-canvas fraction, stronger VLM visual preference; baseline retains slightly more PosterQuiz-style information and runs faster.
AI.conclusion: POSTERHARNESS provides a reusable evaluation component for scientific poster generation with explicit failure logging (rejections, not hidden plausible outputs), and the work is characterized as regime comparison rather than a superiority claim.

title: DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling draft generation from target verification. While recent parallel drafters efficiently propose long token sequences in a single forward pass, they suffer from rapid acceptance decay due to a lack of inter-token dependencies. Furthermore, indiscriminately verifying these extended blocks wastes critical batch capacity on tokens with high rejection risks, severely degrading throughput in high-concurrency serving systems. We introduce DSpark, a speculative decoding framework that unifies high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive, load-aware verification. To maintain draft quality, DSpark utilizes a semi-autoregressive architecture, coupling a parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential module, to introduce intra-block dependency modeling and mitigate suffix decay. To optimize system efficiency, DSpark employs confidence-scheduled verification, dynamically tailoring the verification length for each request based on estimated prefix survival probabilities and engine-specific throughput profiles. On offline benchmarks across diverse domains, DSpark substantially improves the accepted length over state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel drafters. When deployed within the DeepSeek-V4 serving system under live user traffic, DSpark successfully mitigates verification waste. Compared to the established production baseline (MTP-1), DSpark accelerates per-user generation speeds by 60 to 85 percent at matched throughput levels. More importantly, by preventing severe throughput degradation under strict interactivity constraints, it enables performance tiers that were previously unattainable, shifting the Pareto frontier of our serving system.

AI.tldr: DSpark is a speculative decoding framework that combines semi-autoregressive parallel drafting with adaptive, load-aware verification to improve LLM inference throughput and latency. It mitigates token acceptance decay via intra-block dependency modeling and optimizes batch capacity via confidence-scheduled verification, achieving 60-85% per-user speedup in production at DeepSeek-V4.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods suffer from (1) rapid acceptance decay in parallel drafters due to lack of inter-token dependencies, and (2) wasted batch capacity from indiscriminately verifying long blocks with high rejection risks, degrading throughput in high-concurrency serving systems.
AI.method: DSpark uses (1) a semi-autoregressive architecture with a parallel backbone plus a lightweight sequential module to model intra-block dependencies and mitigate suffix decay; and (2) confidence-scheduled verification that adaptively adjusts verification length per request based on estimated prefix survival probabilities and engine-specific throughput profiles.
AI.result: DSpark significantly improves accepted length over state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel drafters on offline benchmarks. In production (DeepSeek-V4) under live traffic, it achieves 60-85% per-user generation speedup at matched throughput, and enables previously unattainable performance tiers under strict interactivity constraints.
AI.conclusion: DSpark unifies high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive verification, shifting the Pareto frontier of serving system performance by preventing severe throughput degradation and enabling new performance tiers under interactive constraints.

title: Beyond Compliance: A Large Scale Study on the Completeness and Consistency of the GitHub SBOMs
summary: Modern software development relies heavily on open-source components. Reusing components accelerates innovation but increases exposure to supply-chain attacks exploiting known vulnerabilities. Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) improve software supply chain transparency by enumerating components, their versions, and their provenance. GitHub, the largest open-source development hosting platform, now automatically generates SBOMs for repositories, providing valuable metadata for risk assessment. Yet, it is unclear whether GitHub SBOMs can serve as a reliable source for vulnerability and license analysis, and how incomplete or inconsistent metadata may affect different programming ecosystems. To address this, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 10,000 GitHub repositories across ten programming language ecosystems, evaluating GitHub SBOMs against three other popular SBOM generators: Syft, Trivy, and the Microsoft SBOM Tool. Our study finds a lack of NTIA compliance in GitHub SBOMs, though core metadata is consistently present. We also find that component version and license information availability is highly dependent on the programming ecosystem. Compared with the other three tools, GitHub yields results similar to the Microsoft SBOM Tool and often outperforms Syft and Trivy in providing version and license information. Finally, we discuss potential shortcomings of the GitHub SBOM Tool, directly related to how each ecosystem manages its dependencies.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 10,000 GitHub repositories across 10 programming ecosystems to evaluate GitHub's automatically generated SBOMs for vulnerability and license analysis, comparing them against Syft, Trivy, and Microsoft SBOM Tool. Findings show GitHub SBOMs lack NTIA compliance but provide consistent core metadata, with component version and license availability varying by ecosystem. GitHub performs similarly to Microsoft's tool and often better than Syft and Trivy, but has shortcomings related to ecosystem dependency management practices.
AI.motivation: To determine whether GitHub's automatically generated SBOMs are reliable for vulnerability and license analysis and how incomplete or inconsistent metadata affects different programming ecosystems, given the increasing reliance on open-source components and supply-chain attack risks.
AI.method: Large-scale analysis of 10,000 GitHub repositories across ten programming language ecosystems, comparing GitHub SBOMs against three popular SBOM generators (Syft, Trivy, Microsoft SBOM Tool) for NTIA compliance, metadata completeness, and version/license information availability.
AI.result: GitHub SBOMs lack NTIA compliance overall but contain consistent core metadata. Version and license information availability is highly dependent on the programming ecosystem. GitHub performs similarly to the Microsoft SBOM Tool and often outperforms Syft and Trivy in providing version and license information.
AI.conclusion: GitHub SBOMs have potential shortcomings related to how each programming ecosystem manages its dependencies, and while they are comparable to or better than other tools in some aspects, they are not fully NTIA-compliant, indicating room for improvement in SBOM generation for software supply chain security.

title: Implicit Bias of SGD in Multivariate ReLU Networks: Effective Width Collapse
summary: We study the implicit bias of noisy stochastic gradient descent in training wide two-layer ReLU networks for multivariate regression. In a mean-field regime, the training dynamics are approximated by a Wasserstein gradient flow that converges to a unique stationary measure. We characterize the structure of this stationary measure and the predictor it represents. We show that, despite the network being infinitely overparameterized, the learned predictor admits an effectively finite representation: the input weights and biases align along finitely many directions, leading to an effective width collapse. In particular, the solution function is continuous piecewise affine, with affine regions determined by the cells of a finite hyperplane arrangement. The number of learned directions, and hence hyperplanes, is bounded above by $2\mathcal{P}-1$, where $\mathcal{P}$ denotes the number of linear dichotomies realizable on the training inputs. We further establish a non-redundancy property of the learned representation by proving that each learned direction induces a unique ternary activation pattern on the training data. Consequently, the complexity of the learned predictor is governed by the combinatorial geometry of the training data.

AI.tldr: Noisy SGD in wide two-layer ReLU networks converges to a stationary measure where the learned predictor has finite width, with weights aligning along at most 2P-1 directions (P = number of realizable dichotomies), yielding a piecewise affine function governed by the combinatorial geometry of training data.
AI.motivation: To understand the implicit bias of noisy stochastic gradient descent in training wide two-layer ReLU networks for multivariate regression, specifically how overparameterization leads to finite effective representations through a mean-field analysis.
AI.method: Mean-field regime approximation where training dynamics are modeled as a Wasserstein gradient flow converging to a unique stationary measure; combinatorial geometry analysis of hyperplane arrangements and linear dichotomies.
AI.result: The learned predictor has finite representation: input weights and biases align along at most 2P-1 directions, leading to width collapse. The solution is continuous piecewise affine with regions defined by a finite hyperplane arrangement, and each learned direction induces a unique ternary activation pattern on training data.
AI.conclusion: The complexity of the learned predictor is governed by the combinatorial geometry of the training data, demonstrating non-redundancy and effective finite representation despite infinite overparameterization.

title: HyperVAttention: Efficient Sparse Attention with Spatio-Temporal Clustering for Video Diffusion
summary: Video Diffusion Transformers (VDiTs) have demonstrated significant capabilities in high-fidelity video generation. However, their ability to produce long-duration videos is fundamentally constrained by the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. Recent clustering-based sparse attention methods improve the quality-speed trade-off by grouping semantically similar tokens, but their practical efficiency remains limited by two bottlenecks: substantial clustering overhead and low CTA utilization caused by irregular cluster-induced blocks. We propose HyperVAttention (HVA), a training-free sparse attention framework that addresses both bottlenecks jointly. To reduce clustering overhead, we introduce 3D local-window clustering, which exploits the spatio-temporal locality of video tokens to restrict centroid search to fixed local neighborhoods, and implement it with a custom Triton kernel for efficient execution. We further propose a hybrid clustering strategy that performs full clustering only at anchor steps and updates only subset tokens at intermediate steps, leveraging the temporal stability of cluster assignments across denoising steps. To improve CTA utilization, we present hardware-aware cluster merging that minimizes CTA-aligned execution cost through parallel agglomerative merging, improving block density and approximation fidelity by utilizing idle tile capacity. Together, these components reduce clustering overhead, avoid redundant updates, and better align sparse attention with the fixed tile structure of modern GPU kernels. Experiments on Text-to-Video generation show that HVA establishes a new Pareto frontier for training-free sparse attention in video diffusion, reducing end-to-end latency by up to $2.13\times$ while improving fidelity over existing training-free sparse attention baselines.

AI.tldr: HyperVAttention (HVA) is a training-free sparse attention framework for Video Diffusion Transformers that addresses clustering overhead and low CTA utilization bottlenecks through 3D local-window clustering, hybrid clustering strategies, and hardware-aware cluster merging, achieving up to 2.13× latency reduction with improved fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing clustering-based sparse attention methods for VDiTs suffer from two bottlenecks: substantial clustering overhead and low CTA utilization caused by irregular cluster-induced blocks, limiting their practical efficiency in long-duration video generation.
AI.method: Three key components: (1) 3D local-window clustering exploiting spatio-temporal locality with custom Triton kernel; (2) Hybrid clustering with full clustering at anchor steps and subset updates at intermediate steps leveraging temporal stability; (3) Hardware-aware cluster merging via parallel agglomerative merging to minimize CTA-aligned execution cost.
AI.result: HVA establishes a new Pareto frontier for training-free sparse attention in video diffusion, reducing end-to-end latency by up to 2.13× while improving fidelity over existing training-free sparse attention baselines on Text-to-Video generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HVA effectively reduces clustering overhead, avoids redundant updates, and better aligns sparse attention with GPU tile structures, enabling more efficient long-duration video generation without additional training.

title: The Changing Role of Symbolic Methods in Artificial Intelligence
summary:
Why do intelligent systems need to perform explicit symbolic reasoning? Computer science has traditionally regarded symbolic reasoning as a defining component of intelligence. Yet the remarkable success of modern foundation models raises a fundamental question: if increasingly capable AI systems can operate with little explicit symbolic reasoning, what role do symbolic methods actually play?
  This article argues that explicit symbolic reasoning is not a fundamental property of intelligence, but a computational consequence of operating on simplified models of reality. We propose the Compression Principle: every computational model is a simplified representation of reality, and explicit symbolic reasoning compensates for information omitted during model construction. From this principle, we derive the Modeling--Reasoning Trade-off: as computational models preserve richer representations of the world, the need for explicit symbolic reasoning correspondingly decreases. This perspective provides a unified explanation for both the historical success of symbolic methods and the remarkable effectiveness of modern foundation models.
  Paradoxically, the same development makes symbolic methods increasingly important for humans. As intelligent systems become more capable and more opaque, symbolic representations increasingly serve as interfaces through which humans specify requirements, verify behavior, regulate autonomous systems, and establish trust. We therefore argue that the future of symbolic methods lies not primarily as the computational engine of intelligent systems, but as the symbolic interface between increasingly capable AI systems and the humans who build, govern, and depend upon them.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that explicit symbolic reasoning is not fundamental to intelligence but a computational necessity arising from simplified models of reality. It proposes the Compression Principle and the Modeling–Reasoning Trade-off, explaining both the historical success of symbolic methods and the effectiveness of foundation models. The authors conclude symbolic methods will shift from being the core computational engine of AI to serving as interfaces for human-AI interaction, trust, and governance.
AI.motivation: To reconcile the apparent tension between classical symbolic AI approaches and the success of modern foundation models that operate with little explicit symbolic reasoning, and to answer the fundamental question of what role symbolic methods play in increasingly capable AI systems.
AI.method: Proposes the Compression Principle (every computational model is a simplified representation of reality) and derives the Modeling–Reasoning Trade-off (richer world representations reduce need for explicit symbolic reasoning). The argument is conceptual and theoretical rather than empirical.
AI.result: A unified explanation for both the historical success of symbolic methods and the effectiveness of modern foundation models, along with a paradoxical prediction that symbolic methods become more important for human-AI interaction as systems become more capable and opaque.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic reasoning is not a fundamental property of intelligence but a computational consequence of model simplification. The future role of symbolic methods will shift from being the computational engine of AI to serving as symbolic interfaces for specification, verification, regulation, and trust between humans and increasingly capable AI systems.

title: Can LLMs Really Recover Microservice Failures? A Recovery-Aware Evaluation of Diagnosis-to-Action Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret operational evidence and assist incident response in cloud-native microservice systems. However, recovery-oriented use cases require more than identifying a root cause. After observing symptoms and diagnosing a fault, an operator or agent must translate the diagnosis into a concrete recovery action, apply it to an admissible target, and verify that service health has been restored. Existing RCA and log-analysis evaluations are well-suited to diagnosis, but they do not characterize this subsequent action decision. This paper presents R2Act, a recovery-action evaluation framework for post-diagnosis incident response. R2Act defines an incident schema, quality gate, action-space representation, recovery-validity metrics, offline evaluator, and live-replay protocol. We instantiate the framework as a benchmark dataset of 302 quality-audited Kubernetes incidents from \system. Each incident provides synchronized multi-modal observations, root-cause labels, an incident-specific action space, and annotated valid and invalid recovery plans. We evaluate heuristic, supervised, RCA-oriented, deep log, and LLM-based methods. The strongest RAG-based LLMs reach 91.4\%--99.7\% root-cause service accuracy, yet their recovery validity remains only 36.8\%--60.3\%. Even when both the root-cause service and fault type are correct, recovery-oriented methods still choose invalid actions for 39.5\%--62.0\% of correctly diagnosed incidents. Overall, this work reveals that many recovery failures arise not from missing diagnostic knowledge, but from the difficulty of translating diagnostic evidence into valid recovery actions and admissible targets. This work provides a reproducible, simplified starting point for research and evaluation.

AI.tldr: R2Act is a recovery-action evaluation framework for post-diagnosis incident response in cloud-native systems. It reveals that even when root-cause diagnosis is accurate (91.4%-99.7%), recovery validity remains low (36.8%-60.3%), highlighting translation from diagnosis to valid recovery actions as the core challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA and log-analysis evaluations focus on diagnosis only and do not characterize the subsequent action decision (translating diagnosis into a concrete recovery action, applying it to an admissible target, and verifying service health restoration), despite recovery-oriented use cases requiring more than root-cause identification.
AI.method: R2Act defines an incident schema, quality gate, action-space representation, recovery-validity metrics, offline evaluator, and live-replay protocol. The framework is instantiated as a benchmark dataset of 302 quality-audited Kubernetes incidents with synchronized multi-modal observations, root-cause labels, incident-specific action spaces, and annotated recovery plans.
AI.result: Strongest RAG-based LLMs reach 91.4%-99.7% root-cause service accuracy but recovery validity remains 36.8%-60.3%. Even with correct root-cause service and fault type, recovery-oriented methods choose invalid actions for 39.5%-62.0% of correctly diagnosed incidents.
AI.conclusion: Many recovery failures arise not from missing diagnostic knowledge but from the difficulty of translating diagnostic evidence into valid recovery actions and admissible targets. The work provides a reproducible, simplified starting point for research and evaluation.

title: Reflected Schrödinger Bridge Matching
summary: Recent advances in generative modeling have enabled the efficient computation of Schrödinger bridges (SB) in high-dimensional settings by leveraging partially simulation-free training methods inspired by flow matching. However, these have not covered SBs with reflecting dynamics, a useful model choice with built-in guarantees that generated samples stay in the data domain. Existing alternatives for reflected SBs instead rely on more complex training based on forward--backward SDE theory, requiring expensive higher-order derivatives and sampling entire paths during training. In this article, we introduce a partially simulation-free framework that allows reflected SBs to be trained similarly to flow matching, using a new sampling method and regression target. We demonstrate our results by coupling pairs of well-known high-dimensional image datasets. Using reflected dynamics incurs negligible additional wall-clock time during both training and inference while maintaining or slightly improving generative performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a partially simulation-free framework for reflected Schrödinger bridges that can be trained similarly to flow matching, using a new sampling method and regression target, achieving negligible additional computational cost while maintaining generative performance.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for reflected Schrödinger bridges rely on complex forward-backward SDE training requiring expensive higher-order derivatives and full path sampling. The authors aim to make reflected SBs more computationally efficient and accessible by adapting partially simulation-free flow matching techniques.
AI.method: The authors propose a partially simulation-free framework that uses a new sampling method and regression target, allowing reflected SBs to be trained similarly to flow matching without requiring expensive higher-order derivatives or full path sampling during training.
AI.result: The method couples pairs of high-dimensional image datasets with reflected dynamics, incurring negligible additional wall-clock time during both training and inference while maintaining or slightly improving generative performance compared to non-reflected alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Reflected Schrödinger bridges can be efficiently trained with flow-matching-like methods, providing built-in guarantees that generated samples stay in the data domain without sacrificing computational efficiency or generative quality.

title: MambaLIE: Scene Light Intensity-Boosted Low-Light Image Enhancement with State Space Model
summary:
Images captured by consumer electronic devices, such as mobile phones and digital cameras, often suffer from low-light degradation due to sensor limitations and imaging pipelines, which degrades visual quality and affects downstream vision tasks.
  Existing methods based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers have dominated current low-light image enhancement (LIE) due to their excellent ability to model hierarchical features.
  However, CNNs operate in local receptive fields that cannot model long-range dependencies, while Transformers overcome this problem but incur substantial computational costs.
  To address these challenges, we propose MambaLIE, a Scene Light Intensity-Boosted Low-Light Image Enhancement method based on a State Space Model (SSM).
  We first introduce scene light intensity to improve the structural distribution of illumination, which is then gated with the low-light input to guide enhancement.
  To better model the illumination while maintaining computational efficiency, we propose the Locally Enhanced State Space Model (LESSM) for efficient light enhancement.
  Our LESSM contains two branches: an SSM branch and a Local Enhanced branch, where the former is used to model the long-range dependencies with linear time complexity, while the latter is used to enhance local feature representations.
  Extensive experiments demonstrate that MambaLIE outperforms state-of-the-art CNN-based and Transformer-based LIE methods on four widely used synthetic benchmarks and five publicly available real-world benchmarks in terms of accuracy, speed, and model size, making it suitable for practical deployment on resource-constrained devices.

AI.tldr: MambaLIE is a low-light image enhancement method based on State Space Models (SSM) that combines long-range dependency modeling (via SSM) with local feature enhancement (via a Local Enhanced branch), achieving superior performance over CNN and Transformer baselines across multiple benchmarks with improved efficiency for resource-constrained devices.
AI.motivation: Images from consumer devices suffer from low-light degradation. CNNs cannot model long-range dependencies due to local receptive fields, while Transformers can but incur high computational costs. The goal is to achieve both effective global modeling and computational efficiency for practical deployment.
AI.method: MambaLIE proposes a Locally Enhanced State Space Model (LESSM) with two branches: an SSM branch for long-range dependencies with linear time complexity, and a Local Enhanced branch for local feature representations. Scene light intensity is introduced to improve illumination structural distribution, which is gated with the low-light input to guide enhancement.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art CNN-based and Transformer-based LIE methods on four synthetic and five real-world benchmarks in accuracy, speed, and model size, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices.
AI.conclusion: MambaLIE effectively addresses the trade-off between long-range dependency modeling and computational efficiency in low-light image enhancement, demonstrating practical viability for real-world deployment on consumer devices.

title: AgentGym2: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in De-Idealized Real-World Environments
comment: Accepted as a main conference paper at ACL 2026
summary: Language agents, i.e., LLM agents, progress rapidly and are increasingly deployed in production environments. This trend underscores the urgent need for rigorous and realistic evaluations. However, most existing benchmarks evaluate agents in simplified, idealized settings. They typically rely on pre-packaged tool interfaces, overlook critical steps, and assume inputs are clean and fully specified. Consequently, they understate the difficulty of real deployments, where uncertainty and noise are ubiquitous and agents must proactively explore the environment to uncover new tools. To bridge this gap, we present AgentGym2, a new evaluation framework with task instances grounded in real-world end-to-end working demands. Beyond reasoning and planning, it measures agents' ability to execute end-to-end procedures, discover tools via exploration, compose tools for unseen tasks, and remain robust to noisy and underspecified information. Experiments on 15 proprietary and open-source models show that even SOTA systems like Gemini and GPT-5 struggle on AgentGym2, revealing a substantial gap between the capability of current agents and the demands of real-world applications.

AI.tldr: AgentGym2 is a new evaluation framework for LLM agents that tests real-world capabilities like tool discovery, exploration, robustness to noise, and end-to-end procedure execution, revealing that even top models like Gemini and GPT-5 fall far short of real-world deployment demands.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLM agents in simplified, idealized settings with pre-packaged tools, clean inputs, and overlooked critical steps, failing to capture the uncertainty, noise, and need for proactive exploration in real deployments. This gap underscores the urgent need for more realistic evaluations as agents are increasingly used in production.
AI.method: AgentGym2 provides a new evaluation framework grounded in real-world end-to-end working demands, measuring agents on: (1) executing end-to-end procedures, (2) discovering tools via exploration, (3) composing tools for unseen tasks, and (4) robustness to noisy and underspecified information. Experiments were conducted on 15 proprietary and open-source models.
AI.result: Even state-of-the-art systems like Gemini and GPT-5 struggle significantly on AgentGym2, indicating a substantial gap between current agent capabilities and real-world application requirements.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents, despite rapid progress, are far from ready for real-world deployment due to their inability to handle uncertainty, noise, and the need for proactive tool discovery, as revealed by the AgentGym2 benchmark.

title: Correctness, confidence, and context: Framing software assurance in the AI age
comment: 9 pages, 11 figures, text for invited keynote at FSE 2026 in Montreal
summary:
Software engineering has a complicated relationship with "correctness". We recognize the challenges of full formal rigor as well as many required properties beyond functional correctness. Although we satisfice in practice, we are still stuck in the mindset that we could reason our way to correctness, if only we had enough information.
  Generative AI has introduced a new dimension to assurances: its foundation is statistical rather than formal. Traditional software engineering establishes confidence through rigorous reasoning, domain knowledge and expert judgment. In contrast, generative AI's results are sophisticated predictions, in Valiant's words "probably approximately correct". This inherently limits assurances about the results are to probabilistic assertions. Further, the nuances and implicit associations that guide human judgment are not accessible to its training sets, so that tacit knowledge cannot be incorporated in its models.
  We have many approaches for developing assurances that a software system does what it's expected to do, though most of them focus on the specification of the code rather than the requirements for the system, let alone fitness for purpose. We have failed to develop a systematic understanding of the relative merits of the various approaches. I hope that generative AI will finally force us to tackle this.
  To that end, I will challenge us to think systematically about our assurance techniques. We need ways to make informed, reasoned choices about cost-effective combinations of approaches to devel-oping confidence in our systems.
  We call ourselves software engineers. Let's act like engineers.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that generative AI's statistical (probably approximately correct) nature challenges traditional software engineering's formal reasoning approach to correctness, and urges the field to systematically evaluate and combine diverse assurance techniques to build confidence in software systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional software engineering's mindset of reasoning toward correctness is insufficient given generative AI's statistical foundations; the field lacks systematic understanding of how different assurance approaches compare, and generative AI's emergence forces this issue.
