AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual analysis contrasting traditional formal/rigorous reasoning with generative AI's probabilistic (probably approximately correct) paradigm, and critiques existing assurance approaches for focusing on code specification rather than system requirements or fitness for purpose.
AI.result: Identifies that generative AI produces only probabilistic assertions due to its statistical nature, that tacit knowledge is inaccessible to its training sets, and that current assurance methods lack systematic comparison and cost-effectiveness analysis.
AI.conclusion: The software engineering community must develop systematic frameworks for making informed, reasoned choices about cost-effective combinations of assurance techniques to build confidence in systems, particularly in light of generative AI's challenges to traditional correctness notions.

title: LLM-Guided Transportation Hub Capacity Planning with Textual Business Inputs
summary: While traditional hub capacity planning models optimize effectively for quantitative inputs, they often fail to digest qualitative business context. We propose a novel framework where a large language model (LLM) agent iteratively proposes hub capacity decisions guided by natural-language business context descriptions. The key mechanism is a chain-of-thought reasoning protocol: the LLM constructs a structured decision table that maps each contextual item to specific capacity adjustments based on the implied direction and magnitude of changes. The new capacity decision is then validated through a feedback loop with an optimization model, which provides routing-based performance metrics to guide the agent's selection. On a real-world 13-hub freight network in the southeastern US, our framework achieves a 2.8% optimality gap relative to the hidden ground-truth, a significant improvement over the 11.0% gap produced by the traditional optimization model without textual business inputs. This demonstrates that LLMs can serve as a contextual bridge, integrating qualitative business insights into Operations Research workflows.

AI.tldr: An LLM agent with chain-of-thought reasoning integrates natural-language business context into hub capacity planning, achieving a 2.8% optimality gap on a real-world freight network vs. 11.0% from traditional optimization alone.
AI.motivation: Traditional hub capacity planning models optimize quantitative inputs but fail to incorporate qualitative business context, limiting real-world applicability.
AI.method: An LLM agent iteratively proposes capacity decisions using chain-of-thought reasoning to construct a structured decision table mapping contextual items to capacity adjustments; decisions are validated via a feedback loop with an optimization model providing routing-based performance metrics.
AI.result: On a 13-hub freight network in the southeastern US, the framework achieves a 2.8% optimality gap vs. 11.0% from the traditional optimization model without textual inputs.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as a contextual bridge, integrating qualitative business insights into Operations Research workflows to improve capacity planning.

title: CP-WSP: A Declarative CP-SAT Framework for Configurable Multi-Constraint Workforce Scheduling
summary: Workforce scheduling is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem requiring simultaneous satisfaction of labor regulations, coverage requirements, employee preferences and operational objectives. Existing CP formulations typically model simplified instances with 6-12 constraints at shift-level granularity and critically lack explicit support for: mandatory break scheduling with midpoint placement control; acuity weighted workload equity; sub-shift temporal granularity enabling demand-driven staffing; inter-week schedule stability; and cross-midnight shift patterns common in 24-hour operations. This paper presents CP-WSP: a declarative CP-SAT framework enforcing 14 hard constraints as mathematically inviolable requirements (zero regulatory violations by construction) while optimizing 15 soft objectives through a unified weighted penalty function -- all configurable via a JSON specification with no code changes required. Key contributions include: a shift-window variable decomposition enabling mandatory break scheduling with centrality control; acuity-weighted workload equity; multi-granularity temporal resolution from 30 minutes to 2 hours; inter-week schedule stability; a grid-offset preprocessing technique for cross-midnight shifts; and a reproducible 36-configuration benchmark suite for community comparison. Evaluated on INRC-II benchmarks at both hourly and shift-level granularity and on 36 synthetic configurations.

AI.tldr: CP-WSP is a declarative CP-SAT framework for workforce scheduling that enforces 14 hard constraints and optimizes 15 soft objectives via JSON configuration, handling break scheduling with midpoint control, acuity-weighted equity, multi-granularity temporal resolution, inter-week stability, and cross-midnight shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing CP formulations for workforce scheduling lack support for mandatory break scheduling with midpoint placement, acuity-weighted equity, sub-shift temporal granularity, inter-week stability, and cross-midnight shifts, which are critical for real-world 24-hour operations.
AI.method: A declarative CP-SAT framework (CP-WSP) with: shift-window variable decomposition for break scheduling with centrality control; acuity-weighted workload equity constraints; multi-granularity temporal resolution (30min-2h); inter-week stability constraints; grid-offset preprocessing for cross-midnight shifts; and a JSON-based configuration system requiring zero code modifications. The system enforces 14 hard constraints and optimizes 15 soft objectives via a unified weighted penalty function.
AI.result: Validated on INRC-II benchmarks (hourly and shift-level granularity) and 36 synthetic configurations; provides a reproducible benchmark suite for community comparison.
AI.conclusion: CP-WSP enables declarative, configurable workforce scheduling with 14 hard constraints and 15 soft objectives, demonstrating that complex real-world scheduling requirements (break placement, acuity equity, multi-granularity, stability, cross-midnight shifts) can be encoded via CP-SAT without code changes.

title: AI Agent Pull Requests on GitHub: Frequency, Structure, and Merge Conflict Rates
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21186464
summary: AI coding agents can create and submit pull requests (PRs) to a common repository at the same time; however, there is little research on the frequency of such concurrent submissions or the cost associated with them. In this study, we use the AIDev-pop dataset (33,596 PRs across 2,807 repositories) to perform the first large-scale empirical analysis of concurrency among agent-authored PRs. We find that under exact temporal overlap, 40.2% of repositories have co-active agent-authored PR pairs, and these co-active pairs account for 79.4% of all PRs submitted by an AI agent. When examining co-activity within a conventional one-week collaboration period, these percentages increase to 53.4% and 95.0%, respectively. For the vast majority of co-active PR pairs, both PRs were authored by the same agent (intra-agent), whereas only 0.5% of co-active pairs were cross-agent, and these were located in only 122 of the 2,807 total repositories examined (approximately 4.3%). Furthermore, we replayed actual three-way git merge operations on 747 unique co-active pairs (one per repository) to determine the rate of textual conflict when merging the two PRs in each pair. We found that the rate of textual conflict was significantly greater for cross-agent pairs than for intra-agent pairs: 41.7% versus 19.8%, respectively, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. Finally, we developed a classification system based upon the output of git's conflict detection, and determined that the majority of conflicts result from changes to source code files (84.4% of conflicted files) rather than dependency manifest files, and that nearly 42% of the conflicts we observed were structural (modify/delete or add/add). Because these metrics capture only the textual layer, they represent a conservative lower bound on the cost associated with uncoordinated AI teammates working together.

AI.tldr: Large-scale analysis of 33,596 AI-agent-authored PRs across 2,807 repositories reveals that 40.2% of repositories have concurrent agent PRs under exact temporal overlap (79.4% of all agent PRs), with only 0.5% being cross-agent. Cross-agent merges cause significantly higher textual conflict rates (41.7% vs 19.8%), and the majority of conflicts are in source code files (84.4%) with 42% being structural.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents can submit PRs concurrently to shared repositories, but the frequency and cost of such concurrent submissions are largely unknown, motivating a large-scale empirical analysis.
AI.method: Used the AIDev-pop dataset (33,596 PRs from 2,807 repos). Measured co-activity at exact temporal overlap and within one-week windows. Replayed three-way git merges on 747 unique co-active pairs to compute textual conflict rates. Developed a conflict classification system based on git's conflict detection output.
AI.result: 40.2% of repos have co-active agent PR pairs under exact overlap (79.4% of all agent PRs); 53.4% and 95.0% within one week. Only 0.5% were cross-agent (4.3% of repos). Cross-agent conflict rate: 41.7% vs intra-agent: 19.8%. 84.4% of conflicts in source code; 42% were structural conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Uncoordinated AI agents working concurrently incur significant coordination costs, measured conservatively via textual merge conflicts; these represent a lower bound on the true cost.

title: Phase-Preserving Trimodal Transformer for Tropical Forest Biomass Estimation Using Optical and PolInSAR Data
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, one of which is a TikZ
summary: The accurate estimation of Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) in mature tropical forests remains a critical challenge in remote sensing, primarily due to the saturation of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) signals in high-density areas and persistent cloud cover affecting optical imagery. To overcome these physical limitations, we propose the Trimodal Coherent Co-attention Transformer (TCCT), a physics-informed deep learning architecture. The TCCT natively fuses optical surface reflectance (Landsat-5) with complex-valued Polarimetric SAR Interferometry (PolInSAR) data from both P and L bands. Unlike traditional fusion methods, our architecture employs complex-valued encoders to preserve spatial phase coherence, coupled with a dynamic co-attention mechanism that acts as an adaptive gating module, reducing the weight of cloud-corrupted optical pixels and shifting reliance to microwave phase data. We also derived a localized spatial allometric calibration model via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization, tailored to the specific wood density of the Paracou region in the Amazon basin. Evaluated using a two-stage protocol, the TCCT first underwent a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation to establish robust global weights (achieving a global RMSE of 4.19 m). Subsequently, following a localized spatial fine-tuning phase over 200 epochs, the model attained an absolute RMSE of 3.78 m and an $R^2$ of 0.33 for Canopy Height Models (CHM), outperforming standard Random Forest, CNN, and Vision Transformer baselines. Our ablation study confirms that preserving phase coherence mitigates deep-canopy signal saturation. When converted to AGB, the fine-tuned TCCT map yielded a Relative RMSE (rRMSE) of 4.51% in dense forest areas above 50 Mg/ha. By meeting the European Space Agency (ESA) BIOMASS mission requirement of less than 20% error, the TCCT provides a robust framework for continuous carbon stock mapping in tropical biomes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Trimodal Coherent Co-attention Transformer (TCCT), a physics-informed deep learning architecture that fuses optical (Landsat-5) and complex-valued PolInSAR (P/L bands) data for accurate Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) estimation in mature tropical forests. It achieves RMSE of 3.78 m for Canopy Height Models and 4.51% rRMSE for AGB estimation, meeting ESA BIOMASS mission requirements.
AI.motivation: Accurate AGB estimation in mature tropical forests is hindered by SAR signal saturation in high-density areas and persistent cloud cover in optical imagery, creating a critical need for methods that overcome these physical limitations.
AI.method: The TCCT uses complex-valued encoders to preserve spatial phase coherence from PolInSAR data, a dynamic co-attention mechanism as an adaptive gating module to down-weight cloud-corrupted optical pixels, and a localized spatial allometric calibration model via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization tailored to regional wood density. Evaluation follows a two-stage protocol: 5-fold cross-validation then localized fine-tuning.
AI.result: Global RMSE of 4.19 m after cross-validation; after fine-tuning, absolute RMSE of 3.78 m and R² of 0.33 for Canopy Height Models, and 4.51% rRMSE for AGB in dense forests above 50 Mg/ha, outperforming Random Forest, CNN, and Vision Transformer baselines.
AI.conclusion: Preserving phase coherence mitigates deep-canopy signal saturation, and the TCCT meets the ESA BIOMASS mission requirement of <20% error, providing a robust framework for continuous carbon stock mapping in tropical biomes.

title: OmniDS: Dual-Stream Context Fusion for Omnidirectional Depth from Fisheye Cameras
summary: Omnidirectional depth estimation from multi-fisheye camera rigs is complicated by visibility conflicts: wide baselines cause different cameras to observe different portions, or even different faces, of the same object, so aggregating their features into a unified equirectangular (ERP) representation under fixed projection produces ambiguous matching evidence near occlusion boundaries and thin structures. Although existing methods mitigate this by down-weighting unreliable views, they do not resolve the underlying discrepancy because context formation and cross-view fusion remain tied to rigid fisheye-to-ERP sampling. We present OmniDS, an iterative depth refinement framework that replaces rigid aggregation by combining dynamic context fusion with consensus-aware multi-view similarity. A dual-stream encoder pairs a lightweight CNN for geometric detail with a frozen DINOv3 for semantic priors; their features are reprojected into ERP space at each refinement step via learned view weighting and deformable cross-attention with geometric distortion bias. In parallel, a multi-view consensus volume captures global cross-camera agreement through group-wise correlation and feature variance, regularized by a 3D U-Net. For efficient deployment, we distill the dual-stream representation into a single MobileNet-based encoder. OmniDS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OmniThings, OmniHouse, and Sunny benchmarks while maintaining competitive inference speed. Project page and codes are available at https://parkchaesong.github.io/omnids.

AI.tldr: OmniDS is an iterative depth refinement framework for omnidirectional depth estimation from multi-fisheye cameras that replaces rigid aggregation with dynamic context fusion and consensus-aware multi-view similarity, achieving SOTA performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Omnidirectional depth estimation from multi-fisheye camera rigs suffers from visibility conflicts caused by wide baselines, where different cameras observe different portions or faces of the same object. Existing methods only down-weight unreliable views but fail to resolve the underlying discrepancy because context formation and cross-view fusion remain tied to rigid fisheye-to-ERP sampling.
AI.method: OmniDS uses a dual-stream encoder (lightweight CNN for geometric detail + frozen DINOv3 for semantic priors), reprojects features into ERP space via learned view weighting and deformable cross-attention with geometric distortion bias at each refinement step. A multi-view consensus volume captures global cross-camera agreement via group-wise correlation and feature variance regularized by a 3D U-Net. The dual-stream representation is distilled into a single MobileNet-based encoder for efficient deployment.
AI.result: OmniDS achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniThings, OmniHouse, and Sunny benchmarks while maintaining competitive inference speed.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic context fusion and consensus-aware multi-view similarity effectively resolve visibility conflicts in multi-fisheye omnidirectional depth estimation, and the model can be efficiently distilled for deployment without sacrificing performance.

title: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
summary: Self-distillation is a promising recipe for self-improvement in language models. In this setting, a model can serve as its own teacher when given privileged information, such as a solution to a math problem. This seems especially appealing for thinking models, which can use test-time reasoning to absorb the privileged information. Surprisingly, we show that privileged self-distillation degrades thinking models on long reasoning traces: across five Qwen3 and OLMo thinking models evaluated on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, privileged-context distillation causes a relative drop of up to 17% in avg@16 accuracy. The degradation scales with the amount of privileged context withheld from the student and is most pronounced at long rollout budgets, where thinking models otherwise obtain their largest gains. This failure mode is not specific to self-distillation: on-policy distillation (OPD) improves thinking models, but privileged OPD reverses these gains. Our diagnostics link this failure mode to how privileged teacher context reshapes learning at high-entropy forking positions, where multiple continuations remain plausible and may lead to different reasoning paths. Privileged context lowers fork rates in thinking-model rollouts but not in instruction-model rollouts. This leads to an interesting dichotomy, where privileged context can help instruction-tuned models but hurts stronger thinking models. The effect is visible when the student begins a self-correction branch, where privileged OPD penalizes sampled reconsideration tokens that vanilla OPD supports. Thinking models trained with a privileged teacher produce fewer verification, backtracking, and hedging markers, even after length normalization. These findings indicate that self-distillation for strong thinking models requires attention to token-level signal, especially around correction and reasoning steps.

AI.tldr: Privileged self-distillation (where teacher has extra solution context) degrades thinking models' long reasoning traces, causing up to 17% relative accuracy drop on math benchmarks, by reducing verification, backtracking, and hedging behaviors at high-entropy forking positions.
AI.motivation: Self-distillation seems appealing for thinking models that use test-time reasoning to absorb privileged information (e.g., math solutions), but it is unknown whether this actually helps or hurts such models.
AI.method: Evaluated five Qwen3 and OLMo thinking models on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 under privileged-context distillation vs. on-policy distillation, analyzing fork rates, token-level signals (verification, backtracking, hedging), and length-normalized rollout behaviors.
AI.result: Privileged distillation causes up to 17% relative avg@16 accuracy drop; degradation scales with privileged context withheld and is worst at long rollout budgets. Privileged OPD reverses gains from vanilla OPD. Privileged context lowers fork rates in thinking models but not instruction models, and reduces self-correction markers.
AI.conclusion: Self-distillation for strong thinking models requires careful attention to token-level signal, especially around correction and reasoning steps, as privileged context harms the very reasoning behaviors that make thinking models effective.

title: Dashboard2Code: Evaluating Multimodal Models on Reconstructing Interactive Dashboards
summary: Automatic data visualization generation has advanced rapidly with multi-modal large language models, yet existing efforts largely focus on static charts and overlook the interactive dashboards commonly used for real-world data exploration. We introduce Dashboard2Code, a novel task that requires a model to proactively explore an interactive dashboard, acquire and integrate feedback from its own interactions (e.g., clicking and filtering), and generate code that reproduces the target dashboard. To support comprehensive evaluation, we present DashboardMimic, the first Plotly+Dash benchmark for Dashboard2Code, comprising 180 carefully designed and manually verified dashboard-code pairs spanning three difficulty levels and covering eight common real-world interaction patterns. We further propose an automated evaluation framework tailored to dashboards that combines code semantic analysis with dynamic interaction-based testing to assess visual and interaction consistency, showing strong agreement with human judgments. Experiments across a range of open- and closed-source multi-modal models reveal that even the strongest systems struggle on high-complexity dashboards and that a substantial performance gap remains between open-source and closed-source models on the Dashboard2Code task.

AI.tldr: Dashboard2Code is a new task requiring models to interactively explore and reproduce dashboards from code; the paper introduces DashboardMimic benchmark (180 Plotly+Dash pairs across 3 difficulty levels and 8 interaction patterns) and an automated evaluation framework showing that even strong models struggle on complex dashboards with a gap between open- and closed-source models.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic visualization generation focuses on static charts and ignores interactive dashboards commonly used in real-world data exploration, motivating the need for a task and benchmark that models proactive exploration and code generation for interactive dashboards.
AI.method: The authors define Dashboard2Code as a task where models must proactively explore dashboards via interactions, integrate feedback, and generate reproducing code. They create DashboardMimic, a Plotly+Dash benchmark with 180 dashboard-code pairs across three difficulty levels and eight interaction patterns. An automated evaluation framework combining code semantic analysis and dynamic interaction-based testing is proposed.
AI.result: Experiments across open- and closed-source multi-modal models show that even the strongest systems struggle on high-complexity dashboards, and a substantial performance gap exists between open-source and closed-source models on this task.
AI.conclusion: Dashboard2Code is a challenging task that reveals limitations of current multi-modal models in handling complex interactive dashboards, highlighting the need for further advancements especially for open-source models.

title: A Structural Interpretation of GELU and Threshold-Transmission Activations via the First-Order Loss Function
summary: The Gaussian Error Linear Unit is usually motivated as the expected output of an input-dependent stochastic Bernoulli gate. This work gives a complementary interpretation based on the Gaussian complementary first-order loss function: GELU is the signal-transmission term of the expected surplus of a hard linear gate with a Gaussian random threshold. This view separates loss accounting from forward signal transmission and generalises to a threshold-transmission family that includes ReLU, GELU, SiLU/Swish, and hard swish as special cases. The uniform-threshold case recovers a hard-swish-like compact piecewise-polynomial gate with an explicit threshold-width parameter, yielding fixed- and learned-width variants. Controlled experiments on compact vision and language models show that calibrated or learned uniform-threshold gates are consistently competitive with GELU, ReLU, and SiLU/Swish, improve over them in most tested settings, and use the finite transition region nontrivially.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a new interpretation of GELU using the Gaussian complementary first-order loss function, showing it as the signal-transmission term of a hard linear gate with a Gaussian random threshold. This leads to a threshold-transmission family encompassing ReLU, GELU, SiLU/Swish, and hard swish. A uniform-threshold variant yields a compact piecewise-polynomial gate with explicit width control, and experiments show it is competitive with or outperforms standard activations in compact vision and language models.
AI.motivation: To provide a complementary interpretation of GELU based on loss accounting and to generalize it into a threshold-transmission family that includes common activation functions as special cases, while introducing a practical uniform-threshold variant.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret GELU via the Gaussian complementary first-order loss function, then generalize to a threshold-transmission family. They introduce a uniform-threshold (hard-swish-like) variant with an explicit threshold-width parameter, tested in both fixed and learned configurations on compact vision and language models.
AI.result: Calibrated or learned uniform-threshold gates are consistently competitive with GELU, ReLU, and SiLU/Swish, improve over them in most tested settings, and use the finite transition region nontrivially.
AI.conclusion: The threshold-transmission perspective provides a principled framework for understanding and designing activation functions, with the uniform-threshold variant offering a practical, competitive alternative to existing activations.

title: Natural Language Camera Movement Understanding
summary: Understanding camera movement in natural language is critical for training and evaluating video generation models, among other applications. However, we demonstrate that existing vision-language models (VLMs) fail this task in surprising ways, frequently confusing translation with rotation, left with right, and object movement with camera movement. To address these limitations, we establish natural language camera movement understanding as a standalone research task. We introduce a two-level cinematographic taxonomy and an extensive, atomic benchmark featuring both real and synthetic videos. Furthermore, we curate a large-scale, multi-source training set enhanced by targeted camera movement augmentation. Our fine-tuned VLM-8B outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro by 10% and 11% on our benchmark's real and synthetic videos, respectively. Despite these gains, a significant gap remains relative to human performance, underscoring the need to promote and facilitate future research on natural language camera movement understanding.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models fail to understand camera movement in natural language, frequently confusing translation/rotation, left/right, and object/camera motion. The authors establish this as a standalone task, introduce a taxonomy and benchmark (real + synthetic videos), curate a large-scale training set with camera movement augmentation, and fine-tune a VLM-8B that outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro by 10-11%, though still below human performance.
AI.motivation: Understanding camera movement in natural language is critical for training/evaluating video generation models, yet existing VLMs surprisingly fail at this task, confusing translation with rotation, left with right, and object movement with camera movement.
AI.method: Establish camera movement understanding as a standalone task; introduce a two-level cinematographic taxonomy; build an atomic benchmark with real and synthetic videos; curate a large-scale multi-source training set with targeted camera movement augmentation; fine-tune a VLM-8B.
AI.result: Fine-tuned VLM-8B outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro by 10% on real videos and 11% on synthetic videos. A significant gap relative to human performance remains.
AI.conclusion: Significant progress is made in VLM-based camera movement understanding, but the gap to human performance underscores the need for future research in this area.

title: ClassicLogic: A Knowledge-Driven Benchmark of Classic Puzzle Games for Evaluating Compositional Generalization
summary: Compositional generalization, the ability to understand and produce novel combinations of known components, remains a fundamental challenge for modern artificial intelligence. While few benchmarks exist, many focus on linguistic tasks and lack complex, explicit compositional structures. We introduce ClassicLogic, a new benchmark suite designed to evaluate an agent's ability to learn and compose problem-solving strategies. The benchmark consists of four classic logic puzzles: Sudoku, KenKen, Kakuro, and Futoshiki. Its core innovation is a hierarchical, explicit knowledge base for each game, where complex solving strategies are formally defined as compositions of simpler, foundational strategies. This structure allows for fine-grained evaluation of an agent's reasoning capabilities, from learning basic rules to applying multi-step compositional strategies to solve puzzles of increasing, mathematically validated difficulty. The open-source benchmark provides a challenging new testbed for advancing neuro-symbolic and other advanced AI reasoning systems.

AI.tldr: ClassicLogic is a benchmark suite of four classic logic puzzles (Sudoku, KenKen, Kakuro, Futoshiki) featuring a hierarchical, explicit knowledge base to evaluate compositional generalization in AI agents, from basic rule learning to multi-step compositional strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for compositional generalization are predominantly linguistic and lack complex, explicit compositional structures, motivating the need for a benchmark with formally defined hierarchical reasoning strategies.
AI.method: The benchmark constructs four classic logic puzzles with a hierarchical, explicit knowledge base where complex solving strategies are formally defined as compositions of simpler foundational strategies, enabling fine-grained evaluation across validated difficulty levels.
AI.result: The benchmark provides an open-source testbed capable of evaluating reasoning from basic rules to multi-step compositional strategies with mathematically validated difficulty progression.
AI.conclusion: ClassicLogic offers a challenging new testbed for advancing neuro-symbolic and other advanced AI reasoning systems in compositional generalization.

title: Cam2Sim: Neural Scenario Reconstruction for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving Simulation
comment: In proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26) - Tools and Datasets track
summary: Simulation-based testing enables safe and repeatable evaluation of autonomous driving systems, but its effectiveness is limited by the gap between synthetic simulator outputs and real-world camera observations. To address this problem, we present Cam2Sim, a tool that transforms real-world driving recordings into playable CARLA simulation scenarios. Starting from camera images and poses, Cam2Sim reconstructs road geometry, ego trajectories, parked vehicles, and simulation assets, and augments the reconstructed environment with Gaussian Splatting to render camera observations that resemble the original recording. The framework supports ROS-based data extraction, parked-vehicle detection, OpenStreetMap-based map generation, CARLA scenario construction, Gaussian Splatting training, trajectory replay, and closed-loop execution with a system under test. We validate Cam2Sim on a real-world urban-driving scenario with a camera-based end-to-end driving model, comparing reconstruction quality, image-generation quality, and closed-loop behavior against both a simulation-only baseline and the real-world target. Results show that Gaussian-Splatting-based rendering reduces the visual gap with respect to standard simulator rendering and improves behavioral similarity to the real-world reference runs. The artifact is publicly available at https: //github.com/ast-fortiss-tum/cam2sim, and a screencast showing the tool is available at https://youtu.be/KmZ74l1__lI

AI.tldr: Cam2Sim transforms real-world driving recordings into CARLA simulation scenarios by reconstructing road geometry, trajectories, and assets, then uses Gaussian Splatting to render realistic camera observations, reducing the sim-to-real visual gap and improving behavioral similarity in closed-loop testing.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based testing for autonomous driving is limited by the visual gap between synthetic simulator outputs and real-world camera observations, reducing the validity of test results.
AI.method: Cam2Sim takes camera images and poses, reconstructs road geometry, ego trajectories, parked vehicles, and simulation assets, augments the environment with Gaussian Splatting for realistic rendering, and supports ROS-based data extraction, OpenStreetMap-based map generation, CARLA scenario construction, trajectory replay, and closed-loop execution.
AI.result: Gaussian-Splatting-based rendering reduces the visual gap compared to standard simulator rendering and improves behavioral similarity to real-world reference runs in closed-loop evaluation with a camera-based end-to-end driving model.
AI.conclusion: Cam2Sim effectively bridges the sim-to-real gap for autonomous driving simulation testing by reconstructing real-world scenarios with enhanced visual fidelity, enabling more valid closed-loop evaluations.

title: Validation-Induced Shapley Shifts: How Validation Structure Distorts Data Valuation
summary: Shapley values are widely used to attribute value to training data based on their marginal contribution to performance on a validation set. Existing practice often assumes these values are stable once the training data and model are fixed. In this work, we uncover a systematic vulnerability: even modest changes to the validation set, such as introducing noises, cause directional shifts in Shapley distributions. As noises are added, Shapley values of training samples compress toward zero. We trace this to a noise-induced neighborhood reshuffling effect: perturbations alter the local rank order between validation and training samples, flattening the valuation landscape. Using the KNN-Shapley framework, we show through synthetic and real data that these shifts are consistent and reproducible. Our findings challenge the assumption of Shapley stability and reveal a new axis of fragility in data valuation. We propose normalization and boundary-aware validation strategies to mitigate these distortions and enable more robust, interpretable valuation in machine learning marketplaces.

AI.tldr: Shapley values for data valuation are unstable under validation set perturbations, compressing toward zero due to noise-induced neighborhood reshuffling, and the paper proposes mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: To challenge the common assumption that Shapley values are stable once training data and model are fixed, by uncovering a systematic vulnerability where even modest validation set changes cause directional shifts in Shapley distributions.
AI.method: Using the KNN-Shapley framework, the authors introduce noise perturbations to validation sets and analyze the resulting shifts in Shapley values through both synthetic and real data experiments. They trace the phenomenon to a noise-induced neighborhood reshuffling effect that alters local rank order between validation and training samples.
AI.result: Shapley values of training samples compress toward zero as validation set noise increases. This compression is consistent and reproducible under the KNN-Shapley framework. The root cause is identified as noise-induced neighborhood reshuffling that flattens the valuation landscape.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a new axis of fragility in data valuation, challenging the assumption of Shapley stability. The authors propose normalization and boundary-aware validation strategies to mitigate distortions and enable more robust, interpretable valuation in machine learning marketplaces.

title: CURE: Controllable Unified Image Restoration for Complex Degradations
summary: The presence of composite degradations poses a significant challenge, since the underlying corruption factors exhibit complex and interdependent interactions. Even when the degradation types are known, accurately restoring the image remains difficult due to the intertwined nature of their effects and the need for selective control during the recovery process. To address this, we introduce CURE, a unified framework that enables controllable restoration in complex degradation settings by learning disentangled and adjustable representations. CURE is driven by four complementary objectives. First, an identity embedding is incorporated, along with a reconstruction constraint, to ensure that the model can reproduce the input image when restoration is unnecessary. Second, the ratio control mechanism blends the identity embedding with degradation-specific embeddings using user-regulated mixing ratios, allowing continuous control over restoration intensity. Third, an intermediate loss is applied to supervise stepwise outputs, each encouraged to tackle the removal of only a single degradation factor within a composite mixture. Finally, a permutation-invariant loss ensures that the model achieves consistent restoration quality regardless of the order in which multiple degradations are addressed. Since CURE modifies only the training strategy and not the underlying network architecture, it can be seamlessly integrated into existing controllable restoration models. Experiments demonstrate that CURE delivers state-of-the-art performance on composite degradation benchmarks, while enabling both selective and jointly fused restoration through flexible modulation of embedding ratios. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/bo-oseng/CURE.

AI.tldr: CURE is a unified framework for controllable image restoration under composite degradations, which learns disentangled representations via four complementary objectives (identity embedding, ratio control, intermediate loss, permutation-invariant loss) and achieves state-of-the-art performance without modifying network architecture.
AI.motivation: Composite degradations (e.g., blur + noise + compression) are challenging because corruption factors interact in complex, interdependent ways. Even when degradation types are known, restoring images accurately is difficult due to intertwined effects and the need for selective control during recovery.
AI.method: CURE introduces four objectives: (1) identity embedding with reconstruction constraint to reproduce input when unnecessary; (2) ratio control mechanism blending identity and degradation-specific embeddings via user-regulated ratios for continuous restoration intensity; (3) intermediate loss supervising stepwise outputs to remove single degradation factors; (4) permutation-invariant loss ensuring consistent quality regardless of degradation order. The framework modifies only training strategy, not architecture.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on composite degradation benchmarks. Enables both selective and jointly fused restoration through flexible modulation of embedding ratios.
AI.conclusion: CURE can be seamlessly integrated into existing controllable restoration models without architectural changes, achieving superior results on complex multi-degradation scenarios.

title: Reason, Reward, Refine: Step-Level Errors Corrections with Structured Feedback for Physics Reasoning in Small Language Models
summary: Physics reasoning fails structurally in small language models: an error at any step propagates forward, corrupting every inference that follows. Limited domain knowledge, hallucination under multi-step derivation, and distributional sensitivity compound this failure. We propose a step-level reward framework that identifies the first reasoning error, generates targeted structured feedback, and trains the model to revise its solution via policy gradient with KL regularization, without exposing it to ground truth solutions as generation targets. Unlike annotation-dependent step-level methods, no preference data construction is required and the external verifier operates exclusively at training time. Across five physics benchmarks, our framework delivers accuracy gains of 17-20% over CoT prompting and 10-16% over the strongest baseline, reduces calculation errors from 56.9% to 23.5%, and reduces miscomprehension errors from 22.3% to 12.0% in the best observed cases. Conceptual errors reduce from 89.7% to 68.7%, yet persist as the hardest failure mode across all conditions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a step-level reward framework that identifies the first reasoning error in physics problems, generates structured feedback, and trains SLMs via policy gradient with KL regularization—without requiring ground-truth solutions or preference data—achieving 17-20% accuracy gains over CoT and significantly reducing calculation, miscomprehension, and conceptual errors.
AI.motivation: Physics reasoning in small language models fails structurally due to error propagation, limited domain knowledge, multi-step hallucination, and distributional sensitivity; existing step-level methods require costly preference data or annotation.
AI.method: A step-level reward framework that detects the first reasoning error, generates targeted structured feedback, and uses policy gradient with KL regularization for revision training; an external verifier operates only at training time with no ground-truth exposure or preference data construction.
AI.result: Accuracy gains of 17-20% over CoT prompting and 10-16% over strongest baseline; calculation errors reduced from 56.9% to 23.5%; miscomprehension errors from 22.3% to 12.0%; conceptual errors from 89.7% to 68.7% (still the hardest failure mode).
AI.conclusion: The step-level reward framework effectively mitigates structural reasoning failures in small LMs without annotation overhead, though conceptual errors remain a persistent challenge.

title: A Temporal Reasoning Benchmarking Framework for LRMs via Difficulty-controlled and Dynamic Test Generation
comment: Accepted to ISSTA 2026. 23 pages including references, 3 figures
summary:
Defining the reasoning boundaries and ensuring the reliability of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) remains a critical challenge. Current benchmarks primarily rely on static datasets susceptible to data contamination or synthetic tasks lacking fine-grained difficulty control. Furthermore, standard outcome-based evaluations often conceal reasoning flaws by neglecting the reasoning process.
  To address these limitations, we introduce TRACE, a testing framework that models temporal reasoning as constraint satisfaction problems via Allen's Interval Algebra. This approach enables precise regulation of logical complexity and incorporates a Trace-Based Verification Oracle to validate reasoning faithfulness. Using this framework, we construct TRACEBench, an extensive benchmark comprising 1,200 synthesized test instances across graded difficulty levels. We employ TRACE to evaluate eight widely used LRMs on TRACEBench. The results confirm a strong negative correlation between model performance and our difficulty metric (Pearson's r approximately -0.96), validating the effectiveness of our difficulty control mechanism. Moreover, our trace-based analysis exposes significant discrepancies between reasoning validity and final answers, revealing a high spurious guessing rate of approximately 28% in mid-sized models. In addition, we diagnose scale-dependent failure modes, ranging from Degenerative Loops in small models to Reasoning Explosion in advanced architectures. TRACE thus provides a robust, automated platform for benchmarking the true temporal reasoning capabilities of LRMs.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a testing framework for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that models temporal reasoning as constraint satisfaction problems using Allen's Interval Algebra, enabling precise difficulty control and verification of reasoning faithfulness. Using TRACEBench (1,200 instances), the authors find a strong negative correlation (r≈-0.96) between model performance and difficulty, reveal a ~28% spurious guessing rate in mid-sized models, and diagnose scale-dependent failure modes like Degenerative Loops and Reasoning Explosion.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for LRMs suffer from static datasets prone to data contamination, synthetic tasks lacking fine-grained difficulty control, and outcome-based evaluations that conceal reasoning flaws by ignoring the reasoning process.
AI.method: TRACE models temporal reasoning as constraint satisfaction problems via Allen's Interval Algebra, incorporates a Trace-Based Verification Oracle to validate reasoning faithfulness, and constructs TRACEBench with 1,200 synthesized test instances across graded difficulty levels.
AI.result: Strong negative correlation (Pearson's r≈-0.96) between model performance and difficulty metric; ~28% spurious guessing rate in mid-sized models; identification of scale-dependent failure modes (Degenerative Loops in small models, Reasoning Explosion in advanced architectures).
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides a robust, automated platform for benchmarking the true temporal reasoning capabilities of LRMs, exposing significant discrepancies between reasoning validity and final answers.

title: Rethinking AI-Generated Text Detection: A Strong Baseline and the Distribution-Shift Problem That Remains
summary: Recent AI-generated text detection work often introduces a new benchmark together with a specialized detector tailored to it. We revisit this practice from a baseline-first perspective. Across several benchmarks, we show that a plain, fully fine-tuned RoBERTa matches or exceeds the specialized detectors those benchmarks are built around. This suggests that much of the recent architectural complexity is not what drives strong in-distribution detection. The remaining challenge is the distribution shift. The same strong baseline degrades sharply when the topic domain or generating model changes at test time, and simply adding more source data does not close the gap. We identify a key failure mode: under distribution shift, the detector can assign high-confidence machine labels to human-written text from unseen domains. We then study two lightweight domain adaptation methods to address this problem: $K$-shot adaptation with first-order MAML over LoRA adapters, and a per-sample confidence-weighted ensemble built on top of the adapted detector. Overall, our results suggest that progress in AI-generated text detection should be measured not only by in-distribution performance, but also by robustness under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: A plain fine-tuned RoBERTa matches or exceeds specialized AI-text detectors in-distribution, but degrades under distribution shift; lightweight domain adaptation (MAML+LoRA and confidence-weighted ensembling) helps, but the core challenge remains robustness to shift.
AI.motivation: Much AI-generated text detection work introduces new benchmarks with specialized detectors, but it is unclear whether architectural complexity actually drives performance. The authors revisit this from a baseline-first perspective to assess whether simpler models suffice and where real challenges lie.
AI.method: (1) Compare a fully fine-tuned RoBERTa against specialized detectors across multiple benchmarks. (2) Evaluate distribution shift robustness (topic domain & generating model changes). (3) Apply two lightweight domain adaptation methods: K-shot adaptation with first-order MAML over LoRA adapters, and a per-sample confidence-weighted ensemble built on top.
AI.result: RoBERTa matches/exceeds specialized detectors in-distribution. Under distribution shift, performance degrades sharply; a key failure mode is assigning high-confidence machine labels to human-written text from unseen domains. Adding more source data does not close the gap.
AI.conclusion: Progress in AI-generated text detection should be measured by in-distribution performance and robustness under distribution shift; lightweight domain adaptation methods offer some mitigation but the distribution shift problem remains a central challenge.

title: Text-to-Image Generation for Projector-Camera System Registration
summary: Establishing correspondence between projector and camera images in a procam (projector + camera) system is essential for achieving high-resolution pixel matching, referred to as procam registration. The highest accuracy is typically obtained using structured light patterns (e.g., stripes or blobs). However, these methods are often inefficient and lack meaningful information for human viewers. Although some have explored the use of natural images, these often fail to provide a sufficient distribution of features to achieve comparable accuracy. Additionally, existing methods struggle to cope with environmental factors such as surface textures and variations in brightness due to ambient light or changes in camera exposure. To address these limitations, we propose a method based on deep neural networks. Our approach aims to generate a single natural image from text-based prompts that not only appears realistic but also possesses rich spatial features to enhance registration accuracy in procam applications. We have developed a deep neural network trained on a synthesized dataset that simulates potential geometric and photometric distortions encountered in a procam system illuminating a relatively smooth object (see Figure 1). Our trained network predicts the correspondence between projector and camera images, significantly improving registration accuracy across various procam configurations. By jointly considering the naturalness and feature richness of the projector images, our method minimizes visual disruptions in projected content without sacrificing precision. A user study confirms that our technique enhances perceived naturalness and usability compared to existing methods, validating its practical utility in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep neural network method that generates a single natural image from text prompts, rich in spatial features, to improve projector-camera registration accuracy while maintaining visual naturalness, outperforming traditional structured light and natural image approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing procam registration methods using structured light patterns achieve high accuracy but are inefficient and lack meaningful visual information for viewers. Natural image methods fail to provide sufficient feature distribution for comparable accuracy and struggle with environmental factors like surface textures and brightness variations.
AI.method: A deep neural network trained on a synthesized dataset simulating geometric and photometric distortions in procam systems. The network generates a single natural image from text-based prompts that balances visual realism with rich spatial features, then predicts correspondence between projector and camera images.
AI.result: Significantly improved registration accuracy across various procam configurations. A user study confirmed enhanced perceived naturalness and usability compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method minimizes visual disruptions in projected content without sacrificing registration precision, validating its practical utility in real-world procam applications.

title: EvoAgentBench: Benchmarking Agent Self-Evolution via Ability Transfer
summary: Agent self-evolution in long-horizon LLM systems is largely procedural: useful experience is not merely stored information, but reusable procedures for searching, debugging, and verification. Yet current evaluations do not isolate this form of transfer. Agent benchmarks test single-episode task solving; memory benchmarks target information retention rather than procedural reuse. We introduce EvoAgentBench, a benchmark for agent self-evolution via Ability-guided transfer across four agentic domains: web research, algorithmic reasoning, software engineering, and knowledge work. EvoAgentBench extracts trace-grounded Abilities from agent executions, canonicalizes them into operational units, and builds domain-specific Ability Graphs linking tasks that share procedural overlap. By design, every test task is backed by verified training-side Ability support. Across a 528/267 train/test split, two scaffolds, and three backbones, curated Ability content transfers reliably across model families, but no current automatic method sustains positive gain in all settings. EvoAgentBench shifts self-evolution evaluation from aggregate accuracy comparison to fine-grained diagnosis of experience encoding, routing, and uptake. The benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/EverMind-AI/EvoAgentBench.

AI.tldr: EvoAgentBench is a new benchmark that evaluates agent self-evolution through procedural ability transfer across four domains (web research, algorithmic reasoning, software engineering, knowledge work), using trace-grounded Ability Graphs. Results show curated ability content transfers reliably but no automatic method sustains positive gains universally.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks fail to isolate procedural reuse — agent benchmarks test single-episode task solving, while memory benchmarks test information retention rather than reusable procedures (searching, debugging, verification). Agent self-evolution needs evaluation of how experience transfers as operational procedures.
AI.method: EvoAgentBench extracts trace-grounded "Abilities" from agent executions, canonicalizes them into operational units, and builds domain-specific Ability Graphs linking procedurally overlapping tasks. Uses a 528/267 train/test split across two scaffolds and three backbone models.
AI.result: Curated Ability content transfers reliably across model families, but no current automatic method achieves sustained positive gain in all settings across all four domains.
AI.conclusion: EvoAgentBench shifts self-evolution evaluation from aggregate accuracy comparison to fine-grained diagnosis of experience encoding, routing, and uptake, highlighting the gap between curated and automatic ability transfer.

title: An Exploration of Agentic Information Fusion for Test Maintenance Prediction
summary:
Test maintenance is a critical, yet costly, activity - particularly as codebases rapidly evolve. To assist, we present MAST, a multi-agent framework that predicts which test cases require maintenance following changes to the production code. This identification task is necessary as a precondition to any subsequent maintenance activities, but remains challenging due to the complex relationships between production and test code. MAST advances the state-of-the-art by integrating multiple analyses -- including static, lexical, and semantic analyses - through an intelligent fusion and post-check procedure and by focusing on a realistic use and evaluation setting - i.e., standardized input formats, repository-level analyses, and the ability to infer relations between test and production artifacts rather than assuming a pre-existing mapping.
  We evaluated MAST on 21 industrial Java repositories from Ericsson AB, considering situations where test maintenance both was and was not required in the ground truth. MAST yielded superior precision to a state-of-the-art baseline - resulting in a higher accuracy, F1, and F2 score - with only some loss in recall. Our ablation study demonstrates the value of each analysis in producing the final recommendations. MAST illustrates the potential of multi-agent systems that can fuse multiple information sources when performing software testing tasks.

AI.tldr: MAST is a multi-agent framework that predicts which test cases need maintenance after production code changes, using fused static, lexical, and semantic analyses. Evaluated on 21 industrial Java repositories from Ericsson, it achieves superior precision and F-scores over baselines, with some recall loss.
AI.motivation: Test maintenance is critical yet costly as codebases evolve. Identifying which test cases require maintenance after production code changes is necessary but challenging due to complex production-test code relationships.
AI.method: MAST is a multi-agent framework integrating static, lexical, and semantic analyses through intelligent fusion and post-check. It uses standardized input formats, repository-level analyses, and infers production-test relations instead of assuming pre-existing mappings.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 industrial Java repositories from Ericsson, MAST achieved superior precision, accuracy, F1, and F2 scores compared to a state-of-the-art baseline, with only some recall loss. Ablation study confirmed the value of each analysis component.
AI.conclusion: MAST demonstrates the potential of multi-agent systems fusing multiple information sources for software testing tasks, advancing the state-of-the-art in test maintenance prediction.

title: PIEFS: Physics-Informed Eigenfunction Features with Learnable Scaling
summary: Spectral methods are widely used to construct representations from the geometry of data, but they often rely on a fixed kernel, graph Laplacian, or manually selected feature scaling. We propose Physics-Informed Eigenfunction Features with Learnable Scaling (PIEFS), a supervised neural representation-learning framework with a spectral inductive bias, based on a modified Dirichlet energy. In PIEFS, scalar coordinate maps are trained under empirical Gram orthogonality, a supervised linear readout, and a Dirichlet penalty in which the input gradient is transformed by a learnable metric $A(x)=Λ(x)U(x)$. The diagonal factor $Λ(x)$ controls anisotropic scaling, while the orthogonal factor $U(x)$ is parameterized by a structured product of Givens rotations. This construction yields task-adaptive Dirichlet-regularized coordinates rather than eigenfunctions of a fixed supervision-independent operator. Experiments on synthetic, tabular, and image-based benchmarks study the effect of identity, diagonal, and rotation-scaling metrics, and compare the resulting coordinates with classical baselines and NeuralEF. The results support PIEFS as a compact supervised spectral representation method and identify optimization stability, validation on explicit operator eigenproblems, and richer metric parameterizations as the main directions for future work.

AI.tldr: PIEFS is a supervised neural representation-learning framework that uses a learnable metric (with anisotropic scaling via diagonal factors and rotations via Givens products) within a modified Dirichlet energy to produce task-adaptive spectral coordinates, outperforming fixed-kernel spectral methods and NeuralEF on synthetic, tabular, and image benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Spectral methods for data representations rely on fixed kernels, graph Laplacians, or manually selected feature scaling, limiting their adaptability to downstream tasks.
AI.method: PIEFS trains scalar coordinate maps under three losses: (1) empirical Gram orthogonality, (2) supervised linear readout, and (3) a Dirichlet penalty with a learnable metric A(x)=Λ(x)U(x), where Λ(x) is a diagonal factor for anisotropic scaling and U(x) is an orthogonal factor parameterized by a structured product of Givens rotations.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic, tabular, and image benchmarks show PIEFS outperforms classical spectral baselines and NeuralEF, with the rotation-scaling metric providing the most task-adaptive representations.
AI.conclusion: PIEFS is a compact supervised spectral representation method; future work should focus on optimization stability, validation on explicit operator eigenproblems, and richer metric parameterizations.

title: RIGS-Refiner: Risk-Guided Recursive Refinement in Prediction Space for Colonoscopy Polyp Segmentation
summary: Post-refinement can improve colonoscopy segmentation after host inference, but many designs still rely on extra correction heads or multi-stage pipelines with non-negligible parameter or computational cost. For polyp segmentation, host predictions are often already reasonable globally, with remaining errors clustered around ambiguous boundaries and difficult local structures. These residual errors matter in colonoscopy images because useful masks need correct lesion coverage and clean contour delineation across subtle mucosal transitions. This setting favors selective local repair in prediction space over reprocessing the entire mask. We therefore propose RIGS-Refiner, a lightweight post-refinement plugin for risk-guided recursive refinement in prediction space. Starting from a frozen host anchor prediction, RIGS-Refiner extracts lightweight image priors and prediction cues, applies risk-guided update, and writes back residual corrections through a shared recursive cell. The module adds only +519 parameters and +0.631 GFLOPs, keeping the refinement path compact for deployment. Experiments use Kvasir-SEG for training and Kvasir, ClinicDB, ColonDB, and ETIS for evaluation under two frozen hosts, namely PraNet and SegFormer-B0. Results show consistent gains on both hosts and a favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-off against representative post-refinement methods. Code is available at https://github.com/tyui99/RIGS-Refiner.

AI.tldr: RIGS-Refiner is a lightweight post-refinement plugin for colonoscopy/polyp segmentation that uses risk-guided recursive refinement in prediction space, adding only +519 parameters and +0.631 GFLOPs, achieving consistent segmentation improvements on Kvasir-SEG, Kvasir, ClinicDB, ColonDB, and ETIS datasets with PraNet and SegFormer-B0 hosts.
AI.motivation: Host predictions for polyp segmentation are often globally reasonable but have clustered residual errors around ambiguous boundaries and subtle mucosal transitions. Existing post-refinement methods rely on extra correction heads or multi-stage pipelines with non-negligible parameter/computational cost. There is a need for selective local repair in prediction space rather than full mask reprocessing.
AI.method: RIGS-Refiner: a risk-guided recursive refinement plugin operating in prediction space. It extracts lightweight image priors and prediction cues from a frozen host anchor prediction, applies risk-guided update, and writes back residual corrections through a shared recursive cell. The refinement path is compact (+519 params, +0.631 GFLOPs).
AI.result: Consistent segmentation gains on Kvasir-SEG, Kvasir, ClinicDB, ColonDB, and ETIS datasets using two frozen hosts (PraNet and SegFormer-B0). Achieves favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-off against representative post-refinement methods.
AI.conclusion: RIGS-Refiner demonstrates that lightweight, selective local repair in prediction space is effective for polyp segmentation refinement, offering a parameter-efficient and computationally cheap alternative to existing post-refinement approaches.

title: MoP-JEPA: Hard-Assigned Predictor Mixtures for Stochastic JEPA World Models
summary: JEPA world models predict the next latent state with a single deterministic predictor trained by latent regression. We show that this fails structurally when the environment is stochastic: at a branching transition, the regression-optimal predictor outputs the conditional mean of the successor embeddings, a point between the true next states that corresponds to no state at all. We prove this collapse for deterministic and gated mixture-of-experts predictors, and prove that MoP-JEPA's hard-assigned predictors converge instead to a quantizer of the transition distribution: one head per successor mode, enumerable in a single forward pass, which is the interface a planner consumes. On official OGBench offline data with leak-free evaluation, planning over single-predictor rollouts performs poorly ($0.02$--$0.09$ success) while planning over our predicted modes reaches up to $0.85$, ahead of deterministic, gated-MoE, and variational predictors on every task. Because multi-prediction evaluation invites coverage freeloading, a verification protocol is part of the method: an input-agnostic codebook control, a shuffled-context test, router-gated readouts, transition-precision guards, and a verified-route criterion in which the model proposes its transition graph blind and ground truth is used only to check the result. Under this criterion our method outperforms the strongest soft alternative on all three mazes ($2$--$5\times$), and the protocol identifies the remaining gap in that baseline's raw scores as routes through predicted transitions that do not exist. The same model executes in the real environment, placing second of seven against the published OGBench baselines on the hardest maze. Multimodal dynamics decide whether a JEPA world model can plan at all; a mixture of predictors with hard assignment is a minimal and verifiable fix.

AI.tldr: JEPA world models fail under stochastic dynamics because regression-optimal predictors collapse to meaningless conditional means. The paper proposes MoP-JEPA with hard-assigned mixture-of-predictors heads that quantize transition distributions, enabling effective planning (0.85 success vs 0.02-0.09 for single-predictor) and introduces a verification protocol to prevent coverage freeloading. The method outperforms baselines on OGBench mazes and validates with real-world execution.
AI.motivation: Standard JEPA world models use a single deterministic predictor trained via latent regression, which structurally fails in stochastic environments. At branching transitions, the regression objective produces the conditional mean of successor embeddings—a point that does not correspond to any real state—making planning impossible. The paper aims to fix this collapse and enable reliable planning under multimodal dynamics.
AI.method: The method replaces the single predictor with a mixture-of-predictors (MoP) using hard assignment (MoP-JEPA), where each predictor head specializes to one successor mode, producing a quantizer of the transition distribution enumerable in one forward pass. A verification protocol is introduced: input-agnostic codebook control, shuffled-context test, router-gated readouts, transition-precision guards, and a verified-route criterion where the model proposes transitions blind and ground truth only checks results.
AI.result: Single-predictor rollouts achieve only 0.02-0.09 success on OGBench offline data; MoP-JEPA reaches up to 0.85 success, outperforming deterministic, gated-MoE, and variational predictors on every task. Under the verified-route criterion, MoP outperforms the strongest soft alternative by 2-5× on all three mazes. The protocol identifies the baseline's scores as partly inflated by non-existent transitions. In real-world execution, MoP-JEPA places second of seven on the hardest maze.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal dynamics determine whether a JEPA world model can plan at all. A mixture of predictors with hard assignment provides a minimal and verifiable fix for planning under stochastic transitions, and the verification protocol is essential to detect coverage freeloading and ensure predicted transitions correspond to actual environment dynamics.

title: E-CoDrive: A Co-Simulation Framework for Testing Energy-Critical Driving Scenarios
comment: In proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26) - Tools and Datasets track
summary: Autonomous driving research has largely focused on safety while giving limited attention to non-functional aspects such as energy consumption and sustainability. As Autonomous Electric Vehicles (AEVs) become increasingly common in urban traffic, understanding how complex traffic dynamics influence their energy consumption is paramount to test whether AEVs can complete trips before battery depletion. To support energy-aware scenario-based testing of AEVs, we present E-CoDrive, a framework for reproducible closed-loop driving co-simulations that integrates an energy consumption model, a micro-traffic simulator, and a high-fidelity driving simulator to test AEV software stacks in urban scenarios. This tool paper describes the architecture of E-CoDrive and demonstrates its applicability by testing an Autoware-based AEV stack. Our evaluation shows that varying traffic conditions produce substantial differences in vehicle energy consumption. The artifact is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32244783, and a screencast showing the tool is available at https://youtu.be/yX9fWHqCvgc.

AI.tldr: A framework called E-CoDrive is presented for energy-aware scenario-based testing of Autonomous Electric Vehicles (AEVs) through closed-loop driving co-simulations integrating energy consumption, micro-traffic, and high-fidelity driving simulators.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving research has largely focused on safety while giving limited attention to non-functional aspects such as energy consumption and sustainability. Understanding how complex traffic dynamics influence AEV energy consumption is paramount to test whether AEVs can complete trips before battery depletion.
AI.method: E-CoDrive is a framework for reproducible closed-loop driving co-simulations that integrates an energy consumption model, a micro-traffic simulator, and a high-fidelity driving simulator to test AEV software stacks in urban scenarios.
AI.result: Varying traffic conditions produce substantial differences in vehicle energy consumption, demonstrated by testing an Autoware-based AEV stack.
AI.conclusion: E-CoDrive enables energy-aware scenario-based testing of AEVs, supporting assessment of whether AEVs can complete trips before battery depletion under different traffic dynamics.

title: Social Networks of LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in interacting populations, raising the question of what such populations come to believe collectively. Whether a population aggregates genuine knowledge or collapses into a false consensus directly affects how much such systems can be trusted. Classical social-network models assume that the network itself determines how beliefs combine. This assumption breaks down for LLM agents, whose limited attention takes in only part of what they are exposed to, so these models overstate how much information a population actually pools and cannot tell genuine consensus from herding. We introduce SNLA, a framework that models how much each agent actually influences others, rather than merely how the network connects them. This influence depends on each agent's position in the network and on how sharply attention focuses. Theoretically, we show on a tractable proxy that narrow attention causes herding, where the effective sample size stays bounded regardless of population size, while wide attention recovers wisdom-of-crowds behavior only when the exposure graph is undirected and degree-regular. Empirically, a controlled testbed validates these predictions directly, and the herding-wisdom transition reproduces on operator-controlled variants of three multi-agent LLM benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SNLA models belief formation in LLM agent populations, showing that narrow attention causes herding (bounded effective sample size) while wide attention recovers wisdom-of-crowds only under specific network conditions, validated on a controlled testbed and three multi-agent LLM benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Classical social-network models assume the network itself determines belief aggregation, but this assumption fails for LLM agents whose limited attention only captures part of their exposure, causing overestimation of information pooling and inability to distinguish genuine consensus from herding.
AI.method: The paper introduces SNLA (Social Network with Limited Attention), a framework that models each agent's actual influence based on network position and attention sharpness, rather than just connectivity. Theoretical analysis uses a tractable proxy, and empirical validation uses a controlled testbed and three multi-agent LLM benchmarks.
AI.result: Narrow attention causes herding with bounded effective sample size regardless of population size; wide attention recovers wisdom-of-crowds only when the exposure graph is undirected and degree-regular. Predictions are validated in a controlled testbed and reproduced on operator-controlled variants of three multi-agent LLM benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The herding-wisdom transition depends on attention breadth and network structure, with implications for trustworthiness of LLM agent populations.

title: Lightweight Polyp Segmentation via a Gain-Aware Prediction-Space Recursive Controller
summary: While lightweight polyp segmentation is highly desirable for low-cost deployment, reported performance gains often stem from upgraded backbone encoders, complex decoders, or heavy refinement branches. Consequently, it remains difficult to isolate whether a lightweight correction mechanism is inherently effective on its own. We address this limitation by formulating refinement as a prediction-space recursive correction task, introducing a recursive controller that operates directly on backbone logits. Under a fixed recursion budget, this controller aggregates discrepancy and uncertainty evidence, updates a compact state tracking recent correction utility, and applies additive residual logit corrections. By design, this correction path remains small, host-portable, and deployment-explicit. Utilizing a unified Kvasir-trained protocol, we evaluate our approach across seven lightweight backbones on Kvasir-SEG and three transfer datasets, measuring segmentation accuracy (Dice/IoU) alongside deployment efficiency (parameters, GMACs, and peak memory). The controller yields consistent improvements in the source domain, achieves competitive performance against both training-side baselines and heavier structural refiners on representative hosts, and delivers selective transfer gains with minimal static overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/tyui99/Gain-Aware-Prediction-Space-Recursive-Controller.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, prediction-space recursive controller for polyp segmentation that refines backbone logits using discrepancy and uncertainty evidence, achieving consistent improvements across multiple backbones and datasets with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing lightweight polyp segmentation methods often conflate gains from backbone upgrades or complex decoders with the effectiveness of the correction mechanism itself. The authors aim to isolate and evaluate a purely lightweight, host-portable refinement approach that works directly on prediction logits.
AI.method: A recursive controller operates on backbone logits under a fixed recursion budget. It aggregates discrepancy and uncertainty evidence, updates a compact state tracking recent correction utility, and applies additive residual logit corrections. The correction path is small, host-portable, and deployment-explicit.
AI.result: Evaluated on Kvasir-SEG and three transfer datasets with seven lightweight backbones, the controller yields consistent improvements in the source domain, achieves competitive performance against training-side baselines and heavier refiners, and delivers selective transfer gains with minimal static overhead.
AI.conclusion: The proposed recursive correction mechanism is inherently effective on its own, offering a lightweight, plug-and-play refinement module that improves segmentation accuracy without requiring complex decoder redesigns or heavy structural modifications.

title: MetaSkill-Evolve: Recursive Self-Improvement of LLM Agents via Two-Timescale Meta-Skill Evolution
summary: Recent LLM agents tackle increasingly long-horizon, open-ended tasks, and external skills, reusable procedural knowledge supplied to the agent, further extend this capability. However, a fixed, hand-authored skill is rarely optimal, and cannot adapt to the diversity of tasks an agent encounters. Self-improving agents address this by rewriting their own skill files from execution traces, yielding meaningful gains on challenging benchmarks. Yet such self-evolution remains non-recursive: it improves only the task skill (what the agent does) while the improvement procedure (how it improves) is authored once and held fixed. We introduce MetaSkill-Evolve, a two-timescale framework that makes agentic skill improvement recursive: every branch carries both a task skill $s$ and a branch-local meta-skill $m=(ψ,σ,α,π,\varepsilon)$ whose five components parameterise the Analyzer, Retriever, Allocator, Proposer, and Evolver agents of the improvement pipeline. Task skills evolve on a fast loop while the meta-skill evolves on a slower one under the same pipeline applied to itself, with no additional model or objective. With all five pipeline agents sharing a single frozen backbone, MetaSkill-Evolve outperforms no-skill, static-skill, and single-level evolution baselines on three agentic benchmarks (OfficeQA, SealQA, ALFWorld), improving held-out test accuracy over the raw backbone by +23.54, +16.09, and +1.92 points respectively.

AI.tldr: MetaSkill-Evolve introduces a recursive two-timescale framework where both task skills and meta-skills (the improvement procedure itself) evolve, enabling self-improving agents to not only refine what they do but also how they improve.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improving agents can rewrite task skills from execution traces but the improvement procedure remains fixed and non-recursive, limiting adaptability across diverse tasks.
AI.method: A two-timescale framework where task skills evolve on a fast loop and meta-skills (parameterized by five components: Analyzer, Retriever, Allocator, Proposer, Evolver) evolve on a slower loop under the same pipeline applied to itself, using a single frozen backbone with no additional model or objective.
AI.result: Outperforms no-skill, static-skill, and single-level evolution baselines on OfficeQA (+23.54), SealQA (+16.09), and ALFWorld (+1.92) in held-out test accuracy over the raw backbone.
AI.conclusion: Recursive meta-skill evolution enables more effective and adaptive agentic improvement, achieving significant gains across diverse benchmarks with minimal overhead.

title: Teaching LLMs a Low-Resource Language: Enhancing Code Completion in Pharo
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) unlocked new possibilities in automated code writing, becoming the backbone of most code completion tools. While LLMs excel in mainstream languages, they often lack support for the so-called low-resource languages where training data is scarce. As a result, these languages lag behind in the quality of code completion tooling available to their communities. A concrete example is Pharo, a Smalltalk-inspired language whose IDE currently offers only single-token completion. In this work, we report on our experience bringing LLM-based code completion to Pharo. First, we describe an end-to-end pipeline that combines Pharo-specific data curation, continued pre-training and fine-tuning of open code LLMs. Second, we introduce a set of Pharo code completion benchmarks designed to evaluate whether models (i) learn Pharo's syntax and (ii) accurately complete masked Pharo code from real-world GitHub repositories.
