Through experiments on various datasets, we demonstrate that OCDM effectively infers the causal structure of multistage processes, outperforming existing methods.

AI.tldr: OCDM is a novel causal discovery method for multistage processes that incorporates hierarchical/sequential process knowledge to infer causal structures, using a knowledge-informed order-inferring algorithm and a stochastic gated neural network pruning technique for computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods produce counterintuitive results for multistage processes and lack computational efficiency for large datasets, despite multistage processes being prevalent across many fields.
AI.method: OCDM consists of two key components: (1) a structural knowledge-informed order-inferring algorithm that determines causal order by incorporating stage-origin information of variables within an order-based causal discovery framework; (2) a pruning technique using stochastic gated neural networks to eliminate spurious edges from the initial causal graph.
AI.result: Experiments on various datasets demonstrate that OCDM effectively infers the causal structure of multistage processes and outperforms existing methods.
AI.conclusion: OCDM addresses the gap in causal discovery for multistage processes by explicitly incorporating process knowledge (hierarchical and sequential structure) and improving computational efficiency.

title: Semantic Segmentation-Driven Image-Level Diagnosis of Liver Cancers in Hematoxylin and Eosin Histopathology Images
summary: As hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) staining constitutes the primary entry point in routine diagnostic workflows, computer-aided diagnosis from whole-slide H&E images is of particular clinical relevance. However, substantial variability in specimen preparation, staining protocols, and scanning conditions, together with inherent uncertainty in expert pixel-level annotations, makes automated analysis of H&E-stained images challenging. In this study, we propose a semantic segmentation-based framework for image-level diagnosis, grounded in the clinically motivated assumption that each histopathological image corresponds to a single cancer type. Image-level predictions are obtained by assigning the class of the dominant pixel-level label in the segmentation output. To ensure clinical relevance, we adopt the nnU-Net architecture and train it on a publicly available dataset collected in our study with pixel-level annotations for three liver cancer types: hepatocellular cacrcinoma (HCC; 55 images from 30 patients), cholangiocellular carcinoma (CCA; 55 images from 29 patients), and colorectal metastatic adenocarcinoma (CMA; 60 images from 30 patients). Annotations were independently provided by four pathologist. We hypothesize that the combination of stain normalization and semantic segmentation mitigates domain shift and reduces sensitivity to annotation noise. Five-fold cross-validation yielded balanced accuracy of 0.975 (HCC), 0.950 (CCA), and 1.000 (CMA), comparable to results obtained with immunohosthochemical staining and superior to several deep learning models trained on patch-level annotations. The proposed framework has the potential to support pathologists in prioritizing immunohistochemical marker selection, thereby reducing diagnostic costs and turnaround time. Integration with immunohistochemical findings improve overall diagnostic reliability.

AI.tldr: A semantic segmentation framework (nnU-Net) using H&E-stained whole-slide images achieves high diagnostic accuracy (0.975-1.000 balanced accuracy) for three liver cancer types by converting pixel-level predictions to image-level diagnoses, outperforming patch-level deep learning models and approaching immunohistochemistry-level performance.
AI.motivation: H&E staining is the primary entry point in routine diagnostic workflows, but variability in specimen preparation, staining protocols, scanning conditions, and uncertainty in expert annotations make automated analysis challenging. The study aims to develop a clinically relevant computer-aided diagnosis framework from H&E images.
AI.method: A semantic segmentation-based framework (nnU-Net) for image-level diagnosis, assuming each image corresponds to a single cancer type. Image-level predictions are obtained by assigning the class of the dominant pixel-level label. Trained on a dataset of 170 images with pixel-level annotations from four pathologists for HCC, CCA, and CMA. Stain normalization is combined with semantic segmentation to mitigate domain shift and annotation noise.
AI.result: Five-fold cross-validation yielded balanced accuracy of 0.975 (HCC), 0.950 (CCA), and 1.000 (CMA), comparable to immunohistochemical staining and superior to several patch-level deep learning models.
AI.conclusion: The framework has potential to support pathologists in prioritizing immunohistochemical marker selection, reducing diagnostic costs and turnaround time. Integration with immunohistochemical findings can improve overall diagnostic reliability.

title: Auto: The AGI Compiler
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, 1 algorithm. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/auto
summary: Every LLM agent run re-derives its behavior token by token on a frontier model: brilliant, expensive, slow, and unbounded. We present Auto, a compiler that records live agent behavior, measures which parts are secretly deterministic, extracts them into verified programs or distilled specialists, and emits cognition binaries: WebAssembly artifacts whose manifests carry measured guarantees and whose declared capabilities are physically enforced by the sandbox. A tiered runtime executes compiled behavior behind conformally calibrated guards; guard trips deopt to the reference agent, and the captured trace recompiles back down, so nothing is figured out twice. We use "AGI compiler" in one narrow, testable sense: a system that autonomously converts novel experience into permanent, verified, near-free skill while measuring what it does not know. On AUTO-BENCH, a benchmark we introduce and pre-register, 87.1% of 560 recorded frontier-agent spans are witnessed-deterministic (three of the four censused task families measure 100.0%). On a 300-item stream with three scheduled distribution shifts, the closed loop compiles three artifact generations and drives marginal cost from 59 to 2 micro-dollars per item (6.4x end-to-end) at 96.9% parity on witnessed inputs with zero errors. The same stream also quantifies the failure modes: a loose guard silently mislabels 48.9% of compiled answers, and an unfaithful deopt reference causes the verification gate to refuse recompilation. Calibration and reference fidelity, not model capability, decide whether cheap stays correct. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/auto

AI.tldr: Auto is a compiler that records LLM agent behavior, extracts deterministic parts into verified programs, and emits sandboxed WebAssembly artifacts. In a benchmark, it achieves 87.1% determinism, reduces cost from 59 to 2 micro-dollars per item (96.9% parity), but reveals critical failure modes when guards are loose or reference fidelity is poor.
AI.motivation: LLM agents re-derive behavior token-by-token on frontier models, which is expensive, slow, and unbounded. The authors aim to convert novel agent experience into permanent, verified, near-free skill while measuring what remains unknown.
AI.method: Auto records live agent behavior, identifies deterministic segments, extracts them into verified programs or distilled specialists, and compiles them into WebAssembly cognition binaries with capability-sandboxed execution. A tiered runtime uses calibrating guards—guard trips trigger deopt to the reference agent and recompilation with captured traces.
AI.result: On AUTO-BENCH, 87.1% of 560 frontier-agent spans are witnessed-deterministic. On a 300-item stream with three distribution shifts, cost drops from 59 to 2 micro-dollars per item (6.4x end-to-end) at 96.9% parity with zero errors. Loose guards cause 48.9% mislabeling; unfaithful deopt references cause verification gate failures.
AI.conclusion: Calibration and reference fidelity—not model capability—determine whether cheap inference remains correct. The system demonstrates that most agent behavior is secretly deterministic and can be compiled into efficient, verified artifacts, but robustness depends on guard precision and reference trustworthiness.

title: MANCE: Manifold Aware Concept Erasure
summary: Concept erasure aims to remove a target concept from a representation while preserving the other information encoded in it. This is difficult because representations encode many concepts that are often correlated with the erasure target, so removing the target risks damaging them. We propose the Manifold Constraint Hypothesis (MCH): if natural representations concentrate on a structured, lower-dimensional manifold, then interventions should be constrained to that manifold and better preserve other information encoded in the representation during interventions. We instantiate MCH in a new concept erasure method: MANifold aware Concept Erasure (MANCE). MANCE performs iterative updates to the representations using signals from a classifier that predicts a target concept. We estimate the manifold using representations obtained from natural inputs, and then we project the concept removal update to the estimated manifold. We perform extensive evaluation on 119 settings spanning text and vision, including 13 language models, three NLP concepts, and 40 CelebA-CLIP attributes. Employing MANCE on top of previous methods shows consistent improved leakage results. We also introduce MANCE+ and MANCE++, which prepend a closed-form erasure algorithm before employing MANCE, achieving better leakage--surgicality tradeoffs relative to matched full-space updates. MANCE++, our best method, achieves state-of-the-art results on nonlinear concept erasure. These results support MCH in the erasure setting: interventions should be constrained to the natural representation manifold.

AI.tldr: MANCE constrains concept erasure interventions to the natural representation manifold, achieving state-of-the-art leakage-surgicality tradeoffs across 119 text and vision settings.
AI.motivation: Representations encode many correlated concepts, so removing a target concept risks damaging other encoded information; existing methods struggle with this tradeoff.
AI.method: Proposes Manifold Constraint Hypothesis (MCH) — interventions should stay on the natural data manifold. Instantiates as MANCE: iteratively update representations via classifier signals, estimate the manifold from natural inputs, and project removal updates onto it. MANCE+ and MANCE++ prepend closed-form erasure before MANCE for better tradeoffs.
AI.result: Evaluated on 119 settings (13 LMs, 3 NLP concepts, 40 CelebA-CLIP attributes). MANCE improves leakage over previous methods; MANCE++ achieves state-of-the-art nonlinear concept erasure.
AI.conclusion: Results support MCH: constraining interventions to the natural representation manifold better preserves other information while removing target concepts.

title: A Decomposable Probe for Few-Step Diffusion Models: Prompt, Latent, and Score Selectivity across Backbone Families and Distillation Paradigms
summary: Few-step distilled diffusion students cut text-to-image inference from ~50 to 1-8 network evaluations, but the quality gap is usually summarised by a single FID/CLIP scalar that cannot say which axis of the conditioning response changed, nor whether a behaviour comes from the architecture, the distillation objective, or simply from being a diffusion model. We replace the scalar with a decomposable probe that injects controlled perturbations along three layers (prompt encoder, denoiser input, denoiser output) under three modes (mean, variance, scale) and six strengths, reporting a bootstrap-median Bures W2^2 selectivity ratio on Inception features. Under a single matched estimator across 23 models -- five teachers and 18 distilled students spanning five backbone families (SDXL, SD1.5, SD3.5, PixArt-alpha, FLUX), three architecture classes (UNet, DiT, MMDiT), and five distillation paradigms -- the three layers read three empirically separable factors: the prompt layer is a universal prompt-mean response (a sanity channel, not a discriminator), the latent layer reads the prediction type, and the score layer reads the distillation objective. Our main result: within this sweep, the latent layer is a near-binary detector of rectified-flow backbones. Its ratio exceeds 1 across a sustained low-to-mid band only for rectified-flow models (SD3.5, FLUX); no epsilon-prediction model qualifies. A matched epsilon-prediction control (PixArt-alpha) rules out wide-T5 conditioning, and the fingerprint survives adversarial (ADD) distillation as both teacher and student. Two secondary score-layer findings hold under narrower scopes: a canonical 4-step ADD-vs-rest contrast on the UNet families with a non-ADD baseline, and a CI-separated trajectory-rollout early-strength score spike on both UNet and DiT. All ratios are CI-citable under one estimator; we release the per-cell tables and the estimator.

AI.tldr: Replaces scalar FID/CLIP metrics with a decomposable probe that injects controlled perturbations across three layers (prompt, latent, score) to empirically separate factors of diffusion model behavior, finding that the latent layer acts as a near-binary detector of rectified-flow backbones.
AI.motivation: Single scalar metrics (FID/CLIP) cannot diagnose which axis of conditioning response changed in distilled diffusion models, nor attribute behavior to architecture, distillation objective, or being a diffusion model.
AI.method: Designs a decomposable probe injecting controlled perturbations along three layers (prompt encoder, denoiser input/latent, denoiser output/score) under three modes (mean, variance, scale) and six strengths, computing bootstrap-median Bures W2^2 selectivity ratio on Inception features across 23 models.
AI.result: Three layers read three separable factors: prompt layer = universal prompt-mean response, latent layer = prediction type (near-binary detector of rectified-flow backbones; ratio >1 only for SD3.5, FLUX), score layer = distillation objective. Secondary findings: 4-step ADD-vs-rest contrast on UNet, and CI-separated trajectory-rollout early-strength score spike.
AI.conclusion: The latent layer is a robust, near-binary fingerprint for rectified-flow backbones, surviving adversarial distillation; the probe provides CI-citable per-cell selectivity ratios under a single estimator.

title: Beyond the Need for Speed: Energy-Aware Code Generation via Simulation-Guided Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Code models strictly prioritize functional correctness, leaving software energy efficiency as an unoptimized byproduct. Training models to generate energy-efficient code requires reproducible feedback at scale, which physical hardware measurement cannot reliably provide due to variance.
  In this paper, we replace hardware profiling with a deterministic architectural simulation harness to build Green Tea, a corpus of $3.5$ million evaluations across $1{,}474$ C++ problems. We train an energy-aware code model via supervised fine-tuning on energy-contrastive pairs, followed by closed-loop reinforcement learning (GRPO) using simulation-in-the-loop feedback. To rigorously evaluate deployment readiness, we introduce the Correctness-Adjusted Reduction in Energy Total (CARET), a metric that explicitly penalizes code that sacrifices functionality for efficiency.
  On $143$ held-out problems, our simulation-in-the-loop pipeline achieves $12.63\%$ CARET, nearly tripling the gain of fine-tuning alone, and successfully beats the energy efficiency of human-expert references on $58.4\%$ of its valid outputs. Furthermore, our analysis exposes the IPC trap: standard throughput proxies like Instructions-Per-Cycle (IPC) actively misrank true energy efficiency on $67.8\%$ of problems, proving the absolute necessity of direct energy simulation. By releasing our dataset and infrastructure, we bypass the $263{,}000$ CPU-hours required for reproduction, structurally empowering the community to deploy inherently energy-efficient code generation models.

AI.tldr: Green Tea replaces hardware profiling with deterministic architectural simulation to generate energy-contrastive training data, fine-tunes code models via supervised learning and GRPO reinforcement learning with simulation feedback, and introduces the CARET metric to measure energy efficiency without sacrificing correctness. The pipeline achieves 12.63% CARET and beats human experts on 58.4% of outputs, while exposing that IPC misranks true efficiency on 67.8% of problems.
AI.motivation: Code models optimize functional correctness but ignore energy efficiency as a byproduct. Physical hardware profiling is irreproducible and noisy at scale, making it impossible to provide reliable feedback for training energy-aware models.
AI.method: (1) Replace hardware profiling with a deterministic architectural simulation harness. (2) Build Green Tea corpus: 3.5M evaluations across 1,474 C++ problems. (3) Supervised fine-tuning on energy-contrastive pairs. (4) Closed-loop reinforcement learning (GRPO) with simulation-in-the-loop feedback. (5) Introduce CARET metric to penalize correctness-sacrificing efficiency.
AI.result: 12.63% CARET on 143 held-out problems (nearly 3× gain over fine-tuning alone). Beats human-expert energy efficiency on 58.4% of valid outputs. IPC misranks true efficiency on 67.8% of problems. Released dataset/infrastructure saves 263,000 CPU-hours for reproduction.
AI.conclusion: Direct energy simulation is essential for reliable code energy optimization; throughput proxies like IPC are fundamentally misleading. The released infrastructure empowers community-wide development of energy-efficient code generation models.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Predicting Execution-Consistency Convergence in Text-to-SQL
summary: Repeated LLM calls are the standard way to estimate how trustworthy a Text-to-SQL result is: run the pipeline multiple times, judge each SQL execution, and use the consistency of the verdicts as a confidence signal. The open question is when to stop, when the consistency has converged. We formulate this as a convergence-prediction problem and train a family of lightweight 1-D models that observe the running consistency trajectory and decide, at each step, whether further runs are unlikely to shift it materially, and we benchmark them against a principled Beta-Bernoulli stopping rule and a learned run-count baseline. On the BIRD benchmark and two production customer datasets, our method adapts its stopping point to each user question, halting sooner when consistency converges early and continuing longer when it converges late. We further show that the weak serial correlation between runs lets us permute their order as a training augmentation, controlled by a tunable shuffling weight. Performance stays consistent across the three datasets, and to mimic an imperfect production judge we inject noise into the correct/incorrect verdicts obtained by comparing the generated and ground-truth SQL results, showing that the method still predicts convergence reliably.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to dynamically determine when to stop repeated LLM calls in Text-to-SQL by predicting convergence of consistency verdicts using lightweight 1-D models, outperforming a Beta-Bernoulli stopping rule and a learned baseline on BIRD and production datasets.
AI.motivation: Repeated LLM calls are standard for estimating trustworthiness in Text-to-SQL, but the open question is when to stop sampling. The goal is to avoid unnecessary runs while ensuring consistency has converged, adapting the stopping point per question.
AI.method: Formulates convergence-prediction as a problem for lightweight 1-D models that observe the running consistency trajectory and decide at each step whether further runs would materially shift it. Benchmarked against a Beta-Bernoulli stopping rule and a learned run-count baseline. Uses permutation of run order as a training augmentation controlled by a tunable shuffling weight.
AI.result: On the BIRD benchmark and two production customer datasets, the method adaptively stops earlier when consistency converges early and continues longer when convergence is late. Performance is consistent across datasets and robust to injected noise in verdict evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive stopping method reliably predicts convergence of consistency in Text-to-SQL, even under imperfect judge conditions, making it practical for production deployment.

title: OmniLayout: A Schematic-Coupled Multimodal Benchmark for Constraint-Aware Geometric Reasoning in PCB Layout
summary: Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in 3D spatial reasoning, spatial grounding, and fine-grained geometric understanding. However, their ability to reason about densely packed object placement under strict spatial and functional constraints remains largely unexplored, despite being a fundamental challenge in practical electronic design automation (EDA) workflows. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniLayout, the first benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on printed-circuit-board (PCB) layout placement reasoning under real-world geometric, routing, and connectivity constraints. OmniLayout contains 1,681 industrial-grade schematic-coupled PCB layouts and includes four tasks: (1) geometric reasoning for IC physical placement, with 77.24K placement instances constrained within PCB board boundaries; (2) routability-aware placement reasoning, generating physically valid component placements; (3) electrical functionality, preserving schematic-specified connectivity and electronic functional correctness; and (4) tool-augmented agentic reasoning for invoking external tools to accomplish tasks (1)-(3). Our results reveal substantial limitations of current LLMs in PCB layout placement, including weak geometric reasoning, poor routability optimization, and inconsistent preservation of electrical functionality.

AI.tldr: OmniLayout is the first benchmark evaluating LLMs on PCB layout placement reasoning, containing 1,681 industrial-grade layouts across four tasks. Results reveal LLMs have substantial limitations in geometric reasoning, routability optimization, and electrical functionality preservation.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown progress in 3D spatial reasoning but their ability to handle densely packed object placement under strict spatial and functional constraints—a fundamental challenge in EDA workflows—remains unexplored. OmniLayout bridges this gap.
AI.method: Constructed a benchmark with 1,681 industrial-grade schematic-coupled PCB layouts spanning four tasks: (1) geometric reasoning for IC placement (77.24K instances), (2) routability-aware placement, (3) electrical functionality preservation, and (4) tool-augmented agentic reasoning for tasks (1)-(3).
AI.result: Current LLMs exhibit substantial limitations: weak geometric reasoning, poor routability optimization, and inconsistent preservation of electrical functionality in PCB layout placement tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLMs currently lack the capability to handle real-world PCB layout placement under strict geometric, routing, and connectivity constraints, highlighting a significant gap for practical EDA applications.

title: Latent Programming Horizons in Coding Agents
summary: A coding agent solving a software-engineering task spends dozens of steps reasoning, editing code, and running tests, yet little is known about what the underlying language model internally represents about the program it is working on. We show that the residual streams of language models under coding agents linearly encode properties of the evolving program: a logistic-regression probe on hidden states is able to decode whether the current code parses, passes its test suite, reduces the number of failing tests, and introduces regressions, reaching AUC up to 0.83 for correctness across two models and two benchmarks. Our second finding is more surprising: these representations run ahead of the agent's own edits. Probes trained to predict the outcome of future edits (before they are materialized and written on disk) achieve performance above chance up to roughly 25 steps in advance. We call this the agent's latent programming horizon. As a proof of external validity, we show that the probes transfer across benchmarks without retraining. Our positive results open calls for more research in mechanistic interpretability of coding agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how language models inside coding agents internally represent the state of the evolving program. It finds that residual streams linearly encode program properties (parsing, test passing, regressions) with AUC up to 0.83, and surprisingly, these representations can predict future edits up to ~25 steps in advance—a phenomenon termed the "latent programming horizon." Probes transfer across benchmarks without retraining.
AI.motivation: Little is known about what language models internally represent about the program they are working on during multi-step coding agent tasks.
AI.method: Logistic-regression probes were trained on hidden states (residual streams) of language models under coding agents to decode program properties. Probes also predicted outcomes of future edits before they were materialized.
AI.result: Probes achieved AUC up to 0.83 for correctness across two models and two benchmarks. Future-edit prediction performed above chance up to ~25 steps in advance. Probes transferred across benchmarks without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The latent programming horizon shows that models' internal representations run ahead of actual edits, opening avenues for mechanistic interpretability of coding agents.

title: Directional Curvature from Armijo Backtracking: A Low-Cost Sharpness Probe and a Calibration-Free Learning-Rate Safeguard for Adam
summary: The local sharpness of the loss, the top Hessian eigenvalue $λ_1$, determines the largest stable gradient step, but measuring it normally requires Lanczos or Hessian-vector iterations. We observe that a single Armijo backtracking line search already carries this information at the cost of a few forward passes: the accepted step $α$ brackets the \emph{directional} curvature $q = g^\top H g/\|g\|^2$ within the multiplicative band set by the backtracking factor. Across CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST and Imagenette, $\logα$ tracks $\logλ_1$ at Pearson $-0.91$ to $-0.95$, giving a low-cost online Edge-of-Stability reading. Used once at initialisation, this measurement yields a learning-rate cap (a safeguard, not a faster optimiser) that makes Adam robust to a too-large initial learning rate across more than three orders of magnitude ($10^{-3}$ to $3.0$), at about one percent overhead, and it is a no-op when the chosen rate is already safe. One probe is enough: periodic in-training probing adds no robust benefit. The raw-gradient probe exposes the mechanism but needs a safety factor calibrated to the architecture by a one-minute divergence sweep. Probing along Adam's own update direction removes this calibration: a single fixed safety factor $κ= 2$ avoids divergence on all nine architectures we test and across the full learning-rate grids of all four benchmarks, and the recipe transfers to AdamW unchanged.

AI.tldr: A single Armijo backtracking line search step efficiently measures local loss sharpness (directional curvature), which strongly correlates with the top Hessian eigenvalue. Using this at initialization provides a low-cost learning-rate cap that makes Adam robust to overly large learning rates across a wide range, with minimal overhead and no need for periodic re-calibration.
AI.motivation: Measuring the top Hessian eigenvalue (local sharpness) typically requires expensive Lanczos or Hessian-vector iterations. The authors seek a low-cost alternative that can provide online Edge-of-Stability information and improve optimizer robustness.
AI.method: Use a single Armijo backtracking line search to obtain the accepted step size α, which bounds the directional curvature q = g^T H g / ‖g‖². Show that log α strongly correlates with log λ₁ (Pearson -0.91 to -0.95). Apply this as a one-time learning-rate cap at initialization for Adam. A raw-gradient probe requires architecture-specific safety calibration; probing along Adam's update direction with a fixed safety factor κ=2 eliminates this need.
AI.result: Strong correlation between log α and log λ₁ across CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, and Imagenette. The learning-rate cap makes Adam robust to initial learning rates spanning three orders of magnitude (10⁻³ to 3.0) with ~1% overhead. Periodic in-training probing adds no benefit. Probing along Adam's update direction with κ=2 avoids divergence on all 9 architectures tested and transfers to AdamW.
AI.conclusion: A single Armijo line search at initialization provides a cheap, effective learning-rate safeguard for Adam/AdamW, requiring no periodic re-calibration when using the Adam-direction probe with a fixed safety factor.

title: Defending from GeoLocalization through Adversarial Road Trips
summary: Retrieval-based image geolocalization has emerged as a powerful technique for determining the location of a query image by matching it against a large, geotagged database. The success of deep learning based approaches has raised concerns regarding privacy and safety. A way to protect users from geolocalization is to design adversarial attacks for such methods. In this paper, we introduce RoadTrip Attack (RTA), a novel and highly effective targeted adversarial attack for geolocalization. RTA conceptualizes the adversarial process as finding an optimal distractor journey to a specific, attacker-chosen location. It employs a beam search algorithm to iteratively construct a sequence of incorrect geographic locations that form a path to the target. At each step, the attack generates subtle perturbations to the query image, guiding the geolocalization model toward the next location in this deceptive path. We show that our method is also strong in black-box settings, obtaining highly transferable attacks with less perceptible image artifacts.

AI.tldr: RoadTrip Attack (RTA) is a targeted adversarial attack for retrieval-based image geolocalization that uses beam search to create a deceptive path of locations, guiding the model to a wrong target destination via subtle image perturbations.
AI.motivation: To protect users' privacy and safety from deep learning-based geolocalization by designing effective adversarial attacks that can fool such systems.
AI.method: RTA uses a beam search algorithm to iteratively construct a sequence of incorrect geographic locations forming a path to an attacker-chosen target, adding subtle perturbations to the query image at each step to guide the geolocalization model toward the next location in the deceptive path.
AI.result: The method achieves strong performance in black-box settings with highly transferable attacks and less perceptible image artifacts.
AI.conclusion: RTA is a novel and effective targeted adversarial attack for geolocalization that demonstrates strong transferability and subtle perturbation characteristics.

title: When Does Small Data Work? Accuracy and Efficiency Trade-offs Between Tabular Foundation Models and Conventional Methods for Crowd-State Classification at Hajj and Umrah
summary: Learning from few labeled examples is a central challenge in tabular machine learning, and it becomes the binding constraint in domains where labeling is costly, such as crowd monitoring during Hajj and Umrah. Tabular foundation models, which predict from only a handful of examples without task-specific training, were recently introduced to address this very-few-label regime. In this study we test them on crowd-state classification to assess how much they help when labels are scarce, and we compare them against standard machine learning methods to characterize the accuracy and efficiency trade-offs between the two approaches. Using three real datasets we evaluate different machine learning models, in untuned and tuned forms, against three foundation models. Results show that no single family is best everywhere. The right choice depends on the label budget. When labels are very few, foundation models lead. As labels grow, tuned conventional models catch up and significantly surpass the foundation models on the more structural geometry target. Efficiency separates them further where tuned machine learning models incur a large tuning cost that foundation models avoid, although foundation models reprocess their context at every prediction. We summarize these results as a practical map of which approach to prefer under a given label budget and computational budget.

AI.tldr: This study compares tabular foundation models against standard ML methods for crowd-state classification under low-label regimes, finding that foundation models excel when labels are very scarce, while tuned conventional models catch up and surpass them as labels grow, with efficiency trade-offs depending on computational and label budgets.
AI.motivation: Learning from few labeled examples is a central challenge in tabular ML, especially in costly labeling domains like crowd monitoring during Hajj and Umrah. The paper aims to assess how tabular foundation models help when labels are scarce and compare them against standard ML methods to characterize accuracy and efficiency trade-offs.
AI.method: The study uses three real datasets to evaluate different ML models (in untuned and tuned forms) against three foundation models for crowd-state classification. They compare performance across varying label budgets and analyze computational efficiency.
AI.result: No single family is best everywhere. When labels are very few, foundation models lead. As labels grow, tuned conventional models catch up and significantly surpass foundation models on the more structural geometry target. Efficiency trade-offs exist: tuned ML models incur large tuning costs that foundation models avoid, but foundation models reprocess context at every prediction.
AI.conclusion: The right model choice depends on the label budget. Results are summarized as a practical map of which approach to prefer under a given label budget and computational budget.

title: LBTCap: A Lightweight Bilateral Transformer for Real-Time Remote Sensing Image Change Captioning
summary: Remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) generates natural-language descriptions of semantic changes between paired remote sensing images (RSIs), supporting applications such as urban planning, disaster response, and environmental monitoring. Although recent methods achieve strong captioning accuracy, most overlook computational efficiency and inference speed, which are essential for real-time deployment in practice. To this end, we propose LBTCap, a lightweight RSICC framework built on a bilateral Transformer that jointly models pre- and post-change features for efficient processing of paired RSIs. Specifically, we introduce a bilateral attention mechanism for paired inputs: the two temporal images are projected into separate queries and keys by the same query and key matrices shared across the two images, the value is formed from their concatenation, and the two resulting attention maps are combined by a learnable, structurally bilateral weighting instead of a fixed subtraction. This design keeps both temporal branches explicit while remaining compact, and, together with a truncated backbone and grouped-query attention, LBTCap uses only 39.99M parameters, of which the change-aware encoder accounts for just 2.78M. Extensive experiments on two public RSICC datasets show that LBTCap matches or closely approaches the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods while using far fewer parameters and running at markedly higher inference speed, with the benefit of the bilateral formulation most pronounced in the low-resource setting, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for practical RSICC.

AI.tldr: LBTCap is a lightweight remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) framework using a bilateral Transformer with shared query/key matrices and a learnable bilateral weighting mechanism, achieving SOTA-comparable accuracy with only 39.99M parameters (2.78M in the encoder) and significantly higher inference speed.
AI.motivation: Existing RSICC methods achieve strong captioning accuracy but overlook computational efficiency and inference speed, hindering real-time deployment in practice.
AI.method: LBTCap proposes a bilateral Transformer with: (1) a bilateral attention mechanism using shared query/key matrices for paired temporal images, concatenated values, and learnable bilateral weighting (instead of fixed subtraction); (2) a truncated backbone; and (3) grouped-query attention to minimize parameters.
AI.result: LBTCap uses only 39.99M total parameters (2.78M in the change-aware encoder), matches/closely approaches SOTA accuracy on two public RSICC datasets, achieves markedly higher inference speed, and shows pronounced benefits in low-resource settings.
AI.conclusion: LBTCap demonstrates a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for practical RSICC deployment, making it suitable for real-time applications like urban planning, disaster response, and environmental monitoring.

title: A Unified Algebraic Framework for Classification Performance Evaluation
summary: We propose a unified algebraic framework for classification performance evaluation that encompasses binary, multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, hierarchical, cost-sensitive, and soft-label settings within a single formalism. The foundation is a representation of actual and predicted labels as binary indicator matrices, combined with three aggregation operators -- global, column-wise, and row-wise -- that correspond exactly to micro, macro/weighted, and exemplar averaging. Any binary performance measure expressed in terms of true/positive/negative counts extends automatically to all settings by substituting these operators, generating multiclass and multilabel versions without measure-specific derivations. The framework further accommodates soft classifier outputs via argmax or thresholding, soft ground truth via triangular norms, ordinal classification via membership functions or cumulative encodings, and cost-sensitive evaluation via a cost matrix that subsumes MAE and MSE as special cases. We establish several theoretical results: micro-averaging equals denominator-weighted macro-averaging; the product $t$-norm is the unique one preserving the confusion-matrix partition; skew-invariant measures are characterised as functions of recall and specificity; and micro-precision, micro-recall, and micro-$F_1$ are all equal to accuracy in multiclass settings. Empirical illustrations on synthetic and real data confirm the theoretical findings.

AI.tldr: A unified algebraic framework for classification performance evaluation using binary indicator matrices and three aggregation operators (micro, macro/weighted, exemplar), generalizing binary measures to multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, hierarchical, cost-sensitive, and soft-label settings without measure-specific derivations.
AI.motivation: Existing classification evaluation metrics are derived separately for different settings (binary, multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, etc.), lacking a unifying formalism that can automatically extend a binary performance measure to all these settings without ad-hoc, measure-specific derivations.
AI.method: Represent actual and predicted labels as binary indicator matrices; define three aggregation operators (global/column-wise/row-wise) corresponding to micro/macro/exemplar averaging; substitute these operators into any binary measure expressed via true/positive/negative counts; extend to soft outputs via argmax/thresholding, soft ground truth via t-norms, ordinal via membership/cumulative encoding, cost-sensitive via cost matrix.
AI.result: Micro-averaging equals denominator-weighted macro-averaging; product t-norm uniquely preserves confusion-matrix partition; skew-invariant measures are functions of recall and specificity; micro-precision, micro-recall, and micro-F1 equal accuracy in multiclass settings; empirical validation on synthetic and real data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a mathematically grounded, unified approach to classification evaluation that subsumes numerous existing evaluation paradigms, eliminating the need for measure-specific derivations across different classification settings.

title: From General Actions to Domain-Specific Monitoring: Prior-Adaptive Transfer for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition
summary: Skeleton-based action recognition models have recently shown strong performance on large-scale benchmarks with general actions. However, directly transferring them to domain-specific tasks e.g., healthcare monitoring, is often suboptimal, as such tasks are narrow in scope and may be relevant to only a subset of general motion priors. Moreover, not all pretrained motion patterns are equally useful for a specific task, and retaining less relevant components may hinder adaptation and increase computational cost. To address these challenges, we propose Prior-Adaptive Transfer of Skeletons (PATS), a framework that adapts general skeleton-based models by selectively retaining task-relevant motion priors while filtering redundant ones during transfer. PATS follows a standard pipeline that extracts skeleton signals from videos and employs a spatio-temporal backbone pre-trained on general actions. The key contribution lies in a novel Adaptive Prior Transfer module, which performs model compression as a prior selection mechanism through iterative pruning and refinement. Experiments on two specific action recognition tasks, Alzheimer's detection and fall detection, show consistent improvements in both performance and efficiency over competitive baselines. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: PATS is a framework that adapts general skeleton-based action recognition models to domain-specific tasks by selectively retaining only the most relevant motion priors through iterative pruning and refinement, achieving better performance and efficiency on healthcare tasks like Alzheimer's detection and fall detection.
AI.motivation: Directly transferring general skeleton-based action recognition models to domain-specific tasks (e.g., healthcare monitoring) is suboptimal because these narrow tasks may only benefit from a subset of general motion priors, and retaining irrelevant components hurts adaptation and increases computational cost.
AI.method: PATS uses a standard skeleton extraction pipeline with a spatio-temporal backbone pretrained on general actions, plus a novel Adaptive Prior Transfer module that performs model compression as a prior selection mechanism through iterative pruning and refinement to retain task-relevant motion patterns and filter redundant ones.
AI.result: On Alzheimer's detection and fall detection tasks, PATS achieves consistent improvements in both performance and efficiency over competitive baselines.
AI.conclusion: Selectively transferring task-relevant motion priors via structured pruning is an effective strategy for adapting skeleton-based action recognition models to narrow, domain-specific tasks.

title: OmniOpt: Taxonomy, Geometry, and Benchmarking of Modern Optimizers
summary: Optimizer selection for large-scale model training has become a system-level design decision constrained jointly by compute, memory, tuning budget, and task diversity, yet the landscape of over one hundred methods remains fragmented. We therefore present OmniOpt, a unified survey and benchmark cookbook of optimizers for the research community. OmniOpt rests on four coupled components. First, we treat every optimizer update as a structured transformation through a five-stage meta-pipeline, and show that most methods engage only one or two of these stages. Second, we use norm-constrained linear minimization oracles (LMOs) to unify different optimizers. Third, these two views ground a dual-dimension taxonomy, one dimension assigning each method to a mechanism family and the other recording the measurable training objectives it aims to improve. Fourth, and at the core of this paper, we instantiate the full taxonomy in a unified cross-domain benchmark spanning representative optimizers, model scales, and training regimes from language model pretraining to image classification, systematically analyzing each method family across multiple effect objectives and laying out their trade-offs. OmniOpt thus supplies the research community with an operational coordinate system for selecting optimizers under explicit mechanism and objective assumptions, and charts a direction for the future development of the optimizer community.

AI.tldr: OmniOpt provides a unified survey and benchmark cookbook for optimizer selection in large-scale model training, organizing over 100 methods via a five-stage meta-pipeline, norm-constrained LMO unification, a dual-dimension taxonomy, and a comprehensive cross-domain benchmark spanning language pretraining to image classification.
AI.motivation: Optimizer selection for large-scale training is a system-level design decision constrained by compute, memory, tuning budget, and task diversity, yet the landscape of over 100 methods remains fragmented without a unified framework.
AI.method: (1) A five-stage meta-pipeline treating every optimizer update as a structured transformation; (2) norm-constrained linear minimization oracles (LMOs) to unify optimizers; (3) a dual-dimension taxonomy (mechanism family vs. measurable training objectives); (4) a cross-domain benchmark across model scales and training regimes.
AI.result: Systematic analysis of each method family across multiple effect objectives, revealing trade-offs and providing an operational coordinate system for selecting optimizers under explicit mechanism and objective assumptions.
AI.conclusion: OmniOpt supplies the research community with a unified coordinate system for optimizer selection and charts a direction for future optimizer development.

title: Beyond Post-Quantization: Native Hash Learning with a Dedicated HASH Token
summary: Efficient large-scale image retrieval requires compact representations that preserve semantic similarity under fast Hamming-space search. Deep hashing is appealing, but most existing CNN- and ViT-based methods still follow a post-quantization paradigm, where continuous visual features are first learned and binary codes are then produced by a terminal hash projection or binarization operation. This late code generation creates a feature-to-code discrepancy between the continuously optimized representation space and the discrete Hamming space used for retrieval. To address this limitation, we propose HashViT, a Vision Transformer framework for native hash token learning. Instead of treating hashing as a terminal readout, HashViT introduces a dedicated HASH token that serves as a persistent, hash-oriented retrieval state inside the transformer. The HASH token is structurally decomposed into a Hash Register for direct binary code generation and a Semantic Workspace for preserving auxiliary continuous semantics. To enable effective workspace-to-register interaction, we further design a lightweight Hash Refinement Adapter that progressively refines the Hash Register across transformer layers. As a result, binary-oriented representations are formed through token evolution within the backbone, rather than being abruptly induced by an output-level projection. HashViT is optimized with a unified objective that combines learnable semantic center supervision, class-token similarity distillation, and quantization regularization, encouraging the HASH token to encode semantically structured and compact binary representations. Extensive experiments on three widely used benchmarks demonstrate that HashViT achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive retrieval performance while preserving the efficiency of compact Hamming codes. Code is available at https://github.com/Xinze919/HashViT.

AI.tldr: HashViT introduces a Vision Transformer framework with a dedicated HASH token that enables native hash token learning inside the backbone, avoiding the feature-to-code discrepancy in post-quantization deep hashing methods. It decomposes the HASH token into a Hash Register (binary code) and Semantic Workspace (continuous semantics), uses a Hash Refinement Adapter for progressive refinement, and is optimized with a unified objective. It achieves SOTA retrieval performance on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing deep hashing methods (CNN- and ViT-based) follow a post-quantization paradigm where continuous features are learned first and binary codes are produced late via terminal hash projection, creating a feature-to-code discrepancy between the optimized continuous space and the discrete Hamming space used for retrieval.
AI.method: HashViT: (1) A dedicated HASH token is introduced inside the transformer backbone, decomposed into a Hash Register (for direct binary code generation) and a Semantic Workspace (for auxiliary continuous semantics). (2) A lightweight Hash Refinement Adapter progressively refines the Hash Register across layers. (3) Unified optimization objective combining learnable semantic center supervision, class-token similarity distillation, and quantization regularization.
AI.result: State-of-the-art or highly competitive retrieval performance on three widely used benchmarks while preserving the efficiency of compact Hamming codes.
AI.conclusion: Binary-oriented representations formed through token evolution within the backbone outperform post-quantization paradigms by eliminating feature-to-code discrepancy.

title: Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation is a powerful way to transfer reasoning ability from a strong teacher to a smaller student: the student samples trajectories from its own policy, and the teacher provides dense token-level supervision on the states the student actually visits. However, this supervision is not always reliable: a teacher can assign high likelihood to plausible but incorrect solutions, or low likelihood to correct student solutions that follow different reasoning paths. Unconditionally distilling the teacher can therefore reinforce bad modes or erase useful student behavior. To address these limitations, we introduce RG-OPD: Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation that uses verifier feedback to decide when teacher logits should be trusted. RG-OPD bridges sparse verifier rewards and dense teacher logits, preserving token-level supervision while filtering misleading teacher signals. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, RG-OPD produces stronger distilled students, outperforming both vanilla reverse-KL distillation and the recent TSD-KD baseline. At 1K generation length, RG-OPD improves over reverse-KL by 2.9 points and over TSD-KD by 4.9 points; in the long-generation setting, it improves over the untuned student by 8.2 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/UoC-tail/RG-OPD.

AI.tldr: RG-OPD (Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation) improves knowledge distillation from a strong teacher to a smaller student by using verifier feedback to filter unreliable teacher logits, outperforming vanilla reverse-KL distillation and TSD-KD on reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation is powerful for transferring reasoning ability, but teacher supervision can be unreliable—teachers may assign high likelihood to plausible but incorrect solutions or low likelihood to correct student solutions that follow different reasoning paths. Unconditionally distilling the teacher can reinforce bad modes or erase useful student behavior.
AI.method: RG-OPD uses verifier feedback as a gate to decide when teacher logits should be trusted, bridging sparse verifier rewards and dense teacher logits to preserve token-level supervision while filtering misleading teacher signals.
AI.result: At 1K generation length, RG-OPD improves over reverse-KL by 2.9 points and over TSD-KD by 4.9 points; in the long-generation setting, it improves over the untuned student by 8.2 points.
AI.conclusion: RG-OPD produces stronger distilled students across reasoning and coding benchmarks, effectively addressing the limitations of unreliable teacher supervision in on-policy distillation.

title: GrowFields: Compositional 4D Neural Fields for Topology-Changing Plant Growth
summary: Quantifying plant growth dynamics from sparse longitudinal 3D observations is fundamental for agriculture and plant sciences. Yet, plants pose unique challenges: they undergo intricate non-rigid deformations, exhibit changing topology as new organs emerge, and often lack explicit temporal correspondences between consecutive data acquisitions due to newly formed tissue. Methods designed for general scenes struggle to model topology changes and asynchronous organ growth characteristic of plants. To address these challenges, we introduce GrowFields, a compositional dynamic neural field representation for organ-aware 4D plant growth modelling from point cloud time series. Our approach decomposes a plant into its constituent organs and aligns each organ into its own canonical coordinate frame, isolating intrinsic growth patterns from global plant motion. We then learn a shared continuous neural deformation field that models temporal dynamics across all organs, conditioned on learnable per-organ latent codes capturing organ identity and growth characteristics. The resulting modular yet unified representation naturally accommodates the asynchronous development of plant organs while remaining grounded in the practical setting of organ-level plant tracking. We evaluate GrowFields on growth sequences from four plant species, assessing geometric fitting and organ tracking accuracy using manually annotated leaf-tip trajectories. Results demonstrate consistent improvements in spatial precision, temporal coherence, and morphological fidelity over a range of existing representations.

AI.tldr: GrowFields is a compositional dynamic neural field for 4D plant growth modeling from sparse point cloud time series, decomposing plants into organs with canonical alignment and shared deformation fields to handle topology changes and asynchronous growth, achieving superior geometric and tracking accuracy across four species.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for general dynamic scenes struggle to model plant-specific challenges: non-rigid deformations, topology changes from emerging organs, and lack of temporal correspondences due to newly formed tissue. There is a need for representations that explicitly handle asynchronous organ development and organ-level tracking from sparse longitudinal 3D observations.
AI.method: GrowFields uses a compositional dynamic neural field that: (1) decomposes a plant into constituent organs, (2) aligns each organ into its own canonical coordinate frame to separate intrinsic growth from global motion, (3) learns a shared continuous neural deformation field conditioned on per-organ learnable latent codes that capture organ identity and growth characteristics, enabling modular yet unified modeling of asynchronous organ development.
AI.result: Evaluated on growth sequences from four plant species using geometric fitting quality and organ tracking accuracy (via manually annotated leaf-tip trajectories), GrowFields consistently outperforms existing representations in spatial precision, temporal coherence, and morphological fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The compositional design with per-organ canonical frames and shared deformation fields conditioned on organ-specific latent codes effectively addresses topology changes and asynchronous growth, providing a practical framework for organ-level 4D plant growth modeling from sparse point cloud time series.

title: A Unified Framework for In-Context Learning with Causal and Masked Language Models
summary: In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a central capability of pretrained language models, yet its theoretical analysis has focused primarily on causal language models trained by left-to-right autoregressive prediction, such as GPT-style models. Masked language models instead recover masked tokens from bidirectional context, and their role in ICL remains less understood. We develop a statistical learning framework that represents the context examples by their empirical measure and models prediction as a function of the context and the query. This formulation places autoregressive and masked pretraining objectives within a common excess-risk analysis. Under Wasserstein-type regularity conditions, we relate pretraining with T tasks and N samples per task to k-shot excess risk at inference, obtaining same-order upper bounds for masked and autoregressive objectives. We also study task-distribution shift, where pretraining tasks are sampled from P and inference tasks from Q; the resulting bound contains an additional term controlled by the lifted Wasserstein distance between P and Q. The bounds further imply an order-optimal allocation under a fixed pretraining data budget and refined rates under intrinsic low-dimensional structure. Experiments on controlled function-learning tasks show that the Masked Pair Encoder (MPE) can achieve performance comparable to GPT-2-style causal Transformers, suggesting that ICL behavior is not specific to causal language models.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a statistical learning framework unifying autoregressive and masked language models for in-context learning (ICL), showing that masked models can achieve comparable ICL performance to causal models under same-order excess risk bounds, with analysis covering task-distribution shift and optimal data allocation.
AI.motivation: While ICL has been extensively studied for causal (GPT-style) language models, its theoretical understanding for masked language models remains limited. This paper aims to bridge that gap by providing a unified theoretical framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a statistical learning framework that represents context examples via empirical measure and models prediction as a function of context and query. They conduct excess-risk analysis under Wasserstein-type regularity conditions, relating pretraining (T tasks, N samples per task) to k-shot ICL inference risk. They also analyze task-distribution shift via lifted Wasserstein distance and derive optimal allocation under fixed pretraining budgets.
AI.result: Same-order upper bounds for masked and autoregressive pretraining objectives; an additional term controlled by lifted Wasserstein distance under task-distribution shift; order-optimal allocation under fixed pretraining budget; refined rates under intrinsic low-dimensional structure; and experiments showing Masked Pair Encoder (MPE) matches GPT-2-style causal Transformers on function-learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ICL behavior is not specific to causal language models; masked language models can achieve comparable ICL performance, and the theoretical framework provides unified understanding of both architectures.

title: Pathways of Visual Information Flow in Vision-Language Models
summary: We study how visual information is routed in vision-language models (VLMs). Using causal patching on controlled synthetic and natural datasets, we find that models rely on two distinct pathways to solve visual tasks: A direct pathway, where visual information is retained in image token representations and read out by the final token at later layers, and a text-mediated pathway, where visual information is first transferred to the query tokens and then read out by the final token. Across three visual tasks, we show that pathway selection is task-dependent, and that data distribution and prompt design can also modulate which pathway is used to solve the image-based query. Moreover, using attention knockouts and corrupted-input patching, we find that these pathways are flexible, under certain interventions, models can rely on the text-mediated pathway as a fallback when the usual pathway is ablated. This behavior unifies findings in prior work and shows that ablation-based interventions can reveal what models could do rather than what they normally do. Together, our results provide a mechanistic characterization of visual information flow in VLMs and highlight the flexibility of their internal mechanisms under intervention.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how visual information flows in vision-language models (VLMs), identifying two distinct pathways: a direct pathway (visual info stays in image tokens) and a text-mediated pathway (visual info transfers to query tokens first). Pathway selection depends on task, data distribution, and prompt design. Under ablation interventions, models flexibly fall back to alternative pathways.
AI.motivation: To understand how VLMs route visual information internally and whether they rely on fixed or flexible mechanisms, unifying prior conflicting findings about ablation-based interventions.
AI.method: Used causal patching on controlled synthetic and natural datasets, along with attention knockouts and corrupted-input patching, to trace information flow in VLMs across three visual tasks.
AI.result: Identified two distinct visual information pathways (direct and text-mediated); pathway selection is task-dependent and modulated by data distribution and prompt design; models can flexibly switch to the text-mediated pathway as a fallback when the usual pathway is ablated.
AI.conclusion: VLMs exhibit flexible internal mechanisms for visual information routing, and ablation-based interventions can reveal latent capabilities (what models *could* do) rather than only what they normally do.

title: FedSPM: Routing-Enabled Federated Learning under Dual Heterogeneity via Semiparametric Mixture
summary: Routing-prediction federated learning has emerged as a new paradigm that reframes inter-client heterogeneity as a resource for system-level intelligence: at inference time, the server routes each external query to the best-matched client for prediction. Existing approaches, however, typically treat each client as internally homogeneous, overlooking latent subpopulations within local data. For example, patients with the same diagnosis at one hospital may exhibit morphologically distinct disease subtypes. The coexistence of inter-client and intra-client heterogeneity, which we call dual heterogeneity, can impair both routing and prediction. To address this challenge, we propose FedSPM, a routing-enabled semiparametric mixture framework that represents each client using client-specific latent components. Each component combines a predictive distribution for classification with a feature distribution for routing. To flexibly model feature distributions while effectively sharing information across clients, FedSPM models their density ratios relative to a common nonparametric measure estimated via empirical likelihood. We develop a federated expectation-maximization algorithm that optimizes a tractable surrogate and prove convergence of the exact profiled objective at the standard $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate when the surrogate errors are properly controlled. Experiments on controlled benchmarks and real-world medical data demonstrate consistent improvements in routing and prediction under dual heterogeneity. Code is available at https://github.com/zijianwang0510/FedSPM.

AI.tldr: FedSPM is a routing-prediction federated learning framework that addresses dual heterogeneity (both inter-client and intra-client) by modeling each client with multiple latent components, combining predictive and feature distributions via a semiparametric mixture model with nonparametric density ratios estimated through empirical likelihood, achieving convergence at O(1/√T) rate.
AI.motivation: Existing routing-prediction FL methods treat each client as internally homogeneous, overlooking latent subpopulations within local data (e.g., disease subtypes in the same hospital). This dual heterogeneity (inter-client + intra-client) impairs both routing and prediction performance.
AI.method: FedSPM represents each client using client-specific latent components, where each component combines a predictive distribution for classification with a feature distribution for routing. Feature distributions are modeled via density ratios relative to a common nonparametric measure estimated through empirical likelihood. A federated expectation-maximization algorithm optimizes a tractable surrogate, with proven O(1/√T) convergence.
AI.result: Experiments on controlled benchmarks and real-world medical data demonstrate consistent improvements in both routing and prediction under dual heterogeneity settings.
AI.conclusion: FedSPM effectively handles dual heterogeneity in federated learning by modeling latent subpopulations within clients, improving both query routing and prediction accuracy compared to existing approaches.

title: Brand-as-Memory: Vision-Language Models Encode Causal, Mechanistically Localizable Credibility Priors for News Sources
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read news and web content as images, where the publisher's identity is visually present. We show that VLMs carry a strong source-credibility prior keyed on outlet identity, and study it along three axes. (i) Cross-model benchmark. We introduce CueTrust, a cross-model diagnostic that measures which surface source cue overrides an article's content evidence via a Source-Override Index (SOI). Across seven VLMs and five cues, the vulnerability profile is model- and scale-dependent, and the override is outlet-identity-specific and encoding-invariant, firing from the masthead name, the logo image, or the bare domain, but not from a named author, in-text authority, or page layout (clean negative controls). (ii) Mechanistic account. For the brand cue, we give a full mechanistic account: swapping only the masthead moves credibility across an approximately 11 log-odds range that tracks professional ratings (rho = 0.88 with Media Bias/Fact Check). The prior is dual-coded (name and logo), strengthens with scale, is causally formed at layers 19-21, carried by interpretable seed-stable sparse-autoencoder features, and recurs at the same relative locus in a second model family. It overrides content (about 1.8x) as a signal-magnitude effect within a shared pathway, not a privileged route. Steering the localized direction selectively reduces the override (41% reduction) and generalizes to held-out outlets, confirming the prior is causally used, not merely decodable. Deployed VLMs may thus defer to source identity over the evidence in front of them, a reliability failure we can measure across models, localize, and causally probe. We release the stimulus suite and CueTrust.

AI.tldr: VLMs have a strong source-credibility prior keyed on outlet identity that can override actual article content; the paper introduces CueTrust to measure this, provides a mechanistic account showing the prior is dual-coded (name/logo), localized to layers 19-21, and can be steered to reduce override by 41%.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models increasingly process news and web content where publisher identity is visually present, yet it is unknown whether VLMs carry source-credibility biases that override content evidence, posing reliability risks in deployed systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces CueTrust, a cross-model diagnostic using a Source-Override Index (SOI) across 7 VLMs and 5 cues. Mechanistic analysis uses log-odds tracking, sparse autoencoder features, and causal steering to localize and manipulate the source-credibility prior.
AI.result: The source-credibility override is outlet-identity-specific and encoding-invariant (masthead, logo, domain), but not triggered by named author, in-text authority, or layout. The prior tracks professional ratings (rho=0.88), is dual-coded, strengthens with scale, localizes to layers 19-21, overrides content ~1.8x, and steering reduces override by 41% with generalization to held-out outlets.
AI.conclusion: Deployed VLMs may defer to source identity over evidence, a measurable and causally probeable reliability failure; the authors release the stimulus suite and CueTrust tool.

title: Target-Aware Interaction-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Black-Box Node Injection Attacks on Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in graph representation learning, yet their inherent vulnerability to adversarial attacks poses severe security risks. Especially, black-box node injection attacks have become a major threat to GNNs since they inject malicious nodes without altering the original graph topology. However, they typically decouple the generation of malicious node features and edge connections, thereby resulting in suboptimal attack efficacy under stringent budgets. To address this critical issue, this study proposes a novel Target-aware Interaction-guided Reinforcement learning for Black-box node injection Attacks on GNNs (TIRBA), which formulates the attack as a Markov Decision Process and jointly optimizes node feature generation and edge construction in a heterogeneous action space. Firstly, TIRBA designs a target-aware interaction encoder to fuse information of node features and edges. Further, it introduces a class-center guidance mechanism to utilize prior class distribution information, thereby guiding efficient exploration of the high-dimensional feature space. Finally, a topology difference-aware state value evaluation is adopted to explicitly capture local structural anomalies caused by injected nodes, thereby stabilizing the reinforcement learning training process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed TIRBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art black-box node injection attack methods.

AI.tldr: TIRBA is a reinforcement learning-based black-box node injection attack on GNNs that jointly optimizes malicious node features and edge connections using a target-aware interaction encoder, class-center guidance, and topology difference-aware evaluation, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing black-box node injection attacks decouple malicious node feature generation and edge connection construction, leading to suboptimal attack performance under tight budgets. There is a need for a joint optimization approach to improve attack efficacy.
AI.method: TIRBA formulates the attack as a Markov Decision Process with a heterogeneous action space. It uses: (1) a target-aware interaction encoder to fuse node feature and edge information, (2) a class-center guidance mechanism leveraging prior class distribution for efficient feature space exploration, and (3) a topology difference-aware state value evaluation to capture local structural anomalies and stabilize training.
AI.result: Experimental results show TIRBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art black-box node injection attack methods on GNNs.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing node features and edge connections via reinforcement learning with interaction-aware encoding and topology-aware evaluation yields superior black-box attack performance against GNNs.

title: Present but Not Remembered: Auditing How Frozen VLAs Encode, Deploy, and Steer Visual History
summary: A frozen vision-language-action model (VLA) receives recent observations at every decision step, yet prior work has focused on adding memory rather than asking how existing history is represented and used. We study this temporal axis using layer-resolved linear probing and causal interchange interventions across three VLAs from two architecture families. We find a three-part dissociation. First, past-frame content remains linearly decodable throughout the network. Second, information unique to history beyond the current frame is nearly absent, indicating that stored history is largely a redundant copy of the present. Third, history is causally deployed only when the current frame is heavily degraded, while the action readout progressively loses dependence on history through the network. Although all models encode history similarly, their deployment strategies differ: under the same occlusion, one architecture increasingly relies on history as a fallback, whereas the other relies on it less. We further introduce a training-free temporal deployment audit that distinguishes these regimes. In the fallback regime, re-injecting history neither repairs occlusion nor disambiguates actions, confirming the redundancy of the stored representation. In the other regime, the same intervention reliably steers the predicted action toward the donor history. These results show that steerability depends on how history is deployed rather than whether it is encoded. VLAs do not forget the past; they largely fail to represent it as information distinct from the present. Our findings suggest that future memory augmentation should inject information unique to the past rather than simply more history.

AI.tldr: Frozen vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode past-frame content throughout the network, but this history is largely a redundant copy of the present and is causally deployed only when the current frame is degraded. Different architectures deploy history differently (fallback vs. non-fallback regimes), and steerability depends on deployment strategy, not encoding. Simple history re-injection does not help; future work should inject information unique to the past.
AI.motivation: Prior VLA work has focused on adding memory rather than understanding how existing temporal history is represented and used. The authors aim to dissect whether and how frozen VLAs utilize past observations, and whether the stored history contains information distinct from the present.
AI.method: Layer-resolved linear probing and causal interchange interventions applied to three frozen VLAs from two architecture families, plus a training-free temporal deployment audit to distinguish deployment regimes.
AI.result: (1) Past-frame content is linearly decodable throughout the network. (2) History beyond the current frame carries almost no unique information—it is largely redundant with present. (3) History is causally used only when the current frame is heavily degraded; action readout loses dependence on history through the network. (4) Different architectures exhibit different deployment strategies under occlusion (fallback vs. non-fallback). (5) In fallback regimes, re-injecting history does not repair occlusion or disambiguate actions; in non-fallback regimes, the same intervention steers the predicted action toward the donor history.
AI.conclusion: VLAs encode past information but fail to represent it as something distinct from the present. Future memory augmentation should inject information unique to the past rather than simply more history. Steerability depends on how history is deployed, not whether it is encoded.

title: Dictionaries, Not Darwin: Set-Level Selection Beats LLM Evolution in Scientific Equation Discovery
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as evolutionary engines for scientific discovery: generate candidates, select winners, feed them back as parents, and repeat. We audit whether this loop actually compounds discovery in scientific equation discovery, a setting where finite samples make structure underdetermined and interpolation easy. Under matched LLM-call budgets, parent-conditioned evolution is indistinguishable from fresh independent sampling: median OOD NMSE is 0.045 vs. 0.049, instructed multi-parent crossover is worse, final success is predicted by initial proposal quality, and multiple iteration schemes fail to add solved problems. Operationally, the loop reduces to what it produces: a dictionary of candidate terms. We turn that diagnosis into PTB-Search, a one-generation method for componentized scientific discovery. PTB-Search samples independent LLM proposals once, extracts reusable terms into a per-problem dictionary, and performs train-only set-level sparse selection with least-squares coefficients. Its central principle is that underdetermined data identifies the joint behavior of term sets, not reliable per-term credit. On identical dictionaries and zero additional LLM calls, set-level selectors solve 165--169 of 717 cells, while single-term reductions solve only 74--78. On the official 239-problem LLM-SRBench split, PTB-Search reaches 73.2% Acc0.1 with Llama-3.1-8B and 77.0% with a single-seed DeepSeek-V4 anchor, versus 49.2% for the best reported baseline, using one tenth of the standardized call budget. A program-domain stress test gives a scoped boundary: generation count remains unreliable, while retained external state can help in harder non-linear spaces. Across these results, LLMs are best understood as material suppliers; discovery is carried by external set-level selection over reusable components.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven evolutionary loops for scientific equation discovery offer no benefit over independent sampling due to underdetermined data; the paper proposes PTB-Search, a one-generation method using set-level selection over reusable term dictionaries, achieving 73.2-77.0% accuracy vs. 49.2% for the best baseline with 10x fewer LLM calls.
AI.motivation: To audit whether LLM-based evolutionary discovery loops (generate-select-feedback-repeat) actually compound discovery in scientific equation discovery, where finite samples make structure underdetermined and interpolation easy.
AI.method: PTB-Search: samples independent LLM proposals once, extracts reusable terms into per-problem dictionaries, performs train-only set-level sparse selection using least-squares coefficients, avoiding per-term credit assignment under underdetermined data.
AI.result: Parent-conditioned evolution is indistinguishable from independent sampling (median OOD NMSE 0.045 vs 0.049). Set-level selectors solve 165-169/717 cells vs 74-78 for single-term reductions. PTB-Search achieves 73.2% (Llama-3.1-8B) and 77.0% (DeepSeek-V4) Acc0.1 vs 49.2% best baseline with 1/10th the call budget.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are best understood as material suppliers; discovery is carried by external set-level selection over reusable components. The evolutionary loop reduces to producing a dictionary of candidate terms, and one-generation PTB-Search outperforms iterative schemes.

title: DynaVieW: Schema-Guided World Modeling for Understanding Hierarchical Visual Dynamics
summary: Multimodal LLMs struggle to systematically model the temporal evolution of visual scenes in videos or multi-image sequences. Such inputs require models to predict or simulate multiple levels of dynamic constituents, such as actions taken in the visual sequence, and the associated changes to the visual environment that result. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamic schema-guided world model, DynaVieW, optimized for visual dynamic prediction and simulation. DynaVieW achieves an in-depth understanding of visual dynamics by learning interleaved state-transition sequences, where states cover broad visual scenes from video keyframes, and transitions capture comprehensive dynamic constituents within a hierarchical schema.
