Using an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline and fine-tuned multimodal LLMs with various input settings (raw frames, segmentation-enhanced input, textual descriptions), they establish a strong benchmark showing that ego-centric videos enable nuanced, legally meaningful reasoning beyond traditional accident classification.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal traffic accident understanding relies on expensive infrastructure-camera footage, satellite imagery, or structured crash records, which cannot objectively capture what the driver actually observed before the accident. Ego-view videos directly represent the driver's visual perspective, making them suitable for reasoning about avoidability and driver responsibility.
AI.method: The authors construct an LLM-assisted responsibility annotation pipeline and fine-tune multimodal large language models under multiple input settings, including raw frames, segmentation-enhanced input, and textual descriptions for the task of responsibility distribution estimation.
AI.result: Experimental results establish a strong initial benchmark, demonstrating that multimodal LLMs can effectively perform this nuanced, constraint-based reasoning task.
AI.conclusion: Ego-centric accident videos provide a promising foundation for socially and legally meaningful multimodal reasoning beyond conventional accident classification and explanation tasks.

title: Channel-Adaptive Robust Aggregation for Over-the-Air Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Networks
summary: The growing demand for privacy-preserving, data-intensive applications such as IoT, augmented reality, and autonomous systems positions Federated Learning (FL) as a key enabler in 6G networks. Over-the-Air FL (OTA-FL) leverages the superposition property of the wireless multiple access channel for efficient aggregation via simultaneous transmissions. Existing methods rely on fixed aggregation schedules and do not jointly address noise, fading, and client heterogeneity. We propose CHARGE-FL (CHannel-Adaptive Robust agGrEgation), a framework that adaptively schedules aggregation based on channel dynamics and application readiness. By combining a tailored optimization strategy with a dual-purpose precoding mechanism, CHARGE-FL mitigates channel distortion and bias from partial updates, achieving superior accuracy, stability, and convergence under realistic wireless conditions. Empirical results under realistic wireless conditions show that CHARGE-FL significantly improves accuracy, stability, and convergence over state-of-the-art OTA-FL methods, particularly in straggler-prone and noisy scenarios.

AI.tldr: CHARGE-FL is a channel-adaptive framework for Over-the-Air Federated Learning in 6G networks that dynamically schedules aggregation and uses dual-purpose precoding to jointly address noise, fading, and client heterogeneity, outperforming existing OTA-FL methods under realistic wireless conditions.
AI.motivation: The growing demand for privacy-preserving, data-intensive applications (IoT, AR, autonomous systems) positions FL as a key enabler in 6G, but existing OTA-FL methods rely on fixed aggregation schedules and fail to jointly address noise, fading, and client heterogeneity.
AI.method: CHARGE-FL adaptively schedules aggregation based on channel dynamics and application readiness, combining a tailored optimization strategy with a dual-purpose precoding mechanism to mitigate channel distortion and bias from partial updates.
AI.result: Under realistic wireless conditions, CHARGE-FL significantly improves accuracy, stability, and convergence over state-of-the-art OTA-FL methods, especially in straggler-prone and noisy scenarios.
AI.conclusion: CHARGE-FL effectively addresses key OTA-FL challenges (noise, fading, client heterogeneity) through channel-adaptive aggregation and dual-purpose precoding, achieving superior performance for FL in 6G networks.

title: Token-Based Affordance Grounding with Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Affordance grounding aims to localize image regions that support a specific action, serving as a core capability for physical intelligence and embodied perception. Previous studies have primarily relied on weakly supervised learning with action labels from exocentric images. However, these methods often struggle with visually ambiguous exocentric images containing co-occurring actions; moreover, they fail to distinguish semantically similar actions because existing methods typically rely on brief action phrases that lack rich semantic details for action-specific localization. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) encode rich action semantics and their action-conditioned textual outputs implicitly contain spatial cues, they do not directly provide action-specific spatial localization. To address these problems, we propose TokAG, a zero-shot affordance grounding framework that exploits the token-level semantic-spatial signals in LVLMs to localize action-relevant regions without external supervision. We observe that attention maps associated with different LVLM output tokens vary significantly, with many attending to irrelevant regions such as the background. Thus, we introduce a spatial-aware token-selection mechanism to systematically evaluate each output token and select the one whose attention maps exhibit dominant activation over the target object, instead of relying on arbitrary attention maps. By extracting these object-focused attention maps, we transform the LVLM's implicit semantic signals into zero-shot affordance heatmaps. Our zero-shot framework consistently outperforms prior weakly supervised approaches across multiple benchmarks, improving NSS by 10.7% on the unseen split of AGD20K and by 29.7% on HICO-IIF. The code and models will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: TokAG is a zero-shot affordance grounding framework that uses token-level semantic-spatial signals from LVLMs, with a spatial-aware token-selection mechanism, to localize action-relevant image regions. It outperforms prior weakly supervised methods across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Previous affordance grounding methods rely on weakly supervised learning from exocentric images but struggle with visually ambiguous co-occurring actions and fail to distinguish semantically similar actions due to lack of rich semantic details. LVLMs encode rich action semantics but do not directly provide spatial localization.
AI.method: TokAG proposes a spatial-aware token-selection mechanism that evaluates each LVLM output token's attention maps to select those with dominant activation over the target object, transforming implicit semantic signals into zero-shot affordance heatmaps.
AI.result: The zero-shot framework consistently outperforms prior weakly supervised approaches, improving NSS by 10.7% on AGD20K unseen split and by 29.7% on HICO-IIF.
AI.conclusion: Token-level semantic-spatial signals from LVLMs can be effectively exploited for zero-shot affordance grounding, achieving superior performance without external supervision.

title: Quantize the Target, Quantize the Drafter: Efficient Inference with Qwen3.5-4B
comment: All authors contributed equally. Our submission to Efficient Qwen Competition, ICML 2026 Workshop on AdaptFM
summary: This report describes our approach to the Efficient Qwen Competition, where the goal is to enable low-latency serving of Qwen3.5-4B on a resource-constrained NVIDIA A10G GPU. Our system combines a quantized target model with speculative decoding. To recover accuracy, we apply quantization-aware distillation to the target model while retaining the original quantization grid. To speed up decoding, a block-diffusion drafter specialized for the quantized target model is trained using a two-stage procedure: first learning from the high-precision target and then adapting to the low-precision target. Because the drafter is invoked at every speculative decoding step, we further reduce its overhead with quantization and sliding-window attention, preserving draft-token acceptance while improving long-context decoding latency. As a result, our submission achieves a 6.978$\times$ average speedup over the baseline while satisfying the required quality thresholds, ranking 3rd overall. We hope these results provide useful insights for practical LLM inference. The code and resources are available at https://github.com/nota-github/adaptfm-quant-dflash

AI.tldr: A system combining quantized Qwen3.5-4B with speculative decoding and a block-diffusion drafter achieves 6.978× speedup on A10G GPU, ranking 3rd in the Efficient Qwen Competition.
AI.motivation: Enable low-latency serving of Qwen3.5-4B on a resource-constrained NVIDIA A10G GPU.
AI.method: Combines a quantized target model with speculative decoding. Uses quantization-aware distillation with the original quantization grid for accuracy recovery. Trains a block-diffusion drafter via two-stage procedure (learning from high-precision, then adapting to low-precision target). Reduces drafter overhead with quantization and sliding-window attention.
AI.result: Achieves 6.978× average speedup over baseline while meeting quality thresholds, ranking 3rd overall.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides useful insights for practical LLM inference; code and resources are open-sourced.

title: A Step Towards Robust Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted and presented at the 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence (ECAI 2025), Bologna, Italy
summary: Adversarial robustness in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) remains a significant challenge due to noisy pseudo labels and inherent distributional shifts between the clean source and adversarially perturbed target domains. Existing approaches often fail to achieve an optimal trade-off between robustness and accuracy, as pseudo-labels generated by domain-adapted models tend to introduce classification errors under adversarial attacks. In this work, we propose \textbf{SFT+RL}, a two-stage robust UDA framework that integrates Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on top of CLIP's pre-trained visual encoder. In the SFT stage, we adversarially fine-tune a linear classifier using PGD-based perturbations over the labelled source domain while partially unfreezing CLIP's projection layer. It allows adaptation to adversarial noise while preserving CLIP's rich semantic priors. We introduce a confidence-guided pseudo-labeling strategy in the RL stage to annotate unlabeled target samples progressively. Pseudo labels are filtered using a decaying confidence threshold to balance quality and coverage, and the model is trained on a composite dataset formed by combining clean source samples with high-confidence target samples. Adversarial training is applied to mixed batches of clean and adversarial examples to enhance cross-domain robustness. Comprehensive evaluations on three benchmark datasets OfficeHome~\cite{tomm-ude}, PACS~\cite{pacs}, and VisDA~\cite{visda} demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Notably, \textbf{SFT+RL} achieves average improvements of \textbf{10.2\%} in clean accuracy and \textbf{15.8\%} in adversarial robustness across all three datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: SFT+RL is a two-stage robust UDA framework combining Supervised Fine Tuning (adversarial fine-tuning with PGD perturbations on source) and Reinforcement Learning (confidence-guided pseudo-labeling with decaying threshold) atop CLIP's visual encoder, achieving +10.2% clean accuracy and +15.8% adversarial robustness over SOTA on OfficeHome, PACS, and VisDA.
AI.motivation: Adversarial robustness in UDA is challenged by noisy pseudo labels and distribution shifts between clean source and adversarially perturbed target domains. Existing methods fail to balance robustness and accuracy due to error-prone pseudo-labels under attacks.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) SFT stage adversarially fine-tunes a linear classifier with PGD perturbations on labeled source data while partially unfreezing CLIP's projection layer; (2) RL stage uses confidence-guided pseudo-labeling with a decaying threshold to annotate target samples, trains on composite clean+target dataset with mixed adversarial training batches.
AI.result: On OfficeHome, PACS, and VisDA benchmarks, SFT+RL achieves average improvements of 10.2% in clean accuracy and 15.8% in adversarial robustness over existing state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The SFT+RL framework effectively addresses robust UDA by preserving CLIP's semantic priors while adapting to adversarial noise, and the confidence-guided pseudo-labeling strategy with decaying threshold successfully balances label quality and coverage for cross-domain robustness.

title: Signal or Noise? Understanding Generative Models for Real-World Sensor Time Series
summary: Generative models have changed how machine learning represents complex data distributions, especially in language and vision, yet many real-world systems are observed instead as continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy sensor time series. Existing generative modeling of sensor data, however, remains fragmented across modalities, datasets, and task formulations, limiting a systematic understanding of when, how, and why generative models succeed or fail in real-world settings. To address this gap, we introduce SensorGen, a large-scale study of sensor-signal generation spanning 14 settings across 4 domains, 7 datasets, and 12 signal modalities. Leveraging SensorGen, we systematically evaluate generative models from five major families and uncover three key findings: (1) flow-matching models provide strong overall performance across most settings; (2) signal properties matter, with demographic covariates improving longitudinal generation and time-frequency modeling improving high-frequency signal generation; and (3) generated signals have practical utility beyond visual realism, with scaling improving generation quality and synthetic data improving downstream performance. Together, SensorGen establishes a broader understanding of design choices, evaluation protocols, and failure modes in real-world sensor data generation.

AI.tldr: SensorGen is a large-scale study evaluating generative models for sensor time series data across 14 settings, 4 domains, 7 datasets, and 12 modalities, finding flow-matching models perform best overall, signal properties critically affect generation quality, and synthetic sensor data has practical utility for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing generative modeling of sensor data is fragmented across modalities, datasets, and task formulations, lacking a systematic understanding of when, how, and why generative models succeed or fail in real-world sensor settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce SensorGen, a large-scale benchmark spanning 14 settings across 4 domains, 7 datasets, and 12 signal modalities, and systematically evaluate generative models from five major families (including flow-matching models) on sensor-signal generation.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) flow-matching models achieve strong overall performance across most settings; (2) signal properties matter—demographic covariates improve longitudinal generation and time-frequency modeling improves high-frequency signal generation; (3) generated signals have practical utility beyond visual realism, with scaling improving quality and synthetic data improving downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: SensorGen establishes a broader understanding of design choices, evaluation protocols, and failure modes in real-world sensor data generation, unifying previously fragmented approaches.

title: SAF3R: Dynamic Sparse Attention for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction Transformers
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (F3R) transformers have recently achieved remarkable success. However, scaling them to long image sequences remains challenging, as the quadratic complexity of cross-view global attention quickly becomes the dominant computational bottleneck. While recent efforts attempt to improve efficiency through compressed or sparse attention, they fail to fully exploit the inherent sparsity and dynamic behavior of global attention. In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of global attention across multiple F3R transformers and reveal that attention patterns are highly heterogeneous, dynamic, and extremely sparse across layers and attention heads. Motivated by these findings, we propose SAF3R, a training-free dynamic sparse attention framework tailored to F3R transformers. SAF3R integrates tailored sparse attention mechanisms with offline head profiling and an efficient online adaptation strategy to match input-dependent attention behaviors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAF3R achieves high sparsity ratios while preserving camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction quality, translating into substantial end-to-end speedup on F3R transformers compared to existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/jndeng/SAF3R

AI.tldr: SAF3R introduces a training-free dynamic sparse attention framework for Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction transformers, exploiting heterogeneous and sparse attention patterns to achieve significant speedup while maintaining reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Scaling F3R transformers to long image sequences is bottlenecked by quadratic complexity of cross-view global attention. Existing efficient attention methods fail to exploit the inherent sparsity and dynamic behavior of global attention in these models.
AI.method: SAF3R performs a comprehensive analysis revealing heterogeneous, dynamic, and extremely sparse attention patterns across layers/heads, then proposes a training-free framework integrating tailored sparse attention mechanisms with offline head profiling and online adaptation to match input-dependent attention behaviors.
AI.result: Achieves high sparsity ratios with preserved camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction quality, yielding substantial end-to-end speedup on F3R transformers compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the naturally sparse and dynamic nature of attention in F3R transformers via a training-free sparse framework is an effective approach for efficient 3D reconstruction from long image sequences.

title: On Preserving Geometrical Invariance for Superpixel Image Classification using Graph Transformer
summary: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) for image classification exploit a dense grid of pixels containing redundant information. Consequently, for a larger image dataset, CNNs and ViTs face deployability challenges due to high computational complexity. Representing images as graphs of superpixels offers an efficient alternative that preserves key information while eliminating pixel-level redundancy. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been utilized on such graphs to perform image classification. However, GNNs are known to struggle with capturing long-range dependencies which is important in the domain of image classification. Furthermore, a majority of these superpixel-based image classification approaches do not explicitly preserve translation/rotation invariance. Nevertheless, preserving translation/rotation invariance is important for robust image classification. Thus, this paper proposes SuperGT, a Graph Transformer-based framework for image classification, which captures the long range dependencies, along with a pre-processing scheme that preserves translation/rotation invariance. We evaluate SuperGT on CIFAR-10 dataset and observe that it performs significantly better than many baselines. Furthermore, we note that the overall performance of SuperGT is comparable to the previous state-of-the-art model, namely, ShapeGNN, without relying on coordinates of the boundary points of each superpixel required by ShapeGNN.

AI.tldr: SuperGT is a Graph Transformer framework for image classification that uses superpixel graphs to reduce computational complexity while capturing long-range dependencies and preserving translation/rotation invariance, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art ShapeGNN on CIFAR-10 without needing boundary point coordinates.
AI.motivation: CNNs and ViTs face deployability challenges due to high computational complexity from processing dense pixel grids with redundant information. Existing GNN-based superpixel approaches struggle with long-range dependencies and often fail to preserve translation/rotation invariance, both critical for robust image classification.
AI.method: SuperGT proposes a Graph Transformer-based framework that operates on superpixel graphs, capturing long-range dependencies via attention mechanisms, combined with a preprocessing scheme designed to preserve translation and rotation invariance.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, SuperGT significantly outperforms many baselines and achieves performance comparable to the previous state-of-the-art model ShapeGNN, without requiring coordinates of superpixel boundary points that ShapeGNN relies on.
AI.conclusion: SuperGT effectively addresses the limitations of prior superpixel-based GNN methods for image classification by jointly handling long-range dependencies and geometric invariance, offering a more efficient yet competitive alternative to pixel-dense models and previous GNN approaches.

title: IDEAL-Bench: Indoor Dataset and Evaluation suite for Analyzing 3D Layout reasoning
summary: Spatial question answering is the dominant paradigm for evaluating spatial intelligence in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), but it leaves a complementary axis of spatial competence under-evaluated: holistic 3D layout inference, which predicts every visible object's pose and extent from a single image in a structured form. To this end, we introduce IDEAL-Bench, an evaluation suite that requires VLMs to predict structured 3D layouts on photorealistic indoor scenes across 10 room types, scored along five numerical dimensions and a perceptual render-and-compare protocol. By operating on semantically realistic scenes with full asset substitution under controlled lighting and viewpoint, IDEAL-Bench moves beyond CLEVR-style simple geometric primitives so that any image-space discrepancy reflects spatial reasoning alone. The benchmark is built on IDEAL-Scenes, a procedurally generated dataset of 1,000 re-renderable Blender environments with ground-truth layouts. Evaluating 15 prominent VLMs reveals three findings: the task remains substantially unsolved, with the strongest model reaching only 62.1/100 overall; all models exhibit a sharp asymmetry between object recognition and geometric regression, indicating that current VLMs are trained to describe scenes rather than to measure them; model rankings partially diverge from those on QA-based and primitive-reconstruction benchmarks: top-tier consensus holds, but mid-tier rankings shift substantially. Collectively, these findings establish IDEAL-Bench as a diagnostic suite, targeting the geometric and structural competencies that QA-based evaluation cannot surface, and paving the way towards more rigorous evaluation of spatial intelligence in next-generation VLMs. Together, these findings position IDEAL-Bench as a principled diagnostic for whether future VLMs achieve genuine spatial understanding rather than linguistic approximations of it.

AI.tldr: IDEAL-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating holistic 3D layout inference in VLMs, requiring structured prediction of object poses and extents from single images across 1,000 photorealistic indoor scenes. Testing 15 VLMs reveals the task is largely unsolved (best score 62.1/100), models show a sharp asymmetry between recognition and geometric regression, and rankings diverge partially from QA-based benchmarks, establishing IDEAL-Bench as a diagnostic for genuine spatial understanding beyond linguistic approximation.
AI.motivation: Current spatial intelligence evaluation in VLMs is dominated by spatial question answering (QA), which overlooks holistic 3D layout inference—predicting every visible object's pose and extent from a single image. Existing benchmarks like CLEVR use simple geometric primitives rather than semantically realistic scenes, making it unclear whether image-space errors reflect spatial reasoning or other factors.
AI.method: IDEAL-Bench evaluates VLMs on structured 3D layout prediction across 10 room types, scoring along five numerical dimensions plus a perceptual render-and-compare protocol. It is built on IDEAL-Scenes, a procedural dataset of 1,000 re-renderable Blender environments with ground-truth layouts, featuring semantically realistic scenes with full asset substitution under controlled lighting and viewpoint.
AI.result: Evaluating 15 prominent VLMs shows: (1) the task is substantially unsolved, with the best model reaching 62.1/100; (2) all models exhibit a sharp asymmetry between object recognition and geometric regression; (3) model rankings partially diverge from QA-based and primitive-reconstruction benchmarks—top-tier consensus holds, but mid-tier rankings shift substantially.
AI.conclusion: IDEAL-Bench serves as a diagnostic suite targeting geometric and structural competencies that QA-based evaluation cannot surface, paving the way for more rigorous evaluation of spatial intelligence in next-generation VLMs and distinguishing genuine spatial understanding from linguistic approximations.

title: HiFA4: Training-Free 4-bit FlashAttention on Ascend HIF4 NPUs for LLM Inference
summary:
We present HiFA4, a post-training operator-level design that executes both QK^T and PV in FlashAttention as 4-bit HIF4 Cube GEMMs for LLM inference on Ascend NPUs, while maintaining the online softmax state in FP16. To our knowledge, HiFA4 is the first Ascend-HIF4-targeted design of this kind evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks.
  HiFA4 combines two mechanisms. Smooth-QK applies a calibration-static per-channel equivalent rescaling to Q and K after RoPE, transferring quantization difficulty from K to Q without per-tile online reduction at inference. P-Reordering accumulates the softmax normalizer from the same quantized attention weights P_hat used in the PV GEMM, rather than from a higher-precision reconstruction. We show that this inconsistent formulation introduces a coherent output-scaling error, and validate the effect on a Qwen3-8B Layer-0 MMLU trace, where all 3.6M measured attention tiles exhibit net probability-mass loss with median epsilon_bar = -0.064. P-Reordering also allows the normalizer to be fused into the PV Cube GEMM.
  Across five LLMs, HiFA4 reduces quantization-induced decision drift. On Qwen3-8B, it recovers 37.5% of the accuracy gap introduced by direct HIF4 quantization, narrows the sample-weighted accuracy loss from 1.12 pp to 0.70 pp, reduces BF16-inconsistent MMLU predictions from 16.3% to 8.2%, and cuts MMLU accuracy regressions by 57% (1071 to 465). On Gemma2-9B, mild smoothing keeps HiFA4 within 0.7 pp of BF16 while reducing MMLU regressions by 27%. On LLaMA3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4B, where Smooth-QK is disabled, P-Reordering with the adopted Q-Mean auxiliary still reduces full-set MMLU regressions by 41-52%. A preliminary instruction-scheduling analysis projects a 35.4% critical-path latency reduction relative to BF16 by fusing the softmax normalizer into the PV Cube GEMM; on-hardware validation is left to future work.

AI.tldr: HiFA4 is a post-training operator-level design that executes FlashAttention's QK^T and PV as 4-bit HIF4 Cube GEMMs on Ascend NPUs, using Smooth-QK (calibration-static per-channel rescaling) and P-Reordering (accumulating softmax normalizer from quantized attention weights) to reduce quantization-induced accuracy loss across five LLMs.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient 4-bit quantized FlashAttention inference on Ascend NPUs by addressing the accuracy degradation caused by direct HIF4 quantization of attention operations.
AI.method: HiFA4 uses (1) Smooth-QK: calibration-static per-channel rescaling of Q and K after RoPE to transfer quantization difficulty from K to Q without per-tile online reduction; and (2) P-Reordering: accumulating the softmax normalizer from the same quantized attention weights P_hat used in PV GEMM rather than from higher-precision reconstruction, fusing the normalizer into the PV Cube GEMM.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B: recovers 37.5% of accuracy gap from direct HIF4, narrows sample-weighted accuracy loss from 1.12 pp to 0.70 pp, reduces BF16-inconsistent MMLU predictions from 16.3% to 8.2%, cuts MMLU regressions by 57% (1071 to 465). On Gemma2-9B: within 0.7 pp of BF16, reduces regressions by 27%. On LLaMA3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-4B: regressions reduced by 41-52% with P-Reordering and Q-Mean auxiliary. Projected 35.4% critical-path latency reduction.
AI.conclusion: HiFA4 effectively reduces quantization-induced decision drift across diverse LLMs, with both accuracy recovery and latency improvements, though on-hardware validation of latency projections remains future work.

title: A Vision Based System for Guided and Collaborative Reconstruction of Fragmented Documents
comment: The paper was presented at MetroArchaeo 2024 in Malta. Publication in Springer Proceedings is still delayed
summary: This paper presents the development and evaluation of a collaborative system for real-time reconstruction of fragmented paper documents in the context of cultural heritage preservation. The developed system includes a collaborative robot, or cobot, that can fully manage the positioning of paper fragments using a specially designed vacuum-based suction attachment. This attachment enables gentle and precise positioning, ensuring the preservation of fragile materials. With this device, we are able to achieve a positioning repeatability of 0.57mm for fragments of 8cm^2. The system offers users the flexibility to choose between manual positioning, with visual guidance, or fully automated positioning performed by the cobot. To further improve the reconstruction process, AI methods for image interpretation, specifically for segmentation and positioning tasks, were applied and evaluated for their applicability to template-based reconstruction of damaged paper fragments. Our investigation provides critical insights into the performance of different local feature matching methods under different document types, taking into account rotation, scale robustness, and the degree of damage to the fragments. With a focus on the reconstruction of damaged and optically altered archival material, SE2-LoFTR, a detector-free local feature matching method, was chosen as the preferred method for the system due to its robust performance in our experiments.

AI.tldr: A collaborative robotic system with vacuum-based suction attachment and AI-based image matching (SE2-LoFTR) was developed for real-time reconstruction of fragmented paper documents, achieving 0.57mm positioning repeatability and flexible manual/automated operation modes.
AI.motivation: To preserve cultural heritage by developing a precise, gentle, and flexible system for reassembling fragile fragmented paper documents that reduces human handling and damage risk.
AI.method: A collaborative robot (cobot) with vacuum-based suction attachment for gentle fragment positioning; AI-based local feature matching methods evaluated for segmentation and positioning; SE2-LoFTR selected as the preferred detector-free matching method after comparative experiments.
AI.result: Positioning repeatability of 0.57mm for 8cm² fragments; SE2-LoFTR demonstrated robust performance across different document types, rotation, scale variations, and damage levels.
AI.conclusion: The developed cobot system with SE2-LoFTR matching is effective for template-based reconstruction of damaged archival material, offering both manual and automated positioning modes for cultural heritage preservation.

title: SAD-LoRA: Spectral Alignment for Low-Rank Knowledge Distillation
comment: ICML'26 workshop on CoLoRAI - The 2nd Workshop on Connecting Low-rank Representations in AI, 15 pages
summary: Distilling a fine-tuned teacher into a LoRA-adapted student is a standard recipe for parameter-efficient compression, but output-level KD does not explicitly control which rank-$r$ weight subspace the adapter occupies. We propose \textbf{SAD-LoRA} (\textbf{S}pectral \textbf{A}lignment \textbf{D}istillation), which selects this subspace from the data-weighted student-space reference update $\DWT\Sigx^{1/2}$ and maintains it during training via a differentiable principal-angle loss on $\colspan(B)$. We show that the data-weighted distillation error decomposes exactly into subspace misalignment, within-subspace coefficient mismatch, and irreducible rank residual; standard KD can affect the first term only indirectly through output gradients. On controlled synthetic problems with a flat teacher spectrum, SAD-LoRA reduces the subspace-misalignment term from $51\%$ to nearly zero and lifts final subspace alignment from $0.49$ to $1.00$. On RoBERTa-large to RoBERTa-base distillation across six GLUE tasks, SAD-LoRA improves rank efficiency: at $r{=}4$, it matches or beats the strongest included spectral baseline on five of six tasks, and at $r{=}8$ it gives the best result on SST-2 and CoLA. Ablations identify subspace alignment as the load-bearing component, while coefficient matching is auxiliary.

AI.tldr: SAD-LoRA improves parameter-efficient compression by aligning the LoRA adapter's subspace with a data-weighted reference update through a differentiable principal-angle loss, significantly reducing subspace misalignment and improving rank efficiency on GLUE tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard output-level KD for LoRA-compressed models does not explicitly control which rank-$r$ weight subspace the adapter occupies, leading to suboptimal subspace alignment.
AI.method: SAD-LoRA selects the adapter subspace from the data-weighted student-space reference update $\DWT\Sigx^{1/2}$ and maintains alignment during training via a differentiable principal-angle loss on $\colspan(B)$.
AI.result: On synthetic problems, SAD-LoRA reduces subspace-misalignment from 51% to nearly zero and lifts alignment from 0.49 to 1.00. On RoBERTa-large-to-base distillation across six GLUE tasks, SAD-LoRA at r=4 matches/beats the best spectral baseline on 5/6 tasks; at r=8 it achieves best results on SST-2 and CoLA.
AI.conclusion: Subspace alignment is the critical component for effective LoRA distillation, with coefficient matching playing an auxiliary role; SAD-LoRA offers a principled approach to controlling the adapter subspace explicitly.

title: RADIO1D: Elastic Representations for Condensed Vision Modeling
comment: Published as main conference paper at ICML 2026
summary: This paper challenges the assumption that vision-language models (VLMs) require fixed patch-based 2D vision features. Analyzing fine-tuned vision encoders, we find that representations become increasingly abstract and less spatially coherent during VLM training. Notably, models trained with image-text alignment (such as SigLIP2) develop a small number of specialized tokens that effectively summarize global image content. Building on this, we introduce RADIO1D, which compresses images into a compact, variable-length 1D token sequence using multi-teacher knowledge distillation and an autoencoder design. The resulting representations exhibit strong hierarchical summarization, enabling accurate scene understanding - even with a single token - and support improved composition-aware image retrieval. In VLMs, RADIO1D provides flexible accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs through adjustable token counts, delivering competitive performance on diverse multimodal benchmarks with lower computational overhead and better accuracy.

AI.tldr: RADIO1D compresses images into variable-length 1D token sequences instead of fixed 2D patch-based features, achieving efficient scene understanding with fewer tokens while maintaining or improving VLM performance.
AI.motivation: The assumption that VLMs require fixed patch-based 2D vision features is challenged. The authors observe that fine-tuned vision encoders become increasingly abstract and less spatially coherent, with specialized tokens emerging that summarize global content. This motivates moving beyond rigid spatial grids to more compact representations.
AI.method: Multi-teacher knowledge distillation combined with an autoencoder design to compress images into compact, variable-length 1D token sequences, building on insights from SigLIP2's specialized summarization tokens.
AI.result: RADIO1D enables accurate scene understanding even with a single token, supports improved composition-aware image retrieval, and provides flexible accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs in VLMs through adjustable token counts, delivering competitive multimodal benchmark performance with lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Fixed 2D patch-based representations are not necessary for VLMs; variable-length 1D token sequences offer a more efficient and flexible alternative that can summarize global image content hierarchically while reducing computational overhead.

title: On the effectiveness of reward functions in reinforcement learning for confidence calibration of large language models
summary: In this paper, we consider the setting where large language models (LLMs) are trained using reinforcement learning (RL) to simultaneously improve reasoning accuracy and verbalize its confidence. Our reward scheme uses two functions for rewarding confidence verbalized by the LLM: one when the LLM is correct and a different one when the LLM is incorrect. With a poorly designed reward scheme, the LLM may be incentivized to answer incorrectly so that it can be confident that its answer is indeed incorrect, a phenomenon that we call confidence reward hacking. We propose the concept of non-hackable confidence reward schemes and define a spectrum of such reward schemes for RL confidence calibration training in LLMs. We demonstrate that selective confidence reward hacking can occur in practical datasets with reward schemes that are not designed to be non-hackable. We also demonstrate that the reward scheme with the best calibration to accuracy tradeoff depends on the dataset and the application, and propose using the reward scheme as a hyperparameter to optimize the tradeoffs in accordance to what is important for the application. The code of our experiments is available in https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rl-confidence-calibration-9ED4/README.md.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to train LLMs via RL to improve both reasoning accuracy and confidence verbalization, introduces "confidence reward hacking," defines non-hackable confidence reward schemes, and demonstrates that the optimal reward scheme for calibration-accuracy tradeoff depends on the dataset and application.
AI.motivation: LLMs trained with RL often struggle to verbalize calibrated confidence alongside accurate reasoning; poorly designed reward schemes can incentivize the model to intentionally answer incorrectly to confidently predict its own error, a phenomenon called confidence reward hacking.
AI.method: Two reward functions are used—one for correct answers and one for incorrect ones. The paper formally defines non-hackable confidence reward schemes along a spectrum and treats the reward scheme as a tunable hyperparameter to balance calibration and accuracy.
AI.result: Selective confidence reward hacking occurs in practical datasets under non-hackable designs. The best reward scheme for calibration-to-accuracy tradeoff varies by dataset and application.
AI.conclusion: Non-hackable reward schemes mitigate confidence reward hacking; the reward scheme should be treated as a hyperparameter tailored to application-specific tradeoffs.

title: Probing Identity-Specific Motion Signatures: A Controlled Diagnostic Study
summary: Identity recognition (e.g., person, animal re-identification) has traditionally relied heavily on static appearance cues. Yet motion--consistent, individual-specific dynamics--can provide a complementary and potentially more robust signature, especially when appearance is weak or variable. This raises a fundamental question: when identity-specific motion cues are clearly present, to what extent do modern video models use them for recognition? To investigate this question, we conduct a systematic diagnostic study and introduce BALLER120, a controlled benchmark of 120 professional basketball players performing free-throws. By focusing on the same multi-phase action across individuals, BALLER120 reduces action-level variation and identity-correlated acquisition biases, enabling fine-grained analysis of identity-specific kinematic patterns. We find that modern video models can predict identity accurately from RGB videos, but often rely on static appearance cues such as faces and jersey regions, even when informative motion cues are available. Strikingly, when appearance is suppressed through silhouette-only or skeleton-only inputs, the same model architectures shift toward motion micro-patterns (e.g., foot placement and elbow bending). Despite containing less visual information, appearance-suppressed representations achieve competitive accuracy and stronger robustness to appearance shifts. Our qualitative analyses further show that appearance-suppressed models attend to distinctive motion patterns across individuals. Overall, our study demonstrates that identity-specific motion signatures are present, informative, and learnable, but modern video models may overlook them in favor of easier static shortcuts unless appearance cues are explicitly suppressed.

AI.tldr: Modern video models rely on static appearance cues (faces, jerseys) for identity recognition even when distinctive motion patterns are available; suppressing appearance forces models to use motion micro-patterns (foot placement, elbow bending), achieving competitive accuracy with stronger robustness to appearance shifts.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether modern video models use identity-specific motion cues for recognition, given that motion provides a complementary and potentially more robust signature when appearance is weak or variable.
AI.method: Introduced BALLER120, a controlled benchmark of 120 basketball players performing free-throws; systematically compared model performance on RGB videos vs. appearance-suppressed inputs (silhouette-only, skeleton-only); conducted qualitative attention analyses.
AI.result: Models predict identity accurately from RGB but rely on static cues (faces, jerseys); appearance-suppressed models shift to motion micro-patterns, achieve competitive accuracy, and show stronger robustness to appearance shifts.
AI.conclusion: Identity-specific motion signatures are present, informative, and learnable, but modern video models overlook them in favor of static shortcuts unless appearance is explicitly suppressed.

title: Structure-Specific Representational Priors Causally Control the Grokking Delay
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. Code and artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21132757
summary: Grokking -- generalization arriving long after training-set interpolation -- can be accelerated by structure-agnostic interventions: gradient filtering, weight-norm clamping, geometric penalties on hidden representations. Whether the delay specifically measures the time to form task-structured representations has remained an observational claim. We test it causally by injecting representational priors of varying structural content into a one-layer transformer learning modular addition: a supervised-contrastive auxiliary loss whose positives encode (i) the task's true equivalence structure ($(a+b) \bmod p$), (ii) a coherent-but-wrong sibling structure ($(a-b) \bmod p$), or (iii) a random partition, all with identical loss form, strength, class sizes, and geometry. Whether generalization occurs follows a clean gradation: true structure 22/30 runs; sibling structure, which needs the same periodic features but the wrong combination, 14/15; random partition, satisfiable only by memorization, 0/20 (Fisher exact $p = 1.3 \times 10^{-7}$). A weight-norm-matched control replaying each intervention's norm trajectory onto plain cross-entropy generalizes in 0/15, collapsing into logit-scale saturation, ruling out the norm as mediator. Representation probes show structure formation precedes and predicts generalization in all 95 runs. Only the true structure also accelerates grokking, up to $2.75\times$ faster than baseline, but the acceleration is dose-dependent, bimodal across seeds, and a net wall-clock win only in its strongest cases given the contrastive term's overhead. The grokking delay is, causally, the time to form the right representational structure, where "right" is decided at the level of features rather than labels: coherent-but-wrong structure leaves grokking intact, random structure abolishes it, and only the true structure hastens it.

AI.tldr: This paper causally tests whether grokking delay is the time needed to form task-structured representations by injecting representational priors (true modular addition structure, coherent-but-wrong structure, random partition) into a one-layer transformer. Results show a clean gradation: true structure generalizes (22/30), wrong structure generalizes (14/15) but doesn't accelerate grokking, random structure never generalizes (0/20). Only true structure accelerates grokking up to 2.75x. The grokking delay is causally the time to form the right representational structure at the feature level, not label level.
AI.motivation: To causally test whether the grokking delay specifically measures the time to form task-structured representations, moving beyond observational claims.
AI.method: Injected representational priors via supervised-contrastive auxiliary losses encoding (i) true modular addition structure, (ii) coherent-but-wrong sibling structure (a-b mod p), or (iii) random partition into a one-layer transformer. Used identical loss form, strength, class sizes, geometry. Included weight-norm-matched control.
AI.result: True structure: 22/30 generalize; wrong structure: 14/15 generalize; random partition: 0/20 generalize (Fisher exact p=1.3e-7). Only true structure accelerates grokking (up to 2.75x), dose-dependent and bimodal. Weight-norm control generalizes in 0/15. Representation probes show structure formation precedes and predicts generalization in all 95 runs.
AI.conclusion: The grokking delay is causally the time to form the right representational structure, where "right" is decided at the feature level rather than label level: coherent-but-wrong structure leaves grokking intact, random structure abolishes it, and only true structure hastens it.

title: Moonstone: A Multimodal Foundation Model and Benchmark for Lunar Remote Sensing
summary: Decades of orbital missions have produced multi-modal remote sensing data for the Moon, spanning optical imagery, spectroscopy, thermal emission, radar, gravity, and elemental composition. Yet these datasets remain fragmented across archives, and no benchmark exists for evaluating machine learning on lunar data. We introduce Moonstone, the first multi-modal foundation model benchmark for lunar remote sensing. Our contributions are: (1) a 28-channel, 128 pixels-per-degree (~237 m) global lunar pretraining dataset from seven instrument families across five missions, (2) MG-MAE, a modality-grouped masked autoencoder with per-group convolutional tokenizers, a shared Vision Transformer encoder, attention masking for missing modalities, coverage-adaptive masking for heterogeneous spatial coverage, and spectral continuity regularization for physically plausible reconstructions, and (3) a benchmark of six downstream tasks covering classification, regression, and segmentation. MG-MAE pretrained features outperform scratch baselines on all tasks and surpass both ImageNet-pretrained and vanilla MAE baselines by large margins. Data and code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ayushprd/Moonstone and https://github.com/ayushprd/Moonstone .

AI.tldr: Moonstone is the first multi-modal foundation model benchmark for lunar remote sensing, introducing a 28-channel global lunar dataset (from 7 instruments across 5 missions), a modality-grouped masked autoencoder (MG-MAE) with specialized masking strategies, and a benchmark of 6 downstream tasks where MG-MAE pretrained features significantly outperform scratch, ImageNet-pretrained, and vanilla MAE baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal lunar remote sensing data (optical, spectroscopy, thermal, radar, gravity, elemental) is fragmented across archives with no existing benchmark for evaluating machine learning on lunar data, motivating the creation of a unified benchmark and pretraining framework.
AI.method: The authors construct a 28-channel global lunar dataset at 128 pixels/degree (~237 m) from seven instrument families across five missions. They propose MG-MAE (modality-grouped masked autoencoder) with per-group convolutional tokenizers, a shared Vision Transformer encoder, attention masking for missing modalities, coverage-adaptive masking for heterogeneous spatial coverage, and spectral continuity regularization.
AI.result: MG-MAE pretrained features outperform scratch baselines on all six downstream tasks (classification, regression, segmentation) and surpass both ImageNet-pretrained and vanilla MAE baselines by large margins.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal pretraining with domain-specific masking strategies significantly improves performance on lunar remote sensing tasks, and the open-source benchmark (data and code) enables reproducible ML research on planetary science data.

title: One Framework for All: Cross-Modal Membership Inference for Generative Models
summary: Large generative models across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text modalities have been shown to pose significant privacy risks. One fundamental threat is membership inference attacks (MIA), which aim to determine whether a given data point was used in a model's training set. Although prior work has investigated MIAs against these three classes of generative models, existing approaches treat them in isolation and are not cross-applicable, thereby limiting their real-world utility. To address this limitation, we present the first comprehensive study of a unified membership inference framework that applies across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text modalities. Our approach is grounded in a key modality-agnostic observation: the output distribution of a generative model can approximate its training data distribution. Leveraging this property, we model the distributions of model-generated outputs and auxiliary non-member samples in a shared embedding space, and perform membership inference via likelihood ratio testing. We conduct extensive experiments in a strict black-box setting under both partial-knowledge and zero-knowledge threat models, and evaluate membership inference against both fine-tuning and pre-training data. Experimental results demonstrate our approach's superior performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods, which are typically optimized for a single model class.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive unified membership inference framework applicable across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text generative models, using a modality-agnostic approach based on output distribution approximation of training data and likelihood ratio testing in a shared embedding space.
AI.motivation: Existing membership inference attacks (MIA) against generative models (text-to-text, text-to-image, image-to-text) are treated in isolation and are not cross-applicable, limiting their real-world utility. A unified framework is needed.
AI.method: The framework uses a modality-agnostic observation that a generative model's output distribution approximates its training data distribution. It models distributions of model-generated outputs and auxiliary non-member samples in a shared embedding space, then performs membership inference via likelihood ratio testing under strict black-box settings.
AI.result: Superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods that are optimized for single model classes, evaluated under both partial-knowledge and zero-knowledge threat models for both fine-tuning and pre-training data.
AI.conclusion: A unified MIA framework is feasible and effective across multiple generative model modalities, outperforming modality-specific approaches, which has significant implications for privacy auditing and risk assessment.

title: Do Medical Vision Language Models Actually See? A Counterfactual Grounding Framework and Hard-Negative Contrastive Training for Visually-Reliant Medical VLMs
summary: Large vision language models (VLMs) report strong accuracy on medical question-answering, yet it remains unclear whether they reason from visual evidence or exploit textual shortcuts. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that decouples visual and textual contributions by substituting input images with controlled surrogates blank, pixel-shuffled, image-absent, and CLIP-retrieved hard negatives and derive a suite of grounding metrics including the Visual Reliance Score (VRS) and Visual Hallucination Rate (VHR). We further introduce CORAL (COntrastive Retrieval-Augmented Learning), a 7B-parameter LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-VL-7B trained with a Contrastive Grounding Objective (CGO) that penalises answer invariance under hard-negative image swaps. On a paired controlled evaluation across four closed-form medical VQA benchmarks (PathVQA, PMC-VQA, SLAKE, VQA-RAD; n=400 total), CORAL improves macro accuracy by +6.7 pp (P(Delta>0)=0.988) and reduces VHR by 8.0 pp (P<0.001) over the matched Qwen2.5-VL-7B base; neither MedVLThinker RL variant achieves a significant gain on either metric. Cross-domain diagnostics further reveal that image substitution costs only <=6.5 pp on medical benchmarks versus 48-61 pp on general-domain tasks, situating the grounding gap that CGO targets. We discuss evaluation limitations openly including train/eval benchmark overlap and underpowered secondary metrics and release our framework, training code, and model weights to support reproducible grounding audits of medical VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CORAL, a contrastive retrieval-augmented learning framework that improves visual grounding in medical VLMs by penalizing answer invariance under hard-negative image swaps, achieving +6.7 pp accuracy gain and 8.0 pp reduction in visual hallucination rate over Qwen2.5-VL-7B on closed-form medical VQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs report strong accuracy on medical VQA but it is unclear whether they genuinely reason from visual evidence or exploit textual shortcuts (e.g., priors, label leakage). The paper aims to decouple visual vs. textual contributions and develop methods to enforce genuine visual grounding.
AI.method: (1) A counterfactual evaluation framework using controlled image surrogates (blank, pixel-shuffled, image-absent, CLIP-retrieved hard negatives) to compute Visual Reliance Score (VRS) and Visual Hallucination Rate (VHR). (2) CORAL: a 7B LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-VL-7B with a Contrastive Grounding Objective (CGO) that penalizes answer invariance under hard-negative image swaps.
AI.result: CORAL improves macro accuracy by +6.7 pp (P(Δ>0)=0.988) and reduces VHR by 8.0 pp (P<0.001) over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base across four medical VQA benchmarks (n=400). No significant gains from MedVLThinker RL variants. Cross-domain diagnostics show image substitution costs ≤6.5 pp on medical vs. 48-61 pp on general-domain tasks.
AI.conclusion: CORAL effectively improves visual grounding in medical VLMs, but the small grounding gap in medical benchmarks (≤6.5 pp) versus general-domain tasks suggests limited scope for improvement; the paper discusses evaluation limitations (train/eval overlap, underpowered secondary metrics) and releases resources for reproducibility.

title: How Many Initial Points Does Bayesian Optimization Need?
comment: 4 pages. Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Decision-Making from Offline Datasets to Online Adaptation
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) generally begins with an initialization phase: a batch of $n_0$ uninformed evaluations. The choice of $n_0$ remains largely heuristic, and we empirically observe that the total cost (random initial points plus BO iterations needed to find the global optimum) is U-shaped in $n_0$, i.e., a practitioner wastes resources by selecting either too low or too high a value of $n_0$. We find this tradeoff persists across MLE, Bayesian MCMC, and exact GP hyperparameters, as well as across acquisition functions. Toward the latter, Thompson Sampling appears an exception, with both total cost and simple regret essentially $n_0$-agnostic, though higher in our experiments. We attribute this U-shape to the known boundary issue of variance-driven BO: BO burns early budget on corners of the hypercube before turning inward. We demonstrate this effect using a 3D BO trajectory where the exact hyperparameters are known. We conclude with practical recommendations: use multi-step lookahead BO where possible; otherwise use Thompson Sampling when $n_0$ cannot be tuned, and a generously large $n_0$ when it can.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the impact of the number of initial random evaluations (n₀) in Bayesian Optimization, finding a U-shaped cost curve where both too few and too many initial points waste resources. Thompson Sampling is n₀-agnostic but less efficient, while the U-shape stems from variance-driven BO's tendency to explore boundary regions early. Practical recommendations include using multi-step lookahead BO, Thompson Sampling when n₀ can't be tuned, or a large n₀ when it can.
AI.motivation: The choice of n₀ (number of initial random evaluations) in BO is largely heuristic, and its impact on total optimization cost (initialization + BO iterations to find global optimum) is not well understood, leading to potential resource waste in practice.
AI.method: Empirical study across multiple BO configurations (MLE, Bayesian MCMC, exact GP hyperparameters) and acquisition functions, with trajectory analysis using known exact hyperparameters in 3D to explain the observed U-shaped cost phenomenon.
AI.result: Total cost is U-shaped in n₀ across most settings; Thompson Sampling is n₀-agnostic but yields higher cost/simple regret; the U-shape is attributed to variance-driven BO's boundary issue where early budget is spent on hypercube corners.
AI.conclusion: Use multi-step lookahead BO when feasible; otherwise prefer Thompson Sampling if n₀ cannot be tuned, or a generously large n₀ if it can be tuned.

title: ClinOCR-Bench: A Comprehensive Clinical Scanned Document Dataset for Optical Character Recognition Model Evaluation
summary: Extracting textual information from scanned medical documents, such as external laboratory reports and manually filled forms, has been a major challenge in modern electronic health records (EHRs). Recent advancements in vision language models (VLMs) have shown great promise over traditional OCR tools. However, at this point, most clinical OCR studies were conducted on private, institutional data. To our knowledge, there are few publicly available datasets for evaluating OCR models in the clinical domain. Furthermore, common scanning artifacts that undermine OCR performance are not reflected in those datasets, leaving a systematic evaluation unfeasible. Therefore, we release a publicly available, realistic-looking OCR benchmark dataset, ClinOCR-Bench, with 384 scanned images across 6 subsets: Normal, Handwriting, Poor Quality, Rotation, Tables, and Mix-artifacts. ClinOCR-Bench features: 1) diverse document types and layouts, 2) full coverage of common EHR scan artifacts, 3) protected health information-free, 4) template-aware train/test split, and 5) adequate sample size for OCR benchmarking. Baseline OCR performance was evaluated using state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The dataset and documentation are available on GitHub (https://github.com/ClinOCR-Bench/ClinOCR-Bench).

AI.tldr: ClinOCR-Bench is a publicly available, realistic OCR benchmark dataset for clinical documents containing 384 scanned images across 6 artifact subsets (Normal, Handwriting, Poor Quality, Rotation, Tables, Mix-artifacts), designed to fill the gap of lacking standardized public benchmarks for evaluating VLMs on clinical OCR tasks.
AI.motivation: Extracting textual information from scanned medical documents remains a major challenge in EHR systems. Existing clinical OCR studies use private institutional data with few public benchmarks available, and common scanning artifacts affecting OCR performance are not covered in current datasets, making systematic evaluation infeasible.
AI.method: The authors release ClinOCR-Bench with 384 scanned images across 6 subsets: Normal, Handwriting, Poor Quality, Rotation, Tables, and Mix-artifacts. Key features include diverse document types/layouts, full coverage of common EHR scan artifacts, PHI-free content, template-aware train/test split, and adequate sample size. Baseline OCR performance was evaluated using state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs.
AI.result: A publicly available OCR benchmark dataset (ClinOCR-Bench) with 384 images across 6 artifact subsets, with baseline evaluations using state-of-the-art VLMs. The dataset and documentation are available on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: ClinOCR-Bench addresses the lack of public, realistic clinical OCR benchmarks with diverse artifacts, enabling systematic evaluation of VLM-based OCR methods for clinical document extraction.

title: RL Forgets! Towards Continual Policy Optimization
summary: Continual post-training is becoming a central paradigm for adapting vision-language models to evolving tasks. Recent work has increasingly favored reinforcement learning over supervised fine-tuning, driven by the belief that reinforcement learning is inherently less prone to forgetting. However, the belief remains insufficiently validated, as existing evidence is largely drawn from outdated or homogeneous benchmarks. To revisit this assumption, we introduce MRCL, a Multimodal Reasoning Continual Learning benchmark built from diverse and recently released multimodal datasets. Experiments on MRCL show that reinforcement learning can still suffer from severe catastrophic forgetting during continual post-training. To address this challenge, we propose Continual Policy Optimization (CPO), a replay-free framework grounded in the prior-task behavioral KL objective. CPO uses a theoretically justified parameter-movement regularization to limit policy drift on previous tasks. Extensive experiments across multiple model scales demonstrate that CPO consistently reduces forgetting while preserving, and in some cases improving, pretrained model capabilities. On Qwen3-VL-8B, CPO reduces forgetting by 13.7\% and improves pretrained capability by 7.0\%. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/MaolinLuo/CPO.

AI.tldr: MRCL benchmark reveals RL can still suffer catastrophic forgetting in continual multimodal post-training; CPO (Continual Policy Optimization) with prior-task behavioral KL regularization reduces forgetting by 13.7% while improving pretrained capabilities by 7.0% on Qwen3-VL-8B.
AI.motivation: To revisit the insufficiently validated belief that reinforcement learning is inherently less prone to forgetting than supervised fine-tuning in continual post-training of vision-language models, especially given that existing evidence is drawn from outdated or homogeneous benchmarks.
AI.method: Introduced MRCL (Multimodal Reasoning Continual Learning) benchmark using diverse recent datasets; proposed CPO (Continual Policy Optimization), a replay-free framework using prior-task behavioral KL objective with theoretically justified parameter-movement regularization to limit policy drift on previous tasks.
AI.result: On MRCL benchmark, RL still suffers severe catastrophic forgetting. CPO consistently reduces forgetting while preserving/improving pretrained capabilities. On Qwen3-VL-8B: 13.7% forgetting reduction, 7.0% improvement in pretrained capability.
AI.conclusion: RL is not inherently immune to forgetting in continual multimodal post-training; CPO effectively addresses this via replay-free KL-based regularization, and the approach scales across multiple model sizes.

title: ViPo-MLLM: Visual-Pose Multimodal LLM for Gloss-Free Sign Language Translation
summary: Gloss-free Sign Language Translation (SLT) translates sign language videos into spoken-language sentences without gloss annotations, avoiding costly labeling but requiring fine-grained modeling of hands, body, and facial cues. Existing methods often use single-modality or weakly fused features, limiting performance. We propose ViPo-MLLM, a framework that integrates spatio-temporal RGB and human pose features. Dedicated encoders model intra-modal dynamics and cross-modal attention captures long-range dependencies. The fused representation is conditioned with a structured prompt and processed by an LLM trained with contrastive and language modeling objectives. The proposed model was evaluated on the PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily datasets and achieved new state-of-the-art results on both datasets. Moreover, the ViPo-MLLM model attained competitive performance compared to gloss-based recognition approaches, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed pose cues and cross-modal attention mechanisms.

AI.tldr: ViPo-MLLM integrates spatio-temporal RGB and pose features with cross-modal attention and an LLM decoder to achieve state-of-the-art gloss-free sign language translation on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily, rivaling gloss-based methods.
AI.motivation: Gloss-free SLT avoids costly gloss annotations but requires fine-grained modeling of multi-modal cues (hands, body, face). Existing single-modality or weakly fused features limit performance, motivating a stronger multi-modal fusion framework.
AI.method: ViPo-MLLM uses dedicated encoders for spatio-temporal RGB and human pose features, cross-modal attention for long-range dependencies, a structured prompt for conditioning, and an LLM trained with contrastive and language modeling objectives.
AI.result: Achieved new state-of-the-art results on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily datasets; competitive performance compared to gloss-based recognition approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pose cues and cross-modal attention mechanisms are effective for gloss-free SLT, enabling performance competitive with gloss-based methods without costly annotations.

title: NKI-Agent: Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning and Agentic Tool Use for Neuron Kernel Generation
comment: 7 pages. Accepted at DL4C @ ICML 2026 Workshop
summary: Recent agentic approaches to LLM-based kernel generation have achieved impressive results on CUDA. For emerging AI accelerators such as AWS Trainium and Inferentia, automated kernel generation and optimization remain largely unaddressed. Writing kernels for these chips via the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) is particularly challenging: developers must navigate a multi-engine architecture, tile-based programming, and explicit data movement across multi-level memory hierarchy. Moreover, no publicly-available training data, benchmarks, or tool-augmented agents exist for this domain. We introduce NKI-Agent, the first system combining domain-specific supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with a compile-verify-fix agent loop for NKI kernel generation. We adapt the existing CUDA-Agent framework to Neuron hardware, curate 6,000 NKI kernel generation tasks for training, and construct NKIBench, a 250-task benchmark across three difficulty levels. Evaluated on real Trn1 hardware, NKI-Agent with Claude Opus 4.8 and a rank-aware system prompt achieves a 77.3% pass rate on the 150-task NKIBench. We show that tool use is critical: Opus 4.8 scores 6% in single-shot mode without agent tools. On a 60-task subset, we show that an SFT-trained Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B achieves 25.0% pass rate at 1/100th the cost, outperforming Claude Sonnet 4 (15.0%). We also report that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with binary compilation reward fails to improve over SFT, providing guidance on reward design for RL-based kernel generation.

AI.tldr: NKI-Agent is the first system to combine domain-specific supervised fine-tuning with a compile-verify-fix agent loop for automated NKI kernel generation on AWS Trainium/Inferentia, achieving a 77.3% pass rate on the newly introduced NKIBench benchmark using Claude Opus 4.8.
AI.motivation: Automated kernel generation for emerging AI accelerators (AWS Trainium/Inferentia) via the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) remains unaddressed, with no public training data, benchmarks, or tool-augmented agents available, despite impressive results on CUDA.
AI.method: The system adapts the CUDA-Agent framework to Neuron hardware, curates 6,000 NKI kernel generation tasks, and constructs NKIBench (250 tasks across three difficulty levels). It combines domain-specific supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with a compile-verify-fix agent loop, and also explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with binary compilation reward.
AI.result: NKI-Agent with Claude Opus 4.8 achieves 77.3% pass rate on NKIBench (150 tasks). Opus 4.8 drops to 6% without agent tools. SFT-trained Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B achieves 25.0% at 1/100th cost, outperforming Claude Sonnet 4 (15.0%). GRPO with binary compilation reward fails to improve over SFT.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented agent loops are critical for NKI kernel generation; SFT provides a cost-effective alternative; binary compilation rewards are insufficient for RL-based kernel generation, requiring more sophisticated reward design.

title: From Geometric Labels to Semantic Understanding of Indoor Building Components Using Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: 46 pages, 13 figures, accepted by Automation in Construction journal
summary: Point cloud-based understanding has become an important enabler for facility operation and maintenance involving indoor building components. However, existing methods output only discrete labels without explaining component functions or natural language interactions. This paper proposes Building-MLLM, a point cloud-centered multimodal large language model (MLLM) for indoor components, which models point clouds and instructions to generate responses across Simple Recognition, Complex Captioning, and Multi-Engineering Question Answering tasks. Building-MLLM addresses semantic concentration through four domain-specific mechanisms: Point Information Enhancer for task-relevant semantics, Geometry-Preserving Regularization preventing geometric erosion, fixed textual prefix for domain stabilization, and multi-dimensional LoRA balancing recognition with reasoning. A multi-constraint progressive instruction-generation engine is developed to compile a synthetic point cloud-text dataset with 4198 objects, 37,782 instruction-following pairs, and 47 categories. Experiments show that Building-MLLM achieves 88.00%, 65.10%, and 68.14% on the three task types, respectively, demonstrating superior indoor component language understanding and providing initial generalizability in transfer inference on other real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Building-MLLM is a point cloud-centered multimodal large language model for indoor building components that integrates domain-specific mechanisms (Point Information Enhancer, Geometry-Preserving Regularization, fixed textual prefix, multi-dimensional LoRA) and a multi-constraint progressive instruction-generation engine to handle Simple Recognition, Complex Captioning, and Multi-Engineering Question Answering tasks, achieving 88.00%, 65.10%, and 68.14% accuracy respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing point cloud-based understanding methods for indoor building components output only discrete labels without explaining component functions or enabling natural language interactions, limiting their utility for facility operation and maintenance.
AI.method: Building-MLLM employs a point cloud-centered MLLM with four domain-specific mechanisms: (1) Point Information Enhancer for task-relevant semantics, (2) Geometry-Preserving Regularization to prevent geometric erosion, (3) fixed textual prefix for domain stabilization, and (4) multi-dimensional LoRA balancing recognition with reasoning. A multi-constraint progressive instruction-generation engine compiles a synthetic dataset of 4198 objects, 37,782 instruction-following pairs, and 47 categories.
AI.result: Building-MLLM achieves 88.00% on Simple Recognition, 65.10% on Complex Captioning, and 68.14% on Multi-Engineering Question Answering, with initial generalizability demonstrated on other real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Building-MLLM demonstrates superior indoor component language understanding and provides initial transfer inference generalizability, effectively addressing the semantic concentration problem in point cloud-based indoor component understanding.

title: Learning Task-Sufficient World Models by Synergizing Agentic Exploration and Structured Modeling
summary: Learning and planning in imagination using world models provides an effective paradigm for training agents for decision-making. However, existing approaches often rely on high-dimensional latent spaces or generic visual embeddings that retain many factors irrelevant to control, limiting efficiency and generalization across tasks. To this end, we study how agents can learn world models with representations that are task-specific, minimal, and sufficient for decision-making. We achieve this via a closed-loop synergy between the agent and the world model, in which structured world-model learning distills task-sufficient representations from informative interaction data. On the agent side, agents actively probe the environment to collect informative trajectories that expose task-relevant latent factors, guided by an adaptive curriculum. On the world-model side, we learn structured representations over observations to distill compact, task-sufficient latent states from the collected interaction data. This synergy enables the empirical recovery of task-sufficient latent representations that capture all control-relevant factors. Leveraging these representations, the resulting policies achieve improved sample efficiency and generalization, including generalization across skills, object-skill compositions, and previously unseen tasks on standard continuous-control and robotic-manipulation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a closed-loop synergy between agents and world models, where agents actively collect informative trajectories and world models distill task-sufficient latent representations, improving sample efficiency and generalization across tasks in continuous-control and robotic manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing world model approaches rely on high-dimensional latent spaces or generic visual embeddings that retain many control-irrelevant factors, limiting efficiency and generalization across tasks.
AI.method: A closed-loop synergy: (1) Agents actively probe the environment via an adaptive curriculum to collect informative trajectories exposing task-relevant latent factors. (2) World models learn structured representations over observations to distill compact, task-sufficient latent states from collected interaction data.
AI.result: Empirical recovery of task-sufficient latent representations capturing all control-relevant factors; improved sample efficiency and generalization across skills, object-skill compositions, and unseen tasks on continuous-control and robotic-manipulation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Structured world-model learning with task-sufficient representations, driven by agent-world model synergy, significantly enhances sample efficiency and generalization in decision-making tasks.

title: IPDiff: Diffusion-driven ORSI Salient Object Detection with Information Reconstruction and Multi-Prior Guidance
summary: Existing Salient Object Detection in Optical Remote Sensing Image (ORSI-SOD) methods mainly adopt the static inference strategy, which uses fixed trained model parameters for saliency inference in the testing phase. This means that even if the generated saliency map has errors, it cannot be further optimized. In this paper, we propose the novel IPDiff, a Diffusion-driven ORSI-SOD method with Information Reconstruction and Multi-Prior Guidance. We build IPDiff based on a unique dynamic optimization strategy, which endows IPDiff with the ability to iteratively optimize saliency maps with a dynamic parameter. Specifically, we formulate ORSI-SOD as a conditional diffusion problem in IPDiff. IPDiff first extracts informative conditional priors from ORSIs, including the saliency prior and the hierarchical priors, in the prior network with the assistance of the information reconstruction-driven attention module. The saliency prior can provide positional information of salient objects, while the hierarchical priors can provide specific detail and semantic information of salient objects. Under the guidance of these priors, IPDiff then iteratively denoises random noise as the timestep dynamically changes in the denoising network, generating saliency maps that are close to ground truths. Notably, we simultaneously supervise IPDiff in both spatial and spectral domains through a hybrid loss function to achieve efficient network training. Comprehensive experiments on public ORSSD, EORSSD, and ORSI-4199 datasets demonstrate that our proposed IPDiff achieves the best performance compared to 46 state-of-the-art methods. The code and results of our method are available at https://github.com/MathLee/IPDiff.

AI.tldr: IPDiff is a diffusion-driven ORSI-SOD method that uses dynamic optimization with information reconstruction and multi-prior guidance (saliency and hierarchical priors) to iteratively refine saliency maps, achieving SOTA results on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ORSI-SOD methods use static inference with fixed model parameters, meaning generated saliency maps with errors cannot be further optimized during testing.
AI.method: IPDiff formulates ORSI-SOD as a conditional diffusion problem. It extracts saliency prior (positional info) and hierarchical priors (detail/semantic info) using an information reconstruction-driven attention module. These priors guide iterative denoising of random noise with dynamically changing timesteps. A hybrid loss function supervises both spatial and spectral domains.
AI.result: Achieves best performance compared to 46 SOTA methods on ORSSD, EORSSD, and ORSI-4199 datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dynamic optimization strategy enables iterative refinement of saliency maps, outperforming static inference approaches.

title: Environmental Drivers of Respiratory Disease: A District Level Analysis
summary: Sri Lanka has experienced a decade of progressive forest degradation and rising atmospheric pollution, yet district-level respiratory admissions have paradoxically declined, pointing to the confounding role of healthcare access. This study addresses that gap by constructing an 11-year (2014-2024) panel dataset across all 25 administrative districts, integrating satellite-derived vegetation indices, fire radiative power, pollutant concentrations (particulate matter (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2)), carbon flux metrics and population-normalized respiratory admission rates.
