Two temporally validated XGBoost models were created for annual district-level respiratory rate (R^2 = 0.937) and monthly PM2.5 concentration (R^2 = 0.976) with generalization validated in 21 out of 25 districts (Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) <= 20%). Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis established that cumulative air quality burden is the overwhelming driver of respiratory rate variance (80.1%), ahead of forest degradation (15.6%) and fire activity (4.3%). The Forest-Air-Health (FAH) Risk Index used these SHAP-derived weights to find the districts with the highest risk: Colombo (FAH = 0.802), Gampaha (0.708), and Kalutara (0.682). These findings present the inaugural evidence-based, district-level framework correlating environmental degradation with respiratory health in Sri Lanka, establishing a quantitative basis for focused public health and environmental policy.

AI.tldr: This study develops a machine learning framework using an 11-year panel dataset across 25 Sri Lankan districts to link environmental degradation (air quality, forest cover, fires) with respiratory health outcomes, finding that cumulative air quality burden is the dominant driver (80.1%) of respiratory rate variance, and identifies the highest-risk districts via the FAH Risk Index.
AI.motivation: Despite progressive forest degradation and rising atmospheric pollution in Sri Lanka, district-level respiratory admissions have paradoxically declined, suggesting confounding effects from healthcare access. This study aims to resolve this paradox by constructing a comprehensive environmental-health dataset and quantifying the true relationship between environmental degradation and respiratory health at the district level.
AI.method: Constructed an 11-year (2014-2024) panel dataset across all 25 districts integrating satellite-derived vegetation indices, fire radiative power, pollutant concentrations (PM2.5, NO2, SO2), carbon flux metrics, and population-normalized respiratory admission rates. Two temporally validated XGBoost models were developed (annual respiratory rate R²=0.937; monthly PM2.5 R²=0.976) with generalization validated in 21/25 districts (MAPE≤20%). SHAP analysis quantified feature importance, and the FAH Risk Index was derived using SHAP weights.
AI.result: SHAP analysis revealed cumulative air quality burden as the overwhelming driver of respiratory rate variance (80.1%), followed by forest degradation (15.6%) and fire activity (4.3%). The FAH Risk Index identified Colombo (0.802), Gampaha (0.708), and Kalutara (0.682) as highest-risk districts. Both XGBoost models achieved high predictive performance with strong temporal and spatial generalizability.
AI.conclusion: This study provides the first evidence-based, district-level quantitative framework linking environmental degradation to respiratory health in Sri Lanka, establishing a foundation for targeted public health and environmental policy interventions.

title: Leveraging Pathology Co-occurrence for Test-Time Adaptation in Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
summary: Medical imaging models often degrade when deployed at new clinical sites due to differences in imaging equipment, protocols, and patient populations. Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses this by updating a pretrained model using only unlabeled target data, without access to source data. However, existing TTA methods were designed for single-label classification on natural image benchmarks, minimizing entropy uniformly across all samples without considering label dependencies. This overlooks a key property of multi-label medical imaging: pathologies do not occur independently but exhibit structured co-occurrence patterns. In this work, we propose Co-occurrence Weighted Adaptation (CoWA), which leverages disease co-occurrence patterns as a reliability signal for adaptation. CoWA estimates label co-occurrence structure from model predictions and downweights samples that deviate from expected patterns, enabling adaptation to rely more on consistent predictions while reducing the impact of noisy ones. We evaluate CoWA on chest X-ray benchmarks under domain shifts and demonstrate consistent improvements over established baselines.

AI.tldr: CoWA is a test-time adaptation method for multi-label medical imaging that uses disease co-occurrence patterns as a reliability signal, downweighting samples that deviate from expected co-occurrence patterns to improve adaptation under domain shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing TTA methods are designed for single-label natural image classification and uniformly minimize entropy without considering label dependencies, overlooking the structured co-occurrence patterns of pathologies in multi-label medical imaging.
AI.method: CoWA estimates label co-occurrence structure from model predictions, then downweights samples that deviate from expected co-occurrence patterns, allowing adaptation to rely more on consistent predictions and reduce the impact of noisy ones.
AI.result: CoWA achieves consistent improvements over established baselines on chest X-ray benchmarks under domain shifts.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging disease co-occurrence patterns as a reliability signal for test-time adaptation can effectively improve model performance under domain shifts in multi-label medical imaging.

title: Full-Stack FP4: Stable LLM Pretraining with Quantized Projections, Optimizers, and Attention
summary: Recent NVFP4 pretraining methods mainly target transformer linear layers, leaving optimizer states, optimizer arithmetic and attention underexplored in 4-bit pipelines. This critical gap blocks stable full-stack 4-bit pretraining, as the three core modules exhibit unique numerical failure patterns: linear layers hit hard quantization noise limits with dimension-propagated error amplification; AdamW second moments are heavy-tailed non-negative values fragile to low-precision denominators; attention carries error-prone computation paths demanding strict forward-backward quantization consistency. We propose Full-Stack FP4, the first complete NVFP4 pretraining framework resolving all three stability bottlenecks via module-wise precision strategies. For linear projections, LoRA-SVD lightweight decomposition suppresses quantization noise and breaks the direct-quantization error ceiling, shrinking the linear-only loss gap from 1.40% to 0.61%. For optimizers, we design AdamW second-moment transformation for robust NVFP4 storage and fully support native NVFP4 Newton-Schulz iterations for the Root (Muon) optimizer. For attention, a mixed-precision scheme quantizes Q/K/V and backward dS while guarding vulnerable paths in BF16, paired with unified tensor reuse to sustain forward-backward alignment. We further analyze fast error accumulation in naive low-bit matrix multiplication and the extreme sensitivity of PV / dOV^T attention branches. All modules are plug-and-play with cumulative stability and efficiency improvements. Our 3B/64B-token pretraining validates near-BF16 performance with merely 1.47% loss gap, verifying feasible stable end-to-end NVFP4 LLM pretraining.

AI.tldr: First complete NVFP4 pretraining framework addressing stability bottlenecks in linear layers, optimizer states, and attention via module-wise precision strategies, achieving near-BF16 performance with only 1.47% loss gap in 3B/64B-token pretraining.
AI.motivation: Existing NVFP4 methods focus on transformer linear layers, leaving optimizer states, arithmetic, and attention underexplored. These three modules exhibit unique numerical failure patterns that block stable full-stack 4-bit pretraining.
AI.method: Proposes Full-Stack FP4 with three module-wise strategies: (1) LoRA-SVD for linear projections to suppress quantization noise; (2) AdamW second-moment transformation for robust NVFP4 storage and native NVFP4 Newton-Schulz iterations for Muon optimizer; (3) mixed-precision attention quantizing Q/K/V and backward dS while protecting vulnerable paths in BF16 with unified tensor reuse.
AI.result: Linear-only loss gap reduced from 1.40% to 0.61%. 3B/64B-token pretraining achieves only 1.47% loss gap compared to BF16 baseline, validating feasible stable end-to-end NVFP4 LLM pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Full-Stack FP4 resolves all three stability bottlenecks with plug-and-play modules, proving that stable end-to-end NVFP4 LLM pretraining is achievable with near-BF16 performance.

title: ProxyUp: Training-Free Proxy-Conditioned Video Generation for Controllable Dynamics
summary: Precise control over complex dynamics remains challenging for modern video generative models, as text prompts alone often cannot specify physically plausible, fine-grained motion and interactions. We introduce $\textit{proxy-conditioned video generation}$, where a coarse proxy video from physics-based simulation or real-world recording serves as a dynamics carrier to control foreground object motion. Given a proxy video and a text prompt, the goal is to synthesize a new video that preserves the proxy dynamics while generating novel content and plausible interactions aligned with the prompt. Since paired proxy-target videos are difficult to obtain, we propose $\textbf{ProxyUp}$, a training-free framework built on pretrained video generative models. ProxyUp first inverts the proxy video into an intermediate latent representation and applies $\textbf{region-wise latent noising}$, preserving motion-critical proxy latents while injecting noise into regions intended for text-driven regeneration. To mitigate the distribution mismatch and weak foreground-background coupling introduced by this heuristic latent composition, we further propose $\textbf{Stochastic Flow Relaxation (SFR)}$, which progressively relaxes the composed latent toward the model's learned distribution before ODE sampling. Experiments on both simulation and real-world proxies show that ProxyUp outperforms strong video editing and motion transfer baselines in dynamic fidelity and text alignment.

AI.tldr: ProxyUp is a training-free framework for proxy-conditioned video generation that uses region-wise latent noising and Stochastic Flow Relaxation to control foreground motion via proxy videos while generating novel content aligned with text prompts.
AI.motivation: Precise control over complex dynamics remains challenging for modern video generative models because text prompts alone cannot specify physically plausible, fine-grained motion and interactions.
AI.method: ProxyUp inverts proxy video into latent space, applies region-wise latent noising (preserving motion-critical proxy latents while injecting noise for text-driven regeneration), and uses Stochastic Flow Relaxation (SFR) to progressively relax the composed latent toward the model's learned distribution before ODE sampling.
AI.result: Experiments on simulation and real-world proxies show ProxyUp outperforms strong video editing and motion transfer baselines in dynamic fidelity and text alignment.
AI.conclusion: Proxy-conditioned video generation with ProxyUp enables precise motion control from coarse proxy videos while maintaining compatibility with pretrained video generative models in a training-free manner.

title: Covert Trait Propagation Is Representation Alignment: Mechanistic Evidence from Hidden-Channel Distillation
summary: A student model trained on pure uniform noise can still inherit its teacher's digit-classification ability, provided the two share initialization. Previous work proves this transfer is guaranteed when the teacher's learning rate is small enough, but does not explain where in the network the channel lives or what sets its capacity. Working in an MLP distillation setting on MNIST, we show these channels are not purely informational: geometric alignment gates access to the information the channel carries. Shared initialization makes the output projection W_2 a common coordinate key, and KL gradients reshape the student's input projection W_0 until its hidden representations align with the teacher's. We call this covert trait propagation (CTP). Five experiments support this mechanism: channel closure tracks weight drift, not teacher accuracy; freezing W_0 destroys transfer while freezing W_2 leaves it intact; multi-teacher ensembles cancel out despite each teacher carrying comparable label information; and linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) tracks student accuracy at r=0.98 across a continuous initialization sweep. Applying the same geometric lens to cross-token behavioral entanglement (CTBE) in instruction-tuned LLMs, we find the effect appears to be activated by alignment training, acting on an inherited substrate, and that the standard log-ratio metric produces an apparent frequency bias that is largely a circularity artifact.

AI.tldr: Student models can inherit teacher abilities via shared initialization even when trained on noise, due to geometric alignment of hidden representations (covert trait propagation or CTP), as demonstrated in MLP distillation on MNIST, with implications for CTBE in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed that knowledge transfer via shared initialization occurs when the teacher's learning rate is small, but it did not explain where in the network the communication channel resides or what determines its capacity.
AI.method: The paper works in an MLP distillation setting on MNIST. It identifies that shared initialization makes the output projection W_2 a common coordinate key, and KL gradients reshape the student's input projection W_0 to align hidden representations with the teacher's—termed covert trait propagation (CTP). Five experiments support the mechanism: channel closure tracking weight drift rather than teacher accuracy; freezing W_0 destroys transfer while freezing W_2 leaves it intact; multi-teacher ensembles cancel out; linear CKA correlates with student accuracy at r=0.98. The same geometric lens is applied to CTBE in instruction-tuned LLMs.
AI.result: Geometric alignment (not pure information content) gates access to transferred knowledge. The output projection W_2 serves as a common coordinate frame. The standard log-ratio metric for CTBE produces an apparent frequency bias that is largely a circularity artifact.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge transfer via shared initialization is mediated by geometric alignment of representations, and the same geometric mechanism may underlie CTBE in instruction-tuned LLMs, where alignment training activates the effect on an inherited substrate.

title: Attending to Multimodal Generation One Token at a Time
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate responses autoregressively, integrating visual and linguistic information in an evolving context. Prior work on interpretability has focused on individual layers and circuits (where), leaving the token-level dynamics of multimodal computation during generation (when) underexplored. We address this gap and study attention shifts as per semantic role; tracking model attention to image, text, instruction, and previously generated tokens, One Token at a Time (OTaT). We introduce multimodal tasks that require explicit switching between visual and textual context within a single response. Across two mainstream model families and four open-weight MLLMs of varying sizes, we establish consistent patterns: attention to image peaks at tokens requiring image-derived information, instruction tokens are revisited during task transitions, and attention to previously generated tokens increases as the generation progresses. Causal attention blocking interventions validate the functional role of these trends. We profile model behavior under disrupted attention and observe responses falling back to language priors, or exhibiting cross-modal leakage, denial, or recovery. Finally, informed of the attention dynamics through our novel analysis, we propose a simple test-time intervention to boost attention to the relevant modality at the right time, significantly improving multimodal task performance.

AI.tldr: This paper studies token-level attention dynamics in multimodal LLMs during generation, identifying when models attend to image, text, instruction, or previously generated tokens. The authors propose OTaT analysis, reveal consistent attention patterns across model families, validate them via causal interventions, and introduce a test-time attention intervention that improves multimodal task performance.
AI.motivation: Prior interpretability work on MLLMs focused on where (layers/circuits) multimodal computation occurs, but the token-level temporal dynamics of when models attend to different modalities during autoregressive generation remain underexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose OTaT (One Token at a Time), tracking attention shifts by semantic role across image, text, instruction, and previously generated tokens. They design multimodal tasks requiring explicit visual-textual switching, evaluate on two model families (four open-weight MLLMs), and perform causal attention blocking interventions plus a test-time intervention to boost relevant modality attention.
AI.result: Consistent patterns: attention to image peaks at tokens requiring visual info, instruction tokens are revisited during task transitions, attention to prior tokens increases as generation progresses. Causal blocking causes fallback to language priors, cross-modal leakage, denial, or recovery. The test-time intervention significantly improves multimodal task performance.
AI.conclusion: The token-level attention dynamics reveal a structured temporal pattern in how MLLMs switch between modalities during generation, and this understanding can be leveraged for effective test-time interventions to enhance performance.

title: Knowledge-Informed Local Causal Discovery of Optimal Adjustment Sets
summary: Local causal discovery is a scalable alternative to global structure learning. However, it can struggle to identify valid adjustment sets in data-scarce settings because of finite-sample uncertainty, incomplete local neighborhoods, and unresolved Markov equivalence. Although many application domains provide structured background knowledge, its integration into local causal discovery remains limited. We propose b-LOAD, a knowledge-informed extension of the LOAD algorithm for local discovery of optimal adjustment sets. b-LOAD incorporates prior edge constraints directly into the local structure-learning procedure and uses Meek's rules to expand the discovery frontier dynamically, yielding a knowledge-constrained partially directed graph over the relevant local subgraph. This strategy helps prevent structurally relevant nodes introduced by prior knowledge from being excluded by local search. We prove that, under sound background knowledge, the procedure monotonically refines the admissible equivalence class and can enlarge the set of identifiable causal queries, enabling recovery of optimal adjustment sets that are not identifiable from observational conditional-independence information alone. Empirically, b-LOAD improves downstream causal effect estimation relative to purely data-driven and standard knowledge-augmented baselines, particularly in data-scarce and structurally complex regimes. Results on real-world biological networks show that locally targeted prior knowledge provides the largest gains and remains beneficial under moderate structural noise. These findings position b-LOAD as a scalable approach for converting fragmented domain knowledge into more reliable causal-effect estimation.

AI.tldr: b-LOAD extends the LOAD algorithm by incorporating prior edge constraints and Meek's rules into local causal discovery, enabling better identification of optimal adjustment sets for causal effect estimation, especially in data-scarce settings.
AI.motivation: Local causal discovery struggles with finite-sample uncertainty, incomplete neighborhoods, and unresolved Markov equivalence when identifying valid adjustment sets. Although structured background knowledge exists in many domains, its integration into local discovery remains limited.
AI.method: b-LOAD integrates prior edge constraints directly into local structure learning and applies Meek's rules to dynamically expand the discovery frontier. This yields a knowledge-constrained partially directed graph over the relevant local subgraph.
AI.result: Under sound background knowledge, b-LOAD monotonically refines the admissible equivalence class and enlarges the set of identifiable causal queries. Empirically, it outperforms data-driven and knowledge-augmented baselines in data-scarce and structurally complex settings, with real-world biological network results showing benefits even under moderate structural noise.
AI.conclusion: b-LOAD provides a scalable approach for converting fragmented domain knowledge into more reliable causal-effect estimation, with locally targeted prior knowledge yielding the largest gains.

title: EmCom-Diffusion: Probing Visual Reflection in Emergent Languages via Image Generation
summary: Measuring the extent to which emergent languages encode the visual content of their inputs is an open problem. We refer to this property as visual reflection: the extent to which emergent messages preserve information about their source images that can be recovered without appeal to the speaker-listener pair that produced them. Existing metrics measure it only indirectly, through proxies such as human-defined concept inventories, natural-language captions, structural distance correlations, or Referential Game accuracy, each of which can either miss visual content the message encodes or credit content it does not. We propose EmCom-Diffusion, an evaluation framework that measures visual reflection directly: it reconstructs each input image from its emergent message and compares the reconstruction with the original image itself, rather than with human-defined targets. Concretely, it finetunes a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model on (image, emergent-message) pairs and scores visual reflection as the perceptual similarity between the reconstructed and original images, operating generatively rather than discriminatively. Instantiating it on MS-COCO with a Referential Game, we validate the metric against random and fixed-token baselines under three pretrained visual encoders, and compare it against four existing metrics (CBM, supervised translation, TopSim, and R@1). EmCom-Diffusion captures visual content the other metrics miss.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EmCom-Diffusion, an evaluation framework that measures how well emergent languages preserve visual content from input images by reconstructing images from emergent messages using a finetuned text-to-image diffusion model and comparing reconstructions to originals via perceptual similarity.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for measuring visual reflection in emergent languages are indirect and flawed: they rely on human-defined concepts, natural-language captions, structural correlations, or Referential Game accuracy, which can miss or overcredit visual content. A direct, generative evaluation method is needed.
AI.method: The framework finetunes a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model on (image, emergent-message) pairs, then reconstructs input images from emergent messages. Visual reflection is scored as the perceptual similarity between reconstructed and original images, operating generatively rather than discriminatively. Validation uses MS-COCO with a Referential Game against random/fixed-token baselines and three pretrained visual encoders.
AI.result: EmCom-Diffusion captures visual content that four existing metrics (CBM, supervised translation, TopSim, R@1) miss, and is validated against random and fixed-token baselines under three pretrained visual encoders.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a more direct and comprehensive measure of visual reflection in emergent languages by leveraging generative reconstruction, overcoming limitations of prior discriminative or proxy-based metrics.

title: A Deep Learning-based surrogate model for Severe Accidents in nuclear reactors using ASTEC
summary: Integral codes like the Accident Source Term Evaluation Code (ASTEC) are powerful tools to study the physics of Severe Accidents (SAs) in nuclear reactors. Real time SA simulators can also be helpful in training operators of nuclear plants to react correctly to malfunctions. However, SA simulators can take up to several days per simulation, making their use infeasible for real time applications. In this work we show how to speed up a SA simulator with a fast, Deep Learning based (DL), surrogate model (SM). The SM is built as a combination of a dimensionality reduction stage, via an AutoEncoder, and a time-stepping stage, via a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation. The data on which the SM is trained are obtained from the ASTEC simulator, by sampling a set of operator actions for station blackout (SBO) and loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA). The objective of the developed SM is to approximate multiple spatio-temporal fields for the thermal-hydraulic physics, core degradation, and fission product release modules in ASTEC's vessel domain. The SM predicts simultaneously around $80$ different physical variables (both scalar and fields), maintaining a stable autoregressive rollout up to $50$ thousand time steps. In addition, the AutoEncoder achieves a dimensionality reduction by a factor of over $300$, which allows the SM to predict up to $40$ hours of simulation in under a minute, both on CPU and GPU. This work is the first study of the capabilities and limits of DL based surrogate modeling in approximating the challenging, highly non-linear physics of ASTEC.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Deep Learning-based surrogate model (combining AutoEncoder for dimensionality reduction and Neural ODE for time-stepping) to speed up the ASTEC severe accident simulator from days to under a minute, accurately predicting ~80 physical variables over 50k time steps with a 300x dimensionality reduction.
AI.motivation: Real-time severe accident simulators are essential for operator training but are computationally infeasible (taking days per simulation), necessitating a faster surrogate modeling approach to enable real-time applications.
AI.method: The surrogate model combines an AutoEncoder for dimensionality reduction (300x factor) with a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) for time-stepping, trained on ASTEC simulation data from station blackout (SBO) and loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA) scenarios.
AI.result: The model simultaneously predicts ~80 physical variables (scalars and fields) across thermal-hydraulic physics, core degradation, and fission product release modules, maintaining stable autoregressive rollout up to 50k time steps, and simulating 40 hours in under a minute on both CPU and GPU.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study demonstrating the capabilities and limits of DL-based surrogate modeling for the challenging, highly non-linear physics of ASTEC, showing feasibility for real-time severe accident simulation.

title: Exploring SAM Supervision for Fine-Grained UAV Target Segmentation under Data Scarcity
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) target segmentation remains challenging due to the small size of objects, appearance variations, cluttered backgrounds, and the scarcity of densely annotated data. These factors hinder the performance and practical deployment of lightweight segmentation models in real-world UAV applications. To address this problem, this paper investigates the use of SAM3 (Segment Anything Model 3) as a pseudo-label generator for training compact segmentation networks. Specifically, two supervision paradigms are explored: (i) direct pseudo-supervision using unaltered SAM3-generated masks, and (ii) a refinement strategy that re-applies SAM3 to localized image patches for improved mask quality. Based on these paradigms, a two-stage SAM3-guided pseudo-label generation framework is proposed. In the first stage, SAM3 generates coarse masks for initial object localization. The localized regions are subsequently cropped into patches and processed by SAM3 again to generate fine masks with accurate object boundaries and discard false positives. The resulting coarse and fine masks are then used as pseudo-labels to optimize a lightweight network, termed IPS-Seg, which consists of three components: an IdentityFormer backbone for feature extraction, an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module for multi-scale context aggregation, and a PixelShuffle-based decoder for spatial resolution recovery. Extensive experiments under multiple supervision settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The results show that IPS-Seg achieves a favorable trade-off between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency while benefiting consistently from the proposed pseudo-label generation strategy. These findings highlight the potential of large-scale foundation models as annotation sources for training compact task-specific segmentation networks in low-label vision domains.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage SAM3-guided pseudo-label generation framework to train a lightweight UAV target segmentation network (IPS-Seg), using SAM3-generated coarse and refined masks as supervision signals, achieving a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.motivation: UAV target segmentation faces challenges from small objects, appearance variations, cluttered backgrounds, and scarcity of dense annotations, which hinder lightweight model performance and practical deployment.
AI.method: A two-stage SAM3-guided pseudo-label generation framework is proposed. Stage 1: SAM3 generates coarse masks for object localization. Stage 2: localized patches are cropped and re-processed by SAM3 to produce fine masks with accurate boundaries. These masks serve as pseudo-labels to train IPS-Seg, which comprises an IdentityFormer backbone, ASPP module, and PixelShuffle-based decoder.
AI.result: Extensive experiments under multiple supervision settings show IPS-Seg achieves a favorable trade-off between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency, with consistent benefits from the proposed pseudo-label generation strategy.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale foundation models like SAM3 can serve as effective annotation sources for training compact task-specific segmentation networks in low-label vision domains.

title: Operator-on-F complements value-equivalence: a planning-time diagnostic for latent world models
comment: Accepted at the RLC 2026 World Model Workshop
summary: World-model evaluation for model-based reinforcement learning typically asks whether the learned model predicts reward and value well, which can leave planning-relevant errors in the model's latent rollouts unmeasured. We introduce a complementary diagnostic, operator-on-F, that compares a model's k-step latent pushforward to the environment's on an observable subset F, using the model's own predictor. On a TD-MPC2 size sweep over cheetah-run, reward-prediction error stays within [0.028, 0.091] for every model size - only about 3x variation - so an unnormalized reward-fit check has narrow resolution to distinguish them; the (unnormalized) Bellman residual and reward error themselves have weak relationships with return (Spearman -0.10 and -0.30). Operator error spans 0.28 to 2.62 over the same sizes. At 317M the operator error is 2.62 - an order of magnitude above the 0.28-0.36 cluster - and the planning return collapses to 0.9, while reward-prediction error (0.091) is the highest of the five but stays within the same small [0.028, 0.091] range as the rest of the sweep. The rank correlation between operator error and return loss is -0.90 (anchor-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.90, -0.70] at n=5 sizes; leave-one-out removal of any single size leaves it at -0.80 or stronger). The operator also returns informative, architecture-discriminating estimates in a cross-architecture comparison between TD-MPC2 and a pure-SSL latent world model. The operator diagnostic complements value-equivalence rather than replacing it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "operator-on-F," a complementary diagnostic for evaluating world models in model-based reinforcement learning that measures planning-relevant errors in latent rollouts, showing it better predicts planning performance than traditional reward-prediction error metrics across model scales and architectures.
AI.motivation: Standard world-model evaluation focuses on reward/value prediction accuracy, which misses planning-relevant errors in latent rollouts. The authors seek a diagnostic that better captures model deficiencies that actually degrade planning performance.
AI.method: The operator-on-F diagnostic compares a model's k-step latent pushforward to the environment's dynamics on an observable subset F using the model's own predictor. It is evaluated on TD-MPC2 size sweeps (cheetah-run) and cross-architecture comparisons (TD-MPC2 vs. pure-SSL latent world model).
AI.result: Operator error spans 0.28–2.62 across model sizes (vs. reward-prediction error only 0.028–0.091). Spearman correlation between operator error and return loss is -0.90 (95% CI [-0.90, -0.70]). At 317M parameters, operator error spikes to 2.62 (10× larger than other sizes) while reward error stays within its narrow range. The diagnostic also discriminates between architectures.
AI.conclusion: The operator-on-F diagnostic complements value-equivalence by capturing planning-relevant model errors that reward/value prediction misses. It provides higher-resolution discrimination between models and better correlates with actual planning performance collapse.

title: GeoSAM-Lite: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Onboard Remote Sensing Segmentation
summary: The deployment of large-scale foundation models like Segment Anything Model (SAM) on resource-constrained Earth observation platforms is hindered by prohibitive computational costs and the domain shift between natural and remote sensing imagery. To address these challenges, we propose \textit{Geo}spatial \textit{S}egment \textit{A}nything \textit{M}odel-Lite (GeoSAM-Lite), a lightweight, prompt-free segmentation framework designed for efficient onboard remote sensing segmentation. GeoSAM-Lite incorporates two core innovations: (1) Geospatial-Domain Initialization (Geo-Init), a domain-aware pre-training strategy that distills geospatial priors from a specialized teacher to bridge the domain gap; and (2) Feature Fusion Layers (FFL), which recalibrate spatial features and restore high-frequency boundary cues to overcome the capacity bottlenecks of lightweight backbones. Experiments across representative datasets, with a primary focus on cloud scenarios to evaluate performance under extreme scale variations and complex boundaries, demonstrate that GeoSAM-Lite achieves competitive accuracy while reducing parameters by 92.8\% compared to the heavyweight RSAM-Seg. By establishing a superior Pareto frontier between efficiency and fidelity, GeoSAM-Lite offers a practical solution for real-time segmentation on edge devices.

AI.tldr: GeoSAM-Lite is a lightweight, prompt-free segmentation framework for onboard remote sensing, achieving competitive accuracy with 92.8% fewer parameters than RSAM-Seg via Geospatial-Domain Initialization and Feature Fusion Layers.
AI.motivation: Deploying large foundation models like SAM on resource-constrained Earth observation platforms is hindered by high computational costs and the domain shift between natural and remote sensing imagery.
AI.method: GeoSAM-Lite incorporates (1) Geospatial-Domain Initialization (Geo-Init), a domain-aware pre-training strategy distilling geospatial priors from a specialized teacher to bridge the domain gap; and (2) Feature Fusion Layers (FFL), which recalibrate spatial features and restore high-frequency boundary cues to overcome lightweight backbone bottlenecks.
AI.result: GeoSAM-Lite achieves competitive accuracy while reducing parameters by 92.8% compared to RSAM-Seg, establishing a superior Pareto frontier between efficiency and fidelity on remote sensing datasets (with focus on cloud scenarios).
AI.conclusion: GeoSAM-Lite offers a practical solution for real-time segmentation on edge devices by balancing efficiency and fidelity.

title: Regime-Conditional Stabilisation of LLM-Augmented Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural interface for translating human objectives into reward signals for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), yet the training-time dynamics of this integration remain poorly understood. We show that dynamically updating LLM-generated reward weights during off-policy MARL violates the stationarity assumption of Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) and contaminates the experience replay buffer, whose stored transitions carry reward labels computed under stale shaping weights. We characterise the result as a regime-dependent failure whose severity depends on how competent the unshaped baseline already is. To control it we propose two stabilisation strategies: a Phase-Based Freeze Schedule that enforces strict stationarity within training phases, and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing that bounds per-episode weight drift. We evaluate across three cooperative environments and five random seeds with QMIX, complemented by an exploratory VDN extension, yielding a three-regime taxonomy. In the augmentative regime (Simple Spread), where the baseline is functional (74.4 %), EMA significantly improves success to 86.7 % ($+12.3$ pp, $p<0.01$) while naive dynamic updates collapse it to 15.2 %. In the essential regime (Level-Based Foraging), where the baseline is broken (0.1 %), any shaping unlocks the task (95.9 % under EMA). In the supplementary regime (SMAC 3m), where the baseline is near-saturated (98.8 %), stabilised shaping preserves performance (99.9 %) while unstabilised shaping adds variance without gain. These findings establish reward-signal stationarity as a necessary design constraint and indicate that regime placement is a practical predictor of whether dynamic LLM shaping helps or harms.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that dynamic LLM-generated reward weight updates in off-policy MARL violate stationarity assumptions, contaminating replay buffers and causing regime-dependent failures. Two stabilization strategies (Phase-Based Freeze Schedule and EMA smoothing) are proposed, with three-regime taxonomy showing EMA significantly helps in augmentative (86.7% vs 74.4%) and essential regimes, while preserving performance in supplementary regimes.
AI.motivation: The training-time dynamics of integrating LLM-generated reward signals into cooperative MARL remain poorly understood. Specifically, how dynamically updating LLM-generated reward weights during off-policy learning affects the stationarity assumption of PBRS and experience replay buffers.
AI.method: Two stabilization strategies: (1) Phase-Based Freeze Schedule enforcing strict stationarity within training phases, (2) EMA smoothing bounding per-episode weight drift. Evaluated across three environments (Simple Spread, Level-Based Foraging, SMAC 3m) using QMIX with VDN extension, five random seeds.
AI.result: Three-regime taxonomy identified: (1) Augmentative regime (Simple Spread, baseline 74.4%): EMA improves to 86.7% (+12.3 pp), naive dynamic updates collapse to 15.2%. (2) Essential regime (Level-Based Foraging, baseline 0.1%): any shaping unlocks task (95.9% under EMA). (3) Supplementary regime (SMAC 3m, baseline 98.8%): stabilized shaping preserves performance (99.9%), unstabilized adds variance.
AI.conclusion: Reward-signal stationarity is a necessary design constraint for integrating LLM-based reward shaping into off-policy MARL. Regime placement (baseline competence level) is a practical predictor of whether dynamic LLM shaping helps or harms performance.

title: Sparse-View Surface Reconstruction using Gaussian Splatting through High-Confidence Depth Propagation with Normal Priors
summary: 3D reconstruction from sparse views is a challenging task in 3D computer vision. Recent studies on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved remarkable results with sparse views in novel view synthesis, yet reconstructing high-quality geometric surfaces from sparse views remains a challenge, due to the limited geometry clues and the discreteness of Gaussians. In this paper, we propose a novel 3DGS-based method for high-fidelity surface reconstruction from sparse views. Our key insight is to introduce a normal-guided depth propagation approach, which can extend depth information from high-confidence regions to constrain the depth in low-confidence areas. Additionally, we propose an abnormal depth edge-aware regularization to address depth discontinuities caused by the discreteness of Gaussians. Extensive experiments on DTU and Tanks-and-Temples datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in sparse view surface reconstruction. Project page: https://hanl2010.github.io/DP-GS.

AI.tldr: DP-GS proposes a normal-guided depth propagation and abnormal depth edge-aware regularization for high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from sparse views using 3D Gaussian Splatting, outperforming SOTA on DTU and Tanks-and-Temples.
AI.motivation: 3D surface reconstruction from sparse views is challenging due to limited geometry clues and the discreteness of Gaussians in 3DGS, which hinders high-quality geometric surface recovery.
AI.method: A normal-guided depth propagation approach that extends depth from high-confidence regions to constrain low-confidence areas, plus an abnormal depth edge-aware regularization to address depth discontinuities caused by Gaussian discreteness.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on DTU and Tanks-and-Temples datasets for sparse view surface reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DP-GS method effectively leverages normal-guided depth propagation and edge-aware regularization to achieve high-fidelity surface reconstruction from sparse views, addressing the key limitations of 3DGS in geometry recovery.

title: LeukocyteCount: Automatic Identification and Counting for leukocytes using Deep Learning
summary: Diagnosing and monitoring diseases frequently involves the analysis of human biological samples, with blood analysis being pivotal. Specifically, leukocytes, or white blood cells (WBCs), are essential markers for evaluating the body's defense mechanisms against infections. Traditional methods for WBC counting and classification are labor-intensive and prone to inaccuracies, primarily due to human error. The conventional processes for blood cell analysis, especially those concerning WBCs, are beset with difficulties. These include the laborious nature of manual counting and the susceptibility to errors, which can significantly impact the accuracy and reliability of disease diagnosis and monitoring. This study proposes an automated, machine learning-based solution aimed at mitigating the identified challenges. By employing a hybrid model that integrates Yolov5 for the detection of WBCs, coupled with a finely tuned, pre-trained MobileNetV2 model and a Logistic Regression classifier, the study innovates in the accurate identification, counting, and classification of WBCs into four distinct types. The methodology leverages the BCCD dataset for training and validation purposes. The application of the proposed hybrid machine learning model has yielded remarkable results, demonstrating a detection accuracy rate of 98\% through the Yolov5 stage, and an unparalleled classification accuracy of 99.04\% in subsequent stages utilizing MobileNetV2 and Logistic Regression. Additionally, Our proposed YOLOv5-based RBC detection module achieves an F1 score of 99.73\%, which outperforms the baseline. These findings underscore the model's potential in transforming traditional laboratory practices for WBC analysis, offering a path towards more accurate, efficient, and reliable disease diagnostics and monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid ML model combining YOLOv5, MobileNetV2, and Logistic Regression to automate WBC detection, counting, and classification, achieving 98% detection accuracy and 99.04% classification accuracy on the BCCD dataset, with an RBC detection F1 score of 99.73%.
AI.motivation: Traditional manual WBC counting and classification are labor-intensive, error-prone, and impact disease diagnosis reliability. The need for automated, accurate solutions motivates this work.
AI.method: A hybrid ML pipeline: YOLOv5 for WBC detection, fine-tuned pre-trained MobileNetV2 for feature extraction, and Logistic Regression for classification into four WBC types. Trained and validated on the BCCD dataset.
AI.result: YOLOv5 detection accuracy: 98%; classification accuracy via MobileNetV2 + Logistic Regression: 99.04%; YOLOv5-based RBC detection F1 score: 99.73%, outperforming the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model can transform traditional laboratory WBC analysis, offering more accurate, efficient, and reliable disease diagnostics and monitoring.

title: Self-Improving Diffusion Classifiers with Minority Preference Optimization
summary: Prior studies have demonstrated that diffusion classifiers achieve robust zero-shot classification performance. However, their effectiveness is strongly tied to the pretraining data distribution: they perform well in majority, high-density regions of the data manifold, but are significantly less accurate in minority, low-density regions. Although prior works on minority sampling have focused on generating more minority-like images, what minority sampling fundamentally enables beyond generation remains underexplored. In this paper, we reveal a direct relationship between minority sampling in generation and the perception capability of diffusion classifiers. Specifically, we show that enhancing minority sampling broadens the coverage of underrepresented regions on the data manifold, thereby improving diffusion-based recognition. To exploit this connection, we propose \textit{Self-Improving Diffusion Classifiers with Minority Preference Optimization} (MiPO), which fine-tunes a pretrained diffusion model using minority preference rewards. Using only arbitrary caption data, MiPO generates candidate samples, rewards those that better cover minority regions, and optimizes the model with LoRA and Group Relative Policy Optimization, without additional image data, external foundation models, or external reward models. This enables stable, prompt-adaptive minority sampling and translates low-density generative coverage into improved zero-shot diffusion classification. To sum up, we show that diffusion classifier perception is biased toward majority regions, demonstrate that this bias can be alleviated through minority preference optimization, and evaluate MiPO on five standard datasets.

AI.tldr: MiPO fine-tunes diffusion models using minority preference rewards to improve classification in low-density regions of the data manifold, without requiring additional data or external models.
AI.motivation: Diffusion classifiers exhibit strong bias toward majority, high-density regions and perform poorly in minority, low-density regions. Prior work focused on generating minority samples but did not explore how minority sampling fundamentally improves perception capabilities.
AI.method: Proposes MiPO (Self-Improving Diffusion Classifiers with Minority Preference Optimization): uses arbitrary caption data to generate candidate samples, rewards those covering minority regions better, and optimizes via LoRA and Group Relative Policy Optimization — no extra images, foundation models, or reward models needed.
AI.result: Enhanced minority sampling broadens coverage of underrepresented regions on the data manifold, leading to improved diffusion-based zero-shot classification performance across five standard datasets.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion classifier perception is biased toward majority regions; this bias can be alleviated through minority preference optimization, producing stable, prompt-adaptive minority sampling that translates into improved zero-shot classification.

title: Two Black Boxes, One Solver: Encoder Probing and Decoder Attribution for Neural Multi-Attribute VRP under Hard-Mask and Recourse Decoders
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Bremen, Germany. 8 pages
summary: Neural autoregressive solvers for the Multi-Attribute Vehicle Routing Problem (MAVRP) reach competitive cost but offer no per-step justification, a problem when dispatchers must validate, accept, or compare them. We open two complementary black boxes in one protocol. On the encoder side, linear probes, spontaneous-organization metrics, rank-based richness measures, and discovered-direction analyses with intervention validation characterize how the latent represents constraint families at the graph, node, and edge level. On the decoder side, three attribution methods (gradient, integrated gradients, DeepLIFT) feed three reading angles: abductive, contrastive against the best feasible alternative, and counterfactual (smallest input change that switches the action or restores feasibility). Explanations are scored on fidelity, concentration, stability, sanity, and actionability. Across six variants combining three encoders (Attention baseline, Unimp, UnimpMoe) with two decoders (Hard-Mask, Recourse), we find that graph inductive bias improves both representational predictability and decoder sanity, that the Mixture-of-Experts encoder represents constraints in a distributed rather than axis-aligned way, and that the Recourse training regime, not merely its softer mask, produces policies that represent infeasibility usefully, exposing make-feasible counterfactuals that Hard-Mask policies fail to produce even when fed infeasible alternatives externally.

AI.tldr: This paper opens two black boxes in neural MAVRP solvers: (1) encoder-side analysis via linear probes, richness measures, and discovered-direction analysis; (2) decoder-side attribution via gradient, integrated gradients, and DeepLIFT, evaluated on fidelity, concentration, stability, sanity, and actionability. Key findings: graph inductive bias improves representational predictability and decoder sanity; MoE encoder uses distributed constraint representation; Recourse training enables useful infeasibility counterfactuals absent in Hard-Mask policies.
AI.motivation: Neural MAVRP solvers achieve competitive costs but lack per-step interpretability, preventing dispatchers from validating, accepting, or comparing solutions. The paper aims to explain both the encoder's latent representations and the decoder's action justifications.
AI.method: Encoder-side: linear probes, spontaneous-organization metrics, rank-based richness, discovered-direction analysis with intervention validation. Decoder-side: three attribution methods (gradient, integrated gradients, DeepLIFT) feeding three perspectives (abductive, contrastive, counterfactual). Evaluated across six model variants (Attention/Unimp/UnimpMoe encoders × Hard-Mask/Recourse decoders).
AI.result: Graph inductive bias improves both encoder representational predictability and decoder sanity. MoE encoder represents constraints in distributed (not axis-aligned) fashion. Recourse training enables policies that represent infeasibility usefully and produce make-feasible counterfactuals, which Hard-Mask policies fail to generate even with external infeasible inputs.
AI.conclusion: The protocol successfully opens two complementary black boxes in MAVRP solvers, revealing how inductive biases and training regimes shape both latent representations and decision attributions, with Recourse training particularly enabling actionable counterfactual explanations for infeasibility.

title: City-Level 3D Surface Reconstruction with Viewpoint Orientation Partitioning and Scene Completion
summary: Multi-view 3D surface reconstruction is a longstanding challenge in computer vision. Although recent large-scale reconstruction methods based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieve impressive novel-view synthesis, producing high-quality surfaces over large scenes remains difficult, due to complex geometry, long optimization, and limited memory. In this paper, we propose a novel yet simple partitioning method to efficiently and faithfully reconstruct large-scale scene surfaces. Our key insight lies in a scene partitioning method based on viewpoint orientation. This partitioning approach ensures that views with similar orientations are jointly involved for more accurate depth estimations, leading to precise surface reconstructions and balanced computation on multiple GPUs in parallel. In addition, we propose a strategy to detect and repair missing regions in the initial point cloud caused by sparse viewpoints or insufficient textures, thereby further improving the geometric quality. Extensive experiments on the GauU-Scene, MatrixCity, and UrbanScene3D datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches in surface reconstruction for large-scale scenes. Project page: https://hanl2010.github.io/VOP-GS.

AI.tldr: VOP-GS proposes a viewpoint-orientation-based scene partitioning method for efficient, high-quality 3D surface reconstruction of large-scale scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing large-scale 3DGS methods struggle with producing high-quality surfaces over large scenes due to complex geometry, long optimization, and limited memory. There is a need for an efficient reconstruction method that can handle large-scale scenes faithfully.
AI.method: 1) A scene partitioning method based on viewpoint orientation, grouping views with similar orientations together for more accurate depth estimation and balanced multi-GPU parallel computation. 2) A missing-region detection and repair strategy to recover geometry in sparse-view or low-texture areas, improving overall geometric quality.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on GauU-Scene, MatrixCity, and UrbanScene3D datasets in surface reconstruction for large-scale scenes.
AI.conclusion: The viewpoint-orientation-based partitioning enables efficient, accurate, and scalable large-scale 3D surface reconstruction, with the proposed missing-region repair further enhancing geometric completeness.

title: Beyond travel mode: urban context shapes active mobility's mental health effects over time
summary: Active mobility is widely promoted for sustainable and healthier living, but whether it translates into equitable mental health benefits across individuals and places over time remains unknown. Using causal machine learning and causal deep learning in 264168 UK adults, we find substantial inequalities in individualized effects of active mobility on anxiety, depression, and common mental disorders. These inequalities widen over time and are strongly structured by urban context. For example, anxiety risk at follow-up ranges from a 40.6% reduction to a 10.1% increase across individuals, versus a 10.4% reduction to a 0.1% increase at baseline. Benefits are greatest in greener, safer, less polluted, and less deprived neighborhood environments, with 81.8% of individuals experiencing above-average benefits and mean anxiety risk reduced by 26.4%, versus 10.4% of individuals and 7.4% reduction in the least supportive environments. Urban compact form further modifies these effects through nonlinear interactions with neighborhood environments, amplifying benefits only under supportive conditions. Despite these strong environmental gradients, genetic moderation is negligible. These findings suggest universal active mobility promotion could widen health inequalities if individual and contextual differences are not accounted for.

AI.tldr: Using causal ML on 264,168 UK adults, this study finds that active mobility's mental health benefits are highly unequal across individuals and contexts, with benefits strongest in greener, safer, less polluted areas, and minimal or even harmful effects in unsupportive environments, suggesting universal promotion could widen health inequalities.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the widely promoted active mobility for sustainable living translates into equitable mental health benefits across diverse individuals and places over time, or if inequalities exist that could be exacerbated by universal promotion.
AI.method: Causal machine learning and causal deep learning applied to a large longitudinal cohort of 264,168 UK adults to estimate individualized treatment effects of active mobility on anxiety, depression, and common mental disorders at baseline and follow-up.
AI.result: Substantial inequalities in individualized effects: anxiety risk change ranged from -40.6% to +10.1% at follow-up (vs. -10.4% to +0.1% at baseline). Benefits concentrated in greener, safer, less polluted, less deprived areas (81.8% of individuals above-average benefit, mean -26.4% anxiety risk) versus unsupportive environments (10.4% above-average, mean -7.4%). Urban compact form moderates effects nonlinearly, amplifying benefits only under supportive conditions. Genetic moderation was negligible.
AI.conclusion: Universal active mobility promotion could widen health inequalities if individual and contextual differences are not accounted for, as benefits are strongly environmentally stratified and inequalities widen over time.

title: Rethinking Depth Pruning for Vision Transformers: A Heterogeneity-Aware Perspective
summary: While prior studies have successfully compressed vision Transformers (ViTs) through various pruning techniques, most have concentrated on width pruning to achieve significant reductions in model size. Depth pruning, which removes entire layers from a ViT, is notoriously difficult for accuracy recovery despite its potential to deliver higher speedups, limiting the acceleration achieved by existing joint width-and-depth pruning methods. In this work, we reveal that the failure of existing depth pruning methods lies in their neglect of heterogeneity between different layers, and we introduce HetDPT, a heterogeneity-aware depth pruning method that avoids dimension mismatch. Comprehensive experiments on ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, COCO, and ADE20K validate our method: HetDPT achieves a 1.58$\times$ speedup for DeiT-B while maintaining accuracy and a 1.39$\times$ speedup for DeiT-S with nearly no accuracy degradation. Furthermore, when combined with width pruning, HetDPT+ sets a new state-of-the-art record in extreme ViT pruning, enhancing the acceleration ratio from 4.24$\times$ to 5.19$\times$ for the Isomorphic-Pruning-2.6G configuration while maintaining near-lossless accuracy; our code is available at https://github.com/Efficient-AI-for-All/HetDPT.

AI.tldr: HetDPT is a heterogeneity-aware depth pruning method for Vision Transformers that addresses the failure of existing depth pruning by accounting for inter-layer heterogeneity and avoiding dimension mismatch, achieving 1.58× speedup on DeiT-B and 1.39× on DeiT-S with minimal accuracy loss, and setting SOTA in extreme ViT pruning when combined with width pruning (5.19× acceleration).
AI.motivation: Existing depth pruning methods for ViTs fail because they neglect heterogeneity between different layers, limiting acceleration despite the potential of removing entire layers. Prior work focused on width pruning or joint pruning, but depth pruning's accuracy recovery remains notoriously difficult.
AI.method: HetDPT introduces a heterogeneity-aware depth pruning approach that accounts for layer differences and avoids dimension mismatch when removing entire layers from ViTs. It can also be combined with width pruning (HetDPT+).
AI.result: HetDPT achieves 1.58× speedup for DeiT-B and 1.39× for DeiT-S with near-lossless accuracy on ImageNet-1K/CIFAR-100; HetDPT+ boosts acceleration from 4.24× to 5.19× on Isomorphic-Pruning-2.6G while maintaining near-lossless accuracy, validated on COCO and ADE20K.
AI.conclusion: HetDPT effectively addresses the heterogeneity neglect issue in depth pruning for ViTs, achieving superior acceleration with minimal accuracy degradation, and sets new SOTA in extreme joint width-and-depth pruning scenarios.

title: Lyapunov-Guided Training for Hardware-Safe Neural Networks Under Fixed-Point Arithmetic
summary: Low-precision neural networks are attractive for resource-constrained hardware, but fixed-point arithmetic introduces failure modes that are often hidden by idealised quantisation models. In particular, two's-complement overflow wrapping can corrupt hidden activations by changing both their magnitude and sign, leading to unstable numerical error propagation and severe accuracy degradation. This paper proposes a Lyapunov-stabilised quantisation framework for low-precision neural networks operating under hardware-style wrapping arithmetic. The hidden-state energy is monitored through a layerwise Lyapunov function, and a monotone projection is applied to enforce bounded and non-increasing state evolution across depth. The method is evaluated on MNIST using a compact patch-based transformer under post-training quantisation and quantisation-aware training with fixed-point bit-widths from 4 to 16 bits. Monte Carlo results show that unconstrained wrapped quantisation-aware training collapses to near-chance accuracy across 6-16 bits, with activation overflow rates exceeding 11%. In contrast, the proposed monotone Lyapunov projection suppresses activation overflow to below 0.012% and restores stable low-precision learning, achieving 86.55% accuracy at 12 bits. These results demonstrate that Lyapunov-based state control can act as a hardware-aware stabilisation mechanism for reliable fixed-point neural inference and training.

AI.tldr: A Lyapunov-stabilised quantisation framework prevents numerical instability from fixed-point overflow wrapping in low-precision neural networks, suppressing activation overflow from >11% to <0.012% and restoring stable learning (86.55% accuracy at 12 bits on MNIST).
AI.motivation: Low-precision neural networks using fixed-point arithmetic suffer from two's-complement overflow wrapping, which alters hidden activation magnitude and sign, causing unstable numerical error propagation and severe accuracy degradation—failure modes hidden by idealised quantisation models.
AI.method: The authors propose monitoring hidden-state energy via a layerwise Lyapunov function and applying a monotone projection to enforce bounded, non-increasing state evolution across depth, evaluated on MNIST with a compact patch-based transformer under PTQ and QAT from 4 to 16 bits.
AI.result: Unconstrained wrapped QAT collapses to near-chance accuracy across 6-16 bits (overflow >11%); the proposed method suppresses overflow to <0.012% and achieves 86.55% accuracy at 12 bits.
AI.conclusion: Lyapunov-based state control serves as a hardware-aware stabilisation mechanism for reliable fixed-point neural inference and training.

title: G$^2$TAM: Geometry Grounded Track Anything Model
summary: Human spatial understanding arises from jointly perceiving geometry and semantics, enabling consistent object identification and localization across viewpoints and time. Current video segmentation models depend on explicit object appearance memory banks for instance tracking, yet they remain vulnerable to large viewpoint changes and long-term occlusions. Leveraging the spatial consistency afforded by modern feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, we propose the Geometry Grounded Tracking Anything Model (G$^2$TAM), a unified framework for promptable instance tracking in 3D using only unordered RGB images or videos. G$^2$TAM employs spatially aligned geometric representations as implicit memory, ensuring stable instance identity and localization across frames and views. At its core is a cross-modal spatial encoder that integrates visual and textual prompts into a shared geometric space, enabling end-to-end spatial reconstruction and instance-consistent mask prediction. To support training and evaluation, we construct InsTrack, a large-scale dataset with a dedicated validation split for benchmarking. Extensive experiments show that G$^2$TAM delivers strong cross-view consistency, promptable instance spatial tracking, video object segmentation and spatial reconstruction, establishing a foundation for interactive, geometry-grounded spatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: G$^2$TAM is a unified framework for promptable 3D instance tracking from unordered RGB images/videos, using spatially aligned geometric representations as implicit memory to achieve consistent object identification across large viewpoint changes and occlusions, supported by a new large-scale dataset InsTrack.
AI.motivation: Current video segmentation models rely on explicit object appearance memory banks for instance tracking, which are vulnerable to large viewpoint changes and long-term occlusions. The paper seeks to overcome these limitations by leveraging spatial consistency from feed-forward 3D reconstruction models.
AI.method: G$^2$TAM employs a cross-modal spatial encoder that integrates visual and textual prompts into a shared geometric space, using spatially aligned geometric representations as implicit memory for stable instance identity and localization, enabling end-to-end spatial reconstruction and instance-consistent mask prediction.
AI.result: The method achieves strong cross-view consistency, promptable instance spatial tracking, video object segmentation, and spatial reconstruction. A large-scale dataset InsTrack with a dedicated validation split is constructed to support training and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: G$^2$TAM establishes a foundation for interactive, geometry-grounded spatial reasoning by unifying promptable instance tracking in 3D from unordered RGB images or videos.

title: ManifoldFlow: SPD-Relaxed Stiefel Layers with Learnable Singular Spectrum
summary: Orthogonal and Stiefel layers give neural weights exact spectral control, but they also impose a strong modeling constraint: all represented singular values are fixed at one. Many settings that benefit from an orthonormal basis still need direction-dependent attenuation or amplification. We introduce ManifoldFlow, a minimal relaxation of a fixed-spectrum Stiefel layer that keeps the basis on the Stiefel manifold while learning a bounded positive spectrum through W = Q S^{1/2}, with Q^T Q = I and S positive definite. Since W^T W = S, the eigenvalues of S are exactly the squared singular values of the realized weight, making eigenvalue clipping a direct singular-value control mechanism. Across paired sequence, tabular, and image experiments, the learnable SPD spectrum improves the fixed-spectrum Stiefel counterpart in the reported settings where the Stiefel prior is useful, with the largest gains in recurrent language-model projections. Boundary cases in convolutional classifier heads clarify the intended scope: ManifoldFlow is not a universal dense-layer replacement, but a spectrum-learnable Stiefel relaxation for settings where an orthonormal basis is a useful prior. When the basis should be orthonormal, its spectrum need not be frozen. Code available at https://github.com/Hik289/manifold_flow

AI.tldr: ManifoldFlow relaxes fixed-spectrum Stiefel layers by learning a positive definite spectrum while keeping the basis on the Stiefel manifold, improving performance in settings where orthonormal bases are useful (e.g., recurrent language models), but is not a universal dense-layer replacement.
AI.motivation: Orthogonal/Stiefel layers impose fixed singular values at one, which is too restrictive for tasks needing direction-dependent attenuation/amplification while still benefiting from an orthonormal basis.
AI.method: Factorize weight as W = Q S^{1/2}, where Q^T Q = I (Stiefel manifold) and S is positive definite. The eigenvalues of S equal squared singular values of W, enabling direct singular-value control via eigenvalue clipping.
AI.result: Outperforms fixed-spectrum Stiefel layers in paired sequence, tabular, and image experiments, with largest gains in recurrent language-model projections. Boundary cases in convolutional classifier heads clarify intended scope.
AI.conclusion: When an orthonormal basis is a useful prior, its spectrum need not be frozen; ManifoldFlow provides a spectrum-learnable Stiefel relaxation, but is not a universal dense-layer replacement.

title: InfraNet: Quality-Aware RGB Guidance for Efficient Infrared Object Detection
summary: Robust object detection under adverse visual conditions remains a long-standing challenge for multi-modal perception systems. Existing fusion-based methods typically require both RGB and infrared (IR) inputs, and treat them equally during both training and inference, which compromises their robustness when the RGB modality becomes unreliable or unavailable. In this case, we propose \textbf{InfraNet}, an IR-centric quality-aware framework that regulates RGB guidance during training and supports flexible RGB--IR or IR-only deployment. InfraNet employs an asymmetric architecture where the primary IR pathway extracts multi-scale infrared features for predictions, while the auxiliary RGB pathway provides reliability-controlled supervisory signals. The core of InfraNet is \textbf{QualGate}, a quality-aware fusion module that learns a task-oriented control signal to suppress unreliable RGB guidance and compensate IR features during cross-modal training. Built upon InfraNet, we design two architectural variants: a lightweight IR-only architecture InfraNet-IR and an RGB--IR architecture InfraNet-RGB-IR. Our method is evaluated through extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets (LLVIP, FLIR-Aligned, M$^3$FD, and DroneVehicle), showing strong or competitive accuracy in challenging low-light and adverse weather conditions. Notably, InfraNet maintains high efficiency in IR-only inference, making it both accurate and computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: InfraNet is an IR-centric quality-aware framework for robust object detection under adverse conditions, featuring a QualGate module that adaptively controls RGB guidance and supports both RGB-IR and IR-only deployment with strong performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion-based methods treat RGB and IR modalities equally during training and inference, compromising robustness when RGB becomes unreliable or unavailable under adverse visual conditions.
AI.method: InfraNet employs an asymmetric architecture with a primary IR pathway for multi-scale feature extraction and an auxiliary RGB pathway with reliability-controlled supervision. The core QualGate module learns task-oriented control signals to suppress unreliable RGB guidance and compensate IR features during cross-modal training. Two variants are designed: InfraNet-IR (lightweight IR-only) and InfraNet-RGB-IR.
AI.result: Evaluated on LLVIP, FLIR-Aligned, M^3FD, and DroneVehicle datasets, achieving strong or competitive accuracy in low-light and adverse weather conditions. InfraNet maintains high efficiency in IR-only inference.
AI.conclusion: InfraNet demonstrates that an IR-centric asymmetric design with quality-aware gating can achieve robust detection under adverse conditions while supporting flexible deployment modes and maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Probabilistic Robustness in Medical Image Classification
summary: Deep learning (DL) has shown strong performance in medical image classification, but its trustworthy deployment remains challenging in safety-critical clinical settings, where prediction errors under perturbations may lead to severe consequences. Existing studies mainly focus on adversarial robustness (AR) from a worst-case perspective; however, such settings may be less representative of real medical applications. In this work, we investigate probabilistic robustness (PR) as a more practical measure of model trustworthiness. To this end, we construct a set of natural corruption settings for medical image classification and systematically evaluate commonly used DL models on MedMNIST v2 dataset. Our study provides a statistically grounded perspective on assessing the trustworthiness of DL models, thereby supporting their more trustworthy deployment in medical imaging applications.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates probabilistic robustness (PR) as a more practical measure of trustworthiness for deep learning models in medical image classification, evaluating commonly used models on MedMNIST v2 under natural corruption settings to provide a statistically grounded assessment.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models in medical image classification face trustworthiness challenges due to prediction errors under perturbations, and existing adversarial robustness (AR) from a worst-case perspective is less representative of real medical applications.
AI.method: The authors construct a set of natural corruption settings for medical image classification and systematically evaluate commonly used DL models on the MedMNIST v2 dataset using probabilistic robustness (PR) as the evaluation metric.
AI.result: The study provides a statistically grounded perspective on assessing the trustworthiness of DL models under natural corruption settings, demonstrating that probabilistic robustness is a more practical measure than worst-case adversarial robustness for medical imaging.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic robustness offers a more representative and practical framework for evaluating model trustworthiness in safety-critical clinical settings, supporting more trustworthy deployment of DL models in medical imaging applications.

title: Predicting Therapeutic Outcome via Aligning Patient-Specific Knowledge Graph and Gene-Level Perturbation Representations
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at BIOKDD 2026, held in conjunction with ACM SIGKDD 2026
summary: Accurate prediction of patient-specific therapeutic response from pre-treatment transcriptomes is hindered by the scarcity of matched clinical response labels and post-treatment molecular profiles. Preclinical transfer-learning models can simulate drug-induced expression changes but are often hard to interpret and unstable, whereas knowledge-graph methods provide mechanistic context yet remain static and fail to capture drug-induced transcriptomic perturbation dynamics. We propose PREDIKTOR, a patient-centered multi-view framework that aligns a personalized network view with a transferable transcriptomic perturbation view to predict clinical drug response. For each patient, we construct an individualized gene regulatory network from tumor expression using DysRegNet and augment it with drug-target links from DrugBank; a graph neural encoder yields a drug-centric, mechanistically grounded embedding. In parallel, a frozen condition-specific gene-gene attention model pretrained on LINCS L1000 generates a simulated post-perturbation transcriptomic profile for the same patient-drug pair. We align the two views in a shared latent space via a CLIP-style contrastive objective with drug-context hard negatives, then concatenate the representations for end-to-end response classification. On TCGA, PREDIKTOR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under patient-, drug-, and tissue-split evaluations, and transfers zero-shot to the I-SPY2 trial, improving AUROC by 5.6% over competing methods. The aligned embeddings yield stable gene and pathway attributions that recover known mechanisms, supporting actionable and interpretable precision oncology.

AI.tldr: PREDIKTOR is a patient-centered multi-view framework that aligns personalized gene regulatory networks with simulated transcriptomic perturbation profiles via contrastive learning to predict clinical drug response, outperforming baselines on TCGA and I-SPY2 while providing interpretable mechanistic attributions.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of patient-specific therapeutic response from pre-treatment transcriptomes is hindered by scarcity of clinical response labels and post-treatment molecular profiles. Existing preclinical transfer-learning models are hard to interpret and unstable, while knowledge-graph methods remain static and fail to capture drug-induced transcriptomic perturbation dynamics.
AI.method: PREDIKTOR constructs individualized gene regulatory networks (via DysRegNet) augmented with drug-target links (DrugBank), encoded by a graph neural network for mechanistic embeddings. In parallel, a frozen condition-specific gene-gene attention model pretrained on LINCS L1000 generates simulated post-perturbation transcriptomic profiles. Both views are aligned via CLIP-style contrastive learning with drug-context hard negatives, then concatenated for end-to-end response classification.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on TCGA under patient-, drug-, and tissue-split evaluations. Transfers zero-shot to I-SPY2 trial, improving AUROC by 5.6% over competing methods. Aligned embeddings yield stable gene and pathway attributions that recover known mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: PREDIKTOR supports actionable and interpretable precision oncology by integrating mechanistic network context with transcriptomic perturbation dynamics through a contrastively aligned multi-view framework.

title: CineMobile: On-Device Image-to-Video Diffusion for Cinematic Camera Motion Generation
summary: The growing demand for image-to-video creation on mobile devices has increasingly focused on cinematic motion effects like bullet time, dolly zoom, slow motion, etc. While Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) exhibit strong performance in video generation, their large parameter sizes and multi-step iterative denoising processes lead to substantial computational overhead, making efficient generation on mobile devices challenging. We propose CineMobile to bridge the gap. In particular, CineMobile adopts a three-fold optimization strategy: (1) leveraging a distillation-guided pruning approach to derive a compact yet efficient model that retains the essential video generation capabilities required for cinematic effects; (2) optimizing the compressed model into a 4-step generator via a combination of diffusion distillation and reinforcement learning; (3) employing a hybrid post-training quantization strategy to compress the model footprint to under 1 GB. Experimental results show that compared to the teacher model with the Wan 2.1 architecture, CineMobile achieves a 40x speedup in generation while maintaining comparable visual quality. Specifically, CineMobile generates 49-frame 480p videos with a per-step denoising latency of 0.6s on an NVIDIA H200 GPU and 20s on the MediaTek Dimensity 8400 Ultimate 5G platform, with a peak memory usage of 1.8 GB, demonstrating its practical applicability for mobile-based image-to-video creation.

AI.tldr: CineMobile is a three-fold optimization framework (pruning distillation, 4-step diffusion+RL distillation, hybrid quantization) that compresses a Wan 2.1-based DiT video generation model to under 1 GB, achieving 40x speedup with comparable quality—running 49-frame 480p videos at 0.6s/step on H200 GPU and 20s/step on MediaTek Dimensity 8400 mobile platform.
AI.motivation: The growing demand for mobile image-to-video creation with cinematic effects (bullet time, dolly zoom, slow motion) is hindered by the large parameter sizes and multi-step iterative denoising processes of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), which cause substantial computational overhead and make efficient on-device generation challenging.
