AI.method: Three-fold optimization: (1) distillation-guided pruning to derive a compact model retaining essential cinematic video generation capabilities; (2) compressing the model into a 4-step generator via diffusion distillation combined with reinforcement learning; (3) hybrid post-training quantization to reduce model footprint to under 1 GB.
AI.result: 40x speedup over the Wan 2.1 teacher model with comparable visual quality. Generates 49-frame 480p videos with per-step denoising latency of 0.6s on NVIDIA H200 GPU and 20s on MediaTek Dimensity 8400 Ultimate 5G platform, with peak memory usage of 1.8 GB.
AI.conclusion: CineMobile demonstrates practical applicability for mobile-based image-to-video creation by bridging the gap between high-quality DiT-based video generation and the computational constraints of mobile devices.

title: A Few Teacher Steps Go a Long Way: Cost-Efficient On-Policy Data Augmentation for Agent Post-Training
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop: RLxF: Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback
summary: For LLM agents, supervised fine-tuning is not only about teacher labels' quality, but also about which interaction contexts those labels condition on. Pure behavioral cloning uses full teacher demonstrations, creating a mismatch between teacher-induced contexts seen in training and student-induced contexts encountered at test time. Recent work addresses this mismatch by querying a teacher at contexts reached by the student, often with increasingly elaborate filtering of the teacher's continuations. We instead frame on-policy data construction as a budget-allocation problem: under matched supervision resources, should teacher output be spent on more start-to-finish demos, longer continuations, outcome filtering, or broader coverage of learner-induced contexts? We formalize this design space through the rollout policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and two complementary costs: teacher inference generated before filtering and teacher supervision retained for SFT. Across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev, bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts improve over pure behavioral cloning at matched budgets. On HotpotQA and ALFWorld, where we run the full comparison, few-step continuations match or exceed success-filtered and critical-context-filtered alternatives. Our findings suggest that a few teacher steps, placed at learner-induced contexts, can be a more cost-efficient supervision allocation than longer or more heavily curated teacher completions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes framing on-policy data construction for LLM agents as a budget-allocation problem, finding that bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts outperform pure behavioral cloning and match or exceed more complex filtering approaches under matched supervision budgets across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning for LLM agents suffers from a distribution mismatch between teacher-induced contexts seen in training and student-induced contexts at test time. Prior work addresses this by querying a teacher at student-reached contexts but often uses elaborate filtering. The authors aim to systematically study how to best allocate a fixed supervision budget across different design choices.
AI.method: The authors formalize the design space via rollout policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and two complementary costs (teacher inference before filtering vs. teacher supervision retained for SFT). They compare pure behavioral cloning, success-filtered, critical-context-filtered, and bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts under matched budgets across three benchmarks.
AI.result: Bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts improve over pure behavioral cloning at matched budgets. On HotpotQA and ALFWorld, few-step continuations match or exceed success-filtered and critical-context-filtered alternatives. Longer or more heavily curated teacher completions are not necessarily more cost-efficient.
AI.conclusion: A few teacher steps placed at learner-induced contexts represent a more cost-efficient supervision allocation than longer or more heavily curated teacher completions, suggesting that simple, short on-policy interventions can be highly effective.

title: TestMate: Test-Time Domain Adaptation Aided by Lightweight Vision Foundation Model
summary: Test-Time Domain Adaptation (TTDA) aims to adapt Deep Neural Networks to distribution shifts using only streaming, unlabeled test data in real time. Current methods for semantic segmentation tasks suffer from critical limitations. Entropy minimization techniques require costly backpropagation, risking catastrophic forgetting and producing noisy segmentation boundaries. Memory-bank methods, while backpropagation-free, exhibit slow adaptation, requiring numerous samples to converge and struggle to handle continuous domain shifts. We introduce TestMate, a novel, real-time, and backpropagation-free TTDA framework that overcomes these issues. TestMate leverages generalization capability of a lightweight Visual Foundation Model to guide the adaptation. We use a zero-shot instance segmentation YOLOv8-seg based model to generate unlabeled mask proposals for objects and their parts at multiple scales in real time. These proposals are fused with the primary model via a heuristic, size-ordered competitive scheme, where small, high-confidence regions dominate and refine predictions in surrounding larger, less certain areas. This paremeter-free mechanism enables immediate adaptation from the first frame, inherently avoids catastrophic forgetting and effectively preserves fine object details and boundaries, even for small objects. TestMate can be used as a standalone, efficient refinement module or seamlessly integrated into existing TTDA methods to significantly boost their performance. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results across two benchmark datasets, proving TestMate's effectiveness in three distinct adaptation tasks: TTDA, Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA), and online-TTDA. Code is available.

AI.tldr: TestMate is a real-time, backpropagation-free Test-Time Domain Adaptation framework for semantic segmentation that uses a lightweight vision foundation model (YOLOv8-seg) to generate multi-scale mask proposals, which are fused with the primary model via a size-ordered competitive scheme, achieving state-of-the-art results on TTDA, SFDA, and online-TTDA tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing TTDA methods suffer from costly backpropagation, catastrophic forgetting, noisy segmentation boundaries (entropy minimization), or slow adaptation requiring many samples (memory-bank methods). TestMate aims to overcome these limitations with a real-time, backpropagation-free approach.
AI.method: TestMate uses a zero-shot YOLOv8-seg instance segmentation model to generate unlabeled mask proposals at multiple scales in real-time. These proposals are fused with the primary model's predictions via a heuristic, size-ordered competitive scheme where small, high-confidence regions dominate and refine larger, uncertain areas — a parameter-free mechanism enabling immediate adaptation from the first frame.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results across two benchmark datasets in three adaptation tasks: TTDA, Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA), and online-TTDA. The framework can be used standalone or integrated into existing TTDA methods to boost their performance.
AI.conclusion: TestMate demonstrates that leveraging a lightweight visual foundation model for mask proposal fusion enables real-time, backpropagation-free adaptation without catastrophic forgetting, while preserving fine object details and boundaries. Code is available.

title: Global Logic and Local Search: Dual-Stream Multimodal In-Context Learning for Verifiable Industrial Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted by ECCV 2026. 18 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) show strong few-shot generalization, but industrial anomaly detection remains difficult because defects are small, input resolution is limited, and textual standards are not always grounded in visual evidence. Recent optimization-based methods improve alignment through fine-tuning, but they often require many defective samples, which are unavailable in early deployment. We present Global Logic and Local Search (GLLS), a training-free framework for reference-guided multimodal in-context verification. GLLS uses a Part-Aware Visual-Logical Atlas to organize normal references and structured specifications in the inference context. It combines a Global & Logic Stream, where SAM 3 extracts partially checkable visual facts, with a Fine-Grained & Actions Stream, where MCTS selects local evidence crops under a fixed budget. Experiments on MMAD-QA and additional anomaly detection datasets show consistent gains over matched and general-purpose baselines, while keeping the final diagnostic decision traceable to explicit visual evidence throughout the inspection trace.

AI.tldr: GLLS is a training-free framework for multimodal anomaly detection that uses a Part-Aware Visual-Logical Atlas with two streams (Global & Logic, Fine-Grained & Actions) to perform reference-guided in-context verification without requiring fine-tuning or many defective samples.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection with LMMs is challenging due to small defects, limited input resolution, and misalignment between textual standards and visual evidence. Existing optimization-based methods require many defective samples for fine-tuning, which are unavailable during early deployment.
AI.method: GLLS employs a Part-Aware Visual-Logical Atlas to organize normal references and structured specifications. It operates via two streams: (1) Global & Logic Stream using SAM 3 to extract partially checkable visual facts, and (2) Fine-Grained & Actions Stream using MCTS to select local evidence crops under a fixed budget. The framework is training-free and uses reference-guided multimodal in-context verification.
AI.result: GLLS achieves consistent gains over matched and general-purpose baselines on MMAD-QA and additional anomaly detection datasets, with diagnostic decisions traceable to explicit visual evidence.
AI.conclusion: The training-free GLLS framework effectively addresses the data scarcity problem in early-stage industrial anomaly detection by leveraging structured visual-logical reasoning and MCTS-guided local evidence selection, while maintaining traceability of decisions.

title: Score Distributions, Not Cells: Evaluating Single-Cell Perturbations Under Class Overlap
summary:
Most classification problems assume the classes are roughly separable, so that an individual sample can usually be assigned to one class. Single-cell perturbation data violates this assumption: two perturbations can produce different populations of cells while overlapping so much that an individual cell could belong to either. Per-cell accuracy then measures this overlap rather than model quality. We see this on Tahoe-100M and the Virtual Cell Challenge, where a linear classifier, an MLP, and a Transformer all plateau near macro-F1 0.2-0.3 even though almost every pair of perturbations is statistically distinguishable.
  The fix is to score perturbations across the whole population rather than cell by cell. We average a classifier's per-cell probability vectors over all cells of a perturbation to form a population profile, then rank candidate perturbations by this profile; we call the resulting score the Classifier Discrimination Score (CDS). Taking the top-ranked class recovers the winning perturbation. It needs no retraining, costs linear time in the number of cells, and recovers near-perfect identification from the same weak models. CDS differs from the pseudobulk-based Perturbation Discrimination Score (PDS) used in recent benchmarks only in where the average is taken, raw gene expression for PDS versus a learned discriminative space for CDS, and identifies the true perturbation more reliably on both datasets, with the gap widening as cells grow scarce. Because a metric that misranks the ground truth will misrank the models scored against it, per-cell accuracy and raw-pseudobulk scores should be used with caution when comparing perturbation models.

AI.tldr: Single-cell perturbation data violates the class-separability assumption of standard classification, causing per-cell accuracy to plateau near macro-F1 0.2-0.3. The proposed Classifier Discrimination Score (CDS) averages per-cell probability vectors across all cells of a perturbation to form population profiles, enabling near-perfect perturbation identification without retraining.
AI.motivation: Single-cell perturbation data violates the standard classification assumption of separable classes because two perturbations can produce overlapping cell populations where individual cells could belong to either. This renders per-cell accuracy meaningless—it measures overlap rather than model quality.
AI.method: CDS averages a classifier's per-cell probability vectors over all cells of a perturbation to form a population profile, then ranks candidate perturbations by this profile. It requires no retraining and costs linear time in the number of cells. CDS differs from PDS only in where averaging occurs: raw gene expression (PDS) vs. learned discriminative space (CDS).
AI.result: On Tahoe-100M and Virtual Cell Challenge, linear classifier, MLP, and Transformer all plateau near macro-F1 0.2-0.3. CDS recovers near-perfect identification from the same weak models and identifies the true perturbation more reliably than both per-cell accuracy and PDS, with the gap widening as cells become scarce.
AI.conclusion: Per-cell accuracy and raw-pseudobulk scores (PDS) should be used with caution when comparing perturbation models, as a metric that misranks the ground truth will also misrank models scored against it. CDS provides a more reliable alternative.

title: TRISTAR: Triple-Signal Stair Recognition and Vision-Only Indoor Navigation for Search-and-Rescue Micro-UAVs
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Project repository available at: https://github.com/tavigingu/HawkOps-Indoor-Drone-Navigation-and-TRISTAR-Stair-Climbing
summary: Indoor search-and-rescue (SAR) operations often require rapid situational awareness where GNSS signals are unavailable and human access is difficult or hazardous. While most autonomous aerial systems rely on LiDAR, stereo vision, or specialized depth cameras, such solutions increase both hardware complexity and deployment costs. This paper presents a complete autonomous indoor navigation framework for low-cost unmanned aerial vehicles based exclusively on monocular vision. Implemented on a DJI Tello platform, the system combines monocular depth estimation using Depth Anything V2 with classical computer vision and lightweight deep learning models for scene understanding, victim detection, and hazard recognition. The framework consists of two independent behaviors: (i) corridor exploration with automatic door detection, room entry, OCR-based room identification, and victim inspection; and (ii) autonomous stair ascent based on TRISTAR (TRI-Signal STair Ascent Recognition), a novel triple-sensor fusion method that integrates structural cues (Sobel filtering), texture analysis (multi-scale Gabor filtering), and geometric depth from monocular depth estimation. Evaluation used real indoor flights in a university building. Depth calibration reduced relative depth error from 27.4% to below 10%, while the door detection algorithm reached a precision of 0.93 and an F1-score of 0.91. A dedicated ablation study shows that multi-sensor fusion significantly improves stair-recognition robustness compared to individual sensing modalities, and a failure-case analysis delineates the limits of monocular perception under challenging lighting and reflective surfaces. The results demonstrate that reliable indoor exploration and stair traversal are achievable on resource-constrained platforms without specialized ranging hardware, a practical, cost-effective solution for rapid SAR deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a monocular-vision-based autonomous indoor navigation framework for low-cost UAVs (DJI Tello), featuring corridor exploration with door detection, room identification, victim inspection, and autonomous stair ascent using a triple-sensor fusion method (TRISTAR). Depth calibration reduced relative error to below 10%, door detection achieved 0.93 precision and 0.91 F1-score, demonstrating reliable indoor SAR capabilities without specialized ranging hardware.
AI.motivation: Indoor SAR operations require rapid situational awareness in GNSS-denied environments, but existing autonomous aerial systems rely on expensive hardware (LiDAR, stereo/depth cameras), increasing complexity and deployment cost. There is a need for a low-cost, practical solution using minimal sensors.
AI.method: Complete monocular-vision-based indoor navigation framework on DJI Tello: (1) monocular depth estimation via Depth Anything V2; (2) corridor exploration with door detection, room entry, OCR-based identification, victim inspection; (3) autonomous stair ascent via TRISTAR — triple-sensor fusion of Sobel filtering (structural cues), multi-scale Gabor filtering (texture), and geometric depth from monocular depth estimation.
AI.result: Depth calibration reduced relative depth error from 27.4% to below 10%. Door detection achieved 0.93 precision and 0.91 F1-score. Ablation study confirmed multi-sensor fusion significantly improves stair-recognition robustness over individual modalities. Failure-case analysis identified limits under challenging lighting and reflective surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Reliable indoor exploration and stair traversal are achievable on resource-constrained UAV platforms using only monocular vision, offering a practical, cost-effective solution for rapid SAR deployment without specialized ranging hardware.

title: Minimum Block Width for Universal Approximation by Residual Neural Networks with Inner Width One
summary: In this paper, we study the universal approximation property of residual neural networks, and obtain some new results. For input and output dimensions $d_x$ and $d_y$, and LeakyReLU, ReLU, ReLU-like activation functions, the upper and lower bounds of the block width are established. To achieve $L^p$ approximation $(1\leq p <+\infty)$ on any compact domain, we show that the exact minimum block width is $\max\{d_x,d_y\}$ when the inner width is 1. Furthermore, we show that residual neural networks with block width $\min\{d_x+d_y, \max\{2d_x+1,d_y\}\}$ can achieve uniform approximation on any compact domain under the constraint that each residual branch has inner width 1. Besides, for any activation function family, we prove that residual neural networks with block width less than $\max\{d_x, d_y\}$ cannot approximate all target functions, both in the $L^p$ sense and the uniform sense, regardless of inner width.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes exact minimum block widths for residual neural networks to achieve universal approximation, showing that the minimum block width is max{dx,dy} for Lp approximation when inner width is 1, and proving that block widths below max{dx,dy} cannot achieve universal approximation regardless of inner width or activation function.
AI.motivation: To establish precise theoretical bounds on the minimum block width required for residual neural networks to achieve universal approximation, addressing a gap in understanding the exact architectural constraints for these networks.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis deriving upper and lower bounds on block width for residual NNs with LeakyReLU, ReLU, and ReLU-like activations, considering both Lp and uniform approximation on compact domains.
AI.result: - Exact minimum block width for Lp approximation is max{dx,dy} when inner width is 1. - Block width min{dx+dy, max{2dx+1,dy}} achieves uniform approximation with inner width 1. - Block width < max{dx,dy} cannot approximate all target functions regardless of inner width or activation function family.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides tight theoretical characterizations of the minimum block width needed for residual neural networks to be universal approximators, establishing fundamental limits on their architectural complexity.

title: FDR-Occ: Factorized Dense Routing for Full-Spectrum 3D Occupancy Prediction
summary: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction fundamentally relies on the 2D-to-3D view transformation. Current paradigms predominantly utilize explicit physical projection, which artificially restricts the routing matrix to strict, sparse camera rays. While computationally efficient, this imposes a severe Locality Bottleneck, preventing the network from constructing holistic contextual understanding and degrading sharply when camera extrinsics are unreliable or absent. To break this bottleneck, we abstract view transformation as unconstrained bipartite routing and propose Factorized Dense Routing (FDR). By approximating dense 2D-to-3D mixing through hierarchical tensor contractions, FDR guarantees a fully-global receptive field with tractable, sub-quadratic complexity. Crucially, the mandatory spatial contraction in dense routing exposes a fundamental Resolution-Context Trade-off. To address this, we introduce a Resolution-Context Decoupled Architecture. We factorize the 3D space into a global macroscopic topological anchor (via FDR) and precise local geometric planes (via explicit projection). This decoupling enables global semantic inference and exact surface localization to complement each other without mutual compromise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo benchmarks. More notably, in an uncalibrated setting where physical extrinsics are withheld, our global routing internalizes the implicit multi-camera rig topology and exhibits substantially stronger structural robustness than physical-projection baselines under the same protocol.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Factorized Dense Routing (FDR) to overcome the locality bottleneck of explicit 2D-to-3D projection in vision-based 3D occupancy prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results on Occ3D benchmarks and robust performance even without camera extrinsic calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing 2D-to-3D view transformations rely on explicit physical projection (camera rays), which creates a Locality Bottleneck—restricting the network to sparse, strict geometric correspondences and preventing holistic contextual understanding. This bottleneck severely degrades performance when camera extrinsics are unreliable or unavailable.
AI.method: FDR abstracts view transformation as unconstrained bipartite routing, approximating dense 2D-to-3D mixing via hierarchical tensor contractions with sub-quadratic complexity. A Resolution-Context Decoupled Architecture is introduced: global macroscopic topological anchors via FDR (dense routing) and precise local geometric planes via explicit projection, enabling complementary semantic inference and surface localization.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo benchmarks. In uncalibrated settings (without extrinsic parameters), the global routing internalizes multi-camera rig topology and demonstrates substantially stronger structural robustness than physical-projection baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dense routing breaks the locality bottleneck of explicit projection, and decoupling resolution from context resolves the inherent Resolution-Context Trade-off, making the framework both accurate and robust to missing calibration data.

title: Measuring What Matters: A Unified Evaluation Framework for GNN Explainability
summary: Graph eXplainable AI (G-XAI) is increasingly important for making Graph Neural Networks interpretable and accountable. While a growing number of explainers are available, choosing the right method and assessing the trustworthiness of its outputs remains unclear. Consistent evaluation practices and actionable guidance are still missing, hindering practical adoption. In this paper, we introduce a unified, quantitative benchmarking framework for G-XAI that requires no ground-truth assumptions. We formalize tabular explainability metrics for graph data, evaluating topological structure and node features as independent components. Our large-scale benchmarking study identifies explainers that consistently lie on the Pareto front across metric pairs and tasks, establishing robustly non-dominated solutions - while confirming that no single explainer achieves universal superiority. We distill our findings into actionable G-XAI usability guidelines to support Machine Learning practitioners in evaluating and deploying trustworthy GNN-based pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified, quantitative benchmarking framework for Graph eXplainable AI (G-XAI) that requires no ground-truth assumptions, using tabular explainability metrics adapted for graph data to evaluate topological structure and node features independently. Through large-scale benchmarking, it identifies explainers on the Pareto front across metric pairs and tasks, finding no single explainer universally superior, and provides actionable usability guidelines for practitioners.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of consistent evaluation practices and actionable guidance for choosing and assessing the trustworthiness of G-XAI methods, hindering practical adoption despite the growing number of available explainers.
AI.method: The authors formalize tabular explainability metrics for graph data, evaluating topological structure and node features as independent components, and conduct a large-scale benchmarking study to identify explainers on the Pareto front across metric pairs and tasks without ground-truth assumptions.
AI.result: The benchmarking identifies explainers that consistently lie on the Pareto front across metric pairs and tasks, establishing robustly non-dominated solutions, while confirming that no single explainer achieves universal superiority.
AI.conclusion: The findings are distilled into actionable G-XAI usability guidelines to support ML practitioners in evaluating and deploying trustworthy GNN-based pipelines.

title: Q-TriM: Question-Guided Tri-Modal Attention for Audio-Visual Question Answering
summary: Audio-Visual Question Answering (AVQA) extends classical VQA by requiring joint reasoning over video and synchronized audio. However, many AVQA systems rely on deeply stacked layers of self- and cross attention across text, video, and audio. Such sequential stacking may incur loss of information such as subtle inter-modal cues over the layers, causing errors to accumulate across sequential attention layers during the fusion. We introduce Q-TriM which performs multi-modal fusion in a shallow and parallel manner instead of a deep and sequential manner. For Q-TriM, we propose a novel framework for attention operation incorporating video and audio conditioned on text. As a result, we obtain not only standard cross attention outputs but also Tri-Modal Attention representations in which Query, Key, and Value come from distinct modalities. These attention representations are combined in parallel at a single stage, thus avoiding the multi-modal fusion with deep stacks in order to mitigate error accumulation and depth-induced issues. Q-TriM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three AVQA benchmarks, including substantial gains on MUSIC-AVQA-R, which demonstrates its robustness and out-of-distribution generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/Sunghun95/Q-TriM

AI.tldr: Q-TriM is a novel Audio-Visual Question Answering framework that performs multi-modal fusion in a shallow, parallel manner using Tri-Modal Attention (where Query, Key, and Value come from distinct modalities) instead of deep sequential attention stacks, achieving state-of-the-art results on three AVQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing AVQA systems use deep, sequentially stacked self- and cross-attention layers for fusing text, video, and audio, which causes information loss of subtle inter-modal cues and error accumulation across layers.
AI.method: Q-TriM performs multi-modal fusion in a shallow and parallel manner using a novel Tri-Modal Attention mechanism where Query, Key, and Value originate from three different modalities (text, video, audio). These attention representations are combined at a single stage, avoiding deep sequential stacks.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on three AVQA benchmarks, with substantial gains on MUSIC-AVQA-R, demonstrating robustness and out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.conclusion: Shallow parallel fusion via Tri-Modal Attention effectively mitigates error accumulation and depth-induced issues in AVQA, outperforming deep sequential fusion approaches.

title: Reliability and Identifiability in Persona-Trained Monte Carlo: Variance Decomposition, Stability Bounds, and the Identifiability of Heterogeneous News Reaction
comment: 29 pages. Companion theory paper to arXiv:2606.29556 (framework specification, "Persona-Trained Monte Carlo: Estimating Market-Outcome Distributions via Swarms of Persona-Conditioned Neural Policy Bots in a Limit Order Book"). Theory-only: all proofs given in full, no simulation results reported
summary:
Persona-Trained Monte Carlo (PTMC) estimates distributions of market-outcome functionals by repeatedly simulating limit-order-book interaction among $K$ neural policy bots whose behavioral personas are drawn from a learned heterogeneity distribution $\mathcal{P}$. This paper develops the statistical theory that makes the word "reliable" precise for such estimators.
  We decompose estimator variance into a persona-draw component $σ_P^2$ and a within-run component $σ_w^2$, give unbiased ANOVA estimators of both, and derive the variance-optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget between outer persona draws and inner replications. A coupling-based stability bound quantifies how misestimation of $\mathcal{P}$ and error in the trained policy propagate into the estimand, yielding a three-term total-error budget whose terms are separately estimable; a uniform-in-horizon version holds under a Doeblin condition on the market chain.
  The main contribution is an identification theory for heterogeneous news reaction: under a fixed response nonlinearity, the aggregate impact curve $A(z)=\mathbb{E}_Q[g(ηz)]$ detects heterogeneous news sensitivity through a strict Jensen gap and identifies the distribution $Q$ locally via odd moments and Hausdorff determinacy, with sharp failure when the response family is unknown. We provide $\sqrt{n}$-consistent estimators and a boundary-corrected test of homogeneous news reaction. Two separation theorems delimit when PTMC is provably preferable to homogeneous-population simulators and reduced-form forecasters, formalizing an irreducible Jensen bias floor and the Lucas critique as a minimax limit on intervention extrapolation. All proofs are given in full; guarantees are classified as unconditional (Monte Carlo convergence), conditional worst-case (the error budget), or open (the large-$K$ mean-field limit).

AI.tldr: This paper develops statistical theory for Persona-Trained Monte Carlo (PTMC) estimators, decomposing variance into persona-draw and within-run components, providing ANOVA estimators, variance-optimal compute allocation, coupling-based stability bounds, identification theory for heterogeneous news reaction, and separation theorems comparing PTMC to homogeneous simulators and reduced-form forecasters.
AI.motivation: To make PTMC estimators "reliable" by providing rigorous statistical guarantees, including variance decomposition, error budgeting, and identifiability conditions for heterogeneous agent-based simulations in limit-order-book markets.
AI.method: Variance decomposition into σ_P² (persona-draw) and σ_w² (within-run) with unbiased ANOVA estimators; coupling-based stability bounds for misestimation of P and policy errors; identification theory using Jensen gap, odd moments, and Hausdorff determinacy for heterogeneous news reaction; separation theorems for optimality comparisons.
AI.result: Provides variance-optimal compute allocation, three-term total-error budget, √n-consistent estimators, boundary-corrected test for homogeneous news reaction, and formal Jensen bias floor and Lucas critique as minimax limits.
AI.conclusion: PTMC estimators can be made statistically rigorous with decomposed error sources; heterogeneous population simulators are provably preferable under identified conditions; proofs classify guarantees as unconditional, conditional worst-case, or open (large-K mean-field limit).

title: How Do Diffusion Classifiers Decide? A Bias-Centric Evaluation
summary: Diffusion models have recently been repurposed for zero-shot classification, giving rise to diffusion classifiers that identify the best-matching text prompt by minimizing the noise-prediction error. Despite their growing adoption, how these models make classification decisions remains poorly understood. We introduce ASOB-Bench, a bias evaluation for diffusion classifiers along three dimensions: Attribute binding, Size-Order bias, and Background dependency. These dimensions serve not as an exhaustive taxonomy but as targeted probes of how the text-conditioned reconstruction-error score reaches a decision. Such a perspective is well studied for discriminative vision-language models, yet remains overlooked for diffusion classifiers. Extending an existing framework with five new attribute categories on newly constructed datasets, we find diffusion classifiers are less prone to attribute misbinding than an OpenCLIP baseline; on the established ComCo benchmark they are substantially more susceptible to size-order shortcuts; and on ImageNet-B they suffer far larger accuracy drops, revealing heavy reliance on background over foreground cues. Reconstruction-error heatmaps and U-Net cross-attention visualizations expose the mechanism behind each bias. Because diffusion classifiers share the same denoiser as text-to-image models, these single-pass diagnostics also point toward analogous failure modes in generation. Overall, diffusion classifiers exhibit a distinct bias profile from vision-language models, offering guidance for building more robust diffusion-based models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ASOB-Bench, a bias evaluation framework for diffusion classifiers across three dimensions (Attribute binding, Size-Order bias, Background dependency), finding that diffusion classifiers exhibit a distinct bias profile compared to discriminative vision-language models—less prone to attribute misbinding but more susceptible to size-order shortcuts and background reliance.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing adoption of diffusion models for zero-shot classification, how these models make classification decisions remains poorly understood, particularly regarding their biases compared to well-studied discriminative vision-language models.
AI.method: The authors propose ASOB-Bench, a bias evaluation framework with three dimensions: Attribute binding (5 new attribute categories on newly constructed datasets), Size-Order bias (on the established ComCo benchmark), and Background dependency (on ImageNet-B). They use reconstruction-error heatmaps and U-Net cross-attention visualizations to expose underlying mechanisms.
AI.result: Diffusion classifiers are less prone to attribute misbinding than OpenCLIP baseline; substantially more susceptible to size-order shortcuts on ComCo; and suffer far larger accuracy drops on ImageNet-B, revealing heavy reliance on background over foreground cues.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion classifiers exhibit a distinct bias profile from vision-language models, offering guidance for building more robust diffusion-based models. The single-pass diagnostics also point toward analogous failure modes in text-to-image generation.

title: Machine Learning for Depression Screening and Intervention: an Original Circadian Rhythm Score-based Methodology
summary: Depression screening from large-scale behavioral data is challenged by fragmented circadian indicators, limited interpretability, and the lack of intervention-oriented analysis. Existing approaches typically analyze sleep, activity, and social behaviors in isolation, failing to capture their joint circadian structure. To address this limitation, we first propose the Circadian Rhythm Score (CRS), a composite index that compresses multi-domain daily behaviors into a unified representation of circadian rhythm. CRS is constructed to maximize discriminative power for depression screening while preserving behavioral semantics through non-negativity constraints. Empirical results demonstrate near-lossless compression, where a single CRS retains almost the full predictive capability compared with multiple raw behavioral indicators. Building upon CRS, we develop an interpretable depression screening framework based on gradient-boosted trees and SHAP analysis, revealing nonlinear and saturation-like associations between circadian rhythm and depression risk. Beyond risk prediction, we further integrate interaction modeling and counterfactual regression to estimate heterogeneous and dose-dependent behavioral effects, enabling intervention-oriented reasoning under different circadian contexts. Experiments on the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, n=15,233), demonstrate robust screening performance (ROC-AUC=0.825) and identify actionable behavioral thresholds, including a minimum effective exercise dose of approximately 300 MET-min/week and an optimal restorative nap duration of approximately 65 minutes for sleep-deprived individuals. By bridging supervised representation learning and interpretable modeling, this work provides a scalable framework for depression screening and intervention-aware healthcare data mining.

AI.tldr: Proposes Circadian Rhythm Score (CRS) to compress multi-domain behavioral data into a single interpretable index for depression screening, validated on CHARLS (n=15,233) with ROC-AUC=0.825, and identifies actionable behavioral thresholds (e.g., ~300 MET-min/week exercise, ~65 min nap for sleep-deprived).
AI.motivation: Existing depression screening from behavioral data suffers from fragmented circadian indicators, limited interpretability, and lack of intervention-oriented analysis; sleep, activity, and social behaviors are analyzed in isolation, failing to capture joint circadian structure.
AI.method: (1) CRS: a composite index compressing multi-domain daily behaviors into a unified circadian representation via non-negativity constraints maximizing discriminative power. (2) Interpretable screening framework using gradient-boosted trees + SHAP. (3) Interaction modeling and counterfactual regression for heterogeneous/dose-dependent behavioral effects.
AI.result: Near-lossless compression (single CRS retains almost full predictive capability); ROC-AUC=0.825 on CHARLS (n=15,233); identified actionable thresholds: ~300 MET-min/week exercise, ~65 min nap for sleep-deprived individuals.
AI.conclusion: Bridges supervised representation learning and interpretable modeling, providing a scalable framework for depression screening and intervention-aware healthcare data mining.

title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
summary: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, finding that a simple pipeline (specialized OCR → VLM) outperforms complex multi-component systems. It introduces the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC) dataset and reveals a specialization gap where domain-specific OCR models drastically outperform general-purpose VLMs despite being far smaller.
AI.motivation: VLMs perform poorly on historical manuscripts due to low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy inputs. Current clean-text benchmarks fail to expose these failure modes, motivating a systematic evaluation framework for the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts.
AI.method: The authors benchmark on the CATMuS Latin dataset comparing domain-specific OCR models against general-purpose VLMs. They introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC) with 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations. They evaluate multi-component pipeline variants including RAG and post-OCR correction.
AI.result: Domain-specific OCR models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3× compared to general-purpose VLMs despite having orders of magnitude fewer parameters. The simplest pipeline (specialized OCR → VLM) outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding RAG or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade translation quality.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a complexity paradox for low-resource historical settings: simpler pipelines are more effective. The paper offers a new benchmark (IPC) and practical guidance for deploying translation systems on medieval Latin manuscripts.

title: A Physics-Regulated Neural Framework for Learning 3D Grain Growth Dynamics
summary: Grain growth is governed by the reduction in grain boundary energy and exhibits well-established statistical scaling laws. Developing data-driven surrogates that preserve these physical invariants while remaining computationally scalable remains challenging, especially in 3D. We present 3D-PRIMME (Physics-Regulated Interpretable Machine Learning for Microstructure Evolution) for learning three-dimensional grain growth dynamics. The model is trained using only two consecutive time steps yet accurately reproduces the linear coarsening law and preserves topological statistics over extended time scales. Despite being trained on a $100^3$ grid points with 512 grains, the learned evolution operator is applied to domains up to $1024^3$ grid points with 550000 grains without retraining, maintaining consistent kinetics and grain topology across orders-of-magnitude increases in system size. These results demonstrate that 3D-PRIMME learns a scale-independent and temporally stable local evolution rule, enabling efficient and robust large-scale surrogate prediction of 3D microstructure evolution.

AI.tldr: 3D-PRIMME is a physics-regulated ML model that learns 3D grain growth dynamics from just two time steps, accurately reproducing coarsening laws and topological statistics while scaling from 512 grains (100^3 grid) to 550,000 grains (1024^3 grid) without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven surrogates for grain growth fail to preserve physical invariants (e.g., linear coarsening law, topological statistics) and struggle with computational scalability in 3D.
AI.method: 3D-PRIMME (Physics-Regulated Interpretable Machine Learning for Microstructure Evolution) is trained on only two consecutive time steps of 3D grain growth data (100^3 grid, 512 grains) and learns a scale-independent local evolution rule that can be applied to larger domains without retraining.
AI.result: The model accurately reproduces linear coarsening law and preserves topological statistics over extended time. It generalizes from 100^3/512 grains to 1024^3/~550,000 grains without retraining, maintaining consistent kinetics and grain topology across orders-of-magnitude increases in system size.
AI.conclusion: 3D-PRIMME demonstrates that a temporally stable and scale-independent local evolution rule can be learned for 3D microstructure evolution, enabling efficient and robust large-scale surrogate predictions.

title: ContiStain: Cross-Domain Relation-Preserving Distillation for Continual Multi-Domain Virtual IHC Staining
summary: A unified multiplex virtual staining model enables scalable and non-destructive multiplex analysis from H&E slides while promoting parameter efficiency, shared pathological knowledge, and consistent cross-biomarker representations. However, in clinical practice, data for new biomarkers are typically acquired sequentially over time. Fine-tuning on such temporally arriving data leads to severe performance degradation on previously learned biomarkers, as sequential optimization disrupts the structured relationships among biomarker representations in the latent space. To address this issue, we propose ContiStain, an IHC multi-domain relational distillation framework for continual virtual staining. We first (i) construct a domain-aware structured feature space using a mixture-of-experts (MoE) feature extractor to reduce representation interference across biomarker domains. Based on this stabilized feature space, we then (ii) propose a relation-preserving distillation strategy that explicitly enforces the consistency of cross-domain token-level cosine similarity matrices between learned biomarker domains during continual adaptation. By maintaining cross-domain structural coherence, ContiStain mitigates forgetting while retaining adaptability to new domains. Experiments on the MIST dataset under a four-domain sequential virtual IHC staining setting show improved stability, reducing FID and ConchFID by 11.1 and 60.9 compared to sequential fine-tuning, enabling scalable and robust multi-domain virtual staining. Code is released at https://github.com/ccitachi/ContiStain.

AI.tldr: ContiStain is a continual learning framework for multiplex virtual IHC staining that uses an MoE-based feature extractor and relation-preserving distillation to prevent catastrophic forgetting when new biomarkers are added sequentially, reducing FID by 11.1 and ConchFID by 60.9 over sequential fine-tuning on the MIST dataset.
AI.motivation: Clinical practice requires sequential acquisition of new biomarker data over time, but fine-tuning on new biomarkers causes severe performance degradation on previously learned ones due to disruption of structured latent-space relationships among biomarker representations.
AI.method: ContiStain employs (i) a domain-aware structured feature space built via a mixture-of-experts (MoE) feature extractor to minimize representation interference across biomarker domains, and (ii) a relation-preserving distillation strategy that enforces consistency of cross-domain token-level cosine similarity matrices during continual adaptation.
AI.result: On the MIST dataset under a four-domain sequential virtual IHC staining setting, ContiStain reduces FID by 11.1 and ConchFID by 60.9 compared to sequential fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: By maintaining cross-domain structural coherence, ContiStain mitigates forgetting while retaining adaptability to new domains, enabling scalable and robust multi-domain virtual staining.

title: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment
summary: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. We find that while LLMs can support high-level strategic planning, they currently underperform specialized retrosynthesis models in reliably solving synthesis planning tasks.

AI.tldr: URSA is a new benchmarking framework for evaluating retrosynthesis planning that assesses both commercial feasibility and chemical plausibility. Testing on novel molecules shows specialized deep-learning models outperform LLMs, though LLMs can assist with high-level strategic planning.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols for comparing specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models for synthesis planning.
AI.method: The authors introduce URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment), an evaluation framework that benchmarks synthetic routes from both a formal perspective (convergence to commercially available starting materials) and a chemical plausibility perspective (mimicking expert chemist evaluation). They evaluate both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs on novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes.
AI.result: LLMs underperform specialized retrosynthesis models in reliably solving synthesis planning tasks, though they can support high-level strategic planning.
AI.conclusion: Specialized retrosynthesis models remain superior for reliable synthesis planning, while LLMs may serve as complementary tools for strategic-level planning in drug discovery.

title: CogRad: A Cognitively-Inspired Multi-Agent Framework for Radiology Report Generation
summary: Automated radiology report generation (RRG) can ease radiologist workload, yet most existing systems produce a report in a single forward pass, with no mechanism to check a claim against the image or revisit a finding once stated. We present CogRad, a cognitively inspired multi-agent framework that structures generation around four stages of a radiologist's reading process. A Scout agent discovers anatomical regions directly from image patches via slot attention and assigns region and disease-level triage scores; an Investigator agent concentrates representational capacity on the regions Scout flags as suspicious; a Writer agent compiles these signals into a disease gated visual prefix for a large language model; and a Verifier agent supervises training with a visual entailment loss and, at inference, re-examines its own draft sentence by sentence, regenerating any report it judges insufficiently grounded. On CheXpert Plus, CogRad attains a BLEU-4 of 0.316 and a CIDEr of 0.322, the best scores among the methods we compare against. On IU X-Ray, it attains a BLEU-4 of 0.201 and a CIDEr of 0.724, leading every baseline on every standard NLG metric. We further evaluate CogRad with RadGraph F1, CheXbert F1, and a hallucination analysis to assess clinical accuracy beyond standard text-overlap metrics, complemented by ablation studies and Grad-CAM-based visualizations that characterize each agent's contribution and the model's visual grounding.

AI.tldr: CogRad is a multi-agent framework for radiology report generation that mimics the four-stage reading process of radiologists (scouting, investigating, writing, verifying), achieving state-of-the-art BLEU-4 and CIDEr scores on CheXpert Plus and IU X-Ray datasets, with additional clinical accuracy evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing RRG systems generate reports in a single forward pass without any mechanism to verify claims against images or revisit findings, which limits clinical reliability and grounding.
AI.method: CogRad employs four specialized agents: (1) Scout agent uses slot attention to discover anatomical regions and assign triage scores; (2) Investigator agent focuses representational capacity on suspicious regions flagged by Scout; (3) Writer agent compiles signals into a disease-gated visual prefix for an LLM; (4) Verifier agent supervises training via visual entailment loss and performs sentence-by-sentence re-examination at inference, regenerating insufficiently grounded reports.
AI.result: On CheXpert Plus: BLEU-4 0.316, CIDEr 0.322 (best among compared methods). On IU X-Ray: BLEU-4 0.201, CIDEr 0.724 (leading all baselines on all NLG metrics). Also evaluated on RadGraph F1, CheXbert F1, and hallucination analysis, with ablations and Grad-CAM visualizations.
AI.conclusion: The cognitively inspired multi-agent design with explicit verification and iterative refinement improves both linguistic quality and clinical grounding of generated radiology reports.

title: F-ACVAE: A Federated Adaptive Conditional Variational Auto-Encoder for Privacy-Preserving Intrusion Detection in IoT Networks
summary: The rapid proliferation of Internet of things (IoT) devices has significantly expanded the cyber-attack surface, necessitating robust and privacy-preserving intrusion detection systems (IDS). However, centralized learning approaches often suffer from severe performance degradation due to high-dimensional traffic data, extreme class imbalance, and highly non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across heterogeneous edge devices. To address these challenges, this paper proposes F-ACVAE, a federated adaptive conditional variational autoencoder framework that enables collaborative model training across distributed IoT devices without sharing raw data. F-ACVAE incorporates selective parameter aggregation, where local encoders remain private while globally shared components are synchronized to preserve discriminative latent structures. To further enhance stability under extreme non-IID settings and feature distribution shifts, we introduce a novel constrained momentum Gaussian aggregation (CMGA) strategy that combines update clamping with momentum-based smoothing to mitigate client drift. Extensive experiments on the N-BaIoT dataset demonstrate that F-ACVAE achieves an average accuracy and macro F1-score of 99\%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, the selective aggregation mechanism reduces communication overhead by approximately 62\%, making the framework particularly suitable for resource-constrained IoT environments. These results highlight the effectiveness of F-ACVAE in achieving high detection performance while ensuring privacy preservation and communication efficiency.

AI.tldr: F-ACVAE is a federated adaptive conditional variational autoencoder framework for privacy-preserving intrusion detection in IoT, achieving 99% accuracy and macro F1-score on N-BaIoT while reducing communication overhead by 62% via selective parameter aggregation and constrained momentum Gaussian aggregation.
AI.motivation: IoT devices have expanded the cyber-attack surface, but centralized IDS suffer from high-dimensional data, extreme class imbalance, and non-IID data across heterogeneous edge devices, while sharing raw data raises privacy concerns.
AI.method: Proposes F-ACVAE with (1) federated adaptive conditional variational autoencoder for collaborative training without raw data sharing, (2) selective parameter aggregation (local encoders private, global components synchronized), and (3) constrained momentum Gaussian aggregation (CMGA) combining update clamping with momentum-based smoothing to mitigate client drift under non-IID settings.
AI.result: Achieves 99% average accuracy and macro F1-score on N-BaIoT dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing communication overhead by approximately 62%.
AI.conclusion: F-ACVAE effectively achieves high detection performance, privacy preservation, and communication efficiency, making it suitable for resource-constrained IoT environments.

title: PRISM3D: Probabilistic Refinement and Robust Initialization for Physically Consistent Scene Modeling under Extreme Motion Blur
summary: We address the inverse problem of blind 3D scene reconstruction from extremely motion-blurred images, a scenario where traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines fail. Existing approaches typically circumvent this bottleneck by relying on impractical sharp-image supervision. In this work, we introduce PRISM3D, a unified framework enabling robust reconstruction directly from severely degraded inputs. To overcome the lack of a reliable starting point, we propose a Robust Initialization strategy utilizing deep dense tracking method (VGGSfM) to recover global topology where feature matching fails. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to effectively leverage this paradigm to bootstrap 3D Gaussian Splatting from extreme motion blur. However, while robust, this initialization yields sparse and noisy geometry that causes deterministic optimization to diverge. To resolve this, we propose a coupled solution driven by probability and physics: we adopt a probabilistic formulation for geometric densification via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to robustly populate the sparse priors, while simultaneously modeling physical image formation via continuous Bezier Trajectories. Furthermore, while PRISM3D establishes a highly robust standalone pipeline, the availability of complementary event streams offers an opportunity to push the reconstruction fidelity further. To exploit this, we introduce PRISM3D-E, a multi-modal (RGB + Events) extension that seamlessly integrates high-temporal-resolution events as structural priors to maximize geometric recovery. Because existing datasets lack paired event streams under such severe degradation, we concurrently contribute the PRISM3D-E Benchmark to facilitate rigorous evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that both our standalone RGB framework and its multi-modal extension establish new state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: PRISM3D is a framework for blind 3D scene reconstruction from extremely motion-blurred images, using robust initialization via dense tracking, probabilistic geometric densification via MCMC, and continuous Bezier trajectory modeling. A multi-modal extension PRISM3D-E integrates event streams, and a new benchmark is contributed. Both achieve state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional SfM pipelines fail under extreme motion blur; existing methods rely on impractical sharp-image supervision. The goal is to enable robust 3D reconstruction directly from severely degraded inputs without such supervision.
AI.method: (1) Robust Initialization using deep dense tracking (VGGSfM) to recover global topology; (2) Probabilistic geometric densification via MCMC to robustly populate sparse noisy priors; (3) Physical image formation modeling via continuous Bezier Trajectories; (4) Multi-modal extension PRISM3D-E integrating event streams as structural priors; (5) A new benchmark with paired event data under severe degradation.
AI.result: Both the standalone RGB framework (PRISM3D) and the multi-modal extension (PRISM3D-E) establish new state-of-the-art performance in blind 3D reconstruction from extreme motion blur.
AI.conclusion: PRISM3D provides a highly robust standalone pipeline for 3DGS bootstrapping under extreme blur without sharp-image supervision. The event-based extension further pushes reconstruction fidelity, and the contributed benchmark enables future evaluation.

title: Hierarchical Scaffolding Enables Human-Like Cognitive Selectivity under Data Scarcity
summary: Modern machine learning systems demand extensive datasets for visual recognition. Conversely, humans learn with high efficiency despite severe data limitations, often by acquiring broad categorical structures before refining finer distinctions. Inspired by this contrast, we introduce SCALA (Scaffolded Cognitive Architecture for Learning under limited dAta), a hierarchical learning framework grounded in cognitive psychology that guides models from coarse conceptual structures to fine-grained recognition. Our model exhibits human-like cognitive selectivity by effectively prioritizing task-relevant features while suppressing background distractors, a mechanism that induces a fundamental shift in representation learning. This shift is characterized by accelerated cluster formation, reduced intra-class dispersion, and enhanced semantic separability. Empirically, SCALA achieves significant accuracy improvements under severe data scarcity. Furthermore, this hierarchical scaffolding promotes robust generalization to unseen classes and accelerates the acquisition of novel categories. Collectively, our results establish SCALA as a powerful framework for achieving human-level sample efficiency and resilient category generalization in data-constrained environments.

AI.tldr: SCALA introduces a cognitively-inspired hierarchical learning framework that guides models from coarse concepts to fine-grained recognition, achieving human-like sample efficiency and robust generalization under severe data scarcity.
AI.motivation: Humans learn efficiently from limited data by acquiring broad categorical structures before refining finer distinctions, whereas modern ML systems demand extensive datasets. The paper aims to bridge this gap by designing a framework that achieves human-level sample efficiency.
AI.method: SCALA (Scaffolded Cognitive Architecture for Learning under limited dAta) is a hierarchical learning framework grounded in cognitive psychology that guides models from coarse conceptual structures to fine-grained recognition, incorporating human-like cognitive selectivity to prioritize task-relevant features while suppressing background distractors.
AI.result: The framework induces accelerated cluster formation, reduced intra-class dispersion, and enhanced semantic separability. SCALA achieves significant accuracy improvements under severe data scarcity, robust generalization to unseen classes, and accelerated acquisition of novel categories.
AI.conclusion: SCALA establishes a powerful framework for achieving human-level sample efficiency and resilient category generalization in data-constrained environments.

title: Ghosts Beneath Textures: Texture-Relation Cues for Cross-Paradigm AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated images have proliferated rapidly, motivating extensive research. Most existing AI-generated image detectors are developed and evaluated under image-free generation paradigms, such as noise-based or text-guided generation. However, image-conditioned generation has become increasingly important in practical applications, as it enables more fine-grained control over generated content. Detecting AI-generated images across these two paradigms creates a critical cross-paradigm detection problem that has long been overlooked. To study this problem, we construct ConImageGen, a benchmark for cross-paradigm AI-generated image detection. Evaluations on ConImageGen show that existing detectors fail to generalize reliably across image-free and image-conditioned generation. To address this failure, this paper identifies a cross-paradigm forensic cue and provides a new perspective for generalized AI-generated image detection. Specifically, by suppressing semantic interference, we visualize, for the first time, semantics-irrelevant texture patterns across generation paradigms. These patterns exhibit structured local-global texture relations, indicating a generalizable form of forensic evidence. Motivated by this finding, we shift the focus from directly exploiting explicit artifacts to modeling texture relations and propose DTS-Det, a detection framework that captures and leverages such relations for generalized AI-generated image detection. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our method. DTS-Det achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse evaluation settings, reaching 99.6% ACC on ConImageGen with a 10.5% gain over the best baseline. It also achieves 93.2%/94.1% ACC in cross-dataset evaluation on PicoBanana/RAID and maintains detection rates of 95.2%/88.1% under reconstruction attacks and black-box adversarial attacks, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the overlooked cross-paradigm AI-generated image detection problem (image-free vs. image-conditioned generation), constructs the ConImageGen benchmark showing existing detectors fail to generalize, discovers a generalizable forensic cue based on local-global texture relations, and proposes DTS-Det which achieves state-of-the-art performance (99.6% ACC on ConImageGen, 93.2%/94.1% on cross-dataset evaluation, robust against attacks).
AI.motivation: Existing AI-generated image detectors are developed under image-free generation paradigms (noise-based or text-guided), but image-conditioned generation has become increasingly important. The cross-paradigm detection problem has been overlooked, and existing detectors fail to generalize reliably across these two paradigms.
AI.method: The paper constructs the ConImageGen benchmark, identifies cross-paradigm forensic cues by suppressing semantic interference to visualize semantics-irrelevant texture patterns with structured local-global texture relations, and proposes DTS-Det, a detection framework that models texture relations rather than exploiting explicit artifacts.
AI.result: DTS-Det achieves 99.6% ACC on ConImageGen (10.5% gain over best baseline), 93.2%/94.1% ACC in cross-dataset evaluation on PicoBanana/RAID, and maintains 95.2%/88.1% detection rates under reconstruction and black-box adversarial attacks respectively.
AI.conclusion: Modeling texture relations as generalizable forensic evidence is effective for cross-paradigm AI-generated image detection, offering a new perspective beyond exploiting explicit artifacts.

title: RSPO: Reward-Swap Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn LLM Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning holds significant potential for training large language models (LLMs) to handle multi-turn interactive tasks. However, in long-horizon, multi-turn tasks characterized by sparse outcome rewards, directly training with outcome rewards often results in slow convergence due to the sparsity of signals and the lack of fine-grained feedback. Furthermore, the model may fail to learn successful trajectories that are not sampled during training, thereby limiting its performance. Conversely, while employing customized dense process rewards provides richer signals and accelerates convergence, these surrogate rewards may exhibit potential misalignment with the ground-truth outcome rewards. This inconsistency can bias the training direction and ultimately degrade the model's final performance. In this work, we propose Reward-Swap Policy Optimization (RSPO), a method designed to leverage the rich information from dense process rewards to facilitate training with outcome rewards. By utilizing a reward-swap mechanism, RSPO ensures the diversity of sampled trajectories while guaranteeing consistency between the optimization objective and the true outcome rewards, thereby elevating the performance ceiling of the model. We conduct extensive experiments on two challenging agent benchmarks, WebShop and ALFWorld. By applying our method to various reinforcement learning algorithms, including GRPO, PPO, and GiGPO, we demonstrate that RSPO achieves consistent performance improvements across different baselines and benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RSPO combines dense process rewards with outcome rewards via a reward-swap mechanism to improve reinforcement learning for LLMs in multi-turn tasks, achieving consistent gains across WebShop and ALFWorld benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Outcome rewards in long-horizon multi-turn tasks are sparse, causing slow convergence, while dense process rewards can misalign with true rewards and bias training.
AI.method: Reward-Swap Policy Optimization (RSPO) uses a reward-swap mechanism to leverage dense process rewards for trajectory diversity while maintaining alignment with ground-truth outcome rewards.
AI.result: RSPO achieves consistent performance improvements across multiple RL algorithms (GRPO, PPO, GiGPO) on WebShop and ALFWorld benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: RSPO effectively elevates the performance ceiling of LLMs in multi-turn interactive tasks by combining the benefits of dense process rewards and outcome rewards without misalignment.

title: GeoSelect: Spatial-Program Execution for Training-Free Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
summary: Referring remote sensing image segmentation isolates the object named by a natural-language expression in an aerial image. Existing training-free methods resolve the expression through implicit vision-language activations or region-text similarity, which gives weak control over the spatial, comparative, and ordinal relations that dominate aerial referring: they cannot represent constructions such as the largest ship or the second court from the left. We propose GeoSelect, a training-free pipeline that reframes referring as the execution of a typed spatial program. A frozen, text-only language model synthesises the expression into a small domain-specific language, a well-formedness checker accepts the program, and a deterministic executor runs it. The central abstraction is a single scored candidate set type under which every operator composes: continuous geometric fields realise position and proximity as dense pixel-level maps, while discrete set and order operators add the extremum, ordinal, counted-union, and relational constructions that fields alone cannot express. Because execution is explicit, every intermediate program, field, and ranking is inspectable, and a reliability ladder degrades any failing program to a field-only special case, so every expression returns an answer. GeoSelect attains 58.86 mIoU on RRSIS-D test and 55.27 mIoU on RISBench test, more than twice the best prior training-free method on RRSIS-D, with no referring supervision and on a single GPU. A controlled comparison with candidates and segmenter fixed attributes the gain to explicit execution, not the backbone; an oracle decomposition localises the residual gap to detection recall on RRSIS-D and selection on RISBench, and an exposure audit confirms robustness to pretraining leakage. Code will be released upon acceptance at the project page https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoSelect/.

AI.tldr: GeoSelect is a training-free pipeline for referring remote sensing image segmentation that reframes referring expressions as typed spatial programs executed by a frozen LLM, achieving over 2x mIoU improvement (58.86 on RRSIS-D) compared to prior training-free methods.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free methods for referring remote sensing segmentation rely on implicit vision-language activations or region-text similarity, which fail to handle spatial, comparative, and ordinal relations (e.g., "the largest ship", "the second court from the left") that dominate aerial referring expressions.
AI.method: GeoSelect uses a frozen text-only LLM to synthesize the expression into a typed domain-specific language program, validated by a well-formedness checker and executed deterministically. It introduces a scored candidate set type with: continuous geometric fields (position, proximity as pixel-level maps) and discrete set/order operators (extremum, ordinal, counted-union, relational). A reliability ladder degrades failing programs to a field-only fallback, ensuring every expression returns an answer.
AI.result: GeoSelect achieves 58.86 mIoU on RRSIS-D test and 55.27 mIoU on RISBench test, more than double the best prior training-free method on RRSIS-D, with no referring supervision on a single GPU. Controlled comparisons attribute gains to explicit execution; oracle decomposition localizes residual gaps to detection recall on RRSIS-D and selection on RISBench; exposure audit confirms robustness to pretraining leakage.
AI.conclusion: Explicit programmatic execution of spatial language (via a typed DSL with geometric fields and discrete operators) dramatically outperforms implicit training-free methods for aerial referring segmentation, while maintaining full inspectability and reliability through a degradation mechanism.

title: Trust Region Policy Distillation
summary: Big goals are hard to achieve all at once; breaking them into small steps is wiser. We present Trust Region Policy Distillation (TOP-D), which transforms the notoriously unstable, high-variance On-Policy Distillation (OPD) into a stable training paradigm by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher. Theoretically, we establish a rigorous framework demonstrating that TOP-D inherently controls gradient variance. By providing a formal global convergence analysis alongside a monotonic improvement bound, we mathematically formalize the reliability and stability of the overall training dynamics. Empirically, TOP-D dramatically enhances training stability, sample efficiency, and final performance on mathematical reasoning tasks. More importantly, TOP-D introduces zero additional computational overhead, positioning itself as a promising alternative to the well-established OPD paradigm.

AI.tldr: TOP-D transforms unstable On-Policy Distillation into stable training by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher, with theoretical guarantees on gradient variance control and convergence, achieving superior performance on math reasoning tasks at zero extra cost.
AI.motivation: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is notoriously unstable and high-variance; big goals are hard to achieve all at once, so breaking them into small steps is wiser.
AI.method: Dynamically constructs a proximal teacher to stabilize training; provides theoretical framework for gradient variance control, global convergence analysis, and monotonic improvement bound.
AI.result: Dramatically enhances training stability, sample efficiency, and final performance on mathematical reasoning tasks with zero additional computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: TOP-D is a promising alternative to the established OPD paradigm, offering stable, efficient, and cost-free improvements.

title: SharpSplat: Edge-Regularized 3D Gaussian Splatting for High Fidelity Urban Building Reconstruction from UAV images
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) - 2026
summary: Reconstructing high-fidelity 3D building models from UAV imagery is essential for large-scale digital twin development. However, existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) techniques often struggle with building facades, failing to capture sharp geometric transitions. To address this, we propose a semantic edge regularization framework that supervises 3DGS to produce crisp architectural boundaries. Our method leverages SAM 3 to generate precise building masks, from which we extract architecturally significant edges. During training, we align rendered image gradients with these extracted edges, forcing the Gaussians to converge into sharp structural geometries. Evaluations across campus environments, dense urban centers, and custom residential datasets demonstrate significant improvements in edge fidelity without requiring architectural modifications to the 3DGS pipeline. Our approach proves robust across diverse building types, roof geometries, and urban densities.

AI.tldr: A semantic edge regularization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses SAM-generated building masks and extracted architectural edges to produce sharper geometric boundaries in 3D building reconstruction from UAV imagery.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS techniques fail to capture sharp geometric transitions in building facades, limiting high-fidelity 3D building model reconstruction for large-scale digital twins.
AI.method: Uses SAM 3 to generate building masks, extracts architecturally significant edges, then aligns rendered image gradients with these edges during training to force Gaussian convergence into sharp structural geometries.
AI.result: Significant improvements in edge fidelity across campus environments, dense urban centers, and custom residential datasets, with robustness across diverse building types, roof geometries, and urban densities.
AI.conclusion: The semantic edge regularization framework enhances 3DGS for building reconstruction without architectural modifications to the pipeline, proving effective for crisp architectural boundary capture.

title: Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation with Prefix Replay
summary: We study on-policy distillation (OPD) for agentic tasks, where an LLM agent interacts with an environment over multiple turns and a student imitates a teacher over these multi-turn interaction histories. Fully online OPD is costly because each update requires fresh student rollouts through the environment and teacher queries at visited histories. We propose Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation (ReOPD), an off-environment alternative that reuses pre-collected teacher trajectories as replayed prefixes: the student acts at selected steps, while the teacher provides dense per-step supervision without executing new environment interactions. We show that multi-turn OPD introduces a prefix trap: making histories more student-on-policy improves relevance to the student, but can query the teacher on histories where its target is unreliable. This creates a two-sided distribution shift between student occupancy and teacher reliability. ReOPD addresses this by treating multi-turn OPD as a reliability-aware prefix distribution design and implements it with a simple step-decaying sampling schedule that emphasizes early, lower-shift prefixes. Across mathematical reasoning with Python and search environments over multiple teacher and student model scales, ReOPD preserves or improves OPD-level accuracy, uses zero tool calls during student training, and is at least 4$\times$ faster per training step than OPD. ReOPD therefore turns expensive agent-environment interaction into a reusable offline resource, enabling scalable distillation across tools, tasks, and environments.

AI.tldr: ReOPD is an off-environment distillation method for LLM agents that reuses pre-collected teacher trajectories as replayed prefixes, avoiding costly online environment interactions while preserving or improving OPD-level accuracy with zero tool calls during training and 4x speedup per step.
