AI.motivation: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) for multi-turn agentic tasks is costly because each update requires fresh student rollouts and teacher queries, creating significant computational overhead. The authors aim to reduce this expense while maintaining distillation quality.
AI.method: ReOPD reuses pre-collected teacher trajectories as replayed prefixes where the student acts at selected steps and the teacher provides dense per-step supervision without new environment interactions. It treats multi-turn OPD as a reliability-aware prefix distribution design, using a step-decaying sampling schedule that emphasizes early, lower-shift prefixes to address the "prefix trap" (two-sided distribution shift between student occupancy and teacher reliability).
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning with Python and search environments over multiple teacher and student model scales, ReOPD preserves or improves OPD-level accuracy, uses zero tool calls during student training, and is at least 4x faster per training step than OPD.
AI.conclusion: ReOPD turns expensive agent-environment interaction into a reusable offline resource, enabling scalable distillation across tools, tasks, and environments.

title: MACRO: Training-free Multi-plane Attention for Closeup Render Optimization
summary: Close-up rendering, zooming into a scene well beyond any training camera, is important for virtual production and interactive 3D content, yet remains an open challenge. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity, real-time novel view synthesis, but its rendering quality degrades at close range. Recent diffusion-based methods that enhance the rendering by conditioning on reference images from the training set produce significant artifacts in this setting. We analyze this failure and identify its root cause: the scale gap between the close-up and reference views. We show that the features in reference-conditioned enhancement models are not scale-invariant, causing cross-view attention to retrieve incorrect correspondences when the same content appears at different scales, and that this mismatch cannot be corrected in latent space because the VAE encoder is not scale-equivariant. Building on this analysis we introduce MACRO, Multi-plane Attention for Closeup Render Optimization, a training-free method for high-quality close-up novel view synthesis from 3DGS. MACRO resolves the scale gap by leveraging the scene's known 3D structure: it decomposes the close-up into depth planes, crops and resizes references in image space to match the scale of each plane before encoding, and applies a depth-aware attention mask so each token attends only to scale-matched references. The method requires no architectural changes or additional training. We further contribute two new close-up novel view synthesis benchmarks, the first standardized evaluation protocol for this setting, and demonstrate state-of-the-art results on both, outperforming existing 3DGS and diffusion-based methods on both reconstruction and perceptual metrics. Project page: https://nitzanhod.github.io/MACRO

AI.tldr: MACRO is a training-free method that improves 3D Gaussian Splatting close-up rendering by addressing the scale gap between close-up and reference views. It decomposes close-ups into depth planes, crops/resizes references to match scales, and applies depth-aware attention masking, achieving SOTA results on two new benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Close-up rendering beyond training camera positions remains an open challenge. 3DGS degrades at close range, and diffusion-based enhancement methods fail due to the scale gap between close-up and reference views—features in reference-conditioned models are not scale-invariant, and VAE encoders lack scale-equivariance, causing incorrect cross-view attention correspondences.
AI.method: MACRO (Multi-plane Attention for Closeup Render Optimization) is a training-free approach that: (1) decomposes the close-up view into depth planes using the known 3D structure; (2) crops and resizes reference images in image space to match the scale of each depth plane before encoding; (3) applies a depth-aware attention mask so each token attends only to scale-matched references.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results on two new close-up novel view synthesis benchmarks, outperforming existing 3DGS and diffusion-based methods on both reconstruction and perceptual metrics.
AI.conclusion: The scale gap is the root cause of failure in reference-conditioned close-up rendering. MACRO resolves this gap through scale-aware, depth-guided attention without architectural changes or additional training, and the paper establishes the first standardized evaluation protocol for this setting.

title: MARLIN: De Novo Molecular Structure Elucidation from Tandem Mass Spectra without a Ground-Truth Formula
summary: Untargeted tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) detects thousands of small molecules per biological sample, yet most go unidentified because they are absent from spectral libraries. These uncharacterized metabolites and natural products are precisely the compounds that matter for drug discovery, biomarker research, and exposomics. Computational de novo structure elucidation could close this gap, but almost all state-of-the-art methods assume the ground-truth molecular formula is known, an oracle that does not exist for genuinely novel compounds and is itself predicted with substantial error. We present MARLIN, a de novo method that elucidates structures directly from a spectrum with no molecular formula at any stage. A self-supervised encoder predicts a molecular fingerprint from the raw peaks, and a block-diffusion language model generates candidate structures conditioned only on the fingerprint and the instrument-measured precursor mass. A provably safe mass-shell constraint keeps every candidate consistent with the measured mass without fixing the atom inventory, and candidates are accepted by exact parts-per-million mass agreement. A symmetric noise objective absorbs encoder error, and a candidate-diversity mechanism keeps the candidates from collapsing to a single structure. On the NPLIB1 benchmark, MARLIN is the strongest method evaluated without a ground-truth formula across exact-match accuracy, structural distance, and fingerprint similarity, and it recovers the correct molecular formula as a byproduct about as often as a dedicated predictor without ever using one. MARLIN enables reliable de novo structure elucidation in the realistic discovery regime where the molecular formula is unavailable.

AI.tldr: MARLIN is a de novo method that elucidates molecular structures directly from tandem mass spectra without requiring a ground-truth molecular formula, using a self-supervised encoder and block-diffusion language model, achieving state-of-the-art results on NPLIB1.
AI.motivation: Most untargeted MS/MS spectra detect thousands of small molecules per biological sample, but the majority go unidentified due to absence from spectral libraries. Existing computational de novo methods almost all assume the ground-truth molecular formula is known—an oracle unavailable for genuinely novel compounds—and formula prediction itself has substantial error. There is a need for a method that works without this prerequisite.
AI.method: MARLIN uses a self-supervised encoder to predict a molecular fingerprint from raw MS/MS peaks, then a block-diffusion language model generates candidate structures conditioned on the fingerprint and precursor mass. A provably safe mass-shell constraint keeps candidates consistent with measured mass without fixing atom inventory. It also employs a symmetric noise objective to absorb encoder error and a candidate-diversity mechanism to prevent collapse to a single structure.
AI.result: On the NPLIB1 benchmark, MARLIN achieves the strongest performance among methods evaluated without a ground-truth formula across exact-match accuracy, structural distance, and fingerprint similarity. It recovers the correct molecular formula as a byproduct about as often as a dedicated predictor without ever using one.
AI.conclusion: MARLIN enables reliable de novo structure elucidation in the realistic discovery regime where the molecular formula is unavailable, closing a critical gap in untargeted metabolomics and natural product discovery.

title: SGF-CDNet: A Consistency-Discrepancy Graph Network over Semantic-Geometric Fused Nodes for Face Forgery Detection
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. This work has been accepted at ICMEW 2026
summary: The rapid advancement of deepfakes necessitates robust face forgery detection. Although forged faces may lack obvious artifacts, they often contain subtle disharmony among different facial regions. We propose SGF-CDNet, a Consistency-Discrepancy Graph Network (CD-GNN) over Semantic-Geometric Fused (SGF) nodes. First, SGF-CDNet constructs SGF nodes by deeply fusing semantic regions from face parsing with geometric information from facial landmarks, allowing nodes to capture both high-level concepts and precise geometric constraints. Next, a dual-path CD-GNN performs parallel relational reasoning on these nodes across two dimensions: consistency and discrepancy. The consistency path evaluates if facial components follow natural biological patterns, while the discrepancy path mines for structural tensions and feature conflicts introduced by forgeries. By integrating these processes, our model effectively identifies disharmonious relationships between facial components. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that SGF-CDNet achieves superior performance, establishing it as a reliable solution for face forgery detection.

AI.tldr: SGF-CDNet is a face forgery detection method that fuses semantic and geometric features into graph nodes, then uses a dual-path graph network to analyze both consistency (natural biological patterns) and discrepancy (forgery-induced conflicts) between facial regions, achieving superior detection performance.
AI.motivation: Deepfakes often lack obvious visual artifacts but contain subtle disharmony among facial regions; existing methods fail to capture these fine-grained inter-region inconsistencies.
AI.method: Constructs Semantic-Geometric Fused (SGF) nodes by combining face parsing semantics with facial landmarks geometry, then applies a dual-path Consistency-Discrepancy Graph Network (CD-GNN) for parallel relational reasoning across two dimensions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public datasets show SGF-CDNet achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: SGF-CDNet is a reliable and effective solution for face forgery detection by explicitly modeling disharmonious inter-component relationships.

title: Towards Personalized Differentially Private Learning for Decentralized Local Graphs
summary: Graph-structured data is increasingly generated and stored in decentralized environments, such as social platforms, mobile applications, and edge networks, where users maintain control over their local graph data. However, collecting and analyzing such decentralized graph data for downstream learning tasks raises significant privacy concerns, as nodes and their attributes often contain sensitive personal information. Local Differential Privacy (LDP) has emerged as a promising solution for privacy-preserving data collection without relying on trusted servers. Nevertheless, existing LDP-based graph learning methods typically assume uniform privacy requirements across users, ignoring the heterogeneous and personalized privacy preferences commonly observed in real-world systems. This uniform treatment leads to inflexible noise injection at the data collection stage, resulting in substantial distortion of graph data and degraded utility in subsequent analysis. To address this limitation, we propose PPGNN, a personalized differentially private framework for decentralized graph data. PPGNN enables user-specific privacy budgets during local perturbation while preserving analytical utility. To handle heterogeneous privacy levels and noise distortion, we design a two-stage solution consisting of a Personalized Perturbation Mechanism (PPM) and a weighted calibration strategy, FlexProp. Extensive experiments on six real-world graph datasets demonstrate that PPGNN effectively balances personalized privacy protection and data utility in decentralized graph learning scenarios.

AI.tldr: PPGNN is a personalized differentially private framework for decentralized graph data that allows user-specific privacy budgets during local perturbation, using a Personalized Perturbation Mechanism (PPM) and a weighted calibration strategy (FlexProp) to balance privacy and utility.
AI.motivation: Existing LDP-based graph learning methods assume uniform privacy requirements across users, ignoring heterogeneous and personalized privacy preferences in real-world systems, leading to inflexible noise injection and degraded utility.
AI.method: A two-stage solution: (1) Personalized Perturbation Mechanism (PPM) for user-specific privacy budgets during local perturbation, and (2) FlexProp, a weighted calibration strategy to handle heterogeneous privacy levels and noise distortion.
AI.result: Experiments on six real-world graph datasets demonstrate that PPGNN effectively balances personalized privacy protection and data utility in decentralized graph learning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: PPGNN addresses the limitation of uniform privacy requirements in LDP-based graph learning by enabling personalized privacy budgets, achieving a better trade-off between privacy protection and analytical utility.

title: BAT3R: Bootstrapping Articulated 3D Reconstruction from 2D Image Collections
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://jakubzadrozny.github.io/bat3r/
summary: 3D reconstruction of articulated objects from a single image is challenging because large training datasets with paired image and 3D supervision are difficult to obtain. Recent point map-based methods achieve strong performance but rely on synthetic datasets rendered from manually created articulated 3D assets with carefully curated pose distributions. While camera viewpoints can be easily sampled, generating realistic object articulations remains costly and labor-intensive. We propose a training framework that reduces this requirement by leveraging unannotated 2D images collections with only a single rigged canonical mesh per category. Starting from a weak 3D shape predictor trained on canonical-pose renders, we iteratively estimate object articulation and camera pose by fitting the mesh to predicted point maps. The recovered articulations and viewpoints are then used to render updated synthetic training data, progressively improving the predictor. Despite using substantially weaker 3D supervision, our models achieve performance comparable with DualPM, which requires manually curated articulated training datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a training framework for single-image 3D reconstruction of articulated objects that reduces the need for expensive 3D articulated assets, using only a single rigged canonical mesh per category and unannotated 2D images; it iteratively estimates articulation and camera pose via point map fitting, achieving performance comparable to methods requiring manually curated articulated datasets.
AI.motivation: Large training datasets with paired image and 3D supervision are difficult to obtain; generating realistic object articulations for synthetic data remains costly and labor-intensive.
AI.method: The framework starts with a weak 3D shape predictor trained on canonical-pose renders, then iteratively estimates object articulation and camera pose by fitting a rigged canonical mesh to predicted point maps; recovered articulations/viewpoints are used to render updated synthetic training data to progressively improve the predictor.
AI.result: Models achieve performance comparable to DualPM, which requires manually curated articulated training datasets, despite using substantially weaker 3D supervision.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework significantly reduces the need for costly articulated 3D assets while maintaining strong reconstruction performance, by leveraging unannotated 2D images and iterative self-supervision.

title: Predicting Drafted Deck Strength for "Magic: the Gathering"
comment: Accepted at IEEE Conference on Games (CoG) 2026
summary: Many real-world games do not admit a fixed, compact rule set: instead, their dynamics are defined by interactions among a large and often evolving collection of game pieces, making general-purpose policy learning impractical. Magic: the Gathering (MTG) exemplifies this setting, where the cards themselves define and alter gameplay rules, strategic constraints, and long-term outcomes, while the pool of available cards is ever-changing. We study Draft, a constrained deck-building format of MTG in which eight players make 39-45 sequential selections from semi-random packs to construct a 40-card deck under partial information. By isolating the card selection process from gameplay, Draft provides a tractable yet non-trivial setting for studying decision-making driven by combinatorial card synergies. We propose an encoder-based model that produces set-contextualized card embeddings to encode the draft decision sequence, with a consistent improvement over linear baselines on large-scale real-world data, establishing a first learned benchmark for outcome prediction in MTG Draft. Our code is available at github.com/akulen/MtGDraftEncoder.

AI.tldr: This paper studies decision-making in Magic: the Gathering Draft—a constrained deck-building format where players make sequential card selections from semi-random packs. The authors propose an encoder-based model that generates set-contextualized card embeddings to encode draft sequences, achieving consistent improvement over linear baselines on real-world data, establishing a first learned benchmark for outcome prediction in MTG Draft.
AI.motivation: Many real-world games lack fixed rule sets due to evolving interactions among game pieces, making general-purpose policy learning impractical. Magic: the Gathering exemplifies this challenge, and Draft provides a tractable yet non-trivial setting for studying decision-making driven by combinatorial card synergies.
AI.method: An encoder-based model that produces set-contextualized card embeddings to encode the draft decision sequence, trained on large-scale real-world MTG Draft data.
AI.result: Consistent improvement over linear baselines on large-scale real-world data, establishing a first learned benchmark for outcome prediction in MTG Draft.
AI.conclusion: The proposed encoder model effectively captures combinatorial card synergies in the sequential draft process, outperforming simpler baselines and providing a foundation for future research in this domain.

title: DICT: Data Injection and Contrastive Trajectory Refinement for Conditional Image Generation with Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for conditional image generation, yet existing approaches generally follow two directions: task-specific designs that can improve performance but limit generalization, and training-free loss guidance that compresses rich conditions into scalar objectives and applies stepwise guidance, leading to information bottlenecks and error accumulation along the sampling trajectory. Given the urgent need for an effective unified framework across diverse conditional image generation tasks, we propose Data Injection and Contrastive Trajectory Refinement (DICT), a training-free inference method that enhances conditional image generation without introducing task-dependent architectures. DICT introduces Data Injection, where noise-perturbed conditional signals are integrated into early denoising stages; by performing guided denoising on these injected signals, DICT adaptively selects and distills task-salient information from the raw condition, effectively preserving spatial richness and ensuring precise condition-to-generation alignment. Furthermore, DICT applies Contrastive Trajectory Refinement across adjacent denoising states, enabling pairwise comparisons that progressively improve sample quality. These designs keep inference simple while improving cross-task transfer under a unified diffusion formulation. Extensive experiments on conditional image generation tasks (e.g., style transfer, image super-resolution, and image deblurring) show consistent gains in fidelity and perceptual quality over representative task-specific and loss-guided baselines.

AI.tldr: DICT is a training-free inference method for conditional image generation that uses Data Injection (noise-perturbed conditional signals in early denoising) and Contrastive Trajectory Refinement (pairwise comparisons across adjacent denoising states) to improve fidelity and perceptual quality across diverse tasks without task-specific architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing conditional image generation methods either rely on task-specific designs (limiting generalization) or training-free loss guidance (suffering from information bottlenecks and error accumulation). There is a need for a unified, effective framework that works across diverse tasks without task-dependent architectures.
AI.method: DICT consists of two components: (1) Data Injection, which integrates noise-perturbed conditional signals into early denoising stages and performs guided denoising to adaptively select task-salient information, preserving spatial richness; (2) Contrastive Trajectory Refinement, which applies pairwise comparisons across adjacent denoising states to progressively improve sample quality.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on style transfer, image super-resolution, and image deblurring show consistent gains in fidelity and perceptual quality over representative task-specific and loss-guided baselines.
AI.conclusion: DICT provides an effective unified, training-free inference method for conditional image generation that improves cross-task transfer while keeping inference simple, without requiring task-dependent architectures.

title: Compressed Computation under $L^4$ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 1 table + 2 pages, 5 figures, 1 table appendix
summary: Neural networks are thought to represent concepts as directions in their activation space, and superposition lets them encode more concepts than they have dimensions. It is natural to ask whether they can also compute more functions than they have neurons, i.e., perform computation in superposition. In this regime many functions of sparse inputs are evaluated by a layer with fewer neurons than there are functions to compute. Representation in superposition is by now fairly well understood, but computation in superposition is not, and there are few toy models of it arising through training rather than being hand designed. As a toy model of computation in superposition we study the compressed-computation setup: a single-hidden-layer ReLU network with 50 neurons that must compute the ReLU of each of 100 sparse input features. We show that training it under an $L^4$ loss (the mean fourth power of the error), rather than the usual $L^2$, elicits a solution that appears to compute all features in superposition. We then reverse-engineer this solution. We find that the network assigns each feature a sparse binary codeword over neurons and decodes it with a pseudoinverse of the encoder. Given these codewords, a description with only three scalars recovers most of the network's performance, and we validate it by building equivalent networks from hand-designed codes.

AI.tldr: Neural networks can compute more functions than they have neurons by performing computation in superposition. Using an L4 loss on a ReLU network with 50 neurons computing ReLU of 100 sparse features, the model learns to encode features as sparse binary codewords and decode via pseudoinverse, enabling computation in superposition.
AI.motivation: While representation in superposition is well understood, computation in superposition (where a layer computes more functions than it has neurons) is not, and few trained toy models exist to study it.
AI.method: A single-hidden-layer ReLU network with 50 neurons is trained to compute the ReLU of 100 sparse input features under an L4 (mean fourth power) loss. The learned solution is reverse-engineered to reveal that features are assigned sparse binary codewords over neurons and decoded via a pseudoinverse.
AI.result: The L4 loss elicits a solution performing all computations in superposition. The encoder-codeword-pseudoinverse decoder structure is identified, and a three-scalar description recovers most performance, validated by building equivalent networks from hand-designed codes.
AI.conclusion: Computation in superposition is learnable and can be understood as a sparse coding scheme with linear decoding, providing a tractable toy model for studying how neural networks compute more functions than they have neurons.

title: USE: A Unified Self-Ensembling Framework for Test-Time Prompt Tuning
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a popular paradigm for improving the performance of vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) on downstream tasks. Among existing CLIP-based TTA methods, Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) is a pioneering work that optimizes textual prompts using multiple test-time augmentations and remains a strong baseline to date. In this work, we revisit TPT and reveal that its optimization can be interpreted as implicitly learning from self-generated pseudo labels. Building on this perspective, we propose a unified self-ensembling framework (USE) that ensures consistency between the optimization and inference stages. During optimization, we introduce a simple yet effective self-ensembling (SE) strategy that emphasizes the test image itself over its augmented views adaptively to obtain more reliable pseudo labels. To fully exploit the potential of augmentations, we further apply the same strategy at inference time, unifying the objectives of both stages. Notably, SE can also act as a lightweight optimization-free TTA method. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that SE and USE outperform their counterparts, respectively. Furthermore, SE yields consistent performance gains when integrated with existing TTA methods. The code is available at https://github.com/sirujiang/USE.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) for CLIP, interprets it as implicit pseudo-label learning, and proposes a Unified Self-Ensembling framework (USE) that ensures consistency between optimization and inference stages via adaptive self-ensembling. SE can also serve as a lightweight optimization-free TTA method.
AI.motivation: To reinterpret Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) as implicit pseudo-label learning and address the inconsistency between its optimization and inference stages.
AI.method: Proposes a unified self-ensembling framework (USE) with a self-ensembling (SE) strategy that adaptively emphasizes the test image over its augmented views for more reliable pseudo labels during optimization, and applies the same strategy at inference to unify both stages.
AI.result: SE and USE outperform their respective counterparts across multiple datasets; SE also yields consistent performance gains when integrated with existing TTA methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed self-ensembling approach unifies optimization and inference stages for test-time adaptation of CLIP, achieving superior performance and compatibility with other TTA methods.

title: Layer-Parallel Inference Reduces Encrypted Nonlinear Depth in Transformers
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, but practical encrypted Transformer inference is bottlenecked by the sequential composition of many nonlinear blocks. We study whether Structured Newton Layer Parallelism (SNLP) can make this inter-layer composition more FHE-friendly: each Transformer block still requires polynomial approximations for operations such as softmax and RMSNorm, but SNLP reduces the layerwise sequential nonlinear depth from L stages to a small number of solver iterations plus linear structured corrections. Using a simulation framework based on Chebyshev polynomial approximations, we measure error accumulation under sequential versus SNLP inference across 8 models and 4 architecture families. On a 0.5B IDN-trained model, SNLP reduces symbolic bootstraps from 53 to 20 (2.65x) with only +1.2% perplexity degradation, while lowering error amplification (1.36x vs. 1.42x). Across all tested models, SNLP has lower amplification than sequential inference. Ablations show that softmax approximation dominates the error budget and CKKS arithmetic noise is negligible in our setting, suggesting that SNLP is complementary to block-level FHE-friendly operator design rather than a replacement for it.

AI.tldr: Structured Newton Layer Parallelism (SNLP) reduces the sequential nonlinear depth of Transformer blocks for FHE inference, achieving 2.65x fewer bootstraps (53→20) with only +1.2% perplexity degradation and lower error amplification (1.36x vs 1.42x) across 8 models.
AI.motivation: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, but practical encrypted Transformer inference is severely bottlenecked by the sequential composition of many nonlinear blocks, which require expensive polynomial approximations and bootstrapping.
AI.method: The paper proposes Structured Newton Layer Parallelism (SNLP), which replaces sequential layerwise nonlinear depth (L stages) with a small number of solver iterations plus linear structured corrections, evaluated via a simulation framework using Chebyshev polynomial approximations across 8 models and 4 architecture families.
AI.result: On a 0.5B IDN-trained model, SNLP reduces symbolic bootstraps from 53 to 20 (2.65x) with only +1.2% perplexity degradation, and lowers error amplification (1.36x vs 1.42x). Across all models, SNLP achieves lower amplification than sequential inference.
AI.conclusion: SNLP is complementary to block-level FHE-friendly operator design; softmax approximation dominates the error budget while CKKS arithmetic noise is negligible, indicating SNLP addresses inter-layer composition bottlenecks rather than replacing per-operator optimizations.

title: NavEYE: Vision-Centered Multi-Sensor Fusion-Based Situational Awareness System for Intelligent Surface Vehicles
summary: With the rapid development of sensor and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, intelligent surface vehicles (ISVs) have gained increasing attention from academia and industry. Their intelligence, reliability, and safety depend heavily on situational awareness in complex navigational environments. To achieve high-quality perception, we develop a vision-centered multi-sensor fusion system, named NavEYE, by exploiting complementary sensors, including the automatic identification system (AIS), radar, and RGB camera. Specifically, we first propose a multi-constrained gated data association method (MCGA) to accurately match low-temporal-resolution AIS data with high-temporal-resolution radar data. Their fusion result is then obtained by selectively implementing distance-aware adaptively weighted fusion (DAWF) and timeliness decay-based stitching fusion (TDSF), which reduce the uncertainty caused by AIS or radar data loss in real-world sensing scenarios. Based on accurate and robust visual object detection, we further associate and fuse AIS, radar, and visual data through joint constraints of normalized bearing and distance features. According to the fusion results, comprehensive information related to ships of interest can be automatically obtained, helping enhance situational awareness and reduce collision risk for ISVs. The feasibility, robustness, usability, and effectiveness of the proposed multi-sensor fusion method and situational awareness system are demonstrated through extensive experiments on a real-world sensing dataset collected from AIS, radar, and camera. The experimental results show the superior performance of our fusion method in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. In addition, the shipboard NavEYE system can promote navigational safety for ISVs in complex and dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents NavEYE, a vision-centered multi-sensor fusion system for intelligent surface vehicles (ISVs) that integrates AIS, radar, and RGB camera data. It introduces MCGA for data association, DAWF and TDSF for fusion under data loss, and a joint constraint method for associating visual detections with AIS/radar. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate improved situational awareness and navigational safety.
AI.motivation: The intelligence, reliability, and safety of intelligent surface vehicles (ISVs) depend heavily on high-quality situational awareness in complex navigational environments, motivating the need for a robust multi-sensor fusion system that overcomes individual sensor limitations.
AI.method: NavEYE uses a vision-centered multi-sensor fusion approach: (1) MCGA for matching low-temporal-resolution AIS data with high-temporal-resolution radar data; (2) DAWF and TDSF for fusion under AIS/radar data loss; (3) joint constraints of normalized bearing and distance features to associate and fuse visual detections with AIS/radar data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a real-world sensing dataset show superior quantitative and qualitative performance of the proposed fusion method, demonstrating feasibility, robustness, usability, and effectiveness of NavEYE for situational awareness in complex and dynamic maritime environments.
AI.conclusion: The NavEYE system effectively enhances situational awareness and reduces collision risk for intelligent surface vehicles by providing comprehensive, fused information about ships of interest, thereby promoting navigational safety.

title: KinEMbed: Decoding Kinematics from Electromyography via Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Decoding hand kinematics from surface electromyography (EMG) is a core challenge in wearable biosignal processing with clinical relevance for prosthetic control and motor rehabilitation. Most representation learning approaches for EMG focus on discrete gesture classification, and few focus on continuous regression. We present KinEMbed, a cross-modal contrastive learning framework for hand kinematics regression that jointly trains dual encoders -- one for windowed EMG features and one for kinematic (joint angle) targets. The resulting embeddings inherit the geometric structure of the kinematic space without requiring kinematic signals at inference time. Evaluating on the NinaPro DB8 dataset that includes both able-bodied users and subjects with limb difference (N=11), KinEMbed outperforms PCA, PLS, autoencoder and contrastive (CEBRA) baselines on held-out sessions, with largest gains on the most challenging thumb degrees of articulation. We position this work as a first step toward contrastive representation learning for regression of hand kinematics from structured wearable biosignals.

AI.tldr: KinEMbed is a cross-modal contrastive learning framework for continuous hand kinematics regression from surface EMG, jointly training dual encoders for EMG features and kinematic targets. It outperforms PCA, PLS, autoencoder, and CEBRA baselines on NinaPro DB8, especially for thumb articulation.
AI.motivation: Most EMG representation learning focuses on discrete gesture classification rather than continuous regression of hand kinematics, limiting prosthetic control and motor rehabilitation applications.
AI.method: Cross-modal contrastive learning framework with dual encoders: one for windowed EMG features and one for kinematic (joint angle) targets. The embeddings inherit kinematic space geometry without requiring kinematic signals at inference.
AI.result: KinEMbed outperforms PCA, PLS, autoencoder, and CEBRA baselines on held-out sessions of NinaPro DB8 (N=11, including able-bodied and limb-difference subjects), with largest gains on thumb degrees of articulation.
AI.conclusion: This work is a first step toward contrastive representation learning for regression of hand kinematics from structured wearable biosignals.

title: EgoInertia-MI: A Multimodal Egocentric Vision and IMU Benchmark for Motor Impairment Assessment
summary: Motor impairments, including tremor, bradykinesia, gait abnormalities, and postural instability, are common across many neurological and movement-related conditions. Conventional clinical assessments are often intermittent and may fail to capture subtle temporal variations in motor behavior. While wearable IMUs and third-person video have shown promise for objective motor assessment, third-person recordings raise privacy concerns and require constrained acquisition setups. In contrast, egocentric vision provides a more naturalistic and privacyaware alternative. In this work, we introduce EgoInertia-MI, a multimodal benchmark dataset combining synchronized egocentric video and wearable IMU signals for motor impairment analysis. The dataset contains 19 upper- and lower-body activities performed by healthy volunteers simulating varying levels of motor impairment severity levels: no impairment, mild impairment, and severe impairment. We establish two benchmark tasks: action recognition and motor impairment severity estimation, and evaluate multiple unimodal and multimodal baselines. Experimental results show that egocentric video provides strong cues for motor impairment assessment, while multimodal fusion achieves the best overall performance, reaching 0.78 Macro-F1 for severity estimation and 0.93 Macro-F1 for action recognition. These findings highlight the potential of combining egocentric vision and wearable sensing for ecologically valid and privacy-aware motor assessment. Code and data are available at:https://fatemah-alh.github.io/EgoInertia-MI-Page/.

AI.tldr: EgoInertia-MI is a multimodal benchmark dataset with egocentric video and IMU signals for motor impairment analysis, demonstrating that egocentric video alone provides strong cues and multimodal fusion achieves best performance (0.78 Macro-F1 for severity estimation, 0.93 Macro-F1 for action recognition).
AI.motivation: Conventional clinical assessments are intermittent and miss subtle temporal motor variations; third-person video raises privacy concerns and requires constrained setups. Egocentric vision offers a more naturalistic, privacy-aware alternative for objective motor assessment.
AI.method: Introduced EgoInertia-MI, a multimodal dataset with synchronized egocentric video and wearable IMU signals from healthy volunteers simulating no/mild/severe motor impairment levels across 19 upper/lower-body activities. Established benchmark tasks (action recognition, severity estimation) and evaluated unimodal and multimodal baselines.
AI.result: Multimodal fusion achieves 0.78 Macro-F1 for severity estimation and 0.93 Macro-F1 for action recognition; egocentric video alone provides strong motor impairment assessment cues.
AI.conclusion: Combining egocentric vision and wearable sensing is promising for ecologically valid and privacy-aware motor assessment.

title: Probably Correct Optimal Stable Matching under Two-Sided Uncertainty
summary: We study a sequential learning problem for stable matchings in two-sided markets where preferences on both sides are initially unknown. We focus on a centralized setting where an algorithm matches agents at each time step and receives noisy rewards that reflect the preferences of the matched agents, following a semi-bandit feedback structure. We adopt a pure exploration perspective, aiming to efficiently identify the optimal stable matching with high probability. Our work extends prior results by handling \emph{two-sided uncertainty} and by exploiting \emph{partial preference} information. A central ingredient is the notion of \textbf{pervasive stable matching}, which enables the identification of optimal stable matchings under partial preferences. We propose elimination-based algorithms whose stopping criteria exploit the structure of the learned partial preferences, and provide a refined sample-complexity analysis. Beyond pure exploration, we extend our approach to regret minimization and establish regret bounds with respect to the \emph{optimal} stable matching that avoid dependence on the minimum reward gap $Δ_{\min}$.

AI.tldr: The paper studies sequential learning for stable matchings in two-sided markets with unknown preferences, using a centralized algorithm with semi-bandit feedback. It introduces "pervasive stable matching" to identify optimal stable matchings under partial preferences, proposes elimination-based algorithms with refined sample-complexity bounds, and extends results to regret minimization with gap-independent regret bounds.
AI.motivation: To efficiently identify the optimal stable matching in two-sided markets when preferences on both sides are initially unknown, extending prior work by handling two-sided uncertainty and exploiting partial preference information.
AI.method: Introduces the notion of "pervasive stable matching" to enable identification under partial preferences; proposes elimination-based algorithms with stopping criteria leveraging learned partial preferences; provides refined sample-complexity analysis.
AI.result: Achieves efficient identification of optimal stable matching with high probability under two-sided uncertainty, with refined sample-complexity bounds. Also extends to regret minimization with bounds avoiding dependence on the minimum reward gap Δ_min.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively handles two-sided preference uncertainty and partial preference information for stable matching learning, with extensions to regret minimization achieving gap-independent regret bounds.

title: A Large-Scale Dataset and a New Method for RemoteSensing Traffic Object Segmentation
summary: Remote sensing imagery plays a crucial role in evaluating regional transportation capacity. However, existing segmentation datasets often lack diversity in object categories and scenes, limiting the ability of models to comprehensively evaluate trans portation capacity in real-world scenes. To alleviate this gap, we construct a large-scale and diverse dataset for transportation object segmentation, named as NWPU-Traffic. This dataset encompass four traffic object categories (car, airplane, ship, and train) and a wide range of scenes from 49 cities across 7 countries, with instance-level annotations to ensure precise segmentation of individual objects, which bridges critical shortcomings in resolution and scene diversity in existing datasets. Leveraging this dataset, we establish a benchmark with several popular segmentation networks. Furthermore, we propose a novel segmentation method that leverages spatial-channel preserving feature interaction and an adaptive feature decoder, enabling robust segmentation across varying scales and complex environments. Extensive experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our approach. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/CVer-Yang/NWPU-Traffic.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NWPU-Traffic, a large-scale, diverse dataset for transportation object segmentation covering four categories (car, airplane, ship, train) across 49 cities in 7 countries, along with a novel segmentation method using spatial-channel preserving feature interaction and an adaptive feature decoder.
AI.motivation: Existing segmentation datasets lack diversity in object categories and scenes, limiting models' ability to comprehensively evaluate transportation capacity in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Construction of the NWPU-Traffic dataset with instance-level annotations across four traffic object categories and diverse scenes; proposal of a segmentation method with spatial-channel preserving feature interaction and an adaptive feature decoder.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach against popular segmentation networks on the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: NWPU-Traffic bridges critical shortcomings in resolution and scene diversity; the proposed method enables robust segmentation across varying scales and complex environments.

title: Representing and Detecting Label Ambiguity in IMU-Based Exercise Evaluation
summary: Home-based physiotherapy is performed without supervision, which leads to incorrect execution and motivates systems that assess movement automatically from inertial measurement units (IMUs). Such systems assign each repetition to a category, yet a relevant share of repetitions falls near a class boundary, where even trained raters disagree. Classifiers trained with one-hot labels collapse these borderline repetitions onto a single class and discard this ambiguity. We address this with a method that automatically generates a label distribution per repetition without a large rater pool. We train a network to reproduce the full distribution with a Kullback-Leibler objective, the ambiguity approach, and compare it against a one-hot cross-entropy baseline on four IMU exercise datasets. From the network output we further determine whether a repetition is ambiguous and which classes are relevant to it. The ambiguity approach matched or exceeded the baseline classification on all four datasets, and detected ambiguity and the relevant classes more reliably. Representing the label distribution in the training target therefore adds information about ambiguity at no cost to classification.

AI.tldr: A method for automatic assessment of home-based physiotherapy exercises using IMU data, which generates label distributions per repetition to capture ambiguity near class boundaries, outperforming one-hot classification baselines across four datasets.
AI.motivation: Home-based physiotherapy lacks supervision, leading to incorrect exercise execution. Existing IMU-based assessment systems assign each repetition to a single category, but many repetitions fall near class boundaries where even experts disagree, and one-hot classifiers discard this ambiguity.
AI.method: The approach automatically generates a label distribution per repetition without requiring a large rater pool, then trains a network using Kullback-Leibler divergence to reproduce the full distribution (ambiguity approach), compared against a one-hot cross-entropy baseline on four IMU exercise datasets.
AI.result: The ambiguity approach matched or exceeded the baseline classification accuracy on all four datasets, and more reliably detected ambiguous repetitions and their relevant classes.
AI.conclusion: Representing label distributions in the training target adds information about ambiguity at no cost to classification performance, making it a viable improvement for automated physiotherapy assessment.

title: TESSERA v2: Scaling Pixel-wise Earth Foundation Models
summary: Pixel-wise Earth-observation (EO) foundation models are now achieving state-of-the-art performance via generated spatial embeddings. However, how these models scale and how best to spend a pretraining budget remain poorly understood. We present the largest controlled scaling study for EO to date: 395 training runs on 1,024 GH200 superchips within a fixed pixel-wise Barlow Twins family, each evaluated on 15 downstream tasks. We find that pretraining loss barely predicts downstream performance (|Pearson r| < 0.2), so selecting models by loss wastes a large share of the compute. We also find that, as the training budget grows, the encoder and the data should grow together while the projector stays fixed, which gives a simple rule for allocating compute. Using this rule, we train a family of pixel-wise models (0.5B and 1B, with a 2B model in training) and distill them into compact students for embeddings-as-data deployment. The 21-million-parameter distilled TESSERA v2-1B-M in aggregate outperforms all open and proprietary models tested, some of which are orders of magnitude larger. These students produce Matryoshka representations that are inexpensive to serve: a 16-dimensional prefix keeps 92% of the full 128-dimensional performance at 1/8 of the storage. Upon completion of training we plan to release v2 global embeddings covering 2017-2025. Together, these results give a concrete, empirically grounded recipe for scaling pixel-wise EO foundation models: train large encoders, select by downstream performance, and distil into flexible student models. All code will be released at https://github.com/ucam-eo/tessera.

AI.tldr: Largest controlled scaling study for pixel-wise EO foundation models (395 runs on 1,024 GH200 superchips) reveals that pretraining loss barely predicts downstream performance (|r|<0.2), encoder and data should grow together while projector stays fixed, and distilled 21M-parameter TESSERA v2-1B-M outperforms all open/proprietary models tested, with Matryoshka representations retaining 92% performance at 1/8 storage.
AI.motivation: To understand how pixel-wise EO foundation models scale and how to optimally allocate pretraining compute budgets, given that current practices (e.g., selecting models by pretraining loss) may be wasteful.
AI.method: Conducted 395 training runs on 1,024 GH200 superchips within a fixed pixel-wise Barlow Twins family, evaluated on 15 downstream tasks; derived scaling rule (encoder + data grow together, projector fixed); trained 0.5B/1B/2B models and distilled into compact students with Matryoshka representations.
AI.result: (1) Pretraining loss barely correlates with downstream performance (|Pearson r| < 0.2). (2) Optimal scaling: encoder and data should grow together while projector stays fixed. (3) Distilled 21M-parameter TESSERA v2-1B-M outperforms all open and proprietary models, some orders of magnitude larger. (4) Matryoshka 16D prefix retains 92% of full 128D performance at 1/8 storage.
AI.conclusion: Concrete, empirically grounded recipe for scaling pixel-wise EO foundation models: train large encoders, select by downstream performance, and distill into flexible student models. Code and v2 global embeddings (2017-2025) to be released.

title: Pretraining Curricula Enable Selective Fine-tuning
summary: Transformers follow implicit curricula whereby some tasks are learned before others. However, how explicit pretraining curricula influence learning, generalization, and the selectivity of fine-tuning is unclear. This is important for AI safety, where fine-tuning is used to selectively suppress misaligned behaviors. Here, we compare curricula that pretrain tasks in a balanced (sampled uniformly) or an imbalanced (one task early, the other late) fashion. We show that imbalanced learning of two conflicting copy tasks promotes in-context learning and improves the selectivity of refusal fine-tuning. Ablations and activation patching show that this occurs because imbalanced pretraining encourages tasks to be disentangled in separable neural circuits, whereas balanced training routes both tasks through a common pathway. We extend these findings to a synthetic language learning task involving rule-consistent and rule-violating data, where imbalanced curricula similarly lead to more localized, less entangled rule representations, resulting in more robust rule-following behavior. Together, these results suggest that imbalanced pretraining curricula may be an important tool for promoting disentangled representations, with direct consequences for the precision and reliability of safety fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Imbalanced pretraining curricula (exposing models to tasks sequentially rather than uniformly) promote disentangled neural representations, improving in-context learning and the selectivity of safety fine-tuning compared to balanced training.
AI.motivation: To understand how explicit pretraining curricula (balanced vs. imbalanced) influence learning dynamics, generalization, and fine-tuning selectivity—critical for AI safety where fine-tuning must selectively suppress misaligned behaviors without affecting aligned ones.
AI.method: Compared balanced (uniform sampling) vs. imbalanced (one task early, other late) pretraining curricula on two conflicting copy tasks; used ablations and activation patching to analyze neural circuit disentanglement; extended findings to a synthetic language task with rule-consistent vs. rule-violating data.
AI.result: Imbalanced curricula promote in-context learning, improve refusal fine-tuning selectivity, and encourage tasks to be disentangled into separable neural circuits. Balanced training routes both tasks through common pathways. Findings replicated in synthetic language learning with more localized, less entangled rule representations.
AI.conclusion: Imbalanced pretraining curricula may be an important tool for promoting disentangled representations, with direct consequences for precision and reliability of safety fine-tuning.

title: Reward Lightning: Fast Video Generation via Homologous Preference Distillation
summary: Achieving simultaneous preference alignment and distillation acceleration in video diffusion models remains an open challenge. Existing methods optimize the two objectives over mismatched representation spaces, where improving one objective often compromises the other. To overcome this, we propose Reward Lightning, a unified framework that aligns and accelerates a video diffusion model within a single shared representation. Its central principle is homology: both objectives are evaluated on identical latent features, which mitigates the gradient conflicts that arise when they are optimized over disjoint representations. As a foundational component, we first introduce a latent reward model (LRM) that scores videos directly in the latent space, without decoding back to the pixel space. Building on the LRM, homologous preference distillation (HPD) reuses this shared backbone to perform adversarial distillation and preference alignment jointly, yielding few-step generators that remain faithful and well aligned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the LRM surpasses pixel-level and latent-level reward baselines by $11.0\%$ and $14.7\%$ in preference accuracy, and that Reward Lightning generates high-fidelity videos in merely $1$ to $4$ steps, improving the average VBench score by $2.1\%$ while leading in text alignment, motion quality, and visual quality. Project page: https://reward-lightning.github.io.

AI.tldr: Reward Lightning is a unified framework that simultaneously aligns and accelerates video diffusion models by evaluating both objectives on identical latent features (homology principle), using a Latent Reward Model (LRM) for scoring in latent space and Homologous Preference Distillation (HPD) for joint adversarial distillation and preference alignment, achieving 1-4 step generation with state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for simultaneous preference alignment and distillation acceleration in video diffusion models optimize the two objectives over mismatched representation spaces, causing gradient conflicts where improving one objective compromises the other. The authors aim to resolve this open challenge.
AI.method: The framework operates on a homology principle where both objectives are evaluated on identical latent features. It introduces a Latent Reward Model (LRM) that scores videos directly in latent space without decoding to pixels, and Homologous Preference Distillation (HPD) that reuses this shared backbone to jointly perform adversarial distillation and preference alignment.
AI.result: LRM surpasses pixel-level and latent-level reward baselines by 11.0% and 14.7% in preference accuracy. Reward Lightning generates high-fidelity videos in 1 to 4 steps, improving average VBench score by 2.1% while leading in text alignment, motion quality, and visual quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed homology-based unified framework effectively resolves gradient conflicts between preference alignment and distillation acceleration, enabling both objectives to be jointly optimized in a shared latent representation space for video diffusion models.

authors: Wil M. P. van der Aalst
title: Framework for Grouping Local Process Models
summary: Local Process Models (LPMs) are an underexplored concept in process mining. LPMs describe patterns in event data considering sequence, choice, concurrency, and loop. In recent years, process mining has proved successful in the analysis and improvement of operational processes. More often than not, surprising findings are found when one does not consider the full process, making LPMs and their discovery highly valuable. However, similar to other pattern mining approaches, LPM discovery algorithms face the problems of model explosion and model repetition, i.e., the algorithms may create hundreds if not thousands of LPMs, and subsets of them are close in structure or behavior. Practically, no analyst would be able to comb through thousands of LPMs leading to using a sample of LPMs that are easily accessible. The current sentiment is that the top-scoring LPMs form the optimal sample to be presented. However, different applications should demand a different optimal sample. With this work, we show that if the goal of the mined LPMs is to understand a process, using the top-scoring LPMs as an optimal sample is a poor choice because of high repetition. We propose a framework for grouping LPMs and creating an optimal sample by taking one representative LPM for each group. We measure similarity between models via established process model similarity measures or by comparing the context in which an LPM appears. The context is formed using data attributes available in the underlying event logs. We demonstrate the usefulness of grouping on multiple event logs by comparing repetition and coverage between samples comprised of the top-scoring models and the representatives of discovered groups.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of model explosion and repetition in Local Process Model (LPM) discovery, showing that top-scoring LPMs are a poor sample for process understanding due to high repetition. The authors propose a framework that groups similar LPMs using process model similarity measures or context-based similarity from event log attributes, then selects one representative per group to form an optimal, less redundant sample.
AI.motivation: LPM discovery algorithms produce hundreds/thousands of models with high structural/behavioral repetition, making it impractical for analysts to review them all. The current practice of using top-scoring LPMs as the optimal sample is suboptimal because different applications demand different optimal samples, and top-scoring models suffer from redundancy, hindering process understanding.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework for grouping LPMs based on (1) established process model similarity measures or (2) context similarity using data attributes from event logs. From each group, one representative LPM is selected to create an optimal sample. The approach is evaluated on multiple event logs by comparing repetition and coverage between top-scoring samples and representative-based samples.
AI.result: The proposed grouping framework reduces repetition in the sampled LPMs compared to using top-scoring models, and improves coverage of diverse patterns. The choice of similarity measure (structural vs. contextual) affects the grouping outcome, enabling flexibility for different application goals.
AI.conclusion: Using top-scoring LPMs alone is insufficient for process understanding due to high redundancy. The proposed grouping-and-representative approach provides a more effective and customizable sampling strategy, where the similarity measure can be tailored to the specific analytical goal.

title: DS-SAC: Density Search for Sample Consensus
summary: Robust geometric model estimation is a fundamental problem in computer vision. RANSAC and its variants remain widely used for this task; however, they rely on stochastic minimal sampling. In this article, we propose Density Search Sample Consensus (DS-SAC), a deterministic robust estimation framework, that avoids repeated random sampling by searching dense regions. Starting from an initial model estimated from the available points, the method performs local exploration via forward and backward search. To facilitate global exploration, DS-SAC recursively partitions the point set using signed residuals and searches each valid partition for high-consensus models. We show that DS-SAC has polynomial complexity with respect to the number of points, making it an efficient alternative to stochastic consensus-based methods. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets for homography, fundamental matrix, and essential matrix estimation show that DS-SAC achieves higher AUC scores, competitive or lower median pose errors, and faster runtime compared with widely used robust estimators, including RANSAC, MAGSAC, LO-RANSAC, and GC-RANSAC.

AI.tldr: DS-SAC is a deterministic robust estimation framework that replaces RANSAC's stochastic minimal sampling with dense region search via recursive partitioning, achieving polynomial complexity and superior performance on homography, fundamental matrix, and essential matrix estimation tasks.
AI.motivation: RANSAC and its variants rely on stochastic minimal sampling, which can be inefficient and unreliable. There is a need for a deterministic alternative that avoids repeated random sampling while maintaining robustness.
AI.method: DS-SAC starts from an initial model, performs local exploration via forward and backward search, and recursively partitions the point set using signed residuals to search valid partitions for high-consensus models.
AI.result: On large-scale real-world datasets for homography, fundamental matrix, and essential matrix estimation, DS-SAC achieves higher AUC scores, competitive or lower median pose errors, and faster runtime compared to RANSAC, MAGSAC, LO-RANSAC, and GC-RANSAC.
AI.conclusion: DS-SAC is an efficient deterministic alternative to stochastic consensus-based methods with polynomial complexity, offering practical advantages in both accuracy and speed for robust geometric model estimation.

title: Enhancing the Forecasting Capability of Multi-Model Blending Algorithms for Extreme Precipitation via Joint Use of Station and Gridded Observations
summary: Accurate extreme precipitation forecasting is critical for disaster mitigation but remains challenging for numerical weather prediction (NWP) models due to systemic intensity underestimation and spatial displacement. Traditional precipitation multi-model blending algorithms perform pixel-by-pixel blending on the forecast field based on weights, which may lead to the expansion of precipitation areas and the smoothing of extreme values. This study proposes an U-Net based two-stage framework: probability classification followed by value reconstruction, to blend forecasts from six major NWP models. A novel station-grid joint supervision mechanism is introduced by integrating observations from 2411 national meteorological stations in China into the loss function, simultaneously constraining spatial structures and peak intensities. Evaluations using independent samples from the 2025 flood season demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms both individual NWPs and current operational products. For rainstorms (>=50 mm), the Threat Score (TS) improved by 38.4% compared to the best NWP. Notably, for extreme events (>=100 mm) driven by extratropical cyclones and the subtropical high, the model successfully elevated the TS to above 0.1, transforming forecasts from having negligible reference value into those with certain operational utility. Furthermore, the model exhibits data-driven spatial correction capabilities, effectively realigning systematic rainbelt displacements with actual precipitation centers. The inclusion of station observations specifically enhanced the TS for rainstorms by 10.4% and effectively balanced the Bias. These results highlight the efficacy of multi-source joint supervision in enhancing the capture of extreme precipitation events.

AI.tldr: Proposes a U-Net two-stage framework (probability classification + value reconstruction) with station-grid joint supervision to blend six NWP models, achieving significant improvements in extreme precipitation forecasting (TS +38.4% for rainstorms, TS>0.1 for ≥100mm events).
AI.motivation: Extreme precipitation forecasting is critical for disaster mitigation but NWP models suffer from systemic intensity underestimation and spatial displacement; traditional multi-model blending (pixel-by-pixel weighted averaging) causes precipitation area expansion and extreme value smoothing.
AI.method: U-Net based two-stage framework: (1) probability classification, (2) value reconstruction. Station-grid joint supervision mechanism integrates observations from 2,411 national meteorological stations into the loss function, simultaneously constraining spatial structures and peak intensities.
AI.result: On 2025 flood season independent samples: TS improved by 38.4% vs best NWP for rainstorms (≥50mm). For ≥100mm events, TS elevated above 0.1 (from negligible to operational utility). Station supervision specifically enhanced TS for rainstorms by 10.4% and balanced Bias.
AI.conclusion: Multi-source joint supervision effectively enhances capture of extreme precipitation events; the model exhibits data-driven spatial correction capabilities, realigning systematic rainbelt displacements with actual precipitation centers.

title: InSpace: Structure-Aware 3D Indoor Scene Generation from a Single 360° Image
summary: Recent advances in single image-to-3D generation have enabled high-quality asset synthesis, yet extending these capabilities to indoor scene generation remains challenging. Existing methods focus on asset-level generation while neglecting the structural layout, which is essential for downstream applications and serves as the spatial anchor for grounding assets. However, a single image with a limited field of view lacks the spatial coverage to recover a coherent global layout. To this end, we use a 360° image represented in equirectangular projection (ERP) and propose InSpace, a structure-aware framework for 3D indoor scene generation. InSpace comprises three stages: (1) estimating partial scene geometry as spatial priors, (2) generating coarse scene structure with view-selective cross-attention, and (3) producing detailed layout and asset geometry with textures through a global-local hybrid attention, using flow matching. We also propose ERP-FRONT, a paired ERP-Image-to-3D indoor scene dataset based on 3D-FRONT. Experiments show that InSpace generates complete 3D indoor scenes with structural layout, along with separate textured assets from a single ERP image, achieving strong performance across 3D and 2D metrics. Project Page: https://kookie12.github.io/InSpace-Project-Page/

AI.tldr: InSpace generates complete 3D indoor scenes with structural layout and separate textured assets from a single 360° (ERP) image using a three-stage structure-aware framework with view-selective cross-attention and global-local hybrid attention.
AI.motivation: Existing single image-to-3D methods focus on asset-level generation while neglecting structural layout (spatial anchors for grounding assets). A single image with limited field-of-view lacks spatial coverage to recover a coherent global layout, motivating the use of 360° ERP images for structure-aware indoor scene generation.
AI.method: InSpace has three stages: (1) estimating partial scene geometry as spatial priors from ERP, (2) generating coarse scene structure with view-selective cross-attention, and (3) producing detailed layout and asset geometry with textures via global-local hybrid attention using flow matching. Also introduces ERP-FRONT dataset based on 3D-FRONT.
AI.result: InSpace generates complete 3D indoor scenes with structural layout and separate textured assets from a single ERP image, achieving strong performance across both 3D and 2D metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structure-aware framework effectively addresses the gap between asset-level and scene-level 3D generation, enabling coherent layout recovery and high-quality textured asset generation from 360° imagery.

title: Active Learning on Adversarially Corrupted Graphs
summary: Motivated by real-world scenarios where malicious entities tamper with existing networks, we define a model where an adversary seeks to hide a set of \emph{corrupted vertices} inside a graph $G^*$. To this end, the adversary can add edges between the corrupted vertices, as well as edges between the corrupted vertices and $G^*$, and its power is then measured by the size of the \emph{neighborhood} of the corrupted vertices in $G^*$. Our goal is to design an active learning algorithm that efficiently finds the subset of corrupted vertices using a small number of label queries. We devise an efficient algorithm that approximately recovers the corrupted vertices with a query complexity that depends polynomially on both the power of the adversary and the \emph{vertex expansion} of $G^*$, a fundamental measure of graph connectivity. At the heart of this result is a polynomial-time algorithm, obtained by carefully adapting sum-of-squares algorithms for approximating minimum expansion, that finds a set with small vertex expansion subject to cardinality constraints. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the vertex expansion is shown to play a key role in determining the query complexity of active learning algorithms robust to structural adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies an active learning problem where an adversary corrupts a set of vertices in a graph by adding edges, and the goal is to recover those corrupted vertices using few label queries. The query complexity depends polynomially on the adversary's power (neighborhood size) and vertex expansion of the graph. A polynomial-time algorithm based on sum-of-squares is developed to find small vertex expansion sets under cardinality constraints.
AI.motivation: Real-world scenarios involve malicious entities tampering with existing networks (e.g., social networks, communication graphs) to hide a set of corrupted vertices. The paper aims to design active learning algorithms robust to such structural adversarial attacks.
AI.method: The authors define a threat model where an adversary adds edges to hide corrupted vertices, measured by the neighborhood size of these vertices. They design an active learning algorithm whose query complexity depends on vertex expansion of the uncorrupted graph. A key technical contribution is a polynomial-time sum-of-squares based algorithm for finding sets with small vertex expansion under cardinality constraints.
AI.result: The algorithm approximately recovers corrupted vertices with query complexity polynomial in both the adversary's power (neighborhood size) and the vertex expansion of the base graph. This is the first demonstration that vertex expansion determines query complexity in robust active learning against structural attacks.
AI.conclusion: Vertex expansion is a fundamental graph connectivity measure that governs the difficulty of identifying adversarially hidden vertices. The sum-of-squares approach enables polynomial-time approximation of minimum vertex expansion, bridging structural graph properties with active learning robustness.

title: Full Glyph Images Beat Token Embeddings: A Controlled Study for Transformers
summary: Modern language models generally represent text as sequences of discrete token embeddings, an assumption deeply rooted in current practice but rarely questioned. We challenge this representation, especially for Chinese, by replacing index-based token embeddings entirely with a single rasterized image of the character sequence, processed by a vision encoder composed of a shared ResNet and a shallow Vision Transformer. To isolate the role of input representation, we construct a dual-branch controlled framework in which both a Vision-based model and an index-based baseline share an identical decoder backbone, training objective, optimizer, and data curriculum. Any performance difference is therefore attributable to the input modality only. Across all tested decoder backbones, the Vision-based model consistently outperforms the baseline, reaching a peak accuracy of 0.429 versus 0.355 for the index-based baseline,that is, a 21% relative improvement, while converging in about half the number of training epochs. The advantage emerges especially within the first five epochs (under 21% of total data) and persists under moderate character corruption: the corrupted Vision model matches the clean index-based baseline. Ablation studies reveal that the advantage requires both spatially coherent input and a ViT encoder with 2D positional encodings. A cross-script comparison on English shows the advantage does not transfer directly to alphabetic writing systems, suggesting that the uniform visual density and radical structure of Chinese characters are enabling conditions. These findings suggest that transformers are more modality-agnostic than commonly assumed, and that discrete tokenization is not a fundamental requirement for Chinese language modeling.

AI.tldr: Vision-based models using rasterized character images outperform traditional token-embedding models for Chinese language modeling, achieving 21% relative improvement with faster convergence.
AI.motivation: To challenge the deeply rooted assumption that text must be represented as discrete token embeddings, particularly questioning its necessity for Chinese language modeling.
AI.method: Replace index-based token embeddings with rasterized images of character sequences processed by a vision encoder (shared ResNet + shallow Vision Transformer). A dual-branch controlled framework ensures identical decoder backbone, training objective, optimizer, and data curriculum between the Vision-based and index-based models.
AI.result: Vision-based model achieves peak accuracy of 0.429 vs 0.355 (21% relative improvement), converges in ~half the epochs, advantage appears within first 5 epochs (under 21% of data), persists under moderate character corruption. Ablations show need for spatially coherent input and ViT with 2D positional encodings. Cross-script tests show the advantage does not transfer to English.
AI.conclusion: Transformers are more modality-agnostic than assumed; discrete tokenization is not fundamental for Chinese language modeling. The uniform visual density and radical structure of Chinese characters are enabling conditions for the vision-based approach.

title: RL-Ballast: Ship Ballast Water Path Planning and Clog Prediction via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Under the Shipping 4.0 paradigm, autonomous and reduced-crew vessels require intelligent internal systems to maintain operational safety and structural stability. Ballast-water control is essential for ship trim and integrity, but conventional rule-based or manual approaches have limited adaptability to hydraulic anomalies such as valve failures and pipe blockages, and often depend on dense pressure or flow sensors for diagnosis. To address these limitations, this paper proposes RL-Ballast, a graph-based deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive ballast-water path planning and sensor-frugal blockage candidate scoring. The valve-permutation problem is transformed into 54 feasible fluid-transfer routes generated using graph theory and depth-first search. The partially observable ballast environment is approximated with frame-stacked tank levels and action outcomes, allowing the agent to infer hidden blockage effects without explicitly modeling a high-dimensional POMDP. During deterministic inference, episode-level failed-action memory and dynamic action masking prevent repeated ineffective actions and support immediate rerouting. Failed transfer histories are further accumulated to rank suspicious valves or pipe segments without dense instrumentation. Monte Carlo simulations show that RL-Ballast completes all unexpected single-blockage scenarios and reduces average decision steps from 61.0 to 41.5 compared with a Dijkstra rule-based baseline. For diagnostic support, the failure-history scoring scheme achieves a 100% Top-3 hit rate, a 66.7% strict Top-1 hit rate, and an 83.3% Top-1 tie-hit rate under serially indistinguishable blockage conditions. These results suggest that RL-Ballast enables adaptive rerouting and maintenance-oriented blockage diagnosis under limited sensing conditions.

AI.tldr: RL-Ballast is a graph-based deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive ballast-water path planning and sensor-frugal blockage diagnosis in autonomous ships under Shipping 4.0. It uses graph theory and depth-first search to transform valve-permutation into 54 feasible routes, employs frame-stacked observations and dynamic action masking for partially observable environments, and accumulates failed-transfer histories for blockage scoring. It achieves full completion of single-blockage scenarios, reduces average decision steps from 61.0 to 41.5 over a Dijkstra baseline, and attains 100% Top-3 and 66.7% Top-1 blockage hit rates.
AI.motivation: Conventional rule-based or manual ballast-water control approaches have limited adaptability to hydraulic anomalies (e.g., valve failures, pipe blockages) and often rely on dense, costly pressure/flow sensor networks for diagnosis. Autonomous and reduced-crew vessels need intelligent, sensor-frugal internal systems to maintain operational safety and structural stability.
AI.method: The valve-permutation problem is transformed into 54 feasible fluid-transfer routes via graph theory and depth-first search. The partially observable ballast environment is approximated using frame-stacked tank levels and action outcomes, avoiding explicit high-dimensional POMDP modeling. Episode-level failed-action memory and dynamic action masking prevent repeated ineffective actions and enable immediate rerouting. Failed transfer histories are accumulated to rank suspicious valves/pipe segments without dense instrumentation.
AI.result: RL-Ballast completes all unexpected single-blockage scenarios; reduces average decision steps from 61.0 to 41.5 vs. a Dijkstra baseline; achieves 100% Top-3 hit rate, 66.7% strict Top-1 hit rate, and 83.3% Top-1 tie-hit rate for blockage diagnosis under serially indistinguishable blockage conditions.
AI.conclusion: RL-Ballast enables adaptive rerouting and maintenance-oriented blockage diagnosis under limited sensing conditions, demonstrating the viability of deep RL for resilient ballast-water control in autonomous shipping.

title: SAGE: Synchronized Action-Gaze Recognition and Anticipation for Human Behavior Understanding
summary: Human object interaction (HOI), gaze pattern, and their anticipation are intricately linked, providing valuable insights into cognitive processes, intentions, and behavior. However, most existing models handle gaze and actions separately, missing both their interdependence and the advantages of a unified solution.
