This paper presents a novel unified framework, SAGE (Synchronized Action-GazE), which integrates simultaneous recognition and anticipation of both HOI and human gaze into a single unified end-to-end trainable model. Our approach leverages a transformer-based architecture and incorporates gaze data into spatiotemporal attention mechanisms to simultaneously predict current and future human actions and gaze behavior. We explore this bidirectional relationship between gaze and actions under different scenarios, whether requiring a close-up, detailed view (egocentric) or a wider, more contextual view (exocentric), making our framework versatile for various applications. Additionally, due to lack of datasets for comprehensive analysis of both HOI and gaze in exocentric videos, we establish a new benchmark Exo-Cook to facilitate further research in this domain. Experiments on three benchmark datasets: VidHOI, EGTEA Gaze+, and Exo-Cook show that jointly modeling gaze and actions across current and future frames achieves consistently strong results, often surpassing specialized state-of-the-art models tailored to individual tasks. By unifying actions and attention in a comprehensive way, our work lays the groundwork for more intuitive human-machine interaction.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a unified transformer-based framework that simultaneously recognizes and anticipates human-object interactions (HOI) and human gaze in both egocentric and exocentric videos, achieving strong results across three benchmarks and introducing a new exocentric dataset, Exo-Cook.
AI.motivation: Existing models treat gaze and actions separately, ignoring their interdependence and the benefits of a unified solution for understanding cognitive processes, intentions, and behavior.
AI.method: A transformer-based architecture that incorporates gaze data into spatiotemporal attention mechanisms to simultaneously predict current and future human actions and gaze behavior in a single end-to-end trainable model. The framework handles both egocentric (close-up) and exocentric (wide contextual view) scenarios.
AI.result: On VidHOI, EGTEA Gaze+, and Exo-Cook benchmarks, joint modeling of gaze and actions across current and future frames consistently achieves strong results, often surpassing specialized state-of-the-art models tailored to individual tasks.
AI.conclusion: Unifying actions and attention in a comprehensive manner lays the groundwork for more intuitive human-machine interaction, demonstrating that bidirectional gaze-action modeling is broadly effective across different viewing perspectives.

title: When Do Foundation Models Pay Off? A Break-Even Analysis of Pretrained Time Series Forecasters
summary: Deploying a time series foundation model requires GPU infrastructure, engineering overhead, and carries no guarantee of improvement over XGBoost. We provide the first systematic break-even analysis answering when this investment pays off. Across 30 benchmark datasets, we compare zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned foundation models (Chronos, Moirai, Lag-Llama) against classical baselines (Naive, ETS, ARIMA, XGBoost) at six training set sizes from 2% to 100% of available data. Foundation models outperform classical methods at every evaluated training fraction on 15 of 30 datasets -- GPU deployment is unconditionally justified on these regardless of data volume. On 6 datasets, classical methods surpass zero-shot foundation models with as little as 2% of training data (21-2,768 samples); on the remaining 9, break-even ranges from 24 to 8,361 samples. One robust deployment rule requires no model training: if n_train < 700 and seasonality is non-negligible, use FM zero-shot and skip fine-tuning -- this resolves 10 of 30 deployment decisions immediately. Contrary to common practice, LoRA fine-tuning can actively degrade performance on short series. We operationalise these findings as a two-step decision framework -- compute dataset length and seasonality strength, run a brief 5-10% pilot only if needed -- enabling practitioners to make the FM-versus-classical decision before committing to full infrastructure. Four dataset features motivate mechanistic hypotheses for the remaining cases, though reliable automated prediction at this benchmark scale remains an open problem. Code, benchmark, and decision tools are available at https://github.com/nicolaisi/fm-breakeven.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first systematic break-even analysis comparing time series foundation models (Chronos, Moirai, Lag-Llama) against classical baselines (Naive, ETS, ARIMA, XGBoost) across 30 datasets, showing that GPU deployment is unconditionally justified on 15 of 30 datasets, while break-even points vary widely; the authors propose a two-step decision framework based on dataset length and seasonality strength to help practitioners decide when to invest in foundation models.
AI.motivation: Deploying time series foundation models requires significant GPU infrastructure and engineering costs with no guaranteed improvement over simpler classical methods like XGBoost. Practitioners lack systematic guidance on when the investment in foundation models actually pays off, motivating the need for a rigorous break-even analysis.
AI.method: The authors benchmark zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned foundation models (Chronos, Moirai, Lag-Llama) against classical baselines (Naive, ETS, ARIMA, XGBoost) across 30 datasets at six training set fractions (2%-100%). They analyze break-even points where FMs surpass classical methods and derive a two-step decision framework based on dataset length and seasonality strength.
AI.result: Foundation models outperform classical methods at every training fraction on 15/30 datasets. On 6 datasets, classical methods surpass zero-shot FMs with as little as 2% training data (21-2,768 samples). On 9 datasets, break-even ranges from 24 to 8,361 samples. A simple rule (n_train < 700 + non-negligible seasonality → use FM zero-shot) resolves 10/30 decisions. LoRA fine-tuning can degrade performance on short series.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose an operationalized two-step decision framework enabling practitioners to make FM-versus-classical decisions before committing to full infrastructure. Four dataset features motivate mechanistic hypotheses for remaining ambiguous cases, though reliable automated prediction at this benchmark scale remains an open problem.

title: Paired Uterine Whole-Slide Images and Pathology Reports for Multimodal Computational Pathology
summary: Uterine diseases represent an important category of gynecologic pathology and require accurate histopathological assessment for diagnosis and treatment planning. Whole-slide images (WSI) have enabled the digital transformation of pathology workflows and provided new opportunities for artificial intelligence (AI) in computational pathology. In particular, multimodal models that jointly analyze histopathology images and pathology reports have shown promising potential for automated pathology report generation and AI-assisted diagnosis. However, the development of such systems remains limited by the scarcity of datasets that pair whole-slide images with clinically meaningful pathology reports. Instead, existing pathology datasets focus on patch- or slide-level annotations of a single endpoint (e.g., disease class), which do not fully capture the rich information in full clinical diagnostic workflow reports. Here, we introduce TUM-Uteria, a uterine pathology dataset comprising WSIs paired with diagnostic pathology reports at both the case and slide levels, collected from a tertiary medical center. The dataset contains 216 clinical cases, comprising 455 slide-level WSI-report pairs. The dataset underwent a structured multi-stage validation procedure involving board-certified pathologists to ensure reliable annotations. TUM-Uteria supports research in computational pathology, including whole-slide image analysis, multimodal learning, and automated pathology report generation.

AI.tldr: TUM-Uteria is a uterine pathology dataset of 216 cases with 455 whole-slide images paired with diagnostic pathology reports at both case and slide levels, validated by board-certified pathologists, designed to support multimodal AI research in computational pathology including automated report generation.
AI.motivation: Existing pathology datasets lack paired whole-slide images and clinically meaningful pathology reports, limiting the development of multimodal AI systems for automated report generation and AI-assisted diagnosis in uterine pathology.
AI.method: The dataset comprises 216 clinical cases with 455 slide-level WSI-report pairs collected from a tertiary medical center, with structured multi-stage validation by board-certified pathologists.
AI.result: A comprehensive uterine pathology dataset (TUM-Uteria) with paired WSIs and diagnostic reports at both case and slide levels, with reliable annotations.
AI.conclusion: TUM-Uteria provides a valuable resource for computational pathology research, particularly for multimodal learning, whole-slide image analysis, and automated pathology report generation.

title: Input Pathways Shape Few-Shot, Not Zero-Shot, Binding in Tiny Transformers: A Fully-Enumerable Study
summary: How does the way information reaches a transformer -- as symbolic tokens, a clean per-factor "oracle" code, or an entangled perceptual vector -- shape whether it binds that information compositionally? We study ~6-10K-parameter transformers on finite factored worlds enumerated exhaustively, so every measurement covers the whole input space (zero sampling variance) and the informative routes are information-matched (exact Bayes ceiling 1.0). We report four findings. (1) Endpoint invariance: on held-out binding queries no informative route reaches converged zero-shot composition -- each ends at or below chance despite a ceiling of 1.0, so within a bounded sweep the failure reflects inductive bias under a lookup-sufficient objective, not missing information. (2) A two-factor account of few-shot binding: sample efficiency is best explained by input-pathway parameter sharing and code readability; a dimension-matched control and a graded readability sweep isolate readability from input dimension, and the clean oracle is not the most sample-efficient readable route. (3) A double dissociation: early in training, distributed -- but not index-like -- codes pass through a transient above-chance phase (tracking code format), while few-shot efficiency tracks pathway sharing. (4) Failure anatomy: symbolic routes lose the answer at the readout; index routes mis-bind (the answer stays decodable, yet an input intervention shows the output tracks the wrong slot); entangled routes inherit their input's readability. The central claim is the two-factor account; the endpoint and anatomy results are diagnostic constraints. All code, manifests, and per-seed logs are released for exact reproduction.

AI.tldr: Using ~6-10K-parameter transformers on fully enumerated finite worlds, we find that (1) held-out zero-shot composition fails across all input routes despite exact information matching, (2) few-shot binding efficiency is explained by pathway parameter sharing and code readability (a two-factor account), (3) a double dissociation emerges between transient above-chance composition (code format) and few-shot efficiency (pathway sharing), and (4) symbolic, index, and entangled routes fail via distinct mechanisms (readout loss, mis-binding, inherited unreadability).
AI.motivation: To understand how different input representations (symbolic tokens, oracle codes, perceptual vectors) affect a transformer's ability to bind information compositionally, and to isolate whether failures stem from missing information or inductive bias.
AI.method: Exhaustive enumeration of ~6-10K-parameter transformers on finite factored worlds with information-matched input routes (exact Bayes ceiling 1.0), measuring zero-shot composition, few-shot binding sample efficiency, and training dynamics with diagnostic interventions.
AI.result: (1) Zero-shot composition fails universally at or below chance. (2) Few-shot binding is best explained by two factors: pathway parameter sharing and code readability. (3) Early training shows a double dissociation: distributed codes transiently exceed chance (code format) while few-shot efficiency tracks pathway sharing. (4) Symbolic routes lose answers at readout; index routes mis-bind; entangled routes inherit input readability.
AI.conclusion: The central claim is a two-factor account of compositional binding (pathway sharing + code readability); the endpoint and failure-anatomy results serve as diagnostic constraints for theories of compositional generalization in transformers.

title: SiamJEPA: On the Role of Siamese Student Encoders in JEPA
summary: Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have attracted significant attention in the computer vision and machine learning communities as a promising framework for self-supervised representation learning. Unlike masked autoencoders that reconstruct pixels, JEPA models learn representations by predicting latent embeddings of masked regions. Existing JEPA-based methods, such as I-JEPA and V-JEPA, typically employ a single encoder in the student network. In contrast, using Siamese encoders for student network is more naturally aligned with brain-inspired representation learning frameworks, yet their role in JEPA models remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the effect of Siamese student encoders in JEPA-based representation learning. To this end, we propose SiamJEPA, masked Siamese student encoders equipped with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher network. SiamJEPA can also be viewed as a JEPA formulation of the brain-inspired representation learning model PhiNet. Through extensive experiments on ImageNet linear probing, we demonstrate that Siamese encoders act as an effective regularizer for the JEPA objective, improving representation separability and accelerating learning during the early stages of training. Furthermore, SiamJEPA consistently outperforms comparable single-encoder JEPA variants under limited training budgets and achieves higher linear probing accuracy than Masked Autoencoders (MAE) which requires longer training. Our findings reveal that Siamese student encoders are not merely an architectural choice but constitute an important inductive bias for predictive representation learning. These results provide new insights into the design of JEPA-based models and suggest that incorporating Siamese student architectures offers a simple yet effective approach for improving self-supervised representation learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SiamJEPA, which introduces Siamese student encoders into JEPA-based self-supervised learning. This approach improves representation separability and accelerates early training, outperforming single-encoder JEPA variants and MAE under limited budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing JEPA models (I-JEPA, V-JEPA) use a single encoder in the student network, but Siamese encoders—more aligned with brain-inspired frameworks like PhiNet—remain unexplored in JEPA. The paper investigates whether Siamese student encoders can serve as an effective inductive bias for predictive representation learning.
AI.method: SiamJEPA employs masked Siamese student encoders with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher network, framing it as a JEPA formulation of the brain-inspired PhiNet model. It predicts latent embeddings of masked regions rather than reconstructing pixels.
AI.result: Siamese encoders act as an effective regularizer for the JEPA objective, improving representation separability and accelerating early training. SiamJEPA consistently outperforms single-encoder JEPA variants under limited training budgets and achieves higher linear probing accuracy than MAE (which requires longer training).
AI.conclusion: Siamese student encoders are not merely an architectural choice but provide an important inductive bias for predictive representation learning. Incorporating them offers a simple yet effective way to improve self-supervised learning in JEPA-based models.

title: Lightweight ML-Based Automatic Sleep Staging Framework with Constrained CNN and Mamba for Small-Sample EEG Datasets
summary: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders as well as long-term home sleep monitoring. Portable electroencephalogram (EEG) devices have become the focus of research due to their convenience in data collection. However, current methods still face three major challenges: large parameter sizes that easily lead to overfitting on small datasets, low accuracy in classifying difficult stages such as N1 and REM, unclear optimal training dataset size, and difficulty in deployment. This paper proposes GamSleepNet, a lightweight and low-latency automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework features the FEB module, which combines improved Gabor kernels with learnable filters for feature extraction, uses the Mamba architecture to build a temporal classification network, introduces a novel contrastive loss and a two-stage training strategy, and experimentally validates the optimal dataset size for single-channel EEG sleep staging models. On the Sleepedf dataset, this model achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86 percent with only 30.86 thousand parameters, with all metrics reaching SOTA levels and significantly improving the identification accuracy of challenging sleep stages.

AI.tldr: GamSleepNet is a lightweight (30.86K parameters) single-channel EEG sleep staging framework achieving 87.86% accuracy on SleepEDF by combining improved Gabor kernels, Mamba-based temporal classification, contrastive loss, and a two-stage training strategy, while addressing overfitting, difficult stage classification (N1, REM), and optimal dataset size determination.
AI.motivation: Current automatic sleep staging methods face three major challenges: large parameter sizes causing overfitting on small datasets, low accuracy for difficult stages (N1 and REM), unclear optimal training dataset size, and deployment difficulties. Portable single-channel EEG devices offer convenience but lack effective lightweight solutions.
AI.method: GamSleepNet consists of: (1) a FEB module combining improved Gabor kernels with learnable filters for feature extraction; (2) a Mamba architecture-based temporal classification network; (3) a novel contrastive loss function; (4) a two-stage training strategy; and (5) empirical validation of optimal dataset size for single-channel EEG sleep staging.
AI.result: On the SleepEDF dataset, the model achieves 87.86% overall accuracy with only 30.86K parameters. All evaluation metrics reach state-of-the-art (SOTA) levels, with significantly improved identification accuracy for challenging sleep stages (N1 and REM).
AI.conclusion: GamSleepNet provides a lightweight, low-latency solution for automatic sleep staging from single-channel EEG, effectively balancing model size and accuracy while addressing key challenges in portable sleep monitoring applications.

title: PreSIST: Vision-Language-Informed Object Persistence Prediction in Open-World Scenes
summary: Robots deployed over long periods must reason about environments that change over time. Existing long-term perception systems often address object change reactively, updating their maps only after revisiting a scene and observing that an object has moved. Instead, robots should reason proactively about how long objects are likely to persist using the context in which they appear. For example, a car at a traffic light and a car in a parking spot share the same semantic class, but their contexts imply different persistence durations. We propose PreSIST (Predictive Scene-conditioned Instance Survival over Time), a method for predicting whether an observed object will remain in its last seen pose at arbitrary future times. PreSIST estimates instance-level persistence priors from object properties and scene context, then integrates these priors with a probabilistic persistence filter as observations become available. Its key insight is that the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can relate scene context to likely object use and human activity, enabling persistence prediction before long-term observations are available. We develop two interchangeable variants: PreSIST-Lang, which estimates persistence priors using a VLM, and PreSIST-Vis, a novel vision-only model trained using PreSIST-Lang pseudo-labels for efficient deployment. Experiments on a new dataset of in-the-wild object persistence annotations show that PreSIST-Lang and PreSIST-Vis outperform baselines on open-world persistence prediction.

AI.tldr: PreSIST predicts how long objects will persist in their observed poses by leveraging scene context and vision-language models, outperforming baselines on a new object persistence dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term perception systems reactively update maps after revisiting scenes and detecting object changes, lacking proactive reasoning about object persistence based on scene context.
AI.method: PreSIST uses two variants: (1) PreSIST-Lang, which estimates persistence priors via a VLM by reasoning about scene context and likely human activity, and (2) PreSIST-Vis, a vision-only model trained on pseudo-labels from PreSIST-Lang. Both integrate priors with a probabilistic persistence filter as observations arrive.
AI.result: On a new in-the-wild object persistence dataset, both PreSIST-Lang and PreSIST-Vis outperform baselines in open-world persistence prediction.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware persistence prediction enables proactive long-term robot perception, with VLMs providing a bridge to reason about object lifespan before observations are available.

title: Sensitivity Sampling with Predictions for k-Means Clustering
summary:
We study the problem of k-means clustering on large datasets. The state-of-the-art for the problem is given by coresets-based approaches, which build small weighted summaries of the input and derive approximate solutions with rigorous quality guarantees from them. One of the most popular and advanced approaches to derive coresets for k-means is sensitivity sampling. However, sensitivity sampling requires to compute the importance of each input point with respect to the whole dataset over all possible choices of centers. Since the exact computation of such quantities is unfeasible, current approaches work by approximating the sensitivity values. Nevertheless, the runtime of such approaches is still impractical for large datasets.
  In this work, we propose to reduce the runtime of sensitivity-based approaches for k-means by leveraging predictions to approximate the importance of input points. We first formally prove that current theoretical results on coresets construction via sensitivity sampling hold for coarser approximations of sensitivities compared to the one required by existing approaches. This implies that even fairly noisy predictors can be leveraged for sensitivity-sampling approaches. We then propose a natural predictor, which applies to the common scenario where clustering is performed (over time) on a sequence of datasets from the same problem. We prove that when the datasets in the sequence come from the same (unknown) distribution, centers resulting in a low error on one dataset can be used as predictions for sensitivity sampling in subsequent datasets, with guarantees on their quality. We perform an extensive experimental evaluation showing that our approach significantly improves, in terms of clustering cost vs runtime, over uniform sampling and state-of-the-art sensitivity sampling approaches when applied to sequences of datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using predictions (e.g., from previous datasets in a sequence) to approximate sensitivity values for coreset-based k-means clustering, showing that coarser approximations suffice theoretically and achieving significant runtime improvements experimentally.
AI.motivation: Existing sensitivity sampling approaches for k-means coresets require computing importance scores that are computationally expensive, making them impractical for large datasets.
AI.method: The authors prove that theoretical guarantees for coreset construction via sensitivity sampling hold for coarser sensitivity approximations. They propose a natural predictor leveraging clustering results from previous datasets in a sequence (assuming they come from the same unknown distribution) to approximate sensitivities.
AI.result: Extensive experimental evaluation shows the proposed approach significantly improves the clustering cost vs. runtime trade-off over uniform sampling and state-of-the-art sensitivity sampling methods on sequences of datasets.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging predictions for sensitivity approximation is theoretically sound (coarser approximations suffice) and practically effective, reducing runtime while maintaining clustering quality.

title: Enhancing Implicit Neural Representations with Image Feature Embedding for Unsupervised Cardiac Cine MRI Reconstruction
summary: Cardiac cine Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a critical diagnostic tool that provides dynamic insights for radiologists. To accelerate acquisition, under-sampled k-space data is often used, requiring reconstruction methods that combine coil sensitivity encoding with prior information to recover missing data. Deep learning approaches have gained more attention for leveraging data-adaptive priors. While supervised learning approaches are a common choice, they depend on fully sampled reference data, which is not always available. Unsupervised methods eliminate the need for fully sampled reference data, which can be advantageous in cardiac cine MRI reconstruction. Among them, implicit neural representations (INRs) have shown great potential due to their simple architecture and good quality reconstructions. In this work, we propose an image-domain dual-branch INR framework, termed I-FP-INR, which extends the original INR design by introducing an additional feature-processing branch. This design aims to extract complementary feature embeddings to enhance the overall representation, thereby benefiting reconstruction. Extensive evaluations on both public datasets and in-house data show consistent improvements over baseline methods in reconstruction quality, with strong robustness across varied scenarios.

AI.tldr: I-FP-INR is a dual-branch implicit neural representation framework for unsupervised cardiac cine MRI reconstruction that adds a feature-processing branch to extract complementary embeddings, outperforming baseline methods on public and in-house datasets.
AI.motivation: Cardiac cine MRI reconstruction from under-sampled k-space data is needed to accelerate acquisition, but supervised deep learning methods require fully sampled reference data which is often unavailable. Unsupervised methods, particularly INRs, offer a solution but have limited representation capacity.
AI.method: Proposes I-FP-INR, an image-domain dual-branch INR framework that extends the original INR design by introducing an additional feature-processing branch to extract complementary feature embeddings, enhancing the overall representation for reconstruction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on both public datasets and in-house data demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods in reconstruction quality, with strong robustness across varied scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The dual-branch INR design with a dedicated feature-processing branch effectively improves unsupervised cardiac cine MRI reconstruction quality and robustness without requiring fully sampled reference data.

title: Train Smarter, Not Longer: Memorization-Guided Data Reuse for Efficient LLM Training
comment: Published as a paper at 3rd DATA-FM workshop @ ICLR 2026, Brazil
summary: The training paradigm of large language models has shifted from traditional one-pass training to multi-epoch training, as reasonable reuse of limited high-quality data can improve both model performance and sample efficiency. Meanwhile, excessive repetition introduces the risk of overfitting and diminishing returns. Determining when and how to reuse data effectively thus emerges as a natural but under-explored question. Through a novel observation of model's "Memorization Window" signals derived from loss retention dynamics and downstream evaluation scores, we propose "Memorization-guided Data Reuse", a training paradigm that adaptively determines when and how data should be reused, enabling principled decisions on the number of training epochs and the scheduling of data replays. Our preliminary experiments reveal a consistent memorization-driven regime: performance continues to improve with repetition far beyond current practice (e.g., the commonly cited four-epoch limit). While a full scheduler remains future work, these insights provide a foundation for memorization-aware training schedules, helping to determine reuse budgets and move toward training LLMs smarter rather than longer with limited high-quality data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Memorization-guided Data Reuse," a training paradigm that uses loss retention dynamics and evaluation scores to adaptively determine when and how to reuse data in multi-epoch LLM training. Preliminary experiments show performance improves with repetition far beyond the commonly cited four-epoch limit, suggesting a larger memorization-driven regime for leveraging limited high-quality data.
AI.motivation: While multi-epoch training on limited high-quality data can improve LLM performance, excessive repetition risks overfitting and diminishing returns. The question of when and how to reuse data effectively remains under-explored.
AI.method: The authors observe a "Memorization Window" signal derived from loss retention dynamics and downstream evaluation scores, then propose a training paradigm that adaptively determines data reuse decisions (number of epochs and scheduling of replays).
AI.result: Preliminary experiments reveal a consistent memorization-driven regime where performance improves with repetition far beyond common practice (e.g., beyond the four-epoch limit).
AI.conclusion: These insights provide a foundation for memorization-aware training schedules and help determine reuse budgets, moving toward training LLMs smarter rather than longer with limited high-quality data. A full scheduler is left as future work.

title: Seeing Once is Enough? Online Geometry-Aware Token Pruning for 3D Question Answering
comment: published at ICLR 2026 Workshop on Efficient Spatial Reasoning
summary: Recent Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on 2D question answering tasks. However, extending these models to the 3D question answering remains challenging, as they typically require multiple views of the scene, which incurs substantial computational cost at inference. To mitigate this issue, existing solutions rely on strategic frame selection or token-merging algorithms that require preprocessing in advance all frames of the scene, i.e., an offline fashion. In contrast, we propose the first online token-pruning method that can be integrated seamlessly with current MLLM models for 3D question answering tasks, without additional training and with lower memory usage.Our key insight is to project each input frame into a shared voxel space using depth information and camera pose, identifying spatially-overlapped regions across frames and selectively pruning redundant image tokens before they enter the language model. Our method enables efficient online processing while reducing up to 50% of token usage. We apply this approach to Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, demonstrating improved performance on the ScanQA, SQA3D, and OpenEQA-HM3D benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes the first online token-pruning method for MLLMs in 3D QA tasks, projecting frames into shared voxel space to prune redundant tokens before they enter the language model, reducing up to 50% token usage without additional training.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs for 3D QA require multiple views, causing high computational cost at inference. Prior offline solutions preprocess all frames in advance, which is inefficient. An online token-pruning method is needed to reduce redundancy efficiently.
AI.method: Projects each input frame into a shared voxel space using depth information and camera pose, identifies spatially-overlapped regions across frames, and selectively prunes redundant image tokens before they enter the language model. This is done online without additional training.
AI.result: Reduces up to 50% token usage while improving performance on ScanQA, SQA3D, and OpenEQA-HM3D benchmarks when applied to Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
AI.conclusion: The first online token-pruning method for 3D QA with MLLMs, offering efficiency gains and performance improvements without requiring additional training or offline preprocessing.

title: Geometry-Aware Bayesian Quantification via Compositional Data Analysis
summary: Accurately estimating the unknown target label distribution is the critical first step for adapting to label shift. This task, widely known as quantification or class prevalence estimation, has recently seen significant advances through continuous KDE-based methods which model the density of multiclass classifier posteriors. Posterior vectors might be regarded as compositional data, since they lie on the probability simplex. However, existing KDE-based quantifiers typically rely on Euclidean Gaussian kernels, which ignore simplex geometry and incorrectly assign probability mass outside its boundaries. We introduce a geometry-aware KDE model for multiclass quantification based on log-ratio representations and Aitchison geometry, together with a shrinkage regularization that improves robustness near the simplex boundary. Combined with a maximum-likelihood interpretation of KDE-based quantification, we derive both point-estimation and Bayesian inference procedures for class prevalences. Experiments on 42 datasets across tabular, text, and image domains show that the proposed method is competitive with state-of-the-art quantifiers, often improving over standard KDE-based baselines, while also yielding strong results among Bayesian quantification methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a geometry-aware KDE-based method for multiclass quantification (label shift estimation) that uses log-ratio representations and Aitchison geometry with shrinkage regularization, outperforming standard Euclidean KDE baselines across 42 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing KDE-based quantifiers rely on Euclidean Gaussian kernels which ignore the simplex geometry of posterior probability vectors, assigning probability mass outside simplex boundaries and leading to inaccurate label shift estimation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a geometry-aware KDE model using log-ratio representations and Aitchison geometry, combined with shrinkage regularization for robustness near the simplex boundary. It derives both point-estimation and Bayesian inference procedures using a maximum-likelihood interpretation of KDE-based quantification.
AI.result: Experiments on 42 datasets across tabular, text, and image domains show the method is competitive with state-of-the-art quantifiers, improves over standard KDE-based baselines, and yields strong results among Bayesian quantification methods.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for simplex geometry via Aitchison geometry and log-ratio transforms improves KDE-based multiclass quantification, with shrinkage regularization enhancing robustness near boundaries.

title: Sparse4D-Radar: An Efficient and Robust Framework for Surround-View 3D Object Detection via 4D Radar-Camera Fusion
summary: In recent years, 4D imaging radar has gained wide attention in autonomous driving for its robustness against harsh weather and ability to output target velocity. Nevertheless, mainstream 4D radar-camera fusion methods only support front-view perception, lacking mature solutions for surround-view sensing. Directly expanding these pipelines to full 360° coverage introduces excessive computation cost and limits real-world deployment. To tackle these limitations, this work proposes Sparse4D-Radar, an efficient robust surround-view multi-modal fusion framework. We first design a Deformable Fusion module to embed radar-camera features into sparse queries, constructing the lightweight base version Sparse4D-Radar-Base. Two dedicated modules are further introduced to boost localization accuracy and modality stability: Velocity-Consistency Sampling (VCS) refines features via radar velocity cues for motion awareness, and Adaptive Modality Gating (AMG) dynamically adjusts cross-modal fusion weights according to feature confidence. Combining all components, we build Sparse4D-Radar-Acc for high-precision detection demands. Comprehensive experiments on OmniHD-Scenes verify that our approach achieves state-of-the-art surround-view 3D detection performance. Compared with prior arts, our method obtains over 7% mAP and 10% ODS improvements under complex driving scenes while running at nearly 10 FPS, striking a favorable trade-off among detection accuracy, environmental robustness and inference efficiency. Our open-source code is available at https://github.com/Aiuan/Sparse4D-Radar.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sparse4D-Radar, a surround-view multi-modal fusion framework for 4D imaging radar and cameras that achieves state-of-the-art 3D detection with over 7% mAP and 10% ODS improvements while running at nearly 10 FPS, balancing accuracy, robustness, and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D radar-camera fusion methods only support front-view perception and cannot efficiently scale to full 360° surround-view due to excessive computational costs, limiting real-world autonomous driving deployment.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) a Deformable Fusion module to embed radar-camera features into sparse queries (Sparse4D-Radar-Base); (2) Velocity-Consistency Sampling (VCS) for motion-aware feature refinement using radar velocity cues; (3) Adaptive Modality Gating (AMG) for dynamically adjusting cross-modal fusion weights based on feature confidence (combined as Sparse4D-Radar-Acc).
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art surround-view 3D detection on OmniHD-Scenes, with over 7% mAP and 10% ODS improvements over prior methods under complex driving scenes, operating at nearly 10 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Sparse4D-Radar strikes a favorable trade-off among detection accuracy, environmental robustness, and inference efficiency, providing an open-source solution for practical surround-view autonomous driving perception.

title: Qantara: Bridge-Flow Training for Multi-Paradigm JEPA Control
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://corl-team.github.io/qantara
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) underpin a growing family of latent world models for control from raw pixels, but every existing JEPA world model commits at training time to a single inference paradigm: either trajectory optimisation in a learned dynamics model, or direct behaviour cloning. A single checkpoint that serves both would defer this choice to inference, when deployment constraints (rollout cost, observation accessibility) determine which path wins. We present Qantara, an end-to-end JEPA whose joint training objective pairs a Brownian-bridge interpolant between consecutive clean latents on the state axis with noise-to-data flow matching on the action axis. The same checkpoint serves three inference paradigms without retraining: latent planning, behaviour-cloning action sampling, and inverse dynamics, which we query through a video-inverse composition that first predicts the next latent without action conditioning, then extracts the action. Training concentrates mass on the edges of the (action-time, state-time) noise square, where inference queries the predictor: replacing it with uniform interior sampling drops Push-T planning from 90.1 to 53.3 SR at matched compute. On the LeWM control suite, Qantara reaches a 91.2 SR three-train-seed average and sets new SOTA on OGBench-Cube (+7.7 SR over DINO-WM, +19.7 over LeWM). From the same weights, the behaviour-cloning and video-inverse paths reach 82-83 SR on Push-T and 71-73 SR on Cube. These results move JEPA world models from single-paradigm planners to multi-paradigm controllers.

AI.tldr: Qantara presents a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with a unified training objective (Brownian-bridge interpolant + noise-to-data flow matching) that enables three inference paradigms—latent planning, behaviour-cloning action sampling, and inverse dynamics—from a single checkpoint, achieving SOTA results on LeWM and OGBench-Cube while enabling multi-paradigm control.
AI.motivation: Existing JEPA world models commit at training time to a single inference paradigm (either trajectory optimization in learned dynamics or direct behavior cloning), forcing users to choose before deployment constraints are known. The goal is to defer this choice to inference time, allowing a single checkpoint to serve multiple paradigms based on runtime constraints like rollout cost and observation accessibility.
AI.method: Qantara is an end-to-end JEPA with a joint training objective that combines: (1) a Brownian-bridge interpolant between consecutive clean latents on the state axis, and (2) noise-to-data flow matching on the action axis. This concentrates training mass on the edges of the (action-time, state-time) noise square where inference queries the predictor. Three inference paradigms are supported: latent planning, behaviour-cloning action sampling, and a video-inverse composition (predict next latent without action conditioning, then extract action via inverse dynamics).
AI.result: Qantara achieves 91.2 SR (three-train-seed average) on LeWM control suite, sets new SOTA on OGBench-Cube (+7.7 SR over DINO-WM, +19.7 over LeWM). From the same weights, behaviour-cloning and video-inverse paths reach 82-83 SR on Push-T and 71-73 SR on Cube. Uniform interior sampling (vs. edge-concentrated training) drops Push-T planning from 90.1 to 53.3 SR at matched compute.
AI.conclusion: Qantara moves JEPA world models from single-paradigm planners to multi-paradigm controllers, enabling a single checkpoint to serve latent planning, behaviour cloning, and inverse dynamics inference paradigms without retraining.

title: The Multipath Blind Spot: $K$-Agnostic Robust Calibration for Sparse-Anchor Metric Depth from Frozen Foundations
summary: Monocular depth foundations predict domain-general relative depth but lack absolute scale; a handful of sparse metric anchors from a range sensor can calibrate them to metric depth, an attractive alternative to metric-supervised training. Existing sparse-anchor calibration methods, however, assume the anchors are clean, whereas real sensors produce outliers that are present with the wrong value -- time-of-flight multipath, mixed pixels -- not merely missing. We show that the established residual-on-CFA calibration recipe collapses under such outliers, and that the strongest publicly deployed method, VI-Depth, has a structural multipath blind spot: robust to missing anchors, it falls behind an unprotected baseline on three of four datasets when anchors are present but wrong. We propose Multipath-Robust Anchor Calibration (MRAC), a parameter-free, inference-time wrapper that gates anchors by foundation consistency -- a Theil--Sen fit and a median-absolute-deviation test against the foundation's own relative-depth ordering -- before a single call to the calibration head. MRAC adds no learned parameters, runs its selection in $\approx 50\,μ$s on CPU, and serves anchor budgets $K \in [5,200]$ from one checkpoint. On a $320$-cell benchmark with a same-backbone, same-architecture control, MRAC strictly wins $84\%$ of same-backbone cells across all four outlier families and, against VI-Depth, wins all twelve corrupted multipath cells and all sixteen KITTI cells, reducing KITTI multipath AbsRel by $3.2\times$ ($0.489$ to $0.151$) at zero retraining.

AI.tldr: Real-world range sensor outliers break existing sparse-anchor monocular depth calibration methods. MRAC is a parameter-free, inference-time wrapper that uses foundation consistency (Theil-Sen fit + MAD test) to gate anchors before calibration, achieving robust metric depth without retraining. It strictly outperforms VI-Depth and baselines across diverse outlier types, reducing KITTI multipath AbsRel by 3.2×.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse-anchor calibration methods assume clean anchors, but real sensors (e.g., time-of-flight) produce outliers with wrong values (multipath, mixed pixels), not just missing data. The established residual-on-CFA recipe collapses under such outliers, and VI-Depth has a structural multipath blind spot.
AI.method: MRAC (Multipath-Robust Anchor Calibration): a parameter-free, inference-time wrapper that gates anchors by foundation consistency. It applies a Theil-Sen fit and median-absolute-deviation (MAD) test against the foundation model's relative-depth ordering to filter outliers before a single call to the calibration head. No retraining or added learned parameters; runs ~50μs on CPU; supports anchor budgets K ∈ [5,200] from one checkpoint.
AI.result: On a 320-cell benchmark with same-backbone, same-architecture control: MRAC strictly wins 84% of cells across all four outlier families. Against VI-Depth: wins all twelve corrupted multipath cells and all sixteen KITTI cells. Reduces KITTI multipath AbsRel by 3.2× (0.489 → 0.151) at zero retraining.
AI.conclusion: MRAC demonstrates that robust anchor selection via foundation consistency is an effective, lightweight alternative to retraining-based approaches for handling real-world sensor outliers in metric depth calibration.

title: Data-Driven Soft Labeling Scales DNA Read Classification to Whole-Body Cell-Type Deconvolution
summary: Cell-type deconvolution, the task of estimating the proportions of constituent cell types in a heterogeneous biological sample, is a core problem in computational biology. Methods that rely on epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation typically operate on aggregated methylation estimates, discarding the pattern-level information carried by individual DNA reads. Existing read-level approaches that exploit this information are scarce, and all remain restricted to few-class settings; scaling them further is an open problem because, at scale, non-discriminative reads dominate and hard labels conflict with the many-to-many mapping between methylation patterns and cell types, preventing classifier convergence. To overcome this, we propose data-driven soft labels that estimate the conditional cell-type distribution for each read, and integrate this scheme into Syto, a new modular framework for read-level classification-based deconvolution. On a whole-body atlas of 39 human cell types, Syto reduces MSE by 2.56$\times$ over SoTA, with gains transferring to an out-of-distribution dataset spanning 16 tissues. Syto lays the foundation for modeling increasingly large cell-type panels, with improved applications in biology and healthcare. The proposed soft-labeling scheme is further translatable to any setting with a many-to-many signal-to-label mapping.

AI.tldr: Syto introduces data-driven soft labels for read-level methylation-based deconvolution, enabling scaling to 39 cell types with 2.56× MSE reduction over state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Existing read-level deconvolution methods are limited to few-class settings because non-discriminative reads dominate at scale and hard labels conflict with the many-to-many mapping between methylation patterns and cell types, preventing classifier convergence.
AI.method: Syto proposes data-driven soft labels that estimate the conditional cell-type distribution for each read, integrated into a modular read-level classification-based deconvolution framework.
AI.result: On a whole-body atlas of 39 human cell types, Syto reduces MSE by 2.56× over state-of-the-art, with gains transferring to an out-of-distribution dataset spanning 16 tissues.
AI.conclusion: Syto lays the foundation for modeling increasingly large cell-type panels with improved applications in biology and healthcare; the soft-labeling scheme is translatable to any setting with a many-to-many signal-to-label mapping.

title: SOV-CAD: Stepwise Orthographic Views Guided CAD Modeling Sequence Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing Computer-Aided Design (CAD) modeling sequences from images is crucial for preserving design intent and supporting parametric editing. However, existing methods typically generate full CAD sequences holistically, overlooking the iterative, feedback-driven nature of human design workflows. We address this limitation by introducing the rich stepwise visual supervision: at each modeling step, the system observes the target's orthographic projections, the projections of the incrementally constructed model, and the active sketch, enabling informed action selection. To effectively leverage this on-the-fly feedback, we propose SOV-CAD, a framework that formulates CAD reconstruction as a sequential decision-making task and employs offline reinforcement learning with a Decision Transformer architecture. This design incorporates continuous visual feedback guided by geometric alignment rewards, resulting in a more accurate and human-like modeling process. Extensive experiments show that SOV-CAD surpasses state-of-the-art methods in CAD sequence reconstruction while exhibiting strong data efficiency. Code of SOV-CAD is available at: https://github.com/LukePhong/SOV-CAD

AI.tldr: SOV-CAD is a framework that reconstructs CAD modeling sequences from images using stepwise visual supervision and offline reinforcement learning with a Decision Transformer, achieving state-of-the-art performance by treating CAD reconstruction as a sequential decision-making task guided by geometric alignment rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing methods generate full CAD sequences holistically, ignoring the iterative, feedback-driven nature of human design workflows. The authors aim to address this by introducing rich stepwise visual supervision that mimics how humans observe orthographic projections at each modeling step.
AI.method: The framework formulates CAD reconstruction as a sequential decision-making task, employing offline reinforcement learning with a Decision Transformer architecture. It incorporates continuous visual feedback from orthographic projections (target, incrementally constructed model, and active sketch) guided by geometric alignment rewards.
AI.result: SOV-CAD surpasses state-of-the-art methods in CAD sequence reconstruction and exhibits strong data efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The approach produces more accurate and human-like modeling processes by leveraging stepwise visual feedback, demonstrating the value of reinforcement learning for iterative CAD sequence reconstruction.

title: Non-Convex Sparse Reinforcement Learning via Non-Monotone Inclusions
summary:
This work delivers two key contributions: one to efficient feature selection in reinforcement learning
  (RL), the other to the theory of non-monotone inclusions. On the RL side, the estimation bias inherent
  in conventional regularization schemes is addressed by augmenting classical least-squares
  temporal-difference (LSTD) policy evaluation with the sparsity-inducing, non-convex projected minimax
  concave (PMC) penalty. Because the PMC penalty is weakly convex, the resulting fixed-point problem is
  no longer monotone; instead, it falls under a broader class of non-monotone inclusions involving the
  sum of a monotone Lipschitz operator and a hypomonotone operator. On the theory side, novel convergence
  conditions are developed for the forward-reflected-backward splitting (FRBS) method applied to this
  broader class of non-monotone inclusion problems. Under mild conditions, Lyapunov stability and the
  existence of a limit point of the sequence of FRBS iterates are established; alternatively, under the
  weak Minty variational inequality assumption, exact convergence is guaranteed. Numerical tests on
  benchmark datasets show that the proposed FRBS iterates, applied to the non-convexly regularized LSTD
  problem, substantially outperform state-of-the-art feature-selection methods, especially when many
  noisy features are present.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a non-convex PMC penalty to LSTD for bias-aware feature selection in RL, and provides convergence theory for the FRBS method applied to the resulting non-monotone inclusion problem, with strong empirical results on noisy benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional regularization in RL policy evaluation introduces estimation bias, and existing monotone inclusion solvers cannot handle the weakly convex (hypomonotone) structure induced by non-convex sparsity-inducing penalties like PMC.
AI.method: Augment LSTD with the non-convex PMC penalty, casting the fixed-point problem as a non-monotone inclusion (monotone Lipschitz + hypomonotone operator). Apply the forward-reflected-backward splitting (FRBS) method and derive convergence conditions under Lyapunov stability and weak Minty variational inequality assumptions.
AI.result: FRBS iterates converge (limit point existence under mild conditions; exact convergence under weak Minty VI). On benchmark datasets, the non-convexly regularized LSTD with FRBS substantially outperforms state-of-the-art feature selection methods, particularly with many noisy features.
AI.conclusion: The PMC-regularized LSTD combined with FRBS provides effective, bias-reducing feature selection in RL, and the theoretical analysis extends splitting methods to a broader class of non-monotone inclusions.

title: FRFDet: Efficient UAV Small Object Detection with Symmetric Sampling and Scalable Fusion
summary: Small object detection in Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery remains challenging under adverse conditions, including complex weather, low illumination, and sensor noise. These challenges mainly stem from severe background clutter, fine-grained detail degradation, and suboptimal semantic-spatial feature fusion, which jointly hinder robust small-object representation. To this end, we propose FRFDet, a lightweight yet effective single-stage detector tailored for UAV-based small object detection. FRFDet proposes two plug-and-play modules: Inverse Bidirectional Sampling (IBS) and Scale-Feature Relationship Cross-Fusion (SFRCF). IBS preserves critical spatial details via channel expansion-compression and bidirectional pattern reconstruction, improving feature alignment. SFRCF explicitly models scale-dependent fusion behaviors, revealing that inter-group element-wise multiplication favors compact models, while inter-group additive fusion benefits larger architectures. Extensive experiments on VisDrone, UAVDT, HazyDet, and MS COCO demonstrate that FRFDet achieves state-of-the-art performance among lightweight detectors with low computational cost, compact parameters, and fast inference, making it well suited for resource-constrained UAV platforms.

AI.tldr: FRFDet is a lightweight single-stage detector for UAV small object detection that uses two plug-and-play modules (IBS and SFRCF) to handle adverse conditions, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low computational cost on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Small object detection in UAV imagery under adverse conditions (complex weather, low illumination, sensor noise) is hindered by background clutter, detail degradation, and suboptimal feature fusion, motivating the need for a lightweight yet effective detector suitable for resource-constrained UAV platforms.
AI.method: Proposes FRFDet with two modules: (1) Inverse Bidirectional Sampling (IBS) for preserving spatial details via channel expansion-compression and bidirectional pattern reconstruction; (2) Scale-Feature Relationship Cross-Fusion (SFRCF) for modeling scale-dependent fusion behaviors, where inter-group element-wise multiplication benefits compact models and inter-group additive fusion benefits larger architectures.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance among lightweight detectors on VisDrone, UAVDT, HazyDet, and MS COCO, with low computational cost, compact parameters, and fast inference.
AI.conclusion: FRFDet is well-suited for resource-constrained UAV platforms, effectively addressing the challenges of small object detection under adverse conditions through its plug-and-play modules.

title: The Map Behind the Flow: Finite-Step Gradient Descent as a Dynamical System
summary:
Many phenomena of deep learning are dynamical: they concern not only which minima exist, but how gradient descent reaches, avoids, or selects among them. Edge-of-stability behavior, sharpness oscillations, catapult phases, balancing, and movement toward flatter representations are effects of the training map itself, and are poorly captured by the small-step gradient-flow limit.
  This paper studies fixed-step gradient descent as a discrete dynamical system in a hierarchy of exactly solvable models retaining basic structures of deep learning: depth, factorization, width, data coupling, activation, and stochasticity. The starting point is the balanced scalar reduction of a deep linear chain, giving a quartic loss and a cubic gradient map whose post-edge behavior is explicit. Under the natural large-depth scaling, this dynamics converges to a universal Ricker-type map. The edge of stability is therefore not a breakdown of optimization, but the first bifurcation of the training map.
  Embedding the scalar dynamics back into factored models turns these regimes into learning phenomena. Finite steps break conservation laws of gradient flow and contract factorization imbalance; residual oscillations move parameters toward flatter, more balanced representations. Wider linear networks produce a ladder of spectral edges, so the optimal learning rate can lie beyond the first edge. Data coupling, nonlinear activations, and stochastic targets preserve the same organizing principle: finite-step oscillations drive alignment, balancing, and representation selection. Thus the learning rate is not merely a numerical stability parameter. It is a structural parameter of the training dynamics, determining its attractors and shaping the representations gradient descent selects.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes fixed-step gradient descent as a discrete dynamical system using exactly solvable models, showing that the edge of stability is a bifurcation of the training map, and finite-step oscillations drive alignment, balancing, and representation selection in deep learning.
AI.motivation: Many deep learning phenomena are dynamical (edge-of-stability, sharpness oscillations, catapult phases, balancing) but are poorly captured by the small-step gradient-flow limit, motivating the need to study fixed-step gradient descent as a discrete dynamical system.
AI.method: The paper builds a hierarchy of exactly solvable models preserving deep learning structures (depth, factorization, width, data coupling, activation, stochasticity), starting from a balanced scalar reduction of a deep linear chain that yields a quartic loss and cubic gradient map, which under large-depth scaling converges to a universal Ricker-type map.
AI.result: The edge of stability is the first bifurcation of the training map, not a breakdown of optimization. Finite steps break conservation laws of gradient flow, contract factorization imbalance, and drive residual oscillations toward flatter, more balanced representations. Wider linear networks produce spectral ladders where optimal learning rates can exceed the first edge. These principles generalize across data coupling, nonlinear activations, and stochastic targets.
AI.conclusion: The learning rate is not merely a numerical stability parameter but a structural parameter of training dynamics, determining attractors and shaping the representations gradient descent selects.

title: Real-Time LiDAR Gaussian Splatting SLAM
summary: We present a real-time LiDAR-based framework for Gaussian Splatting SLAM that tightly couples fast G-ICP registration with spherical rasterization-based dense mapping for large-scale sequences. Leveraging LiDAR geometry rather than appearance, we reuse tracking-estimated local covariances to initialize Gaussians with range-aware scales and to derive surface normals for geometry-aware map optimization. We further introduce a covariance-derived geometry score that measures local complexity and drives pruning in planar regions and selective densification in structurally rich areas, while optimized Gaussians and LiDAR-specific confidence cues are fed back to improve tracking robustness. On the Newer College dataset, our method achieves an F-score of 86.78\% using purely online trajectories at real-time speed ($>$20 FPS), and additional experiments on other datasets confirm its stability and scalability.

AI.tldr: A real-time LiDAR-based Gaussian Splatting SLAM framework that tightly couples fast G-ICP registration with spherical rasterization-based dense mapping, achieving 86.78% F-score on Newer College dataset at >20 FPS.
AI.motivation: To develop a real-time LiDAR SLAM system that leverages Gaussian Splatting for dense mapping while tightly coupling tracking and mapping through covariance reuse, geometry-aware optimization, and LiDAR-specific confidence feedback.
AI.method: Tightly couples fast G-ICP registration with spherical rasterization-based dense mapping; initializes Gaussians using tracking-estimated local covariances with range-aware scales; derives surface normals for geometry-aware map optimization; uses a covariance-derived geometry score to drive pruning in planar regions and densification in structurally rich areas; feeds optimized Gaussians and LiDAR-specific confidence cues back to improve tracking.
AI.result: Achieves 86.78% F-score on Newer College dataset using purely online trajectories at real-time speed (>20 FPS); additional experiments confirm stability and scalability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LiDAR-based Gaussian Splatting SLAM framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and real-time performance for large-scale sequences by tightly coupling tracking and mapping through geometric covariance reuse and feedback.

title: ImputeECG: Deep Learning Reconstruction of Complete 12-Lead Electrocardiograms from Incomplete Recordings for Cardiac Assessment
summary: Complete digital 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) are essential for AI-enabled cardiovascular assessment, yet many clinical ECG records, particularly those digitized from ECG images, remain incomplete because of short display formats, incomplete waveform digitization, lead loss, or signal corruption. We developed ImputeECG, a mask-conditioned one-dimensional Transformer autoencoder that completes 12-lead, 10-s ECGs while retaining all observed samples. The model was trained on PTB-XL and evaluated on PTB-XL and CPSC2018 under simulated incomplete settings, with additional real-world validation in a 43,633-record Kailuan clinical cohort after ECG image digitization. Metrics were computed over originally missing regions, with analyses of morphology and downstream diagnostic utility. On PTB-XL, ImputeECG reduced missing-region MAE by 41.7-51.0% and MSE by 54.0-63.7% versus the strongest baseline, with lower errors in R-peak timing, RR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, and P-wave, QRS-complex, and T-wave reconstruction. On CPSC2018, ImputeECG reduced MAE by 49.7-51.9%, supporting external generalization. In downstream multi-label classification, ImputeECG restored performance to 92.28% AUROC and 33.88% AUPRC in the most incomplete PTB-XL setting, approaching complete-ECG performance. On CPSC2018, completed ECGs achieved 94.75-95.89% AUROC and 78.83-81.86% AUPRC across settings. In Kailuan, ECG completion improved zero-shot sex prediction AUROC from 82.6% to 85.8% and reduced age prediction MAE from 10.72 to 9.87 years after image-based ECG digitization. These findings support ECG completion as a practical strategy for converting incomplete ECG records into AI-ready 12-lead, 10-s digital signals and extending the usable scope of ECG archives for digital cardiac assessment.

AI.tldr: ImputeECG is a mask-conditioned 1D Transformer autoencoder that completes incomplete 12-lead, 10-s ECGs. It significantly reduces reconstruction error (MAE 41.7-51.9% reduction), restores diagnostic classification performance close to complete-ECG levels (e.g., 92.28% AUROC), and improves downstream tasks like sex/age prediction in real-world clinical cohorts, demonstrating practical utility for converting incomplete ECG archives into AI-ready digital signals.
AI.motivation: Complete 12-lead ECGs are essential for AI-based cardiovascular assessment, but many clinical records—especially those digitized from ECG images—are incomplete due to short display formats, incomplete waveform digitization, lead loss, or signal corruption, limiting their usability for AI analysis.
AI.method: ImputeECG uses a mask-conditioned 1D Transformer autoencoder trained on PTB-XL, designed to complete missing portions of 12-lead, 10-s ECGs while preserving all observed samples. Evaluation was done under simulated incomplete settings on PTB-XL and CPSC2018, plus real-world validation on a 43,633-record Kailuan clinical cohort after ECG image digitization.
AI.result: On PTB-XL, ImputeECG reduced MAE by 41.7-51.0% and MSE by 54.0-63.7% vs. baselines, with lower errors across key ECG intervals. On CPSC2018, MAE reduced by 49.7-51.9%. Downstream classification AUROC reached 92.28% (most incomplete PTB-XL setting) and 94.75-95.89% on CPSC2018. In Kailuan, zero-shot sex prediction AUROC improved from 82.6% to 85.8%, age prediction MAE from 10.72 to 9.87 years.
AI.conclusion: ECG completion with ImputeECG is a practical strategy for converting incomplete ECG records into AI-ready 12-lead, 10-s digital signals, extending the usable scope of ECG archives for digital cardiac assessment.

title: HCSU: A Dataset and Benchmark for Fine-Grained Historical Calligraphy Style Understanding
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 17 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
summary: Automated fine-grained perception of calligraphy styles--a task vital to cultural heritage preservation--remains a critical challenge for Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), largely constrained by existing datasets that suffer from modal mixture and flattened labels. To bridge this gap, we introduce HCSU, the first comprehensive dataset tailored for fine-grained Historical Calligraphy Style Understanding. HCSU comprises 39,307 meticulously curated character images from 49 historically prominent calligraphers across 10 dynasties, systematically decoupling authentic ink manuscripts (Tie) from stone rubbings (Bei) to resolve the long-standing modal mixture problem. Moving beyond conventional flattened labels, HCSU provides hierarchical expert-written aesthetic descriptions, enabling two rigorous evaluation protocols: fine-grained style discrimination and interpretable aesthetic reasoning. Extensive evaluations reveal a persistent gap between calligraphy-related knowledge and visually grounded style perception: state-of-the-art LVLMs show non-trivial performance but remain sensitive to script-level, textual, and source-specific cues, and often struggle to ground aesthetic judgments in fine-grained brushwork evidence. Ultimately, the HCSU benchmark exposes fundamental limitations in current multimodal architectures, aiming to inspire the evolution of expert-level visual reasoning for cultural heritage preservation. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Tongji209/HCSU.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HCSU, the first comprehensive dataset for fine-grained Historical Calligraphy Style Understanding, containing 39,307 character images from 49 calligraphers across 10 dynasties. It decouples ink manuscripts from stone rubbings, provides hierarchical expert-written aesthetic descriptions, and establishes two evaluation protocols. Evaluations show LVLMs struggle with grounded fine-grained style perception despite some knowledge.
AI.motivation: Automated fine-grained perception of calligraphy styles remains a critical challenge for LVLMs, constrained by existing datasets that suffer from modal mixture and flattened labels.
AI.method: HCSU dataset: 39,307 curated character images from 49 calligraphers across 10 dynasties, decoupling ink manuscripts (Tie) from stone rubbings (Bei), with hierarchical expert-written aesthetic descriptions. Two evaluation protocols: fine-grained style discrimination and interpretable aesthetic reasoning.
AI.result: State-of-the-art LVLMs show non-trivial performance but remain sensitive to script-level, textual, and source-specific cues, and often struggle to ground aesthetic judgments in fine-grained brushwork evidence.
AI.conclusion: The HCSU benchmark exposes fundamental limitations in current multimodal architectures and aims to inspire the evolution of expert-level visual reasoning for cultural heritage preservation.

title: Hyperparameter Transfer in Graph Neural Networks
summary: The performance of deep learning models crucially depends on the settings of hyperparameters like learning rate, initialization scale, and weight decay. Hyperparameter transfer aims to make near-optimal hyperparameter settings consistent across model scale, so that large models can be optimized by proxy tuning their smaller, cheaper-to-optimize counterparts. While transfer principles are well-studied in the context of dense neural networks in language and vision tasks, they remain comparatively under-explored for graph neural networks (GNNs). We develop and validate a transfer parameterization for GNNs trained with SGD, Adam, and AdamW. Through theoretical scaling analyses and controlled experiments, we show that the proposed parameterization yields stable feature updates, learning rate transfer, and improved performance as width and depth increase. For SGD, we identify graph-dependent first-layer correction factors and show that their use can accelerate early training in graphs with sparse bag-of-words inputs. For Adam, we explore how different message passing normalizations affect early- and late-training transfer behavior, illustrating the importance of message passing normalization and advocating for an associated hyperparameter. For AdamW, we adapt a parameterization that allows for the joint transfer of weight decay and learning rate. Together, these results provide a practical recipe for scaling GNNs across a variety of learning tasks and training scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and validates transfer parameterizations for GNNs trained with SGD, Adam, and AdamW, showing that the proposed methods yield stable feature updates, learning rate transfer, and improved performance as width and depth increase.
AI.motivation: Hyperparameter transfer principles are well-studied for dense neural networks in language and vision but remain under-explored for graph neural networks (GNNs).
AI.method: The authors develop transfer parameterizations via theoretical scaling analyses and controlled experiments for GNNs under SGD, Adam, and AdamW. For SGD, they identify graph-dependent first-layer correction factors. For Adam, they study message passing normalization effects on transfer. For AdamW, they adapt parameterization for joint weight decay and learning rate transfer.
AI.result: The proposed parameterization yields stable feature updates, learning rate transfer, and improved performance with increasing width and depth. Graph-dependent correction factors accelerate early training for sparse bag-of-words inputs under SGD. Message passing normalization critically affects Adam transfer behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical recipe for scaling GNNs across various learning tasks and training scenarios.

title: Beyond Scene Priors: Fine-Grained Traffic Scene Reasoning with Benchmarking and Query-Guided Small-Object Focus
summary: In safety-critical traffic scenarios, answering complex questions relies on minute, localized visual cues. However, standard Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) tend to over-attend to backgrounds, overwhelming crucial small objects during visual-language alignment, a failure mode we term 'critical evidence dilution.' Furthermore, existing visual question answering (VQA) datasets rarely expose this flaw, as they lack large-scale, distractor-heavy evaluations that require pinpointing local evidence. To bridge this evaluation and architecture gap, we introduce the Fine-Grained Traffic Reasoning Benchmark (FGTR-Bench) and the Text-Guided Small-Object Reasoning MLLM (TSR-MLLM). FGTR-Bench comprises 40,236 single-image Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs) created via multi-agent generation, consistency checks, and expert audits, alongside a disjoint 4,947-sample blind test split. To resolve evidence dilution, TSR-MLLM, built on Qwen3-VL-4B, uses a query-conditioned Text-Guided Small-Object Focus (TG-SOF) map. Applied once at the decoder boundary, the map adds sparse Top-K gated residuals to the most question-relevant vision slots while leaving text tokens unchanged. Together with lightweight decoder adaptation, TSR-MLLM preserves single-pass inference without external detectors or image re-encoding. Under matched settings, TSR-MLLM outperforms the strongest 4B baseline by 2.1 points on FGTR-Bench (74.1% overall), with larger gains on evidence-local tracks. Furthermore, it remains competitive on DriveQA-V (CARLA Signs) under greedy decoding without task-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FGTR-Bench (40,236 fine-grained traffic VQA questions) and TSR-MLLM, a 4B MLLM that uses a Text-Guided Small-Object Focus map with sparse Top-K gated residuals at the decoder boundary to solve the "critical evidence dilution" problem where standard MLLMs over-attend to backgrounds and miss small crucial objects. TSR-MLLM outperforms the strongest 4B baseline by 2.1 points on FGTR-Bench while maintaining single-pass inference without external detectors.
AI.motivation: Standard MLLMs over-attend to backgrounds, diluting critical small-object evidence ("critical evidence dilution") during visual-language alignment in safety-critical traffic scenarios. Existing VQA datasets lack large-scale, distractor-heavy evaluations requiring pinpoint local evidence, creating both an evaluation and an architecture gap.
AI.method: (1) FGTR-Bench: 40,236 MCQs via multi-agent generation, consistency checks, expert audits, with a 4,947-sample blind test split. (2) TSR-MLLM: Built on Qwen3-VL-4B, uses a query-conditioned Text-Guided Small-Object Focus (TG-SOF) map applied once at the decoder boundary, adding sparse Top-K gated residuals to question-relevant vision slots while leaving text tokens unchanged, with lightweight decoder adaptation.
AI.result: TSR-MLLM outperforms the strongest 4B baseline by 2.1 points on FGTR-Bench (74.1% overall), with larger gains on evidence-local tracks. It remains competitive on DriveQA-V (CARLA Signs) under greedy decoding without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and architecture effectively address the critical evidence dilution problem in traffic VQA, achieving superior fine-grained reasoning without sacrificing inference efficiency or requiring external detectors.

title: Beyond Modality Fusion: Deep Ensembles for Multimodal Classification
summary:
In multimodal classification, late-fusion approaches classify concatenated modality-specific features extracted by unimodal neural networks.
  When modality imbalance is pronounced, various regularization techniques have been proposed to balance the learning process and overcome the inferior performance of late-fusion networks.
  In contrast, this work demonstrates that multimodal data can be effectively classified without any explicit modality fusion, using deep ensembles of unimodal networks.
  We systematically compare deep ensembles to late-fusion networks at equal parameter count and show that ensembles consistently outperform state-of-the-art late-fusion methods designed to address modality imbalance.
  This advantage also holds over intermediate-fusion techniques we evaluated and over hybrid methods that combine unimodal and multimodal predictions.
  We propose and empirically validate a method for selecting the number of models per modality in an ensemble, avoiding computationally expensive exhaustive search.
  Under extreme modality imbalance and small ensemble sizes, the heuristic indicates that ensembles of unimodal models trained solely on the stronger modality are preferable; as the ensemble scales up, incorporating models from the weaker modality becomes beneficial.
  Both predictions align with our empirical findings.
  To systematically explore the challenges of optimizing multimodal models, we propose a synthetic multimodal framework that allows control over both the number of modalities and their predictive strength; our findings are consistent across synthetic and real-world datasets.
  Finally, by fitting scaling laws to bimodal datasets, we estimate the asymptotic performance of ensembles.

AI.tldr: Deep ensembles of unimodal networks outperform late-fusion and intermediate-fusion methods in multimodal classification, especially under modality imbalance, without requiring explicit fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing late-fusion approaches for multimodal classification suffer from modality imbalance, requiring various regularization techniques. This work questions the necessity of explicit fusion, exploring whether ensembles of unimodal networks can be a simpler and more effective alternative.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of deep ensembles of unimodal networks vs. late-fusion and intermediate-fusion networks at equal parameter counts. Proposed a heuristic for selecting the number of models per modality to avoid exhaustive search. Introduced a synthetic multimodal framework for controlled experiments. Fitted scaling laws to estimate asymptotic ensemble performance.
AI.result: Ensembles consistently outperform state-of-the-art late-fusion and intermediate-fusion methods. Under extreme modality imbalance and small ensembles, models trained solely on the stronger modality are preferable; with larger ensembles, incorporating weaker modality becomes beneficial. Findings are consistent across synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal data can be effectively classified without explicit fusion via deep ensembles. The proposed heuristic for model allocation per modality is validated empirically, and scaling laws provide insights into asymptotic behavior.

title: Perceiving Better Moments: Cover Frame Reselection and Enhancement for Live Photos with the Live2K Dataset
summary: Modern smartphones capture Live Photos, short video bursts surrounding a still image, offering a dynamic and engaging photographic experience. However, the cover photo and video components are generated by two distinct imaging pipelines: the photo stream undergoes full computational photography processing, while the video stream is constrained by real-time efficiency and heavy compression.
